                                       Preface



On behalf of the Conference Committee, we welcome you to the proceedings of the
2025 International Conference on Algorithms and Architectures for Parallel Processing
(ICA3PP 2025), which was held in Zhengzhou, China from October 30 – November 2,
2025. ICA3PP 2025 was the 25th in this series of conferences (started in 1995) that are
devoted to algorithms and architectures for parallel processing. ICA3PP is now recog-
nized as the main regular international event that covers the many dimensions of par-
allel algorithms and architectures, encompassing fundamental theoretical approaches,
practical experimental projects, and commercial components and systems. This confer-
ence provides a forum for academics and practitioners from countries around the world
to exchange ideas for improving the efficiency, performance, reliability, security, and
interoperability of computing systems and applications.
    A successful conference would not be possible without the high-quality contribu-
tions made by the authors. This year, ICA3PP received a total of 543 submissions from
authors in various countries and regions. Each paper underwent a single-blind review
process by at least three reviewers. Based on rigorous peer reviews by the Program
Committee members and reviewers, 158 regular papers were selected to be presented at
the conference, giving an acceptance rate of 29%. We also accepted 104 research papers
and 48 special session papers. In addition to the contributed papers, distinguished schol-
ars were invited to give keynote lectures, providing us with the recent developments in
diverse areas in algorithms and architectures for parallel processing and applications.
    We would like to take this opportunity to express our sincere gratitude to the Program
Committee members and 305 reviewers for their dedicated and professional service. We
highly appreciate the General Chairs, Didier El Baz, Zizhong Chen, and Gudula Runger,
for their help and support in organizing the conference. Then we would like to express
our appreciation to the four program vice-chairs, Rong Gu, Deze Zeng, Jiawei Huang,
and Zhe Peng, for their leadership in managing the various tracks of the conference. We
would also like to give our sincere thanks to the Local Chairs, Jihong Ding, Yi Jiang,
Song Zhang, Zhicheng Liu, Chunfeng Du, Zecan Yang, and Xin Nie, for their hard work
and commitment to the success of the conference. Our heartfelt thanks also go to the
Workshop Chair Shaojun Zou for his efforts in organizing the wonderful special sessions
and enriching the technical discourse. We are also deeply appreciative of the Publicity
Chairs, Jia Hu, Jing Guo, and Wenxuan Zhang, for their tireless efforts in promoting
the conference. We are so grateful to the publication chairs, Binbin Zhou and Lan Yan,
and the publication assistants for their dedicated support in overseeing the publication
process. Thanks also go to Registration Chairs Yuan Tian and Tingting Han, and Web
Chairs Jiawei Wang and Ren Li. Our deepest thanks also go to the Steering Chairs, Yang
Xiang, Wanlei Zhou, Yi Pan, Laurence T. Yang, and Weijia Jia, for their continuous
leadership and support throughout the planning and execution phases of the conference.
We must also say “thank you” to all the volunteers who helped us at various stages of
this conference. Moreover, we were so honored to have many renowned scholars be part
vi       Preface

of this conference. Finally, we would like to thank all speakers, authors, and participants
for their great contribution to and support for the success of ICA3PP 2025!

       Abstract. High performance computing is essential for complex fusion
       simulations, especially for guiding-center drift-orbit integration, which
       accurately describes important physical phenomena in Tokamak devices,
       such as high-energy particle transport, current actuation, and energy
       deposition. In this paper, we develop a two-level parallel strategy for
       the Tokamak guiding-center drift-orbit integration program (ORBIT) on
       the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer that combines thread-level and
       process-level optimizations. Thread-level improvements include compu-
       tation data optimization, out-of-order output optimization, and parti-
       cle tracking optimization, while process-level optimization methods are
       based on particle independence to develop new communication domain
       and data processing methods to reduce latency and improve scalability.
       On a single core group, thread-level optimization provides up to 12.02x
       speedup. When expanded to 2,048 processes (133,120 cores), the two-
       level optimized program has a strong scaling eﬃciency of 66.6% and a
       weak scaling eﬃciency of over 98% on a 16-process benchmark. This app-
       roach greatly accelerates ORBIT and enriches the application ecosystem
       of the Sunway system.


       Keywords: High performance computing · Tokamak · Guiding-center
       drift-orbit integration method · Sunway supercomputer · ORBIT


1    Introduction

With the development of nuclear fusion technology, stable high-temperature
plasma conﬁnement has become the core challenge to achieve controllable nuclear
fusion [1]. Tokamak [2] maintains a self-sustaining fusion reaction by conﬁning
the plasma with a precise magnetic ﬁeld. However, the guiding-center motion
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 3–24, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_1
 4      M. Song et al.

 behavior of plasma under extreme conditions, such as fast ion orbit loss, neoclas-
 sical transport, and magnetic island interaction, presents signiﬁcant challenges to
 long-pulse operation and the conﬁnement of high-energy particles [3]. By reduc-
 ing the six-dimensional phase space to the evolution of ﬁve-dimensional ﬁeld
 line coordinates, the orbit tracking method based on the guiding-center approx-
 imation provides an eﬀective means for studying high-energy particle transport
 and Alfvén-wave instabilities [4]. Numerical integration of the guiding-center
 equations, typically with fourth-order Runge–Kutta schemes and ﬁeld-line coor-
 dinate mapping, requires frequent access to magnetic-equilibrium data and high-
 dimensional interpolation [5].
     The Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer, an upgraded successor to Sunway
 TaihuLight [6], incorporates the SW39000 heterogeneous many-core processor
 and forms a new-generation fusion-simulation platform. Its the platform com-
 bines a multi-tier distributed computing architecture with high mixed-precision
 performance, providing the guiding-center drift-orbit code ORBIT [7] with pow-
 erful coupled-ﬁeld solving capability for its simulations. Cooperative design
 between Management Processing Element (MPE) and Computation Processing
 Elements (CPEs), together with a globally scalable memory hierarchy, enables
 eﬃcient dynamic reconstruction of unstructured magnetic-surface data and six-
 dimensional phase-space discretization during orbit integration [8].
     This work performs thread-level and process-level parallel optimizations of
 the ORBIT code on the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer. At the thread level,
 particle losses in ORBIT make the CPEs output results in an indeterminate
 order. We have successfully eliminated the problem of out-of-order data output
 by utilizing Remote Memory Access (RMA) and Direct Memory Access (DMA)
 technology; this method can be applied to any application in which the CPEs
 cannot determine their ﬁnal write addresses beforehand. Because ORBIT parti-
 cles are inherently independent, we also introduce a particle tracking optimiza-
 tion that assigns each particle to a dedicated CPE. Each CPE owns the entire
 life cycle of a particle—initialization, orbit advancement, and ﬁnal output—
 which improves computational eﬃciency, reduces the number of data transmis-
 sions between MPE and CPE, fully utilizes data locality, and evenly distributes
 tasks. At the process level, the data that need to be exchanged are placed in
 the interleaved segment of the SW39000 processor. Moreover, a new communi-
 cation domain is created to lower inter-process overhead. Optimizing the data-
 movement path and processing logic further increases the program eﬃciency and
 improves the performance of large-scale particle-orbit simulations.
     The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

(1) We propose a scheme for the SW39000 processor that eﬃciently exploits
    the CPEs shared Local Data Memory (LDM) resources and performs the
    data preprocessing on the MPE, thereby maximizing spatial locality and fully
    utilizing CPE memory capacity.
(2) We develop a solution to the out-of-order data output problem between the
    MPE and the CPEs. The monitor CPE exchanges data among the CPEs via
       Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration    5

    RMA, and interacts with the MPE via DMA, to allocate arrays of appropriate
    size, achieving eﬃcient data transfer and better use of memory of the MPE.
(3) In addition, we leverage the intrinsic independence of particles to track each
    particle’s entire life cycle, and we optimize inter-process communication by
    taking advantage of the architecture of the Sunway Bluelight II supercom-
    puter and the SW39000 processor.

     The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 presents the
 background. Section 3 analyses the Tokamak guiding-center drift-orbit inte-
 gration program. Section 4 describes the thread-level parallel optimization of
 ORBIT. Section 5 details the process-level parallel optimization of ORBIT.
 Section 6 reports the experimental results and analysis. Section 7 describes
 related work. Finally, Sect. 8 concludes the paper.


 2      Background
 2.1     Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration Method

 In tokamak and other controlled-fusion devices, the motion of charged particles
 is highly complex, and direct orbit tracking is both diﬃcult and computationally
 expensive. Guiding-center drift-orbit integration is employed to model particle
 trajectories, and can better analyze the particle dynamics, drift eﬀects, and
 overall plasma conﬁnement performance [9].
     The guiding-center drift-orbit integration method is an eﬃcient numerical
 technique based on the guiding-center approximation. It computes drift tra-
 jectories in electromagnetic ﬁelds and motion along magnetic ﬁeld lines. This
 method approximates the long-term, large-scale motion of particles in strong
 magnetic ﬁelds by tracking the center point of the cyclotron motion of charged
 particles [10]. Its chief advantage is very high computational eﬃciency, which
 makes it well suited to studies of particle transport in magnetically conﬁned
 and space plasmas. The key task is to integrate the guiding-center equations.
 In this study, we use guiding-center Eq. (1) that is not limited to Boozer coor-
 dinates [11]; equal-arc-length, PEST, and straight-ﬁeld-line coordinates .ψp , .θ,
 and .ζ, together with the parallel velocity and the particle energy, completely
 determine the particle position and velocity.

                     .B = g(ψp ) ∇ζ + I(ψp ) ∇θ + δ(ψp , θ, ζ) ∇ψp               (1)
    .B denotes the magnetic ﬁeld, .ψ the toroidal ﬂux, .ψp the poloidal ﬂux, .θ
 the poloidal angle coordinate, .ζ the toroidal angle coordinate, and .g, .I, and .δ
 are equilibrium functions. Numerical values for the guiding-center equations are
 supplied by the plasma magnetic-ﬁeld distribution, that is, the equilibrium ﬁeld.
 Magnetic-equilibrium data are obtained by solving the Grad–Shafranov equation
 with the Equilibrium Fitting (EFIT) code [12]. In a Tokamak, the equilibrium
 ﬁeld is usually expressed through the poloidal-ﬂux function .ψ (R, Z), which
 satisﬁes the Grad–Shafranov Eq. (2).

 EFIT solves the nonlinear partial diﬀerential Eq. (2) by iteratively adjusting the
 free functions .p(ψ) and .F (ψ) until the computed .ψ, magnetic ﬁeld, and pressure
 proﬁles agree with the measured data. After the experimental data are loaded,
 the program performs interpolation and spline ﬁtting, thus producing smooth
 magnetic-ﬁeld and ﬂux Eq. (1).
     In the guiding-center drift-orbit method, Eq. (1) is solved with a high-

 precision and good stability, making it suitable for numerically solving most ordi-

.tn denotes the current time level, .yn is the phase-space state vector of the

 vector at the next time level.
     ORBIT is a numerical simulation code designed for particle tracking
 and guiding-center drift-orbit calculations in Tokamak plasmas. It is chieﬂy
 used to study charged-particle transport, drift-orbit losses, and energetic-
 particle dynamics in magnetically conﬁned fusion devices. Given an equilibrium
 magnetic-ﬁeld conﬁguration from an external solver, ORBIT integrates parti-
 cle trajectories numerically and supports detailed analyses that include particle
 collisions, wave–particle interactions, and Poincaré-section diagnostics.

2.2     The Sunway Bluelight II Supercomputer

Figure 1 depicts the architecture of the SW39000 processor. The chip contains
six core groups (CGs). Each CG comprises one management processing ele-
ment (MPE) and one computation processing elements cluster (CPE Array).
The CPE Array is an 8 * 8 mesh of 64 computing processing elements (CPEs).
Within this mesh, every four adjacent CPEs form a subcluster that shares a local
management unit and incorporates a router. Each CG has a dedicated memory
controller (MC) connected to 16 GB of DDR4 memory that delivers 51.2 GB/s
of bandwidth. Data transfer among CPEs in the same array is handled through
a Remote Memory Access (RMA) interface.




                  Fig. 1. SW39000 many-core processor architecture.


   Each CPE contains a 256 KB Local Data Memory (LDM). For memory
access, the CPE can access main memory directly through discrete gld/gst
operations, or it can employ Direct Memory Access (DMA) to transfer data
from the main memory into the LDM. During computation, the CPE reads
and writes solely through its LDM. The LDM can be partitioned into three
conﬁgurable regions: the private region, the contiguous shared region, and the
CPE data-cache region.
   The Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer is the next-generation Sunway sys-
tem following Sunway TaihuLight. It employs entirely domestically developed
components, including processors, network chipsets, storage, and management
systems, and has served as a comprehensive technology test bed for exascale com-
puting. The machine comprises 512 compute nodes that house 1,024 SW39000
many-core processors, providing 6,144 management processing elements (MPEs)
and 393,216 computation processing elements (CPEs) in total. A single proces-
sor delivers peak speeds of 12.48 TFLOPS in double-precision ﬂoating point,
13.956 TIPS in single-precision ﬁxed point, and oﬀers a memory bandwidth of
282 GB/s. The entire system attains a peak performance of 14.3 PFLOPS.
8      M. Song et al.

3   Analysis of the Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit
    Integration Program

This section analyses the hotspot functions of the Tokamak guiding-center drift-
orbit integration program (ORBIT) and describes the challenges encountered
in implementing its parallel optimization on the Sunway Bluelight II supercom-
puter.
    During the performance assessment and correctness veriﬁcation of ORBIT,
we combined explicit time stamping, the gprof proﬁler, and the SWLU hotspot
analyzer provided by the Sunway supercomputer to obtain a detailed proﬁle of
the code’s behavior, including per-function execution time, call frequency, call
relationships, and runtime bottlenecks. To ensure the reliability and accuracy of
the numerical results, we used Poincaré-section distributions as an independent
benchmark for checking the physical correctness of the program output.
    Poincaré-section data are obtained by projecting a high-dimensional dynam-
ical system or particle-orbit simulation onto a two-dimensional cross section,
producing a clear and stable topological pattern. By comparing the simulated
section with theoretical or reference data and examining diﬀerences in point
locations, densities, and orbit shapes, one can directly and eﬃciently detect
integration errors or implementation defects and thereby verify the correctness
of the ORBIT program results.
    We proﬁled the code on the single MPE of the SW39000 processor. The
functions of the ORBIT program include Field, Ptrba, Onestep, Update, and
Others. The Field function is responsible for calculating the local magnetic ﬁeld
vector and related equilibrium quantities in the Tokamak during particle propul-
sion; the Ptrba function calculates the perturbation ﬁeld; the Onestep function
updates the particle coordinates and velocity; the Update function counts and
processes all particle states; and the Others category includes reading equilib-
rium data, outputting Poincaré-section distribution data, etc. Hotspot functions
include Field, Ptrba, Onestep, and Update, which account for 32.10%, 30.70%,
17.42%, and 12.81% of the total execution time, respectively. The Others func-
tion accounts for 6.97% of the total execution time. In each iteration of the
Onestep and Update calculations, the Field and Ptrba functions are invoked.
Excessive iterations make the Field and Ptrba functions particularly time-
consuming.
    During the advancing phase in ORBIT, no inter-particle forces inﬂuence the
motion of other particles. Each particle possesses its own velocity, charge, and
mass. The functions that update the particle state and the surrounding magnetic
ﬁeld operate independently of other particles, and the data used by Onestep and
Update, as well as by Field and Ptrba, are highly similar. Based on this feature,
the data reuse rate is improved through the optimization of particle tracking.
    Based on the characteristics of ORBIT and the hardware architecture of the
Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer, we identify four major challenges faced in
parallel optimization:
       Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration      9

(1) Data is discrete and large: When the original program reads the equi-
    librium data, the data are discrete and the data volume is too large. In the
    step of advancing the particles, the eﬃciency of using gld/gst to obtain data
    from the MPE is low. The LDM space of the CPEs is only 256 KB, which
    cannot store the data required for the CPEs computation.
(2) Out-of-order output: Particle losses occur while particles are being
    advanced, so although a ﬁxed number of particles are assigned to each CPE,
    the number that complete is unknown in advance; consequently, the CPEs
    cannot guarantee that their output data appear in the correct order.
(3) Frequent DMA communication: When the functions Field, Ptrba,
    Onestep, and Update are executed on the CPEs, it leads to frequent updates
    of computing data, increasing the time consumption of DMA communication.
    In addition, the activation and recovery frequency of the CPEs increases.
(4) High overhead for large-scale problems: As the number of processes
    increases, collecting the results of particle transport leads to more and more
    frequent communication between processes, and processing data that require
    interaction also consumes a signiﬁcant amount of time.

     To address these challenges, we propose a ﬁne-grained, generic two-level par-
 allelization scheme, built on the Sunway many-core processor architecture and
 the overall architecture of the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer. The scheme
 comprises thread-level and process-level parallelization. At the thread level, we
 develop computational data optimization, out-of-order output optimization, and
 particle tracking optimization, targeting challenges (1), (2), and (3), respectively.
 At the process level, we present a new communication domain method to tackle
 challenge (4).


 4      Thread-Level Optimization for ORBIT

 This section presents the thread-level optimization of ORBIT within a single
 CG, including computational data optimization, out-of-order output optimiza-
 tion, and particle tracking optimization. The three optimizations are progressive:
 out-of-order output optimization is built on computational data optimization,
 and particle tracking optimization, in turn, is built on out-of-order output opti-
 mization.


 4.1     Computational Data Optimization

 The purpose of computational data optimization is to discard unnecessary data,
 speed up data transfer between the MPE and the CPEs, exploit the spatial
 locality, and make eﬃcient use of the limited LDM space. According to Sect. 3,
 the functions Field, Ptrba, Onestep, and Update together account for 93.03%
 of the execution time of the ORBIT program. Field and Ptrba need the dis-
 tribution data of particles in spatial position, energy, and pitch angle, and the
 position of particles can be generated by the random variable .x in Eq. (8).
 10      M. Song et al.


                                dn     dn dx
                                .    =        = fψ                           (8)
                                dψ     dx dψ
     Furthermore, the particle energy distribution follows the Maxwell distribu-
 tion, that is, .en (k) = maxwell (tdum ), where the parameter .tdum denotes the
 plasma temperature in keV. The data required by these hotspot functions are
 highly scattered and very large, and transferring them with gld/gst operations
 is ineﬃcient. Therefore, we employ the more eﬃcient DMA transfers between
 the MPE and the CPEs.
     The computational data optimization includes two steps: preprocessing the
 data on the MPE, the use of LDM shared space and the choice of mode.
(1) Preprocessing the data on the MPE
    In the ﬁrst part, we reconstruct the original array data and only keep the data
 required by the hotspot function. The data processing is completed by the MPE.
 As shown in Fig. 2, ﬁrst, before using the CPEs to process the hotspot function,
 the calculation part of the array data in the hotspot function is extracted, and the
 MPE calculates the subscript of the array data in advance. Secondly, use Boolean
 arrays to ﬁlter duplicate data, and then build a new array to store the data
 actually required for the computing task. Then, establish a mapping relationship
 between the computing task and the new array, and create an array to save the
 mapping relationship. Finally, Calculate the amount of data .N (in KB) actually
 required for the computing task.
    The CPEs of SW39000 support LDM continuous shared space, which is a
 space used by the CPEs for shared access to LDM within the array. The CPEs
 can access the LDM space of other CPEs. In LDM continuous sharing mode,
 each CPE in the array provides LDM space of the same capacity for continuous
 addressing. The capacity of the LDM space provided by each CPE for sharing can
 be divided into seven capacity adjustments: 0 KB, 4 KB, 8 KB, 16 KB, 32 KB,
 64 KB, and 128 KB. As shown in the lower left part of Fig. 2, the continuous
 sharing mode includes single cluster, double cluster, four cluster, and full array
 sharing modes, which facilitates nearby access to diﬀerent working sets.
(2) The use of LDM shared space and the choice of mode
     The second part concerns the use of the LDM shared space and the choice of
 its operating mode. The “read-only data” set includes the actual data .N ; among
 the hotspot functions, Field requires the most “read-only data” (282.31 KB),
 while Onestep uses the largest amount of “computational data” (197.5 KB).
 Consequently, we allocate 32 KB of LDM of each of the CPEs as contiguous
 shared space for “read-only data”, reserving the remainder as private space for
 intermediate variables and results. As shown in Fig. 2, we select the four-cluster
 contiguous share mode, providing a total shared LDM of 512 KB. Before the
 CPEs execution, arrays .B and .C are transferred via DMA into this shared
 space. Since the original array .A is scattered while array .B is contiguous, the
 CPEs leverage spatial locality to accelerate memory access, reducing MPE–CPE
 communication overhead and improving overall performance.
      Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration    11




                       Fig. 2. Computational data optimization.


4.2     Out-of-Order Output Optimization

When we use computational data optimization, the situation that the CPE can-
not guarantee that the data is output in the correct order occurs. This is because
during the particle propulsion phase, particle collisions and external disturbances
are also performed, resulting in particle escape during the movement of the
plasma. The collision eﬀect randomizes the particle pitch angle, which pushes
some particles into the “loss cone” and thus escapes directly along the open mag-
netic ﬁeld lines. The ORBIT program uses the diﬀusion-drift (Fokker–Planck)
Eq. (9) to describe the pitch angle scattering:
                              ∂f   1 ∂      ∂f       ∂
                          .      =      Dξξ      −      Aξ f                     (9)
                              ∂t   2 ∂ξ     ∂ξ       ∂ξ
   .f is the particle distribution function, .ξ = cos α the pitch-angle cosine, .Dξξ
the diﬀusion coeﬃcient, and .Aξ the drag term. External magnetic perturbations
are represented by Eq. (10).

                                 δB = ∇ × α(ψ, θ, ζ) B
                                 .                                              (10)
    These resonant perturbations change particle trajectories, break closed ﬂux
surfaces, and create random magnetospheres and island chains, allowing trajec-
12     M. Song et al.

tories to cross ﬂux surfaces and escape the plasma. The perturbation amplitude
α is expanded in harmonics.
.




                    Fig. 3. Out-of-order output optimization.


    We take an optimization approach for out-of-order output from the CPEs.
Firstly, the monitor CPE is selected from the CPE array. According to the
characteristics of the hardware architecture of the Sunway Bluelight II super-
computer and SW39000 many-core processor, the distance between the cluster
of the CPEs aﬀects the communication delay between the CPEs. Through the
RMA communication test on the CPE array, this paper takes the RMA commu-
nication test between the CPE 0 and other CPEs as an example. As shown in
the upper part of Fig. 3, the RMA communication delay between the CPE 0 and
the CPEs 1, 8 and 9 is 47 beats. When the inter-cluster distance of the CPEs
increases by 1, the communication delay increases by 6 beats. Selecting CPE 0
as the monitor CPE to communicate with other CPEs, the communication delay
will reach 4,113 beats. The RMA communication test is carried out on diﬀerent
CPEs, and the CPE 27 is selected as the monitor CPE to communicate with
other CPEs. The communication delay will be reduced to 3,729 beats, which
meets the standard of low communication delay and more stable communica-
tion. Therefore, we choose the CPE 27 as the monitor CPE, and the other 63
CPEs in the CPE array are responsible for the computing task as the computing
CPEs.
    After selecting the monitor CPE, computing CPEs initially store processed
data within their local LDM and propagate data volumes to the monitor CPE via

RMA. The monitor CPE aggregates the collective data volume while computing
transfer addresses for individual computing CPEs. Subsequently, it performs a
DMA transfer of the total data volume to the MPE, which allocates a storage
array of adequate capacity in main memory. Concurrently, the monitor CPE
broadcasts computed transfer addresses to all 63 computing CPEs through an
RMA operation. Finally, computing CPEs execute DMA transfers from their
local LDM to the main-memory storage array using assigned addresses. The
detailed steps are given in Algorithm 1.

4.3      Particle Tracking Optimization
We execute each hotspot function on the CPE array separately, resulting in
frequent data transfer in and out of the CPE array. This method is a phased
thread-level optimization. Although it is generally applicable to applications, it
cannot make deeper optimizations for the characteristics of ORBIT programs
and SW39000 processors. When the MPE calls the CPEs to accelerate the pro-
cessing of computing tasks, it needs to start the CPE array and pass in data.
After the CPEs complete the computing task, they transmit data to the MPE,
and the MPE recycles the CPE array. Frequent startup and recovery of the CPE
array will incur additional time consumption, increase communication overhead,
and result in low execution eﬃciency.
14     M. Song et al.




                        Fig. 4. Particle tracking optimization.


     According to Sect. 3, particles have natural independence, and the data of
hotspot functions are highly similar. Therefore, we adopt the method of tracking
the entire movement process of particles instead of the previous staged method.
Each CPE is bound to a diﬀerent particle group and is responsible for the entire
life cycle of the particle. As shown in Fig. 4, we reconstructed the data layout of
the hotspot functions and merged the serial code between the hotspot functions
into the function. Not only that, the Field function, Ptrba function and Runge–
Kutta algorithm are integrated into the Onestep function. The Field and Ptrba
functions are integrated into the Update function, and the Onestep function,
Update function and serial code are organized and merged. When executing the
integrated function in the CPE array, the number of data input and output is
reduced to once from the startup and recovery of the CPE array, and the data
reuse rate is improved.


5    Process-Level Optimization for ORBIT
This section introduces the process-level parallel optimization solution for
ORBIT. Based on the “thread-level parallel optimization for ORBIT”, we car-
ried out the “process-level parallel optimization for ORBIT” and optimized the
cluster communication and data processing of the SW39000 processor.
    According to the characteristics of the guidance center equation, the particles
in the ORBIT program have natural independence. The position and velocity
of the particle can be completely described by a set of independent parameters,
including the magnetic ﬂux coordinate system .(ψp , θ, ζ), the parallel velocity,
and the energy of the particle. The determination of these parameters depends
only on the size .B of the magnetic ﬁeld at the location of the particle and
the functions .I and .g. The movement of any particle is independent of other
particles and is only related to its own initial conditions and local magnetic ﬁeld
characteristics. This weak coupling between particles and the locality of the
initial conditions indicate that each particle moves independently in the local
magnetic ﬁeld environment where it is located, and the solution of its trajectory
   Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration      15

is suitable for parallel processing. Therefore, as shown in Fig. 5, we implement
process-level parallel optimization by assigning particle groups to diﬀerent CGs.
In the annular cross-section diagram, the particles are divided into diﬀerent
particle groups, and each CG is responsible for the entire life cycle of diﬀerent
particle groups.




                  Fig. 5. Particle groups are assigned to the CGs.


   On the SW39000 processor, main memory uses virtual addressing and is
divided into two regions: the contiguous segment and the cross segment. The
contiguous segment is private to each CG, laid out in a continuous address range
and accessible directly by both the management and compute cores of that group.
The cross segment is a shared region across all CGs on the same chip, and it can
be accessed by every CG, enabling eﬃcient data exchange within the chip.




              Fig. 6. New communication domain and cross segment.


    As the number of processes increases, the frequency of communication
between processes also increases. In the process-level optimization of the ORBIT
program, we take the method of establishing a new communication domain to
optimize the MPI cluster communication between SW39000 processors. Since
process 0 is the root process of the entire communication domain, in order to
facilitate process communication. As shown in Fig. 6, select the local CG 0 in each
processor, create a new communication domain containing all CGs 0, and when
data needs to be exchanged between CGs, ﬁrst, put the data to be exchanged
into the cross segment, so that the CGs in the same processor can directly oper-
ate the data without communication. Then, when the CGs between processors
16       M. Song et al.

exchange data, MPI communication is performed through the CGs in the newly
created communication domain, so as to achieve the purpose of reducing the
frequency of communication between processes. The detailed steps are given in
Algorithm 2.

6     Evaluation
6.1    Configuration

We use the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer to evaluate the ORBIT program
for two-level parallel optimization. The speciﬁc hardware and software used are
shown in Table 1. In order to verify the universality of the scheme, all test input
data are small, medium, and large scale. The principle of setting the data scale
is to give full play to the computing power of the Sunway Bluelight II supercom-
puter and reﬂect the impact of diﬀerent data scales on the optimization eﬀect.
All results are averaged over ﬁve rounds.

6.2    Performance of Various Parallel Optimizations

In thread-level parallel optimization, the number of simulated particles is set to
100,000, 500,000, and 1,000,000, corresponding to small, medium, and large data
scales. The principle of setting the data scale is to give full play to the computing
power of the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer and show the impact of diﬀerent
   Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration        17

              Table 1. Hardware and software used for optimisation.

        Hardware Computer        Sunway Bluelight II Supercomputer
                 Processor model SW39000
                 Number of nodes 171
                 Number of cores 133 120 (2 048 MPEs and 131 072 CPEs)
                 Memory          32 768 GB
        Software System            Sunway Linux 4.4.15
                 Compiler          mpicc and sw9gcc




     Fig. 7. Speedup ratio of thread-level optimization under diﬀerent schemes.


data scales on the optimization eﬀect. To test thread-level parallel optimization,
a single-core group of one MPE and 64 CPEs is used on the SW39000 CPU.
    Figure 7 shows the speedup achieved by the three thread-level optimization
schemes. Under the ﬁrst scheme, computational data optimization, we observe
speedups of 2.01x to 2.07x across the three data scales. Building on that, the
out-of-order output optimization delivers speedups of 4.11x to 4.55x. Finally,
the particle tracking optimization, applied on top of the out-of-order output
optimization scheme, achieves speedups of 9.92x to 12.02x.
    In computational data optimization, we design a memory access scheme based
on the LDM continuous sharing mode. We preprocess the data in the MPE,
reconstruct the array and mapping relationship, and design a memory access
18     M. Song et al.

scheme based on the actual amount of data required for the task. In out-of-order
output optimization, based on the characteristics of the hardware architecture of
the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer and the SW39000 many-core processor,
we select the best monitor CPE in the CPE array, design the collaborative work
of RMA and DMA, realize the data exchange between the MPE and the CPE
in the CPE array, solve the problem of out-of-order output of the CPEs, reduce
the communication overhead between the MPE and the CPE, and improve the
utilization of main memory resources. In particle tracking optimization, we use
the natural independence of particles to integrate multiple hot functions in the
ORBIT program and the serial code parts between them, avoiding the delay
caused by frequent startup and recovery of the CPE array and improving the
data reuse rate.
    According to our analysis, as shown in Fig. 8, compared with the original
program, the proportion of the total execution time occupied by the four func-
tions, Field, Ptrba, Onestep and Update, is signiﬁcantly reduced, from 93.03%
to 27.77%, and thread-level parallel optimization has achieved good results.




                   Fig. 8. Hotspots of thread-level optimization.


    In process-level parallel optimization and two-level parallel optimization
(including thread-level parallel optimization and process-level parallel optimiza-
tion), the number of simulated particles is set to 7,168,000, 15,360,000 and
27,648,000 respectively, corresponding to small, medium, and large data scales.
The process-level parallel optimization and two-level parallel optimization of the
ORBIT program are tested with diﬀerent numbers of processes (16, 32, 64, 128,
256, 512, 1,024, 2,048). As the number of processes increases, the number of
      Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration          19

particles that the CPEs need to process becomes smaller and smaller. After the
CPE array is accelerated in the two-level parallel optimization, the hotspot time
ratio in the program shrinks much faster than that of the process-level optimiza-
tion. Therefore, as the number of processes increases, the speedup ratio of the
two-level parallel optimization gradually decreases relative to the process-level
parallel optimization.
    Figure 9 shows the execution time and speedup ratio of process-level parallel
optimization and two-level parallel optimization at diﬀerent process scales. We
use the execution time of the program in 16 processes as a benchmark. Under
the test of three data scales, the two-level parallel optimization is compared
with the process-level parallel optimization, and the speedup ratios are as high
as 42.79x, 44.46x, and 45.74x, respectively. When the number of processes is
2,048, compared with the process-level parallel optimization, the two-level par-
allel optimization maintains a speedup ratio of 20.59x, 25.43x, and 29.37x at
diﬀerent scales. This shows that the two-level parallel optimization program can
make full use of the hardware resources of the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer
to handle more computing tasks. As the number of computing tasks increases,
the two-level parallel program shows better acceleration performance in a large
number of processes.




      Fig. 9. Execution time and speedup of process-level and two-level parallelism.




6.3     Scalability
In the strong scalability test, three diﬀerent particle sizes were set, namely
7,168,000, 15,360,000 and 27,648,000, corresponding to small-scale, medium-
scale and large-scale input data respectively. The program execution time with
16 processes was used as the benchmark time to calculate the parallel eﬃciency
of the program with other numbers of processes. The program used is a two-level
parallel optimization scheme.
    The parallel eﬃciency of the two-level parallel optimization scheme reaches
51.54% at a small scale, 60.19% at a medium scale, and 66.61% at a large scale.
As shown in Fig. 10, a, b, and c represent the parallel eﬃciency of the two-
level parallel optimization program at diﬀerent data scales. The horizontal axis
20     M. Song et al.

represents the number of processes used in the test, starting from 16 processes
and gradually increasing to 2,048 processes. The vertical axis represents the
parallel eﬃciency of the two-level parallel optimization program as the number of
processes increases. As shown in Fig. 10, when the number of processes increases
to 512 processes and above, the parallel eﬃciency of the program decreases.




                   Fig. 10. Strong scalability of diﬀerent sizes.


    There are two reasons for this. The ﬁrst reason is that as the number of
processes increases, the number and delay of MPI communications also increase;
the second reason is that as the number of processes used increases, the program
needs to create more ﬁles to store output data, which causes the scalability of
the program to decrease as the number of processes increases.
    In the weak scalability test, three particles with diﬀerent data scales were
set. In order to keep the computational workload of each process unchanged, the
speciﬁc number of particles was set to 100,000 * N, 600,000 * N, and 1,200,000
* N, where N is the number of processes used, corresponding to small scale,
medium scale, and large scale, respectively. The program execution time of 16
processes was used as the benchmark test time to calculate the parallel eﬃciency
of the program using diﬀerent numbers of processes. Similarly, the program used
was a two-level parallel optimization program.




                    Fig. 11. Weak scalability of diﬀerent sizes.
      Parallel Optimization of Tokamak Guiding-Center Drift-Orbit Integration      21

    Figure 11 shows the weak scalability of the two-level parallel optimization
program under diﬀerent numbers of processes and data sizes. When the number
of processes is 2,048, the program maintains a parallel eﬃciency of 98.37% to
99.38% under diﬀerent data sizes. This is because the particles in the program
have natural independence. After our optimization in Sect. 5, the data process-
ing speed within the processor is improved and the communication frequency
between processes is reduced.

7      Related Work
At present, many studies have explored the Tokamak guiding-center drift
orbit integration method, covering both theoretical and application optimiza-
22     M. Song et al.

tions. [13,14] evaluated a high-order Hamiltonian guiding-center theory with
polarization correction and gyroscopic invariance, demonstrating high accuracy
in conserving energy and canonical angular momentum in various magnetic con-
ﬁgurations. [15] proposed a high-order Hermite interpolation to reconstruct
divergence-free magnetic ﬁelds, preserving canonical momentum and magnetic
moment, and enabling accurate trajectory integration and robust Poincaré cross-
section analysis.
    The guiding-center drift-orbit integration method has been widely applied
in nuclear fusion simulations. [16] developed the relativistic guiding-center
orbit program (RGCO) to study high-energy electron conﬁnement, enabling full
ﬁrst-wall particle tracking in cylindrical coordinates. [17] proposed a fourth-
order Runge–Kutta-based method for accurately simulating particle trajectories
and drifts in dynamic ﬁelds. Leveraging Jacobian self-diﬀerentiation and spline
smoothing, [18] achieved eﬃcient, accurate coordinate transformations, improv-
ing speed and handling discontinuities and singularities eﬀectively.
    In the past decade, the Sunway supercomputer has achieved remarkable suc-
cess, with three projects [19–21] winning the Gordon Bell Prize. [19] developed
large-scale nonlinear earthquake simulation software on Sunway TaihuLight, sus-
taining performance above 18.9 PFLOPS. [20] created an ultra-scalable implicit
solver for non-hydrostatic atmospheric dynamics, achieving 7.95 PFLOPS and
488 m resolution. [21] built a high-performance tensor-based quantum circuit
simulator, reducing sampling time to 304 s and setting a milestone in classical
simulation.


8    Conclusion
This paper implements the parallel optimization of the ORBIT program based
on the Sunway Bluelight II supercomputer. A two-level parallel scheme is pro-
posed for the parallel optimization of ORBIT, including thread-level and process-
level optimization. At the thread level, three acceleration schemes are proposed
within a single-core group, including calculation data optimization, output disor-
der optimization, and particle tracking optimization; at the process level, based
on the characteristics of the hardware architecture of the Sunway Bluelight II
supercomputer and the SW39000 many-core processor, the particle swarm allo-
cation is designed in combination with the natural independence of particles in
ORBIT, and the cross-segment and new communication domain in the SW39000
processor are used to process data, reduce the number of inter-process commu-
nications, and improve the execution eﬃciency of the program. Experimental
results show that compared with the original program, the optimized program
can achieve a speedup ratio of 12.02x within the single CG. When expanded to
2,048 processes and 133,120 cores, the optimized ORBIT still maintains good
strong scalability and weak scalability.

          Accelerating Graph Sampling in GNN
         Systems Through Accuracy-Aware Data
                         Reuse

    Yuchun Wang, Nan Jiang, Qi Wu(B) , Hengshan Yue, and Xiaohui Wei

  College of Computer Science and Technology, Jilin University, Changchun, China
    {wyc23,jiangnan22}@mails.jlu.edu.cn, {wuqi,yuehs,weixh}@jlu.edu.cn



       Abstract. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become fundamen-
       tal tools for processing and analyzing graph-structured data. However,
       when handling large-scale graph data, GNNs face exponential compu-
       tational and memory challenges. While sampling-based training frame-
       works alleviate this issue, the sampling process itself becomes a perfor-
       mance bottleneck. Although existing optimizations like feature caching
       strategies and Uniﬁed Memory Access (UMA) kernels enhance memory
       eﬃciency, they overlook the redundant computation problem in sam-
       pling: the repeated sampling of identical nodes across diﬀerent layers
       leads to resource wastage (consuming an average overhead of 15%). To
       address redundant computation, prior work proposes a complete cross-
       layer reuse strategy, eliminating redundancy by restricting each node to
       be sampled only once per mini-batch and indiscriminately reusing results.
       However, our work shows this indiscriminate reuse will destroy vertex
       neighbor diversity and reduce training stability to a certain extent, thus
       degrading the accuracy of GNN. (Training stability refers to the smooth
       convergence of the loss function during optimization, avoiding oscilla-
       tions or divergence that impede model convergence.)
          In this paper, we propose an accuracy-aware sampling framework
       that accelerates sampling while preserving model accuracy. Speciﬁcally,
       by dissecting two critical execution phases in GNN training—feature
       aggregation and backpropagation—we introduce dual-dimensional vertex
       selective metrics for accuracy-aware cross-layer sampling-result reuse: (1)
       Coordinately considering in-degree and neighbor label entropy to iden-
       tify nodes with high neighbor diversity, whose reuse is blocked to pre-
       serve structural information, and (2) Considering gradient norm metric
       to identify nodes that signiﬁcantly inﬂuence parameter update directions,
       whose reuse is blocked to ensure training stability. Merging them all, our
       approach achieves up to 2.74× speedup on DGL while keeping accuracy
       loss within 1.5%.


       Keywords: Graph Neural Networks (GNN) · Sample-based GNN
       Training · Cross-layer Reuse

1    Introduction
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), owing to their ability to jointly model graph
structural semantics and node attributes, are a core methodology in domains
such as social network analysis [1], recommendation systems [2], biomedical
graph modeling [3], and knowledge graph reasoning [4]. However, when applied
to real-world graphs containing hundreds of millions of nodes and tens of bil-
lions of edges [5,6], the multi-layer message-passing mechanism of GNNs leads
to exponential growth in both computational cost and memory usage, posing
severe scalability challenges for traditional full-graph training approaches [7–9].
    To address this issue, sampling-based GNN training frameworks [10] are
widely adopted. By constructing hierarchical subgraphs through neighborhood
sampling, these methods constrain computation within a manageable scope [11].
A typical training workﬂow involves: (1) randomly selecting a batch of target
nodes to form a mini-batch; (2) recursively sampling k-hop neighbors to form a
subgraph; and (3) performing message passing and model optimization on this
subgraph. However, as graph sizes continue to increase, the sampling phase itself
accounts for a non-negligible portion of overall training time.
    Several prior works seek to optimize the sampling process. For example,
PaGraph [12] employs a degree-based feature caching strategy to preload fre-
quently accessed node features into GPU memory, thereby reducing I/O over-
head; PyTorch-Direct [13] proposes a Uniﬁed Memory Access (UMA)-based GPU
communication kernel for feature retrieval, signiﬁcantly improving transmission
eﬃciency. Although these approaches achieve considerable memory performance
gains, they often overlook redundant computations during sampling. In practice,
the same node may be sampled multiple times across diﬀerent layers, resulting
in wasted resources. Figure 1b illustrates the proportion of redundant sampling
relative to the total number of sampling operations during sampling-based GNN
training across several real-world graph datasets. We show in Fig. 1b that such
redundant sampling can consume up to 15% of total sampling eﬀort on average.
    To mitigate this, MariusGNN [14] introduces a complete cross-layer reuse
strategy, restricting each node to be sampled at most once per mini-batch and
globally reusing its sampling result across all layers. However, this coarse-grained
mechanism indiscriminately reuses both highly sensitive and low-risk nodes, lead-
ing to: (1) destruction of neighbor diversity in sampled nodes, impairing GNNs’
ability to dynamically capture local structural variations; (2) potential loss oscil-
lations or even divergence, substantially impacting model accuracy and conver-
gence speed.
    To overcome these limitations, we propose an accuracy-aware sampling
framework designed to identify and protect critical nodes whose sampling reuse
would signiﬁcantly impact model performance, thereby maintaining accuracy
while improving eﬃciency. Through theoretical analysis and empirical vali-
dation, we discover that only a small subset of critical nodes signiﬁcantly
aﬀects training eﬀectiveness when their sampling results are reused. Building on
this insight, we dissect two crucial execution phases in GNN training—feature
aggregation and backpropagation. Based on this analysis, we introduce dual-
                                  Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN         27

dimensional vertex selective metrics for accuracy-aware cross-layer sampling-
result reuse: (1) Neighbor diversity preservation: An in-degree + neigh-
bor label entropy composite metric identiﬁes nodes with highly diverse neigh-
bor information (excluded from reuse); (2) Training stability assurance: A
gradient norm metric detects nodes signiﬁcantly inﬂuencing parameter update
directions (excluded from reuse). By precisely identifying and reusing only appro-
priate node sets, our method enhances training eﬃciency while preserving model
accuracy. In summary, we make the following key contributions:

1. We analyze the feature aggregation phase and backpropagation process in
   GNNs, proposing an in-degree and neighbor label entropy composite metric
   from the neighbor diversity perspective and a gradient norm metric from the
   parameter update contribution perspective to ﬁlter out nodes signiﬁcantly
   impacting model accuracy, which are excluded from reuse.
2. We design an accuracy-aware sampling framework (AARSampler) that accel-
   erates training through cross-layer reuse of non-sensitive nodes’ sampling
   results while conﬁning accuracy loss within acceptable bounds.
3. Extensive evaluations of the proposed AARSampler under various conﬁgu-
   rations demonstrate that it achieves up to 2.74× speedup over DGL [15],
   while keeping the accuracy loss within 1.5%.


2     Background
2.1   GNN

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an essential tool for processing and analyz-
ing graph-structured data. A graph G = (V, E) consists of a set of vertices V and
edges E, which represent relationships between vertices. In addition, each node
has a dense feature vector encoding its attributes. GNNs take advantage of both
the graph’s topological structure and the features of vertices to learn meaning-
ful representations, enabling applications such as social network analysis, fraud
detection, and molecular property prediction. GNNs operate through iterative
representation learning, reﬁning node representations by aggregating neighbor
information at each layer. At the k-th layer, the feature vector of a vertex v,
             (k)
denoted as hv , is updated based on information from its neighbors N (v). This
process can be mathematically described as follows:

                    v = Aggregate     {h(k−1) | u ∈ N (v)}
                                  (k)
                   a(k)                 u



                         v = Update
                                    (k)
                        h(k)            h(k−1)
                                         v     , a(k)
                                                  v

    Here, the Aggregate function collects and combines information from neigh-
boring vertices, while the Update function incorporates the aggregated informa-
tion to reﬁne the current vertex’s feature vector. These functions vary across
GNN models, allowing for ﬂexibility in adapting to diverse graph-based tasks.
28      Y. Wang et al.

2.2   Sample-Based GNN Training

Traditional GNN training typically requires each node to aggregate the features
of all its neighboring nodes. While this aggregation method eﬀectively captures
the rich structural information in the graph, as the graph size grows, especially in
large-scale real-world graphs like social networks or knowledge graphs, the train-
ing process faces signiﬁcant challenges. Speciﬁcally, the dramatic increase in the
number of nodes, edges, and their high-dimensional features leads to prohibitive
computational and memory costs, making traditional methods non-scalable. To
address this issue, sampling-based GNN training methods are proposed. These
methods reduce computational and memory overhead by sampling each node’s
neighboring nodes and constructing local subgraphs instead of using the full
graph. Speciﬁcally, each iteration randomly selects a mini-batch of nodes and
constructs layer-wise subgraphs via sampling. Then, during each layer of train-
ing, nodes update their representations by aggregating the features of their neigh-
boring nodes. Afterward, the loss for the current mini-batch is computed, and
the model parameters are updated through backpropagation. The training pro-
cess optimizes the model through multiple iterations, with parameter updates
occurring after each training step. Ultimately, training ends when predeﬁned
termination conditions are met.

2.3   Related Work and Motivation

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) demonstrate great potential in processing and
learning from large-scale graph data. However, as the graph size increases, tra-
ditional training methods face signiﬁcant computational bottlenecks. Therefore,
optimizing the GNN training process becomes a crucial research direction. Deep
Graph Library (DGL) [15], a popular GNN framework, employs techniques such
as batch processing, distributed training, and mixed-precision training to sig-
niﬁcantly enhance the overall eﬃciency of GNN training. Pytorch-direct [13]
leverages uniﬁed virtual memory (UMA), allowing GPUs to directly access CPU
memory without explicit data copying. Many studies also focus on optimizing
the sampling phase of GNN training. For example, PaGraph [12] introduces a
degree-guided feature caching strategy that preloads high-degree node features
into GPU memory to reduce data transfer overhead.
    Although signiﬁcant progress is made in optimizing sampling-based GNN
training, existing methods primarily focus on improving the utilization of com-
putational and memory resources while often overlooking repeated computations
during the sampling process. Figure 1a illustrates the phenomenon of redun-
dant sampling in multi-layer GNN training. As shown in Fig. 1a, in multi-layer
GNNs, the same node may be repeatedly sampled by nodes from diﬀerent layers,
resulting in multiple sampling computations across layers—this phenomenon is
referred to as inter-layer redundancy. For example, node A in the Fig. 1a is
sampled and computed in two separate layers. Similarly, within the same layer,
diﬀerent nodes may sample the same neighbor nodes, leading to repeated com-
putations for those neighbors. This is known as intra-layer redundancy. For
                                  Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN         29

instance, node C in the Fig. 1a is sampled and computed twice within the same
layer.




Fig. 1. Visualization and Quantitative Analysis of Redundant Sampling in Sampling-
Based GNN Training.

    Figure 1b presents that the ratio of inter-layer redundant sampling ranges
from 4% to 26%, indicating a signiﬁcant amount of duplicated computation and
considerable room for optimization during the sampling process. Although DGL
[15] globally deduplicates the set of source nodes sampled by all target nodes
within the same layer—ensuring that each neighbor is included only once per
layer and thereby completely eliminating intra-layer redundancy—the issue of
inter-layer redundancy remains unaddressed. Several studies attempt to address
this issue. For example, MariusGNN [14] adopts a complete cross-layer reuse
technique (CCR), which directly reuses sampled neighbors from earlier layers
throughout the entire mini-batch, thereby avoiding redundant sampling and
computation of the same nodes. This approach reduces computational over-
head and memory access costs, leading to improved sampling eﬃciency. Figure 2
presents the accuracy comparison between DGL and CCR when training the
Flickr dataset using the GCN model and the OGBN-Arxiv dataset using the
GraphSAGE model. As shown in Fig. 2, the CCR strategy leads to a decrease
in GNN accuracy. While this method reduces computational and memory over-
head while enhancing sampling eﬃciency, its coarse-grained indiscriminate reuse
mechanism compromises neighbor diversity. The equivalent reuse of both highly
sensitive and low-risk nodes damages structural heterogeneity in sampled neigh-
borhoods, impairing GNNs’ ability to capture local dynamic variations and
resulting in model accuracy degradation. Furthermore, indiscriminate reuse may
induce loss oscillations or even divergence, thereby substantially reducing train-
ing accuracy and convergence speed.
Motivation. As shown in Fig. 1b, the proportion of redundant computation
is substantial, indicating signiﬁcant optimization potential. Although complete
reuse strategies can reduce redundant computations, they often lead to accu-
racy degradation. Therefore, it is crucial to carefully select the nodes that are
suitable for reuse. Reducing the computational cost caused by redundant sam-
pling while maintaining accuracy is essential. We observe that certain nodes
play a more critical role in inﬂuencing the training outcomes of GNNs. To this
end, in Sect. 3, we dissect two critical GNN execution phases—feature aggrega-
tion and backpropagation—and propose key node screening metrics from dual
30      Y. Wang et al.




           Fig. 2. Impact of Complete Reuse Strategy on GNN Accuracy.


dimensions: neighbor diversity preservation and parameter update contribution.
Building on these foundations, in Sect. 4, we design the accuracy-aware sampling
framework AARSampler.


3     Accuracy-Aware Cross-Layer Reuse Strategy
This section primarily introduces accuracy-aware selective cross-layer reuse tech-
niques, focusing on how to select appropriate nodes for cross-layer reuse during
GNN training. Speciﬁcally, this section presents several selection criteria for
evaluating the impact of nodes on training accuracy. Using these criteria, it is
possible to identify which nodes have a greater contribution to the ﬁnal train-
ing outcome, thus optimizing the cross-layer reuse strategy to improve training
eﬃciency while maximizing accuracy retention.

3.1   Feature Aggregation-Based Reuse Selection Criteria
In the forward propagation of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), nodes update
their own features by aggregating information from their neighbors. In sampling-
based GNN training, ensuring the diversity of sampled neighbors for each node is
crucial. Blindly reusing sampling results may impair the fairness and randomness
of sampling, thus undermining neighbor diversity and ultimately degrading the
model’s accuracy. Figure 3 illustrates the variation in neighbor diversity under
diﬀerent node degrees and neighbor label entropies.
    Two key conditions that undermine neighbor diversity are identiﬁed as fol-
lows:
    First, a high in-degree is a fundamental prerequisite for ensuring neighbor
diversity. When a node’s in-degree is signiﬁcantly greater than the sampling
fanout (the number of neighbors to be sampled for each vertex), the potential
space of sampling combinations increases dramatically (e.g., given a fanout of 2,
a node with 10 neighbors generates C(10, 2) = 45 distinct combinations). This
structural condition lays the foundation for diversiﬁed information aggregation.
As shown in Fig. 3a, when the in-degree equals the fanout (e.g., only 2 neighbors),
the sampling result is unique, and reuse has no eﬀect. However, for a high-
degree node with 10 neighbors, as illustrated in Fig. 3b, reusing a ﬁxed sampling
                                   Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN           31

result compresses the original rich combination space into a single deterministic
pattern. This reduces sampling randomness, compromises neighbor diversity, and
negatively impacts model accuracy.




     Fig. 3. Illustration of Sampling Combination Diversity for Diﬀerent Nodes.


    Second, the diversity of neighbor labels further determines how signiﬁcantly
reusing high-degree node samples aﬀects model performance. Even for nodes
with the same high in-degree, their impact on the model varies based on the
label diversity of their neighbors. In real-world scenarios, some neighbors may
belong to the same class (i.e., with identical labels and similar features), and can
thus be approximated as homogeneous. If the label distribution among neighbors
is skewed (e.g., in Fig. 3b), only three eﬀective combinations exist from a label
perspective, and the damage to diversity caused by reuse is limited. In contrast,
as shown in Fig. 3c, a node with balanced label distribution among its neighbors
has up to 12 eﬀective label combinations. Reusing samples for such high-degree
nodes with diverse neighbor labels signiﬁcantly reduces sampling randomness,
disrupts information propagation paths, and causes more pronounced degrada-
tion in the ﬁnal predictive accuracy of the GNN model. Therefore, we introduce
label entropy as an additional metric to quantify the diversity of a node’s
neighbor types. This metric helps assess how much reusing the sampling results
of a node would disrupt the neighbor diversity. The formula for label entropy is
as follows:
                                         K
                              H(v) = −         pi log2 pi
                                         i=1
where H(v) is the label entropy of node v; pi is the probability that the neighbors
of node v belong to the i-th label (i.e., the proportion of neighbors with the i-th
label); and K is the total number of label categories.
    Nodes with higher label entropy generally have more diverse neighbor infor-
mation, while nodes with lower label entropy have more homogeneous neighbor
information. The higher the label entropy, the more diverse the node’s neighbor
information.
Heuristic #1: For nodes with high in-degrees and high label entropy, due to
the diversity of their neighbor information, directly reusing their sampling results
may not capture the full range of their diversiﬁed information, leading to a loss in
accuracy. Hence, it is recommended to avoid reusing sampling results for nodes
with high in-degrees and high label entropy.
32      Y. Wang et al.

3.2   Parameter Update Contribution-Based Reuse Selection Criteria

In the backpropagation of GNNs, the process begins by computing the loss based
on the output. Gradients of node embeddings are then calculated top-down along
the graph structure, followed by aggregation to obtain weight gradients for each
layer. Finally, weights are updated via optimizers (e.g., SGD or Adam) to pro-
gressively minimize the loss.
    Nodes exhibiting high gradient norms demonstrate signiﬁcant sensitivity to
the loss function, where neighborhood variations can readily trigger gradient
instability. Reusing sampling results for such nodes ampliﬁes gradient estima-
tion errors, consequently inducing loss oscillations and convergence delays dur-
ing training, which substantially compromises model accuracy and convergence
speed.
    A key challenge arises from the need to dynamically identify these nodes
that exhibit high gradient norms, as each epoch requires recomputing losses
and executing backpropagation. Fortunately, we observe that the set of high-
gradient-norm nodes exhibits remarkable stability across training epochs: the
Fig. 4 shows the overlap ratio between the high-gradient-norm node set in each
epoch and the high-gradient-norm node set in the ﬁrst epoch. Each epoch shares,
on average, over 70% of high gradient norm nodes with the ﬁrst epoch. These ver-
tices typically include Hard-to-classify vertices (e.g., decision boundary vertices)
and Structurally distinctive vertices (hub vertices or isolated vertices).




            Fig. 4. Stability of High-Gradient Node Sets Across Epochs.


    Based on this observation, we eﬃciently identify critical nodes by computing
and dynamically updating a protection set after the ﬁrst epoch, thereby sys-
tematically preventing sampling reuse for high-gradient nodes. We adopt the
Frobenius norm of a node’s gradient as an indicator of its inﬂuence on
training. The Frobenius norm incorporates gradient information across all fea-
ture dimensions and sampling instances, providing a comprehensive measure of
a node’s overall impact on parameter updates. It is deﬁned as follows:
    For a node’s gradient matrix G ∈ Rd×m , its Frobenius norm is

                                           d   m
                                G F =                2
                                                    gij
                                          i=1 j=1
                                   Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN         33

where d is the embedding dimension (feature dimension), m is the number of
neighbor sampling instances, and gij is the gradient of the i-th feature dimension
at the j-th sampling.
Heuristic #2: Nodes with high Frobenius norms have a substantial inﬂuence on
the direction of parameter updates. Reusing their sampling results may introduce
biased gradient estimates, slow convergence, and degrade model performance.
Therefore, during training, special caution should be taken when handling these
nodes’ samples to avoid excessive reuse and to ensure model stability and per-
formance.


4     Implementation
This section proposes an Accuracy-Aware Cross-layer Reuse strategy
based on dynamic node importance identiﬁcation, aiming to reduce
redundant sampling computation overhead while preserving model accuracy.




             Fig. 5. The design of Selective Cross-layer Reuse Strategy.




4.1   Design Overview

The overall framework of the strategy is shown in Fig. 5 and consists of three com-
ponents: (1) Preprocessing Phase: Based on Heuristic #1, high-importance
nodes are identiﬁed via multi-dimensional feature analysis to construct the initial
“Reuse Protection Node Set (RPNS),” which marks critical nodes unsuitable for
cross-layer reuse. (2) Gradient-Based Protection Update Phase: After the
ﬁrst training epoch, Heuristic #2 is applied to dynamically expand the RPNS by
incorporating node gradient information. (3) Sampling Reuse Phase: Within
each mini-batch, a dynamically updated reuse list is maintained to enable eﬃ-
cient reuse of sampled neighborhoods.
34     Y. Wang et al.

   These techniques eﬀectively control the reuse of sampling information across
GNN layers while maintaining training accuracy and reducing computational
overhead.


4.2   Design Details
(1) Preprocessing Phase The preprocessing phase constructs the initial
Reuse Protection Node Set (RPNS) through single-stage screening. The
speciﬁc process is as follows:
Structural Feature Joint Screening (Heuristic #1): We ﬁrst identify the
top 20% of nodes by in-degree as high-degree nodes, placing them into set S1a .
    Next, we compute neighbor label entropy for nodes in S1a , then select the
top 40% with the highest entropy values into set S1 , identifying nodes exhibiting
high neighbor diversity.
Protection Set Generation: We take S1 as the initial RPNS. This RPNS
is used to constrain which nodes’ sampling results should not be reused across
GNN layers during training.


(2) Gradient-Based Protection Update Phase (Heuristic #2) After the
ﬁrst training epoch, we compute the gradient norm of each node and select the
top 10% highest-norm nodes to form the set Sgrad . We union Sgrad with the cur-
rent RPNS to produce the updated RPNS. This dynamic update ensures that
nodes with signiﬁcant contributions to model updates remain protected from
sampling reuse, further preserving accuracy while reducing redundant computa-
tion.


(3) Sampling Reuse Phase To achieve eﬃcient and controlled sampling reuse,
we maintain a dynamic Reuse List during each mini-batch:
Reuse List Maintenance Mechanism: In each mini-batch training iteration,
the system caches sampled neighborhoods of non-protected nodes in the Reuse
List to avoid redundant computation. The implementation proceeds as follows:
(a) Pre-Sampling Check
    Before performing any sampling, the target node is ﬁrst checked against the
RPNS :
If the node ∈ RPNS: Perform the sampling operation as usual, but do not
cache the result to preserve the dynamic behavior of critical nodes.
If the node ∈ / RPNS: Proceed to the reuse decision ﬂow.
(b) Reuse Decision Flow
    For nodes outside the RPNS, the system then queries the Reuse List:
Hit in Reuse List: Immediately reuse the cached neighbor set and skip the
sampling computation.
Miss in Reuse List: Perform neighbor sampling as usual, then insert the newly
obtained neighbor set into the Reuse List for future reuse.
                                  Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN          35

5     Evaluation
5.1   Experimental Setup
1. Environments: We conduct our experiments on a server running Ubuntu
   24.04 LTS with an Intel Xeon Gold 6133 CPU (40 cores), 62 GB main memory,
   and two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs (each with 24 GB memory). The
   software environment includes GCC 13.3.0, CUDA 12.4, PyTorch 2.1.0, and
   DGL v2.4.0+cu121.
2. Datasets: In our experimental evaluation, we select four publicly available
   graph datasets: two large-scale social networks—Reddit [16] and Tolokers—as
   well as the Flickr dataset and Ogbn-arxiv [17] from the Open Graph Bench-
   mark (OGB). For the OGB dataset, we use the oﬃcial training split provided
   by OGB; for the remaining datasets, we follow the data partitions provided
   by DGL [15].
3. Parameter Settings: In our experiments, we employ multiple widely used
   parameter conﬁgurations for comparative evaluation [16,18]. Speciﬁcally, the
   batch size (i.e., the number of sampled nodes per iteration) is set to 1024,
   2048, 4096, and 8192; the graph sampling fanout tuples are set to (10, 10, 10)
   and (15, 15, 15). By combining diﬀerent batch sizes with sampling densities,
   we can comprehensively assess our method’s training eﬃciency and model
   performance.
4. Models: To evaluate our method, we employ three of the most common and
   representative GNN architectures: GCN [19], GraphSAGE [20], and GIN [21].
   For all models, we use a three-layer architecture with a hidden dimension of
   128. (For the GIN model, however, we set the hidden dimension to 32 to
   mitigate overﬁtting, as deeper hidden layers in GIN are more prone to this
   issue.)
5. Baselines: We compare against two baseline implementations:
   (a) DGL [15], a state-of-the-art GNN framework;
   (b) MariusGNN [14], which employs complete cross-layer reuse in its sam-
       pling process to accelerate sampling-based GNN training. We only com-
       pare the sampling optimization strategy in MariusGNN [14].
   In our evaluation, we measure both the performance of their sampling modules
   and the ﬁnal GNN training accuracy.


5.2   Parameter Selection

To determine the optimal protection ratio combination, this study systematically
evaluates the impact of label entropy selection ratio (α), degree selection ratio
(β), and gradient norm selection ratio (γ) on the Accuracy Recovery Ratio.
1. Synergistic Eﬀect of Label Entropy and Degree Ratios
As shown in Fig. 6a, which presents the accuracy recovery ratio of GNN training
through selective reuse of node sets ﬁltered by diﬀerent combinations of label
entropy and degree selection ratios, it is observed that when selecting the top 20%
by degree and top 40% by label entropy, the accuracy recovery ratio exceeds 50%
36     Y. Wang et al.

while protecting only 8% of nodes. To balance protection eﬃciency and accuracy
beneﬁts, we select the combination of β = 20% and α = 40%.
2. Independent Eﬀect of Gradient Norm Ratio
As shown in Fig. 6b, which displays the accuracy recovery ratio using node sets
ﬁltered by diﬀerent gradient norm selection ratios, the gradient norm threshold
γ exhibits a critical point eﬀect on accuracy recovery. Within the range of γ ≤
10%, the recovery ratio increases rapidly, while when γ > 10%, the growth rate
decreases signiﬁcantly. Thus, γ = 10% is determined as the optimal threshold,
eﬀectively capturing most critical nodes while preventing excessive protection.
3. Parameter Conﬁguration Selection
The optimal parameter combination established through the above experiments
(α = 40%, β = 20%, γ = 10%) is adopted as the default conﬁguration for the
following experiments.




        Fig. 6. Eﬀects of Parameter Selection on Accuracy Recovery Ratio.




5.3   Performance Results

We compare our proposed accuracy-aware cross-layer reuse strategy (AAR)
against the native DGL [15] neighbor sampler and the complete cross-layer reuse
sampler (CCR) from MariusGNN [14], evaluating both sampling time overhead
and training accuracy.

1. Sampling Performance Comparison
    – Sampling Time Speedup: Figure 7 shows the sampling time speedup of
      our method (Accuracy Aware Reuse, AAR) and the cross-layer reuse sam-
      pler from MariusGNN [14] (Complete Cross-layer Reuse, CCR) compared
      to the native DGL [15] sampler under various datasets and parameter set-
      tings. The results indicate that AAR achieves an average sampling time
      speedup of 1.78× (with a maximum of 2.74×), while MariusGNN [14]
      achieves an average speedup of 1.95× (up to 2.76×).
                                   Accuracy-Aware Sampling Reuse in GNN          37

    – Sampling Workload Speedup: Figure 8 compares the actual total
        number of sampling operations (i.e., the number of eﬀective neighbor sam-
        plings) for AAR and MariusGNN [14] against the DGL [15] native sampler
        under diﬀerent datasets and parameter settings. AAR achieves an average
        sampling workload speedup of 1.80× (up to 2.90×), whereas MariusGNN
        [14] reaches an average of 1.97× (with a maximum of 2.94×).
        Although AAR’s sampling time speedup is slightly lower than that of
        MariusGNN [14], it still achieves a 63% reduction in sampling time com-
        pared to native DGL [15], signiﬁcantly improving sampling eﬃciency. Fur-
        thermore, as the batch size and fanout values increase, the redundant
        computation problem becomes more severe, thereby leading to a more
        pronounced acceleration eﬀect.
2. Training Accuracy Comparison Figures 9, 10, 11 present the ﬁnal train-
   ing accuracy achieved by our method, the native DGL [15] sampler, and
   the MariusGNN [14] cross-layer reuse sampler across diﬀerent GNN mod-
   els. To provide a clearer visual comparison of accuracy diﬀerences, the plots
   only show results from epochÂă5 onward. As shown, MariusGNN [14]’s blan-
   ket reuse of all nodes incurs an average accuracy drop of 3.84% (peaking at
   4.83%). In contrast, our approach strictly bounds accuracy loss to less than
   1.5% (1.01 ± 0.32%) while still maintaining substantial speedup.
   In summary, our method achieves eﬃcient acceleration of sampling-based
   GNN training by signiﬁcantly reducing sampling time and computational
   overhead, all while keeping accuracy loss within acceptable limits.
