6    Conclusion
In this paper, we propose AARSampler, an accuracy-aware sampling framework.
Speciﬁcally, by analyzing two key stages in GNN training—feature aggregation
and backpropagation—we introduce a two-dimensional vertex selection metric
for accuracy-aware cross-layer reuse of sampling results. By reusing the sampling
results of insensitive nodes across layers, the sampling process is accelerated
while keeping the training accuracy loss within a controllable range. We system-
atically evaluate AARSampler on four graph datasets combined with three dif-
ferent GNN models under various parameter settings. Experimental results show
that, compared with DGL, AARSampler achieves an average 1.78× speedup in
the sampling phase while controlling the training accuracy loss within 1.5%,
signiﬁcantly improving training eﬃciency.

         Scalable Distributed Index Construction
           for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS

           Xiangyu Liu1 , Meiling Wang2 , and Yiming Zhang1(B)
                    1
                      NICE Lab, Xiamen University, Xiamen, China
                     xiangyul@stu.xmu.edu.cn, sdiris@gmail.com
                        2
                          Huawei Theory Lab, Shenzhen, China
                             wangmeiling17@huawei.com



       Abstract. In high-dimensional vector spaces, approximate nearest
       neighbor search (ANNS) is essential for modern database and AI sys-
       tems. Graph-based ANNS has become increasingly popular owing to
       its balance between search eﬃciency and accuracy. However, building
       indexes for extremely large graphs remains challenging: single-node index
       construction can take a long time (days or even weeks) due to limited
       memory, computation, and I/O resources, while distributed index con-
       struction suﬀers from workload imbalance, network and I/O bottlenecks
       during index merging, and poor hardware utilization. This paper presents
       SD-GAC, a scalable distributed index construction framework for large-
       scale graph-based ANNS. SD-GAC introduces a ﬁne-grained partitioning
       and packing scheme to ensure balanced distribution of index construction
       workloads, a communication-eﬃcient merging algorithm that prefetches
       and batches all required neighbor data in a single pass, and a NUMA-
       aware construction algorithm that maximizes local memory and cache
       utilization. Evaluation shows that SD-GAC signiﬁcantly reduces index
       construction time and achieves near-linear speedup with increasing com-
       putational resources.


       Keywords: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) ·
       Distributed Graph Index Construction · Scalability


1    Introduction

Today deep learning models can embed almost all types of data, including
speech, vision, and text information, into multi-dimensional vectors with tens
or even hundreds of dimensions. Such vectors are critical for complex semantic
understanding tasks [19,22]. To enable eﬀective vector analysis, vector nearest
neighbor search (NNS) systems have become critical system components for an
increasing number of online services like search and recommendation. To satisfy
the strict query latency requirement for these online services, vector search sys-
tems often resort to approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS), to locate as
many correct results as possible (i.e., query accuracy).
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 43–58, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_3
44     X. Liu et al.

    ANNS in highdimensional spaces refers to ﬁnd top-k vectors most similar
to a given query vector. It has a wide range of applications in many ﬁelds,
including data mining [27], search engines [33], and AI-driven recommendation
systems [12,35]. Speciﬁcally, fueled by the recent prosperity of Large Language
Models (LLMs) [3,15,31,34], ANNS systems have become a crucial compo-
nent of modern AI infrastructure. Current studies explore four index types for
ANNS: Tree-based [20,28], Hash-based [10,13,26], Quantization-based [9,11],
and Graph-based methods [7,25]. Among these, graph-based algorithms have
demonstrated superior performance, establishing themselves as the industry
standard [5,6] and attracting substantial academic interest [8,23]. Although
numerous studies have explored optimizations for search performance, research
on improving index construction eﬃciency remains limited, which is increasingly
critical in real-world applications. However, single-node solutions can take a long
time (days or even weeks) [32] due to limited memory, computation power, and
I/O resources. For instance, building an graph index on tens of millions of vectors
typically requires about 10 h [5,17], billion-scale datasets may extend construc-
tion time to ﬁve days, even with relaxed construction parameters [25]. Thus,
construction eﬃciency has become a bottleneck in modern vector databases [21],
as it directly impacts the ability to rapidly release new services with up-to-date
data and high search performance [24].
    To overcome these limitations, distributed index construction has emerged
as a promising solution. By partitioning data and harnessing parallel compu-
tations across multiple computing nodes, distributed indexing can dramatically
reduce construction time, enabling eﬃcient and timely handling of billion-scale
datasets. However, distributed index construction introduces several unique and
signiﬁcant challenges. Firstly, workload imbalance across nodes can lead to inef-
ﬁcient resource usage, where some servers become idle prematurely, while others
continue processing overloaded tasks. Secondly, inter-node data transfers during
index merging phases can create substantial network and I/O bottlenecks, oﬀset-
ting the beneﬁts gained from parallel execution. Finally, modern server hardware
commonly employs Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architectures; ignor-
ing NUMA-awareness in distributed systems may severely degrade performance
by causing excessive remote memory accesses and suboptimal cache utilization.
    In order to address the challenges mentioned above, we propose SD-
GAC, a Scalable Distributed Graph-based ANNS Construction Framework for
extremely large datasets. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as
follows:

– We design a ﬁne-grained partitioning and packing strategy to achieve near-
  optimal workload balance across distributed nodes, signiﬁcantly reducing idle
  time and resource underutilization.
– We propose a NUMA-aware index construction algorithm that co-locates
  computation and memory access, maximizing memory bandwidth and mini-
  mizing remote memory latency.
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS             45

– We introduce an eﬃcient cross-node graph merging mechanism that min-
  imizes network and I/O bottlenecks by leveraging precomputed mappings
  and bulk communication.
– We provide a comprehensive experimental evaluation on billion-scale datasets,
  demonstrating substantial improvements in build time and scalability.



2     Background and Motivation
2.1   Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

Nearest Neighbor Search (NNS) involves ﬁnding the closest data point to a given
query point within a dataset. Formally, consider a dataset D consisting of n
points, each represented as a d-dimensional vector {x1 , x2 , ..., xd }. Given a query
point q, also represented by a d-dimensional vector {q1 , q2 , ..., qd }, and target k,
the goal is to ﬁnd k points {p1 , p2 , ..., pk } ∈ D such that the distance d(pi , q)
is minimized. The choice of distance metric, such as Euclidean or Hamming
distance, typically depends on the embedding model used to generate the vectors.
    However, the NNS problem becomes computationally challenging in high-
dimensional vector spaces due to the curse of dimensionality [14], which makes
exhaustive linear searches impractical on large-scale datasets [30]. To address
this issue, Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) algorithms have been
developed, where the goal is to retrieve k neighbors which are close to being
optimal. The accuracy of the ANNS is typically measured as recall. Let the
set of the exact k-nearest vectors be X, and the vectors returned by an ANNS
algorithm be Y , where |X| = |Y | = k. Then recall@k is deﬁned as |X∩Y            k
                                                                                     |
                                                                                       ,
meaning the proportion of exact k-nearest vectors the algorithm ﬁnds.
    To meet diverse accuracy and performance requirements, several ANNS algo-
rithms such as tree-structure based [20,28], hashing based [10,13,26] and quanti-
zation based approaches [9,11] have been proposed over the past decades. Among
the various techniques, ANNS algorithms using graphs [7,18] are considered as
the most promising solution, with great potential. In graph-based ANNS, the
vectors in the dataset are organized as a directed graph where each node of the
graph represents a vector, and the edges of the graph represent the neighboring
relationship of the vectors. This structure allows graph-based approaches to bet-
ter capture neighbor relationships and traverse fewer points during the search,
leading to higher eﬃciency and accuracy compared to other methods.


2.2   On-Disk Graph-Based Index Construction

In super large-scale vector search scenarios, the memory cost can become
extremely expensive. For example, many commercial recommendation systems
such as Alibaba [7] usually require TB-scale memory space to accommodate
billion-scale vectors. To support billion-scale ANNS with graph-based index,
SSDs are used because of their cost-eﬀectiveness [25,29], with the majority of
46     X. Liu et al.




           Fig. 1. Workﬂow of On-disk Graph-based Index Construction.


vector indices stored on SSDs and a moderately-sized DRAM used as working
memory.
    Figure 1 shows the construction process of the disk-based graph index, which
consists of three phases: (1) To reduce the number of fetching full-precision vec-
tors, on-disk graph-based ANNS systems always maintain a copy of in-memory
compressed vectors using product quantization (PQ) [16], and use PQ distance as
an approximation when inserting neighbors to the candidate set during search. It
ﬁrst samples the dataset and divides the sampled set uniformly into sub-spaces,
with each vector containing some of the sub-vectors. Then, these sub-vectors
are clustered by using k-means to generate a codebook, which contains a set
of centroids of all clusters. The codebook allows each sub-vector to be approxi-
mated by its nearest centroid. Once all codebooks are generated, the full dataset
is streamed and compressed using the codebooks. (2) As the dataset can reach
billion-scale, it cannot be fully loaded into memory at once for index construc-
tion, it is common practice to partition the dataset using k-means clustering.
The dataset is divided into k clusters (i.e., shards), where k is determined based
on the ram budget, ensuring that the construction of each shard does not exceed
memory constraints. Each data point is then assigned to its l closest cluster
centers (typically l = 2 suﬃces). (3) After the dataset is partitioned, each shard
is built sequentially. Then, all the shard indexes are merged into a single index
by taking the union of all the edges in each shard’s graph. The ﬁnal index is
stored as multiple records on SSD pages, each of which represents one node of
the graph. A record includes the full-precision vector and a neighbor list which
consists of the IDs of neighbors.

2.3   Distributed Systems Demands and Challenges
As real-world datasets continue to expand, single-node solutions are increasingly
inadequate. Business applications such as e-commerce and online advertising rou-
tinely involve billions or even trillions of vectors, making the memory capacity,
computational power, and I/O bandwidth of a single node signiﬁcant bottle-
necks. As shown in Table 1, global rebuilds are both resource-hungry and time-
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS       47

consuming. For example, rebuilding a one billion vector index [25] for DiskANN,
a recent disk-based system, needs 1100 GB DRAM, 32 vCPUs, for 2 days. When
limiting resources to 64 GB memory and 16 vCPUs, the rebuilding time becomes
signiﬁcantly longer, e.g., 5 days for DiskANN. This stressful setting could also
lead to a catastrophic drop in query performance due to severe computational
resource starvation. Consequently, distributed systems have become essential
to support large-scale similarity search and eﬃcient index construction. While
distributed systems oﬀer the potential to handle large-scale datasets, they also
introduce numerous challenges:

                        Table 1. Build time of DiskANN.

                                  Memory CPU       Time
                        DiskANN 1100 GB 32 cores 2 days
                                64 GB 16 cores 5 days




      Fig. 2. Load imbalance in the construction process for Deep1B dataset.


Workload Imbalance: One of the primary challenges in distributed index con-
struction is achieving an even distribution of data partitions across all servers.
When the dataset is divided, variations in partition sizes can result in certain
servers being assigned signiﬁcantly more vectors than others. This imbalance
leads to situations where some nodes complete their index construction tasks
much earlier and remain idle, while others continue processing larger partitions.
As shown in Fig. 2, the build time of the shard with the largest number of vec-
tors is 7.3× longer than the build time of the shard with the smallest number
48     X. Liu et al.

of vectors. As a result, overall resource utilization decreases and the total index
construction time is dictated by the slowest, most heavily loaded node.
Network and I/O Bottlenecks: Data transfer between distributed nodes can
incur signiﬁcant latency, especially when handling large volumes of data. Dur-
ing the index merge stage, inter-node communication (e.g., fetching neighbor
data, synchronizing shards) can create network and I/O bottlenecks that severely
impact overall system performance. Therefore, minimizing network traﬃc and
optimizing data transfer strategies are crucial for achieving high throughput and
low latency.




                           Fig. 3. SD-GAC framework.




3     Design
3.1   System Overview
As shown in Fig. 3, SD-GAC has three key techniques: distributed PQ compu-
tation, balanced partition and distributed graph merge. These techniques are
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS     49

designed to address the main challenges in large-scale graph-based index con-
struction. Speciﬁcally, distributed PQ computation accelerates the quantization
process by parallelizing computation on multiple nodes, thus overcoming the
bottleneck of single-node processing. Balanced partition ensures that each node
is allocated nearly the same amount of data, thus alleviating load imbalance
and maximizing the eﬃciency of parallel construction. Finally, distributed graph
merge eﬃciently integrates locally constructed subgraphs into the global index,
minimizing the frequent and expensive communication overhead typically asso-
ciated with merging, and thereby addressing the scalability challenge.

3.2   Distributed PQ Computation
Distributed Product Quantization (PQ) computation is a critical component
within our proposed framework, speciﬁcally designed to address the scalabil-
ity bottleneck commonly encountered during quantization in large-scale graph-
based index construction. Traditional PQ implementations suﬀer from limited
throughput and signiﬁcant latency due to the resource constraints inherent to
single-node systems. To overcome these limitations, our framework implements
a distributed batch-based PQ computation strategy.


Algorithm 1. Distributed PQ Pivots Generation
Require: Training data X ∈ RN ×d , number of clusters K, number of PQ chunks M
Ensure: PQ pivots for each chunk, saved to ﬁle
 1: // rank = 0 is the master node
 2: if rank = 0 then
 3:    Divide the d dimensions into M feature chunks: {C1 , ..., CM }
 4:    Assign a subset of chunks to each server
 5:    Broadcast chunk assignment and chunk oﬀsets to all ranks
 6: end if
 7: All servers receive chunk oﬀsets and assigned chunk range [s, e)
 8: // Lines 8-9 are executed in parallel on multiple nodes
 9: for chunk i = s to e − 1 do
10:    Run K-means on XCi to get K pivots
11: end for
12: Gather all local pivots from workers to rank 0
13: if rank = 0 then
14:    Save PQ pivots to ﬁle
15: end if



    As illustrated in Algorithm 1, the process begins with the master node (rank
= 0) dividing the d-dimensional feature space into M chunks, each representing a
subset of coordinates (Line 3). The master then assigns a subset of these chunks
to each server and broadcasts the chunk assignment and corresponding oﬀsets
to all participating nodes (Lines 4-5). Upon receiving their respective chunk
assignments (Line 7), all servers proceed in parallel to process their allocated
50      X. Liu et al.

chunks: for each assigned chunk i, the server extracts the data corresponding
to the dimensions of chunk i and performs K-means clustering to obtain K
cluster centers (pivots) (Lines 9–11). Once the local pivots for all chunks have
been computed, they are gathered from all servers to the master node (Line 12),
which then writes the consolidated PQ pivots to disk (Line 14). This workﬂow
enables eﬃcient parallel generation of PQ pivots by distributing the computation
of feature chunks across multiple nodes.


Algorithm 2. Distributed PQ Encoding
Require: Raw dataset X ∈ RN ×d , PQ pivots {P1 , ..., PM }, batch size B
Ensure: PQ codes for all data points
 1: if rank = 0 then
 2:    Load PQ pivots
 3: end if
 4: for batch b = 1 to N/B do
 5:    if rank = 0 then
 6:       Subtract centroid: x ← x − c
 7:       Scatter the batch to all ranks (each receives ≈ B/p points)
 8:    end if
 9:    Each rank receives assigned data points
10:    // Lines 11-14 are executed in parallel on multiple nodes
11:    for all assigned point x do
12:       for chunk i = 1 to M do
13:         Extract xi (chunk’s dimensions)
14:         Find closest pivot id: qi = arg minj xi − Pi,j
15:         Store qi as x’s code for chunk i
16:       end for
17:    end for
18:    Gather encoded results to rank 0
19:    if rank = 0 then
20:       Write all gathered PQ codes of the batch to disk
21:    end if
22: end for


    After the PQ pivots have been generated and collected as described above,
the distributed encoding of the raw dataset proceeds as shown in Algorithm 2.
Initially, the master node loads the precomputed PQ pivots into memory (Line
2). The encoding is performed in batches to accommodate large-scale data: for
each batch (Line 4), the master node ﬁrst subtracts the centroid from each vector
and then scatters the batch to all worker nodes, ensuring that each node receives
an approximately equal number of data points (Lines 6–7). Once the data has
been distributed, each worker processes its assigned points in parallel (Line 9).
For every assigned point x, and for each PQ chunk i, the worker extracts the
relevant subset of dimensions, computes the nearest codeword in the correspond-
ing codebook Pi , and stores the resulting code (Lines 12–16). After all assigned
points in the batch have been encoded, the encoded results are gathered from
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS      51

all workers to the master node (Line 18), which then writes the PQ codes of the
current batch to disk (Line 20). This distributed encoding workﬂow eﬃciently
utilizes the available computational resources and enables scalable compression
of billion-scale datasets.




                   Fig. 4. NUMA-aware building architecture.




3.3   Balanced Partition and NUMA-Aware Building
To address load imbalance in distributed settings, we implement the balanced
partitioning algorithm. We ﬁrst divide each vector into a number of small par-
titions (with the number of partitions exceeding the number of machines), then
employ the best-ﬁt bin-packing algorithm [4] to aggregate these small parti-
tions into larger partitions, so that the number of resulting partitions matches
the number of machines. This ﬁne-grained partitioning and packing strategy
leads to more balanced workload allocation, thereby preventing scenarios where
some servers become idle after ﬁnishing their assigned tasks while others are
still actively constructing the index. By minimizing partition size variance, our
approach maximizes resource utilization and improves the overall eﬃciency of
distributed index construction.
     To further accelerate the build within each server, we implement a NUMA-
aware index construction strategy. Modern multi-core servers often use Non-
Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) architectures, where memory access is faster
when data resides on a processor’s local node than on a remote node. As shown
in Fig. 4, SD-GAC is designed to take advantage of this heterogeneous memory
hierarchy by distributing partitions (shards) across NUMA nodes. To minimize
remote memory accesses, SD-GAC employs aﬃnity-based scheduling and sup-
ports work stealing within each NUMA node to mitigate workload imbalances.
Partitions are bound to speciﬁc CPU cores, ensuring that each partition is always
processed by the same core to maximize cache utilization. By co-locating com-
putation with the relevant data, SD-GAC reduces remote memory accesses, sat-
urates memory bandwidth, and ultimately decreases build time.
52      X. Liu et al.

3.4   Parallel Graph Merge


Algorithm 3. Distributed Parallel Shard Graph Merge
Require: Global node set V , partitioned among P servers by global ID (e.g., server
    i merges neighbors for Vi = [i · N/P, (i + 1) · N/P )), precomputed mapping from
    node to server.
Ensure: Final merged global graph index.
 1: // Step 1: Precompute node-to-server mapping based on global IDs
 2: Each server determines its assigned range Vi and the mapping for all nodes.
 3: // Step 2: Prefetch all needed neighbor lists from remote servers
 4: for each remote server j do
 5:   Request all neighbor lists for nodes in Vi that are owned by j.
 6:   Receive all requested neighbor lists in a single batch (contiguous by construc-
      tion).
 7: end for
 8: // Step 3: Parallel merge of neighbor lists
 9: for all node v in Vi in parallel do
10:    Gather all kbase neighbor lists for v (local + remote).
11:    Merge and deduplicate neighbors; select up to max_degree per node.
12: end for
13: // Step 4: Parallel and ordered file writing
14: Each server writes merged results to the ﬁnal index ﬁle at precomputed oﬀsets,
    matching the global node ID order.



    As illustrated in Algorithm 3, the merge process begins by partitioning the
global node set by ID, such that each server is responsible for merging the neigh-
bor lists for a contiguous range of nodes. The mapping from each node to its
assigned server is precomputed and distributed in advance, ensuring that the
assignment aligns with the ﬁnal output ﬁle layout (Line 2). Prior to merging,
each server prefetches all necessary neighbor lists from remote servers in a single,
bulk I/O operation, taking advantage of the fact that the requested nodes on
each server are stored contiguously in memory (Lines 4–7). With all relevant
neighbor lists locally available, each server proceeds to merge and deduplicate
the neighbors for each of its assigned nodes in parallel (Lines 9–12), selecting up
to the target degree for each node. Finally, since the task partitioning matches
the ﬁnal global ﬁle order, each server can write its merged results directly to
the appropriate oﬀset in the output index ﬁle, enabling eﬃcient and potentially
parallel ﬁle I/O (Line 14).
    This strategy eliminates network I/O bottlenecks during the merge because
each server aggregates all required neighbor information from remote servers in
a single, bulk request, leveraging the fact that the needed data is stored contigu-
ously on the sender side. As a result, each remote server only needs to serve a
single sequential data transfer per requesting server, minimizing communication
rounds and avoiding excessive small or random-access network I/O. Moreover,
once all required data has been fetched, the entire neighbor merging process for
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS       53

each assigned node can be performed independently and in parallel, without fur-
ther synchronization or communication. By aligning the task partitioning with
the ﬁnal ﬁle layout, each server can also write its results directly to the output
ﬁle at precomputed oﬀsets, enabling parallel and sequential disk I/O, further
reducing contention and maximizing throughput. Together, these design choices
ensure that both computation and I/O resources are eﬃciently utilized, leading
to signiﬁcant improvements in distributed merge performance.


4     Evaluation

In this section, we seek to answer the following questions:

– How eﬃciently does SD-GAC build the vector index? (§4.1)
– Does SD-GAC aﬀects search performance? (§4.2)
– How do SD-GAC’s individual techniques impact overall performance? (§4.3)

System Setup: We use 10 servers, each with two AMD EPYC 7763 CPUs (64
cores per CPU, 128 cores in total) and 512GB RAM. SD-GAC is built on top of
the distributed version of DiskANN [25], which is implemented using the MPI [2]
library.
Datasets and Metrics: In our experiments, we use two standard billion-scale
datasets [1] that have been widely used by previous studies, as illustrated in
Table 2. We use query per second (QPS) to evaluate the performance. The query
accuracy is evaluated by Recall@10, which represents the proportion of the top-
10 results containing the ground-truth nearest neighbors for an ANNS query.


                         Table 2. Datasets (One Billion)

                  Dataset Dimension Raw Data Size Data Type
                  SIFT1B 128          119 GB        uint8
                  DEEP1B 96           358 GB        ﬂoat32




4.1   Construction Time

We evaluate the construction time with diﬀerent number of servers, for single-
node we use the original implementation of DiskANN, for distributed we use
the implementation of SD-GAC, each server uses 128 threads. The results are
shown in Fig. 5. As shown in Fig. 5a and Fig. 5b, SD-GAC achieves 2.4× and
16.8× speedup at two and ten nodes on the SIFT1B dataset, and 2.3× and
12.1× speedup on the DEEP1B dataset, respectively, compared to the single-
node baseline. This substantial speedup is primarily attributed to the eﬃcient
54     X. Liu et al.




                       Fig. 5. Build time of diﬀerent datasets.


parallelization of index construction across multiple servers, which allows SD-
GAC to fully exploit distributed memory, CPU, and I/O resources. Addition-
ally, SD-GAC employs NUMA-aware scheduling and optimized data partition-
ing, minimizing load imbalance and ensuring that computational resources are
utilized eﬀectively at all nodes. The lower speedup on DEEP1B is due to its
larger data size (ﬂoat32), which increases network transmission time. Notably,
the speedup exceeds the ideal linear scaling. This is because, in the single-node
baseline, the constructed index must be frequently written to SSD, incurring
signiﬁcant I/O overhead. In contrast, SD-GAC maintains the constructed sub-
graphs in distributed memory throughout the build process and only writes to
disk when necessary, substantially reducing the amount and frequency of SSD
writes.




             Fig. 6. QPS comparison between SD-GAC and DiskANN.




4.2   Search Performance
We use 64 threads for search, and the results are shown in Fig. 6, the results for
SD-GAC were obtained using an index constructed with 10 nodes. As shown, the
Scalable Distributed Index Construction for Large-Scale Graph-Based ANNS     55




                       Fig. 7. Ablation study of SD-GAC.


QPS of SD-GAC is comparable to that of DiskANN across diﬀerent recall rates.
The ﬁgure demonstrates that QPS increases as the recall rate decreases, which
aligns with expectations. Notably, the QPS values of SD-GAC and DiskANN
are closely matched, with SD-GAC exhibiting only minor ﬂuctuations. This
demonstrates that our distributed construction approach in SD-GAC signiﬁ-
cantly accelerates index build time while maintaining search performance.
    Such improvements not only enable timely index updates for rapidly growing
datasets but also allow the system to eﬃciently scale to larger data volumes and
adapt to dynamic, real-world workloads. Consequently, SD-GAC delivers both
high eﬃciency and ﬂexibility for large-scale vector search applications.


4.3   Ablation Study

To quantify the impact of each key optimization in our distributed index con-
struction framework, we conduct an ablation study by incrementally enabling
the following techniques: NUMA-aware construction, parallel graph merge, and
load balance. Test results are averaged over the sift1B and deep1B datasets The
baseline is the original distributed construction without any of these optimiza-
tions, and the total build time is normalized to 1.0.
    As shown in Fig. 7, enabling NUMA-aware construction reduces the build
time by 8%, lowering the normalized build time to 0.92. Incorporating paral-
lel graph merge further reduces the build time by 11% relative to the previous
stage, resulting in a normalized value of 0.82. Finally, introducing load bal-
ance achieves an additional 33% reduction based on the previous conﬁguration,
further decreasing the build time to 0.55. This stepwise improvement clearly
56      X. Liu et al.

demonstrates that each proposed technique contributes to the overall eﬃciency
of the index construction process.
    Overall, the combination of all three optimizations results in a 45% reduction
in total build time compared to the baseline. These results highlight the eﬀective-
ness of our system design in addressing scalability bottlenecks for billion-scale
vector indexing.


5    Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed SD-GAC, a distributed framework designed to accel-
erate graph-based vector index construction for billion-scale datasets. Our app-
roach addresses the key challenges of distributed index construction, including
workload imbalance, network and I/O bottlenecks, and suboptimal hardware
utilization. By leveraging ﬁne-grained partitioning, a NUMA-aware schedul-
ing strategy, and communication-eﬃcient shard merging, SD-GAC signiﬁcantly
reduces construction time while maintaining high accuracy. Through extensive
experiments, we demonstrated that SD-GAC achieves substantial improvements
in build time, with near-linear speedup as the number of nodes increases. Addi-
tionally, the framework scales eﬀectively across large datasets, making it well-
suited for modern vector search systems that require fast and eﬃcient index
construction.

                   Concurrent Interval Tree

                Kapil Kumar Attinagaramu(B) and Praveen Alapati

     Computer Science Engineering Department, Supercomputer Lab. École Centrale
            School of Engineering, Mahindra University, Hyderabad, India
    KapilKumar20pcse002@mahindrauniversity.edu.in, praveena@cse.iitm.ac.in



        Abstract. Interval trees are fundamental data structures for managing
        and querying overlapping intervals, and are widely used in scheduling,
        network monitoring, and database conﬂict resolution domains. However,
        supporting such operations eﬃciently in multi-threaded environments
        remains a substantial challenge due to synchronization bottlenecks and
        contention. In this work, we introduce a novel concurrent interval tree
        that addresses scalability and contention challenges in multi-threaded
        settings. This design is built on the concurrent AA Tree (CAA Tree).
        Our approach departs from traditional interval tree implementations by
        allowing multiple high-values to be stored within a single node using a
        thread-safe structure. It signiﬁcantly improves space utilization and, in
        turn, helps to improve performance while identifying overlapping inter-
        vals. The proposed structure is designed for eﬃcient concurrent insert,
        delete, and overlap operations across diverse workloads. This is achieved
        through a combination of a relaxed balancing approach and a lazy
        deletion mechanism, which together reduce structural contention and
        improve cache locality. Our implementation achieves an average speedup
        of 22.87× over its sequential version when the number of threads is 64
        and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art implementations.


        Keywords: Multi-Threading · Concurrent Interval Trees ·
        Synchronization · Logical Ordering · Contention-Resilient


1     Introduction
The growing use of multicore processors in modern computing systems has made
the design of eﬃcient concurrent data structures increasingly important. While
sequential search trees continue to serve as fundamental components in applica-
tions such as databases, network routing, and task scheduling [1], they are not
well-suited for multi-threaded environments. Their performance tends to degrade
under concurrent workloads due to serialization and synchronization bottlenecks.
To overcome these limitations, various concurrent search tree designs have been
proposed, which enable parallel access across threads while maintaining cor-
rectness. However, building such structures introduces new challenges, including
maintaining structural balance, ensuring consistency during concurrent updates,
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 59–78, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_4
60     K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

and minimizing contention, all while preserving the expected logarithmic time
complexity of search operations.
    Among the various concurrent data structures, interval trees play a partic-
ularly important role due to their ability to eﬃciently support range queries in
logarithmic time [3,4]. Interval trees were originally proposed by Pal et al. [2],
have found widespread application in domains such as task scheduling, net-
work monitoring, and genome sequencing [5]. Conventional interval tree imple-
mentations frequently rely on self-balancing trees such as AVL or Red-Black
trees. Although these data structures ensure that the tree remains balanced and
thereby guarantee logarithmic time complexity for search, insertion, and dele-
tion operations—they introduce notable challenges in concurrent environments.
Maintaining balance in AVL and Red-Black trees involves structural modiﬁca-
tions such as rotations and color or height updates after insertions and deletions.
In a concurrent setting, these operations must be carefully coordinated to pre-
serve the tree’s invariants, often requiring the use of locks or other synchroniza-
tion mechanisms. The need to synchronize access during rebalancing operations
can lead to thread stalls, reduced parallelism, and decreased scalability. In par-
ticular, operations that trigger rotations or propagate structural changes up the
tree may block other threads, resulting in performance bottlenecks as the number
of threads increases.
    In this paper, we introduce a novel concurrent interval tree constructed on
top of the Concurrent AA Tree (CAA Tree) [6], a self-balancing structure specif-
ically designed for concurrent execution. Unlike traditional balancing strategies
that rely on multiple types of complex rotations, the CAA Tree employs a sin-
gle rotation (skew and split) and leverages logical ordering to reduce synchro-
nization overhead. These characteristics make it especially amenable to eﬃcient
and scalable interval management in multithreaded settings. A central chal-
lenge in designing concurrent interval trees is eﬃciently supporting duplicate low
endpoints while allowing access to multiple high endpoints. Conventional data
structures often lack this capability, resulting in poor scalability. Our proposed
structure addresses this limitation by representing each node as a multi-valued
entity that stores multiple high values for a single low value using a thread-
safe ConcurrentHashMap. This compact representation reduces node prolifer-
ation and minimizes contention, thus improving throughput for interval-dense
workloads. Eﬀective memory management also contributes to high performance
in concurrent data structures. By reducing unnecessary node creation and struc-
tural changes, the use of multi-valued nodes decreases the frequency of rebalanc-
ing operations. Additionally, we incorporate a lazy deletion mechanism in which
logically deleted nodes are removed asynchronously by a dedicated background
thread.
    Our experimental evaluation compared to state-of-the-art approaches (see
[7]) shows that the proposed concurrent interval tree outperforms existing
designs in throughput, contention resilience, and cache eﬃciency. Beyond the
general beneﬁts of the CAA framework, our design tackles interval-speciﬁc chal-
lenges: multi-valued nodes reduce node proliferation for overlapping intervals,
                 Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree      61

relaxed balancing minimizes costly rebalancing cascades during interval-heavy
updates, and lazy deletion defers structural removals to lower contention dur-
ing deletions. These optimizations, combined with ﬁne-grained synchronization,
yield high scalability across diverse workloads and thread counts.


2   Background
This section introduces the structural foundations of the proposed Concurrent
Interval Tree (CIT), focusing on how each node represents and manages inter-
vals in a way that supports high concurrency. Each node is designed to capture
a collection of intervals that share the same starting point (low value), while also
facilitating eﬃcient querying and updating in a dynamic environment. Speciﬁ-
cally, a node maintains three key components: the low value, a multi-valued set
of high endpoints, and a max ﬁeld indicating the largest high value in its sub-
tree. The low value serves as the primary key to ordering nodes within the tree.
The max value enables early pruning during range or overlap queries. Mean-
while, high values associated with the same low value are stored in a thread-
safe ConcurrentHashMap, allowing for eﬃcient handling of overlapping intervals
without redundant node creation.




                Fig. 1. Structure of a multi-valued node with size n.



    As shown in Fig. 1, this multi-valued node structure enables the CIT to com-
pactly store multiple intervals with the same starting point. By avoiding the
insertion of separate nodes for each such interval, the structure improves both
space utilization and traversal eﬃciency, which are the two essential factors in
high-performance concurrent settings.
    Figure 2 illustrates the step-by-step insertion of intervals into the CIT. The
process begins with inserting the interval (20, 45), which becomes the root node.
As the tree is initially empty, no rebalancing is required. The next interval,
(15, 19), is inserted as the left child of (20, 45), which triggers a skew operation
to maintain the AA Tree invariant, making (15, 19) the new root (Fig. 2(c)).
    The insertion of (25, 50) adds a right child to (20, 45) and requires a split
operation to restore balance, incrementing the level of (20, 45) and updating
the root’s maximum high value to 50. As additional intervals such as (10, 18),
(20, 30), and (25, 45) are inserted, the structure distinguishes between new low
62      K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati




Fig. 2. Inserting the (low, high) values: (20, 45), (15, 19), (25, 50), (10, 18), (20, 30),
(25, 45), and (34, 55).


values and duplicates. For duplicate low values (e.g., 20 and 25), the correspond-
ing high values are added to the node’s internal ConcurrentHashMap, preserving
the tree’s structure while increasing interval density within each node. The ﬁnal
interval, (34, 55), is inserted as the right child of (25, 50). Since this insertion does
                  Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree         63

not violate any AA Tree invariants, no rebalancing is necessary. This incremental
and localized insertion strategy ensures that the tree remains balanced through
lightweight skew and split operations while eﬃciently accommodating overlap-
ping intervals. By leveraging multi-valued nodes and limiting structural changes,
CIT minimizes synchronization overhead and improves memory locality, making
it well-suited for multi-threaded execution.
    Deletion in CIT also beneﬁts from this design. Figure 3 shows the deletion
process for intervals (10, 18) and (15, 19). When removing (10, 18), the node is
simply detached, and its child (15, 19) is reconnected to the root node. The
deletion of (15, 19) leads to a temporary imbalance, which is then corrected
through level adjustments and rebalancing operations. These corrective steps
are lightweight and follow the same principles as the AA Tree’s rotation-based
balancing.




Fig. 3. Deleting the (low, high) values: (10, 18) and (15, 19). Here, the red cross
indicates a logically deleted node that satisﬁes conditions for physical removal. (Color
ﬁgure online)


    A key advantage of the CIT deletion process lies in its lazy deletion strategy.
If a node still contains other high values, only the speciﬁc interval is removed from
the ConcurrentHashMap, leaving the node intact. If the node becomes empty,
it is logically marked for deletion but not immediately removed from the tree.
Instead, a dedicated background maintenance thread performs physical deletion
in a safe and non-blocking manner. This thread ensures that marked nodes
are removed only when they are leaves or have a single child, thus preserving
structural consistency without interfering with active operations.
    Overall, the design choices in CIT, including multi-valued nodes, relaxed
balancing, and deferred deletions, allow the data structure to maintain correct-
64      K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

ness while signiﬁcantly improving throughput and scalability under concurrent
workloads.


3     Concurrent Interval Tree
3.1   Node Structure


                          Table 1. Fields of a CIT Node

                   ﬁnal int low
                   volatile int max
                   volatile int level
                   volatile boolean mark
                   volatile concurrentHashMap<> instance
                   volatile Node left, right, parent, pred, succ
                   volatile ReentrantLock succLock
                   volatile ReentrantLock treeLock



Table 1 outlines the structure of a node in the CIT. Each ﬁeld is carefully
designed to support thread-safe operations and preserve the structural and
semantic correctness of the tree during concurrent accesses and modiﬁcations.
The low ﬁeld represents the lower bound of an interval and serves as the node’s
primary key for ordering within the tree. The max ﬁeld stores the highest upper
bound among all intervals in the subtree rooted at this node. This value is essen-
tial for eﬃciently pruning subtrees during overlap or range queries. The level
ﬁeld represents the node’s depth in the tree and is used to enforce balance
through skew and split operations.
    To facilitate eﬃcient deletions, each node includes a mark ﬂag indicating
whether the node is logically deleted. A value of true means the node is marked
for deferred deletion and will be physically removed later by a dedicated mainte-
nance thread. The instance ﬁeld holds a thread-safe ConcurrentHashMap that
maps each low endpoint to a set of high endpoints. This design enables a single
node to represent multiple overlapping intervals that share the same starting
point. The pointers left, right, and parent maintain the physical structure of
the tree, allowing standard traversal and modiﬁcation operations such as inser-
tion, deletion, and rebalancing. Furthermore, pred and succ are used to maintain
logical ordering between nodes based on order traversal. This logical ordering
supports eﬃcient operations that require range-aware navigation, such as range
queries and concurrent traversal.
    To ensure thread safety, each node includes two ﬁne-grained locks: succLock
and treeLock. The succLock protects the logical successor and predecessor
links, allowing concurrent threads to update the ordering information safely.
                 Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree     65

Meanwhile, the treeLock guards the physical structure during critical operations
such as insertions, deletions, or structural adjustments to maintain balance. By
combining logical ordering, multivalued node representations, and ﬁne-grained
locking mechanisms, the CIT node structure supports scalable, high-throughput
operations in multithreaded environments while maintaining correctness and low
contention.


3.2   Concurrent Operations on Interval Tree

The concurrent interval tree supports a rich set of operations essential for manag-
ing dynamic interval datasets in multithreaded environments. These operations
include getAllOverlaps, insert, delete, and range queries, all implemented on
the CAA Tree framework. This subsection focuses on the semantics and imple-
mentation of these operations, including their correctness guarantees through
linearization points [8,9].
    The getAllOverlaps operation retrieves all intervals that overlap with a given
query range (queryLow, queryHigh). An interval (low, high) overlaps with the
query if any of the following conditions are met: (i) partial left-aligned over-
lap where low ≤ queryLow ≤ high, (ii) partial right-aligned overlap where
queryLow ≤ low ≤ queryHigh, (iii) complete containment where the interval
fully encloses the query range with low ≤ queryLow and high ≥ queryHigh,
(iv) complete containment in reverse where the query range fully encloses the
interval with queryLow ≤ low and high ≤ queryHigh, or (v) exact match
where low = queryLow and high = queryHigh. The Algorithm 1 eﬃciently
detects these cases through selective traversal, reducing redundant checks and
improving throughput. These ﬁve cases represent the complete set of geometric
relationships in which an interval may overlap with a query range. The algorithm
eﬃciently detects all such cases through a combination of subtree pruning and
targeted traversal, eliminating redundant checks and improving throughput.
    Among all supported operations, getAllOverlaps provides the most compre-
hensive functionality. It generalizes both the contains and exists_Overlap meth-
ods. The contains operation can be viewed as a special case of getAllOverlaps
which checks for exact interval matches, while exists_Overlap terminates as soon
as the ﬁrst overlapping interval is found. Given the overlap in logic, and due to
space constraints, we present only the getAllOverlaps method in this section,
as it subsumes the others and captures the core traversal and overlap detection
strategies of the CIT.
getAllOverlaps operation: The getAllOverlaps method performs a recur-
sive traversal of the CIT to identify all intervals that overlap with a given query
range (queryLow, queryHigh), as shown in Algorithm 1. It is designed to be
selective and eﬃcient, using subtree pruning to minimize unnecessary traver-
sal and inspection. The procedure begins by checking if the current node is
nil, indicating the end of a branch, the recursion terminates immediately. This
avoids further computation and ensures that only relevant portions of the tree
are examined [6].
66       K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

Algorithm 1. Identifying All Overlapping Intervals
1: procedure getAllOverlaps(queryLow, queryHigh, current)
2:    if current = nil then
3:        return
4:    end if
5:    nodeLow ← current.low
                                                  Step 1: Check for Overlaps in the Current Node
 6:   if queryLow ≤ current.max and queryHigh ≥ nodeLow then
 7:       if current.instance = nil then
 8:           for each high ∈ current.instance.keySet() do
 9:              if queryHigh ≥ high then
10:                  Process the overlapping interval
11:               end if
12:            end for
13:        end if
14:    end if
                                         Step 2: Traverse Left Subtree Only If Overlap is Possible
15:    if current.lef t = nil and queryLow ≤ current.max then
16:        getAllOverlaps(queryLow, queryHigh, current.left)
17:    end if
                                       Step 3: Traverse Right Subtree Only If Overlap is Possible
18:    if current.right = nil and queryLow ≤ current.max then
19:        getAllOverlaps(queryLow, queryHigh, current.right)
20:    end if
21: end procedure



    Next, in Step 1, the algorithm checks whether the query range potentially
overlaps with the intervals stored at the current node. This is done by comparing
the query range with the node’s max and low values. If an overlap is possible, the
algorithm inspects all high values stored in the node’s instance map. For each
high endpoint high associated with the low value of the node, if queryHigh ≥
high, then the interval (current.low, high) is reported as overlapping.
    Step 2 focuses on exploring the left subtree. This traversal is conditional and
only performed if the query range may intersect with intervals stored on the left,
speciﬁcally if queryLow ≤ current.max. This condition prevents unnecessary
descent into subtrees that cannot possibly contain relevant intervals.
    Similarly, Step 3 handles traversal of the right subtree under the same prun-
ing condition. By evaluating subtree relevance using the max ﬁeld at each node,
the algorithm eﬀectively reduces the search space and improves throughput
under concurrent execution.
    This overlap detection strategy is highly concurrency friendly. It involves no
locking or modiﬁcation of the data structure, allowing multiple threads to per-
form read-only overlap queries without contention. Furthermore, the algorithm
naturally supports generalizations such as exact containment or partial matches,
making it versatile for a wide range of interval query applications.
Insert Operation: The insert operation in the CIT is designed to support
high throughput, concurrent insertions while maintaining correctness through
ﬁne-grained synchronization, logical ordering of nodes, and relaxed rebalancing.
The algorithm, presented in Algorithm 2, begins by locating the appropriate
position for insertion. This is achieved through a search operation that identiﬁes
the node whose low value matches the new interval or is closest to it. The parent
of this node is also recorded to support structural updates during insertion. Based
                     Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree                  67

 3:    parent ← node.parent
 4:    pred ← (node.low ≥ low)?node.pred : node
 5:    while not TrySuccLock(pred) do
 6:        continue                                        Retry until predecessor lock is acquired
 7:    end while
 8:    succ ← pred.succ
 9:    while not TrySuccLock(succ) do
10:         SuccUnlock(pred)                        Release predecessor lock if successor lock fails
11:         continue
12:     end while
13:     if low > pred.low and low ≤ succ.low then
14:         if succ.low=low then
15:             if node.mark=true then
16:                 node.mark ← f alse
17:                 SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
18:                 return true                              Linearization Point: Successful insert
19:             end if
20:             val1 ← node.instance.PutIfAbsent(high, high)
21:             if high > node.max then
22:                 node.max ← high
23:             end if
24:             SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
25:             if val1 = null and high=node.max then
26:                 UpdateMax1(node.parent)
27:             end if
28:             return (val1 = null)               Linearization Point: Interval added successfully
29:         else if (low < node.low and node.lef t = nil) or (low > node.low and node.right =
   nil) then
30:            SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
31:            continue                                                            Retry insertion
32:        else
33:            newN ode ← Node(low, high, nil)
34:            newN ode.succ ← succ
35:            newN ode.pred ← pred
36:            succ.pred ← newN ode
37:            pred.succ ← newN ode
38:            SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
39:            if low < node.low and node.lef t=nil then
40:                node.lef t ← newN ode
41:                newN ode.parent ← node
42:            else if low > node.low and node.right=nil then
43:                node.right ← newN ode
44:                newN ode.parent ← node
45:            end if
46:        end if
47:    else
48:        SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
49:        return false                                       Linearization Point: Insertion failed
50:    end if
51:    while true do
52:        node ← SkewAndSplit(node)
53:        if node=nil then
54:            break
55:        end if
56:        if node.parent = nil then
57:            node ← node.parent
58:        else
59:            break
60:        end if
61:    end while
62:    if high > newN ode.parent.max then
63:        UpdateMax1(newNode.parent)
64:    end if
65:    return true                                Linearization Point: Insert operation completes
66: end procedure

Algorithm 3. Update Max Values After Insertion
 1: procedure UpdateMax1(node)
 2:    previous ← null, parent ← null
 3:    lef tM ax, rightM ax ← 0
 4:    while true do
 5:        parent ← node.parent
 6:        if not TryLock(parent) then
 7:            continue
 8:        end if
 9:        if not TryLock(node) then
10:             Unlock(parent)
11:             continue
12:         end if
13:         lef tM ax ← node.lef t.max
14:         rightM ax ← node.right.max
15:         node.max ← max(lef tM ax, rightM ax)
16:         if previous = null then
17:             Unlock(previous)
18:         end if
19:         previous ← node
20:         node ← node.parent
21:         if previous.max ≤ node.max then
22:             break
23:         end if
24:     end while
25:     if previous = null then
26:         Unlock(previous)
27:     end if
28:     if IsLockedByCurrentThread(parent) then
29:         Unlock(parent)
30:     end if
31: end procedure



on the outcome of this search, the algorithm determines the correct predecessor
and successor nodes to which the new interval will be logically linked. To ensure
consistency and avoid interference from other concurrent threads, the algorithm
next acquires locks on both the predecessor and successor nodes. The locking
mechanism is optimistic and non-blocking, if the lock on the successor cannot
be obtained, the predecessor lock is released, and the procedure is retried. This
retry strategy avoids deadlocks and minimizes contention in high-concurrency
scenarios.
    Once the locks are acquired, the algorithm checks whether the successor
already contains a node with the same low value. If such a node exists and is logi-
cally marked for deletion, it is reactivated by setting its mark ﬁeld to false. This
step is considered a linearization point, as the previously deleted node becomes
immediately visible and valid for future operations. If the node is active, the
algorithm attempts to insert the high value into the node’s ConcurrentHashMap
using putIfAbsent. This data structure allows multiple high values to coexist
under the same low key, thereby avoiding redundant node creation and eﬃciently
representing overlapping intervals. If the insertion is successful, the node’s max
ﬁeld is updated if the new high value exceeds the existing maximum. This suc-
cessful update marks another linearization point, as the interval becomes visible
to other threads.
                 Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree     69

    If the low value does not already exist in the tree, a new node is created.
The node is initialized with the given interval and is logically linked by updating
the succ and pred pointers of its neighbors. Once these links are updated, the
locks are released. The new node is then physically inserted into the tree by
updating either the left or right child pointer of its parent, depending on its
key. The logical linking of the node to its in-order neighbors constitutes another
linearization point, as the node is now visible for range-based operations.
    Following insertion, the AA Tree may become temporarily imbalanced. To
restore its invariants, the algorithm invokes a sequence of skew and split opera-
tions, as prescribed in the CAA Tree structure [6]. These operations rebalance
the tree using a simpliﬁed strategy that avoids complex rotations and supports
concurrent updates more eﬃciently than traditional self-balancing trees. After
structural balance is restored, the algorithm veriﬁes whether the inserted high
value is greater than the maximum ﬁeld of the parent node. If so, the updateMax1
procedure is invoked, as shown in Algorithm 3 to propagate the new maximum
value up the tree. This update is carried out incrementally and employs ﬁne-
grained locking to reduce contention and avoid blocking concurrent operations.
The propagation stops as soon as the max value of a parent node is found to be
larger than or equal to the current value, ensuring minimal overhead.
    The insert operation ends with true, indicating that the interval has been
successfully added to the tree. This return point serves as the ﬁnal linearization
point, after which the interval is fully integrated and visible to all concurrent
queries and updates. Together, the key linearization points in the insert pro-
cedure occur when a logically deleted node is reactivated, when a high value
is successfully inserted into an existing node, when a new node is created and
logically linked, and when the operation completes successfully. The algorithm
design eﬀectively balances correctness, responsiveness, and scalability, making it
suitable for concurrent workloads with a long interval.
Remove Operation: The remove operation in the CIT is responsible for delet-
ing a speciﬁc interval (low, high) while preserving the correctness and concur-
rency guarantees of the tree. Since a single node in CIT may contain multiple high
values for the same low value, a successful removal often involves only deleting a
high value from the node’s internal map rather than removing the entire node.
Structural updates are minimized and balancing is preserved through incremen-
tal adjustments of auxiliary ﬁelds, such as the maximum value. The algorithm,
shown in Algorithm 4, is designed to support ﬁne-grained concurrency through
localized locking and logical deletion.
    The operation begins by locating the node corresponding to the speciﬁed low
value using a search procedure. If the node is not found, or if the high value
does not exist within the node’s ConcurrentHashMap, the operation terminates
immediately by returning false. If the target node is located, it is locked to
prevent concurrent modiﬁcations. This initial step ensures thread safety and
consistency while examining and potentially modifying node content.
    After acquiring a lock on the node, the algorithm proceeds to establish logical
ordering by identifying and locking the node’s predecessor and successor. These
70       K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

 1: procedure Remove(low, high)
 2:    node ← nil, parent ← nil, node1 ← nil
 3:    pred, succ, Lnode ← nil
 4:    while true do
 5:       node ← Search(low)
 6:       if not TryLock(node) then
 7:           continue
 8:       end if
 9:       if node.low = low and ContainsKey(node.instance, high) then
10:            pred ← (node.low ≥ low)?node.pred : node
11:            if not TrySuccLock(pred) then
12:                TreeUnlock(node)
13:                continue
14:            end if
15:            succ ← pred.succ
16:            if low > pred.low and low ≤ succ.low then
17:                if not TrySuccLock(succ) then
18:                    SuccUnlock(pred), TreeUnlock(node)
19:                    continue
20:                end if
21:                if succ.low = node.low then
22:                    SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred), TreeUnlock(node)
23:                    return false                          Linearization point: Interval not found
24:                end if
25:                node ← succ
26:                f lag ← Remove(node.instance, high)
27:                if not IsEmpty(node.instance) then
28:                    if high = node.max then
29:                        node.max ← FindLargestValue(node.instance)
30:                    end if
31:                end if
32:                if Size(node.instance) = 0 then
33:                    node.mark ←                       Linearization point: Node logically deleted
34:                end if
35:                SuccUnlock(succ), SuccUnlock(pred)
36:                TreeUnlock(node)
37:                if high > node.max then
38:                    UpdateMax2(node.parent, node.max)
39:                end if
40:                return true                    Linearization point: Interval successfully removed
41:            else
42:                SuccUnlock(pred), TreeUnlock(node)
43:                return false                 Linearization point: Interval not found or reordered
44:            end if
45:        else
46:            TreeUnlock(node)
47:            return false                              Linearization point: Target node not found
48:        end if
49:     end while
50: end procedure



locks are acquired in sequence to avoid deadlock. If either lock acquisition fails,
any previously acquired locks are released and the process is retried. Once both
locks are successfully acquired, the algorithm veriﬁes that the successor node
still matches the expected low value to prevent inconsistencies due to concurrent
modiﬁcations. If this check fails, the operation aborts and releases all locks.
     If the successor node contains the desired low value and the high value is
found within its instance map, the high value is removed. If additional high values
remain in the node after removal, and if the removed high value was equal to the
node’s max ﬁeld, the node’s max value is updated using the largest remaining
                  Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree   71

high value. If the instance map becomes empty, the node is marked for deletion
by setting its mark ﬂag to true, indicating that the node is logically deleted but
not yet physically removed. The marking step constitutes a key linearization
point, signifying that the interval is no longer visible to other threads. After
updating or marking the node, the algorithm releases all acquired locks to allow
concurrent operations to proceed. If the removed high value was the maximum
in its subtree, the algorithm invokes the updateMax2 procedure (Algorithm 5)
to propagate the new maximum value up the tree. This function iteratively
moves up the parent chain, locking each node and updating its max ﬁeld only
when required. The propagation halts as soon as a parent node’s existing max
value is larger than the newly computed one. This lazy propagation technique
reduces contention and ensures eﬃcient maintenance of the max ﬁeld across the
tree’s hierarchy. Once all updates have been applied, the operation concludes by
returning true, indicating that the interval was successfully removed. If at any
point the interval is not found or a locking failure occurs, the operation safely
aborts and returns false. These return points serve as linearization boundaries
that deﬁne the moment the remove operation takes eﬀect or fails.


Algorithm 5. Update Max Values After Deletion
 1: procedure UpdateMax2(node, new_max)
 2:    previous ← null, parent ← null
 3:    lef tM ax, rightM ax, high ← node.max
 4:    while true do
 5:        parent ← node.parent
 6:        if not TryLock(parent) then
 7:            continue
 8:        end if
 9:        if not TryLock(node) then
10:             Unlock(parent)
11:             continue
12:         end if
13:         node.max ← new_max
14:         lef tM ax ← node.lef t.max
15:         rightM ax ← node.right.max
16:         node.max ← max(lef tM ax, rightM ax)
17:         if previous = null then
18:             Unlock(previous)
19:         end if
20:         previous ← node
21:         node ← node.parent
22:         if high < node.max then
23:             break
24:         end if
25:     end while
26:     if previous = null then
27:         Unlock(previous)
28:     end if
29:     if IsLockedByCurrentThread(parent) then
30:         Unlock(parent)
31:     end if
32: end procedure



    Importantly, physical deletion of logically marked nodes is deferred to a ded-
icated thread for background maintenance. This thread continuously traverses
72      K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

the tree in logical order and safely removes marked nodes only when they are
leaves or have a single child, as discussed in prior work on the CAA Tree [6]. This
deferred cleanup mechanism minimizes contention and avoids interference with
primary operations such as insertions or queries, allowing the tree to maintain
structural integrity and responsiveness in highly concurrent environments.
    The remove operation introduces several critical linearization points through-
out its execution. These include the moment the function determines that an
interval is not present and returns false, the point at which the high value is
successfully removed from the ConcurrentHashMap, the act of logically mark-
ing a node for deletion, and the propagation of updated max values via the
updateMax2 method. The ﬁnal linearization point occurs when the function suc-
cessfully completes and returns true. By combining logical deletion, ﬁne-grained
locking, and asynchronous cleanup, the remove operation ensures both correct-
ness and scalability for interval deletions in multithreaded settings.


4     Correctness
The correctness of the CIT is established by inheriting the synchronization and
consistency principles of the underlying CAA framework. All core operations—
insert, remove, and getAllOverlaps—adhere to thread-safe execution and lin-
earizability guarantees derived from the CAA’s structured locking and logical
ordering.

4.1   Synchronization
CIT reuses the ﬁne-grained locking model of CAA, which separates logical order-
ing from physical structure using dual locks: succLock for logical links and
treeLock for structural modiﬁcations. This design minimizes contention and
supports parallelism. As in CAA, locks are acquired in a ﬁxed order (prede-
cessor, successor, then node) to prevent deadlocks. Synchronization is further
aided by CIT’s use of a thread-safe ConcurrentHashMap to manage multiple
high endpoints per node without introducing locking overhead. Lazy deletion is
inherited as well: deleted nodes are marked using a volatile mark ﬂag and physi-
cally removed later by a background maintenance thread, ensuring non-blocking
updates.

4.2   Linearizability
CIT deﬁnes clear linearization points for all operations, many of which are anno-
tated directly in Algorithms 2 and 4. For insert, the operation is linearized
when a logically deleted node is reactivated, when a new high value is success-
fully inserted into the map, or when a new node is linked into the logical order.
In remove, linearization occurs when the high value is removed, when the node
is logically marked deleted, or when the operation returns failure after valida-
tion. The getAllOverlaps operation is read-only and lock-free, and its traversal
                 Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree    73

over immutable ﬁelds (low, max, instance) ensures safe concurrent execution,
maintaining linearizability without synchronization.
   Overall, correctness in CIT is ensured by reusing CAA’s proven concurrency
control mechanisms and extending them with safe, scalable handling of interval-
speciﬁc logic.


5   Experimental Evaluation
We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed CIT to assess its per-
formance under diverse workloads and compare it with leading concurrent inter-
val tree implementations. The experiments were designed to capture through-
put, memory eﬃciency, and energy usage across varying dataset sizes and thread
counts.
    The evaluation used input datasets containing 2 × 105 , 2 × 106 , and 2 ×
10 intervals, all generated using a uniform distribution with Java’s built-in
  7

random() method. The experiments were carried out on a dual socket Intel(R)
Xeon(R) Platinum 8260 server with 48 cores (96 threads), 512 GB of memory and




Fig. 4. The average throughput of concurrent interval search trees across diﬀerent
workloads and problem sizes by varying the number of threads. Higher is better.
74     K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati

Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, running Java implementations built using OpenJDK 19.0.2.
To ensure the reliability of our benchmark results, we intentionally limited our
measurements to 64 threads, despite the hardware’s ability to support up to 96
simultaneous threads. This decision was driven by the need to minimize the inﬂu-
ence of confounding factors such as operating system-level interference, artifacts
introduced by hyperthreading, and various sources of measurement noise, such
as increased resource contention, cache thrashing, and unpredictable scheduling
overhead. By capping the thread count, we aimed to create a more controlled
and reproducible testing environment, allowing our results to more accurately
reﬂect the performance rather than being skewed by system-level artifacts.
    To benchmark the performance of CIT using CAA, we compared it against
three state-of-the-art concurrent interval tree implementations referenced in
Chap. 5, Sect. 5.5 of this thesis [7]: (i) CAVL, a concurrent AVL tree using
logical ordering [10], (ii) CTreap, a concurrent treap combining BST and heap
properties [11], (iii) CBST, a contention-friendly binary search tree with hand-
over-hand locking [12].
    While more recent designs have emerged—for example Lock-Free Augmented
Trees (2024) that provide augmentation for range queries and order statistics
in a lock-free fashion [19], Wait-free Trees with Asymptotically-Eﬃcient Range
Queries (2023) supporting count-in-range operations [20], and EEMARQ (2022)
oﬀering linearizable range queries with lock-free reclamation [21]—these either
do not directly handle interval-based queries or lack publicly available imple-
mentations for interval trees with overlapping intervals. Therefore, the chosen
baselines remain the most relevant and reproducible for evaluating CIT.
Workload Distributions: We evaluated performance using three representa-
tive workloads, each denoted by the format XC-YI-ZD, where C, I, and D cor-
respond to the respective proportions of Contains, Insert, and Delete opera-
tions. The selected workloads (30C-35I-35D, 50C-25I-25D and 90C-9I-1D ) span
a spectrum of access patterns, ranging from balanced read-write distributions
to highly read-dominated scenarios. This diversity allows us to simulate varying
contention proﬁles and stress diﬀerent aspects of system behavior. By employ-
ing these standardized mixes consistently across all performance and system-
level evaluations, we ensure a comprehensive and comparative assessment of the
system under distinct operational conditions.
Throughput Analysis: Throughput, measured in millions of operations per
second (MOPS), serves as the primary performance metric. Figure 4 reports the
average throughput achieved by each implementation across multiple workloads
and dataset sizes. CIT consistently outperforms the other structures, particularly
at higher thread counts, due to its eﬃcient synchronization model and relaxed
balancing strategy.
    The performance advantages of CIT, built on the CAA tree, stem from three
key design choices. First, the use of multivalued nodes allows multiple inter-
vals that share the same low endpoint to be stored compactly, signiﬁcantly
reducing tree height and frequency of rebalancing. Second, its internal use of
ConcurrentHashMap enables fast, atomic access to high values within a node,
                 Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree      75




Fig. 5. The average number of cache misses per operation (ANCMP) across diﬀerent
workloads and problem sizes. Lower is better.


allowing frequent contains and delete operations to complete in constant time.
Third, the lazy deletion mechanism delegates physical removals to a background
maintenance thread, ensuring that insertions and queries can proceed without
disruption. These optimizations lead to a highly scalable structure. On a dataset
with 2 × 105 intervals, CIT achieves a 22.87× speedup over its sequential base-
line with 64 threads. Against competing implementations, it delivers an average
speedup of 1.3× over CAVL, 1.5× over CTreap, and 1.68× over CBST. These
results demonstrate the resilience of the CIT in high contention and its suitability
for concurrent interval workloads.
Analysis of Cache Misses: The behavior of the cache plays a critical role in
the performance of concurrent data structures. Poor cache eﬃciency can intro-
duce signiﬁcant memory latency, especially when multiple threads access shared
resources. We employed perf tool [14] to monitor cache references and cache
misses. As a metric for cache eﬃciency, we used the Average Number of Cache
Misses Per Operation (ANCMP). As shown in Fig. 5, CIT records fewer cache
misses across all workloads, beneﬁting from improved spatial locality through
compact node layouts and shorter traversal paths.
76     K. K. Attinagaramu and P. Alapati




Fig. 6. The average performance per joule (PPJ) across diﬀerent workloads and prob-
lem sizes, varying the number of threads from 1 to 64. Higher is better.


Analysis of Energy Consumption: Beyond throughput, we also evalu-
ated the energy eﬃciency of each implementation. Energy measurements were
obtained using the jRAPL framework [17,18], which provides access to processor-
level energy counters via Intel’s RAPL interface. We report energy eﬃciency
in terms of Performance Per Joule (PPJ), deﬁned as the number of operations
executed per unit of energy. As illustrated in Fig. 6, CIT achieves higher energy
eﬃciency than competing designs, due to its reduced contention, lightweight
synchronization, and compact node representation. The experimental ﬁndings
reinforce the eﬀectiveness of the CIT design, built on top of the CAA tree. This
streamlined execution delivers high throughput, improved cache location, and
better energy eﬃciency across various workloads and input sizes. These char-
acteristics make CIT a strong candidate for real-time interval management in
high-performance multithreaded systems.


6    Conclusion
This work presents the design and implementation of a CIT, built upon the
Concurrent AA Tree (CAA Tree), to eﬃciently support interval-based queries
                  Scalable and Contention-Resilient Concurrent Interval Tree         77

in multithreaded environments. By incorporating a relaxed balancing strategy,
lazy deletion mechanisms, and a multivalued node structure, the CIT minimizes
synchronization overhead and contention while improving spatial locality and
cache eﬃciency. A dedicated background maintenance thread handles deferred
physical deletions, allowing insertions and deletions to proceed with minimal
disruption to concurrent operations.
    Experimental results demonstrate that the CAA-based interval tree con-
sistently outperforms leading concurrent data structures such as CAVL trees,
CTreaps, and CBSTs in throughput, cache eﬃciency, and energy usage across
diverse workloads. The design exhibits excellent scalability and maintains its
performance advantages even as the number of threads increases, making it well
suited for modern multicore systems. As future work, we plan to perform abla-
tion studies to quantify the contribution of each design choice and to evaluate the
structure under skewed interval distributions (e.g., Gaussian, Zipﬁan), providing
further insight into the robustness of CIT across real-world workloads.
