       Abstract. The integration of blockchain and edge computing oﬀers a
       promising solution to key challenges in Internet of Things (IoT) appli-
       cations, including data security, transmission reliability, and computility
       demands. This paper focuses on the total system revenue in IoT applica-
       tion scenarios and proposes a resource allocation method for blockchain
       networks based on edge computing, which mitigates resource waste by
       adjusting block rewards. First, an IoT-blockchain architecture supported
       by the edge server’s computilities is proposed. The revenue models for
       IoT devices and the edge server incorporating the Gompertz function
       are constructed, and the resource allocation problem is formulated as
       a nonlinear programming (NLP) with the objective of maximizing the
       total system revenue. The Gompertz function eﬀectively characterizes
       the relationship between block rewards and total computilities, thereby
       suppressing resource waste caused by IoT devices’ excessive pursuit of
       block rewards. Then, to address the challenge of solving this NLP prob-
       lem, an improved particle swarm optimization algorithm based on chaotic
       dynamics and adaptive inertia parameters (CAPSO) is designed. The
       introduction of the Logistic chaotic mapping enhances the algorithm’s
       global search ability, while the adaptive inertia weights improve conver-
       gence speed and solution accuracy. The experimental results demonstrate
       that the proposed method outperforms three traditional heuristic algo-
       rithms, achieving both higher system revenue and faster convergence.

       Keywords: Edge computing · Blockchain network · Internet of
       Things · Resource allocation · Chaotic mapping · Particle swarm
       optimization


1    Introduction
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a vast system that integrates various objects,
devices, services, technologies, and individuals through the Internet. By enabling
interconnectivity, it facilitates data communication, information sharing, and
collaborative interactions among all things, thereby optimizing resource alloca-
tion, improving production models, and enhancing user experiences. Currently,
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 79–100, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_5
80     Q. Su et al.

IoT has been widely adopted in smart city applications such as transportation,
ﬁnance, healthcare, agriculture, and logistics [1]. However, with the surge in
the number of IoT devices and the amount of data transmitted between them,
IoT applications face many challenges in terms of data integrity, transmission
reliability, and other aspects [2,3].
    Blockchain is inherently a tamper-proof, secure, and decentralized distributed
ledger. By integrating distributed storage, consensus mechanisms, and crypto-
graphic techniques, it oﬀers robust solutions to data security challenges in IoT
applications [4,5]. As a result, the convergence of IoT and blockchain has become
an emerging trend across various domains, including ﬁnance, supply chain man-
agement, healthcare, and public governance [6].
    Consensus mechanisms represent a core technology of blockchain. Current
IoT-blockchain applications predominantly adopt Proof of Work (PoW) as the
consensus algorithm, where blockchain nodes must complete substantial compu-
tational tasks to compete for the right to generate new blocks. However, when
IoT devices participate in blockchain networks, their constrained computilities
and limited battery capacity struggle to support PoW’s operational demands.
    Fortunately, the widely favored edge computing can alleviate the computa-
tional limitations of IoT devices to some extent by providing necessary compu-
tational resources through task oﬄoading at locations close to these devices [7].
When confronted with substantial resource demands from numerous IoT devices,
eﬀective resource allocation of edge servers becomes crucial. First, IoT devices
receive corresponding cryptocurrency rewards when obtaining block creation
rights and writing transactions into blocks. To prevent IoT devices from being
addicted to block rewards and causing computility waste, the resource alloca-
tion method should reasonably control the block rewards. Second, while receiving
rewards, IoT devices must also pay corresponding fees to edge servers that pro-
vide computational resources. The resource allocation method should maximize
total system revenue while meeting IoT devices’ resource requests as much as
possible. Existing research has made progress in winner determination, resource
pricing, social welfare maximization, and cost minimization in resource alloca-
tion [8,9], but few studies have introduced reward control mechanisms to mitigate
resource wastage in this process.
    Based on the above discussion, this paper investigates the resource allocation
problem for maximizing system revenue in IoT-blockchain application scenarios
and proposes an edge computing-based resource allocation method for blockchain
networks. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

– We construct an edge computing-powered IoT-blockchain architecture and
  formulate the resource allocation problem as a nonlinear programming model
  for total system revenue maximization. Within the revenue models for both
  IoT devices and the edge server, we incorporate the Gompertz function [10]
  from economics to characterize the relationship between block rewards and
  total computilities. This approach eﬀectively mitigates resource waste from
  excessive reward-seeking by IoT devices by dynamically adjusting block
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network       81

  rewards through the Gompertz function’s ﬂexible response to computational
  demands.
– We design an enhanced particle swarm optimization algorithm based on
  chaotic dynamics [11] and adaptive parameters (CAPSO) to solve the resource
  allocation problem. Speciﬁcally, the Logistic mapping function from chaotic
  dynamics is introduced to enhance the algorithm’s global search ability, while
  the adaptive inertia weights are employed to improve both convergence speed
  and solution accuracy. This tailored integration provides a speciﬁc solution
  to the NLP challenges in IoT-blockchain resource allocation, distinguishing it
  from generic swarm intelligence methods. Comparative experiments demon-
  strate that our algorithm achieves faster computation speed and yields higher
  system rewards compared to conventional heuristic approaches.

    The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews
related work on IoT resource allocation, blockchain-enabled and edge computing-
assisted resource optimization. In Sect. 3, we present the system architecture,
develop revenue models for both IoT devices and the edge server, and formulate
the resource allocation problem as a mathematical programming. Section 4 pro-
poses an improved particle swarm optimization algorithm incorporating chaotic
dynamics and adaptive parameters, with detailed explanations of the algorithmic
procedures. Section 5 evaluates the performance of our approach through com-
parative experiments with three heuristic algorithms. Finally, Sect. 6 concludes
the work and outlines directions for future research.


2   Related Works

The rapid development of IoT technology has brought signiﬁcant convenience to
users while simultaneously elevating expectations for quality of service (QoS). In
this context, eﬃcient resource management and scheduling has become a critical
approach to fulﬁll these growing demands. Existing research has demonstrated
substantial progress in resource allocation optimization across various IoT appli-
cation domains, particularly in Internet of Vehicles (IoV), smart healthcare sys-
tems, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks, and industrial IoT environ-
ments. Liang et al. [12] formulated the resource allocation problem in IoV as a
semi-Markov decision process incorporating both a resource reservation strategy
and a secondary resource allocation mechanism, and proposed a dedicated hier-
archical reinforcement learning algorithm. Song et al. [13] proposed a secure and
eﬃcient fog-assisted wearable healthcare IoT system, which leverages physical
layer security techniques and quantum-inspired resource allocation to enhance
the conﬁdentiality and performance of the system. Chen et al. [14] investigated
the UAV deployment problem in UAV-assisted IoT networks with diverse QoS
requirements for IoT devices, and proposed a QoS-guaranteed joint power allo-
cation and data rate maximization placement scheme. Abdullah et al. [15] stud-
ied the resource allocation and task oﬄoading problem in satellite-assisted IoT
networks, considering energy eﬃciency, network throughput, and fairness, and
82     Q. Su et al.

developed an outer approximation algorithm to obtain an -optimum solution.
Chakraborty et al. [16] investigated the QoS-aware resource allocation problem
in industrial IoT-enabled edge networks to ensure low delay, and high revenue
for executing federated learning (FL). Then authors proposed a coalition game-
and utility theory-based scheme to ﬁnd the optimal solutions. The above studies
have focused more on the performance of IoT systems, such as energy consump-
tion, latency, and resource utilization, while lacking discussions on the security
of data and applications.
    Given the vast number of heterogeneous IoT devices with varying capa-
bilities and security levels, device interconnection and data transmission face
numerous potential security risks, including leakage of sensitive medical and
social data, as well as tampering and forgery of critical engineering and com-
mercial information [17]. Establishing trust among massive IoT devices in ubiq-
uitous access networks to ensure lifecycle security and privacy is an urgent chal-
lenge for various IoT applications. Blockchain technology, fortunately, provides
a secure and trustworthy environment for these requirements. Zhang et al. [18]
proposed a blockchain-based FL framework to support trustworthy and reliable
FL paradigms in IoT systems. Their approach incorporates an accuracy-driven
incentive mechanism and a committee-based participant selection scheme, along
with a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-enabled resource allocation algorithm.
Liang et al. [19] investigated the cost optimization for vehicular users in inte-
grated IoT systems through vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) and vehicle-to-vehicle
(V2V) transmission tasks, and proposed a blockchain-based vehicular identity
authentication algorithm and a delay-weighted fair bandwidth allocation algo-
rithm. Hou et al. [20] proposed a distributed Gale-Shapley spectrum allocation
algorithm based on matching theory, which addresses the complexity of battle-
ﬁeld frequency usage and the high requirements for real-time and mobility. The
proposed method features blockchain-enabled decentralized management and
smart contract-based automated allocation. Chen et al. [21] proposed an intel-
ligent computation oﬄoading scheme for joint resource allocation and control
in big-data IoT scenarios, in which a blockchain-based fair incentive mechanism
and a dual actor-critic neural network structure with inverse gradient updates
are designed.
    The aforementioned studies reveal that due to the resource limitations of IoT
devices and the high computility demands of blockchain node deployment, tasks
often need to be completed with the assistance from entities with relatively abun-
dant resources. The integration of blockchain and edge computing can realize reli-
able and incentive-aware access to distributed edge resources, while eﬀectively
coordinate and control the interaction behaviors between IoT devices [22,23]. To
achieve resource allocation and privacy preservation in KubeEdge-based edge
computing, Lingayya et al. [24] designed a privacy-preserving, multi-layered
blockchain-enabled data aggregation mechanism that ensures secure and trans-
parent transactions while enhancing trust in dynamic edge environments. Zhang
et al. [25] investigated computation oﬄoading in a mobile edge computing-
enabled blockchain system involving one edge computing allocation center, mul-
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network         83

tiple edge service providers, and numerous miners. They proposed a two-phase
oﬄoading strategy combining contract theory with matching game to incentivize
participation from both edge service providers and miners in market transac-
tions. Wang et al. [26] proposed a UAV-assisted MEC network architecture and
a comprehensive data processing ﬂow, where UAVs collaborate with base stations
to serve as edge servers and blockchain nodes. The study addressed an optimiza-
tion problem minimizing total data processing time by jointly considering UAV
positioning, data oﬄoading, and resource allocation. Zhang et al. [27] investi-
gated a D2D-assisted edge oﬄoading strategy for blockchain mining tasks. To
mitigate consensus failure risks caused by device mobility, the movement trajec-
tories were predicted. To determine the optimal resource demands and pricing,
the interaction between miners and suppliers was modeled as a Stackelberg game.
Xie et al. [28] introduced edge computing to enhance blockchain’s computational
capabilities, and proposed a breakeven-based truthful double auction mechanism
and a critical value-based double auction mechanism to handle supply-demand
matching and resource allocation respectively.
    To conclude, research on integrating blockchain with edge computing in IoT
applications can be summarized into the following categories: blockchain pro-
vides a truthful platform for edge resource deployment and transactions, edge
computing oﬀers suﬃcient computilities for blockchain consensus mechanisms,
and block reward-based incentive mechanisms promote the maximization of sys-
tem utility or social welfare in edge resource allocation. Inspired by this, we pro-
pose an edge resource allocation method with controlled block rewards. Unlike
existing studies that utilize block rewards to encourage IoT devices and edge
servers to participate in trading activities, this paper applies the Gompertz func-
tion for the ﬁrst time to dynamically adjust block rewards according to computil-
ities, thereby preventing resource waste caused by IoT devices over-requesting
resources due to reward addiction. The resource waste here refers to the failure
of over-requesting resources to exert their eﬀectiveness, which diﬀers from the
resource eﬃciency mentioned in previous studies. Resource eﬃciency empha-
sizes high resource utilization and minimal idle resources. Furthermore, while
chaotic mapping has been widely applied in medical diagnosis, image encryp-
tion, power systems, and engineering design [11], its application in blockchain
networks for edge resource allocation to IoT devices remains unexplored. We
employ the simplest chaotic mapping to enhance the diversity of solutions dur-
ing resource allocation, helping particles escape local optima and potentially
accelerating convergence.


3   System Modeling and Problem Formulation
In this section, we ﬁrst present the system architecture of the IoT-blockchain
network, then develop revenue models for both IoT devices and the edge server,
and ﬁnally formulate the resource allocation problem as a nonlinear program-
ming model aimed at system revenue maximization. All notations used are sum-
marized in Table 1.

3.1    System Architecture

We consider an edge computing-powered IoT-blockchain system as illustrated in
Fig. 1. The system comprises a set of lightweight blockchain nodes {1, 2, ..., N }
consisting of N IoT devices, and an edge server deployed in proximity to these
nodes. The IoT devices communicate with the edge server via wireless networks
for data transmission. Each IoT device maintains a local copy of the blockchain
ledger, with all distributed ledgers synchronized through a consensus algorithm.
    The system operation proceeds through four sequential phases:

(1) Resource request. Due to the relatively limited computational capabilities of
    IoT devices, when performing PoW, in addition to their local computilities
    li ,where i ∈ {1, 2, ..., N }), they also need to request additional computational
                     A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network       85




           Fig. 1. The edge computing-powered IoT-blockchain system.


    resources from the edge server. Let qi = {ri , di } denote the request tuple
    submitted by IoT device i to the edge server, where ri represents the amount
    of computational resources requested, and di is the unit price device i is
    willing to pay for the resources.
(2) Resource allocation. The edge server acts as both a resource provider and
    a decision-maker. Upon receiving requests from IoT devices, it determines
    the resource allocation strategy based on the overall revenue of the system.
    Let xi be the decision variable representing the amount of computational
    resources allocated by the edge server to IoT device i. To avoid resource
    wastage, the allocated resources should not exceed the amount requested by
    device i, that is,
                             0 ≤ xi ≤ ri , ∀i ∈ 1, 2, ..., N .                (1)
    Second, the total resources allocated to all IoT devices are constrained by
    the edge server’s available capacity S R , satisfying
                                    N
                                          xi ≤ S R .                          (2)
                                    i=1

    Furthermore, in large-scale systems, the aggregate resource requests from
    IoT devices surrounding the edge server typically far exceed its resource
    capacity, thus yielding
                                    N
                                          ri > S R .                          (3)
                                    i=1
(3) Generating new blocks and recording transaction. After obtaining resources,
    IoT devices perform PoW. The device that earns the block qualiﬁcation
86        Q. Su et al.

    writes transactions into a new block and broadcasts it across the blockchain
    network. Subsequently, all IoT devices update their respective copies of the
    blockchain ledger accordingly.
(4) Paying fees. Upon completion of these procedures, each IoT device pays the
    edge server two types of fees: the resource cost di · xi , and its shared portion
    of the block reward (i.e., the mining reward) BiES = Bi · (1 − ρi ), where ρi is
    the proportion of the block reward retained by IoT device i, and Bi denotes
    the reward earned by IoT device i for generating a new block.

   The resource allocation problem addressed in this paper aims to maximize
the total system revenue. Next, we will elaborate on the revenue models for both
IoT devices and the edge server.


3.2     Revenue Modeling for IoT Devices

The revenue Ri of IoT device i is the diﬀerence between its income and expen-
diture. The income consists of i’s block reward, while the expenditure includes
not only the two types of fees described in Step (4) of Sect. 3.1 but also the
costs related to energy and resources incurred by the device’s own computilities.
Let πi be the cost coeﬃcient, then the expenditure and revenue of device i are
respectively given by:
                           Ci = di · xi + BiES + πi · li ,                   (4)
                                    Ri = Bi − Ci .                               (5)
      Therefore, the total revenue of all IoT devices in the system can be expressed
as:
                                            N
                                   RIoT =         Ri .                           (6)
                                            i=1

      Next, we provide a detailed discussion on the block reward Bi for IoT device
i.
    The size of a block is related to the number of transactions recorded in it. Let
bi be the size of the new block generated by IoT device i, and si be the number
of transactions recorded in the new block. Their relationship can be expressed
by a linear function:
                                    bi = κ · si + a.                             (7)
Here, κ is the correlation coeﬃcient, representing the contribution of each trans-
action to the block size, and a denotes the size of the ﬁxed portion of the block
structure, including metadata.
    In practical applications, even if an IoT device generates a new block, it does
not guarantee that the block will be successfully added to the blockchain. When
a node generates a new block, it broadcasts the block to the entire network so
that other nodes can verify it and update their ledgers. However, multiple nodes
may generate blocks simultaneously, in which case the network determines which
block is added to the main chain based on propagation delays and information
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network        87

synchronization. The Poisson distribution is widely used in the literature to
model block generation intervals and orphan block rates in blockchain systems
[29]. Consequently, we assume that the process of an IoT device generating a new
block and successfully adding it to the blockchain follows a Poisson distribution.
The probability of success is pi = e−λ·θ(bi ) , where λ is the Poisson distribution
parameter, θ(bi ) = σ · bi denotes the block propagation time, and σ is a given
delay factor. The parameter λ encompasses uncertain factors like network con-
gestion and node computility distribution, while the propagation delay θ(bi ) is
the core determinant of this probability. The larger the block, the slower it prop-
agates, and the higher the risk of being replaced by other competing blocks (i.e.,
becoming an orphan block). Therefore, the probability pi eﬀectively captures the
risk that a block generated by IoT device i fails to be appended to the chain due
to propagation delay.
    Since the value of cryptocurrency is inﬂuenced by various factors, it is chal-
lenging to model the variation in block rewards using precise mathematical for-
mulas. Therefore, this paper focuses solely on the relationship between block
rewards and the total computilities participating in PoW. Generally, the more
computilities is used, the greater the rewards provided by the system. However,
this may lead IoT devices to become overly ﬁxated on rewards, continuously
requesting resources from the edge server, thereby causing resource contention
and waste. To address this, we introduce the Gompertz function from economics
to describe the functional relationship between block rewards and the total min-
ing computilities:
                                                 −γ·φ
                               g(φ) = α · e−β·e       ,                         (8)
where φ represents the total computilities participating in PoW, i.e., φ =
   N          N
   i=1 li +   i=1 xi . The function g(φ) denotes the reward distibution varying
with φ, with a value range of [0,1]. Parameters α, β and γ are positive con-
stants, where α represents the upper limit of the reward distribution ratio (i.e.,
the maximum proportion of rewards the system is willing to allocate), β controls
the oﬀset at which the reward begins to increase signiﬁcantly, and γ governs the
growth rate of the reward with respect to computility, respectively.
    The Gompertz function is traditionally employed to model “S-shaped” phe-
nomena, such as economic and population growth, where growth rates ini-
tially accelerate, then decelerate, and ﬁnally saturate [10]. This behavior closely
matches our reward control objective: initial investments in computility yield sig-
niﬁcant reward growth to incentivize participation, but as the total computilities
expand, the reward growth diminishes and asymptotically approaches the upper
limit α. This mechanism eﬀectively curbs the ineﬃcient resource investment that
results from an excessive pursuit of rewards.
    In conclusion, the block reward for IoT device i can be derived as:

an improved particle swarm optimization algorithm to eﬃciently obtain near-
optimal solutions.


4    Improved Particle Swarm Optimization Algorithm

Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) has been widely adopted for solving opti-
mization problems owing to its simple implementation and rapid search speed.
Nevertheless, this method has notable limitations including susceptibility to local
optima convergence and signiﬁcant performance dependence on constant inertia
factors. To overcome these shortcomings, this paper proposes a improved particle
swarm optimization algorithm based on chaotic dynamics and adaptive param-
eters (CAPSO) for solving the aforementioned resource allocation problem, as
detailed in Algorithm 1. The proposed approach utilizes the Logistic chaotic
mapping to enhance search capability and population diversity, thereby prevent-
ing premature convergence. Additionally, it implements an iteration-dependent
adaptive inertia weight strategy that transitions from large to small parameter
values during the optimization process, eﬀectively improving both convergence
speed and solution accuracy.
    In Algorithm 1, particles search for the optimal position by continuously
moving in an N -dimensional space. Each particle’s position represents a feasible
solution (x1 , x2 , · · · , xN ) to the problem, while its ﬁtness value corresponds to
the objective function value under this solution, namely the total system revenue.
After at most Imax iterations, the global optimal position X gbest found by the
algorithm serves as the global optimal solution to the problem, and the optimal
                 g
ﬁtness value Rbest       is the maximum total system revenue.
    The speciﬁc steps of Algorithm 1 are described as follows:
    First, line 1 generates an initial set of solutions and corresponding initial sys-
tem revenue within the solution space in O(L · N ) time. The position matrix X ,
velocity matrix V , and chaotic matrix C for L particles are initialized randomly,
all of which are L × N -dimensional matrices. Each row in C is a random vector
introduced for each particle to avoid falling into local optima. The initial ﬁtness
values Rpbest (an L-dimensional vector) are calculated according to the objective
function (14), with each dimension recording a particle’s local optimum. The
initial local optimal positions for all particles X pbest (an L × N matrix) are set to
                                                         g

that each particle’s movement distance is progressively shortened to prevent
overshooting the optimal position due to excessive step size.

    Before entering the inner loop, the algorithm has to record the previous
iteration’s optimal position X g∗                     g∗
                               best and ﬁtness value Rbest (lines 4–5) to determine
whether to terminate the outer loop early (lines 20–21). If the diﬀerences in both
the optimal position and ﬁtness value between two consecutive outer iterations
are smaller than a predeﬁned small positive threshold , it indicates that the
algorithm has converged, and thus the outer loop is terminated prematurely.
                       A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network          91

    Within the inner loop, each particle’s current position X [i2 ] is updated based
on its previous position by adjusting both the chaotic vector C [i2 ] and velocity
V [i2 ] (lines 7–9). The chaotic vector C [i2 ] is used to enhance the search ran-
domness and is updated via the Logistics mapping function. Here, the tunable
parameter ξ ∈ [0, 4] ensures that each chaotic value generated by the map-
ping remains within the interval [0,1]. The particle velocity, which represents
its movement direction, is determined by three vectors: the inertia direction
V [i2 ], the local optimal direction X pbest − X [i2 ], and the global optimal direc-
tion X gbest − X [i2 ]. The inertia weight w indicates the signiﬁcance of the original
movement direction, while c1 and c2 serve as weighting coeﬃcients for the local
and global optimal directions, respectively, with τ being a random parameter.
A larger value of any of these coeﬃcients (w, c1 , c2 or τ ) results in the particle
exhibiting a stronger tendency to move in the corresponding direction.
    To satisfy constraint (1), the algorithm bounds the updated particle position,
where xmax corresponds to the current particle’s resource request ri2 , and xmin is
                                         p
set to 0 (line 10). The ﬁtness value Rcur   of the current particle is then computed
using the objective function (14) (line 11). Through comparison, the algorithm
decides whether to update the particle’s local optimal position X pbest [i2 ] and
ﬁtness Rpbest [i2 ], as well as the global optimal position X gbest and ﬁtness Rbeg
                                                                                    st
                                                   g
(lines 12–17). If the global optimal solution X best from any outer iteration vio-
lates constraint (2), resources are reallocated to each IoT device proportionally
(lines 18–19).
    As can be seen from the above analysis, the overall time complexity of Algo-
rithm 1 is at most O(L · (N + Imax )), meaning it can obtain an approximate
optimal solution to the problem in polynomial time.
    Moreover, Algorithm 1 is not an in-place algorithm and requires auxiliary
space during its execution. The initialization phase requires O(L · N ) space for
relevant matrices, vectors, and variables, while the for loop uses an additional
O(N ) space for temporary vectors and variables. Therefore, the overall space
complexity of the algorithm is O(L · N ).


5    Experiments and Results Analysis

We conducted simulation experiments on resource allocation in a blockchain
network scenario consisting of one edge server and multiple IoT devices using
the MATLAB platform. The experimental parameter settings are speciﬁed in
Table 2. Each group of experiments was executed 50 times with randomized
samples, and the results were averaged to mitigate the inﬂuence of randomness.
    The comparative baselines include the traditional Particle Swarm Optimiza-
tion (PSO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), and Simulated Annealing (SA). In PSO,
the inertia weight was ﬁxed at 0.5, while the two acceleration constants were
the same as those in CAPSO. For GA, the initial population size was set to 10
with crossover and mutation probabilities of 0.8 and 0.02, respectively. The SA
algorithm was conﬁgured with an initial temperature of 100 and a cooling rate
of 0.9.
92     Q. Su et al.

                      Table 2. Main parameter conﬁguration

                 Parameter Value           Parameter Value
                 li          [0, 100]      μ         1
                 ri          [100, 1200] κ           0.1
                 πi          [0.1, 1]      a         1
                 si          [50, 100]     α         1
                 ti          [0.01, 0.1]   β         [1, 2]
                 λ           0.1           γ         [0.003, 0.007]
                 σ           0.005         ξ         [0, 4]
                 A           80000         H         [0.8, 3]



    The evaluation metrics encompass both total system revenue and conver-
gence rate. Maximizing the total system revenue is the primary objective of the
resource allocation problem in this paper, and the results obtained by four meth-
ods are all near-optimal values. Convergence rate is measured by the number of
iterations required for system revenue stabilization, which reﬂects execution eﬃ-
ciency of each algorithm. For CAPSO, this speciﬁcally refers to the number of
outer-loop iterations.


5.1   Impact of IoT Device Scale

In this set of experiments, we examined the impact of the scale of IoT devices
changing from 10 to 100 on the performance of several algorithms. The swarm
size of PSO and CAPSO, the resource capacity of the edge server, the maximum
iterations, the mining diﬃculty, and the chaos parameter were set to 30, 10000,
100, [1, 2], and 4, respectively.




                      Fig. 2. The impact of IoT device scale.
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network        93

    Figure 2(a) illustrates that as the number of IoT devices increases, the total
system revenue obtained by CAPSO initially decreases gradually before show-
ing a slow upward trend. In contrast, the other three methods exhibit a rapid
decline in system revenue. Notably, CAPSO consistently maintains the highest
total system revenue among all four approaches, indicating it is more suitable
for resource allocation in large-scale applications. The performance gap becomes
more pronounced with increasing IoT devices, as traditional heuristic algorithms
are more prone to becoming trapped in local optima. While these suboptimal
solutions allocate resources to most devices, the ﬁxed resource capacity of the
edge server leads to progressively diminishing individual allocations, signiﬁcantly
reducing the probability of completing PoW and obtaining mining rewards. For
CAPSO, the ergodicity and randomness of the Logistic chaotic mapping eﬀec-
tively mitigate the algorithm’s tendency to fall into local optima while enabling
concentrated resource allocation to devices with high block rewards and low
operational costs. Consequently, when the number of IoT devices grows from 10
to 50, the decrease in total revenue is not signiﬁcant. As the number of devices
continues to increase, the optional range of devices that can successfully com-
plete PoW and obtain high mining rewards expands slightly, so the total system
revenue gradually increases again.
    Figure 2(b) shows the convergence of the four algorithms under three diﬀerent
numbers of IoT devices. As the number of IoT devices increases, although the
convergence rates of all four methods gradually slow down, CAPSO consistently
exhibits the fastest convergence among them. Speciﬁcally, when N = 10, they
converge at the 36th, 11th, 58th, and 94th iterations, respectively. When N = 50,
the ﬁrst two methods converge at the 40th and 21st iterations, respectively,
whereas the latter two fail to converge even after reaching the preset maximum
iteration of 100. When N = 100, the ﬁrst three methods converge at the 49th,
30th, and 73rd iterations, respectively, while SA does not converge. The rapid
convergence of CAPSO is attributed to the combined eﬀects of chaotic mapping
and adaptive inertia weights, which dynamically adjust the movement direction
and step size of particles, enabling them to approach the optimal solution more
eﬃciently.

5.2   Impact of IoT Device Requirements
In this set of experiments, we investigated the impact of increasing the resources
requested by each IoT device from [100, 400] to [500, 1200] on the performance
of the four algorithms. The swarm sizes of PSO and CAPSO, the number of
IoT devices, the edge server’s resource capacity, the maximum iterations, the
diﬃculty coeﬃcient, and the chaos parameter were set to 30, 20, 10000, 50, [1,
2] and 4, respectively. Here, [a, b] indicates that the resource demand per IoT
device is randomly selected as an integer value within this interval.
    Figure 3(a) shows that as resource demand increases, the total system revenue
of the four methods initially rises and then declines. In all cases, CAPSO achieves
the highest total revenue. This phenomenon primarily stems from block rewards
being constrained by the Gompertz function. With the growing demand from IoT
94     Q. Su et al.




                  Fig. 3. The impact of IoT device requirements.


devices and the continuous investment of the edge server’s resources, the total
computilities of the system increases, causing the function g(φ) to undergo a
change process from 0 to 1. Consequently, the total system revenue ﬁrst increases.
When g(φ) reaches 1, the total revenue attains its maximum value (observed
when resource demand falls within the range [300, 800]). After that, even if the
edge server still have allocatable resources, block rewards no longer increase,
while resource costs continue to rise, leading to a subsequent decrease in total
revenue. This clearly demonstrates the eﬀectiveness of the function in curbing
resource waste.
    This demonstrates that when an IoT device attempts to obtain higher
rewards by requesting more resources, it not only reduces its own revenue but also
diminishes the total system revenue, which contradicts both individual rational-
ity and system goals. Therefore, the device will not proactively request excessive
resources, nor will the system allocate them, thereby avoiding resource wastage.
    As shown in Fig. 3(b), when the resource demand is in the range [100, 400],
the ﬁrst three methods converge at the 36th, 19th, and 23rd iterations, respec-
tively. When the demand increases to [500, 1200], these methods converge at
the 41st, 24th, and 37th iterations, respectively. SA does not converge under
either of the two value ranges. It can be seen that as resource demand grows,
the iterative process of the algorithms in ﬁnding the optimal solution gradually
slows down. Nevertheless, the proposed method always maintains the highest
execution eﬃciency among the four approaches.


5.3   Impact of Particle Swarm Scale

This set of experiments examined the impact of varying the particle swarm
size from 10 to 100 on the performance of PSO and CAPSO. The number of
IoT devices, the edge server’s resource capacity, the maximum iterations, the
diﬃculty coeﬃcient, and the chaos parameter were set to 20, 10000, 50, [1, 2]
and 4, respectively.
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network        95

    The selection of population size directly inﬂuences both the search scope
and search speed of the algorithms. Generally, a larger population size leads
to broader search coverage but also increases computational complexity (for
instance, in CAPSO, the number of particles determines the inner loop itera-
tions). The trend of the total system revenues of PSO with varying particle num-
bers in Fig. 4(a) aligns with this general principle. A wider search range makes it
easier to escape local optima, thereby yielding a larger objective function value.
However, CAPSO is notably less sensitive to the number of particles compared
to PSO, primarily because the search capability and convergence speed of our
method depend heavily on chaotic mapping and adaptive inertia weights.




                    Fig. 4. The impact of particle swarm scale.


   Figure 4(b) illustrates the convergence of the two methods under diﬀerent
particle swarm scales. First, for all three tested particle sizes, the convergence
speed of CAPSO is faster than that of PSO. Second, for each method, the wider
the search range, the higher the eﬃciency in locating the optimal solution, so
the algorithm can converge faster.

5.4   Impact of Chaotic Parameter
This set of experiments investigated the impact of the parameter ξ in the Logistic
chaotic map varying from 0 to 5 on CAPSO. The number of IoT devices, the
particle swarm size, the edge server’s resource capacity, the maximum iterations,
and the mining diﬃculty were set to 20, 30, 10000, 50, and [1, 2], respectively.
    According to the properties of the Logistic chaotic map, chaotic behavior
(i.e., the generated sequence has pseudorandomness) only occurs when ξ ∈ [0, 4].
As ξ approaches 4, the chaotic values become more uniformly distributed in the
[0,1] interval, which enhances the global search capability of CAPSO. Figure 5a
demonstrates this relationship through the variation of the system revenue with
ξ. When ξ = 0, CAPSO degenerates into PSO with adaptive inertia weights,
yielding lower system revenue. As ξ increases, the chaotic behavior intensiﬁes
96     Q. Su et al.




                      Fig. 5. The impact of chaotic parameter.


and the total system revenue gradually improves. The system achieves maxi-
mum revenue at ξ = 4 when full chaos emerges. Beyond ξ ∈ [0, 4], the chaotic
phenomenon disappears, and the chaotic values may either escape from [0, 1]
or diverge. The sharp decrease of system revenue at ξ = 5 in Fig. 5a exactly
conﬁrms this behavior.
    Figure 5(b) further reveals that as ξ increases from 0 to 4, CAPSO converges
at the 33rd, 30th, 26th, 23rd, and 21st iterations respectively. This monotonically
improving convergence rate indicates that the chaotic mapping also accelerates
optimal solution discovery.


5.5   Impact of Mining Diﬃculty




             Fig. 6. System revenues under diﬀerent mining diﬃculties.


This set of experiments investigated the impact of the diﬃculty coeﬃcient for
IoT devices to successfully mine blocks and obtain rewards on the overall system
                      A Resource Allocation Method of Blockchain Network       97

revenue. The number of IoT devices, the particle swarm size, the edge server’s
resource capacity, the maximum iterations, and the chaos parameter were set to
20, 30, 10000, 50, and 4, respectively.
    Figure 6 demonstrates that as the diﬃculty coeﬃcient gradually increases,
the total system revenue sharply declines. This is evident because, as derived
from Eq. (9), the block reward for each IoT device is inversely proportional to
the diﬃculty coeﬃcient. An increase in the diﬃculty coeﬃcient leads to a reduc-
tion in block rewards, thereby decreasing the total system revenue even if costs
remain constant. However, in practice, when the mining diﬃculty rises, miners
tend to request more resources and consume additional electricity, resulting in
a signiﬁcant increase in costs.

6   Conclusion
Edge computing provides a favorable guarantee for IoT devices with insuﬃ-
cient computilities to participate in blockchain networks. Aiming to maximize
the overall system revenue, this work proposed a resource allocation scheme for
blockchain networks that alleviates resource waste by controlling block rewards.
First, we established revenue models for IoT devices and the edge server based on
block rewards introduced with Gompertz function, and formulated the problem
as a NLP problem. Second, we designed an improved particle swarm optimiza-
tion algorithm, termed CAPSO, which leverages chaotic mapping and adaptive
inertia weights to tackle the NLP challenges inherent in IoT-blockchain resource
allocation. This tailored approach enables CAPSO to quickly locate the global
optimal solution, distinguishing it from generic heuristic methods. Through com-
parative experiments, we demonstrated that CAPSO signiﬁcantly outperforms
the other three heuristic algorithms in terms of both total system revenue and
convergence speed.
     However, this work does not consider the issue of resource pricing, simply
trading resources based on unit prices submitted by IoT devices while neglecting
incentive compatibility during resource allocation. Aﬃne maximization auctions,
which oﬀer distinct advantages including truth, collusion resistance, support for
multi-dimensional attributes, high computational eﬃciency, and design ﬂexibil-
ity, present a promising solution [30]. Our future work will focus on implementing
aﬃne auction smart contracts in IoT-blockchain ecosystems, while employing
federated learning and reinforcement learning techniques to dynamically opti-
mize aﬃne parameters, thereby addressing both pricing and trust challenges
in resource allocation. Furthermore, the current framework considers only a
single-edge-server scenario. When numerous surrounding IoT devices compete
for resources or maintaining consensus mechanisms requires more resources, the
limited capacity of a single edge node may fail to ensure stable system operation.
Computing power network is an emerging information infrastructure designed
to interconnect and orchestrate massive distributed computing nodes, provid-
ing integrated services with guaranteed resources and network performance for
various IoT applications [31]. Consequently, we also plan to explore resource
scheduling mechanisms in blockchain-empowered computing power networks.

           A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking
           Method for Sparse LU Factorization

Zhen Hu, Dongliang Xiong(B) , Kai Huang, Changjun Wu, and Xiaowen Jiang

     College of Integrated Circuits, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 311200, China
            {huzhen,xiongdl,huangk,wuchangjun,jiangxw}@zju.edu.cn



       Abstract. In sparse LU factorization, nonzero elements after symbolic
       factorization tend to distribute in diagonal and right-bottom region
       of sparse matrices. However, regular 2D blocking on this non-uniform
       distribution structure may lead to workload imbalance across blocks.
       Besides, existing matrix features fail to guide us eﬀectively in blocking.
       In this paper, we propose a structure-aware irregular blocking method
       for numerical factorization. A novel diagonal block-based feature is intro-
       duced to eﬀectively characterize the local nonzero distribution of sparse
       matrices. Based on this, we further propose an irregular blocking method
       that adjusts block sizes according to the local distribution of nonzeros.
       The strategy utilizes ﬁne-grained blocks in dense regions and coarse-
       grained blocks in sparse regions, adequately balancing the nonzeros of
       blocks both within the same level and across levels in the dependency
       tree. Experiments demonstrate that, on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, our
       proposed irregular blocking method achieves average speedups of 1.50×
       and 3.32× over PanguLU and the latest SuperLU_DIST, respectively.
       In addition, it achieves speedups of 1.40x and 3.84x over PanguLU and
       SuperLU_DIST on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.


       Keywords: blocked sparse LU factorization · nonzero distribution ·
       irregular blocking · load balance


1    Introduction
Solving the sparse linear system Ax = b [6] is a crucial part of many scientiﬁc and
engineering problems. There are two ways to solve Ax = b: direct methods that
obtain an exact solution in a ﬁnite number of steps and iterative methods that
obtain an exact solution through continuous iteration. Sparse LU factorization is
a commonly used direct method for solving linear systems. It factors the sparse
matrix A of the linear system into a lower triangular matrix L and an upper
triangular matrix U , i.e., A = L × U . The direct LU factorization [9] method
can obtain a more accurate solution and is widely used in scientiﬁc computing
and simulation.
    Typical sparse LU factorization is divided into three phases: (1) reorder-
ing; (2) symbolic factorization; (3) numerical factorization. The purpose of the
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 101–118, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_6
102    Z. Hu et al.




                       Fig. 1. Time breakdown of SuperLU


reordering phase is to reduce ﬁll-in nonzeros and maintain numerical stabil-
ity. Then, the symbolic factorization phase is used to determine the nonzero
structure of matrices L and U . Finally, the numerical factorization phase per-
forms ﬂoating-point operations to obtain the speciﬁc nonzero values. As shown
in Fig. 1, among these phases, the numerical factorization phase is the most
time-consuming, accounting for 50% to 95%. At the same time, there are long
dependency chains between tasks in numerical factorization of sparse matrices.
A dependency tree [19] is a data structure that is used to represent the depen-
dencies between tasks in the factorization of a sparse matrix.
    Preprocessing sparse matrix to blocks or aggregating similar rows or columns
into supernodes [10] can make numerical factorization easier to parallelize. How-
ever, existing solvers such as SuperLU_DIST [17], UMFPACK [5] and PAR-
DISO [21] exploit dense Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) libraries [12],
which reduce computational eﬃciency due to excessive ﬁll-ins introduced to
aggregate more similar columns. KLU [8] is a direct solver in circuit simula-
tion, based on the Gilbert-Peierls left-looking algorithm. It achieves good per-
formance by permuting the matrices into Block Triangular Form (BTF), but can
only execute factorization in serial. Basker [2] partitions the matrix to a block
triangular form where each diagonal block is further partitioned using nested
dissection [16], generating a number of independent sub-matrices. It performs
well in highly sparse matrices, but performs poorly in high density matrices [3].
    Unlike these solvers, PanguLU [14] uses a simpler regular two-dimensional
blocking method and stores it with a compressed format, then selects either
sparse kernels or dense BLAS libraries for computation based on the density
of blocks. However, sparse matrices after symbolic factorization demonstrate a
structure similar to the Bordered Block Diagonal (BBD) structure [4]. It fea-
tures with nonzero elements concentrated in the right-bottom region. Regular
  A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method for Sparse LU Factorization       103

2D blocking will lead to more nonzero elements in blocks near the bottom and
right boundaries, and fewer nonzero elements in blocks near the left and upper
boundaries. This will cause the last level of the dependency tree during numerical
factorization a large computational load and a longer execution time, aﬀecting
the overall performance of numerical factorization. Additionally, it will lead to
signiﬁcant diﬀerences in the number of nonzero elements between blocks, causing
workload imbalance during parallel computation and further impacting overall
performance. Therefore, under the premise of sparse storage and computation,
eﬃcient preprocessing blocking is crucial for improving numerical factorization
performance. Besides, sparse matrices have various structure in real world. Exist-
ing matrix features, like density and average nonzeros per row or column, can
only provide coarse and one-dimensional information of sparse matrices. Pan-
guLU constructs a selection tree considering matrix dimension and total number
of nonzeros after symbolic factorization to decide the block sizes [15], which fails
to select the optimal ones for most sparse matrices.
    To mitigate the load imbalance caused by the various non-uniform distribu-
tion structure of nonzeros in sparse matrices, we need to address the following
two challenges: (1) how to eﬃciently obtain the nonzero distribution structure
of the matrix after symbolic factorization. (2) how to determine the blocking
strategy to alleviate load imbalance.
    In this paper, we propose a structure-aware irregular blocking method. Unlike
PanguLU blocking sparse matrices into blocks with the same size, our proposed
method partitions them adaptively according to the nonzero distribution struc-
ture of sparse matrices. The imbalance of nonzeros across blocks can be well
alleviated through multiple block sizes. Firstly, since the sparse matrix after
symbolic factorization has a symmetric structure [1], we introduce a diagonal
block-based pointer to exploit the two-dimensional distribution characteristics of
the sparse matrix. Then, based on the two-dimensional distribution characteris-
tics of the sparse matrix, our proposed blocking method performs coarse-grained
blocking in dense regions and ﬁne-grained blocking in sparse regions to obtain
the speciﬁc blocking positions. Finally, we conduct experiments on various kinds
of test matrices from SuiteSparse Matrix Collection [8] on the platform with 4
NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
    The comparisons between our work with some existing relevant solvers is
shown in Table 1 and the contributions of our work are as follows.
– A diagonal block-based feature, which is described by percentage of nonzeros
  along the diagonal, is proposed to characterize global and partial nonzero
  distribution of sparse matrices. It can be obtained from common compressed
  formats.
– A structure-aware irregular blocking strategy is proposed based on the
  nonzero distribution of sparse matrices to alleviate workload imbalance of
  nonzeros.
– Experimental results show that our proposed irregular blocking method can
  achieve signiﬁcant speedups over PanguLU and the latest SuperLU_DIST in
  numerical factorization.

2     Background
2.1     Sparse LU Factorization
Sparse LU factorization needs symbolic factorization to predict the symbolic
pattern of the LU factors without considering the numerical values. But it will
induce extra ﬁll-ins. As shown in Fig. 2, in order to minimize ﬁll-ins, reorder-
ing algorithms [11] tend to reorder matrix into a good one just like the below
structure [4]. As a result, after symbolic factorization, most nonzero elements are
located in the right-bottom region. Besides, blocking technique is an optimiza-
tion method by exploiting the data locality. Blocked sparse LU factorization is
considered except for the extremely sparse matrices.




Fig. 2. Diﬀerent structure lead to diﬀerent ﬁll-ins. (a) A structure leads to full ﬁll-ins.
(b) A structure leads to no ﬁll-in.




2.2     Right-Looking Blocked LU Factorization
In numerical factorization phase, right-looking LU algorithm is widely used in
solvers like SuperLU and PanguLU. The right-looking blocked LU algorithm [20],
  A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method for Sparse LU Factorization     105

which treats two-dimensional matrix blocks after preprocessing as input, is
described in Algorithm 1. These loop nests show that data dependences are
frequent. At each level i, only after the factorization of diagonal block Bi,i ,
row(U) panels Bi,∗ and column(L) panels B∗,j have been performed, the entire
tailing sub-matrices can be updated. And the ith iteration can only be executed
after the (i − 1)th iteration have been ﬁnished. However, sparsity brings empty
blocks which can reduce the computation and data dependency, then introduces
more parallelism. Computation only need to be performed on non-empty blocks
as shown in Fig. 3. This example adopts regular 2D blocking before numerical
factorization and partitions the original matrix into several 3 × 3 blocks. And it
consists of a dependency tree with 3 levels.


Algorithm 1. Right-looking Blocked LU Factorization
Require: a p × p block matrix B
Ensure: B = [Bi,j ]i=1:p,j=1:p
 1: Construct blocks Bi,j , ∀i, j
 2: for i = 1 to p do
 3:   Bi,i → Li,i Ui,i {Factorize the diagonal block}
 4:   for j = i + 1 to p do
 5:      Bi,j ← L−1
                  i,i Bi,j {Factorize U panel}
                       −1
 6:      Bj,i ← Bj,i Ui,i  {Factorize L panel}
 7:   end for
 8:   for j = i + 1 to p do
 9:      for k = i + 1 to p do
10:         Bk,j ← Bk,j − Bk,i Bi,j {Update submatrix}
11:       end for
12:   end for
13: end for




               Fig. 3. Example of a sparse blocked LU factorization.
106     Z. Hu et al.

3     Motivation
3.1   Ineﬀective One-Dimensional Matrix Features
The nonzero distribution of a sparse matrix is critical for researchers to accel-
erate the computation. However, the most common features, like matrix dimen-
sion and density, only reﬂects the features of the whole matrix. Other features,
like average number of nonzero elements per row or the standard deviation of
nonzero elements in each row, only reﬂect the one-dimensional feature of the
sparse matrix. PanguLU selects a ﬁxed size of regular blocking according to the
matrix order and the density of the matrix after symbolic factorization, which
can not obtain an optimal block size for the performance of numerical factor-
ization as shown in Fig. 4. While blocked LU factorization algorithm performs
computation with block granularity, it is more important to focus on its two-
dimensional features, which have not been explored.




Fig. 4. The numerc factorization time varies with diﬀerent regular block size of a sparse
matrix. PanguLU makes choices of block size from 300, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000. But it
selects a worse size according to the matrix dimension and density.



3.2   Unbalanced Nonzeros
Regular 2D blocking method partitions matrix into blocks with the same size.
However, nonzero elements are distributed non-uniformly, which leads to blocks
with unbalanced nonzeros. Besides, since most of nonzero elements locate at the
right-bottom region, the density of blocks nearing right and bottom region are
generally higher than those near left and up region [3]. As shown in Fig. 5, the
number of nonzero elements in block n is much more than that in block a. This
imbalance causes most of the time for numerical factorization to be spent on
the last dense blocks. This issue will be more severe in parallel computing as
the time diﬀerence between blocks induced by load imbalance. Therefore, it is
necessary to partition blocks according to the sparsity of region.
    A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method for Sparse LU Factorization     107




Fig. 5. Example of a dependency-level tree of a regularly blocked sparse matrix. (a)
Sparse matrix A with regular blocking. (b) The dependency tree of A based on level.


4     Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method
4.1    Overview

In this paper, we propose a structure-aware irregular blocking preprocessing
method for sparse LU numerical factorization. The ﬂoating point operations in
numerical factorization is related with the number of nonzeros after symbolic
factorization. The sparse matrix is stored by Compressed Sparse Column (CSC)
format. In the preprocessing phase, we propose a conversion algorithm to get
a diagonal block-based pointer from CSC pointer. The diagonal block-based
pointer stores the number of nonzeros in diagonal sub-matrix. The percentage
of nonzero values distributed along the diagonal can be obtained by dividing
the value in the pointer by the total number of nonzero values. To balance the
number of nonzeros in blocks, we sample uniformly 1000 points of the nonzeros
distribution to guide us in blocking the sparse matrix. The strategy of ﬁner-
grained blocks in dense regions while allocating coarser blocks in sparse regions
induces blocks with multiple sizes. Workload imbalance can be alleviated through
balance the number of nonzeros both within the same level and across levels in
the dependency tree.
108    Z. Hu et al.

4.2   Diagonal Block-Based Feature

Compressed sparse column (CSC) is a common compressed format for sparse
matrix. It utilizes three arrays: column pointer, row index, and value. The col-
umn pointer array stores the index in the value array of the ﬁrst nonzero element
of each column. Row index array stores the row index of each nonzero element.
And the value array stores the value of nonzero elements of in column order.
According to column pointer array, we can get the number of nonzero elements
in each column. It can be useful for matrix computation based on columns, like
column-wise sparse matrix multiplication [18]. Blocked sparse matrix factoriza-
tion regards blocks as the computational granularity, while compressed sparse
column (CSC) only reﬂect the row distribution of the sparse matrix and cannot
eﬀectively guide the performance optimization for blocked matrix factorization.
    Considering the symmetry of the sparse matrix after symbolic factoriza-
tion [14], a diagonal block-based array can be obtained from compressed sparse
column pointer, which contains the number of nonzero elements in the sub-
matrix [0 : n, 0 : n], where n is the row/column index, as shown in Fig. 6.
The conversion algorithm from arrays of CSC to diagonal block-based pointer is
shown in Algorithm 2.




 Fig. 6. Example of compressed sparse column pointer and diagonal block pointer.


    After normalizing the index and value of diagonal block pointer, we get the
feature, i.e., a percentage array of nonzero distribution along the diagonal. When
taking them as the x-axis and y-axis, respectively, the resulting curve explicitly
shows both global and local distribution features of the sparse matrix.
    As shown in Fig. 7, for linear matrices, the number of nonzero increases uni-
formly along the diagonal. Therefore the nonzero percentage curve based on
diagonal block pointer shows a linear feature. For uniformly distributed matri-
ces, the number of nonzeros in a block is proportional to the area of the diagonal
block. As we can see, the percentage curve of uniformly distributed matrices
shows a quadratic feature. We can roughly infer the structure of sparse matrix
by the global feature of the curve. In addition, the local distribution of nonze-
ros can also be captured. As shown in Fig. 8, ﬁgure (a) shows a sparse matrix
  A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method for Sparse LU Factorization          109


Algorithm 2. Extracting Diagonal Block Pointer
Require: matrix dimension n, ∗columnpter, ∗rowidx
 1: Initialize num[n] = 0
 2: for i = 0 to n − 1 do
 3:    for j = columnptr[i] to columnptr[i + 1] − 1 do
 4:       index ← rowidx[j]
 5:       if index > i then
 6:          num[index] ← num[index] + 1
 7:       end if
 8:    end for
 9: end for
10: blockptr[0] ← 0
11: for i = 0 to n − 1 do
12:    num[i] ← 2 × num[i] + 1
13:    blockptr[i + 1] ← blockptr[i] + num[i]
14: end for
15: return ∗blockptr




Fig. 7. (a) A linear structure matrix. (b) An uniform distribution structure matrix.
(c) Percentage of nonzeros based on diagonal pointer of (a). (d) Percentage of nonzeros
based on diagonal pointer of (b).
110     Z. Hu et al.

with some local dense blocks. The nonzero percentage curve based on diago-
nal block pointer shows partial quadratic trends in dense region with obvious
discontinuities. Also, when there are relatively dense rows and columns along
the diagonal, there are signiﬁcant jumps in the curve. The curve in ﬁgure (d)
shows many jumps because the sparse matrix has relatively dense rows/columns
here. Therefore, the diagonal block-based pointer contains the two-dimensional
distribution information of a sparse matrix, which can be exploited to guide us
in accelerating the block-based matrix computation, like blocked sparse matrix
factorization.




Fig. 8. (a) A sparse matrix with some local dense regions. (b) A sparse matrix with
some dense rows or columns. (c) Percentage of nonzeros based on the diagonal pointer
of (a). The partial quadratic trends in the curve indicates that there are local dense
regions. (d) Percentage of nonzeros based on the diagonal pointer of (b). The jumps in
the curve indicates that there are relatively dense rows and columns.




4.3   Irregular Blocking Method Based on Nonzero Distribution

Considering the locality of the nonzero distribution after symbolic factorization,
an irregular blocking method is proposed as described in Algorithm 3. The algo-
rithm adopts the strategy of blocking ﬁner-grained blocks for dense regions while
allocating coarser blocks for sparse regions.
  A Structure-Aware Irregular Blocking Method for Sparse LU Factorization      111

    We sample uniformly 1000 points from the percentage of nonzeros array as
input. The algorithm calculate the percentage diﬀerence between two consecu-
tive points or points separated by a step interval. If the percentage diﬀerence
exceeds a threshold, this indicates that the diagonal region between these two
indexes contains a signiﬁcant number of nonzero elements, and the larger index
should be marked as a blocking position (P1 ). Otherwise, if the diﬀerence does
not exceed the threshold, we regard that the diagonal region between the two
indexes contains fewer nonzero elements and can be skipped without blocking,
while increasing the skip counter l. It is hard to set the threshold to distinguish
the dense or sparse regions. As we have observed in the nonzero percentage curve
in Sect. 4.2, the percentage of nonzeros based on diagonal pointer of a matrix with
linear structure show a linear feature. Considering the nonzero after symbolic
factorization mainly distribute along the diagonal, we regard the linear diﬀerence
as the threshold, i.e. step/sample_pointers. Also, to prevent excessive accumula-
tion of nonzero elements caused by consecutive skips, when l reaches max_num,
blocking must still be performed and a blocking position (Pm ) marked. The pro-
cess described above continues until the index reaches the dimension N of the
matrix. The algorithm eventually outputs a blocking position pointer array that
records all blocking boundaries. We choose step and max_num to be 2 and 3
respectively. The parameters are determined empirically based on a large number
of parameter tuning experiments.


Algorithm 3. Structure-aware irregular blocking method
Require: Percentage array pct[sample_points], matrix dimension N
 1: ptr[0] = 0
 2: for index i = 0 to sample_points do
 3:   if pct[i + step] − pct[i] ≥ threshold then
 4:      k ←k+1
 5:      ptr[k] ← (i + step) ∗ N/sample_points {Dense region}
 6:      l←0
 7:   else if l ≥ max_num then
 8:      k ←k+1
 9:      ptr[k] ← (i + step) ∗ N/sample_points {Avoid too large blocks}
10:       l←0
11:    else
12:       l ←l+1
13:    end if
14: end for
15: return blocking position ∗ptr



    An example is shown in Fig. 9. We ﬁrst sample uniformly a proper number of
points from the percentage array of nonzero distribution, which means a prelimi-
nary regular blocking into some basic blocks. Then according to the diﬀerence of
distribution percentage between two sample points, we merge a certain number
112     Z. Hu et al.

of basic blocks in sparse regions. The ﬁnal blocking scheme is shown in Fig. 9(c).
The blocking positions are denoted by P0 , P1 , ... , P5 , where P0 = 0 and P5 = N .




Fig. 9. Example of the irregular blocking method. (a) Initial matrix sampled in posi-
tion marked by dashed lines. (b) Coarse-grained blocking in a sparse region. (c) Final
blocking.

5.2      Performance on A Single GPU
We ﬁrst evaluate the performance of the numerical factorization of our work
compared with PanguLU and SuperLU_DIST in a NVIDIA A100 GPU. Pan-
guLU selects the size of block from 200, 300, 500, 1000, 2000 and 5000 according
to the order of matrix and number of nonzeros after symbolic factorization. We
also run PanguLU with all those block sizes mentioned above, and select the best
performance for comparison. In numerical factorization, both PanguLU and our
work use sparse kernels for computation, while SuperLU uses dense kernels. The
experimental results in Table 4 show that the geometric mean speedups of our
work in numerical factorization can achieve 1.50x and 3.32x, compared with
PanguLU and SuperLU_DIST, respectively.
    The sizes of most blocks partitioned by our work are generally larger than
those of PanguLU. Large blocks contain relatively more nonzero elements, which
can improve the utilization rate of the GPU. The speedup over SuperLU_DIST
is mainly due to the computation of sparse kernels.

superiority of our irregular blocking over the regular blocking.

important factor that aﬀects performance, especially when dealing with the irreg-

is very obvious, resulting in a more signiﬁcant speedup.

with a size of 300 regularly. And there is little data dependence in ASIC_680k,

5.4   Preprocessing Cost

Regular blocking with the same size in PanguLU makes preprocessing easier
and more eﬃcient. Irregular blocking needs to store sizes of block in a size
array. The array will be frequently looked up in the preprocessing phase to
perform irregular blocking, which causes a longer time of preprocessing. Since the
performance in numerical factorization accounts for the largest proportion of the
whole LU factorization, it is acceptable to improve the performance of numerical
factorization at the cost of increased preprocessing time. Besides, optimizing the
performance of preprocessing will be our research in the future.


6     Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a novel diagonal block-based feature, which is described
by percentage of nonzeros along the diagonal, can characterize global and local
nonzero distribution of sparse matrices. Furthermore, a structure-aware irregular
blocking method is proposed based on the local nonzero distribution. The irreg-
ular blocking method adopts the strategy of ﬁne-grained in dense regions and
coarse-grained in sparse regions. This strategy can balance the number of nonzero
elements between levels in the dependency tree and the number of nonzero ele-
ments among blocks within the same level. Experiments on test sparse matrices
show that our proposed irregular blocking method achieves speedups of perfor-
mance in numerical factorization compared with PanguLU and SuperLU_DIST.
On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, it achieves geometric means of 1.50x and 3.32x,
respectively. Also, it achieves speedups of 1.40x and 3.84x over PanguLU and
SuperLU_DIST on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
