                A Deep Reinforcement Learning
             Algorithm with Ordered Action Space
            for Budget-Aware Workflow Scheduling
                    in Heterogeneous Clouds

    Yanfen Zhang1 , Longxin Zhang1(B) , Lili Du1 , Zhihua Wen1 , Buqing Cao1,2 ,
                         Sheng Lin1 , and Jianguo Chen3
     1
      School of Computer Science and Artiﬁcial Intelligence, Hunan University of
                        Technology, Zhuzhou 412007, China
                         longxinzhang@hut.edu.cn
  2
    Key Laboratory of Intelligent Sensing System and Security (Hubei University),
                Ministry of Education, Wuhan 430062, China
3
   School of Software Engineering, Sun Yat-Sen University, Zhuhai 519082, China



          Abstract. The optimization problem of makespan for cloud workﬂow
          scheduling under budget constraints presents signiﬁcant challenges due
          to the heterogeneity of cloud resources and the complexity of task depen-
          dencies. Although existing deep reinforcement learning scheduling algo-
          rithms show promise in addressing the inherent limitations of traditional
          methods, they often lack awareness of budget constraints and struggle
          to manage the dynamic action space induced by budgetary considera-
          tions. To address this issue, a perception coeﬃcient generation mecha-
          nism speciﬁcally designed to adhere to budget constraints is proposed.
          Additionally, an ordered action space mapping method is developed to
          facilitate the transition from continuous to discrete actions. Leverag-
          ing these two innovations, the twin delayed deep deterministic policy
          gradient (TD3) framework is leveraged to propose a budget-constrained
          workﬂow scheduling algorithm called PO-TD3, aimed at generating fea-
          sible and eﬃcient scheduling solutions. The experimental results show
          that compared to the baseline algorithms, the PO-TD3 algorithm con-
          verges eﬃciently, achieving a 100% success rate in generating scheduling
          schemes that satisfy budget constraints. Additionally, it achieves opti-
          mal performance in minimizing makespan, with an average reduction of
          61.43% compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.


          Keywords: Budget-aware · Deep reinforcement learning ·
          Heterogeneous cloud computing · Makespan · Workﬂow scheduling


1        Introduction
Cloud computing operates on a pay-per-use business model that leverages virtu-
alization technologies to provide various essential resources, such as computing
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 119–136, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_7
120     Y. Zhang et al.

and storage, within an internet environment [1]. A heterogeneous cloud com-
puting platform consists of a series of clusters of virtual machines (VMs) that
employ diﬀerent infrastructures and management technologies. These VMs are
interconnected through communication or business networks and are deployed
on disparate hosts in a decentralized manner [2]. Cloud computing plays a cru-
cial role in the management of large-scale workﬂows and in the processing of
computationally intensive tasks due to its robust computational capabilities. A
workﬂow application comprises numerous tasks with dependency constraints and
is typically modeled using directed acyclic graph (DAG) [3]. This study imposes
budget constraints on the entire workﬂow and aims to minimize the makespan
while strictly adhering to these budgetary limitations.
    For budget-constrained workﬂow scheduling in heterogeneous clouds, heuris-
tic algorithms are often susceptible to task priority hierarchies, resulting in sub-
optimal solutions. Meanwhile, meta-heuristic algorithms typically require greater
computational resources to converge on optimal solutions. Conversely, the deep
reinforcement learning (DRL) approach formulates workﬂow scheduling as a
Markov decision process (MDP) [4], oﬀering a robust framework for addressing
the workﬂow scheduling challenge. However, most current research on DRL mod-
els primarily focuses on the workﬂow scheduling problem with multi-objective
optimization or emphasizes cost minimization under deadline constraints. In con-
trast, there is a notable scarcity of studies utilizing DRL models to address the
makespan minimization problem under budget constraints.
    In response to this gap, a perception coeﬃcient generation (PCG) mecha-
nism is developed to ensure adherence to budget constraints, and a scheduling
framework based on the twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3)
[5] methodology is designed in this study. A DRL scheduling framework, named
PO-TD3, is proposed to eﬀectively tackle the challenges posed by dynamic action
spaces under budget constraints by exploring an ordered action space (OAS)
mapping approach, with the objective of minimizing makespan in heterogeneous
cloud environments. The main contributions of this study are summarized below:

• It creates a PCG mechanism by utilizing a population-based evolutionary
  model within a meta-heuristic framework. This mechanism generates percep-
  tion coeﬃcients for each task in the workﬂow, which in turn establishes the
  upper limit of the disposable cost for each task, ensuring strict adherence to
  the budget constraints of the workﬂow.
• It explores the OAS mapping approach to facilitate transitions from continu-
  ous to discrete actions within an ordered action space, which comprises can-
  didate VMs arranged by their ﬁnish times. This strategy allows for eﬀective
  scheduling decisions related to task-VM assignments.
• It proposes a budget-constrained workﬂow scheduling algorithm, PO-TD3,
  by integrating the PCG mechanism with the OAS mapping method within
  the TD3 framework. The feasibility and eﬃciency of the PO-TD3 algorithm
  are validated through comparative experiments with similar target scheduling
  algorithms.
      A Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithm with Ordered Action Space       121

   The remainder of this study is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a
review of related work. Section 3 describes the scheduling model and problem
formulation. Section 4 presents the proposed PO-TD3 algorithm. Section 5 dis-
cusses the experimental results and analyses. Finally, Sect. 6 summarizes the
conclusions and outlines future work.


2   Related Work

In recent years, researchers have explored heuristics, metaheuristics, and DRL
methods to address the challenges posed by complex workﬂow scheduling.
    Heuristic algorithms develop suitable scheduling rules by leveraging a priori
knowledge of the workﬂow. Zhang et al. [6] explored a scheduling strategy based
on a predictive makespan matrix, focusing on the minimization of makespan
in heterogeneous cloud environments. Kaur et al. [7] introduced the concept of
virtual task clustering, which reduces data transfer time to zero by reallocating
tasks to more energy-eﬃcient VMs on the same host. This approach achieves
both energy savings and makespan reduction while adhering to deadline con-
straints. Zhang et al. [8] conducted their research under budget constraints,
employing iterative adjustments of task-resource mappings to reduce the length
of the critical path.
    Meta-heuristic algorithms have demonstrated distinct advantages in the
realm of workﬂow scheduling. Li et al. [9] proposed a meta-heuristic algorithm
known as the mutation-driven and population grouping poor and rich optimiza-
tion algorithm (MG-PRO), which is speciﬁcally designed for scheduling work-
ﬂows with budget constraints in cloud environments to minimize the makespan
of workﬂows. Kushwaha and Singh [10] enhanced a meta-heuristic scheduling
algorithm based on the Archimedean optimization approach, which possesses
lower computational complexity. However, this method is highly sensitive to the
initial population settings and parameter conﬁgurations.
    DRL leverages the representation learning capabilities of deep neural net-
works to address the limitations of traditional reinforcement learning in high-
dimensional state spaces. Tang et al. [2] modeled the task scheduling problem as a
MDP and proposed a DRL-based task scheduling algorithm for multi-cloud envi-
ronments, aiming to optimize both cost and makespan according to diverse user
requirements. Chen et al. [11] developed a green-aware scheduling algorithm for
high-performance computing clusters, utilizing a multi-action DRL framework
to simultaneously optimize renewable energy utilization through proximal policy
optimization.
    However, heuristic algorithms exhibit a strong dependence on predeﬁned
rules, while meta-heuristic scheduling algorithms demonstrate a high degree of
complexity in parameter conﬁguration and the determination of relevant thresh-
olds. Both types of algorithms tend to perform poorly when confronted with
workﬂows characterized by diverse structural traits. Consequently, this study
focuses on the scheduling problem of budget-constrained workﬂows and employs
122     Y. Zhang et al.

the DRL method for research. The objective is to design an eﬃcient schedul-
ing algorithm that minimizes the makespan of workﬂows while satisfying budget
constraints.


3     Model and Problem Formulation
This section introduces the workﬂow scheduling model, outlining the constraints
and optimization objectives addressed in the research.


3.1   Workflow Scheduling Model
Heterogeneous cloud resource pools composed of VM instances that vary in pro-
cessing power and lease prices are considered [12]. Let V = {v1 , ..., vk , ..., v|V| }
represent the set of VM instances, with |V| denoting the total number of
rented VM instances. We assume that all VM instances are provisioned by
the same data center and utilize the same average bandwidth bw [3]. A work-
ﬂow application is typically modeled as a DAG, denoted as G = {N , E},
where N = {n1 , ..., ni , ..., n|N | } represents a collection of |N | nodes, each cor-
responding to an individual task that constitutes the workﬂow. E represents
the set of directed edges, while ei,j ∈ E indicates that task ni must complete
its execution before task nj commences. pred (ni ) = {nj ∈ N |ej ,i ∈ E} and
succ(ni ) = {nj ∈ N |ei,j ∈ E} denote, respectively, the set of direct predecessors
and the set of direct successors of task ni . In a workﬂow DAG, an entry task
nentry is deﬁned as a task with no predecessors, whereas an exit task nexit is
characterized as a task with no successors.


3.2   Problem Formulation

Assuming that task ni is assigned to a VM vx and task nj is assigned to a VM
vy , with the size of the data transferred between ni and nj denoted as TDi,j ,
the communication time is denoted as CTi,j , which can be assessed by

                                     TDi,j /bw , if x = y;
                          CTi,j =                                                  (1)
                                     0,          otherwise.

    The start time and ﬁnish time (FT) of a task ni executing on a VM vk are
denoted as STi and FTi , respectively. Their computational expressions are as
follows:
                 STi = max RTk ,         max          FTj + CTj ,i   ,             (2)
                                      nj ∈pred(ni )

                                FTi = STi + ETi,k ,                                (3)
where RTk represents the ready time of VM vk , and ETi,k indicates the execution
time required for task ni to be processed on VM vk .
      A Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithm with Ordered Action Space               123

   The makespan M of a workﬂow is deﬁned as the total time from the start of
execution to completion. Its computational expression is as follows [13]:

                                M (G) = max FTi .                                     (4)
                                          ni ∈N

   The execution cost of a task ni on a VM vk is denoted as Cost(ni , vk ), which
can be evaluated by
                          Cost(ni , vk ) = ETi,k × Pk ,                       (5)
where Pk is the unit execution price of VM vk . The scheduling cost C of a
workﬂow is deﬁned as the sum of the execution costs of all tasks in the workﬂow
on the VM.
    We investigate the budget-constrained workﬂow scheduling problem, aiming
to assign workﬂow tasks to VMs while adhering to budget constraints B. The
objective is to minimize the makespan by determining the optimal start and
ﬁnish times for each task. The optimization problem can be formally deﬁned as
follows:
                              M inimize : M (G),                             (6)
                               Subject to : C(G) ≤ B.                                 (7)


4     PO-TD3 Algorithm
The PO-TD3 algorithm encompasses three essential components: the PCG mech-
anism, the OAS mapping method, and the TD3 algorithm. Speciﬁcally, the PCG
mechanism is designed to meet the budget constraints of the workﬂow. The OAS
mapping method is integrated into the Actor-Critic framework of the TD3 algo-
rithm, aimed at assisting in optimizing the decision-making process by eﬀectively
assigning the appropriate VMs to individual tasks within the workﬂow to min-
imize the makespan. This section elaborates on the implementation principles
of the PO-TD3 algorithm and presents its core formulation. The pseudo-code of
the PO-TD3 algorithm is provided in Algorithm 1.

4.1   PCG Mechanism
Given that makespan and execution cost represent a pair of conﬂicting variables,
a reduction in makespan typically results in an increase in cost. Perception coef-
ﬁcients are established for each task within the workﬂow, denoted as the set
                              ∗
ξ ∗ = {ς1∗ , ..., ςi∗ , ..., ς|N                                ∗
                                 | }. The perception coeﬃcient ςi ∈ [0, 1], which dictates
                                ∗
the disposable cost Ci associated with task ni , can be calculated by

                         Ci∗ = Cmin
                                i
                                    + ςi∗ × (Cmax
                                              i
                                                  − Cmin
                                                     i
                                                         ),                           (8)
       i                                                             i
where Cmin represents the minimum execution cost of task ni , and Cmax    denotes
the maximum execution cost of task ni .
   The objective of designing the perception coeﬃcients is to establish an upper
bound on the cost that can be allocated to a task by pre-assigning the disposable
124     Y. Zhang et al.

cost to each task within the workﬂow. When assigning VMs to tasks, PO-TD3
will disregard any VMs with costs exceeding the task’s cost ceiling, thus prevent-
ing the execution costs associated with the scheduling solution from breaching
the budget constraint. To accomplish this, the PCG mechanism is proposed to
determine the value ςi∗ of the perception coeﬃcient, ensuring that the sum of the
disposable costs of the tasks adheres to the budget constraint of the workﬂow:
                                       |N |
                                              Ci∗ ≤ B.                                 (9)
                                      i=1

    Inspired by the concept that metaheuristics seek optimal solutions through
an iterative optimization mechanism, the design of the PCG mechanism is based
on the population evolution model. This model encompasses the generation of
the initial population, the formulation of evaluation rules, and the exploration
and exploitation of the population.
    (1) Generation of Initial Population. A random initial population P =
{X1 , ..., Xd , ..., Xδ } is generated within the search space to represent δ sets of
perception coeﬃcients, serving as the starting point for the search. In this con-
text, δ indicates the population size, with individual Xd = {x1 , ..., xi , ..., x|N | } in
the population representing a set of perception coeﬃcients, and xi ∈ [0, 1] denot-
ing the value of the perception coeﬃcient corresponding to task ni . According
to the design objectives of the PCG mechanism, the ﬁtness value fd of individ-
ual Xd is determined by the sum of the disposable costs associated with the
corresponding tasks of individual Xd :
                                               |N |
                                      fd =            Ci∗ ,                           (10)
                                              i=1

where Ci∗ is calculated according to Eq. (8), with ςi∗ = xi .
   (2) Formulation of Evaluation Rules. The scheduling problem addressed
considers cost as a constraint. Speciﬁcally, the scheduling cost is required to
meet the budget constraint without necessitating minimization. This implies
that the closer the cost approaches the budgeted value, the more eﬃciently it
can be utilized to reduce the makespan, provided that the cost remains within
the budget constraint. Therefore, for any two sets of perception coeﬃcients in
the population, X1 and X2 , the following three evaluation rules are formulated:
• If neither set satisﬁes the budget constraint, the set with the smaller corre-
  sponding sum of task disposable costs is considered preferable.
• If both sets satisfy the budget constraint, the set with the corresponding
  sum of task disposable costs that is closer to the budgeted value is deemed
  preferable.
• If one of the sets satisﬁes the budget constraint while the other does not, the
  set that meets the budget constraint is preferred.
   (3) Exploration and Exploitation of the Population. In population-
based meta-heuristic optimization algorithms, the exploration of the globally
      A Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithm with Ordered Action Space                  125

optimal solution relies on the iterative updating of each individual’s position
within the search space. This process encompasses two fundamental components:
exploration and exploitation. The weighted average algorithm (WAA) [14] is
a meta-heuristic optimization method grounded in the concept of a weighted
average position. Given the eﬀectiveness and reliability of WAA in balancing
exploration and exploitation, the exploration and exploitation strategies of WAA
are adopted as the position update mechanism for individuals in the population.
This approach aims to enhance the eﬃcient convergence of the PCG mechanism
and to obtain a set of perception coeﬃcients that satisfy the budget constraint.
    During the optimization process, each iteration requires determining whether
the best individual Xbest = {x1 , ..., xi , ..., x|N | } of the population obtained in that
iteration satisﬁes the budget constraints. Once the best individual Xbest in the
population is identiﬁed as meeting the budget constraint (i.e., fbest ≤ B), the
                                                                      ∗
iteration is stopped. The ﬁnal solution ξ ∗ = {ς1∗ , ..., ςi∗ , ..., ς|N | } is determined as
Xbest = {x1 , ..., xi , ..., x|N | }, indicating that the perception coeﬃcient ςi∗ for task
ni is equal to xi .
    Based on the PCG mechanism, the PO-TD3 algorithm ensures adherence to
the essential prerequisite of budget constraints.


4.2    OAS Mapping Method

The workﬂow scheduling problem is formulated as a MDP [15], denoted as
 O, A, r, π, γ . In this formulation, o ∈ O represents the observation values, a ∈ A
signiﬁes the actions, and r(o, a) : O × A → R denotes the reward function. The
agent’s policy, represented by π, predicts the action distribution based on the
observation values at the current time step t, while γ is the discount factor.
Assuming that the distribution of observations is represented by ρ, the Q-value
function can be expressed as
                                                     T
                  Q(ot , at ) = Eot ∼ρ,at ∼π(ot )          γ j rt+j |ot , at ,          (11)
                                                     j=0


where T is the termination time step.
   (1) Observation Space
The observation value ot is deﬁned as follows:

                                  ot = ωt , ϑt , Ct , Mt ,                              (12)

where ωt = t/T represents the current scheduling progress, ϑt = (B − Ct )/Ct
denotes the degree of violation of the current budget constraint (with ϑt = 0
indicating that the constraint is satisﬁed), Ct signiﬁes the total cost of the current
scheduling, and Mt indicates the current makespan.
   (2) Action Space
Due to budget constraints, when assigning VMs to tasks, the algorithm only
considers VMs with a cost less than or equal to the task’s disposable cost as
candidates. As a result, the set of available VMs corresponding to diﬀerent tasks
126         Y. Zhang et al.

varies, which leads to a dynamically changing action space at each time step.
Given this variability, it is not feasible to directly output the probability distri-
bution in the discrete action space for action selection. In light of this situation,
a two-stage decision-making approach is adopted.
                                        (1)
• Determine the output result at (i.e., the action output at of the policy
  network) within the continuous action space.
                                                 (1)
• Design an OAS mapping method to convert at into the discrete action space,
                (2)
  resulting in at , which will be used to identify the VM for executing the task.

     The OAS mapping method based on ordered action spaces is explored to

facilitate the completion of the transformation at → at . At the current time
step t, the decision-making mechanism of the agent aims to assign VM to task
nt . The OAS mapping method is established through three key deﬁnitions: VM
ﬁltering, FT sorting, and action localization.

Definition 1. VM Filtering.

   The disposable cost Ct∗ of task nt is calculated using Eq. (8), where the per-
ception coeﬃcient ςt∗ is obtained through the PCG mechanism prior to decision-
making. OAS traverses the queue Lt of available VMs for the VM acquisition
task nt , considering only those VMs whose usage cost is not greater than the
task’s available budget, while excluding any VMs deemed inappropriate due to
their usage cost.
Definition 2. FT Sorting.
    All VMs in Lt are sorted in ascending order based on the FT of task nt
to generate a queue Lt = {l1 , l2 , ..., lLen }, which represents an ordered discrete
action space. Here, Len denotes the length of the queue Lt .

Definition 3. Action Localization.
      (1)
    at is employed to compute a precise index for locating a target VM in queue

Lt , thereby establishing the implicit mapping from at to at :
                                              (1)

where ind determines at = lind , indicating the assignment of task nt to the
ind -th VM in queue Lt for execution.
    (3) Reward Function
The feedback reward rt received by the agent for taking action at under observa-
tion ot is deﬁned as rt = −Mt , with the objective of minimizing the makespan.

4.3   TD3 Algorithm
Given the focus on continuous action outputs, the TD3 [5] algorithm is selected to
train the policy model. The TD3 algorithm adopts the Actor-Critic architecture
and includes three sets of key neural networks: (1) the online actor network πθ
with parameter θ and its target network πθ− with parameter θ− ; (2) the online
critic network Qφ with parameter φ and its target network Qφ− with parameter
φ− ; and (3) the second online critic network Qψ with parameter ψ and its target
network Qψ− with parameter ψ − . The actor network (i.e., the policy network)
outputs deterministic actions and maximizes the Q-value of the critic evaluation
through the policy gradient. The double critic networks estimate the Q-value
separately and independently, constructing the target value through the minima
operation to mitigate the overestimation of the Q-value. All target networks
utilize a soft update mechanism [15] to ensure training stability.
    The proposed PO-TD3 algorithm, as outlined in Algorithm 1, involves the
agent continuously interacting with the environment during the training process
(lines 5–22). At the current time step t, the agent’s action is determined by
the OAS mapping method according to the current observation ot (lines 8–
11). After executing the action, the agent receives an immediate reward rt and
obtains the environment observation ot+1 at the next time step (line 12). The
tuple (ot , at , rt , ot+1 ) is then stored in the replay buﬀer RB (line 13). When the
size of the experience data in the replay buﬀer reaches a speciﬁed batch size b,
PO-TD3 randomly samples a batch of historical experience data from the buﬀer
to train the network and update the network parameters (lines 15–20).


5     Experiments and Analyses
This section details the experimental setup, including the baseline algorithms
and performance metrics used in the comparative experiments. This evaluation
aims to assess and validate the eﬀectiveness of the PO-TD3 algorithm.

5.1   Experimental Settings
The programming language employed is Python 3.9, and the deep learning frame-
work is developed using the PyTorch 2.5.1 platform. The experiments utilize 32
heterogeneous VM instances, with conﬁguration parameters informed by Ama-
zon EC2 [2] to determine the types and pricing of the VM instances.

Datasets. Two typical real-world scientiﬁc workﬂow applications [6] are
employed as test datasets for the experiments, illustrated in Fig. 1. These work-
ﬂow applications include the LIGO workﬂow in the ﬁeld of gravitational physics
and the Gaussian elimination (GE) parallel application. Furthermore, to com-
prehensively assess the eﬀectiveness of the PO-TD3 algorithm, the experiments
have been conducted across various scales for both types of workﬂow task sets,
categorized into small, medium, and large scales, as deﬁned below: (1) Small:

Baseline Methods. To evaluate the performance of the PO-TD3 algorithm,
a comparison is made with a meta-heuristic scheduling algorithm and a DRL
scheduling algorithm.

• MG-PRO [9]: This algorithm is a meta-heuristic scheduling approach aimed at
  minimizing workﬂow makespan while adhering to budget constraints, aligning
  with the research objectives of the PO-TD3 algorithm. For the comparative
  experiments, the parameter settings from the original MG-PRO study are
  employed, with a population size set to 50 and a maximum of 1000 iterations.
• TD3 [5]: This refers to the original TD3 algorithm. To assess the eﬀective-
  ness of the PO-TD3 algorithm, both the TD3 and PO-TD3 algorithms utilize
  the same observation space, action space, and parameter settings during the
  comparison experiments. However, it is important to note that the TD3 algo-
  rithm does not incorporate the PCG mechanism or the OAS mapping method,
  which are utilized in the PO-TD3 algorithm.

Performance Metrics. Three performance metrics are employed to assess
whether the scheduling schemes produced by the PO-TD3 algorithm and two
baseline algorithms meet budgetary constraints and optimize the makespan. This
evaluation aims to validate the eﬀectiveness and applicability of the PO-TD3
theoretical model.
   (1) Success Rate. A fundamental characteristic of a feasible scheduling
scheme is that the cost incurred in executing the corresponding workﬂow remains
130    Y. Zhang et al.

strictly within a predeﬁned budget constraint. To facilitate a clear and intuitive
analysis of the performance of both the PO-TD3 algorithm and the baseline
algorithms in adhering to these budget constraints, the concept of success rate is
introduced [9]. Speciﬁcally, under each set of predeﬁned experimental conditions,
multiple independent experiments are conducted, and statistics are collected
regarding whether the scheduling solution generated from each experiment com-
plies with the predeﬁned budget constraints. The formula for the success rate
SR is as follows:
                                           χ∗
                                    SR =      ,                              (14)
                                            χ
where χ∗ denotes the number of times a feasible scheduling solution is obtained
in χ experiments. In this study, χ = 10. A higher success rate indicates better
performance of the algorithm.
   (2) Makespan. Experiments are conducted to compare and analyze the
makespan of the PO-TD3 algorithm and the baseline algorithms across diﬀer-
ent workﬂow scheduling environments. The analysis is conducted along three
dimensions: budget constraints (Experiment 1), task sizes (Experiment 2), and
the number of VMs (Experiment 3).
   Experiment 1: We employ a medium-scale dataset to evaluate the perfor-
mance of the PO-TD3 algorithm alongside baseline algorithms for scheduling the
LIGO and GE workﬂows under varying budget constraints in terms of makespan.
To investigate the inﬂuence of budget constraints on the algorithms in greater
detail, we introduce a budget factor β to establish predetermined budgets with
diﬀerent levels of constraint for each workﬂow [3]. Then, the budget constraints
B(G) of the workﬂow G can be determined by

                              B(G) = β × Cmin (G),                            (15)

where β ∈ [1.0, 1.4] with a variation step of 0.1. Cmin (G) denotes the lower bound
on the cost associated with executing workﬂow G, representing the minimum cost
necessary for the completion of workﬂow scheduling. When β = 1.0, the budget
is at its most restricted state. As the value of β rises, the budget constraint
becomes increasingly relaxed.
    Experiment 2: We maintain a constant budget constraint looseness (β =
1.4) and ﬁx the number of VMs (|V| = 12). We evaluate the makespan of the
PO-TD3 algorithm in comparison to baseline algorithms by employing two types
of workﬂows, each containing three task sizes: small, medium, and large.
    Experiment 3: We maintain a constant budget constraint looseness (β =
1.4) and utilize a medium-scale dataset to evaluate the makespan of the PO-TD3
algorithm in comparison to baseline algorithms. The number of VMs is set to 6,
12, 18, and 24, respectively.
    (3) Convergence. To compare and analyze the convergence characteristics
of the three algorithms, a medium-scale LIGO dataset with a budget constraint
relaxation degree of β = 1.4 is utilized for testing.

5.2   Results and Analysis
Success Rate Analysis. The experimental results presented in Table 2 indicate
that the average success rate of the MG-PRO algorithm for scheduling two types
of workﬂows is 80.67%. However, it becomes increasingly challenging to identify
a solution that adheres to the budget constraint when the budget is tightly con-
strained (β = 1.0), particularly in medium and large-scale datasets, where the
algorithm essentially fails to yield a feasible scheduling solution, resulting in a
success rate of 0. In comparison to the MG-PRO algorithm, the performance of
the TD3 algorithm is slightly inferior. Speciﬁcally, in the small-scale test scenario
of the LIGO workﬂow, TD3 requires the relaxation of the budget constraint to
β = 1.2 to identify a scheduling solution that meets the speciﬁed criteria. In con-
trast, the proposed PO-TD3 algorithm, as a DRL scheduling method, achieves
a 100% success rate. PO-TD3 demonstrates superior performance in satisfying
budget constraints, attributed to the budget constraint-aware capabilities of the
PCG mechanism. Notably, the design of the perception coeﬃcients within the
PCG mechanism establishes an upper threshold for the disposable cost asso-
ciated with each task. This eﬀectively ﬁlters out infeasible action choices in
advance, thereby ensuring that the generated scheduling plan complies with the
budget constraints.

132    Y. Zhang et al.

generate more eﬀective scheduling solutions, thereby minimizing makespan when
budget constraints are eased. Conversely, TD3 relies solely on the reward func-
tion to guide the learning process, which limits its eﬀectiveness in addressing the
budget-constrained workﬂow scheduling problem. In comparison with the TD3
and MG-PRO algorithms, PO-TD3 achieves the minimum makespan, demon-
strating optimal performance with average reductions of 66.74% and 56.03%,
respectively.

workﬂow scheduling. The integration of the PCG mechanism and OAS mapping

Convergence Analysis. The convergence curves of the three algorithms
applied to the LIGO workﬂow are illustrated in Fig. 5. In each iteration, the
cost data presented in Fig. 5(a) corresponds to the makespan data depicted in
Fig. 5(b), collectively reﬂecting the total scheduling cost and makespan gener-
134     Y. Zhang et al.

ated by the scheduling schemes employed by the algorithms during that round.
During the initial phase of training for the TD3 algorithm (approximately the
ﬁrst 50 iterations), the cost curve exhibits a decreasing trend. This trend is
attributable to the necessity of adhering to the budget constraint, which serves
as a fundamental prerequisite. The immediate rewards derived from the schedul-
ing environment guide the algorithm towards learning strategies that fulﬁll this
budget constraint. However, cost and makespan represent conﬂicting objectives;
as the cost gradually decreases, the makespan of the workﬂow tends to increase.
Although TD3 ultimately converges to a state that satisﬁes the budget con-
straint, its convergence appears premature, indicating a failure to continue in-
depth learning regarding strategies to minimize the makespan once the budget
constraint is met. In contrast, MG-PRO initially prioritizes cost reduction to
explore feasible solutions that comply with the budget constraint, subsequently
shifting its optimization focus toward minimizing the makespan. Consequently,
the makespan curve for MG-PRO demonstrates an initial increase followed by a
decrease. While MG-PRO outperforms TD3 in satisfying the budget constraint
and reducing makespan, PO-TD3 demonstrates superior convergence behavior.
The cost curves presented in Fig. 5(a) demonstrate that the cost incurred by PO-
TD3 at each iteration can be strictly controlled within the budget constraint, a
capability that can be attributed to the PCG mechanism it employs. Further-
more, the reward function of the PO-TD3 algorithm is exclusively inﬂuenced by
the makespan, allowing it to consistently focus on strategies aimed at optimizing
the makespan throughout the 300 iterations. This commitment results in a more
favorable convergence eﬀect regarding the minimization of makespan.




      Fig. 5. Convergence curves of the three algorithms on the LIGO workﬂow.



6     Conclusion and Future Work
A DRL-based scheduling algorithm, PO-TD3, is proposed to address the work-
ﬂow scheduling problem with budget constraints in heterogeneous cloud envi-
      A Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithm with Ordered Action Space            135

ronments while minimizing makespan. The PCG mechanism incorporated in the
PO-TD3 algorithm establishes an upper limit on the available cost for each task
by generating perception coeﬃcients, thereby ensuring that the entire workﬂow
adheres to budget constraints. Additionally, the OAS mapping approach eﬀec-
tively tackles the challenges posed by the dynamic action space and successfully
facilitates the transition from continuous to discrete actions. A series of compara-
tive experiments on scientiﬁc workﬂows validate the eﬀectiveness of the PO-TD3
algorithm, which demonstrates superior convergence performance against base-
line algorithms, achieving a 100% success rate in meeting budget constraints
and an average reduction of 61.43% in the makespan metric. Future work will
focus on developing workﬂow scheduling algorithms that not only satisfy budget
constraints but also address task privacy and security requirements, aiming to
provide more practical and secure solutions for workﬂow scheduling.

          STM-WFBP: Selective Tensor Merging
            Method in Distributed Learning

    Pingping Dong, Qingfen Yi, Lianming Zhang(B) , and Wensheng Tang(B)

                       Hunan Normal University, Changsha, China
                             {zlm,tangws}@hunnu.edu.cn



       Abstract. Communication is an important constraint for distributed
       deep learning training, and eﬃcient communication scheduling methods
       such as tensor merging accelerate distributed training by merging ten-
       sors from model layers. However, existing optimizations perform tensor
       merging greedily, failing to consider the occurrence of tensor stagnation
       for successive merging of multiple layers, resulting in suboptimal train-
       ing performance. In this paper, we propose the selective tensor merging
       method STM-WFBP to guide the tensor merging process. This method
       intelligently determines whether the solvable layers are eﬀectively merged
       and selects the eﬀectively merged layers, thus avoiding the phenomenon
       of tensor retention. Experimental results on two GPU clusters show that
       the STM-WFBP achieves a 4%-12% optimization in iteration time over
       existing methods, which proves its eﬀectiveness.


       Keywords: Distributed deep learning · Communication scheduling ·
       Gradient communication


1    Introduction

In recent years, artiﬁcial intelligence technology represented by deep learning has
made breakthroughs in application areas such as image recognition [1], speech
recognition [2] and autonomous driving [3]. As the deep neural network model
structure becomes more and more complex, the number of network layers and
parameters keeps increasing, the performance improvement of a single comput-
ing engine enters a bottleneck. Distributed deep learning is commonly used to
accelerate the training of deep neural networks (DNNs) [4,5], and data parallel
training is one of the popular methods for distributed deep learning training. In
a cluster of N nodes, data parallel training divides the data into N batches and
assigns them to these N nodes, each node processes the assigned training data
and completes the forward propagation and backpropagation, and at the end of
each training iteration, each node needs to synchronize the computed gradients
to update the global model parameters [6–8]. However, with the increase in the
number of computing nodes and the dramatic increase in model parameters,
the communication between nodes increases signiﬁcantly, and communication

 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 137–150, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_8
138    P. Dong et al.

gradually becomes a performance bottleneck [9–11]. For example, the computa-
tional power of Nvidia GPU has grown 30 times in the past 10 years, while it
took about 15 years to increase the network speed from 10Gbps to 100Gbps.
Therefore, optimizing communication performance is crucial in distributed deep
learning [12,13].
    In mainstream deep learning engines such as PyTorch [14], TensorFlow [15],
and MXNet [16], the DNN training process can often be represented as a directed
acyclic graph (DAG) (Fig. 1). DAG consists of two sets of computational opera-
tions and one set of communication operations. Since these two types of opera-
tions do not occupy the same resources, communication tasks can overlap with
computing tasks [17]. Based on this, the researchers overlapped backpropaga-
tion with gradient communication and proposed a wait-free backpropagation
algorithm WFBP [18] (Fig. 2(a). Due to the relatively few parameters of many
DNN layers, the amount of gradient communication data is small, and the wait-
free backpropagation algorithm introduces communication overhead every time
a gradient transmission is performed, which leads to low network utilization. In
recent years, researchers Yang et al. [19] have noticed this problem and proposed
a single-layer communication SyncEASGD method (Fig. 2(b), which merges the
gradients of all layers of DNN after the backpropagation of each iteration is com-
pleted, which can reduce most of the communication overhead, but the compu-
tational task and the communication task do not overlap. Shi et al. also noticed
this problem and proposed a tensor merging method MG-WFBP (Fig. 2(c) to
reduce communication overhead by merging adjacent layer gradients and overlap-
ping communication tasks with computational tasks [20]. However, the gradient
merging method MG-WFBP greedily merges tensors, resulting in the tensors of
multiple layers being merged and unable to be transmitted in time, making the
training iteration time suboptimal.




              Fig. 1. Dependency DAG in distributed DNN training.


   In order to solve this problem, we ﬁrst formulate the communication schedul-
ing problem in distributed training as an optimization problem with the goal
of minimizing the total training time of each iteration. Then, a selective ten-
sor merging wait-free backpropagation STM-WFBP method is proposed. Our
main contribution consists of three parts. First, we were the ﬁrst to propose
the Selective Tensor Merge Wait-Free Backpropagation Algorithm STM-WFBP,
which well solves the important shortcomings of the Fusion Tensor Wait-Free
     STM-WFBP: Selective Tensor Merging Method in Distributed Learning     139

Backpropagation MG-WFBP method. Second, we implemented the STM-WFBP
algorithm on PyTorch. Third, we veriﬁed the performance of STM-WFBP on
two GPU clusters and compared it with WFBP, SyncEASGD, and MG-WFBP.




                      Fig. 2. Timeline of the four methods.




2   Related Work

There is a lot of work to alleviate the communication bottleneck of distributed
training, and we mainly focus on the communication scheduling aspect. Com-
munication scheduling can be done by changing the execution order of commu-
nication tasks and computing tasks to overlap computing and communication
tasks, or by using the idea of pipelines to optimize scheduling. We summarize
the relevant work in this aspect of communication scheduling.
    Due to the layered structure of DNN models, communication tasks can over-
lap with computation tasks, making part of the communication cost hidden
in the computation time [21]. The classical wait-free backpropagation algorithm
WFBP [18] can enter communication immediately after the computation is com-
pleted without waiting for the completion of computation in all layers. DeAR
[22] transmits tensors by dividing them into small tensor blocks and according
to the priority. In order to increase the overlap degree of communication and
computation, Song et al. proposed an overlap-aware start-up shared wait-free
backpropagation algorithm [23]. US-Byte [24] schedules tensor blocks of varying
140     P. Dong et al.

sizes in a near-optimal order, thereby improving bandwidth utilization and min-
imizing the time for one iteration. TriRace [25] introduces 3D communication
scheduling, enabling eﬃcient computation and communication overlap. DRFT
[26] transforms the training problem into a knapsack problem and discovers new
overlapping opportunities in the training to eliminate computational bubbles
altogether. ASC-WFBP [27] utilizes simultaneous communication of tensors to
improve network bandwidth utilization. PACE [28] and Prophet [29] discuss the
optimal tensor partitioning strategy in priority scheduling. Bytedscheduler [30]
makes use of priority scheduling to overlap communication with forward com-
putation. Hashemi et al. ﬁnd a ﬁxed scheduling order for the tensor by using
critical path analysis, and propose two heuristic algorithms-Time-Independent
Communication Scheduling Algorithm, TIC, and Time-Associated Communica-
tion Scheduling Algorithm TAC, which are collectively referred to as TicTac
[31]. Jayarajan et al. considered the order of parameter consumption and pro-
posed a priority based parameter scheduling algorithm P3 [32]. SyncEASGD
[19] combines all tensors into a single transmission once all the layers have been
computed. MG-WFBP combines tensors based on backpropagation time and
communication time of each layer to improve communication eﬃciency.
    Despite many advances in communication scheduling, MG-WFBP greedily
performs tensor layer merging and ignores its communication waiting time, lead-
ing to communication idling and tensor stalling.


3     Preliminaries
In this section, we introduce the WFBP training iteration time model and the
All-Reduce communication model. For ease of presentation, we summarize the
frequently used mathematical notations in Table 1.

3.1   WFBP Iteration Time Modeling
For DNNs with L layers, in WFBP, the communication of layer l can overlap
with the backpropagation of layer l − 1, and the communication can only start
when layer l satisﬁes the following two conditions: (1) the backpropagation of
layer l has been completed; and (2) the communication of layer l + 1 has been
completed. The time axis of WFBP is shown in Fig. 2(a). Assuming that the
starting moment of forward propagation is 0, the moment tlb , when layer l starts
to compute the gradient, can be expressed as:

                                 tf             if l = L
                         τbl =                                                (1)
                                 τbl+1 + tl+1
                                          b     if 1 ≤ l < L

Layer l starts communicating at the moment τcl , which can be expressed as:

                         τbl + tlb                     if l = L
                 τcl =                                                        (2)
                                      c , τb + t b
                         max τcl+1 + tl+1  l     l
                                                       if 1 ≤ l < L

         Notation Description
         N        The number of computing nodes in the cluster

         b        Transmission and computation time per byte of all-reduce

         tb       Backpropagation time per iteration

The training iteration time includes forward propagation time, back propagation
time and gradient aggregation communication time, and one iteration training
time of WFBP can be expressed as:

                  titer = τc1 + t1c = max τc2 + t2c , τb1 + t1b + t1c            (3)


3.2   All-Reduce Communication Model

Assuming an even number of compute nodes in the cluster, the cost of peer-to-
peer communication can be modeled as α + βM , where α is the startup time, β
is the communication time per byte, and M is the message size. Then given N
computing nodes, the time cost of all-reduce can be summarized as:

                                 Tar = a + b × M                                 (4)

For a given cluster, the time cost of an all-reduce operation is a linear function of
the message size M with intercept a and slope b. We verify this linear model in the
experimental section later. Distributed training communication requires multiple
invocations of the all-reduce operation. However, in each all-reduce operation,
there is a startup overhead a that is independent of M . Moreover, Tar(M1 ) +
Tar(M2 ) > Tar(M1 + M2 ), i.e., transmitting a single all-reduce operation of size
M1 + M2 is more eﬃcient than transmitting a message of size M1 and a message
of size M2 , respectively.
142      P. Dong et al.

4     Methodology
4.1    Problem Formulation

Definition 1. Ordinary merger Layer. Layer r is an ordinary merger layer if
it is merged into layer r − 1 to defer its communication.

Definition 2. Ordinary Layer. A layer r is called an ordinary layer if it is not
an ordinary merged layer.

    Each layer is either a ordinary merger layer or a ordinary layer. Our goal is to
minimize the iteration time by ﬁrst obtaining the ordinary merge layer and then
selecting a valid ordinary merge layer merge layer among the ordinary merge
layers. We denote the above two layer types by lm and lc, respectively, and use
D(r)(D(r) ∈ {lm, lc}) to denote the type of the layer r. Given a network model
with L layers, the solution is denoted as:

        D=       D(1) , . . . , D(k) , . . . , D(L) | D(r) ∈ {lm , lc } and 1 ≤ r ≤ L      (5)

Our goal is to ﬁnd a D to minimize the iteration time, which can be expressed
as:
                        t = max{τc2 + t2c , τb1 + t1b } + t1c             (6)


4.2    Theoretical Analysis

Assuming that layer L, L − 1, ..., Layer 3 is a ordinary layer and Layer 2 is a
ordinary merge layer, then Layer 2 and Layer 1 are merged for transmission and
the iteration time can be expressed as:

                          tt = max{τc2 , τb1 + t1b } + Tar (m1 + m2 )                      (7)

Comparing Eq.(6) and Eq.(7), we need to ﬁnd the conditions under which Layer
2 is an ordinary merger layer.

    tt = max{τc2 , τb1 + t1b } + Tar (m1 + m2 ) < t = max{τc2 + t2c , τb1 + t1b } + t1c    (8)

This will be discussed in the following scenarios.
Condition 1: τc2 > τb1 + t1b . then Eq.(8) can be simpliﬁed as:

                 τc2 + a + b × (m1 + m2 ) < τc2 + 2a + b × (m1 + m2 )                      (9)

Since a > 0, Eq.(9) holds and the iteration time is shorter when layer 2 is a
ordinary merge layer.
Condition 2: τc2 + t2c < τb1 + t1b . then Eq.(8) can be simpliﬁed as:

                τb1 + t1b + a + b × (m1 + m2 ) < τb1 + t1b + a + b × m1                   (10)
      STM-WFBP: Selective Tensor Merging Method in Distributed Learning       143

Eq.(10) clearly does not hold, so layer 2 is the ordinary layer.
Condition 3: τc2 < τb1 + t1b < τc2 + t2c . then Eq.(8) can be simpliﬁed as:

            τb1 + t1b + a + b × (m1 + m2 ) < τc2 + 2a + b × (m1 + m2 )        (11)

Eq.(11) can be reduced to:
                                  τb1 + t1b < τc2 + a                         (12)
If Eq.(12) is true, then the second layer can be set as a ordinary merge layer
so that the iteration time will be shorter. In summary, for Eq.(8), the iteration
time can be reduced by setting the second layer as a ordinary merge layer under
conditions 1 and 3. The layer type judgment for each layer is as follows:

                         lm   if τbr−1 + τbr−1 < τcr + a and r > 1
                 τcr =                                                        (13)
                         lc   otherwise

When determining the layer type of each layer of a DNN, there are cases where
multiple consecutive layers are ordinary merger layers. Figure 3 shows a 5-layer
network model where layers 5 and 4 are ordinary merger layers, then these two
layers wait for layer 3 to ﬁnish its computation and merge with layer 3 for
transmission. For layer 5 that needs to wait for layer 3 to complete its computa-
tion before it can communicate, its communication wait time, or communication
deferral time, t5p is greater than the saved communication startup overhead.
Therefore, we chose to leave the 5th ordinary merge layer unmerged so that
neither communication idleness nor tensor stalling occurs. Layers 4 and 3 are
also ordinary merger layer, and there is no lagging since the communication in
layer 4 is communicated after the communication in layer 5 is completed, when
the computation in layer 2 has already been completed. In summary, after judg-
ing the layer type of each layer of the model, since the continuous merging of
multiple layers will lead to a tensor lagging situation, which will not reduce the
iteration time instead, it is necessary to dynamically update the communication
start moment of each layer and the communication postponement time of the
ordinary merger layer in a timely manner, and carry out selective merging for
the ordinary merger layer.

4.3   STM-WFBP Algorithm
Suppose there is a homogeneous distributed cluster of N nodes. We can measure
the startup time and per-byte communication time of the all-reduce of Eq.(4)
by NCCL-tests, so that the all-reduce communication time can be estimated for
any message size. For the forward propagation and back propagation times, we
can obtain the forward propagation and back propagation times for each layer
of the model through several baseline tests before formally training the model.
So, the all-reduce startup overhead, the moment of computation completion at
each layer, and the moment of communication at each layer are all known.
    For Algorithm 1, we take these known quantities as input and want to get
the layer type D for each layer of the model and the tag S for whether or not to
144     P. Dong et al.




                 Fig. 3. An example of training a 5-layer network.


merge. The algorithm ﬁrst assumes all layers as ordinary layers, and determines
whether the layer is an ordinary merger layer by checking Eq. (12) (line 3), and
if the layer is an ordinary merger layer, it needs to update the actual moment
of the start of communication between the layer and all lower layers (line 8–15).
It is also necessary to calculate the communication deferral time for the layer
number higher than that layer (line 16–18). The STM-WFBP algorithm further
evaluates the ordinary merging layer to determine whether to merge. The time
complexity of STM-WFBP is O(L2 ). The algorithm is executed only once before
formal training begins.

5     Experimental Evaluation
5.1   Experimental Setup
In order to verify the eﬀectiveness of the STM-WFBP algorithm, we conducted
experiments. The experimental platform includes two GPU clusters, 2-node and
4-node. The environment is deployed as Ubuntu 22.04, Horovod 0.19.1, NCCL
2.4.2, OpenMpi 4.0.1 and PyTorch 1.9.0.
We selected two datasets and ﬁve DNN models. The data consists of the cifar10
dataset and the cifar100 dataset, with Cifar10 consisting of approximately 50,000
training images and 10,000 validation images across 10 categories. The cifar100
dataset consists of approximately 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images
across 100 categories. The ﬁve DNN models include GoogleNet, ResNet-50,
ResNet-152, DenseNet-201, and DenseNet-161, and the training settings of the
DNN models are shown in Table 2. We compare STM-WFBP with three repre-
sentative baselines. (1) WFBP, which is the default optimization used by most
deep learning frameworks. (2) SyncEASGD, a communication mechanism that
merges all layer tensors and performs a single communication. (3) MG-WFBP,
an eﬃcient communication mechanism that ﬁnds corresponding tensor fusion
schemes for diﬀerent DNN models.

and SMG-WFBP algorithms on two clusters. To study the improvement of the
STM-WFBP algorithm in overall training time compared to the other three algo-
rithms, we recorded the average training time for 100 iterations when training

and 6.

In addition, to study the overlap of computation and communication in the
training of the STM-WFBP algorithm and three other algorithms, we measured
the non-overlapping communication time. For the same DNN model, the com-
putation time for each iteration remains almost constant, so the non-overlapping
communication time can eﬀectively reﬂect the overlap between computation and
communication (Figs. 7 and 8).
Non-overlapping communication time = iteration time - computation time; the
smaller the non-overlapping time, the higher the degree of overlap between com-
putation and communication. The results of the average non-overlapping com-
munication time for ﬁve DNN models iterating 1000 times measured on two
clusters are shown in Fig. 5(b) and Fig. 6(b). The SyncEASGD algorithm has
a large non-overlapping communication time because its communication is not
hidden. The MG-WFBP algorithm wastes some overlapping time due to delays
in the communication of partial tensors.

6     Conclusion
In this paper, we emphasize that tensor merging should not be done greedily.
To this end, we propose the algorithm STM-WFBP. This algorithm performs
selective merging of tensors, which eﬀectively merges tensors to reduce the com-
munication startup time, and also prevents multiple layers of tensors from being
in the communication wait phenomenon. Through experiments on two diﬀerent
clusters, we verify that on ﬁve deep neural networks, the STM-WFBP algorithm
can achieve shorter training times than WFBP, SyncEASGD and MG-WFBP.

             Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems

          Sihao Cheng1,2 , Yunfei Gu1(B) , Chentao Wu1 , and Jie Meng2

       Abstract. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remark-
       able capabilities across diverse natural language processing and other
       complex tasks. However, multi-agent deployments of LLMs often suf-
       fer from signiﬁcant inference overhead caused by a great deal of con-
       text and repeated tokens across agents, resulting in high Time-To-First-
       Token (TTFT) and elevated computational costs. To address these chal-
       lenges, we propose EACC (Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache), a system
       that enables position-independent reuse of key-value (KV) caches across
       agents by semantically chunking the prompt and managing reusable KV
       pairs through a globally accessible Agent Context Cache. EACC decou-
       ples context storage from computation, supports distributed deployment,
       and integrates with existing Position-Independent Caching (PIC) tech-
       niques such as CacheBlend and EPIC for selective recomputation. Our
       evaluation across multiple datasets and LLM backends demonstrates that
       EACC achieves up to 82.4% reduction in TTFT, while maintaining out-
       put accuracy, thereby oﬀering a scalable and eﬃcient inference infras-
       tructure for multi-agent services.


       Keywords: Large Language Models · Multi-Agent Systems ·
       Position-Independent Caching · Distributed Inference


1    Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are foundational to the development of intel-
ligent agents capable of autonomous thinking, decision-making, and interaction
with external tools. While single-agent frameworks have shown a promising
prospect, they become ineﬃcient in handling complex tasks requiring special-
ization and decomposition. Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) address this by dis-
tributing subtasks across multiple domain-speciﬁc agents. However, such archi-
tectures introduce massive redundancy in prompt tokens—due to repeated sys-
tem prompts, tool descriptions, and inter-agent communication—amplifying the
computational cost, particularly in the preﬁll stage of LLM inference [3,21].
Recent studies highlight that preﬁll computation dominates inference latency
and that over 80% of tokens in MAS contexts are repeated [40]. Traditional
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 151–171, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_9
152     S. Cheng et al.

preﬁx caching fails in this setting due to its reliance on exact preﬁx align-
ment. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) strategies like CacheBlend [44] and
EPIC [17] alleviate this limitation but are not directly optimized for multi-agent
scenarios.
    To bridge this gap, we present EACC, a system tailored for multi-agent
LLM inference that enables reusable context sharing at the chunk level. EACC
introduces a global Agent Context Cache (ACC), which maps prompt chunks to
their corresponding KV caches, allowing for eﬃcient lookup, sharing, and reuse
regardless of chunk position. Integrated with a distributed Chunk KV Store
and a cache-aware inference scheduler, EACC maximizes KV cache reuse and
optimizes inference routing to minimize TTFT and boost throughput in both
single-node and distributed deployments. Our results show that EACC achieves
up to 82.4% TTFT reduction and 18.9% end-to-end latency reduction, while
maintaining consistent accuracy in tasks such as question answering and tool
invocation.
    In summary, the contributions of our work are as follows:
– We identify key ineﬃciencies in multi-agent LLM serving, including redundant
  preﬁll computations due to lack of structured context sharing, ineﬀective
  reuse of KV caches in non-preﬁx settings, and suboptimal task scheduling
  in distributed environments.
– We propose EACC, a novel system that enables position-independent, chunk-
  level context cache reuse through a globally ACC, decoupling prompt chunk
  management from computation. We design and implement a distributed
  Chunk KV Store and a cache-aware Inference Instance Router, allowing eﬃ-
  cient cache lookup, transmission, and task scheduling across instances to opti-
  mize system throughput.
– We integrate two state-of-the-art PIC mechanisms, CacheBlend and EPIC,
  into EACC and explore their trade-oﬀs in multi-agent scenarios.
– We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets and LLMs, demon-
  strating that EACC achieves up to 82.4% reduction in TTFT and 94.7%
  token hit ratio, while maintaining inference quality across diverse workloads.


2     Preliminaries
2.1   Inference of LLMs
Mainstream LLMs, typically based on Transformer architecture, have inference
processes divided into two stages: prefill and decoding, each exhibiting completely
diﬀerent computational characteristics and costs [3,31,47].
   In the preﬁll stage, each token is processed through Transformer layers. In
each layer, tokens are converted to queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) to
compute attention scores, which are used to generate output tokens. The com-
putational complexity of the preﬁll stage is dominated by the self-attention mech-
anism, whose complexity is .O(N 2 ) with respect to the input length .N [3,31,33].
Key-value pairs (KV cache) are then stored to avoid redundant computations in
      EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems         153

the decoding stage. The ﬁrst output token is generated at the same time to ini-
tialize the decoding stage. The metric Time To First Token (TTFT) [21,33, 47]
captures the elapsed time until the ﬁrst token is produced and is closely approx-
imated by the preﬁll latency.
    During decoding, cached KV pairs are used to generate new tokens in an
autoregressive manner. The complexity of this stage is .O(N ), as it only interacts
with historical KV pairs, making it more eﬃcient than the preﬁll stage [16, 33,47].



2.2   LLM-Based Agent
Single Agent. While an LLM generates outputs based on given inputs, it lacks
the capability for continuous interaction with users or external systems [20].
Furthermore, LLMs cannot retrieve real-time information or adapt dynamically
to runtime conditions and external environments, which often leads to halluci-
nations [19] and limited task performance. External tools and self-thinking are
needed to enhance the LLM’s ability [22,30].




Fig. 1. An agent automatically performs tasks,       Fig. 2. The architecture
interacts with environments and achieve self-        of multi-agent systems.
evolution.


    The concept of an Agent was introduced to address these limitations [8, 25,
45]. An agent perceives its environments, makes decisions, and interacts with
external media to compensate for the LLM’s limitations, such as invoking APIs
or querying databases [11]. By specifying the agent proﬁle (system messages,
tools description, etc.) and integrating external information (documents) and
context (memory) [16, 27, 42], the LLM’s power get greatly enhanced. However,
the length of the prompt has been increased due to injecting more contextual
information into it, signiﬁcantly expanding the preﬁll consumption. Figure 1
illustrates the agent as a bridge between the user and the LLM.
154      S. Cheng et al.

Multi-agent. Single-agent systems are limited in handling complex tasks com-
prising multiple subtasks. Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) address this challenge by
decomposing complex tasks into simpler subtasks, each handled by specialized
agents, thereby improving overall eﬃciency [12, 24,28, 32, 38]. MAS accomplishes
complex objectives through collaboration among agents, where each specializes
in distinct domains or functionalities such as code generation or web search-
ing [24,26]. Figure 2 depicts this collaborative architecture, and Fig. 6 illustrates
the task decomposition process.

2.3    Preﬁx Caching and Position-Independent Caching
In multi-user and multi-request inference environments, reusing KV caches
substantially reduces redundant computations and preﬁll overhead [16, 31,47].
Two prevalent techniques are Prefix Caching (PC) [17, 21, 46] and Position-
Independent Caching (PIC) [14, 17,44], both aiming to optimize TTFT.




Fig. 3. The reuse of the preﬁx cache.    Fig. 4. One Scenario where preﬁx matching
                                         fails.


    Preﬁx Caching relies on exact longest-preﬁx matching among requests (an
example is shown in Fig. 1), allowing the system to bypass recomputing the
KV caches of the matched preﬁx [21,46]. However, PC requires strict preﬁx
alignment, since each token’s KV cache is position-dependent, limiting its appli-
cability in MAS scenarios. As illustrated in Fig. 2, even identical text segments1
cannot share KV caches if their preceding preﬁxes diﬀer (Figs. 3 and 4).
    In contrast, PIC treats repeatable prompt chunks as cache units, enabling
reuse regardless of their position within the prompt. Once the KV cache for a
chunk is computed, it is stored and reused in subsequent requests containing the
same chunk. Preﬁll is only executed on chunks absent from the cache. This mech-
anism resembles dynamic linking in software systems [17,18]. However, naïvely
concatenating cached KV pairs can disrupt attention mechanisms and degrade
output quality [3,14,44]. To address this, selective recomputation of a small
subset of cached tokens is performed to restore cross-chunk attention. Represen-
tative methods include CacheBlend [44] and EPIC [17], which diﬀer mainly in
their algorithms for selecting tokens for recomputation. The overall architecture
of PIC and the selective recomputation scheme are depicted in Fig. 5.
1
    We alternatively refer to them as prompt chunks as well.
          EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems      155




Fig. 5. An abstract of PIC mechanism. ① Preﬁll for the prompt chunks for the ﬁrst
time. ② Save the KV pairs to the cache. ③ One user makes a subsequent reuqest. ④
Check if there are any repetitions in the prompt chunks and reuse the cached KVs.
⑤ Perform the normal preﬁll computation for the uncached chunks and selectively
compute a portion of KVs for the cached tokens. ⑥ Decode, and return the result to
the user.


2.4        Relationship Between Token Hit Ratio and Preﬁll Consumption
As discussed in Sect. 2.1, preﬁll latency dominates inference delay for long inputs.
To reduce redundant computation, inference services cache KV pairs of processed
contexts (Sect. 2.3). In scenarios such as multi-turn dialogues, long context con-
catenation, or multi-agent services, eﬃcient hit of KV cache can signiﬁcantly
reduce the preﬁll overhead.
    Formally, let an inference request contain .L tokens, among which .Lhit tokens
hit the KV cache directly, and the remaining .Lmiss = L − Lhit tokens require
computation during preﬁll. We deﬁne the Token Hit Ratio as:

3     Deficiency in Multi-Agent Serving Systems
However, as the number of agents in MAS increases, the system’s total token con-
sumption grows approximately linearly with the agent count. Additionally, inter-
agent communication—such as using one agent’s output as another’s input—
introduces a substantial amount of redundant tokens. Together, these factors
exacerbate the inference burden, leading to increased latency. Prior work [40]
reports token duplication ratios as high as 86% in such systems. Although some
optimizations have been proposed [21,43, 46], several critical limitations remain
unresolved.

3.1   Lack of Structured Context Sharing
Despite the prevalence of token duplication in MAS—often manifested as
repeated prompt chunks including system messages, tool descriptions, historical
interactions, and intermediate agent outputs [26,38]—there is a notable absence
of eﬀective mechanisms for structured and systematic context sharing. Further-
more, the tight coupling between context management and computation impedes
the reuse of intermediate representations such as key-value (KV) caches, causing
redundant preﬁll computations upon each agent invocation.
    A ﬁne-grained agent context sharing framework capable of identifying and
reusing shared prompt chunks would substantially reduce redundant computa-
tion, accelerate token generation. While preliminary eﬀorts have investigated
cache reuse across diﬀerent requests and agents, their designs lack extensibility
and ﬂexibility to handle the dynamic and interdependent contexts typical in
MAS.

3.2   Underutilization of KV Cache Reuse
Requests in MAS add system prompts [7], tool results, and communication
between agents [40], amplifying the high token consumption of LLMs. There-
fore, preﬁx caching (discussed in Sect. 2.3) is used to reduce the redundant preﬁll
consumptions. However, as can be seen from Fig. 7, the shared prompt chunks
do not always appear in the form of preﬁxes, limiting the gains could obtain in
this setting. Exploring the application of position-independent caching to MAS
might be a crucial step in improving system performance.

3.3   Insuﬃcient Multi-agent Scheduling
As MAS scales to handle hundreds or thousands of agents and the capacity of KV
vectors becomes extremely large, eﬃcient scheduling becomes crucial to ensure
high throughput. However, current scheduling strategies lose the opportunity to
batch agents with overlapping prompt chunks and to improve token hit ratio [23,
41], especially in a distributed employment. A cache-aware scheduling policy can
exploit context overlap among agents to improve system-wide resource eﬃciency
and reduce latency.
      EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems        157

execution of agents based on the spe-   accomplish the task. Prompt chunks of the
ciﬁc task.                              same color represent the communication and
                                        repeated tokens between agents.


4     System Design
To address the challenges identiﬁed in multi-agent serving systems, we propose
EACC, a system optimized for eﬃcient inference in MAS. EACC decouples con-
text management from computation, employs structured caching, and introduces
position-independent prompt chunk caching with eﬃcient indexing mechanisms.
This design maximizes reuse of context and KV caches across requests and
agents. Furthermore, EACC supports cache-aware routing and eﬃcient schedul-
ing in distributed deployments. Notably, EACC is orthogonal to any speciﬁc PIC
mechanism, allowing seamless integration with methods such as CacheBlend or
EPIC. The overall architecture is illustrated in Fig. 8, which organizes the work-
ﬂow into four core components: Agent Context Cache (ACC), Chunk KV Store,
Prompt Chunks Handler, and Inference Instance Router.

4.1   Agent Context Cache
The Agent Context Cache (ACC) serves as a global context index accessible by
all inference instances in the system. Each user input is segmented into chunk-
level units, termed prompt chunks. ACC maintains mappings from these prompt
chunks to their corresponding KV caches. Each chunk serves as a unit of cache
reuse and is loaded into the inference engine during preﬁll. Each entry in ACC
contains the two main attributes:
• Chunk Hash: A SHA256-based hash serves as a unique identiﬁer, enabling
  eﬃcient retrieval.
• KV Cache Mapping Information: Metadata for fast cache lookup,
  including instance identiﬁers where the KV cache resides and their memory
158    S. Cheng et al.

  addresses. Replication of the same chunk’s KV cache across multiple instances
  is supported.
    Crucially, ACC’s KV mappings are position-independent; cache reuse is based
on chunk-level KV caches indexed by hash rather than strict preﬁx matching.
Thus, prompt chunks can be reused regardless of their positions within requests,
overcoming limitations of traditional preﬁx caching. This broader coverage bet-
ter supports dynamic and interdependent inference typical of MAS, eﬀectively
reducing TTFT.




Fig. 8. The system design of EACC. The numerical sequence represents the workﬂow
of a certain task.




4.2   Chunk KV Store
The Chunk KV Store caches KV pairs of individual prompt chunks separately.

Management and Chunk-Level Access on Cache. Following vLLM’s app-
roach [21], the Chunk KV Store organizes KV caches in a block-based manner.
The block size is conﬁgurable, with a default of 16 tokens. The cache manager
exposes CRUD interfaces, and employs a Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction
policy to balance simplicity and eﬀectiveness.
    Aligned with ACC’s chunk-level indexing, the Chunk KV Store treats each
chunk’s KV cache as an independent access unit, enabling chunk-level loading
and writing. Upon generation of a new chunk’s KV cache, the store allocates new
blocks, writes KV data, and maintains slot mappings, supporting subsequent
retrieval for preﬁll acceleration.

Global Distributed Caching. The Chunk KV Store is deployed across the
cluster, leveraging local high-bandwidth memory (HBM) resources per node and
supporting cache transmission. Each inference instance hosts a Chunk KV Store
      EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems         159

separately, and supports ﬂexible conﬁguration of cache capacity based on node
resources. Due to write-once-read-many semantics and capacity-based eviction,
multiple replicas of the same chunk’s KV cache may exist across instances with-
out requiring consistency protocols.


4.3   Prompt Chunks Handler
The Prompt Chunks Handler is responsible for prompt processing and cache
reuse management.


Semantic Chunking. Upon receiving a request, the handler segments the input
prompt .P into semantically meaningful chunks .C = {C1 , C2 , . . . , Cn }. Each
chunk is the minimal unit for KV cache reuse and uniquely identiﬁed by its hash
value .H(Ci ), where .H(·) denotes the hashing function.


Preprocessing of Prompt Chunks. Prompt Chunks Handler iterates
through all the chunks, encodes each chunk .Ci into token sequence .Ti , and
records the starting and ending positions of .Ti , which will be used later for con-
catenating its KV. Meanwhile, the Prompt Chunks Handler also accesses ACC
to check whether the corresponding KV of .Ci is already cached. If it is found,
it results in a cache hit (the corresponding KV is denoted as .KVih ) and records
the instances .IN S h where the KV is saved, meaning the chunk can be reused
without recomputation. Otherwise, it results in a cache miss (the corresponding
KV to be computed is denoted as .KVim ).


 KV Transmission Control. Preprocessed metadata is forwarded to the Infer-
 ence Instance Router (see Sect. 4.4) for routing and KV transmission deci-
 sions. Once the inference instance is determined, and successful retrieval of the
 KV pairs for the cached chunks, Prompt Chunks Handler loads cached KV
 pairs .KV h = {KVih | if Ci triggers a cache hit} into the inference engine
 in preparation for the incremental preﬁll phase. Speciﬁcally, only uncached
.KV     = {KVim | if Ci triggers a cache miss} are to computed during this
     m

 preﬁll. Beyond that, a few tokens of cached .KV h are recomputed to restore the
 cross-attention between prompt chunks.


4.4   Inference Instance Router

The Inference Instance Router schedules inference tasks by routing them to
appropriate execution instances, optimizing throughput through balancing token
hit ratios and instance loads. Algorithm 1 details the scheduling logic.
    Given a set of prompt chunks .{Ci | i = 1, 2, . . . , n}, the router queries the
cache status in metadata and computes the cached token counts per instance
