4.5     Workﬂow

 Figure 8 illustrates the complete workﬂow. The Prompt Chunks Handler seg-
 ments the input prompt into chunks .C = {Ci | i = 1, 2, . . . , 5}, with KVs of
 certain chunks (.C1 , C4 , C5 ) cached in the system. Each chunk is encoded, and
 metadata along with cache status for cached chunks .{KVih | i = 1, 4, 5} is
 recorded. The aggregated metadata is passed to the Inference Instance Router,
 which selects the optimal inference instance. If some required KVs are absent
 locally, remote transmissions are triggered. During inference, all cached KVs
.{KVi | i = 1, 4, 5} are loaded into the inference engine. The engine computes
       h

.{KVi     | i = 2, 3} incrementally for uncached chunks .C2 and .C3 , and selec-
       m

 tively recomputes .{KVih | i = 1, 4, 5} for cached chunks .{Ci | i = 1, 4, 5} to
 restore cross-attention across chunks. Decoding then proceeds to generate the
 ﬁnal output, producing new KVs for the output chunk. Finally, the inference
 results are returned to the user, and an asynchronous process writes newly gen-
 erated .{KV2 , KV3 , KVoutput } back to Chunk KV Store for future reuse. Since
 the write operation and result return are executed in parallel, it will not aﬀect
 the end-to-end latency. ACC is then updated accordingly to maintain mappings
 between the chunks and their cached KVs.


5      Implementation

We implement a prototype of EACC based on vLLM v0.4.1 [9], an eﬃcient infer-
ence framework for large language models. vLLM leverages advanced memory
management techniques such as PagedAttention [21] to reduce memory foot-
print and improve throughput. However, its built-in preﬁx caching mechanism
restricts the reuse of prompt chunks, limiting eﬃciency gains in multi-agent sce-
narios. To overcome this, EACC replaces traditional preﬁx caching with a PIC
foundation. Additionally, we implement inter-instance communication for KV
cache transmission and provide concise APIs for inference, status querying. The
distributed deployment can be seen in Fig. 9.


5.1     Selective Recomputation

Our work respectively integrate two types of PIC mechanisms into EACC, eval-
uate them, and verify the eﬀectiveness of EACC3 . Our implementation modiﬁes
the attention module’s forward pass within vLLM to support selective token
recomputation. For uncached chunks, all token KVs are computed fully. For
cached chunks, only a subset of tokens undergo KV recomputation. Speciﬁ-
cally, CacheBlend selects a proportion of tokens with high KV deviation (termed
HKVD tokens) for recomputation, whereas EPIC recomputes a ﬁxed number of
initial tokens per cached chunk.
 3
     Since the application of Prompt Cache [14] makes it unacceptable for the inference
     accuracy in MAS, we integrage CacheBlend [44] and EPIC [17] into our system,
     which we refer to as .EACC CB and .EACC E .
162     S. Cheng et al.




Fig. 9. The distributed inference cluster managed by Ray hosts multiple LLMEngine-
Actors, each with local Chunk KV caches and model weights. Global Agent Context
Cache coordinates cache reuse across instances. FastAPI provides online inference APIs
supporting streaming and asynchronous responses.



5.2   Distributed Deployment
EACC leverages the Ray framework [10] to build a scalable inference cluster
supporting distributed deployment and parallel task scheduling. Ray provides
robust task orchestration, actor lifecycle management, and resource scheduling,
enabling elastic scaling and eﬃcient load balancing.
   Each LLM inference instance is encapsulated as an LLMEngineActor bound
to a dedicated GPU, hosting its own Chunk KV Store and model weights. KV
cache transmission across nodes is implemented via PyTorch [13] tensor com-
munication primitives. To coordinate global context caching and scheduling, an
independent actor manages the global ACC, accessible by all inference instances.


5.3   RESTful APIs with FastAPI

We build RESTful APIs using the FastAPI framework [35], enabling end-to-end
online inference services capable of handling high concurrency and streaming
responses typical in agent-based workﬂows.
    The primary API interfaces are summarized in Table 1. Clients invoke gen-
erate.remote to trigger online inference and receive asynchronous token streams
via an AsyncGenerator. For streaming requests, EACC returns partial outputs
in real time using StreamingResponse; for non-streaming requests, the complete
ﬁnal result is returned once inference concludes.
      EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems      163

 /encode            POST Encode the input prompt into a token sequence

 /health            GET     Instance health check endpoint



6     Evaluation
As discussed earlier, EACC accelerates the preﬁll stage by partitioning prompts
into reusable chunks stored as KV pairs. In this section, we present a comprehen-
sive set of experiments to validate the eﬀectiveness of EACC. We aim to answer
the following questions: (1) How do prompt segmentation strategies and seg-
mentation granularity reduce redundant computation for repeated chunks? (2)
Can the PIC mechanism eﬀectively restore cross-attention and preserve infer-
ence quality? (3) In a real multi-agent online inference environment, can the
inference routing algorithm maximize the KV reuse ratio and thereby improve
throughput?


6.1   Setup
Testbed and Models. EACC is deployed on a two-node cluster. Each node is
equipped with two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs and an Intel Xeon 4216
CPU, with one inference instance per node. The LLM cache engine and Chunk
KV Store are deployed on separate GPUs within the same node. Nodes com-
municate via InﬁniBand (IB) [29] network interfaces with 100 Gbps bandwidth,
enabling eﬃcient cross-node KV cache transmission. For simplicity, experiments
on prompt chunking are conducted on a single node, except for those in Sect. 6.5.
We evaluate our approach using two open-source LLMs: Mistral-7B-Instruct-
v0.2 [39] and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct [2].


Baselines. To thoroughly assess EACC, we integrate it with two PIC mech-
anisms: CacheBlend [44] and EPIC [17], denoted as .EACC CB and .EACC E ,
respectively. For both methods, we vary the parameters controlling selective
recomputation. In .EACC CB -.r, .r denotes the recomputation ratio of cached
tokens. In .EACC E -.k, .k denotes the number of tokens recomputed in each cached
chunk. As EACC is implemented atop vLLM [9], which natively supports preﬁx
caching, we compare against both standard vLLM and vLLM with preﬁx caching
enabled.


Datasets. We evaluate EACC on four datasets: Agent-conversations-retrieval-
tool [6], Xlam-function-calling-60k [36], Squad (Stanford Question Answering
164    S. Cheng et al.

Dataset) [34] and 2WikiMQA [15]. Agent-conversations-retrieval-tool simulates
dialogues between multiple agents in real-world applications. Xlam-function-
calling-60k contains a large number of function call records, mainly used to
test an agent’s inference capabilities in tool invocation tasks. The prompts in
Squad contain historical memory information, simulating the need for LLMs to
enhance their abilities via historical memory in agent applications. 2WikiMQA is
a knowledge question-answering dataset covering various topics from Wikipedia
which can be divided into reusable chunk units.


Metrics. We adopt the following metrics to quantify EACC’s beneﬁts:

– Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) [21,33,47]: The elapsed time from receiv-
  ing a request to generating the ﬁrst output token.
– Token Hit Ratio (see Sec. 2.4): Higher values indicate reduced computa-
  tional cost in the preﬁll stage.
– F1 Score [4]: Measures the model’s answer accuracy.
– End-to-End (E2E) Latency [5,37]: The total time from request submission
  to receipt of the complete response in an online inference service.

Since EACC only modiﬁes the system-level cache reuse and preﬁll logic, with-
out changing the decoding computation, the per-request metrics TBT [33] and
TPOT [1,47] should remain unaﬀected. Therefore, these metrics are excluded
from the following experiments (Fig. 11).




                  Fig. 10. Token hit ratios in diﬀerent datasets.




6.2   Eﬀectiveness of Reducing Redundant Computation

In this experiment, we emulate multi-agent workﬂows on the datasets described
above to evaluate whether EACC can eﬀectively reduce redundant computation
and lower preﬁll latency. For Agent-conversations-retrieval-tool, Xlam-function-
calling-60k, and Squad, we preselected 200 samples for inference to warm up
the Chunk KV Store, thereby simulating a state in which the cache becomes
saturated after a period of operation. For 2WikiMQA, 160 samples were used
for this warm-up phase. Following this, 20 requests were randomly drawn from
the remaining data to assess the performance gains from cache reuse.
     EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems         165




      Fig. 11. EACC signiﬁcantly reduces TTFT while maintaining accuracy.



 Results. The results demonstrate that EACC signiﬁcantly improves both
 TTFT and token hit ratio. As illustrated in Fig. 10, vLLM exhibits a token
 hit ratio of zero, as it recomputes all tokens from scratch. In contrast, EACC
 achieves the highest token hit ratio, reaching up to 94.7%, owing to its chunk-
 level caching mechanism. As discussed in Sec.2.4, TTFT exhibits a strong nega-
 tive correlation with token hit ratio; thus, EACC’s high hit ratio translates into
 optimal TTFT, delivering up to 82.4% improvement.
     Moreover, the observed ﬂuctuation in F1 score is generally within 30%, indi-
 cating that EACC can balance accuracy and latency eﬀectively. Notably, setting
.r = 15 for EACC.      and .k = 8 for EACC.E yields a favorable trade-oﬀ between
                   CB

6.3   Cache Granularity Analysis
This experiment investigates how the semantic granularity of chunking inﬂuences
KV reuse and preﬁll eﬃciency in EACC. While maintaining the core principle
of semantic segmentation, we adjust chunking granularity, i.e., the ﬁneness of
semantic divisions, by employing three strategies: (1) Coarse: splitting only at
major semantic boundaries (e.g., between system prompt and user prompt);
(2) Moderate: further splitting system messages according to functional cate-
gories; and (3) Fine: partitioning at the smallest variable unit within a sentence
(e.g., variables or timestamps). An example is presented in Fig. 12. Using the
Xlam-function-calling-60k dataset, we ﬁx the total context length per request
while varying chunk granularity to assess its eﬀect on token hit ratio and accu-
racy. The results are illustrated in Fig. 13.
    As chunk size increases, a greater number of identical tokens is required for
a match, resulting in a reduced token hit ratio. Even small changes within a
chunk can degrade its reusability, reducing EACC’s caching advantage. How-
ever, smaller chunks have stronger inter-chunk semantic dependencies. If only a
limited subset of tokens is selectively recomputed, cross-chunk attention restora-
tion may be incomplete, thereby impacting inference quality. For EACC.E , the
ﬁrst .k tokens in each chunk are recomputed regardless of chunk length. As the
number of chunks increases, the total recomputed tokens grow, and when chunk
size becomes excessively small, we can speculate that TTFT may increase rather
than decrease.
    In theory, the intersection point between hit ratio and accuracy curves rep-
resents the optimal balance between computational gains from cache reuse and
inference quality. The choice of semantic chunking strategy constitutes an inte-
gral part of the system’s optimization space, warranting further exploration in
future work.


6.4   Position Independence Veriﬁcation
We further examine the position independence property of EACC by ﬁxing the
input prompt and chunking strategy while altering the source positions of the
prompt chunks. In this setting, a chunk appears at diﬀerent positions within
the original prompt across trials, thereby carrying diﬀerent positional encod-
ings. This enables evaluation of the impact of positional variation on the PIC
mechanism.
   As shown in Fig. 14, altering chunk positions has negligible impact on both
TTFT and F1 score. The total number of tokens requiring computation remains
constant, resulting in stable TTFT. Moreover, EACC consistently restores
cross-attention information through selective recomputation, preserving infer-
ence accuracy. These results conﬁrm that EACC is agnostic to the positional
arrangement of chunks in the input, thereby enhancing cache reuse ﬂexibility
and system robustness.
      EACC: Eﬃcient Agent Context Cache Sharing for Multi-Agent Systems         167

diﬀerent chunk orders.                cation strategies.


6.5   Distributed Cache Load Balancing and Transmission Eﬃciency
To evaluate the impact of KV cache transmission and reuse in a distributed
environment—particularly within multi-node inference clusters—and to investi-
gate how load balancing and inter-node cache transmission aﬀect system perfor-
mance, we conduct experiments using the Xlam-function-calling-60k dataset and
the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model. We set the batch size to 4 and compare two
request allocation strategies: a random allocation strategy and the cache-aware
allocation strategy described in Algorithm 1.

Results. The TTFT and E2E latency results for the two strategies are shown
in Fig. 15. Under the cache-aware allocation strategy, although KV data is trans-
mitted across nodes, the cross-node KV transmission introduces negligible addi-
tional overhead to TTFT. On average, cache transmission accounts for only
13.1% of the total TTFT. Consequently, TTFT under the cache-aware strategy
still outperforms the random allocation baseline.
     While the reduction in TTFT contributes only marginally to the overall
improvement in E2E latency, the cache-aware strategy’s consideration of load
balancing leads to a decrease in end-to-end latency. This advantage is expected
to become more pronounced as the number of nodes increases. The high eﬃciency
of cross-node KV transmission ensures that even in distributed environments,
EACC’s performance is optimized, eﬀectively supporting inference tasks in large-
scale MAS.


7     Future Work
Our prototype, developed on vLLM v0.4.1 [9], currently lacks support for CPU-
based model weight oﬄoading, which constrains our experimentation with large
model architectures. Notably, state-of-the-art techniques such as CacheBlend [44]
and EPIC [17] are also developed based on this version. Our primary focus, how-
ever, lies in the design and evaluation of cache algorithms and system architec-
ture rather than the deployment of large models in this iteration of the research.
Future work will involve migrating the EACC framework to the latest versions of
168     S. Cheng et al.

vLLM that incorporate model oﬄoading capabilities. This migration will enable
us to experiment with large-scale language models and further evaluate their
scalability and eﬀectiveness in realistic scenarios.


8     Conclusion
This paper presents EACC, a system-level framework designed to mitigate
redundancy and ineﬃciency in multi-agent LLM serving. By decoupling context
storage from computation and enabling position-independent KV cache reuse
through semantic prompt chunking, EACC eﬀectively reduces preﬁll latency
and improves overall system throughput. The framework supports distributed
deployment and eﬃcient scheduling, and it integrates seamlessly with existing
PIC techniques. Experimental evaluations on diverse datasets and models show
that EACC achieves up to 94.7% token hit ratio, leading to as much as 82.4%
reduction in TTFT and 18.9% reduction in end-to-end latency, while maintain-
ing model accuracy. These results position EACC as a promising solution for
optimizing large-scale multi-agent services, with broad applicability in conver-
sational AI, and automated decision-making scenarios.

       AccuGraph: Memory-Eﬃcient Full-Graph
           GNN Training on a Single GPU
            via Subgraph Accumulation

         Liyang Wu1 , Menghan Jia1(B) , Lizhi Zhang1 , Yahui Wu1 ,
    Gongqingjian Jiang1 , Jiezhong He1 , Chunye Gong1,2 , and Yinghui Gao3
   1
    College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense
                   Technology, Changsha, Hunan 410073, China
{wuly58,jiamenghan12,zhanglizhi15,wyh,jianghydro,jiezhonghe}@nudt.edu.cn
       2
         National Supercomputer Center in Tianjin, Tianjin 300457, China
               3
                 Academy of Military Science, Beijing 100000, China



       Abstract. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential for
       graph-based applications. Full-graph GNN training is a commonly used
       approach because it enables more comprehensive aggregation of neigh-
       bor information. However, full-graph training requires loading the entire
       graphs into GPU memory, often exceeding GPU memory limits when
       training on large graphs. To address this, we propose accumulated sub-
       graph training method, which decomposes a computationally expensive
       full-graph update into multiple smaller, accumulated subgraph updates,
       while preserving exact mathematical equivalence. However, a naive
       implementation of this approach incurs serious redundant CPU-GPU
       data transfers and GPU computations. To address this challenge, we pro-
       pose AccuGraph, an improved accumulated subgraph training method
       that incorporates two complementary optimizations: (1) topological sim-
       ilarity based nodes pre-sorting strategy to allocate structurally similar
       nodes in to the same sub-batch, which increases intra-batch neighbor
       overlap and lessens duplicated neighbors across batches; and (2) hybrid
       redundancy caching and reuse technique, which prunes residual redun-
       dancy and reuses the cached embeddings of high-frequency nodes and
       cross-batch nodes, thus reducing repeated data transfers and computa-
       tions. Experimental results demonstrate that optimized AccuGraph sub-
       stantially reduces memory consumption while preserving training accu-
       racy, achieving up to a 11.5× speedup in training time. Notably, it com-
       pletes training on the 111M-node ogbn-papers100M dataset within 5 s
       using less than 15 GB of GPU memory, enabling large-scale GNN train-
       ing on consumer-grade hardware.


       Keywords: GNNs · Full-graph training · Memory eﬃciency

1   Introduction
Graph neural networks (GNNs) [1,17,29,30] have emerged as the dominant
paradigm for learning from graph structure data: By aggregating information
from neighbors across multiple layers, GNNs integrate structural patterns with
node features and achieve strong performance on tasks such as link prediction
[20], node and graph classiﬁcation [18,25], and community detection [14].
    Full-graph training is a widely adopted paradigm in GNN training. Com-
pared with mini-batch training [21,26], which risks accuracy degradation due to
biased gradient estimates and sampling-induced loss of topological information
[5,10,28], full-graph training serves as a promising paradigm for its eﬀectiveness
brought by full-batch gradient descent and full-neighbor aggregation semantics.
However, this approach requires loading the entire graph and features into GPU
memory, which becomes infeasible for large graphs due to out-of-memory (OOM)
errors.
    To enable GNN training under constrained GPU memory, gradient accumu-
lation [8] has emerged as an eﬀective solution. This technique works by accu-
mulating gradients across multiple micro-batches before executing parameter
updates, thereby simulating the large-batch training while maintaining memory
eﬃciency. Inspired by this, we propose accumulated subgraph training method,
which decomposes a full-graph update into a sequence of accumulated subgraph
computations. First, the training nodes are partitioned consecutively into sub-
batches. A sub-batch denotes a subset of training nodes calculated together
each forward propagation. Second, for each sub-batch we construct its batch
subgraph by expanding the target nodes’ L-hop neighborhood. Third, generate
the sub-batch node embeddings via forward propagation and calculate gradients
of each batch via backward propagation. Forth, gradients from each subgraph are
accumulated, and a single parameter update is applied after all subgraphs have
been processed. By applying global degree normalization, which uses a consis-
tent normalization factor across batches, this scheme preserves the mathematical
equivalence to full-graph gradient computation under standard assumptions.
    However, a naive implementation of the approach suﬀers from substantial
redundant CPU–GPU data transfers and repeated GPU computations. These
redundancies arise because of the extensive neighbor overlap among sub-batches,
a consequence of the inherent structural dependencies among nodes in graph
data. To mitigate this challenge, we extend the accumulated subgraph training
approach by incorporating two complementary optimizations, which together
deﬁne AccuGraph. First, we propose to execute topological similarity based
nodes pre-sorting (T SP S) before consecutive partitioning, which implicitly allo-
cates structurally similar nodes to the same sub-batch. By increasing intra-batch
neighbor overlap, T SP S raises batch density and reduces overlapped structures
between batch subgraphs. Second, to deal with the remained uneliminated redun-
dancy, we design a hybrid redundancy caching and reuse technique (HCR), in
which overlapped structures are pruned and cached intermediate embeddings
of redundant nodes are reuse in the pruned subgraphs, thus alleviate repeated
data transfers and computations. Speciﬁcally, we adopt hybrid caching strat-
174     L. Wu et al.

egy to manage the embedding of nodes with diﬀerent characteristic of repeated
occurrence for better memory utilization.
    By executing two typical GNNs on four representative datasets, we show
that AccuGraph can achieve full-graph training under constrained memory bud-
gets, while maintaining the same-level accuracy. With optimization, AccuGraph
achieves up to 11.5× speedup in per-epoch training time over the vanilla baseline.
Experiment results demonstrate that AccuGraph can complete a single epoch
training pass on the ogbn-papers100M(with 111 million nodes) within 5 s using
less that 15 GB memory, enabling large-scale graph processing on consumer
hardware.
    In summary, we make the following contributions.
– To the best of our knowledge, we are the ﬁrst to propose accumulated sub-
  graph training method to achieve full-graph training on large graphs with
  tight GPU memory constraint.
– We further analyze the redundancy challenge introduced by the naive accu-
  mulated subgraph training approach. To mitigate it, we propose the T SP S
  strategy to reduce overlapped structures between batch subgraphs, and intro-
  duce the HCR technique to diminish the residual overlaps.
– Our implementation and evaluation show that AccuGraph enables full-graph
  training on large graphs on single GPU. By alleviating the redundancy prob-
  lem, AccuGraph signiﬁcantly improves both training speed and memory uti-
  lization compared to the vanilla baseline.


2     Background and Motivation
2.1   Graph Neural Networks
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of deep learning models designed
for graph-structured data. They operate via message passing, where structural
information and node/edge features propagate through the network to generate
context-aware node representations.
    A typical GNN stacks multiple layers, with the number of layers L deﬁn-
ing the network depth and the receptive ﬁeld size. Speciﬁcally, an L-layer GNN
enables each node to aggregate features from its L-hop neighbors through suc-
cessive nonlinear transformations. Given a graph G(V, E), where V and E are
the sets of nodes and edges respectively, each node v ∈ V has a raw feature
vector xv . The computation at the lth layer is formulated as:

                       hlv = φl (hl−1  l l−1
                                  v , ψ (hu , ∀u ∈ N (v), W
                                                            l−1
                                                                )               (1)

where hlv is the feature of node v at layer l, N (v) denotes the set of neighbors of
v, ψ l aggregates neighbor features, the aggregated information will be computed
using parameters W l−1 , and φl applies nonlinear transformations to the outcome.
The initial node features correspond to h0v = xv . Diﬀerent GNN models mainly
diﬀer in their message aggregation, activation functions, and ways of handling
graph topology.
                                                                AccuGraph      175

2.2   Existing Full-Graph Training Paradigms

Aligned with fundamental objectives of deep learning models, the core goal
in training GNNs is to learn a mapping that captures dependencies between
node features and corresponding labels, enabling accurate predictions for unseen
nodes.
    Two common methods for training GNNs are mini-batch training and full-
graph training. Mini-batch training methods [21,26] compute gradients on a sub-
set of nodes at each iteration to stochastically approximate the full gradient, and
each training epoch consists of multiple iterations. It often combine with various
neighbor sampling techniques [3–5,28] to alleviate the memory bottleneck caused
by neighbor explosion. While reducing computation cost, they introduce the risk
of biased gradient estimates and may discard edges that capture important topo-
logical information [27], potentially degrading the learned representations [10].
    By contrast, full-graph training serves as a promising GNN training method
for its eﬀectiveness brought by full-neighbor aggregation semantics and full-batch
gradient descent [10,15,24]. In each epoch, full-graph methods perform forward
and backward propagation over the entire graph, computing node representa-
tions based on all nodes and edges. The gradients are then calculated using the
loss on the whole training set to update the model parameters. The integrity of
information aggregation and the stability of convergence enable full-graph train-
ing to achieve superior predictive accuracy [7,9,10]. It is equivalent to training
on a batch that contains all nodes in training set, hence the term full-batch
training.
    Since memory usage scales with graph size, full-graph training becomes
impractical for large graphs under limited GPU memory. This poses signiﬁcant
challenges as real-world graphs continue to grow in size. To cope with this scala-
bility problem, distributed training systems [2,15,16,23] have been developed for
partitioning and parallelizing computations across multiple GPUs or machines.
However, distributed system demands substantial hardware resources, setting a
signiﬁcant barrier for researchers without access to multiple GPUs or large-scale
computing infrastructure.
    Consequently, we are motivated to scale full-graph training on large-scale
graphs on consumer hardware.


3     A Naive Accumulated Subgraph Training Method
3.1   Definition

Gradient accumulation strategy simulates larger batch training by accumulating
gradients from multiple batches before performing parameters update. Inspired
by the technique, we propose a method that scales stable full-graph training to
large graphs under limited GPU memory without accuracy compromise.
    In what follows, we formalize this idea as accumulated subgraph training with
global degree normalization, which is referred as accumulated subgraph training
in the remainder of this paper for notational convenience.
176    L. Wu et al.

   Here, we introduce the concept of a sub-batch, deﬁned as a subset of training
nodes that are calculated together in a single forward propagation. Unlike a
conventional mini-batch in SGD, which is typically sampled i.i.d. to yield an
unbiased gradient estimate, a sub-batch can be formed by simple consecutive
partitioning for convenience without degrading model performance.
   The procedure of accumulated subgraph training is as follows:
1. Partition the training set Bf ull into K sub-batches {B1 , . . . , BK }.
   To correctly perform message passing and capture all relevant neighborhood
   information for nodes in Bi , it is necessary to include their multi-hop neigh-
   bors in a localized subgraph rather than considering these nodes in isolation.
2. Thus, for each Bi , construct batch subgraph Si by the following steps.
   (a) First, expand all immediate neighbors of the sub-batch nodes.
   (b) Then, iteratively expand the newly reached nodes for L − 1 additional
       steps to cover all L-hop neighbors required by an L-layer GNN.
   (c) The induced subgraph, containing both target nodes and all their
       expanded neighbors, is then indexed and loaded with raw features.
   Figure 2 presents schematic illustrations of batch subgraphs.
3. For each batch subgraph Sk :
   (a) Perform a forward pass to compute k (θ), which is the loss of Bk . For
       GNN models with normalization layers, apply global degree normalization
       by using each node’s degree in the full graph (rather than its batch-local
       degree) when normalizing messages.
   (b) Perform a backward pass to obtain its gradient contribution gk =
                                        K
       ∇θ k (θ), accumulating G = k=1 gk .
4. After processing all K batches (i.e., at the end of the epoch), apply the update:
   θ ← θ − η G, where η is the learning rate.




             Fig. 1. Workﬂow of naive accumulated subgraph training.


    Figure 1 depicts the process of 3) and 4). Mathematically, this procedure
exactly recovers the full-batch gradient descent update. The use of global degree
normalization ensures that normalization factors match those in a true full-graph
pass, thus preserving the equivalence in both optimization trajectory and ﬁnal
solution.
                                                               AccuGraph      177




Fig. 2. Comparison of two sub-batch partitioning schemes and their eﬀect on batch-
subgraph size and inter-batch redundancy.


3.2   Challenges
Though accumulated subgraph training enables true full-graph gradient compu-
tation under strict memory budgets, the intrinsic high overlap in the graph’s
topology does induce critical bottlenecks. With the phenomenon of neighbor
explosion, batch subgraphs usually severely overlap across sub-batches, which
cause redundant CPU to GPU transfers and GPU computation.
    On one hand, the expansion to multi-hop neighborhoods signiﬁcantly ampli-
ﬁes structural redundancy. As the number of hops increases, the size of each
subgraph grows rapidly (see Fig. 2), causing many nodes and edges to appear
repeatedly across multiple batch subgraphs. We also test on the igb-small [11]
and ﬁnd that, setting batch size to 8192, the constructed batch subgraphs on
average contains about 58860 nodes when L = 1 and 399823 nodes when L = 2.
This exponential growth not only increases memory consumption but also leads
to duplicated computations during training. On the other hand, as illustrated in
Fig. 2 (Scheme A vs. Scheme B), consecutive partitioning of the original training
nodes tends to scatter topologically related nodes across diﬀerent sub-batches.
When the partitioning ignores the graph’s inherent community or cluster struc-
ture (Scheme A), nodes that share many neighbors are split across batches. The
resulting batch subgraphs exhibit little intra-batch neighbor overlap but sub-
stantial inter-batch overlap, which inﬂates the overall size of subgraphs. In the
example, nodes 2, 4, 9, 11 recur in two sub-batches under Scheme A and there-
fore incur repeated host–device transfers and redundant recomputation of their
intermediate embeddings. By contrast, grouping nodes with high topological
similarity into the same sub-batch (Scheme B) concentrates neighbors locally
and increases intra-batch overlap while reducing overlap across batches. Thus,
reordering the training set substantially mitigates redundancy.
    To address the redundancy challenge, we propose a topological similarity
based nodes pre-sorting strategy that promotes intra-batch neighborhood cohe-
178    L. Wu et al.

sion, eﬀectively constraining subgraph size inﬂation and alleviating redundancy.
For the intrinsic redundancy that cannot be eliminated by partitioning alone,
we further introduce a hybrid redundancy caching and reuse technique to signif-
icantly reduce redundant data transfers and duplicated computations through
pre-computed intermediate embedding caching and reuse. We incorporate the
above design techniques into AccuGraph, an GNN training framework that
enables full-graph training on large graphs with limited GPU memory, and the
details of our design are presented in Sect. 4.




                      Fig. 3. Workﬂow of AccuGraph framework.




4     The AccuGraph Framework
4.1   Overview
In this section, we describe the workﬂow of our system and highlight the com-
ponents where we introduce optimizations.
    The overall workﬂow is depicted in Fig. 3. Given a dataset and model, Accu-
Graph ﬁrst treats the entire training set as a single full batch and employs
the Betty [26] memory-estimation procedure to predict whether a full-batch
update will trigger OOM errors. Speciﬁcally, we estimate the memory consump-
tion base on model parameters and input & output sizes, allowing feasibility
to be assessed without executing on the GPU. AccuGraph executes full-batch
training whenever the estimated memory consumption falls within the device’s
available capacity. Full-batch updates deliver superior performance provided suf-
ﬁcient GPU memory is available. Otherwise, the framework falls back to accu-
mulated subgraph training.
    Because the order of training nodes aﬀects the result of consecutive partition-
ing, AccuGraph ﬁrst applies a topological similarity based pre-sorting strategy
to the training nodes, which is one of the main innovations of this paper. On
the sorted node sequence, AccuGraph then determines a suitable batch size by
reusing the memory estimates mentioned above in a binary-search procedure:
Starting from the largest power-of-two not exceeding the number of training
nodes and halving as needed, the search ﬁnds the maximal usable batch size
(always powers of two) that satisﬁes the memory constraint. Once the batch size
                                                                  AccuGraph    179

is ﬁxed, sub-batches and their corresponding batch subgraphs are pre-generated
and reused across all epochs, eliminating per-epoch construction overhead. Dur-
ing training, these pre-generated batch subgraphs are processed sequentially
and optimized using the proposed hybrid redundancy caching and reuse tech-
nique, which combines a static cache for frequently recurring embeddings with a
dynamic cache for locally recurring nodes. Section 4.2 and 4.3 provide detailed
descriptions of our two optimizing techniques.


4.2   Topological Similarity Based Nodes Pre-Sorting Strategy

Since the node ordering directly determines which nodes are placed in the same
batch, our objective is to improve the internal density of each batch, i.e., the
structural similarity among its nodes, by reordering the training set prior to par-
titioning. Although structural similarity can also be measured using higher-order
neighbors (e.g., two-hop or beyond), the number of common ﬁrst-order neigh-
bors provides a more direct and tractable indicator of topological relatedness.
Accordingly, we adopt the Common Neighbors (CN ) Metric to measure pairwise
node similarity:

                 CN(x, y) = |N (x) ∩ N (y)| =                     1.           (2)
                                                  u∈N (x)∩N (y)


For two nodes x, y ∈ V , a larger CN(x, y ) reﬂects stronger structural similarity.
    However, directly computing the CN values for all node pairs and subse-
quently sorting the entire set by similarity is computationally prohibitive, and
in fact NP-hard for large graphs. To overcome this, we design a heuristic pre-
sorting algorithm that leverages local graph structural properties to approximate
similarity-based ordering while remaining scalable.
    The method is motivated by the following observation: Within the subgraph
induced by the out-neighbors of a given set S , the node v with the maximal
in-degree tends to have substantial overlap in predecessors with S . This indi-
cates that v shares the strongest topological connection with S . Similarly, other
nodes with relatively high in-degree in this induced subgraph also exhibit closer
connections with S . This property enables the set S to function as a trigger set,
serving as the seed for grouping topologically similar nodes. By selecting nodes
with the highest in-degrees from this induced subgraph, we can naturally cluster
together nodes that are structurally similar.
    The eﬀectiveness of this procedure strongly depends on the quality of the
trigger set. If S is chosen at random, the maximum in-degree in the induced
subgraph tends to be small, which weakens the ability to cluster nodes with
strong similarity. To mitigate this, our algorithm begins by sampling a con-
nected small subgraph as the initial trigger set Sinit , thereby ensuring inherent
connectivity. We then select g nodes, where g denotes the grouping size during
sorting—that exhibit the highest in-degrees within the subgraph induced by the
out-neighbors of Sinit .
180     L. Wu et al.

    Once the ﬁrst node group is selected, it is extracted along with its incoming
edges to avoid re-selection. Since some of their predecessors may still serve as in-
neighbors of other nodes, they remain in the graph. These remaining predecessors
are naturally chosen as the next trigger set for two reasons: (1) They ensure
continuity of the sorting process, and (2) since some of them may also be common
in-neighbors of the nodes in the previously selected group, they provide a natural
source of similarity for the next grouping. The algorithm then iteratively repeats
this procedure—using the current trigger set to identify new node groups while
dynamically updating the triggers—until all nodes are exhausted.
    After generating all node groups, we perform an additional adjustment to
their sequential order to address potential imbalances in node degree. Although
local degrees within subgraphs are not identical to global degrees, they remain
strongly correlated. As a result, the groups produced in generation order tend to
be arranged from higher to lower degree. Under ﬁxed batch-size constraints, this
ordering creates an imbalance: Earlier batches containing higher-degree nodes
induce much larger subgraphs, which restricts batch size due to GPU memory
limits, while later batches underutilize available memory.
    To alleviate this imbalance, we apply a simple reordering heuristic:
1. Arrange all groups in their generation order.
2. Reverse the second half of the list.
3. Interleave the reversed second half with the ﬁrst half.
    To preserve intra-batch density and retain the spatial locality beneﬁts from
contiguous node expansion, the grouping size g must be a divisor of the batch
size. Accordingly, AccuGraph sets g to a smaller power of two, ensuring com-
patibility with the batch size.
    Importantly, this pre-sorting strategy optimizes structural compactness with-
out compromising predictive accuracy under accumulated subgraph training. It
provides a scalable and eﬀective mechanism for constraining subgraph size inﬂa-
tion and mitigating redundancy across batches.

4.3   Hybrid Redundancy Caching and Reuse Technique
Although duplicated neighbors across batches can be diminished by our TSPS
strategy, overlapped structure between batch subgraphs is unavoidable given
real-world graph topologies.
    Our framework employs full-neighborhood aggregation and uses gradient
accumulation to simulate full-batch gradient descent. Consequently, within an
epoch the intermediate embedding of a given node computed in diﬀerent batches
is exactly the same; this makes the caching and reuse of these embeddings accu-
rate and lossless from the perspective of model correctness. Motivated by this
observation, we prune the overlapped structure in batch subgraphs, cache the
redundant intermediate embeddings, and reuse them across batches to reduce
repeated transfers and recomputation without sacriﬁcing accuracy.
    As recurrence frequency and temporal locality diﬀer across nodes, we parti-
tion redundant nodes into two categories and adopt distinct caching strategies
                                                                AccuGraph      181

for each. The ﬁrst category, High-frequency (HF ) nodes, comprises nodes that
appear as neighbors in a large fraction of batch subgraphs. They are identiﬁed
after ﬁnalizing the batch sequence. We ﬁrst compute the predecessor set Pi for
each batch Bi . Given K total sub-batches, we deﬁne the occurrence frequency
of a node v as
                            freq(v) = |{Bi | v ∈ Pi }|,                     (3)
and then deﬁne the high-frequency index HFi(v) as
                                         1
                              HFi(v) =     freq(v),                            (4)
                                         K
expressed as a percentage. Consistent with real-world graphs’ scale-free proper-
ties, the node frequency distribution also follows a power-law pattern: A small
fraction of nodes exhibit high HFi values while most nodes have low indices.
Given a threshold τ , we classify the set of HF nodes as

                           H(τ ) = { v | HFi(v) ≥ τ }.                         (5)

Lowering τ increases |H(τ )| and hence the static cache footprint. In practice we
choose τ to balance redundancy reduction against the additional memory cost,
which dependents on the number of HF nodes and embedding dimensionality.
Intermediate embeddings for HF nodes in H(τ ) are precomputed and stored in
the static cache within a whole epoch.
    Apart from HF nodes, some nodes naturally reappear across neighboring
batch subgraphs. The continuity introduced by T SP S strengthens batch locality,
which in turn ampliﬁes the presence of these recurrent nodes. They are deﬁnes as
another category of redundant nodes, cross-batch (CB ) nodes. While HF nodes
are deﬁned globally, CB nodes are a local, per-batch notion and are identiﬁed on
a per-layer basis. We explicitly exclude any node pre-classiﬁed as a HF node from
the CB sets; consequently, the CB designation applies only to nodes that are not
already labeled as HF . Here a layer k of a batch subgraph denotes the set of nodes
at k-hop distance from the nodes in sub-batch. A node is classiﬁed as a CB node
for layer k if it appears at the same layer of both the current batch subgraph and
an adjacent batch subgraph; such nodes are further labeled as previous-batch
CB or next-batch CB depending on whether the adjacent occurrence is in the
preceding or the following batch. Consequently, each batch has a distinct set of
CB nodes for every layer k. CB nodes are detected dynamically during batch
pre-generation, and the ﬁrst batch has no previous-batch CB nodes.
    Concretely, we expand direct neighbors of the current sub-batch ﬁrst and
proceed iteratively to larger hop distances. During these subsequent expansions,
expansion into nodes already designated as HF or previous-batch CB is sup-
pressed to avoid redundant inclusion. Before ﬁnalizing a batch subgraph, we
prefetch the node set for the next batch and mark those nodes that will occupy
the same layer k in the next batch subgraph as next-batch CB nodes.
    Figure 4 illustrates structural diﬀerences between complete and pruned batch
subgraphs for 2-layer GNNs, along with their respective forward propagation
processes. During forward propagation on full-neighborhood batch subgraphs,
182    L. Wu et al.




Fig. 4. Illustration of two subgraph structures for a 2-layer GNN (sub-batch size =
2) and the proposed workﬂow for embedding reuse and caching on pruned batch sub-
graphs. To simplify the ﬁgure, we de-emphasized the two-hop neighbors of the target
nodes and their related edges.


information is aggregated layer by layer. For pruned batch subgraphs, interme-
diate embeddings of nodes whose neighbor expansion have not been suppressed,
i.e., nodes 3 & 4, are computed. These embeddings are then concatenated with
cached embeddings to construct complete inputs for the output layer. Compared
with complete batch subgraphs, pruned batch subgraphs require transferring less
data to GPU, since redundant nodes such as 5, 6, and 7 have their intermediate
embeddings cached rather than repeatedly calculated, and have no need for there
dependency data. Speciﬁcally, the embedding of HF node 7 is fetched from the
static cache, and the embeddings of previous-batch CB nodes 5 & 6 are retrieved
from the dynamic cache. All HF node embeddings, including that of node 7, are
precomputed prior to processing any pruned batch subgraph and remain ﬁxed
in the static cache for the duration of the epoch; by contrast, the dynamic cache
is refreshed after each batch to store newly computed CB embeddings. In this
example, after the current batch the dynamic cache is updated to hold embed-
dings of CB nodes 4 & 5. The persistence of node 5 across consecutive batches
demonstrates that cross-batch nodes may recur in multiple sequential batches.
The representations of output nodes 1 & 2 are subsequently computed. Thus, this
method eﬀectively reduces redundant data transfers and duplicate computations
during training.


5     Experiment

In this section, we empirically evaluate the proposed framework AccuGraph,
targeting at answering the following major questions:

– How does it improve performance while reducing maximum memory con-
  sumption and maintaining the accuracy? (Sect. 5.2)
– How do the two technologies alleviate redundancy (Sect. 5.3)?
– How do the key parameters in the two technologies inﬂuence the latency and
  memory footprint related performance (Sect. 5.4 and Sect. 5.5)?
                                                                AccuGraph     183

5.1   Setups
Environments. All the experiments are conducted on a machine with 1
NVIDIA 3090 GPU (24 GB memory), 1 24-core Intel Xeon CPUs (2.40 GHz),
and 256 GB DDR4 host memory. The machine is installed with Ubuntu 18.04,
CUDA library v11.3. Our experiments are carried out on DGL [22], an open-
source framework for graph neural networks.


                           Table 1. Dataset statistics

            Dataset     Feat. Dim. #Nodes      #Edges       Avg degs.
            Small       1,024      1,000,000   12,070,502   12.07
            Medium      1,024      10,000,000 120,077,694 12.07
            Products    100        2,449,029   61,859,140   25.26
            Papers100M 128         111,059,956 1,615,685,872 14.55




Datasets. We evaluate our method on four large-scale, real-world graphs
(Table 1): Products and Papers100M from the Open Graph Benchmark [6], and
Small and Medium from the Illinois Graph Benchmark [11]. Node features for
Papers100M, extracted from the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG) [19], are
128-dimensional vectors computed as the mean of word2vec embeddings over
all words in each paper’s title and abstract, trained on the full MAG corpus;
Products, representing an Amazon product co-purchasing network, uses 100-
dimensional vectors obtained by applying PCA to the high-dimensional bag-of-
words count vectors of product names and descriptions; Small and Medium, built
primarily on MAG with additional human-annotated labels from both MAG and
the Semantic Scholar Corpus [12], employ 1,024-dimensional Sentence-BERT
embeddings of paper titles and abstracts. Since high-dimensional features might
introduce redundancy and noise, and require substantial computational and stor-
age overhead during training, we follow the PCA-based preprocessing pipeline
of Products to compress them to 256 dimensions, eﬀectively removing linear
correlations, suppressing noise, and streamlining resource consumption.


GNN Models. All our experiments were conducted on two representative mod-
els, GCN [13] and GraphSage [5]. For GraphSage, we evaluate both the mean and
pooling aggregators, denoted Sage-Mean and Sage-Pool, respectively, to capture
their diﬀering memory requirements during training. Every model uses two lay-
ers with a hidden size of 128. We ﬁx the random seed across all runs to eliminate
variability from random initialization, especially for the accuracy evaluations in
Sect. 5.2.

5.2   Overall Results

We ﬁrst assess peak memory consumption and accuracy progression across three
training paradigms: full-graph training, naive accumulated subgraph training,
and our method. Experiments use Products and Small datasets, which support
naive full-graph training under our hardware constraints, with batch sizes set to
4,096 and 8,192 respectively for subgraph training methods. For clarity in the
ﬁgures, the naive accumulated subgraph training method is abbreviated as naive
subgraph in the legends of Figs. 5, 6 and 7.
    In our overall experiments, we ﬁrst demonstrate that accumulated subgraph
training substantially reduces the maximum memory consumption compared to
naive full-graph training, as shown in Fig. 5, while our optimized method further
lowers the peak memory footprint. Importantly, both subgraph-based approaches
maintain full-graph-level accuracy. As shown in Fig. 6, the accuracy curves of all
three methods are almost perfectly overlapped.

    When memory is abundant, our framework guarantees performance identi-
cal to full-graph training, as ensured by the workﬂow illustrated in Fig. 3. For
brevity, we omit the speciﬁc numerical results in this case. However, when mem-
ory is constrained to a lower budget, as speciﬁed in Table 2, naive full-graph
training fails due to OOM errors (Fig. 7), whereas both naive accumulated sub-
graph training and our optimized method execute successfully. Moreover, our
method achieves a substantial speedup over the unoptimized baseline. Figure 7
reports the best attainable performance for each method: Our approach achieves
a 2.7×–11.5× speedup in per-epoch runtime on Products, 4.2×–5.4× on Small,
1.3×–1.9× on Papers100M, and 2.1×–3.2× on Medium.
    This speedup stems from two factors. First, both of our optimizations eﬀec-
tively reduce structural redundancy, which accelerates training even with a ﬁxed
batch size by lowering both data transfer time and computation time. Second,
both methods shrink the scale of batch subgraph given ﬁxed batch size and
186    L. Wu et al.

therefor reduce the maximum memory consumption. This enables our frame-
work to adopt larger batch sizes under the same memory budget, as depicted in
Table 2. We will further demonstrate in Sect. 5.3 that both strategies eﬀectively
reduce redundancy for a ﬁxed batch size, and in Sects. 5.4 and 5.5 that this
redundancy reduction directly saves transfer and computation time, while also
contributing to lower peak memory usage. All these experiments are conducted
on the Products and Small datasets, with batch sizes ﬁxed at 4,096 and 8,192,
respectively.

5.3   Redundancy Reduction

This experiment compares four training variants: no optimization (baseline),
T SP S only, HCR only, and T SP S +HCR, in terms of the accumulated number
of nodes per epoch (i.e., the total distinct nodes transferred/processed when
iterating over all subgraphes). For the T SP S experiments we ﬁx the group size
g to 256 for the ogbn-series datasets and to 512 for the igb-series datasets.
For HCR we ﬁx the high-frequency threshold parameter τ to 70. To make cross-
dataset comparisons intuitive, the plotted values for each dataset are normalized
by the baseline (no-optimization) result for that dataset; reported percentages
below represent relative reductions with respect to this baseline (i.e., a 10%
reduction means the normalized value is 0.90).
    The measured reductions in accumulated nodes are as follows. T SP S alone
reduces accumulated nodes by approximately 8%, 31%, 27%, and 32% on Prod-
ucts, Small, Papers100M, and Medium, respectively. HCR alone yields reduc-
tions of roughly 82%, 25%, 8%, and 32% on the same datasets. When both
strategies are applied together, the reductions become larger: about 75%, 44%,
34%, and 60%. These results are summarized in Fig. 8.
    The eﬀectiveness of each optimization varies across datasets due to diﬀer-
ences in graph topology, such as community structure and degree distributions.
In particular, for the Products dataset, applying both T SP S and HCR yields
                                                                AccuGraph      187

slightly less improvement than using HCR alone. We observe that this is because
T SP S increases overlap within a batch, which reduces the frequency of HB nodes
appearing across diﬀerent batch subgraphs. In other words, given the same τ , the
number of HB nodes observed on a uniform dataset after sorting is lower under
T SP S. Since Products exhibits a strong power-law degree distribution, a large
number of HB nodes exist before sorting, and the decrease in HB nodes under
T SP S has a relatively large impact that is not fully compensated by the ben-
eﬁts of T SP S. Nevertheless, the combination of T SP S and HCR consistently
achieves meaningful redundancy reduction across all datasets.




Fig. 9. Sensitivity of g in the T SP S strategy on accumulated node count, peak GPU
memory, and latency for Small and Products.




5.4   Sensitivity Analysis on g in T S P S Strategy.

To evaluate the impact of the grouping size g in our topological similarity based
nodes pre-sorting strategy, we perform a sensitivity analysis across datasets.
Since g controls the number of nodes grouped during sorting, it directly inﬂuences
batch density and thus redundancy reduction.
    Figure 9(a) shows that smaller g generally leads to greater redundancy reduc-
tion, measured by the decrease in accumulated node count. For example, g = 256
reduces accumulated nodes by about 35% on Small and 8% on Products, with the
diﬀerence attributable to their distinct graph structures. The beneﬁt of reduc-
ing g exhibits diminishing returns and is not strictly monotonic. We observe a
knee near g = 256, where g = 128 unexpectedly yields more accumulated nodes.
188    L. Wu et al.

This suggests that overly ﬁne-grained grouping fragments locality and degrades
neighborhood clustering, making g ∈ [256, 512] preferable.
    Figure 9(b) indicates that maximum GPU memory usage closely follows the
trend of accumulated nodes, conﬁrming that pre-sorting reduces the size of batch
subgraphs, including the largest subgraph that determines peak memory. There-
fore, when memory footprint is the primary concern, we recommend g = 256
for Products and g = 512 for Small. This reduction also aligns with decreased
host–device tansfer latency, since fewer distinct nodes require transfer. Although
absolute transfer times are small, a statistically consistent downward trend is
observable in Fig. 9(c,d).




Fig. 10. Sensitivity of τ in the HCR workﬂow on accumulated node count, peak GPU
memory, and latency for Small and Products.




5.5   Sensitivity Analysis on τ in HCR Technique
To evaluate the impact of the high-frequency threshold τ in our hybrid redun-
dancy caching and reuse technique, we performed a sensitivity study. Since low-
ering τ expands the scope of redundant nodes pruned and increases the number
of node embeddings retained, it is associated with the accumulated node count,
transfer/computation overhead as well as peak memory consumption.
    Figure 10(a) shows that, reducing τ yields substantial redundancy reductions
on our datasets. When τ is set to 60, the accumulated node count decreases by
87% on Products and 31% on Small. The magnitude of the eﬀect depends on
graph topology: Products, with a stronger heavy-tailed degree distribution, pro-
duces many HF nodes that are amenable to static caching, whereas on Small
                                                                 AccuGraph       189

most nodes appear rarely across intermediate layers (our statistics show > 99%
of nodes occur at ≤ 10% frequency), limiting HCR’s beneﬁt. Associated trans-
fer/computation overhead also declined with the trend (Fig. 10(c,d)).
    However, as lowering τ increases the static cache footprint because more τ
embeddings must be stored. Consequently, the curve of peak GPU memory con-
sumption exhibits ﬂuctuations, particularly for Small. By contrast, Products,
which beneﬁts more from HCR, generally show a downward trend in peak mem-
ory usage. These ﬁndings demonstrate that optimal τ selection must be adapted
to graph topology, trading oﬀ redundancy elimination against available memory.

6   Conclusion
In this paper, we presented AccuGraph, a framework for scaling full-graph
GNN training to large graphs under limited GPU memory. Based on the accu-
mulated subgraph training method we proposed, AccuGraph decomposes full-
graph propagation into accumulated subgraph computations to reduce memory
requirements while preserving mathematical equivalence to full-graph training.
To address the redundancy challenge inherent in the naive approach, we intro-
duced a topological similarity based node pre-sorting strategy to diminish dupli-
cated neighbors across batches, along with a hybrid redundancy caching and
reuse technique that further prunes a portion of overlapped structures between
subgraphs. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that AccuGraph
enables full-graph training on a 111M-node graph on a single GPU and achieves
up to 11.5× speedup in training time with the optimizations.

        Abstract. For the real-time computing issues of Internet of Things
        devices (IoTD) in urban scenarios, this paper proposes a multi-unmanned
        aerial vehicles (UAV) collaborative mobile edge computing (MEC) net-
        work framework. In this framework, the UAVs avoid obstacles while
        communicating with ground-based IoTDs via probabilistic LoS chan-
        nels. Subsequently, aiming to minimize the average delay of IoTD, we
        formulate an optimization problem that jointly optimizes connection
        scheduling, resource allocation, and three-dimensional (3D) trajectories
        of UAVs. To avoid long training times, a lightweight DRL based on knowl-
        edge distillation is proposed to optimize the ﬂight trajectory. Specif-
        ically, we train the obstacle avoidance teacher model and the service
        teacher model separately, then perform model distillation according to
        the teacher weights, and update the teacher weights by minimizing the
        loss. Additionally, a low-time complexity greedy algorithm is designed
        to solve the connection scheduling problem, and the computing resource
        allocation problem is addressed through optimization theory. Compared
        to benchmarks, our algorithm signiﬁcantly reduces the average latency
        of IoTDs while compressing the network size by 93%, and eﬀectively
        reduces training time.


        Keywords: Multi-UAV · Resource Allocation · Knowledge Distillation


1     Introduction
The rapid development of 5G has accelerated the development of smart cities and
spawned a series of latency-sensitive applications, such as intelligent transporta-
tion and digital twins [1]. However, most IoTDs cannot meet the delay demands
due to their limited computing resources. Fortunately, UAV-assisted MEC pro-
vides a viable solution [2]. Due to their rapid deployment capability, enhanced
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 195–214, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_11
196    H. Liu et al.

line-of-sight transmission probability, and ability to carry powerful computing
resources, UAVs have been widely utilized in edge computing networks.
    The computing oﬄoading and trajectory planning problems in multi-UAV-
assisted systems have been extensively studied [3,4]. However, some trajectory
optimization studies are limited to open-space scenarios, whereas in reality, the
impact of obstacles on channel conditions and ﬂight paths cannot be neglected.
Moreover, for computing oﬄoading problems, solving them with DRL requires a
huge action space and state space, which inevitably increases training costs [5].
Additionally, the sparse rewards designed for UAV obstacle avoidance may aﬀect
the gradient of the objective function’s reward, potentially aﬀecting algorithm
convergence [6].
    Fortunately, knowledge distillation (KD) enables neural networks to achieve
lightweight deployment while maintaining performance [7–9]. Additionally, KD
can distill policies from multiple teacher models into a single student model,
enhancing both robustness and training eﬃciency. However, diﬀerent teacher
models may exhibit distinct decision-making. When conﬂicting knowledge is
distilled into the student model, it may lead to performance degradation [5].
Therefore, it is crucial to select appropriate weights for diﬀerent teacher models
during the distillation.
    To address the aforementioned challenges, this paper focuses on designing
lightweight DRL algorithms for multi-UAV-assisted IoTDs oﬄoading comput-
ing scenarios with obstacle avoidance. The main contributions of our work are
summarized as follows:
– In consideration of real-world 3D obstacles and channel conditions, a multi-
  UAV-assisted edge computing network is proposed. Within this network,
  UAVs are edge servers that assist IoTDs with task oﬄoading and computing
  while simultaneously avoiding obstacles. We jointly optimize the 3D ﬂight
  trajectory, connection scheduling, and computing resource allocation to min-
  imize the average latency of IoTD.
– For 3D trajectories of UAVs optimization, a DRL algorithm based on
  improved KD is proposed. The algorithm integrates a pre-trained obstacle-
  avoidance teacher model and a service-oriented teacher model, employing
  adaptive teacher weights for distillation. Meanwhile, we design a low-time
  complexity greedy algorithm to solve the connection scheduling problem. As
  for computing resource allocation, we solve it using optimization theory.
– Finally, we evaluate the performance of our proposed DTAC algorithm
  through simulations. Compared with the benchmark algorithms, DTAC per-
  forms better in terms of convergence, training time, average delay and cover-
  age of IoTDs, even with a reduced network size.
   The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we summarize
recent related work. Section 3 provides a detailed introduction to the system
model. In Sect. 4, we solve the connection scheduling problem using heuristic
algorithms, optimize resource allocation using optimization theory, and then
combine them with a lightweight DRL to solve the original problem. Comparison
results are presented in Sect. 5. Section 6 concludes the paper.

2   Related Work
DRL enables rapid decision-making in complex environments, yet its deployment
is constrained by high training costs. KD is a promising model compression
and transfer learning technique that transfers knowledge from DRL models to
a lightweight network, thereby improving deployment eﬃciency. This section
reviews and summarizes research on the application of these two technologies in
MEC.
    Li et al. [10] proved that short-job-ﬁrst (SJF) is better than other queuing
algorithms when handling queue tasks. The average user latency was optimized
by a scheduling algorithm based on SJF combined with DRL. Bibi et al. [11]
investigated the total service latency minimization problem for vehicles and pro-
posed a two-stage DRL solution. They optimized vehicle transmission power by
DDPG in the ﬁrst stage, followed by computing resource allocation using DQN
in the second stage. Li et al. [12] formulated a system energy consumption min-
imization problem and proposed a Beta-distribution-based IPPO algorithm to
jointly optimize connection scheduling, communication, and computing resource
allocation. Zhang et al. [13] proposed a framework for multi-UAV-assisted vehicle
networking. They optimized spectrum resource allocation and ﬂight trajectory
problems through the MADDPG algorithm to minimize the average task com-
pletion latency.
    Reviewing the above work, solving communication problems in multi-UAV-
assisted MEC through DRL is a promising approach, but high-dimensional state
and action spaces can aﬀect training time and convergence.
    Chen et al. [14] proposed a multi-teacher policy distillation-based DRL algo-
rithm to maximize proﬁt through joint optimization of transmission bandwidth
and oﬄoading decisions. By employing advantage value functions, the method
maintained distillation stability and performance. Experimental results demon-




                             Fig. 1. System Model.
198     H. Liu et al.

strated simultaneous network compression and proﬁt improvement. However,
this work predeﬁned UAV hovering positions without considering tra jectory
optimization and computing resource allocation. Zhu et al. [15] introduced a
priority mechanism to maximize rewards by connection scheduling optimiza-
tion, utilizing a teacher distillation framework for knowledge transfer. This work
mainly focuses on the optimization of oﬄoading decisions, without considering
resource allocation, trajectory optimization, and multi-teacher knowledge trans-
fer. Wang et al. [16] developed a KD-based multi-agent DRL framework that
enhances transmission eﬃciency through optimized beamforming coordination
and resource allocation. However, this work did not account for potential per-
formance degradation in the student model caused by knowledge discrepancies
among diﬀerent teacher models during the distillation process.
    Currently, there are still some issues worth studying in multi-UAV-assisted
MEC, such as research on 3D trajectories for UAV obstacle avoidance, research
on reducing DRL training time, and the problem of ensuring model perfor-
mance while achieving model compression under multi-teacher knowledge trans-
fer. Therefore, this paper will study the above issues.


3     System Model

As shown in Fig. 1, the proposed edge computing network framework com-
prises N IoTDs, M UAVs, and multiple building obstacles of the same size.
We assume each UAV and IoTD is equipped with both communication circuits
and processing units. Let τ denote the time slot size, with N = {1, 2, ..., N },
M = {1, 2, ..., M }, and T = {1, 2, ..., T } representing the sets of IoTDs, UAVs,
and time slots respectively. In each time slot, every IoTD needs to process a task
with stochastic size. The coordinates of the UAV is qm [i] = (xm [i], ym [i], zm [i])
and the coordinates of the IoTD is qn [i] = (xn [i], yn [i], 0). The task characteris-
tics are deﬁned by a triple Ψn [i] = (Dn [i], Fn [i], T max ), where Dn [i] denotes the
data size of task, Fn [i] represents the required CPU cycles of processing task,
T max speciﬁes the maximum tolerable delay threshold.


3.1   UAVs’ Mobility Model

To formalize the 3D UAV mobility model, we deﬁne φm [i] denotes the vertical
ﬂight angle of the m-th UAV in the i-th slot, θm [i] represents the horizontal ﬂight
angle, and vm [i] indicates the ﬂight speed. Subject to the following constraints:

                           0 ≤ φm [i] ≤ π, m ∈ M, i ∈ T ,                          (1)

                          0 ≤ θm [i] ≤ 2π, m ∈ M, i ∈ T ,                          (2)
                         0 ≤ vm [i] ≤ v max , m ∈ M, i ∈ T .                       (3)

Consequently, the 3D Euclidean coordinates of UAVs are updated by the follow-
ing equations:
                ⎧
                ⎨ xm [i] = xm [i − 1] + vm [i] cos φm [i] cos θm [i]τ,
                  ym [i] = ym [i − 1] + vm [i] cos φm [i] sin θm [i]τ,     (4)
                ⎩
                  zm [i] = zm [i − 1] + vm [i] sin φm [i]τ.

   Furthermore, accounting for architectural obstacles in urban environments,
each UAV must satisfy the following altitude and region constraints:

                     xmin ≤ xm [i] ≤ xmax , m ∈ M, i ∈ T ,                  (5)


                     y min ≤ ym [i] ≤ y max , m ∈ M, i ∈ T ,                (6)


                     z min ≤ zm [i] ≤ z max , m ∈ M, i ∈ T ,                (7)


                                     Γ       ζ κ.                           (8)
where ζ represents the total area, κ denotes the region occupied by obstacles,
and the UAV movable region Γ is the complement of the obstacle region within
the total area ζ.
   In order to prevent collisions between UAVs, we have:

                ||qm [i] − qj [i]||2 ≥ dmin , ∀m, j ∈ M, i ∈ T , n = j.     (9)

4     Algorithm Design
To address the above problems, we ﬁrst propose a knowledge distillation-based
DRL algorithm for solving the 3D ﬂight trajectories of UAVs, and then design
heuristic algorithms to resolve the connection scheduling. Finally, computing
resource allocation is solved by optimization theory.

4.1   Overall Algorithm Design
We design two teacher models specializing in training UAV service and obsta-
cle avoidance policies, respectively. Speciﬁcally, the service policy is for UAVs
to control trajectories to optimize the average latency of IoTD and the obstacle
avoidance policy for UAVs is controlling trajectories to avoid collision with obsta-
cles. Then, we import the two trained teacher models into the student model
for distillation training. During the student model’s training, we assign distinct
adaptive weights to each teacher model to facilitate prioritized knowledge trans-
fer. Weight updates are performed dynamically by combining the Q-value loss
of the teacher model and the student target model.

Service Teacher Model. The ﬂight trajectories of UAVs have Markov char-
acteristics. To apply DRL, we deﬁne the states, actions, and reward function in
the service teacher model as follows:
         Average Delay Minimization Strategy for Multi-UAV Assisted MEC            203

1) State: si = {qm [i], ∀m ∈ M, i ∈ I}, where qm [i] is the coordinates of the
   m-th UAV in the i-th time slot.
2) Action: ai = {Δφm [i], Δθm [i], Δvm [i], ∀m ∈ M, i ∈ I}, where Δφm [i] is the
   increment of the vertical ﬂight angle, Δθm [i] is the increment of the horizontal
   ﬂight angle and Δvm [i] is the increment of the speed.
3) Reward : Based on our optimization objective and constraints C4-C6,C8,C13
   the reward function is deﬁned as:
                                  1     T        N
                        riser =                         n [i] − pb [i],
                                                       tcom                        (27)
                                  N     i=1      n=1

   where pb [i] represents the penalty for all UAVs violating the boundary con-
   straint C4-C6, collision constraints between UAVs C8 and energy consump-
   tion constraint C13.


Obstacle Avoidance Teacher Model. The state space and action space set-
tings for the obstacle avoidance teacher model are the same as those of the
service teacher model. We design the reward function for the obstacle avoidance
teacher model as follows:
    Reward : Based on the constraints C4-C8 and C13, the reward function is
deﬁned as:
                          riobs = rmov [i] − pb [i] − po [i],              (28)
In order to encourage UAVs that learn obstacle avoidance policy to explore the
area better and ﬁnd reasonable positions, we have set UAV movement reward
rmov [6]. po [i] represents the penalty for all UAVs violating the obstacle collision
constraint C7.


Student Model. The reward function for the student model is designed as
follows:
    Reward : Based on optimization objective and constraints C4-C8,C13, the
reward function is deﬁned as:
                          1       T      N
                   ri =                         n [i] − pb [i] − po [i].
                                               tcom                                (29)
                          N       i=1    n=1

    In our model, UAVs act as agents, and the system model is modeled as the
environment. In each time slot, the agent observes its state si , executes action
ai through policy π, obtains reward ri , and moves to the next state si+1 . The
process terminates until it reaches the maximum time step I.
    Compared to classical DRL methods, SAC optimizes policy stochasticity
through entropy regularization, eﬀectively reducing the possibility of local opti-
mal convergence [23]. The algorithm’s objective maximizes both cumulative
rewards and policy entropy, with its actor network updated through the fol-
lowing loss function:

           Lsac,π = Eπ [α log π(ai | si ) − min(Q1 (si , ai ), Q2 (si , ai ))] ,   (30)

Among them, α is the regularization factor that balances reward and entropy,
while Q1 (si , ai ) and Q2 (si , ai ) are obtained from two critic networks. The SAC
critic network is updated using the following loss function:
                                  1                      2

where yi is the target Q-value, which is obtained from the target critic network.
Target Q-value can be expressed as:

   yi = ri + γ (min(Q1− (si+1 , ai+1 ), Q2− (si+1 , ai+1 )) − α log πθ (·|si+1 )) ,    (32)

Here, Q1− (si+1 , ai+1 ) and Q1− (si+1 , ai+1 ) are obtained from two target critic
networks respectively. We need to adjust the regularization coeﬃcient to help
the agent adjust its actions for policy improvement. The loss function of the
regularization coeﬃcient α is deﬁned as:

                           L(α) = E [−α log (ai |si ) − αH0 ] .                        (33)

where H0 is entropy and it used to measures the randomness of policy.
    SAC is an eﬃcient reinforcement learning algorithm that performs well in
solving continuous action control problems. However, when the environment
becomes more complex, especially when multiple constraints involve diﬀerent
         Average Delay Minimization Strategy for Multi-UAV Assisted MEC         205

reward signals, their gradients may aﬀect each other, leading to slow conver-
gence during the learning process [6].
   KD facilitates knowledge transfer between models, enabling student policy to
better inherit policies from diﬀerent teachers [14]. Each teacher model provides
knowledge through its Q-values and action distributions, requiring the student
network to minimize Q-value errors while approximating teachers’ action distri-
butions. The distillation loss is represented by mean square error (MSE) between
the student’s Q-values and a weighted combination of teachers’ Q-values:

           Ldis,Qo = E (Qstu,o (si , ai ) − Q̂tea (si , ai ))2 , ∀o ∈ {1, 2},   (34)

where the weighted combination of teacher’s Q value is deﬁned as Q̂tea (si , ai ) =
  K
  k=1 wk Qtea,k (si , ai ), wk represents the weight of the k-th teacher model, and
Qtea,k (si , ai ) represents the Q value of the k-th teacher model.
   Policy distillation loss is achieved by calculating the Kullback-Leibler (KL)
divergence between the student and the teacher policy. Then, performing a
weighted sum:
                                K
                  Ldis,πstu =         wk DKL (πstu (·|s) πtea,k (·|s)) .        (35)
                                k=1

   We can minimize its loss function to update the student model’s critic net-
work:
                        LQstu,o = Lsac,Qo + Ldis,Qo ,                     (36)
The actor network of the student model can be updated using the following loss
function:
                         Lπstu = Lsac,πstu + Ldis,πstu .                 (37)
    The performance of each teacher model may vary at diﬀerent stages of train-
ing. To integrate multiple teacher models for guiding the student’s learning, an
adaptive weight-adjusted method is proposed. We adjust the inﬂuence of teach-
ers on student models by updating teacher weights. The update is performed by
minimizing the diﬀerence between the weighted teacher Q-value and the student
target Q-value. The loss function can be expressed as:

                     Lw = E (Q̂tea (si , ai ) − Qtar (si , ai ))2 ,             (38)

where Qtar (si , ai ) is the student target Q-value and its function can be denoted
as Qtar (si , ai ) = min(Qstu,1− , Qstu,2− ).

model, and a student model. We use pseudocode in Algorithm II to outline the
speciﬁc algorithm ﬂow. Firstly, we train the obstacle avoidance teacher model
and the service teacher model separately using Algorithm I , and save their
model parameters (line 1). Then, we initialize the student model parameters
