14:         Update Qstu,1 and Qstu,2 by minimizing their loss function according to
    (36);
15:         Update πstu by minimizing (37);
16:         Update entropy regularization coeﬃcient α by formula (33);
17:         Update Qstu,1− and Qstu,2− through soft update;
18:         Update wobs and wser according to its loss function (38);
19:     end for
20: end for



and the teacher model weights. From lines 7 to 10, the student agent obtains
action ai through policy and enters into a new state si+1 after interacting with
the current state si . Based on the current location of the UAV, we can solve
the connection scheduling problem using Algorithm III. Then, based on the
connection scheduling solution, the computing resource allocation problem can
be solved by the convex theory. We can get rewards ri based on the above
solution. Subsequently, store (si , ai , ri , si+1 ) into the replay buﬀer and update the
neural network using batch sampling. It should be noted that the loss function of
the student model is composed of distillation loss and training loss (lines 14–15).
The weights of the teacher model are dynamically updated according to the loss
function (line 18). Since we have discussed the relevant knowledge of student
model updates in the previous section, it will not repeated here.

4.2   Scheduling Algorithm

Similar to [24], given UAV coordinates, we propose a low-complexity greedy
algorithm for solving IoTD connection scheduling. Although this method is not
globally optimal, the algorithm can quickly obtain a suboptimal solution without
aﬀecting the training time.

    As shown in Algorithm III , ﬁrstly, we initialize all IoTDs to perform local
computing and initialize the amount of data processed on each UAV Dm (line 1).
Then, initialize the preselected UAV set Lm for each IoTD, check the coverage
relationship between the IoTD and each UAV, and calculate the transmission
delay between the IoTD and each UAV (lines 3–10). Subsequently, we store the
UAV id m, transmission delay ttr  n,m [i], and the amount of data processed on the
UAV Dm into set Lm .
    IoTD prioritizes UAV with the smallest data load, thereby obtaining more
computing resources while also considering load balancing. Therefore, traverse
each IoTD, if the transmission delay is less than the local computing delay and
constraint (23) is satisﬁed, the IoTD oﬄoads the task to the UAV with the lowest
data load Dm (lines 12–17). In addition, update the amount of data processed
on this UAV Dm (line 18). If the above conditions are not met, remove the UAV
from the set (line 21) and continue traversing the other UAVs in the set (lines
14–22).

5.1   Benchmark Algorithm

To evaluate the performance of DTAC, several algorithms are proposed for com-
parison as follows:
Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) [25]: We set the parameters
of the DDPG algorithm and network architecture to be the same as those of the
teacher model in DTAC. DDPG is used to optimize the trajectories of the UAVs.
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) [26]: The parameters and network architecture of
the SAC are identical to those of the teacher model in DTAC. SAC is used to
optimize the trajectories of the UAVs.
SAC Algorithm Based on knowledge distillation (DAC): The teacher
model and student model of DAC are the same as DTAC but do not consider
updating teacher weights. DAC is used to optimize the trajectories of the UAVs.


5.2   Performance Evaluation

We will evaluate the performance of the DTAC algorithm based on comprehen-
sive performance, convergence, ﬂight trajectory, and average delay.


Comprehensive Performance: As shown in Table 2, we will evaluate the per-
formance of the algorithms in terms of network structure, network size, training
time, and reward. Speciﬁcally, the training time for DTAC and DAC is composed
of the training time for the teacher model and the student model. It can be seen
that DAC and DTAC have short training times. Although DAC reduces the net-
work size compared to SAC, the knowledge conﬂict between teacher models dur-
ing the distillation process leads to the degradation of accumulated rewards in the
student model. DTAC achieves lightweight while introducing a teacher weights
update mechanism, which can reduce the performance impact of knowledge con-
ﬂicts on the student model. DDPG does not introduce an entropy mechanism,
resulting in low eﬃciency of agents in environment exploration, which may cause
the algorithm to fall into a local optimal solution.

6     Conclusion

Based on the consideration of obstacle avoidance, this paper proposes a multi-
UAV-assisted mobile edge computing network to minimize the latency problem
of IoTD in urban scenarios. We comprehensively consider the 3D dynamic trajec-
tories of UAVs, connection scheduling, and computing resource allocation, with
the goal of minimizing the average latency of IoTD task. We design a knowledge
distillation-based lightweight deep reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize
the 3D ﬂight trajectories of UAVs. In addition, a low-time complexity greedy
algorithm is proposed to solve the connection scheduling problem. Based on
connection scheduling, the computing resource allocation problem is solved by
convex theory. Simulation results show that our algorithm maintains good per-
formance while reducing the network size by 93%. Future work will explore the
improvement of UAV collaboration through multi-agent reinforcement learning.

    Peijun Dong1 , Hang Tao1 , Yang Zhao1 , Wei Shi2 , and Hanjiang Luo1(B)

       Abstract. Multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) have been
       widely utilized for underwater search missions. However, traditional
       multi-AUV collaborative search methods based on multi-agent reinforce-
       ment learning (MARL) suﬀer from a cold start problem due to the lack
       of prior knowledge, which hinders eﬃcient cooperation in the early stage
       of search operations. Furthermore, due to harsh environments and unsta-
       ble underwater acoustic communication links, it is diﬃcult for AUVs to
       obtain timely information, which reduces collaborative search eﬃciency
       among AUVs. To address these challenges, we integrate the reasoning
       capabilities of large language models (LLMs) into MARL framework,
       and propose an LLM-enhanced multi-AUV cooperative search scheme.
       In this scheme, to tackle with the cold start problem, we leverage LLMs to
       infer a target probability map (TPM) from the search task and under-
       water terrain information. Then, we use TPM to guide AUV’s search
       and alleviate the cold start problem caused by unfamiliarity with the
       new environment in the early stage of search operations. Moreover, we
       design an information forecaster (Forecaster) using LLMs, which infers
       the states of disconnected AUVs under unstable link interruptions from
       historical data and incorporates into TPM’s updates enhancing coop-
       eration eﬃciency. Finally, we design the scheme based on multi-agent
       deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), improving the eﬃciency
       of multi-AUV collaborative search. The eﬀectiveness of the proposed
       scheme is veriﬁed through simulations.


       Keywords: Cooperative search · Large language models · Information
       fusion · Target probability map · Multi-agent reinforcement learning


1    Introduction
Multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) have been widely used in mar-
itime emergency search operations, as these are capable of performing tasks that
individuals cannot perform alone [1]. However, to carry out underwater emer-
gency search missions leveraging multiple AUVs eﬃciently faces signiﬁcant chal-
lenges under complex environments. As multi-AUV collaborative search tasks
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 215–235, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_12
216    P. Dong et al.

typically require coordination and decision-making among multi-AUV [2], the
harsh environments and communication constraints of underwater acoustic links
(e.g., unstable links, low data rates and high delays) make it diﬃcult for multi-
AUV to eﬀectively search the targets [3,4]. Although there have been remark-
able advances of MARL in collaborative multi-agent applications in recent years,
(e.g., as a powerful framework enabling agents to learn optimal strategies through
interactions with the environment and other agents [5]), as shown in Fig. 1, when
these are utilized in multi-AUV cooperative search operations, several challenges
persist.




Fig. 1. The scenario of multi-AUV collaborative search based on target probability
map under underwater acoustic communication.


     A prominent issue is the cold start problem [6,7]. During the cold start
phase, agents begin to explore the environment from an unfamiliar state due
to the absence of prior knowledge, resulting in ineﬃcient behaviors in the early
stages. The AUV collaborative search methods based on MARL also have a cold
start problem. Due to the lack of the ability to combine task and environmental
information for reasoning with prior knowledge, AUVs have insuﬃcient prior
knowledge to search important areas, which reduce the eﬃciency of collabora-
tive search in the early stage of exploration. Leveraging the extensive knowl-
edge database, experience, and powerful reasoning capabilities of large language
models (LLMs), it is possible to generate contextually relevant prior knowledge
based on task information and environmental information [8]. This makes LLMs
a promising tool for mitigating the cold start problem in MARL [7]. In particular,
LLMs can assist agents in quickly adapting to complex cooperative tasks.
     In order to further enhance the eﬃciency of multi-AUV collaborative search,
it is critical for AUVs to exchange and fuse information in a timely manner. One
critical usage of timely information exchange and fusion is to construct a target
probability map, so as to facilitate the coordination eﬃciency of multi-AUV [9].
                           LLM-Enhanced Multi-AUV Collaborative Search          217

However, when the communication link is unstable [10], it becomes diﬃcult for
AUVs to obtain real-time information and fail to update the target probability
map in a timely manner, thereby reducing the eﬃciency of collaborative search
operations. To mitigate this issue, Zhu et al. [11] used the polar kalman ﬁlter to
predict the states of AUVs under unstable communication conditions. The pre-
dicted results are integrated into the search map as compensation data, thereby
improving the eﬃciency of collaborative search among AUVs. Wu et al. [12] pro-
posed a predictive compensation method to address the unstable communication
issue by integrating the least squares method and the extended kalman ﬁlter for
unstable communication compensation. However, these methods are sensitive to
system noise parameters and have poor generalization and scalability.
    To address these issues, as LLMs possess strong comprehension and reason-
ing capabilities [5,13], in this paper, we ﬁrst propose to leverage LLMs to tackle
the challenges in the multi-AUV collaborative search tasks. We utilize LLMs to
generate eﬀective prior knowledge based on task information, thereby enhancing
AUV decision-making during the exploration phase. Furthermore, we investi-
gate to guide the LLM to infer the state information of disconnected AUVs
under unstable communication conditions and integrate the inferred data into
the MARL framework. This is achieved by incorporating the inference results
into the reward mechanism to improve the decision-making of AUVs and enhance
the eﬃciency of multi-AUV collaborative search. The main contributions of this
paper are summarized as follows.
– To address the cold start problem in MARL-based multi-AUV cooperative
  search, we leverage LLMs to infer the initial target probability map based on
  complex search task and terrain information, mitigating the cold start issue.
– To tackle with the untimely target probability map fusion caused by unstable
  links, we utilize LLMs to predict the information of disconnected AUVs based
  on historical data, mitigating redundant searches resulting from untimely
  information fusion.
– We evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithms through simulations.
  The results show that the algorithms enhance the eﬃciency of multi-AUV
  collaborative search.
The structure of the rest of this paper is as follows. Section 2 introduces the
related work. Section 3 provides a detailed description of the models. Section 4
presents the scheme design. Section 5 presents the performance evaluation.
Section 6 concludes the paper.


2   Related Work
In MARL, the cold start problem arises when agents struggle to eﬀectively initial-
ize their policies due to the lack of prior knowledge, leading to slow or suboptimal
learning performance. Traditional approaches to addressing this issue typically
include pre-trained, imitation learning, and expert knowledge. These methods
can quickly provide baseline behavioral patterns, reducing the time that agents
218    P. Dong et al.

spend blindly exploring the environment. However, they also exhibit limitations.
Pre-trained models [14] may fail to generalize well to speciﬁc task environments,
imitation learning [15] depends on high-quality demonstration data, and expert
knowledge [16] can introduce subjective biases and is often diﬃcult to scale.
    In order to further improve the eﬃciency of AUV collaborative search, it is
critical for AUVs to exchange and fuse search information in a timely manner
when performing search tasks. The research on communication in multi-AUV
systems mainly includes two types: reliable communication and unstable com-
munication. At present, most of multi-AUV cooperative target search methods
are based on the assumption of reliable communication conditions [17], and the
capability of these methods signiﬁcantly relies on reliable communication. Cai
et al. [18] proposed a fuzzy clustering-based target probability map construction
method that improves information fusion and search eﬃciency among AUVs.
Liu et al. [19] proposed a distributed multi-AUV collaborative search system
that enhances robustness and enables eﬀective information exchange and fusion
through a time-stamped mechanism. When the communication link is unstable,
the search performance of these methods will be seriously aﬀected. Research on
unstable communication includes the work by Jia et al. [20], who proposed a
multi-AUV asynchronous update search strategy based on high-capacity oppor-
tunistic communication to maximize target search performance under unstable
communication conditions. However, their study does not address how to miti-
gate the negative impacts of communication instability. Zhu et al. [11] proposed
using a polar kalman ﬁlter to predict AUV states under unstable communica-
tion, integrating the predictions into the search map to enhance collaborative
search eﬃciency. However, this method is highly sensitive to parameter settings
and exhibits poor generalization performance and scalability.

3     System Model
3.1   Multi-AUV Collaborative Search Model
In order to eﬀectively search for target, AUVs should continuously update their
environmental states through information exchange. To this end, the target prob-
ability map model should be built. This paper considers a typical scenario of
multi-AUV collaborative search based on target probability map under underwa-
ter acoustic communication [19]. As shown in Fig. 1, which is deﬁned as follows.
(1) The two-dimensional search area A of size Lx ×Ly is discretized into Nx ×Ny
grid, pmn indicates the likelihood that the target exists in the grid (m, n). (2)
The initial position of the target is unknown, and the target moves a constant
speed. (3) There are N AUVs, denoted as B = {b1 , b2 , . . . , bN }, the AUVs are
equipped with sonars, acoustic communication equipment. Each AUV can sense
the search area through sensors at a distance of Rs . The term ﬁeld of view
(FOV), denoted as F OVi (t), represents the sensing coverage area of AU Vi at
time t. In addition, each AUV can communicate with neighbors, and the acous-
tic communication range is denoted by Ra . When the distance between AUVs
exceeds Ra , communication may become unstable, leading to data transmission
failure.
                               LLM-Enhanced Multi-AUV Collaborative Search             219

3.2   Target Probability Map Update Model

The target probability map (TPM) is used to represent the probability of the
presence of a target at diﬀerent locations within the search area. It helps AUVs
navigate towards potential targets more eﬃciently. As AUVs gather information
and make detections, the TPM is updated to reﬂect changes in the likelihood of a
target being present in various parts of the search area. The TPM is derived using
the sonar detection model and the Bayesian formula [21]. The sonar detection
probability Pd is given by

                                PD · exp − D
                                           Rs
                                             s
                                               ,         0 < d ≤ Ds
                        Pd =                                          ,                (1)
                                PF ,                     d > Ds

where PD represents for the sonar’s detection precision, PF represents the sonar’s
false alarm probability, Rs represents the detection distance, and Ds is the max-
imum detection distance of the sonar.
    In multi-AUV cooperative search tasks, each AUV maintains a TPM repre-
senting the entire search area in a grid. Each grid cell (m, n) corresponds to a
probability value pimn (t), indicating the probability estimated by the i-th AUV
that a target exists in that cell at time t. At each time step, the AUV updates
the probabilities of grid cells within its sensing range based on its own sonar
detection results using Bayesian update. The update formula is as follows.

               ⎧ i
               ⎪
               ⎪pmn (t − 1),                             if the cell is not observed
               ⎪
               ⎪
               ⎪
               ⎪
               ⎨       pdi · pimn (t − 1)
  pimn (t) =                                    ,        if observed and O(t) = 1 ,    (2)
               ⎪ pfi + (pdi − pfi )pimn (t − 1)
               ⎪
               ⎪
               ⎪
               ⎪      (1 − pdi ) · pimn (t − 1)
               ⎪
               ⎩                                    ,    if observed and O(t) = 0
                 1 − pfi + (pfi − pdi )pimn (t − 1)

where pdi denotes the detection probability of AUV i, pfi denotes its false alarm
probability, and O(t) represents the detection result at the current time (1 indi-
cates target detected, 0 indicates no detection).


3.3   Search Information Fusion Model

To compensate for the limited detection capability of each AUV, an information
fusion mechanism is constructed to accelerate convergence towards a consistent
and accurate TPM across all AUVs. After AUV updates its TPM based on
the observed information, each AUV enters a communication and fusion phase,
integrating information from neighbors to jointly optimize the TPM.
    The set of AUVs within the communication range of AUV i at time t, includ-
ing itself, is deﬁned as

                       Ni (t) = {j     μi (t) − μj (t)     Ra } ∪ {i},                 (3)
220    P. Dong et al.

where μi (t) is the position of AUV i at time t, and Ra is the distance of acoustic
communication. The fusion weights wij (t) assigned to neighbors are deﬁned as
                                ⎧
                                ⎪
                                ⎨ρ,        j=i
                      wij (t) = di (t)−1 , j ∈ Ni (t), j = i ,
                                    1−ρ
                                                                                (4)
                                ⎪
                                ⎩
                                  0,       j∈/ Ni (t)

where ρ ∈ (0, 1) is the self-weight coeﬃcient, and di (t) = |Ni (t)| is the number
of neighbors including AUV i itself. Each AUV converts its cell-wise probability
estimate to the log-odds form [19]

                                                 pimn (t)
                          Limn (t) = ln                        ,               (5)
                                               1 − pimn (t)

where pimn (t) is AUV i’s probability estimate for cell (m, n). Then, it performs
weighted fusion of log-odds from its neighbors
                                        N
                          L̃imn (t) =         wij (t) · Ljmn (t).              (6)

The result is converted back to probability space
                                                   1

                                       1 + exp −L̃imn (t)

   This log-odds-based fusion framework improves numerical stability and
ensures that each AUV incrementally aligns its TPM with those of its neighbors.
Repeated over time and across the entire search space, this mechanism enhances
shared situational awareness and signiﬁcantly improves the collaborative search
eﬃciency of the AUV swarms.


4     Scheme Design
4.1   Scheme Description
In this section, we propose an LLM-enhanced MARL-based multi-AUV collab-
orative search scheme to enhance the eﬃciency of AUV collaborative search.
As shown in Fig. 2, to address the cold start problem in MARL, we employ
LLMs to infer key search regions based on search task and terrain information,
thereby generating initial TPM to guide early AUV behavior. In addition, to
mitigate untimely information fusion caused by limited acoustic communica-
tion, we use LLMs to infer missing observations from historical communication
data, improving coordination among AUVs. Finally, we model the problem as
a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), and design LLM-
enhanced multi-auv collaborative search algorithm (LEMACS) based on multi-
agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG).
                            LLM-Enhanced Multi-AUV Collaborative Search          221




                       Fig. 2. The architecture of LEMACS.


4.2   Cold Start Solutions with LLM-Generated Initial TPM
In this subsection, we propose a method for generating an initial TPM using
LLMs to address the cold start problem in MARL. We leverage LLMs to infer key
search areas based on complex task and terrain information, and integrate them
into an initial TPM. At the beginning of AUV training, this TPM is provided to
the AUVs. By accessing the high-probability areas identiﬁed in the TPM, AUVs
can obtain high reward values and quickly develop eﬀective strategies during the
early search stage. This method mitigates the cold start problem caused by a lack
of prior knowledge in early exploration. As shown in Fig. 2, the method consists
of three components: TPM Reasoner, TPM Conﬁrmer, and TPM Generator.
– TPM Reasoner: As shown in Fig. 3, we encapsulate the given task informa-
  tion {search task} and terrain information {regions} into an dataset {ENV
  Data}. Subsequently, it is provided to TPM Reasoner for inference, in order
  to obtain information about important search areas {TPM Data}.
                           ⎧
                           ⎪
                           ⎪  ((X1 , X2 ), (Y1 , Y2 ), P1 ), region 1
                           ⎪
                           ⎪
                           ⎨((X3 , X4 ), (Y3 , Y4 ), P2 ),   region 2
              T P MData =       .                                     ,   (8)
                           ⎪
                           ⎪    ..
                           ⎪
                           ⎪
                           ⎩
                              ((Xm , Xn ), (Ym , Yn ), Pk ), region k

  where (Xi , Xj ) denotes the horizontal range of the region, (Yi , Yj ) denotes the
  vertical range, and Pk represents the probability weight of the corresponding
  region.
– TPM Confirmer: If a single LLM is used to independently generate the
  entire TPM information, it may produce inaccurate or invalid outputs, and
  is prone to cause system crashes due to format inconsistencies. To ensure the
  accuracy of the inferred information, we design a TPM Conﬁrmer to verify
  the correctness of the reasoning. This additional validation step by the TPM
222    P. Dong et al.

  Conﬁrmer enhances the reliability and scientiﬁc soundness of the generated
  TPM information. After receiving the inferred {TPM Data}, the TPM Con-
  ﬁrmer evaluates its accuracy and validity based on the task information and
  terrain data. If the inferred prior knowledge from the TPM Reasoner is found
  to be inaccurate, a feedback instruction {inaccurate} is returned to trigger
  re-reasoning. If the data is accurate, it is encapsulated into JSON format.
  Then, the conﬁrmed {TPM JSON} is unpacked using the json.load function.
  The unpacked information is stored in the prior knowledge buﬀer for use by
  the TPM Generator.
– TPM Generator: In order to enable the AUV to correctly utilize the TPM,
  important search regions are extracted from the prior knowledge buﬀer. By
  increasing the probability values at the corresponding positions of these key
  regions to speciﬁed multipliers, a normalized TPM is constructed.




                         Fig. 3. TPM Reasoner Prompt.


    The primary procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1. In this algorithm, we
use LLMT P M Reasoner (EN VData ) to infer the key search areas (T P MData ), use
LLMT P M Conf irmer (T P MData ) to further conﬁrm the inference information to
prevent errors or omissions of important search area information, and ﬁnally use
TPM Generator to draw the LLMs inference of important search area informa-
tion into TPM (P (t) = {pmn (t)}), which is provided to AUVs before training
begins.

4.3     LLM-Enhanced Update of TPM Under Communication
        Constraints
Underwater acoustic communication instability may cause some AUVs to lose
connection with others, resulting in failed information exchange and delayed
updates of the TPM, thereby reducing cooperative search eﬃciency. As shown
in Fig. 2, to address this issue, we propose a method that leverages LLMs to
infer the observations of disconnected AUVs based on historical communication
data (H.P.C Data: heading direction, position, channel information), thus com-
pensating for the missing TPM updates. The method consists primarily of a
component named Forecaster.
– Forecaster: When AUVi exceeds the acoustic communication range with
  other AUVs or encounters with unstable links, communication interruptions
  may occur. AUVi determines the set of disconnected AUVs at time t as
                               N̄i (t) = {j       μi (t) − μj (t) 2 > Ra } ,               (9)
    where N̄i (t) denotes the set of AUVs that are beyond the acoustic range of
    AUVi at time t. For each AUV j ∈ N̄i (t), AUVi retrieves the last received
    data packet from time step t − 1 as
                         Hj (t − 1) = {μj (t − 1), vj (t − 1), Cj (t − 1)} ,              (10)
224       P. Dong et al.

      where
      • μj (t − 1) = (xj (t − 1), yj (t − 1)) is the position;
      • vj (t − 1) = (vjx (t − 1), vjy (t − 1)) is the heading direction;
      • Cj (t − 1) = {(mk , nk , pmk nk ) | k = 1, . . . , M } is the set of TPM obser-
        vations, where each entry corresponds to an observed grid cell (mk , nk )
        and its associated probability pmk nk .




                                    Fig. 4. Forecaster Prompt.


  The historical data packet {HIS Data} submitted to the LLM for inference
  is composed by aggregating all Hj (t − 1) from disconnected AUVs

                       Hj (t − 1) = μj (t − 1), vj (t − 1), Cj (t − 1) | j ∈ N̄i (t) .   (11)
           j∈N̄i (t)

  As shown in Fig. 4, To improve inference accuracy, the LLM is provided with
  essential prior knowledge, including AUV motion dynamics model, sonar sens-
  ing mechanism, examples of heading-direction-to-position transitions. The
  inference result for each disconnected AUV can be expressed in a uniﬁed
  JSON format {Fore JSON}. For example, the information prediction for the
  missing AUVj is as follows.
                   ⎧
                   ⎪ "Heading direction" : (vjx (t), vjy (t)),
                   ⎨
       "AUV j" = "Position" : (xj (t), yj (t)),                          (12)
                   ⎪
                   ⎩                                      LLM
                     "Channel information" : (m, n, pmn (t)), . . . .
                            LLM-Enhanced Multi-AUV Collaborative Search           225

   Then, the conﬁrmed {Fore JSON} is unpacked using the json.load func-
   tion. The unpacked information {Fore Data} is stored in the history data
   buﬀer. Subsequently, AUVi retrieves from the historical buﬀer the "Channel
   information": (m, n, pLLMmn (t)), . . . of the disconnected AUVs at time t, as
   inferred by the LLM, modiﬁes its TPM (P (t) = {pmn (t)}) using the predicted
   data, and performs information fusion with the AUVs maintaining stable com-
   munication. This approach eﬀectively compensates for TPM update delays
   caused by the loss of communication.


4.4   Dec-POMDP Formulation
Each AUV is limited by the partially observable environment and cannot per-
ceive global information. Therefore, we formulate the problem as a POMDP,
represented by the tuple S, O, A, P, R , deﬁned as follows.

– State Space: S = {s1 , s2 , . . . , sN }, representing the states of N AU Vi . Each
  state si is deﬁned as
                                    si = {μi , vi , gi , ci },                    (13)
  where μi , vi , gi and ci denote the position, speed, target probability map
  value, and communication status of AU Vi , respectively.
– Observation Space: O = {o1 , o2 , . . . , oN } is the joint observation space of all
  agents, where oi is the partial observation information obtained by the ith
  AUV from the global state. The information observed by the ith AUV is
  represented as
                         oi = {μi , vi , gi , μother , dother , ci },            (14)
  where μother denotes the position matrix of other AUVs, dother = μother −
  μi denotes the position distance between the i th AUV and other AUVs,
  respectively.
– Action Space: A = {a1 , a2 , . . . , aN }, representing the set of all joint actions
  of multiple AUVs.
                                       ai = {bi , ϕi },                           (15)
  where bi and ϕi denote the acceleration and angular velocity of AU Vi , respec-
  tively.
– State Transition Probability: P is the probability function of state transition,
  which can be expressed as P : S × A → S.
– Reward: R = {r1 , r2 , . . . , rN } represents the joint reward of all AUVs. We
  design a reward function to evaluate the behavioral decisions of each AUV.
  The reward is deﬁned as

                    ri = λ · rprob + β · rf ind + θ · rcol + δ · rcomm ,         (16)

   where λ, β, θ, δ ∈ R represent the weight coeﬃcients for each part of the
   reward.
226    P. Dong et al.

  Target probability reward rprob : To encourage AUVs moving to areas
  with higher probabilities. The probability reward is deﬁned as

                                      grid(m,n)∈F OV pmn
                            rprob =                        ,                (17)
                                           NF OV
  where NF OV is the number of grid cells within the AUV detection range,
  pmn represents the probability of target existence for each small square in the
  search range.
  Target reward rf ind : The core of the target search problem is to locate
  the target. Upon discovery, a signiﬁcant reward is given to encourage search,
  deﬁned as
                                   rf ind = rdet ,                           (18)
  where rdet is a constant representing the ﬁxed reward for successfully ﬁnding
  the target.
  Collision penalty rcol : To ensure safe distances between AUVs, penalize
  AU Vi when AU Vi is too close to a neighboring AU Vk (where k ∈ N and
  k = i) if the distance dik is less than a safety threshold dmin , deﬁned as

                             max(0, dik − dmin ),   if dik < dmin
                   rcol =                                         ,         (19)
                             0,                     otherwise

  when the distance between AU Vi and AU Vk is less than the safety distance
  dmin .
  Communication reward rcomm : To enhance information exchange between
  AUVs, we design a communication reward to facilitate the acquisition of
  information among the AUVs as follows.
                                                dik
                                  rcomm = 1 −       ,                       (20)
                                                Ra
  where Ra is the distance for underwater acoustic communication, and dik is
  the distance between AU Vi and AU Vk .


4.5   LEMACS Algorithm
To achieve collaborative search for AUVs, we utilize MADDPG to coordinate and
control AUVs in order to search for targets as quickly as possible. The LEMACS
algorithm is outlined in Algorithm 2. Firstly, we use the TPM inferred by Algo-
rithm 1 as the initial TPM (P (t) = {pmn (t)}) for AUVs. The TPM serves as
the prior knowledge for AUVs to overcome cold start problem, and it contains
terrain information that AUVs need to focus on searching. The probability of
the terrain that needs to be searched in TPM is higher than that of ordinary
areas. Driven by rewards, AUVs will search important areas and then ordinary
areas during the search process, thereby reducing the large number of invalid
searches caused by the lack of prior knowledge in the early stage of search and
                               LLM-Enhanced Multi-AUV Collaborative Search                227

eﬀectively solving cold start problem. Secondly, when communication between
AUVs becomes unstable, we use a forecaster to estimate the states of the dis-
connected AUVs, and use the predicted information ("Channel information":
  (m, n, pLLM
          mn (t)), . . . ) to modify own TPM, thereby reducing the problem of
delayed TPM (P (t) = {pmn (t)}) updates caused by unstable communication.
    During the training process, each AUV acts as an agent. The joint observa-
tions are x = (o1 , . . . , oN ), with next state x after actions a = (a1 , . . . , aN ). Each
agent interacts with the environment and stores experiences in D. Each AUV
(agent) employs four neural networks: actor μξi , target actor μξi , critic Qωi , and
target critic Qωi , with parameters ξi , ξi , ωi , and ωi . The actor is updated by


Algorithm 2. The LEMACS Algorithm
 1: Initialize actor and critic networks of each AUV with random parameters ξi , ωi .
 2: Initialize target networks: ξi ← ξi , ωi ← ωi .
 3: Initialize replay buﬀer D and history data buﬀer B.
 4: Obtain initial TPM P (t) by Algorithm 1 with inputs T and M.
 5: Initialize TPM G ← P (t) = {pmn }.
 6: for episode = 1 to E do
 7:    Initialize exploration process N (t) and G ← G.
 8:    Receive initial observation x of all AUVs.
 9:    for t = 1 to T do
10:        for AUV i = 1 to N do
11:           if communication is interrupted then
12:              Identify disconnected set N̄i (t) = {j μi (t) − μj (t) 2 > Ra }.
13:              Retrieve {HIS Data} = {Hj (t−1) | j ∈ N̄i (t)} from B.
14:              F OREJSON ← LLMF orecaster (HISData ).
15:              Unpack the F OREJSON and store in buﬀer B.
16:           else
17:              Cache channel data to buﬀer B.
18:           end if
19:           Update G with buﬀer B using Eq. (7).
20:        end for
21:        For each agent, take action ai = μξi (oi ) + N (t).
22:        Observe new state x , reward r.
23:        Store (x, a, x , r) into replay buﬀer D.
24:        x←x.

26:           Sample mini-batch of S from D.
27:           Update actor μξi using Eq. (21).
28:           Update critic Qωi using Eq. (22) and (23).
29:        end for
30:        Update target networks using Eq. (24).
31:     end for
32: end for

5     Performance Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate the performance of the LLM-generated initial TPM
by comparing the inference accuracy, inference time, and computational cost, in
preparation for addressing the cold start problem. Then, we distribute the initial
TPM to each AUV to carry out the search tasks. Finally, we validate the eﬀec-
tiveness of the LLM-enhanced TPM update under communication constraints
and conduct experiments. To illustrate the eﬀectiveness of the search strategy,
we use the search time, search success rate and energy consumption to evaluate
the search performance.

5.1   Environment Settings

The scenario assumes that multi-AUV search for underwater targets. In order to
ensure the authenticity of regional underwater terrain data, the coral reef map
dataset of Arizona State University (ASU) and the terrain data of the Dongsha
Islands and other regions are used to build the marine terrain data [22]. The
search area is divided into 1600 square grids in a 10 km × 10 km area, and
the grid length is 250 m. Table 1 lists other simulation parameters used in the
experimental setup.


5.2   Cold Start Solutions with LLM-Generated Initial TPM
      Performance

To evaluate the performance of diﬀerent LLMs in search tasks, we compare
four LLM application programming interfaces (APIs): Llama, GPT, Qwen, and
DeepSeek.
   Table 2 compares LLMs in generating initial TPM for AUVs across two tasks:
task 1, with two terrain area (simpler), and task 2, which adds two more terrain
area (more complex). In the Llama series, Llama-3.1-405B model achieved 100%
and 90% accuracy for task 1 and task 2, respectively. In the GPT series, both
GPT-4 and GPT-4o also reached 100% and 90% accuracy, with excellent perfor-
mance and minimal processing time, but GPT-4 incurs high API costs per expert
message. The cost is too high, which is not conducive to large-scale deployment.
Within the Deepseek series, Deepseek r1 attained 95% and 90% accuracy, but
suﬀers from slow inference, for search tasks that require urgent time, this will
be a fatal disadvantage. Deepseek v3 achieved 100% and 90%, showing strong
results. In the Qwen series, Qwen-2.5-72B and Qwen-max both reached 100%
and 90% accuracy, with Qwen-max oﬀering faster completion time. In addition,
Qwen 2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B are locally deployed, with smaller parameters,

5.3   LLM-Enhanced Update of TPM Under Communication
      Constraints Performance
Table 3 illustrates the performance of various LLMs as Forecaster. The Forecaster
predicts other AUVs’ information based on historical data, a process that may
occur repeatedly during a mission. Llama-3.1-405B achieved 89% accuracy with
a 6.54 s average runtime, showing good performance. In the GPT series, GPT-4
and GPT-4o reached 95.83% and 91.66% accuracy with runtimes of 4.11 s and
3.88 s, respectively. Both performed excellently, but GPT-4 costs $0.06111 per
use, whereas GPT-4o is signiﬁcantly cheaper at $0.01126. In addition to the
lower cost, GPT-4o also responds faster than GPT-4, making it more suitable
for large-scale applications. In the Deepseek series, Deepseek r1, though bidirec-
tional, struggled with mathematical and logical inference and had long runtimes.
Deepseek v3 achieved 76.67% accuracy. In the Qwen series, Qwen-QwQ-32B and
Qwen-max achieved 85% and 90% accuracy, with Qwen-max oﬀering shorter
runtimes. Additionally, Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B were deployed locally.
Their smaller size ensured fast, cost-free runs, though with limited performance
in information inference.

In this section, we evaluate the overall performance of the proposed algorithm
using three selected LLMs to execute the task: LEMACS (GPT-4o), LEMACS

(Qwen-max), and LEMACS (Llama-3.1-405B). To verify the eﬀectiveness of the
proposed algorithm, we introduce the following two baseline reinforcement learn-
ing methods for comparison.

– MADDPG method [23]: The Actor network generates continuous actions to
  control the AUV, and uses random sampling methods to obtain experience
  tuples for training. The other parameters of the MADDPG are conﬁgured to
  be identical to those in our algorithm.
– HCCC method [20]: A multi-AUV asynchronous update search strategy
  based on high-capacity chance communication to maximize target search per-
  formance under unstable communication condition, but HCCC lacks LLM
  enhanced mechanism.

gence speed and search quality of LEMACS (Qwen-max) are higher than those
of LEMACS (Llama-3.1-405B). In HCCC, AUVs maintain a shared TPM via
limited communication. However, the lack of LLM enhancement limits prior
knowledge and delays TPM updates, resulting in slower search performance.
MADDPG uses neither a TPM nor LLM enhancement, leading to a lack of data

6     Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed an LLM-enhanced multi-AUV cooperative search
scheme. Firstly, we model the updating process of environmental information and
TPM. Subsequently, we solve the cold start problem by using the initial TPM
inferred by the LLM as prior knowledge. Furthermore, under communication
constraints, we improve the timeliness of TPM updates by predicting the state
information of AUVs with disrupted communication. Finally, we formulate the
cooperative search task as a Dec-POMDP and proposed the LEMACS algorithm,
which enhances the eﬃciency of multi-AUV cooperative search. In future work,
we plan to evaluate the proposed scheme on real-world AUV hardware platforms,
and improve the performance further of the proposed scheme.

         CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition Using
           Spatial-Temporal Features and Attention

Wenping Yu1(B) , Jianhao Wang1 , Yusong Dong1 , Zhewen Li1 , and Jianzhong Zhang2
   1 Tianjin University of Science and Technology, Artificial Intelligence Institute of Tianjin
              University of Science and Technology, Tianjin 300457, China
                             yuwenping@tust.edu.cn
2 Nankai University, Computer Science Institute of Nankai University, Tianjin 300350, China



        Abstract. In this paper, we propose a CLSA human activity recognition (HAR)
        method based on channel state information (CSI) to address the challenges of
        environmental noise and feature overfitting. The method adopts a hybrid deep
        learning architecture that combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a
        Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network and an attention mechanism. Raw
        CSI data are first denoised using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to preserve
        activity-related information while suppressing random noise. The preprocessed
        data are then passed through the CNN layer to extract spatial features using a
        two-layer Conv1D structure. These spatial features are further processed by a
        two-layer stacked LSTM network to model temporal patterns. The output of the
        final LSTM layer is then fed into the attention layer, where weights are dynamically
        assigned to emphasize the contextual relevance of key activity segments. Finally,
        the classification layer is used to categorize the activities. The experimental results
        show that the CSI-based human body recognition method proposed in this paper
        outperforms models such as LSTM and CNN and some recognition methods on
        real datasets. The average recognition accuracies of up to 90.09% and 89.64%
        are achieved in two different environments, respectively, providing an effective
        method for activity recognition.

        Keywords: Wireless sensing · Human activity recognition · Channel state
        information · Neural network


1 Introduction
Human Activity Recognition (HAR) [1–3] has been a prominent area of study for more
than ten years. Conventional HAR techniques are usually categorized into two main
groups: vision-based and sensor-based approaches. Vision-based methods [4, 5] rely on
cameras or static images to interpret human motion through visual processing. Although
they can yield accurate results in controlled conditions, their effectiveness often dimin-
ishes with changes in lighting or camera placement, which restricts their real-world
adaptability. On the other hand, sensor-based techniques [6] require individuals to wear
or carry specialized equipment. While these methods tend to offer more consistent results
in various environments, they can be expensive and intrusive, potentially leading to user
discomfort and limited long-term usability.

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 236–253, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_13
                                          CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition          237

     In response to these limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to Channel State
Information (CSI) as an alternative solution for activity recognition. CSI, which reflects
the way Wi-Fi signals are influenced by human movement due to multipath effects,
captures fine-grained changes in signal transmission at the physical layer. This enables
systems to detect and classify human activities by observing how signals fluctuate in
each environment [7]. CSI-based HAR methods bring several benefits over traditional
approaches. They remain effective in poorly lit or visually obstructed areas since they
do not depend on image clarity or direct line-of-sight. These methods can also utilize
existing Wi-Fi networks, which help reduce installation costs and eliminate the need
for extra hardware. Furthermore, because they do not require physical contact with the
user, CSI-based systems offer a non-intrusive, privacy-conscious alternative to wearable
technologies.
     The rapid development of machine learning and deep learning has significantly
boosted their application in CSI-based human activity recognition. Because distinct
human movements lead to unique variations in CSI signals, many researchers have
applied different learning algorithms to identify these patterns and improve recogni-
tion performance [8]. Yet, even with these advancements, CSI-based HAR continues to
encounter several important challenges. Current models often overfit to environmental
features in the source domain, resulting in poor generalization to the target domain. To
address these issues, prior studies have employed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
or Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to extract spatial or temporal features
but usually use them alone or combine them without addressing the interference of noise
with key activity segments in CSI data. In contrast, this paper proposes the CLSA model,
which integrates CNN, LSTM network and attention modules for CSI-based HAR. The
attention mechanism dynamically assigns weights to emphasize the most relevant activ-
ities segments while mitigating environmental interference. As mentioned earlier, CSI
data are often affected by multipath effects and environmental dynamics, which can
introduce irrelevant or noisy fluctuations into the data. The attention mechanism excels
in such scenario by focusing on the most informative parts of the signal — such as sub-
tle changes in amplitude or phase that are closely related to human activities — while
downplaying irrelevant or noisy components. This selective focus enhances the model’s
ability to capture discriminative features for accurate activity recognition.
     To conclude, this work introduces the CLSA framework—an approach to HAR
that integrates CNN, LSTM, and attention mechanisms. The system begins by feeding
preprocessed CSI data into a two-layer Conv1D structure to capture spatial features.
Next, the extracted features are fed into a two-layer stacked LSTM network to model
temporal patterns, in the activity sequences. An attention mechanism is then applied,
where weights are computed using a Tanh activation function and normalized with
Softmax to generate a context vector that aids in classification. Experiments on a real-
world dataset show that this method achieves a recognition accuracy of 90.1%.

2 Related Work
Research in activity recognition has evolved along two primary paths: traditional
machine learning methods and modern deep learning approaches. Classic few-shot
learning techniques often employ well-known classifiers like decision trees, random
238        W. Yu et al.

forests, support vector machines (SVMs), and k-nearest neighbors (KNNs) [9]. These
approaches depend on labeled data to classify both training and test samples into pre-
defined categories. For instance, Venkatnarayan et al. [10] introduced WiMU, a system
for recognizing user activities by matching incoming CSI signals to a reference library
using a traversal matching algorithm. In another study, Yang et al. [11] tackled the high
computational cost of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by proposing a transformation
algorithm within the Spiking Neural Network (SNN) framework. Their method converts
trained ANN neurons into spike sequences, allowing SNNs to operate more efficiently
without sacrificing accuracy.
    With the rise of deep learning, this technology has gradually developed in various
fields. In contrast to traditional machine learning, which often depends on manually
crafted features, deep learning models automatically learn useful representations from
data by training on large, labeled datasets and refining their parameters through back-
propagation [12]. This shift has removed reliance on handcrafted descriptors, enabling
models to build layered, abstract features that better capture the complexity of input data
[13]. Leveraging these strengths, researchers have made significant progress in advancing
activity recognition technologies. WiSign [14], for instance, leverages Power Spectral
Density (PSD) to segment CSI data autonomously, deriving amplitude and phase fea-
tures to train a five-layer Deep Belief Network (DBN). In another approach, HandFi
[15], developed by Sruthi et al., processes denoised CSI signals through time-frequency
transformations, extracts spatial features via CNN and classifies outputs using support
vector machines.
    While modern deep learning architectures have enhanced recognition accuracy,
robustness, and generalization, persistent challenges remain in CSI-based systems. Data
quality inconsistencies and environmental variability during collection continue to hin-
der performance, highlighting the need for refined preprocessing methods and innovative
model designs to bridge existing gaps.


3 Method

The CLSA HAR method, illustrated in Fig. 1, follows a three-stage process: data collec-
tion, data preprocessing and activity recognition. In the initial stage, wireless devices are
used to collect CSI embedded in Wi-Fi signals. Next, during preprocessing, the raw CSI
data is processed using the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which helps reduce ran-
dom noise. In the final stage, activity recognition is performed using the CLSA model.
This model integrates a two-layer Conv1D structure to extract spatial features, a stacked
two-layer LSTM network to model temporal patterns, and an attention mechanism to
focus on the key informative segments of the activity data.


3.1 Data Collection

CSI is a detailed metric used in wireless communication to describe how signals behave
as they travel through the environment. It reflects the impact of physical phenomena
like diffraction, reflection and scattering on the signal’s transmission. In most cases, CSI
data are collected using an Intel 5300 wireless network interface card, which can extract
                                          CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition          239




                            Fig. 1. Overall recognition process.


information from 30 subcarriers for each communication link. These subcarriers carry
multiple packets, with each packet represented by a set of complex values such as shown
below.

                                    A(f) = |A(f)| A(f)                                  (1)

    In the above equation, f represents the signal frequency, |A( f )| represents the ampli-
tude loudness and A( f ) represents the phase. Based on Eq. (1), the CSI in Orthogonal
Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) system can be expressed as:

                                Y(f) = A(f) · X(f) + N(f)                               (2)

    In the above equation, f represents the signal frequency, Y(f ) represents the received
signal and X(f ) represents the transmitted signal and N(f ) represents the random noise
signal in the environment.
    In MIMO systems, CSI is extended to a matrix form. The channel matrix for M ×
N antennas is:

                             A = [h1, h2, h3, · · · , h30]M×N                           (3)

   In the above equation, M and N are the number of antennas used at the transmitter
and receiver terminal, respectively, with a total of 30 subcarriers per antenna pair.


3.2 Data Preprocessing

In this paper, the raw CSI data will be preprocessed by DWT to suppress the inherent
random noise components. As a time-frequency analysis technique, the DWT decom-
poses the signal into local wavelet basis functions to achieve characterization across
time and frequency domains. The technique uses window operations to divide the sig-
nal into different frequency bands. The transformation contains scaling and translation
240        W. Yu et al.

parameters that allow the window resolution and position to be adjusted to synchronize
the time-frequency for subsequent processing, as shown in equation.
                                    √                   ∗
                      Wf (a, b) = 1/ | a |     f(t) ·       ((t − b)/a) dt              (4)

     During DWT processing, the raw CSI data begins with a multistage decomposition
by orthogonal mirror filtering. Specifically, the low-pass filter extracts approximate coef-
ficients (representing signal features, referred to as low-frequency information), whereas
the high-pass filter separates detail coefficients (corresponding to high-frequency noise
components, termed detail components). DWT is mainly accomplished by decompo-
sition. The input CSI data is decomposed by the first step to get the low-frequency
information 1 and detail component 1. The obtained low-frequency information decom-
posed by the first step is again subjected to the discrete transform operation to get
the low-frequency information 2 and detail component 2. This process is repeated itera-
tively until the n-level decomposition stage, ultimately producing n levels of hierarchical
low-frequency information and corresponding detail components. The denoising pro-
cess leverages the inherent property that noise is present in the detail coefficients of
the wavelet decomposition. By selectively eliminating these detail components at each
decomposition level through thresholding operations, the raw CSI data is effectively
purified while preserving its essential characteristics.
     Fig. 2 illustrates a comparison of the time-varying characteristics of CSI amplitude
before and after preprocessing using a two-axis plot. Before denoising, the CSI data
(left) displays substantial high-frequency noise, leading to irregular amplitude varia-
tions with minimal recognizable structure. After applying DWT (right), the noise is
significantly suppressed, and the amplitude profile becomes smoother while preserv-
ing activity-relevant features. This contrast highlights DWT’s effectiveness in removing
random noise while preserving the integrity of activity-relevant information, thereby
providing a reliable foundation for subsequent feature extraction.




                  Fig. 2. Comparison of CSI before and after preprocessing.




3.3 Activity Recognition
Fig. 3 illustrates the CLSA HAR process, including spatial and temporal feature extrac-
tion, attention weighting, and final classification. The diagram highlights the sequential
                                           CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition            241

architecture comprising the CNN layer (with Conv1D and pooling operations), the LSTM
layer (a two-layer stacked structure), and the attention mechanism, demonstrating the
hierarchical data flow from input to final classification. It particularly emphasizes the
attention layer’s function in re-weighting key temporal features to enhance classification
performance.




                         Fig. 3. Recognition process of CLSA model.



CSI Spatial Feature Extraction. CNN [16, 17] are effective for dimensionality reduc-
tion, enabling compression of spatial feature maps to reduce parameters and computa-
tional complexity while retaining salient features. Therefore, a CNN module is employed
to extract spatial features from preprocessed CSI data.
    Specifically, the CNN layer takes the preprocessed CSI data as input and applies
convolutional and pooling operations. As shown in Fig. 4, a two-layer one-dimensional
convolutional (Conv1D) structure is adopted due to its efficacy in modeling time-series
data such as CSI. The first Conv1D layer employs 64 filters with a kernel size of 5 and a
stride of 1. The second layer expands to 128 filters with a kernel size of 3 and a stride of 2,
capturing fine-grained spatial correlations among subcarriers by progressively expanding
the receptive field. A ReLU activation function is applied after each convolution to
enhance non-linear feature representation. Same padding is applied to preserve the input
length. Max-pooling layers follow each convolutional layer, using a pooling size of 2
and stride of 2, enabling gradual dimensionality reduction and improving translation
invariance. To further mitigate overfitting caused by environmental noise, a Dropout
layer with a rate of 0.3 is applied. The final output from the CNN layer is a compressed
spatial feature vector passed to the LSTM layer for temporal modeling.




                               Fig. 4. CNN network structure.
242        W. Yu et al.

CSI Temporal Feature Extraction. The LSTM network [18], a specialized variant of
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), remains particularly effective for modeling sequen-
tial or temporal data. It is specifically designed to mitigate gradient vanishing and explo-
sion issues that occur in traditional RNNs during the processing of long sequences. LSTM
network incorporates a memory cell architecture regulated by three gating mechanisms—
input, forget, and output gate—as illustrated in Fig. 5. This architecture allows the net-
work to retain important information over long sequences while discarding irrelevant
inputs, thereby enabling effective modeling of long-term dependencies. Consequently,
an LSTM network is employed to extract temporal features from the CSI data.




                                 Fig. 5. LSTM basic units.


    In the LSTM layer, the spatial features compressed by the CNN module are seg-
mented by time steps and expanded into 128-dimensional vectors. A two-layer stacked
LSTM with 128 hidden units in each layer is employed to extract temporal features. At
each step, the LSTM cell receives the current input vector and the previous hidden state,
and performs gating operations using forget, input, and output gate to update the internal
cell state and produce the temporal features.
    The forget gate determines which information to discard from the previous cell state
by examining both the current input and the hidden state from the previous time step.

                               ft = σ Wf · ht−1 , xt + bf                               (5)

   The input gate decides what new information will be updated into the cell state. It
similarly makes decisions by looking at the current input and the previous hidden state.

                               it = σ Wi · ht−1 , xt + bi                               (6)

                            Ct = tanh WC · ht−1 , xt + bc                               (7)
                                          CSI-Based Human Activity Recognition           243

    The cell state constitutes the core memory mechanism in LSTM structure, function-
ing as persistent memory storage for retaining long-range temporal features. This mem-
ory vector undergoes systematic modification through coordinated operations involving
both forget and input gate. Specifically, the forget gate selectively attenuates historical
information patterns, while the input gate counterpart regulates the integration of novel
feature representations into the memory repository.

                                  Ct = ft · Ct−1 + it · Ct                               (8)

   The output gate decides the next hidden state by considering both the current input
and the previous hidden state, producing an output that is influenced by the cell state.

                              ot = σ Wo · ht−1 , xt + bo                                 (9)

                                    ht = ot · tanh (Ct )                                (10)

    After the above steps, the final output features are passed to the next LSTM layer (the
input dimension of the second layer is 128, and the output dimension remains 128) to
capture higher-level temporal features. Finally, the output of the last layer in the LSTM
layer is sent to the attention layer for further processing as the total output of the entire
LSTM layer.
Attention Mechanism. The attention mechanism computes the relevance between time
steps in the input sequence. By assigning higher weights to informative segments that
contribute significantly to classification, it enhances the model’s focus on key activity
segment while suppressing irrelevant environmental noise.
    In the attention layer, the output of the LSTM layer is used as input to compute
attention scores. These scores are calculated using a Tanh activation applied to a linear
transformation involving a learnable weight matrix and bias term. The scores are then
normalized using the Softmax function and used to compute a weighted sum of the
LSTM layer outputs, resulting in context data. This data emphasizes key activity phases
while retaining temporal structure, thereby enhancing the overall discriminative capacity
of the model.
Classifications. The attention-weighted features are passed into the classification layer
for final activity prediction. This layer consists of a two-layer fully connected network,
where the first layer compresses the feature representation, and the second layer projects
the compressed features into the activity label space. Finally, a Softmax classification
function is applied to generate probability distribution across the five activity classes.


4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Equipment
CSI data is collected using an Intel 5300 wireless network interface card (NIC) in con-
junction with the open-source CSI Tool. The Intel 5300 NIC allows flexible configu-
ration of antenna states and related parameters via command-line interface. The CSI
244           W. Yu et al.

Tool facilitates the extraction of CSI from Wi-Fi signals. Experiments are conducted
on a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network with a channel bandwidth of 20 MHz, using a TP-Link
router with three antennas as the transmitter, and an Ubuntu 14.04 desktop equipped
with a three-antenna NIC as the receiver. CSI collection is achieved by connecting both
transmitter and receiver to the same local Wi-Fi network.


4.2 Experimental Procedure

During the setup phase of the experimental environment, the signal transmitter (commer-
cial wireless router) and receiver (computer device equipped with Intel 5300 wireless
card) are configured according to the requirements. However, one thing to keep in mind
is that the router is required to create a wireless network without a password because
the firmware of the CSI Tool does not have enough code space for storing beamforming
software paths and encryption software paths. After checking for errors, the collection
can begin. The data collection process requires the collector stand between the transmit-
ter and receiver with the CSI Tool running and perform the activities in a prearranged
sequence. The collection arrangements relating to collected activity and personnel are
shown in Table 1 and 2. Table 1 lists the information about the participants involved in the
experiment. The study involves five volunteers, whose height and weight are recorded.
Table 2 outlines the predefined human activities and their corresponding definitions for
recognition tasks. Based on nature and duration of activity, five common activity cate-
gories are defined: slide, sweep, stand, crouch and bend. Each activity lasted 5 s and 60
samples were collected per subject. The same process was used to complete the collec-
tion task for the remaining activities, then the collected files were named according to
the prescribed format. Finally, all data files were organized and categorized.

4.3 Evaluation Indicators

In practical applications, choosing the right evaluation metrics is essential for assessing
and optimizing recognition. For the experiments in this study, the evaluation metrics
included accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Accuracy is the primary metric for
measuring overall correctness, reflecting the proportion of correctly identified activities.
Precision indicates accuracy by calculating the ratio of correctly recognized activities
to all activities predicted as positive. Recall evaluates the ability to identify the actual
target activities by measuring how many were correctly recognized. F1 score, which is
the harmonic means of precision and recall, offers a balanced evaluation of the overall
performance.


4.4 Experiments with Different Scenarios

Experiments were conducted in two different scenarios to evaluate the robustness of the
CLSA model in complex environments. Fig. 6 presents the confusion matrices for the
CLSA model under these two settings. In each matrix, rows represent the true activity
classes, while columns indicate the predicted classes as recognized by the model. In
the office environment, the recognition accuracy for most activities is relatively high.
Specifically, slide (91.95%), sweep (91.21%), and crouch (91.11%) each achieve over
90% accuracy. The accuracy for stand is slightly lower at 87.5%, with common mis-
classifications such as crouch (4.17%) or sweep (4.17%). In the classroom environment,
the recognition accuracy for slide (94.25%) and crouch (92.22%) further improves,
while the performance on sweep (89.01%) and stand (85.42%) slightly declines com-
pared to the office setting. This performance degradation may be attributed to more
complex background interference present in the classroom. Notably, stand exhibits a
higher misclassification rate, with a 6.25% chance of being misidentified as bend. The
246       W. Yu et al.

accuracy for bend also slightly decreases to 87.5%. Overall, the proposed CLSA model
achieves robust recognition across different environments, attaining average recognition
accuracies of 90.09% in the office and 89.64% in the classroom.




              Fig. 6. Confusion matrix of different activities in two scenarios.


    In addition, to evaluate the comprehensive performance of the model, the precision,
recall, and F1 score for each activity were also compared. Fig. 7 compares the precision,
recall, and F1 score for each activity in the two scenarios. The stand activity in the
office scenario had the highest precision rate of 94.38%, while the crouch activity only
had 91.11% recall rate due to the smaller range of motion. The F1 score of the sweep
activity in the classroom scenario is 91.53%, which is significantly better than the other
activity, indicating that the model is more accurate in capturing the temporal features of
high-frequency activity. However, the bend activity may be affected by environmental
interference and its performance is relatively weak. Through the above experiments, it
is verified that scenario differences will have a certain impact on model performance.

4.5 Experiments with Different Models

Fig. 8 compares the recognition effects of the CLSA model and the other six models
(LSTM network, CNN, SVM, RNN, KNN, GRU) on five types of activities through con-
fusion matrices. The six models achieved average accuracy of 86.8%, 85.65%, 82.47%,
82.66%, 86.49% and 88.09% respectively. GRU has the best overall performance. Its
accuracy rates of slide (87.36%), sweep (89.01%), stand (88.54%), crouch (88.89%) and
bend (86.42%) exceed 85% and the misclassification rate is generally low, especially in
sweep and stand activity. KNN and LSTM network are second. The accuracy of bend
activity in KNN is 0.85, but the probability of bend activity being misclassified as crouch
activity is slightly higher (5%); while SVM and RNN perform poorly. SVM has the low-
est accuracy rates for slide and bend activity, and RNN has significant misclassification
of sweep activity. CNN is balanced overall, but bend accuracy is slightly lower. In con-
trast, the CLSA model that combines spatiotemporal features and attention weighting
248       W. Yu et al.

has the highest recognition accuracy among similar models, verifying the effectiveness
of its hierarchical feature fusion mechanism.

model with six baseline models (LSTM network, CNN, SVM, RNN, KNN, GRU) in
terms of precision, recall, and F1 score. CLSA model achieved an F1 score of more
than 88% in all five activities in the office scenario, significantly higher than GRU and
LSTM network, thanks to the enhancement of key time step features by the attention

mechanism, while SVM had the lowest recall rate in the bend activity due to its reliance

the complementary integration of CNN and LSTM networks. In addition, due to the
vanishing gradient problem, the average F1 score of RNN was only 82.65%, while CLSA
model alleviated this defect through the LSTM gating mechanism and the score increased
to 90%. Experiments show that the CLSA model has a better overall performance than
the other six models.

To analyze how the introduction of the attention mechanism in this paper’s method
affects the classification results. In the real dataset, ablation experiments are designed to
compare the recognition effects of different models. The experiments are still conducted
in two scenarios: office and classroom. One group adopts the method of this paper, using
CNN, LSTM network and attention mechanism for activity recognition and the other
group removes the attention mechanism on this basis for recognition, and the model’s
name is abbreviated as CLS. Experiments have shown that in both office and classroom
scenario, the accuracy, recall and F1 score of this method are higher than those of the
CLS model. At the same time, the introduction of the attention mechanism has a higher
distinction effect on easily confused activities (Table 3, 4).

4.7 Experiments with Different Methods

To further verify the role of the proposed CLSA HAR method in activity recognition
in different scenarios, it is compared with two different methods: CrossScene and CSI-
MTGN. In two different scenarios, office and classroom, the two methods are used to
recognize the five collected activities respectively and the recognition results are shown
in Table 5. From the table, the CLSA method performs optimally in the office scenario
(90.09%) and ranks second in the classroom scenario (89.64%), demonstrating strong
overall stability, while the CSI-MTGN has the highest accuracy in the classroom scenario
(90.03%), but its performance in the office scenario is slightly lower than that of the
CLSA. The CLS method is close to the same accuracy in both types of scenarios, which
indicates that its adaptability is more balanced. In contrast, the CrossScene method
has the weakest performance in both scenarios (81.2% and 76.9%), especially in the
classroom scenario, where the accuracy decreases significantly, which may need to
be further optimized. In addition, the CLS and CLSA methods had smaller scenario
differences (both below 1.5%) and stronger generalization ability, while the CSI-MTGN
and CrossScene had larger differences (1.83% and 4.3%, respectively), suggesting that
they are more sensitive to scenario changes.

5 Conclusion

This paper proposes a CLSA HAR method to address the issue that current CSI-based
approaches tend to overfit environmental features in the source domain, while failing
to extract effective features in the target domain, thereby resulting in reduced recogni-
tion accuracy. First, the raw CSI data is preprocessed using the DWT, which effectively
suppresses random noise while preserving activity-relevant information. Then, in the
recognition stage, spatial features are extracted using a two-layer Conv1D structure and
temporal dependencies are modeled using a two-layer stacked LSTM network. On this
basis, an attention mechanism is applied to assign feature weights, thereby enhancing
the contextual representation of key activity segments. The experimental results show
that on real-world datasets containing five activities, the CLSA model achieves aver-
age recognition accuracy of 90.09% and 89.64% in office and classroom scenarios,
which are improved compared to models such as LSTM networks, CNN, SVM, RNN,
KNN and GRU as well as some of the different recognition methods. Furthermore, the
effectiveness of the attention mechanism is validated through ablation studies, which
significantly improves the differentiation of easily confusable activities such as Slide
and Sweep. In future work, we plan to expand the dataset with higher-quality activ-
ity samples to further enhance recognition performance and overall model robustness.
Although this paper has achieved certain results in HAR research, several limitations
remain. Constrained by experimental equipment and environmental factors, the largest
dataset in the experiments only included 5 participants and 5 action categories. Further-
more, the recording environment was set in relatively stable scenarios, lacking validation
in complex settings, which to some extent limits the model’s generalization capability.
Future research should consider optimizing experiments in multiple dimensions. First,
constructing larger open datasets encompassing diverse ages, body types, complex envi-
ronments (e.g., shopping malls, outdoor settings), and group interaction scenarios could
enhance model generalization. Second, integrating CSI with computer vision and sensor
modalities through multimodal fusion could improve recognition robustness in complex
scenarios. In summary, CSI-based wireless sensing technology holds great promise in
human-machine interaction and intelligent security. Future research should focus on
breakthroughs in datasets and algorithms to advance the transition of this technology
from idealized environments to practical applications.
