           Abstract. Base placement is particularly critical for navigation manip-
           ulation tasks in environments, where improper placement can severely
           hinder task execution if the object’s kinematics are not properly taken
           into account. In this work, we present MoMa-Pos, a framework that
           determines the base placement for mobile manipulators in such envi-
           ronments. MoMa-Pos leverages a graph-based neural network to predict
           object importance and selectively reconstructs the environment by pri-
           oritizing task-relevant key objects, enhancing computational eﬃciency
           and ensuring that only essential kinematic details are processed. More-
           over, MoMa-Pos integrates inverse reachability maps with environmental
           kinematic properties to determine feasible base placement tailored to the
           speciﬁc robot model. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MoMa-Pos
           outperforms existing methods in both real and simulated environments,
           oﬀering improved eﬃciency, precision, and adaptability across diverse
           settings and robot models.


           Keywords: Base Placement · Mobile Manipulator · Graph-Based
           Neural Network · Reachability Maps


1        Introduction
Mobile manipulators, which integrate a mobile base with a robotic arm, have
emerged as vital components in modern intelligent systems. In particular, they
serve as key enablers of Cyber-Physical-Social Systems (CPSS), bridging compu-
tational intelligence, physical interaction, and human-centered applications. By
B. Shao and N. Cao—Contributed equally to this work.
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 254–270, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_14
        MoMa-Pos: Base Placement Determination for Mobile Manipulation          255

autonomously perceiving, planning, and acting in dynamic human environments,
these robots function as essential interfaces between cyber, physical, and social
domains. They are increasingly deployed in real-world settings such as smart
homes and assisted living spaces, where they perform navigation-manipulation
tasks—such as approaching appliances or interacting with articulated objects like
doors and drawers [1–3]. The success of such tasks critically depends on accurate
base placement [4–7], as suboptimal positioning can severely limit manipulation
performance, particularly under ﬁxed-base constraints where the base remains
stationary during interaction.
    However, the determination of feasible base placement remains challenging,
particularly in household environments that contain both rigid and articulated
objects [8]. Physically interacting with articulated objects requires robots to be
kinematically aware of these objects’ speciﬁc joint movements and constraints
during manipulation. For instance, when opening a fridge door, the robot must
account for the door’s rotational movement and position itself correctly to exert
the necessary force along the appropriate kinematic trajectory. Therefore, kine-
matic modeling of these articulated objects is essential. While technologies in this
area have advanced considerably [9], the associated computational costs remain
signiﬁcant. The cumulative modeling time of all objects in a given scenario can
be substantial, further worsening the overall eﬃciency of robotic systems. Addi-
tionally, a feasible base placement is highly dependent on the robot model. Robots
with shorter arms, such as Stretch [10], need to place themselves closer to target
objects.
    Existing approaches in computing base placement present several limitations.
The basic methods [11,12] set speciﬁc base placement areas empirically, without
accounting for critical factors such as the kinematics of articulated objects and
speciﬁc robot models, which limits their applicability in complex scenarios. More
advanced methods use inverse reachability maps [13], relying on computed kine-
matic solutions to guide base placement [13–16]. However, these approaches over-
look the kinematic complexities of articulated objects, where complex motion
and conﬁguration dependencies impose constraints that extend beyond the limi-
tations of reachability maps. Worse still, these methods typically incur high com-
putational costs, making them impractical for real-time applications. Learning-
based approaches predict feasible base placements by considering the kinematic
properties of objects, the environment, and speciﬁc robot models [4,8,17–19].
However, they require extensive data collection and training, often tailored to
predeﬁned robot-environment pairs, which limits their generalizability to real-
world applications. Given these limitations, there is a pressing need for an eﬃ-
cient and generalizable framework that incorporates object-kinematic awareness
and adaptability to various robot models.
    This work introduces MoMa-Pos, a framework designed to determine base
positioning for mobile manipulators prior to executing navigation-manipulation
tasks. A central aspect of MoMa-Pos is its ability to prioritize key objects in
the scene, enabling eﬃcient modeling without processing every object in the
environment. By leveraging a graph-based neural network, our method predicts
256     B. Shao et al.

the importance of task-relevant objects, allowing for focused computation on
critical elements. This selective modeling integrates advanced algorithms like
URDFormer [9], facilitating accurate kinematic representations where necessary.
The determination of base placements in MoMa-Pos is distinguished by its inte-
gration of two critical factors: the use of inverse reachability maps to account
for robot-speciﬁc constraints, and the incorporation of objects’ kinematic con-
straints from the environment. Such dual strategy reﬁnes potential base place-
ment areas, balancing physical feasibility with task-speciﬁc eﬃciency, leading to
enhanced precision and adaptability. The main contributions of this paper are
summarized as follows:

1. We propose MoMa-Pos, a novel framework that determines feasible base
   placements prior to task execution.
2. We prioritize task-relevant objects by leveraging a graph-based neural net-
   work, instead of modeling all objects in the environment. This selective mod-
   eling reduces computational cost and improves planning eﬃciency by focusing
   only on key objects.
3. We integrate inverse reachability maps (to capture robot-speciﬁc kinematic
   limits) and object-level kinematic constraints (to account for articulation and
   interaction dependencies). This dual-constraint strategy leads to reﬁned can-
   didate base placements that are both physically feasible and task-eﬃcient.
4. We evaluate MoMa-Pos in both simulated and real-world environments across
   various tasks. Results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms
   existing approaches in terms of task success rate, and computational eﬃ-
   ciency.


2     Problem Statement
In this section, we deﬁne the problem of determining the feasible base placement
in an environment, denoted as Env O , which contains a set of objects represented
as O = {o1 , o2 , · · · , oN }. Each object oi is characterized by its 3D position opi and
3D bounding box obi . The target object within these is speciﬁed as ot , and the
mobile manipulator is tasked with manipulating object ot . As shown in Fig. 1,
this robot model r consists of a base, a body, and an arm, which is denoted by
the tuple,
                                       r = rb , rh , rl                                 (1)
where rb represents the base dimensions (rx , ry , rz ) (width, length, height), rh is
the body height, and rl is the arm extension length. The robot’s 2D base place-
ment is denoted by rp , which is assumed to be vertically aligned with the arm
base. The objective is to determine a feasible base placement rp∗ for navigation-
manipulation tasks. The position must meet two critical criteria: the arm must
be able to compute collision-free trajectories for task execution, and the base
must avoid collisions with any objects in Env O .
   To obtain the position opi and bounding box obi for each object oi , the robot
ﬁrst scans the environment to collect 3D point cloud data and videos. The point
         MoMa-Pos: Base Placement Determination for Mobile Manipulation              257

cloud is processed by a pre-trained Mask3D model [20] to segment objects and
extract their corresponding 3D bounding boxes. After removing outliers based
on a distance threshold, the remaining points are used to compute an axis-
aligned 3D bounding box, with opi deﬁned as its geometric center. Additionally,
the video data is used to select RGB images with optimal views for further
kinematic modeling.




Fig. 1. Our mobile manipulator includes a base, a body, and an arm. The symbol Δr
refers to the horizontal distance between the base’s placement and the end-eﬀector in
the x-y plane. rb refers to the base dimensions, rh is the body height, and rl is the arm
extension length. For explanations of additional symbols, see Sect. 2.




3     The MoMa-Pos Framework
   The proposed MoMa-Pos mainly consists of four phases, including object
importance prediction for kinematic modeling, kinematic modeling of key
objects, base placement determination, and navigation to feasible base place-
ment, which are indicated in Fig. 2.

3.1   Object Importance Prediction for Kinematic Modeling
The objective of object importance prediction is to select a subset of objects,
S, from the object set O for kinematic modeling, enabling eﬃcient computa-
tion. Rather than directly select the objects in an environment, we evaluate
each object’s importance and select those with an importance score exceeding a
predeﬁned threshold α. This approach provides ﬂexibility; if the initial selection
is insuﬃcient, lowering the value of α can encompass additional objects [21].
We develop a prediction model, f : O × O → (0, 1], where the output, f (oi , ot ),
represents the likelihood of including object oi in S based on its importance
relative to the target object ot . Due to the challenges of obtaining precise labels
for all objects in diverse environments [21], we adopt an unsupervised learning
258       B. Shao et al.




Fig. 2. Framework of MoMa-Pos. The framework is composed of four key phases.
Phases 1 and 2 form the task-speciﬁc kinematic perceptual modeling, while Phases 3
and 4 focus on base placement determination and guided navigation. In Phase 1, key
objects in the scene are prioritized to enable eﬃcient kinematic modeling. In Phase
2, kinematic modeling is conducted for these key objects, supporting the subsequent
object-kinematic-aware base placement determination. In Phase 3, potential base place-
ment areas are identiﬁed by considering both robot-speciﬁc constraints and environ-
mental kinematics. Finally, in Phase 4, the robot navigates to the feasible position,
ensuring physical feasibility and adaptability for task execution.


approach, guided by the observation that an object’s importance is often corre-
lated with its spatial proximity to ot and its size, obi . This correlation enables us
to infer importance without exact labels.

      foreach vi ∈ V do

      S←∅
      foreach oi ∈ O do
         if f (oi , ot ) > α then
             S ← S ∪ {oi }
      return S
    As shown in Algorithm 1, our method structures within a graph-based archi-
tecture to calculate spatial proximity between objects oi and ot while considering

object size obi . In Env O , each object oi is represented as a node vi ∈ V , with
attributes such as size obi . The spatial relationships between objects are captured
by edges E ⊆ V × V . An edge (vi , vj ) exists if object oi is spatially related to
oj (e.g., on, in, or inside). The direction of the edge indicates spatial hierar-
chy, and the weight is deﬁned as 1/distxy (oi , oj ), where distxy is the horizontal
distance between oi and oj . We have explored several algorithms to quantify
the spatial proximity between nodes vi and vt . After a thorough evaluation, we
ultimately selected the DeepWalk algorithm [22] due to its superior ability to
capture the required spatial information. Node sequences are generated through
biased random walks, with the transition probability P (vi , vj ) weighted by the
function,
                                           1
                 w(vi , vj ) = norm                    + norm (size(oj ))        (2)
                                     distxy (oi , oj )
This bias ensures the walks reﬂect both spatial distance and object size, gener-
ating sequences that better capture object importance,

                                  ⎩
                                   0,                     otherwise

where N (vi ) represents the set of nodes adjacent to vi . After obtaining node
embeddings, we compute the importance score for each object oi by calculat-
ing the cosine similarity of its embedding to that of the target object vt . Only
objects with a score exceeding a threshold α can be included in the set S . It
should be noted that the threshold α is adjustable, starting from a high value
and decreasing if the system requires more objects to achieve the optimal per-
formance.

3.2   Kinematic Modeling of Key Objects
Here, we aim to perform the kinematic modeling of key objects in the simulation
environment. Key objects can be articulated and rigid. The kinematic modeling
is only needed for articulated objects. While for rigid objects, we simply use their
bounding boxes to approximate. Note that non-target articulated objects are also
considered as rigid ones for eﬃciency. These models will aid in the base placement
computation for navigation planning and predict manipulation waypoints [23] for
articulated objects, enabling the eﬀective execution of real-world manipulation
tasks. To achieve this, we employ the state-of-the-art model, URDFormer, an
end-to-end model based on Vision Transformers (ViT), which excels at capturing
an object’s kinematic structure through URDF models transformed from a single
input image. However, URDFormer typically encounters two major problems
when grounding the model to real-world objects, i.e., the input image of the
model and the misalignment with real-world objects, respectively.
    For the ﬁrst problem, based on our observation and exploration, we ﬁnd that
the viewpoint of the input image signiﬁcantly aﬀects the modeling accuracy,
and the frontal view images can generate the best results. Therefore, we design
260     B. Shao et al.

an algorithm to select the optimal viewpoint image of the target object from
video streams, ensuring the input to URDFormer is optimal for more accurate
kinematic modeling. This process involves using Detectron2 [25] to detect the
target object in each video frame, followed by sorting the frames based on the
object’s central position in the image. We then ﬁne-tuned a ResNet50 model [24],
trained on a dataset we created, which includes 1,000 labeled images (frontal and
non-frontal) of over 20 everyday objects such as refrigerators and microwaves,
to classify whether the object in each frame is facing forward. The loss function
used for training is deﬁned as follows,
                                 N
                         1
                LBCE = −       [yi log(ŷi ) + (1 − yi ) log(1 − ŷi )]          (4)
                         N i=1

where N is the number of training samples, yi ∈ {0, 1} denotes the ground-truth
label indicating whether the object in the i-th image is frontal (1) or not (0),
and ŷi ∈ (0, 1) is the predicted probability that the object is frontal. This binary
cross-entropy loss encourages the model to assign high conﬁdence to correct
predictions while penalizing incorrect classiﬁcations. The ﬁrst best image, which
is classiﬁed as “frontal”, is selected as the input for URDFormer to generate an
initial URDF model with interactive structures.
    For the second problem, to address the limitations of using a 2D single-image
input, which can cause misalignment of the URDF model with the real-world 3D
environment, we correct the model by incorporating precise 3D information from
point clouds. Speciﬁcally, we use 3D bounding boxes generated by Mask3D [20] to
align the object’s size and pose, ensuring the URDF model accurately simulates
an interactive environment that mirrors the real world. Finally, after inputting a
recorded environment video, our algorithm selects the best frontal image of the
target object and uses 3D bounding boxes to align the object’s size and pose,
generating an accurate URDF model. This enables the precise location of action-
able parts on articulated objects at any angle, ensuring real-world alignment.
The location data at each angle are used to generate the object’s manipulation
waypoints.

3.3   Base Placement Determination
To determine the base placement, we ﬁrst calculate the potential area for base
placements (denoted as A), where the requirement of no collisions with surround-
ing objects must be satisﬁed. The ﬁnal base placement is then reﬁned by further
integrating both the robot’s constraints and the objects’ kinematics constraints.
    To obtain an initial robot’s potential base placement area A, we consider
both the robot’s model r and the target object’s position opt to avoid collisions.
The potential area A is calculated according to the following equation:
           A = rp | distxy (rp , opt ) ≤ Δr, ∀i, ¬overlap rp , rb , opi , obi    (5)
Here, Δr represents the allowable horizontal distance between a base placement
rp and the target opt , illustrated in an orange line in Fig. 4. The overlap function
        MoMa-Pos: Base Placement Determination for Mobile Manipulation          261

checks for collisions between the robot’s base and surrounding objects oi by
comparing their positions and boundaries. More speciﬁcally, Δr is calculated as,

                        Δr =    (rl )2 − (op.z
                                           t −r −r )
                                               z  h 2                           (6)

where rl is the arm extension range (shown in green in the ﬁgure), derived from
the robot’s DH matrix. The z-axis distance between rp and op.z  t is indicated by
|op.z
  t   − r z
            − r h
                  |, marked as a blue line in the ﬁgure.
    To reﬁne A, we integrate an inverse reachability matrix to prevent self-
collision and incorporate an improved potential ﬁeld method to avoid poten-
tial interference with furniture and obstacles due to their kinematic constraints.
Speciﬁcally, we design a two-step process to meet the constraints of robot’s and
object’s kinematics, respectively.
 Algorithm 2. Base Placement Determination
  Input: opt : target object position, {oi }: surrounding objects,   r: robot
          model
  Output: P : feasible base placement set
  A←∅
  foreach candidate position rp do
     if distxy (rp , opt ) ≤ Δr and ¬overlap(rp , {oi }) then
         A ← A ∪ {rp }
   // Robot’s Kinematic Constraints
   IRM ← InverseReachabilityMatrixOﬄine(r) ;            // computed offline
   IRMshifted ← Translate(IRM, opt )
   Ak ← A ∩ IRMshifted
   // Object’s Kinematic Constraints
   P ← ∅ foreach rp ∈ Ak do
      if LineSegment(rp , opt ) intersects any BBox(oi ) then
          F (rp , z) ← 0
      else
                              1
          F (rp , z) ←                    P ← P ∪ {rp }
                       distxy (rp , opt )
   return P
– Robot’s Kinematic Constraints: Utilizing the inverse reachability matrix,
  we can obtain the value of points in A without considering the kinematic
  structure. Real-time online computation of the inverse reachability matrix
  IRM requires long computation time, so we calculate it oﬄine. We then
  translate the IRM by shifting its center from rp to opi . The shifted matrix
  IRMshift allows us to precompute feasible base placements within the area A.
  By selecting base placements directly from the matrix, it is easy to get base
  placements satisfy the robot’s kinematic constraints Ak .
– Object’s Kinematic Constraints: Inspired by the potential ﬁeld
  method [26], we propose a novel approach to address the impact of the kine-
  matic structure of the target object at the base placement. For each point
262     B. Shao et al.

   in the incorporated trajectory, the target object ot exerts an attractive force.
   For each candidate base placement rp , we sample a 3D position (rp , z) and
   connect it to opt with a line. If this line collides with the bounding box of any
   furniture (such as actionable parts), the potential value of the potential ﬁeld
   F (rp , z) is set to zero, indicating that the robot cannot reach the target from
   this position. Otherwise, we calculate F (rp , z) = 1/distxy (rp , opt ). As shown
   in Fig. 3, diﬀerent kinematic constraints of the same object, such as varying
   opening angles, may result in very diﬀerent base placements.

   The overall procedure is summarized in Algorithm 2. The ﬁnal potential
value is the sum of the value from the inverse reachability matrix and the value
from the potential ﬁeld. As shown in Fig. 3, positions with higher ﬁnal potential
values are more feasible.

ment, while the three subﬁgures on the right focus on key task-relevant objects in the
simulation. Green circles indicate potential robot standing positions and red diamonds
represent targets, such as the fridge door handle. In example (1), when the door handle
changes position, the corresponding feasible placement map is also changed, consistent

3.4   Navigation to Feasible Base Placement

In the reﬁned area A, we use the Latin Hypercube sampling method to sample
M 2D positions rip , with higher potential values suggesting better feasibility. We
balance potential values with navigation costs, rather than simply selecting the
lowest potential position and checking feasibility with RRTconnect [27]. This
resembles the Open Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) [28], where the robot
does not return to its starting position.
    Given the large number of sampled positions, we group them into smaller
sets, each containing T candidates. Within each set, the optimal path is deter-
mined by solving the Open TSP, using edge weights that combine both distance
distxy (rip , rjp ) and potential values. The edge weight is computed as,

                  cost(ri , rj ) = dist(rip , rjp ) + F (rjp ) − F (rip )       (7)

Algorithms ranging from exact methods [29] to heuristic approaches [30] can
be used, depending on the size of T . The search continues until a collision-free
trajectory is found, and the corresponding base placement rp∗ is selected.
Lemma 1 (MoMa-Pos is complete). Given any object importance scorer f :
O × O → (0, 1], threshold α ∈ [0.0, 1.0], and M sampled positions, M ∈ [1, ∞),
if the motion planner PLAN is complete, then MoMa-Pos is complete.

Proof. Given the codomain of f excludes 0, an α > 0 exists such that ∀o ∈
O, f (o, o) ≥ α. With M → ∞, a feasible position, if existent, will be sampled
eventually. Given PLAN’s completeness, MoMa-Pos also achieves completeness.
Hence, for any task and an inﬁnite number of samples, MoMa-Pos will identify
at least one solution, assuming one exists, through PLAN.



4     Experiments

In our experiments, we aim to address the following questions:
Q1: How does MoMa-Pos’s capability of determining feasible base placements?
Q2: How eﬃcient is the object importance predictor for eﬃciency in kinematic
modeling?
Q3: How accurate is the kinematic modeling?
Experimental Setup: In the real robot experiment, we construct a home
environment in a controlled laboratory setting, as illustrated in Fig. 4. The scene
includes ﬁve rigid objects (e.g., table, apple, and cup) and two articulated objects
(i.e., fridge and microwave). The rigid objects and microwave are placed ran-
domly on the table, which has a variable position, while the fridge remains
ﬁxed. The mobile manipulator, as shown in Fig. 1, consists of an AgileX-based
mobile platform and a Realman 63-F robotic arm, equipped with a Realsense 435
camera for RGB images, depth images, and point cloud data acquisition. The
mobile manipulator is tasked with grasping rigid objects (i.e., apple and cup)
264      B. Shao et al.




Fig. 4. Real Robot Demonstration. We implemented MoMa-Pos on a real robotic
system comprising an AgileX mobile platform and a Realman-63F robotic arm. The
robot’s task in this setup is to open a fridge door. In the ﬁrst ﬁgure, MoMa-Pos predicts
key objects in the environment, with these objects highlighted by colored outlines.
Meanwhile, the manipulation waypoints are predicted and indicated by yellow circles.
Next, MoMa-Pos performs kinematic modeling, representing rigid objects as boxes and
articulated objects using URDFormer. A feasible base placement is then selected, taking
into account robot-speciﬁc constraints and the kinematic properties of the environment.
The ﬁnal two ﬁgures illustrate the robot successfully completing navigation, where the
trajectory is indicated in a dashed black line, and ﬁxed-base manipulation tasks using
the predicted waypoints.


and opening articulated items. For the fridge and microwave, we open them to
90 ◦ during the experiments. The methods for determining base placements are
evaluated across ﬁve trials per task, with each scene featuring a distinct object
conﬁguration. The robot’s initial position is kept consistent across all trials.
For manipulation, the spatial positions of the objects and the actionable parts
(e.g., door handles) of articulated objects are determined using Mask3D [20] and
URDF model. We then employ the RRTconnect algorithm, implemented via the
open-source OMPL library [31], to compute corresponding manipulation trajec-
tories. For navigation, we utilize the Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) [32],
chosen for its responsiveness and stability in complex dynamic environments,
ensuring high precision and safety. Details are available on our website.
    We also perform simulated robot experiments. In contrast to the real-
world setup, the simulation involves a greater number of everyday objects (30,
including a fridge, microwave, and cup) and more tasks, totaling 500. In the
simulation, the 3D positions of objects and their actionable components are
directly accessible. The simulation tool is supported by the GitHub project1 [33].
Our experiments were conducted on a computer with an AMD EPYC 7452
processor (32 cores, 64 threads), an Nvidia GTX 2080 GPU, and 128GB of
RAM.
Baselines: We compare our method with the following reimplemented baselines,
which are inspired by original data-driven approaches:

– Habitat [34]: For rigid objects such as tables, the feasible base placement
  closest to the target is selected, ensuring it is navigable. For articulated
  objects like fridges, the feasible base placement is determined based on a

1
    https://github.com/AutonoBot-Lab/BestMan.
         MoMa-Pos: Base Placement Determination for Mobile Manipulation         265

  ﬁxed position relative to these objects, guided by prior experience, while also
  ensuring no collisions with the environment.
– M3* [4]: Based on the original method, the area is divided into 5 × 5 cm
  cells. For rigid objects, the closest navigable position is selected, prioritizing
  navigation cost. For articulated objects, base placements are sampled until a
  feasible one is found. Unlike the original, which uses reinforcement learning
  to optimize placement, this baseline lacks optimization, potentially increas-
  ing costs. We use * to denote diﬀerences. Additionally, while the original
  allows dynamic base repositioning, our method uses ﬁxed-base manipulation,
  requiring setup adjustments.
– Reuleaux [13]: Similar to M3*, it starts by designating a speciﬁc area,
  divided into 5 × 5 cm cells. It then evaluates how easily the robot can reach
  the target without obstacles. The robot chooses its feasible base placement
  randomly, prioritizing those with the highest reachability to ensure optimal
  accessibility.
Diﬀerent from MoMa-Pos, none of these three baselines account for object kine-
matics, which may lead to suboptimal manipulation performance, particularly
when handling articulated objects.
Rating Criteria: To ensure a fair comparison, all baselines are evaluated in
a complete working environment. These methods do not account for the kine-
matic information of articulated objects, treating all objects as simple bounding
boxes, thus saving time on kinematic modeling. We evaluate the performance
of all approaches using the following metrics: task execution time (Time), mea-
sured in seconds; navigation cost (Cost), measured in meters; and success rate
(SRate). For a more detailed breakdown of time consumption in determining
feasible base placement, we measure the time spent in each key step of the
process, which includes three stages: predicting object importance, performing
kinematic modeling, and determining base placement. The time allocated for
modeling not only includes the modeling process itself but also the integra-
tion of modeled objects into the simulator. To focus on the core task eﬃciency,
we exclude navigation time from task execution, as robot movement speed can
introduce variability unrelated to task completion. Instead, the navigation cost
metric measures spatial eﬃciency, ensuring it doesn’t aﬀect task performance
evaluation. For non-articulated tasks, success means grasping the target with-
out collisions, while for articulated tasks, success means interacting successfully
and executing the planned trajectory without collisions.

as fridges. This is due to our method’s ability to account for the structure of

not only demonstrates signiﬁcant advantages in success rate and time eﬃciency
with articulated objects but also ensures the low navigation cost for ﬁnding feasi-
ble solutions. In our tests, MoMa-Pos consistently determines a feasible solution
within 18 s.

Object Importance Predictor for Eﬃciency in Kinematic Modeling.
We aim to address Q2 here. Our experimentation begins by setting the thresh-

The achieved success rate of 100% conﬁrms that no crucial object has been
overlooked. Figure 5 illustrates the modeling time for MoMa-Pos and a vari-
ant without the prediction module. It is clear that incorporating prediction in
MoMa-Pos decreases the time cost. It should be noted that for non-articulated
tasks, such as grasping an apple or a cup, kinematic modeling is not necessary,
and therefore no modeling time is required.
    Interestingly, we observed that the importing time for the other three tasks is
greater than that of the “Open Fridge” task. This is because the remaining three
tasks involve physical stacking relationships (e.g., an apple on a table), requir-
ing consideration of more objects in the environment. This observation suggests
that the Importance Predictor is able to eﬀectively handle varying environmen-
tal complexities, demonstrating good robustness in accurately predicting the
importance of objects across diﬀerent task scenarios.


Kinematic Modeling Accuracy. We aim to address Q3 here. Table 2 presents
the accuracy of kinematic modeling. For the Vanilla URDFormer, the generated
object model exhibits signiﬁcant misalignment with the real-world object, result-
ing in a spatial error of approximately 0.38 m, as shown in the table. The spatial
error is calculated based on the real-world dimensions of articulated objects,
with the unit in meters. To improve alignment with real-world objects, we apply
two methods to obtain the bounding box: Omni3D [35] and Mask3D. Omni3D
utilizes RGB images and Mask3D leverages depth data. Compared to Omni3D,
Mask3D demonstrates signiﬁcantly higher accuracy, reducing the modeling error
to 0.04 m.

    We also calculate the average time distribution across all tasks, including

98% of the total time cost) is dedicated to kinematic modeling and determin-
ing feasibility through a sampling-based motion planner, such as RRTconnect.
In contrast, the time spent on candidate selection, including solving the Open
Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), is minimal, accounting for less than 2% of
the total time (less than 0.3 s).

   Our framework is further evaluated using three simulated robots: Fetch, Seg-
way+UR5e, and Husky+UR5e. In all trials, MoMa-Pos achieves a 100% success
rate, demonstrating its robustness across diﬀerent robot models. This highlights
the versatility of our method, which is adaptable to various scenarios. Compared
to baselines, MoMa-Pos signiﬁcantly reduces the eﬀort needed for integrating
kinematic models into the simulator. Note that the simulated experiments do
not involve kinematic modeling steps.
   Additional simulation results are provided in the appendix2 .


5     Conclusion and Future Work
In this work, we introduce MoMa-Pos, a novel framework for the determination of
base placement in mobile manipulators, particularly in environments with both
rigid and articulated objects. MoMa-Pos tackles navigation-manipulation chal-
lenges by selectively modeling relevant objects and using a graph-based neural
network to enhance computational eﬃciency. By integrating inverse reachability
maps and kinematic properties, it ensures precise base placement for speciﬁc
robot models, oﬀering adaptability and physical feasibility in diverse environ-
ments.
    In the future, we plan to expand this work mainly in three directions. First, we
plan to enhance its eﬃciency by reducing computational cost, e.g., the kinematic
modeling time. Second, we intend to extend its generalizability by testing more
application scenarios. Lastly, we intend to improve its modeling applicability by
reﬁning the modeling approach to better capture irregularly shaped articulated
objects.

           Distributed Intelligent Computing
        with Kernel-Wise Deep Neural Network
         Partition over Collaborative Devices

                     Boya Sun, Yinglei Teng(B) , and Nan Wang

 Beijing Key Laboratory of Space-ground Interconnection and Convergence, Beijing
  University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT), Xitucheng Road NO. 10,
                                  Beijing, China
                 {boyasun,lilytengtt,wangnan 26}@bupt.edu.cn



       Abstract. With the proliferation of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) applica-
       tions, model partitioning has attracted increasing attention for address-
       ing the computational bottlenecks of edge AI by oﬄoading portions of
       deep neural networks (DNNs) to cloud servers or IoT devices. How-
       ever, existing DNN partitioning methods often incur signiﬁcant param-
       eter overhead during deployment. Moreover, achieving both low-latency
       inference and privacy preservation in Internet of Things (IoT) networks
       remains challenging due to device heterogeneity and the heightened pri-
       vacy risks of distributed architectures. In this work, we propose a reli-
       able distributed computing framework based on ﬁne-grained convolu-
       tional kernel partitioning, enabling collaborative execution among mul-
       tiple edge devices (EDs). To accelerate inference while balancing power
       and reliability constraints, we jointly optimize kernel allocation, redun-
       dancy strategies, and dynamic resource conﬁguration. To address the
       high coupling of time-scale discrepancies and mixed-variable character-
       istics, we ﬁrst apply the Lagrange multiplier method for problem trans-
       formation, and then design a two-timescale Hierarchical Proximal Policy
       Optimization (HPPO) algorithm decoupling the transformed problem
       into two-layer subproblems. Experimental results show that the pro-
       posed framework signiﬁcantly improves inference speed while ensuring
       computational reliability in distributed edge environments.


       Keywords: DNN partition · Cooperative inference · Distributed
       computing system · Hierarchical reinforcement learning


1    Introduction
Intelligent services based on deep learning have emerged alongside the develop-
ment of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) and the rapid growth of Internet of Things
(IoT) devices at the network edge across various application domains, e.g., smart
home, video surveillance, and healthcare [1–3]. The traditional centralized cloud
computing paradigm oﬄoads AI-based tasks to cloud servers with high compu-
tational capabilities. However, due to the explosion of big data, massive deep
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 271–290, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_15
272     B. Sun et al.

neural network (DNN) service requests may overload of the network and the
cloud server, making it diﬃcult to meet the requirements of upcoming sixth-
generation(6G) IoT systems. Therefore, a shift toward distributed edge comput-
ing, which enables collaboration between the cloud and the IoT devices, oﬀers
a promising approach to addressing these challenges by leveraging the comple-
mentary advantages of both edge computing and cloud computing [4–6].
    The IoT devices with available resources at the edge of the network in crowd-
sourcing scenarios have spawned research on distributed computing for intelli-
gent services [7]. Speciﬁcally, splitting model with appropriate oﬄoad schemes is
a feasible solution to make the most of idle resources at the devices. To adapt to
the limited computing and storage capacities of IoT devices, numerous studies
have focused on identifying partition points in DNN models for oﬄoading, and
on designing inference frameworks to enhance AI service performance, such as
reducing latency and energy consumption. According to research studies [8–10],
ﬁne-grained model partitioning methods that divide each layer of a DNN into
multiple segments enables the partitioned models to execute in parallel on dif-
ferent devices. Compared with the approaches using a single model partition
point [11–15], ﬁne-grained partitioning accelerates inference through paralleliza-
tion. Inspired by the atomicity and independence of the kernel computation, Zhi
et al.. [16] propose a kernel-wise partition method (KPM) in which the convolu-
tional kernels of each convolutional layer are segmented into multiple partitions.
With the input feature map, the inference of a single layer can be divided into
distributed collaborative computations of multiple subtasks. KPM leverages the
independence of convolution operations between kernels, providing a private and
secure solution for collaborative inference. By partitioning and oﬄoading con-
volutional kernels, each collaborative node generates only partial feature map
information. This method retains most of the information even when parts of
the feature map results are missing. Thus, KPM oﬀers a distributed inference
option that supports collaborative computing while ensuring data privacy and
security.
    In addition, computing reliability is considered to represent the likelihood of
the edge computing system operating normally be an important factor in the
distributed collaboration scenario. However, a large number of computing nodes
involved face the key threads of node failure or a service failure, which may
lead to a complete failure or degradation of the overall system. As a general
paradigm, fault tolerance technology can ensure the data integrity and system
availability, avoid data loss and the breakdown of the whole system caused by
local failures. Hence, the intelligent tasks are supposed to be executed separately
over the available devices in parallel to improve the eﬃciency of the services, with
joint consideration of computation amount, power consumption, and wireless
communication traﬃc. At present, the coordination of distributed computing
management for edge intelligent services remains an area that require substantial
exploration. Speciﬁcally, there is a lack of a coordinated computing framework for
joint DNN model ﬁne-grained partitioning and reliable computation to enhance
the execution eﬃciency of AI tasks and system robustness.
                                         Distributed Intelligent Computing     273

    With KPM as the underlying support, in this paper, we propose a reliable
distributed computing framework and establish a collaborative procedure among
multiple edge devices (EDs). To accelerate inference while balancing power con-
sumption and reliability constraints, we jointly optimize kernel allocation, redun-
dancy decisions, and dynamic resource conﬁguration. To solve this problem, we
employ the Lagrange multiplier method for problem transformation and pro-
pose a hierarchical proximal policy optimization (HPPO) algorithm for solu-
tion. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework eﬀectively
reduces the average delay while ensuring the reliability of the distributed com-
puting system.
    The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, the system model
will be described. Section 3 and Sect. 4 provide a joint optimization problem
and the HPPO algorithm, respectively. Section 5 provides experimental results.
Finally, this paper is concluded in Sect. 6.


2     System Model

We consider a distributed computing system establishing upon an edge-cloud
collaborative architecture capable of supporting intelligent computing applica-
tions. Speciﬁcally, a set M = {1, 2, ..., M } is used to denote the heterogenous
EDs that voluntarily participate in crowd computing, each with a cascade of two
buﬀers. The cloud server (CS) is responsible for splitting the intelligent services
and managing the cooperation executions of the EDs. Taking the popular DNN-
type applications as target tasks, the neural network model is partitioned into
portable computational elements based on KPM. Moreover, network resource
is dynamically adjusted to accelerate distributed feature extractions of input
tasks across EDs with respect to the queue states, communication conditions
and power consumption. In our system, time is slotted with duration τ , and
the time slots are indexed by t ∈ T = {1, 2, 3...}. The computational frequency
and channel conditions remain constant within the period of one time slot but
ﬂuctuates separately across various periods.

2.1   Distributed Inference Procedure

Taking the popular inference service of two-dimensional convolutional neural
networks (2DCNNs) as an instance, the distributed computing procedure with
multi-EDs for collaborative computing is depicted in Fig. 1. For the distributed
computing of convolutional layer l (Convl) , l ∈ L = {1, 2, ...L} , the redun-
dancy technology of replication for convolutional kernels is adopted to cope with
the inevitable failures of the participating EDs and support the achievement of
acceptable levels of computational reliability. By exploiting the KPM, the CS
develops a partition strategy to schedule the assignment of kernels, where each
kernel is assigned to multiple distinct EDs. Embedded with the respective part
of the CNN model, the EDs will collaborate to achieve distributed computing,
which encompasses the following three phases.
274    B. Sun et al.




           Fig. 1. The distributed computing procedure based on KPM


(1) Feature map downloading phase: The three-channel feature maps with
    the same size are required as the input intelligent tasks by the EDs. To send
    the tasks eﬃciently, each task is transmitted from CS via broadcast.
(2) Convolutional kernel computing phase: The input tasks are queued up
    for calculation in the computing buﬀer at each ED. As the feature extractor
    that provides the computed weights, the convolutional kernels embedded
    at each ED perform complex matrix computations with the input tasks
    in the computation queue. Diﬀerent numbers of convolutional kernels on
    various EDs extract features from input tasks to varying degrees through
    parallel computing. Supported by the available computing resources, each
    ED generates a portion of output channels for each input task.
(3) Result feedback phase: The computed outputs are queued in the commu-
    nication buﬀer at each ED for sending back to CS, at which the separated
    channels from the cooperative EDs are aggregated and each feature channel
    will be veriﬁed through the majority voting among the redundancies. Note
    that the veriﬁcation time of the result can be neglected due to the powerful
    computing ability. Repeating the partition and aggregation process layer by
    layer, the ﬁnal output is obtained after the fully-connected layer at CS.
                                         Distributed Intelligent Computing     275

The inherent data dependency in CNN models, where the output feature maps
of a preceding layer serve as the input to the subsequent layer, implies that the
distributed execution of convolutional layers must occur sequentially. However,
since the kernel allocation optimization is similar across layers, we focus on the
distributed computation of a single representative layer in the following sections.
For simplicity, we omit the layer index l throughout the remainder of the paper,
as the modeling is identical for each layer.

2.2   Kernel-Wise Partition Model
To quantify the neural network layer, a four-dimensional tuple S I , S O , N, W ,
is adopted, where S I and S O represent the input and output data size, and N
is the number of input/output channels, equal to the total number of convolu-
tional kernel at the current layer. In addition, W is the ﬂoating-point operations
(FLOPs) that can be calculated by the formulas in [17]. With the ﬁne-grained
KPM, each layer of the speciﬁc CNN model can be split into multiple partitions
for distributed computing. Deﬁne N = {1, 2, ..., N } as the kernel set and let xn,m
denote the kernel allocation indicator, where xn,m = 1 represents the n-th ker-
nel is deployed in ED m, and vice versa. Thus, the kernel partition matrix can
be given by X = {xn,m |xn,m = {0, 1} , n ∈ N , m ∈ M}. With the redundant
strategy ρ ∈ ρ = {ρ | ρ > 2, ρ ∈ Z+ } for each kernel, the deployment strategy
satisﬁes the following constraint:

                                   xn,m = ρ, ∀n ∈ N .                          (1)

2.3   Queue Models
To support the distributed computing, each ED m downloads the input task
from CS and uploads the result back to CS. Speciﬁcally, the computation queue
276    B. Sun et al.

is fed by the broadcasted tasks and the upload queue is drained by uploading
results. In addition, the two queues are cascaded by the computation process,
because the departing computed tasks of the former is the arriving results to
be uploaded of the latter. The task arrival rate, task computing rate and task
results upload rate of the cascaded queues are deﬁned for further description of
queue dynamics.

maps, the download rate (in bit/s) from the CS to each ED m, m ∈ M, can be

2.4   Convolutional Kernel Computational Reliability Model

Generally, it is imperative that the distributed system be able to withstand
failures since the participating EDs are not subjected to signiﬁcant dependability
checking and failure-prone nodes can easily join the system. The ρ-modular
redundancy scheme [19] supports to establish a reliable distributed computing
environment by assigning each convolutional kernel to diﬀerent EDs. When the
results are aggregated, the CS produces the majority vote on the redundant
output feature maps to verify the correctness of the parallel-processing results.
To be speciﬁc, the redundancy channel result of each kernel reaching at least
some minimum number of agreements is taken to be the solution.
    Assume that all EDs are independent, and the failure occurrence follows the
exponential distribution with the failure rate νm of ED m. Denote the normal
                                                                        0
working time of ED m before performing distributed computing as Tm         . During
the work interval of ED m, the probability of failures occurring can be formulated
as:                                               0
                                P rm = 1 − e−νm Tm .                           (12)
It should be added that Eq. 12 also indicates that the kernels embedded at ED
m have the same failure rate P rm .
278    B. Sun et al.

    Even while some EDs may be more dependable than others, each redun-
dant copy of the convolutional kernel oﬄoaded to the device cluster is randomly
assigned to the EDs speciﬁed by the convolution kernel oﬄoading scheme. There-
fore, every redundant copy is subject to the same risk of failing validation. The
probability of unsuccessfully executing a backup of kernel n is
                                    1

2.5   Average Delay
The total delay of tasks at each ED comprises queue waiting delay, download
delay, computation delay and upload delay. However, for most tasks that arrive
at the EDs, download process overlaps with the execution of the previously
queued task. In the long-term perspective, the additional download delay is
approximately equal to the duration of the ﬁrst task’s transmission over the air
interface, and is therefore negligible.
    Consequently, the delay of each task at ED m can be equivalent to the time
spent in the queues(including queue waiting delay, computation delay and upload
delay). According to Little’s Law [21], the average delay spent in the queues at
ED m is proportional to average length in the queues, i.e.,
                                          T −1
                                     1
                       Tm = τ lim          E [ϕ (Qm (t))] ,                 (15)
                               T →+∞ T
                                       t=0

                 QC +QU
where ϕ (Qm ) = mAm m .
    Since each ED only computes a subset of the output feature maps, it is
necessary to perform synchronization operations among the collaborative EDs
to obtain the entire feature map results. Through the Bulk Synchronous Parallel
(BSP) mechanism [22], the average delay of a single layer is determined by
the maximum average delay among all EDs. Moreover, a maximum allowable
delay, T max is set as a threshold to determine if the convolutional layer needs
reprocessing to ensure the timeliness of the distributed computing service. That
is,
                          T P = max (Tm ) , T P < T max .                    (16)
                                m∈M

3   Problem Formulation
In this section, we formulate a minimization problem for average delay, which
jointly considers convolutional kernel partitioning, resource scheduling and
redundancy strategy. Additionally, we develop constraints based on kernel-level
computation reliability and ED power consumption to enhance system perfor-
mance and ensure utilization of distributed edge resources.
    First, the cooperative inference system must satisfy the following probabilis-
tic constraint to ensure reliability for each convolutional kernel:

                                     R n ≥ 1 − ε0 ,                             (17)

where ε0 is a small positive number, indicating a strict reliability requirement
for task processing.
    Second, power consumption should be constrained due to the resource limi-
tation of the voluntary EDs. For ED m, the power consumption mainly consists
of the computation power and transmission power for uploading results. The
average total power consumption per time slot for collaborative ED m can be
deﬁned as:
                                     T −1
                                   1
                       pm = lim           E pC         T
                                             m (t) + pm .                   (18)
                            T →+∞ T
                                     t=0

    To minimize the average delay while satisfying reliability and power consump-
tion constraints, we formulate the joint optimization problem of convolutional
kernel partitioning, redundancy strategy, and resource allocation as P0:

                       P0 : min T P ,                                           (19)
                            X ,ρ,F

                            s.t.C1 : xn,m = {0, 1} , ∀n, ∀m,
                           C2 :          xn,m = ρ, ∀n,
                                  m∈M
                           C3 : fm (t) ∈ [0, fm
                                              max
                                                  ] , ∀m,
                                      m , ∀m,
                           C4 : pm ≤ pmax
                           C5 : Rn ≥ 1 − ε0 , ∀n,

where ρ is the redundancy decision positive integer. Constraint C1 and C3 pro-
vide feasible region for the partition and frequency scheduling variables, respec-
tively. Constraint C2 restricts the number of redundancy for each kernel. Con-
straint C4 and C5 are proposed to satisfy power consumption and reliability
requirements of the system, where pmaxm   is the power consumption upper bound
for each ED m ,m ∈ M.
    Obviously, P0 represents a highly complex stochastic optimization problem
involving both discrete and continuous variables. In addition, there is no close-
form expression for the problem due to the time-varying state of the queue and
the long-term average constraint on power. In particular, the queue dynamics
280    B. Sun et al.

introduce strong coupling among multiple decision variables. Moreover, the solu-
tions to the problem involve short-term dynamic change of computing frequency
and long-term joint decisions on convolutional kernel allocation strategy and
redundant strategy, forming a two-timescale stochastic optimization problem.
To make it solvable, we ﬁrst transform the objective function by incorporat-
ing Lagrange multipliers. We then apply a hierarchical reinforcement learning
(HRL) algorithm operating at two time scales to eﬃciently solve the minimiza-
tion problem.


4     Optimization Algorithm

Considering the time-scale separation and temporal correlation characteristics
of Problem P0, the HPPO algorithm is designed to solve it. To handle the com-
plex power consumption constraint, Lagrange multipliers (LMs) are introduced
to convert the constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) P0 into an inﬁ-
nite horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP). Subsequently, a hybrid time-scale
reinforcement learning method is proposed to address the temporal discrepancies
among multiple decision variables.


4.1   Problem Transformation

For the long-term average power consumption constraint C4 , which lacks a
closed-form expression, it is not possible to derive an explicit analytical rela-
tionship between the constraint and the decision variables. Additionally, due to
the inﬁnite time-horizon nature of the long-term average, the constraint can-
not be accurately veriﬁed within a ﬁnite number of iterations. In our work,
we incorporate this constraint into the objective function via LMs for handling
non-closed-form characteristic. For any LM γ , we can formulate the Lagrangian
function as:
                                                   T −1
                                             1
             G(X, ρ, F , γ) = T P + lim            E μ γ(t), f (t)   .      (20)
                                       T →+∞ T
                                               t=0

where μ (γ, f ) =         γm pC         T
                              m − pm − pm . It should be noted that we need
                                   max
                    m∈M
to adjust the value of the LM, γ in each time slot to minimize G while ensuring
the power consumption constraint. Thus, the optimization problem P0 can be
equivalently transformed into the minimization problem as follows:

                             P1 : min G (X, ρ, F , γ) ,                     (21)
                                 X ,ρ,F ,γ

                                 s.t.C1 , C2 , C3 , C5 .

4.2   HPPO Algorithm
Inspired by option-based reinforcement learning approaches that allow the policy
to ﬁnd options over a period of time and to optimize within options on discrete
time slots, we adopt a HRL method to address the reformulated problem P1.
Compared with the traditional reinforcement learning methods, two agents con-
sisting of upper-level agent and lower-level agent respectively responsible for the
optimization over diﬀerent time scales are employed. With the hierarchy intro-
duced in the algorithm, HRL enables complex decision-making across diﬀerent
timescales more eﬃciently.




                   Fig. 2. The architecture of HPPO algorithm


    In our work, we leverage Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [23], an
advanced deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm that combines the
strengths of value-based and policy-based methods and eﬃciently handles both
discrete and continuous action spaces, to solve the optimization problem. As
shown in Fig. 2, there are upper-level agent, lower-level agent and the environ-
ment in our HPPO algorithm architecture. Although the optimization problem
P1 is entangled with a hybrid action space consisting of both discrete actions
in the long-term and continuous action in the short-term, our HRL method
avoids directly handling this hybrid action spaces by decoupling the decisions.
The lower-level agent performs the short-term optimization in the time slots of
each long-term optimization, dynamically adjusting the computational resource
allocation and the LM decisions {F , γ} based on the queue state and channel
282     B. Sun et al.

state. On the other hand, the upper-level agent develops the long-term policy
including kernel partition and the redundancy decisions {X, ρ} to minimize the
average delay while guaranteeing the power consumption constraint. In partic-
ular, the upper-level agent selects the long-term action on the slow timescale,
while the lower-level agent formulates the short-term policy on the fast timescale
within T time slots. The interleaved optimization across various timescales are
performed repeatedly until the training converges. Let πθ denote the actor net-
work for approximating the policy function and Vω denote the critic network
for approximating the value function. Note that θ and ω represent the parame-
ters of actor network and critic network, respectively. The detail design of our
proposed algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1. To transform the problem P1 into
HPPO notations, the following MDP is deﬁned for both the upper-level agent
and lower-level agent.

Long-Term Optimization. The long-term optimization contains the kernel
partition strategy and the redundancy decision developed by the upper-level
agent. The kernel allocation decision X is a binary n×m two-dimensional matrix,
where each element indicates assignment (1) or non-assignment (0). However, the
size of action space grows exponentially with the number of convolutional kernels
and EDs, making eﬃcient exploration intractable. In order to reduce the long-
term action space, we make allocation decisions for each convolutional kernel
sequentially over time, rather than making all allocation decisions simultane-
ously in a spatially uniﬁed manner. By transforming the spatial complexity of
kernel allocation decision into temporal complexity through sequential kernel-
wise decisions, we eﬀectively reduce the dimensionality of the high-dimensional
action space. The state space, action space and reward function are deﬁned as
follows:

(1) State space: The required state information SnE contains the reliability of
    each ED m, m ∈ M, the allocation state of n-th convolutional kernel, and
    index n.

    reward function of the upper-level agent is deﬁned in a piece-wise manner.
    Obviously, the kernel allocation strategy is incomplete when the current ker-
    nel is not equivalent to the length of the kernel period, and the lower-level
    agent is inactive. In this case, the reward function consists of two compo-
    nents: the diﬀerence between the current kernel’s reliability level and the
    reliability constraint, and the absolute diﬀerence between the redundancy
    factor ρ of the current kernel and that of the previous kernel. Note that
    the second component is omitted when the current kernel is the ﬁrst deci-

    while ensuring that the reliability constraint is satisﬁed. Conversely, when
    the current kernel index reaches the full kernel period length, the reward
    function is deﬁned as a joint reward, combining the cumulative intrinsic
    rewards from the lower-level agent (under the current long-term option) and

5     Experiment Results and Discussion
In this section, we will test the performance of the proposed distributed com-
puting framework under diﬀerent parameter settings. In our experiments, we
ﬁrst train the Alexnet model for 100 epochs on the Cifar-10 dataset. We then
focus on the partition and distributed computation of convolutional kernels in
the fourth convolutional layer of AlexNet network. Based on the trained model,
384 convolutional kernels are allocated to 8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 heterogeneous EDs
for distributed computation. All code is implemented in Python3.9 and executed
on a Linux server equipped with one NVIDIA A40 GPU.

5.1   Experiment Setup
The system downlink bandwidth is bD = 1.8M Hz, and the uplink bandwidth
is bU = 0.5M Hz. The transmit power of the CS is pD = 0.1W , and the upload
transmit power is pUm = 1W for each ED m. Note that the experiments focus
speciﬁcally on average computational power consumption per ED. For brevity,
the term ”average power” used in subsequent ﬁgures and discussions refers exclu-
sively to average computational power. Other parameters are listed in Table 1.

5.2   Performance of the Proposed Framework
In Fig. 3, we plot the convergence performance of our proposed scheme. It can
be seen that the proposed scheme converges after 300 episodes with diﬀerent
delay deadlines. Note that the decreasing of T max leads to the decline in the
learning performance of the agent. This is because adjusting the time thresh-
old can reshape the statistical characteristics of rewards, thereby inﬂuencing the
exploration-exploitation balance in reinforcement learning and leading to diﬀer-
ent convergence speeds. Furthermore, compared with more lenient delay dead-
lines tighter time constraint causes the system to reduce the obtained rewards
while ensuring the minimization of average delay.

    Figure 4 illustrates the average power consumption per ED and the delay
per convolutional layer under various value of γ max . In the aforementioned
Lagrangian function, γ plays an important role in balancing the trade-oﬀ between
average delay and average power consumption. When γ max is less than 100,
both the average power consumption and the average delay decrease as γ max
increases. However, when γ max exceeds 100, the average power consumption
decreases but the average delay increases. This behavior likely occurs because
small adjustments to γ max are insuﬃcient to consistently prioritize delay perfor-
mance optimization. In our proposed scheme, meeting the power constraint may
                                          Distributed Intelligent Computing    287




                               Fig. 4. Eﬀect of γ max


take precedence over minimizing delay. Therefore, when γ becomes too large,
the average delay increases signiﬁcantly.


5.3   Comparison with Other Baselines

To further reveal the superiority of the proposed framework, we compare it with
three other schemes.


(1) Proximity-based
    Convolutional Kernel Partition Framework(PCKPF): The convolu-
    tional kernels are allocated to EDs nearest to the CS based on geographical
    proximity. As a classical resource allocation approach in edge computing,
    its simplicity and interpretability establish it as an ideal performance bench-
    mark. In our experiments, tasks are assigned to EDs whose physical distance
    to the CS falls below a predeﬁned threshold, ensuring consistent proximity
    constraints.
(2) Random Convolutional Kernel Partition Framework (RCKPF):
    The convolutional kernel are allocated randomly. Redundancy is set to 5.
    To satisfy power consumption constraints, the computation frequency deci-
    sion is made with PPO algorithm.
(3) Only Convolutional Kernel Partition Framework (OCKPF): An
    average allocation scheme is adopted to distribute power across the EDs.
    The kernel partition and redundancy decisions are made to minimize the
    average delay under reliability constraints. The computation frequency fol-
    lows a random strategy.

   Figure 5 describes the average power consumption per ED and the delay per
convolutional layer under various channel conditions, reliability and ED number.
288     B. Sun et al.




Fig. 5. Average power and average delay varies with changing SNR, reliability and ED
number


Our proposed HPPO is compared to other baselines. It can be seen that HPPO
eﬀectively maintains low latency while ensuring power eﬃciency across diﬀerent
channel conditions, reliability requirement and ED number. As expected, with
the improved channel quality and the increase of the number of EDs, we observe
a reduction in the average execution latency of a single convolutional layer in
four methods in Figs. 5 (a) and 5 (c). It can also be seen in Fig. 5 (b) that when
reliability requirements become more stringent, the system sacriﬁces latency
and power performance to ensure high reliability. In particular, compared with
RCKPF and OCKPF, both PCKPF and our proposed HPPO scheme eﬀectively
reduce average latency and save average energy consumption with the change of
the channel conditions and reliability requirements in Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(b).
However, results show that our proposed scheme outperforms PCKPF in both
average latency and average energy consumption. The underlying reason is that
PCKPF only encourages EDs close to the CS to participate in collaborative
computing to achieve higher transmission rates, whereas in our scheme, the
CNN convolutional kernels have a more lenient ED selection mechanism. This
allows EDs to reduce the computational workload on individual devices through
                                             Distributed Intelligent Computing         289

extensive collaboration. The notable downward trend in the average latency
curve of PCKPF in Fig. 5 (c) can also be attributed to the fact that as the
number of collaborative EDs increases, the number of EDs within the distance
threshold from the CS grows. This leads to more collaborative EDs participating
in computation, thus accelerating task processing speed.
    Overall, the results in Fig. 5 highlight the necessity of jointly optimiz-
ing convolutional kernel allocation, redundancy, and network resources in dis-
tributed computing systems. HPPO balances both short-term resource optimiza-
tion and long-term kernel partitioning redundancy strategies. Ignoring reliability
or resource constraints while focusing solely on minimizing single-layer delay, or
overemphasizing the impact of transmission distance on system performance,
may derail optimization from its original goals, ultimately leading to prolonged
average delay.


6    Conclusion

In this work, we proposed a distributed and reliable inference architecture based
on a kernel-wise model partition method. First, a systematic procedure to estab-
lish collaborative distributed computing among multiple EDs is designed. Sec-
ond, we jointly optimized kernel allocation, redundancy decisions, and dynamic
resource conﬁguration to accelerate inference while balancing power consump-
tion and reliability constraints. Then, we employed the LM method for prob-
lem transformation and proposed a two-timescale HPPO algorithm for solution.
Finally, simulation results demonstrated that the proposed framework eﬀectively
reduced the average delay while ensuring the reliability of the distributed com-
puting system.

R&D Program of China (No.2021YFB3300100).

             Optimization for Heterogeneous Task
           Patterns in Multi-access Edge Computing

            Sihan Li1,2 , Yanqing Wu1,2 , XiaoDong Xu1,2 , and Gang Xu1,2(B)
    1
         College of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University, Hohhot 010021, China
2
        Engineering Research Center of Ecological Big Data, Ministry of Education, Inner
                         Mongolia University, Hohhot 010021, China
                                   csxugang@imu.edu.cn



            Abstract. Edge caching has emerged as an eﬀective solution to reduce
            task processing latency in Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) systems
            by proactively storing potentially executable tasks on edge servers. How-
            ever, most existing studies are based on the assumption of task homo-
            geneity and fail to adequately consider the heterogeneity of task types in
            MEC systems. In real-world scenarios, computation-intensive and access-
            intensive tasks generated by users diﬀer signiﬁcantly in their processing
            procedures and resource demands. The previously adopted single caching
            and oﬄoading strategy falls short in addressing the distinct performance
            requirements of both task types, resulting in ineﬃcient utilization of com-
            puting and caching resources and a notable increase in system latency.
            To address this issue, this paper proposes a Task Pattern Classiﬁcation-
            based Caching and Oﬄoading strategy (TPCO). TPCO builds a uni-
            ﬁed framework to jointly handle both computation-intensive and access-
            intensive tasks, and designs two task-speciﬁc caching strategies: Gated
            Deep Q-Network (GDQN) for computation-intensive tasks and Neural
            Collaborative Filtering-based Caching (NCFC) for access-intensive tasks.
            Furthermore, a Bayesian optimization approach is employed at the global
            level to adaptively allocate storage resources between task types with the
            aim of minimizing system-wide delay. Simulation results show that the
            proposed TPCO framework outperforms existing methods under vari-
            ous conditions and reduces latency by at least 27.93% in heterogeneous
            task scenarios, oﬀering a novel solution for joint caching and oﬄoading
            optimization in MEC systems.


            Keywords: Multi-Access Edge Computing · Heterogeneous
            Workloads · Edge caching · Computation Oﬄoading · Deep
            Reinforcement Learning


1         Introduction
In recent years, the explosive growth of IoT device connections worldwide has
coincided with the widespread adoption of cutting-edge technologies–such as
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 291–310, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_16
292    S. Li et al.

artiﬁcial intelligence, virtual reality, and autonomous driving–on mobile plat-
forms. This convergence has driven a dramatic surge in computational demand,
which, however, far exceeds the limited processing capabilities of mobile devices.
    To address these challenges, Multi-Access Edge Computing (MEC) has
emerged [15]. By deploying compute nodes or servers at the network edge, MEC
brings data processing closer to end users, thereby signiﬁcantly reducing trans-
mission latency and enhancing overall system performance and quality of service.
Consequently, MEC is widely regarded as a key technology for alleviating the
anticipated shortage of large-scale network computing resources. Recent stud-
ies [12] have shown that, within MEC systems, only a small subset of tasks is
requested frequently–that is, task requests exhibit high concentration–leading to
repeated oﬄoading and computation of the same tasks and incurring unneces-
sary transmission and processing delays. To mitigate this issue, caching mech-
anisms have been introduced: by storing high-frequency tasks on edge servers,
redundant processing can be avoided, improving resource utilization and reduc-
ing system latency [22]. Given the limited cache capacity of edge servers–which
can accommodate only a fraction of all tasks–designing eﬀective caching strate-
gies is critical. Most prior work on MEC has focused on a single task type: some
studies [2,6,23] optimize caching for computation oﬄoading by storing interme-
diate data, task ﬁles, or preprocessed results to minimize redundant computation
and maximize edge-computing eﬃciency, with new research in this vein empha-
sizing joint optimization of resource allocation and oﬄoading strategies. Other
studies [7,18,20] concentrate solely on caching popular content–such as audio or
video–at the edge to reduce user access latency and backbone network load.
    However, the above caching strategies do not account for the task hetero-
geneity and diversity in edge computing environments. Most existing strategies
are tailored to single-task scenarios, limiting their applicability. Recent studies
suggest that real-world edge caching scenarios can be categorized based on task
patterns. For instance, in the survey [9], typical tasks in MEC environments are
classiﬁed into computation-intensive tasks and data-delivery tasks, correspond-
ing to application scenarios such as Augmented Reality (AR) and HTML content
access. Similarly, [10] discusses key challenges in edge caching and categorizes
cacheable objects into content caching, data caching, and computation caching.
    Some existing studies [11,21] have attempted to propose a uniﬁed framework
for handling both computational and access-type tasks; however, their task-
request models are overly simpliﬁed and cannot generate heterogeneous tasks
asynchronously [11], and applying a single caching policy in complex scenarios
[21] leads to a mismatch between computing resources and storage capacity.
    In summary, although prior research has made progress in improving cache
hit rates and reducing system latency, the challenges posed by heterogeneous
tasks remain insuﬃciently addressed. To tackle this issue, we propose a dynamic
caching and oﬄoading optimization framework based on task pattern classiﬁ-
cation, aiming to minimize overall latency in complex MEC environments. The
main contributions of this work are as follows: (1) we formulate a system model
tailored for heterogeneous task patterns and derive an analytical expression for
                                                    Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization                     293

total task delay; (2) we design two task-speciﬁc caching strategies–Gated Deep
Q-Network (GDQN) for computation-intensive tasks and Neural Collaborative
Filtering-based Caching (NCFC) for access-intensive tasks–based on diﬀerences
in computational and transmission demands; (3) we decompose the global delay
minimization problem into two subproblems and employ a Bayesian optimization
approach to adaptively allocate shared caching resources between task types,
achieving near-optimal overall performance. The proposed method provides a
promising direction for optimizing task scheduling in heterogeneous MEC sce-
narios.

2     MEC System Model Based on Task Pattern
      Classiﬁcation
2.1   Network Model and Task Pro cessing Flow
In edge computing systems equipped with caching mechanisms, user tasks are
generally classiﬁed into computation-intensive and access-intensive types based
on their resource requirements and processing characteristics. Access-intensive
tasks (e.g., ﬁle downloads, video streaming, and web browsing) are diverse in
type and exhibit high request frequency [4]. These tasks rely primarily on data
transmission and are highly delay-sensitive, making them suitable for proactive
caching of popular content at edge servers to reduce response time. In con-
trast, computation-intensive tasks (e.g., face recognition and natural language
processing) require substantial computing resources and speciﬁc task software,
which can be pre-cached at the edge to avoid repeated uploads [8]. Although
such tasks generally have lower request frequency, they incur high computa-
tional overhead [10] and place greater demands on the coordinated allocation of
communication and computing resources.
294          S. Li et al.

    To support both types of tasks within a uniﬁed model, a Multi-Access Edge
Computing (MEC) network is designed, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The network
architecture comprises multiple user devices, a base station equipped with an
edge server, and a remote cloud server. The edge server is endowed with com-
puting and storage capabilities, along with the ability to proactively cache task-
related data and software, while user devices possess basic local processing power.
