    In each time slot t, the user set K = {Kk | k = 1, 2, . . . , K} represents
the users who are currently in an active state. The tasks generated by users
form the computation-intensive task set F1 = {Ff 1 | f1 = 1, 2, . . . , F1 } and
the access-intensive task set F2 = {Ff 2 | f2 = 1, 2, . . . , F2 }, which together
constitute the overall task set F = {F1 , F2 } = {Ff = 1, 2, . . . , F }. We assume
the system operates over T time slots, with each time slot lasting τ , and t
represents any arbitrary time slot.In each time slot, each user requests to execute
a task from the task set or makes no request. Similar to the approach in [24], by
setting a delay constraint, we can ensure that each task completes its execution
within the current time slot. Let μtk represent the request of user Kk in time
slot t. Speciﬁcally, μtk = 0 indicates that the user does not request any task, and
μtk = Ff indicates that the user requests to execute task Ff .
    The parameters of computation-intensive tasks Ff 1 ∈ F1 include the task
input parameter size If 1 , the data size of the task computation software Sf 1 ,
and the number of computational resources (CPU cycles) required to complete
the task ωf 1 . The computational results are considered negligible if the result
size is too small. Computation-intensive tasks can either be computed locally or
oﬄoaded to an MEC server for computation, where users need to upload the task
parameters and computation software to the edge device. Due to the large size of
computation software and strong interference from cloud-edge transmission, this
paper does not consider oﬄoading tasks to the central server for computation.
                                   Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization             295

    Because large computation software signiﬁcantly occupies cache space, the
number of software packages that can be cached concurrently is limited. Mean-
while, tasks exhibit heterogeneous software sizes and computational complexity,
imposing higher demands on caching accuracy. Therefore, the system updates
its cache in real time based on user requests in each time slot. At the begin-
ning of time slot t, the MEC server ﬁrst makes a caching decision, updating its
cache according to the current user task requests. Under this caching policy, it
then makes an oﬄoading decision–determining whether each task is computed
locally or on the server–and returns the computed results, completing the task
execution process.
    In the access-intensive tasks Ff 2 ∈ F2 , the parameters include the task data
size Df 2 that is requested for download. Due to the large number of access-
intensive task types, real-time cache updates would consume a signiﬁcant amount
of system resources. We set L time slots as a time window and perform cache
updates every L time slots. At the beginning of each time slot, based on the cache
state in the window, requested tasks will be prioritized for retrieval from the edge
device. If the requested task is not cached on the edge device, a request will be
made to the central server to download the required task data. In summary, the
complete ﬂowchart of task execution within a time slot is shown in Fig. 2.
    For the task request model, we assume that all task requests of each user
follow a Markov chain model, as referenced in papers [16,17]. The speciﬁc task

    In the statistical model described above for transition probabilities, the prob-
ability of a user transitioning from any state to the no-request state is R. When
the user has no request, the probabilities of requesting a computation-intensive
task Ff 1 and an access-intensive task Ff 2 at the next time slot follow Zipf [14]
distributions with parameters δ1 and δ2 , respectively. When the user has already
made a request in the current time slot, at the next time slot, the user will tran-
sition with equal probability to one of the N neighboring tasks within the same
task set. N1 and N2 represent the number of neighboring tasks in the correspond-
ing task sets for the requested tasks. This design considers both the long-term
statistical characteristics and short-term correlations of user requests, providing
a better simulation of real-world scenarios.

2.2   Communication Delay Mo del

In the system of this paper, the network available bandwidth between the user
and the edge device is set to B Hz. This bandwidth is evenly divided into M
orthogonal wireless channels to avoid inter-channel interference. It is assumed
that the channel is static, meaning that the user remains stationary during the
task oﬄoading process. To address the issue of insuﬃcient channels, we use Code
Division Multiple Access (CDMA) technology [1] on each channel, allowing users
to share channels when channel resources are limited. Users will select the best
channel M ∗ for oﬄoading based on the channel selection algorithm in Sect. 3.1.
For communication between the remote cloud server and the edge server, we
refer to the range in [25], and set the cloud-to-MEC transmission rate Rcloud
based on the speciﬁc simulation scenario.
    According to Shannon’s formula, the uplink transmission rate at which user
Kk oﬄoads tasks to the MEC server over channel M∗ in time slot t is given by:

3     Two Caching Strategies for Computation
      and Access-Intensive Tasks
3.1   Dynamic Caching and Oﬄoading Mechanism for Computation-
      Intensive Tasks
In this study, we design a dynamic task software caching update mechanism,
GDQN, based on Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), aimed at dynamically
adjusting the system cache and oﬄoading decisions according to task requests
in each time slot. Speciﬁcally, GDQN captures user request features and eval-
uates the value of caching actions based on the system state at time slot t. By
eﬃciently learning in a large action space, we optimize the caching strategy and
eﬀectively reduce system latency.
    In designing the oﬄoading scheme, the system ﬁrst computes the oﬄoading
delay under the current caching strategy βt , ignoring interference from shared
                                                                              local
channels. It then compares this delay with the local computation delay Tk,f      1,t .
If the local delay is smaller, the task is executed locally (αt = 0); otherwise, the
system proceeds to channel selection. The user ﬁrst attempts to oﬄoad on any
idle channel. If no idle channel is available, a greedy algorithm evaluates each
busy channel m by computing the cost :

                                Δm = Tcurrent,m − Tnew,m                         (11)

where Tcurrent,m is the current total transmission delay on channel m and Tnew,m
is the delay if the new task is oﬄoaded via channel m. The channel with the
minimum cost is selected:
                                m∗ = arg min Δm                             (12)
                                               m∈M
                                              Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization          299

Finally, the oﬄoading delay on channel m∗ is compared again with Tk,f       local
                                                                               1,t to
determine the ﬁnal decision αt . This channel selection procedure can also be
applied to edge-to-user transmissions for access-intensive tasks.
     To optimize the caching strategy, we employ a joint framework combining a
Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network and a Dueling Double Deep Q-Network
(DDQN), integrated with 01 knapsack dynamic programming. This framework
aims to eﬃciently select the optimal subset of ﬁles to cache and maximize delay
savings under capacity constraints.
     To model the dynamic evolution of user requests and cache states, we abstract
the system as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The system state comprises two
parts: the user request vector μt and the server cache state bt . By concatenating
these two vectors, we obtain the system state at time slot t, denoted as st =
[μt , bt ], which describes the distribution of task requests and the current cache
usage.
     We design the reward function to quantify the delay savings brought by the
caching strategy. It is deﬁned as the diﬀerence between the total execution delay
under an empty cache and that under the current cache:
                                              Rt = TNt − TCt                                   (13)
where TNt and TCt denote the total delay using oﬄoading policy αt under empty-
cache and current-cache states, respectively.
    To capture the temporal dynamics of user requests, we employ a Gated
Recurrent Unit (GRU) to process the input sequence. At each time slot t, the
sequence {st−L+1 , . . . , st } of length L is fed into the GRU. After the GRU applies
its update and reset gates to update the hidden state, it outputs the hidden
state ht as the temporal feature representation. We then pass ht through a
fully connected layer with ReLU activation to further enrich the feature, where
ft = ReLU(Wf ht + bf ) ∈ R128 .
    Here, Wf ∈ R128×H is a trainable weight matrix. This design enables the net-
work to automatically learn the Markovian features of user requests and predict
future time-slot decisions based on the state sequence.
    The output uses a Dueling network structure [19] to estimate the Q-value
for each ﬁle. Two parallel streams compute the state value V (st ) and the action
advantage A(st , f ), measuring the potential contribution of the state to long-
term return and the gain of caching ﬁle f above average, respectively. The ﬁnal
Q-value is
                                                                      F
                     Q(st , f ) = V (st ) + A(st , f ) − F1                A(st , f )          (14)
                                                                    f =1

The network outputs a length-F vector Q(s), where each component Q(st , f )
evaluates the value of caching ﬁle f . Enumerating all subsets requires O(2F )
actions. To select the optimal cache subset eﬃciently, we integrate a 01 knapsack
dynamic programming algorithm. Formally, we solve
                      F1                               F1
            max             Q(st , f ) zf 1     s.t.          Sf 1 zf 1 ≤ C1 , zf 1 ∈ {0, 1}   (15)
           {zf 1 }
                     f =1                              f =1
300     S. Li et al.

where Sf 1 is the data size of the task computation software and C1 is the cache
capacity for computation tasks. This reduces action selection to O(F · C1 ) poly-
nomial time per slot.
    Finally, we adopt a Double DQN (DDQN) strategy to reduce Q-value over-
estimation and improve stability. The online network parameters θ are updated
by backpropagation, while the target network parameters θ− are synced periodi-
cally.The TD target is yt = rt + γ Qθ− (st+1 , a∗t+1 ), a∗t+1 = arg maxa Qθ (st+1 , a),
and we use the Huber loss for the TD error, J(θ) = Huber(Qθ (st , at ) − yt ). This
decouples action selection and action evaluation, ensuring stable convergence in
large-scale task environments.For clarity, we summarize the detailed steps of the
DDQN inference phase in Algorithm 1.


Algorithm 1. Eﬃcient Caching and Oﬄoading for Computation-Intensive Tasks
Require: Cache capacity C1 , discount factor γ, task sizes Sf 1 , request vector μt , cache
   state bt
1: Initialize networks θ, θ− ; set b0 , μ0
2: for each time slot t do
3:     st ← [μt , bt ], ht ← GRU(st−L+1:t )
4:     ft ← ReLU(Wf ht + bf )
5:     Estimate Q(st , f ) via dueling DDQN
6:     Select cached tasks by solving:

                  max      Q(st , f ) · zf ,   s.t.   Sf 1 zf ≤ C1 , zf ∈ {0, 1}

 7:   Update cache, compute reward Rt = TN t
                                             − TCt
 8:   Update Q via Huber loss and target value yt
 9:   if t mod Tsync = 0 then
10:       θ− ← θ
11:    end if
12: end for




3.2   Caching Mechanism for Access-Intensive Tasks

In multi-access edge computing scenarios, existing deep learningbased caching
schemes often only scale to relatively small task pools. To explore a method suit-
able for large-scale task environments, this paper proposes a cache mechanism
combining interest-awareness and delay-beneﬁt based on the Neural Collabo-
rative Filtering (NCF) framework [5]. NCFC models the usertask interaction
directly to predict each user’s access probability for content items. On this basis,
we introduce a delay-savingdriven global reward Gkf to obtain the globally opti-
mal cache subset.
    First, we transform user attributes and content features through a projection
layer into low-dimensional embedding vectors to model their latent characteris-
tics as inputs to the neural network. For each user Kk and each access-intensive
                                    Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization      301

task Ff 2 , the user and content feature vectors are mapped by embedding layers
into the same latent space, yielding low-dimensional embeddings ek , ef 2 ∈ Rd
(with d = 24), where d is the embedding dimension.
    To capture the interaction between users and content, the model utilizes
both linear interaction via GMF (Generalized Matrix Factorization) and non-
linear interaction via MLP (Multilayer Perceptron). GMF models the linear
relationship between user and content by computing the element-wise product
of user and content embeddings. Speciﬁcally, for user Kk with embedding ek
and access-intensive task Ff 2 with embedding ef 2 , the GMF interaction is given
by hGMF
     k,f 2 = ek     ef 2 where      denotes element-wise multiplication, capturing
the linear compatibility between user and content to produce a linear preference
score.
    In the nonlinear interaction component, we concatenate the user and content
embedding vectors to form a composite feature vector, which is then fed into a
multilayer perceptron (MLP) to capture more complex nonlinear relationships.
This process is represented as hMLPk,f2 = MLP [ek ; ef2 ] , where the MLP architec-
ture has layer dimensions 128 → 64 → 32 and uses ReLU activation functions.
    After concatenating the linear and non-linear branches, we obtain the fused
feature vector hk,f2 = [hGMF        MLP
                           k,f2 ; hk,f2 ]. This fused feature is then mapped to an
unnormalised logit rk,f2 = w hk,f2 + b, where w, b are learnable parameters.
    The network outputs the whole logit vector zk = rk,1 , . . . , rk,F2 ∈ RF2 for
each user in a single forward pass.
    We regard the request of user k in time-slot t as a multi-label classification
problem: the actually requested task is marked 1 while all others are 0. The
model is optimised with BCEWithLogitsLoss, which internally applies the sig-
moid activation and computes a per-dimension binary cross-entropy; therefore
no explicit σ(·) is needed during training.
    At inference, request probabilities are recovered from logits by
                                                     1
                   pk,f2 = σ rk,f2 =                           ∈ (0, 1)          (16)
                                              1 + exp(−rk,f2 )
   After obtaining these probabilities, we deﬁne a delay-diﬀerence-based caching
beneﬁt metric Gkf 2, representing the expected delay savings when user Kk caches
task Ff 2 :
                          Gkf 2 = pk,f2 Tk,f 2,t − Tk,f 2,t
                                         F          T
                                                                            (17)
         T          F
where Tk,f 2,t and Tk,f 2,t denote the execution delays under cache hit and miss,
respectively, as deﬁned in Eq. (5).
   The global caching beneﬁt of task Ff 2 is obtained by summing over all users:
                         K              K
                 Gf2 =         Gkf2 =         P (f2 | k) Tk,f
                                                          F
                                                              2 ,t
                                                                   − Tk,f
                                                                      T
                                                                          2 ,t
                                                                                 (18)
                         k=1            k=1

   Finally, let Gf 2 collect these beneﬁts for all candidate contents. To select the
optimal cache subset under the capacity limit C2 for access-intensive tasks, we
formulate a 01 knapsack problem:
302     S. Li et al.

                       F2                         F2
             max             Gf 2 zf 2    s.t.           Df 2 zf 2 ≤ C2 ,    zf 2 ∈ {0, 1}    (19)
            {zf 2 }
                      f =1                        f =1

   This yields the optimal cache set within each time-slot window, minimizing
the total system delay. The knapsack is solved by dynamic programming in
O(F · C2 ) time.
   In our system, we ﬁrst pretrain a base model on historical data and perform
cache replacement using a sliding time-window mechanism. We deﬁne a cache
window of length L. At the end of each window, the model is ﬁne-tuned on the
newly accumulated interaction data. We then recompute Gf 2 and solve Eq. (19)
to update the cache, thus achieving sliding-window cache replacement.


4     Optimization and Solution

In multi-access edge computing scenarios, the joint optimization of caching and
oﬄoading for heterogeneous tasks (computation-intensive and access-intensive)
presents multidimensional coupling challenges. To address this, we propose a
Task Pattern Classiﬁcation-based Caching and Oﬄoading strategy (TPCO)
framework, which adopts a function-decoupling hierarchical strategy: ﬁrst inde-
pendently model and optimize caching and oﬄoading strategies for each task
type, then perform global resource allocation to achieve the overall system objec-
tive.
    Our optimization goal is to minimize the long-term average task processing
delay of all users per time slot t, subject to the system constraints. Formally,
the problem P is deﬁned as:
                                                            T   K
                                                   1
                                     min         lim                  Tk,t                    (20)
                                    {αt ,βt } T →∞ T
                                                     t=1        k=1



                 s.t.                      Tk,t ≤ τ,        ∀k ∈ K, f ∈ F, t ∈ T             (20a)
                  F
                        βk,f 1,t Sf 1 + βk,f 2,t Df 2 ≤ C,             ∀k ∈ K, t ∈ T         (20b)
                f =1
                                     K
                                           mec
                                          fk,t ≤ fmax
                                                  mec
                                                      ,         ∀t ∈ T                       (20c)
                                    k=1
                             βk,f,t ∈ {0, 1},      ∀k ∈ K, f ∈ F, t ∈ T                      (20d)
                            αk,f,t ∈ {0, 1}, ∀k ∈ K, f ∈ F, t ∈ T                            (20e)
                                      M ∗ ∈ {1, 2, . . . , M }                               (20f)

    In Problem P, constraint (20a) ensures that the total execution delay Tk,t
for each user Kk in any time slot does not exceed the slot length τ , which can
be enforced by selecting an appropriate slot duration. Constraint (20b) requires
                                  Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization       303

that the total size of both types of task software cached at the MEC server in
each time slot does not exceed the cache capacity C. Constraint (20c) guarantees
that the sum of computational resources allocated to all users per time slot does
                                                              mec
not exceed the server’s maximum computation capacity fmax         ; any tasks arriv-
ing when the server is fully loaded will be executed locally. Constraints (20d)
and (20e) deﬁne the feasible values of the caching decision βk,f,t and the oﬄoad-
ing decision αk,f,t , respectively–indicating that task software on the server can
be added, removed, or remain unchanged, and that each user can choose local
computation or MEC oﬄoading. Finally, constraint (20f) speciﬁes that the opti-
mal channel M ∗ selected by the channel selection algorithm is chosen from the
M channels deﬁned in the network model, rather than being newly allocated.

    The speciﬁc expression for Tk,t is given in Eq. (10) of Sect. 2.4, where the
                                                                     C
total delay is composed of the computation-intensive component Tk,f     1,t and the
                                A
access-intensive component Tk,f 2,t . Since these two task types are transmitted
over the uplink and downlink respectively (with frequency isolation ensuring no
interference), the total delay can be decoupled into the sum of their independent
delay contributions. Further assuming that the request volumes and temporal
distributions of the two task types are statistically independent, the global opti-
mization problem P can be decomposed into two subproblems P1 and P2 , cor-
responding to delay optimization for computation-intensive and access-intensive
tasks, respectively. The two subproblems P1 and P2 are deﬁned as follows:

304     S. Li et al.

From the detailed analysis, when task requests are independently distributed, the
only coupling between computation-intensive and access-intensive tasks arises
from the shared cache resource: the total cache capacity C must be divided into
C1 for computation-intensive tasks and C2 for access-intensive tasks, satisfying
C1 + C2 = C. Under ﬁxed cache allocations, we use the GDQN and NCFC
algorithms to solve subproblems P1 and P2 , obtaining the optimal delays ρ1 (C1 )
and ρ2 (C2 ). The global delay optimization problem then reduces to:

                        min ρ1 (C1 ) + ρ2 (C2 ) s.t.   C1 + C2 = C            (23)
                       C1 , C 2

Both ρ1 (C1 ) and ρ2 (C2 ) are obtained by training and evaluating their respective
deep learning models; they lack explicit analytical forms and gradients, constitut-
ing a typical black-box optimization scenario. Therefore, neither gradient-based
convex optimization methods nor standard ﬁrst- or second-order descent algo-
rithms can be directly applied to the global objective. Moreover, the edge system
must complete capacity allocation rapidly within a limited evaluation budget,
which precludes random or heuristic searches with high iteration costs.
    Accordingly, we design a Bayesian optimization scheme: we build a Gaussian
process surrogate model and use the Expected Improvement (EI) acquisition
function to iteratively approach the optimal cache allocation (C1∗ , C2∗ ). Specif-
ically, in the initialization stage, we generate a set of candidates by uniformly
sampling the capacity interval [0, C] and collect initial delay samples through
experiments. In each iteration, we use a Gaussian process (GP) to approxi-
mate the objective function and evaluate the posterior distribution at unexplored
points:
                            f (C1 ) ∼ GP μ(C1 ), κ(C1 , C1 )                   (24)
where μ(·) denotes the mean function, and κ(C1 , C1 ) represents the covariance
kernel that measures the similarity between two cache allocation candidates C1
and C1 . A commonly used choice for κ is the squared exponential (RBF) kernel.
We then deﬁne the acquisition function based on Expected Improvement (EI):

                             EI(C1 ) = E max fmin − f (C1 ), 0                (25)

where fmin is the minimum observed objective value so far. Finally, we update
the candidate set by selecting the point with the largest expected improvement,
           (n+1)
denoted C1       , for the next evaluation. This process repeats until the number
of iterations reaches a preset maximum or the improvement Δf (n) falls below a
convergence threshold. The resulting optimal cache allocation C1∗ , C2∗ is then
applied to the system-level delay minimization problem.


5     Experimental Results and Comparative Analysis
In this section, we evaluate the performance of our proposed NCFC and GDQN
schemes against the following baseline caching strategies. All experiments use
the same oﬄoading mechanism as in our proposals:
                                               Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization                            305

– Random Replacement (Random): Caches every new requested task;
  when the cache is full, the MEC server randomly evicts one of the cached
  tasks.
– Least Frequently Used (LFU): Caches the most frequently requested task
  software; when full, the cached item with the fewest requests is replaced by
  the new task.
– First-In, First-Out (FIFO): The MEC server evicts the task that was
  requested earliest, caching the most recently requested tasks.
– Intelligent popularity-based caching scheme (IPTC) [3]: IPTC builds
  a task value function based on popularity, freshness, and size, and performs
  proactive caching using historical request data to reduce latency. Low-value
  tasks are replaced to maximize cache eﬃciency and system performance.
– Item-based Collaborative Filtering Caching (ITBCF) [13]: Predicts
  each user’s activity level and content preferences using collaborative ﬁlter-
  ing, formulates average hit-rate maximization as a submodular problem, and
  greedily allocates ﬁle caches for each user.
– Dynamic ProgrammingBased Heterogeneous Task Caching (DP-
  HTC) [11]: Dynamic programming is used to iteratively build an optimal
  caching strategy by evaluating the latency reduction and storage cost of each
  task, thereby jointly optimizing data caching for computation-intensive tasks
  and access-intensive tasks.
– Greedy AllocationBased Heterogeneous Task Caching (GA-
  HTC) [11]: Cache the data of computation-intensive tasks and access-
  intensive tasks in descending order of popularity until the caching space is
  exhausted.

Fig. 3. In computational-intensive task scenarios (a) The delay consumption of users
with respect to iteration steps; (b) Comparison of the number of users as a function of
delay.


    Figure 3a shows the delay consumption reduction per training slot for com-
putational tasks with the proposed GDQN scheme, under cache sizes of 3G and
7G. As training slots increase, the delay consumption reduction gradually grows
and reaches its maximum. The proposed scheme converges within 1000 time
slots, while most existing DRL-based caching methods [16] require over 10000
time slots. Experiments show that the proposed method can converge quickly
and stably under diﬀerent cache conditions.
    Figure 3b compares the average per-slot delay of diﬀerent caching schemes
for computation-intensive tasks as a function of the task library size. As the
library size increases, the average per-slot delay of all schemes increases. Our
GDQN-based scheme consistently delivers the best cache prediction and delay
reduction across diﬀerent library sizes. At a library size of 30 tasks, our scheme
                                  Joint Caching and Oﬄoading Optimization         307

reduces delay by 31.6%, 39.1%, 43.9%, and 45.2% compared to the Random,
LFU, FIFO, and IPTC schemes. This is because our method dynamically learns
the dynamics of user requests in each time slot and adjusts the caching strategy
in real-time, allowing it to adapt quickly to varying request volumes.




Fig. 4. Comparison of the cache size as a function of delay in computational-intensive
task scenarios and access-intensive task scenarios.


    Figure 4a shows the eﬀect of MEC server cache size on the average per-
slot delay for the proposed GDQN-based computation-intensive scheme and ﬁve
baseline schemes. As cache size increases, all schemes exhibit decreasing delay. At
a 5GB cache, GDQN reduces delay by 19.3%, 24.2%, 29.3%, and 37.1% compared
to the Random, LFU, FIFO, and IPTC schemes. Beyond 10GB, delays converge
as the edge caches the entire software library.
    Figure 4b compares the average per-slot delay of each caching scheme for
access-intensive tasks as a function of the MEC server’s cache size. GDQN con-
sistently outperforms other caching algorithms across all cache sizes. At 5GB
cache, GDQN reduces delay by 18.2%, 29.8%, 41.2%, and 43.9% compared to
Random, LFU, FIFO, and ITBCF. Unlike the computation-intensive task delay-
cache curve, the delay for access-intensive tasks continues to decrease as cache
size grows, as the task library is large and not fully cached even at 10GB.
    Figure 5a compares system performance with a 10GB cache, evaluating four
cache allocation methods: Bayesian optimization, golden-section search, random
allocation, and uniform sampling allocation (which corresponds to grid search).
A 100-iteration grid search serves as the baseline. By varying the parameter
λ deﬁned in Eq. (1), we examine the algorithm’s performance under diﬀerent
computation-to-access task ratios. Bayesian optimization signiﬁcantly outper-
forms other methods in minimizing average per-slot delay. Despite reducing the
number of iterations by 90%, the proposed method still achieves performance
close to that of the grid search algorithm, with the average delay diﬀerence not
exceeding 3.2%.
308    S. Li et al.

   Figure 5b compares the average per-slot delay of the proposed algorithm,
GA-HTC, and DP-HTC algorithms under heterogeneous task scenarios with
varying cache capacities. The proposed algorithm outperforms both GA and
DP, reducing delay by 36.35% and 27.93% at a 10GB buﬀer.




Fig. 5. (a) Performance Comparison of Cache Allocation Algorithms Under Varying
Task Ratios. (b) Performance Comparison of Caching Algorithms Under Heterogeneous
Task Scenarios. (c) System Delay Variations Under Diﬀerent Cache Allocation Schemes
and Task Request Patterns.


    Figure 5c compares the system’s per-slot delay curves for diﬀerent cache allo-
cation schemes under varying ratios of access-intensive to computation-intensive
task requests. As the proportion of computation-intensive tasks decreases, total
delay declines, since these tasks require more cache and computation resources.
The minimum point on each curve represents the lowest possible system delay.
As the access-intensive share grows, the optimal allocation assigns more cache
to access-intensive tasks to minimize overall delay. These results show that our
algorithm eﬀectively adapts to heterogeneous task mixes and scales across dif-
ferent network conditions.


7     Conclusion
This paper proposes a joint caching and oﬄoading optimization scheme
(TPCO) for heterogeneous tasks in multi-access edge computing (MEC). For
computation-intensive and access-intensive tasks, we design specialized caching
strategies (GDQN and NCFC) and allocate cache resources via Bayesian opti-
mization to reduce total system delay. Future work will explore the algorithm’s
performance in multi-server scenarios to enhance the framework’s scalability and
applicability.

         Abstract. Person retrieval aims to use images of any modality or type
         of the target person as query probes to retrieve and locate the target
         individual in the scene image gallery. However, current researches on
         person retrieval still focuses on the close world with controlled envi-
         ronments and abundant annotations, which limits its applicability to
         the open world in Cyber-Physical-Social Systems (CPSS). Open envi-
         ronments are confronted with challenges such as complex and variable
         scenarios, scarce labels, massive data volume, and scattered storage. To
         tackle these challenges, we propose a novel CPSS-based framework for
         open world person retrieval and its distributed parallel training. This
         framework comprises three tightly integrated components: a physical
         part that includes image data collected from various sensors; a social part
         composed of open world person retrieval models; and a cyber part that
         incorporates distributed parallel training strategies for these models. In
         addition, we introduce a new evaluation index that balances model per-
         formance and computational cost to assess open world person retrieval
         models and their distributed parallel training strategies. We hope that
         this work will contribute to advancing research and practical deployment
         of person retrieval in the open world.


         Keywords: Parallel computing · Deep learning · Open world · Person
         retrieval


1       Introduction: From Close World to Open World
With the improvement of living standards, increasing attention has been paid
to personal and property safety, making security a growing public concern. To
enhance social and public security, video surveillance systems have been increas-
ingly deployed in diverse public spaces such as roads, airports, shopping malls,
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 311–329, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_17
312     L. Yan et al.

hospitals, and schools. These systems play a vital role in risk prevention, emer-
gency response, and the maintenance of urban safety. The video surveillance
market is reportedly valued at 54.42 billion USD in 2024 and is projected to
grow to 88.71 billion USD by 2030 [30]. Beyond public spaces, the adoption of
smart security cameras in private homes is rapidly growing, with the number
of active households expected to reach 578.5 million and household penetration
projected to reach 23.9% by 2029 [31]. The widespread deployment of surveil-
lance systems has resulted in the generation of massive volumes of video data,
necessitating intelligent methods for eﬀective processing and analysis. Among
the key technologies addressing this challenge is person search [2,46], which aims
to identify and locate a target individual within a large-scale gallery of images
using a visible-light photograph as a probe. However, in the open world scenarios
of Cyber-Physical-Social Systems (CPSS) [58,62], a clear visible-light image of
the target person is not always available. For instance, in law enforcement and
criminal investigations, suspects may commit crimes under poor lighting condi-
tions or in surveillance blind spots, making it diﬃcult for visible-light cameras to
capture eﬀective facial or full-body images. In such cases, alternative modalities
such as infrared images or forensic sketches based on eyewitness descriptions may
serve as the only available probe data. In this paper, we focus on the open world
person retrieval task, which involves retrieving and localizing a target individual
within a scene image gallery using a query probe of any modality or type, such
as an infrared image or a sketch, as shown in Fig. 1.




                            ...                                             ...

      Person 1   Person 2

           Query Set                             Gallery Set


        Fig. 1. Illustration of the open world person retrieval task in CPSS.


    Meanwhile, with the rapid development of technologies such as big data
and distributed parallel computing, the ﬂow and transparency of information
related to human society have signiﬁcantly increased. The interactions among
cyberspace, physical space, and social space have become increasingly rapid and
expansive. Consequently, the design and operation of Cyber-Physical Systems
(CPS) [11] should no longer regard humans merely as external entities interact-
ing with the system. Therefore, CPSS [58] are extensions of CPS and is intended
to complement the human and social factors that have been neglected in tradi-
tional CPS. Parallel computing technologies provide CPSS with powerful data
          Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training                             313

processing capabilities, improved responsiveness, and enhanced scalability. The
operational eﬃciency and intelligence of CPSS are highly dependent on dis-
tributed parallel computing technologies.
    At present, the related research on person retrieval primarily focuses on closed
datasets with single scenarios and abundant annotations. However, in the open
world, as illustrated in Fig. 2, surveillance cameras deployed across diverse set-
tings (e.g., schools, parks, supermarkets, stations, and streets) capture data with
highly dynamic imaging conditions and complex scenes. These data are typi-
cally distributed across multiple devices and exhibit massive scale. Under these
circumstances, large-scale manual annotation of data is extremely labor- and
resource-intensive, making extensive annotation infeasible in the open world,
resulting in insuﬃcient labeled samples. These challenges cause existing meth-
ods to suﬀer from limited robustness, transferability, and generalization ability,
yielding suboptimal retrieval performance that fails to meet the demands of
practical intelligent surveillance systems in open environments. Furthermore,
due to the distributed and large-scale nature of surveillance data storage, con-
ventional single-device training paradigms for person retrieval models suﬀer from
slow speed, high maintenance costs, and computational inadequacy, hindering
eﬀective utilization of enormous scale data in the open world. Therefore, to
improve computational eﬃciency, reduce maintenance costs, and fully leverage
the available data, it is urgent to improve the training speed of the model through
distributed parallel training.

    However, most existing distributed parallel training approaches are designed
for classical computer vision tasks such as image classiﬁcation [13] and object
detection [42], rather than for person retrieval. Moreover, inappropriate training
strategies under large-scale data scenarios may lead to a rapid decline in the
model’s generalization performance [20]. Therefore, this paper also investigates
314     L. Yan et al.

how to design targeted distributed parallel training strategies for person retrieval
algorithms in the open world.
    To address the challenges of complex and dynamic scenarios, limited sample
annotations, decentralized large-scale data in the open world, we propose a novel
framework based on CPSS for open world person retrieval and its distributed
parallel training. This framework deeply integrates the interactions among the
cyber, physical, and social spaces, fully accounting for the complexity and speci-
ﬁcity of open world person retrieval. It consists of three closely related parts: (1)
the physical part, comprising image data collected from various sensors; (2) the
social part, encompassing open world person retrieval models; and (3) the cyber
part, which includes distributed parallel training strategies of person retrieval
models. The proposed framework overcomes the limitations of previous studies
where individual components were treated in isolation. By organically combin-
ing the physical, social, and cyber components, it establishes a comprehensive
ecosystem spanning data acquisition, model processing, and eﬃcient training.
    Furthermore, to more comprehensively evaluate the performance of person
retrieval models and their distributed training strategies in the open world, we
propose a novel evaluation index. Conventional metrics often focus unilaterally
on either computational cost or model performance, failing to accurately reﬂect
a model’s comprehensive capabilities in complex and dynamic conditions of the
open world. In contrast, the proposed metric innovatively integrates both com-
putational cost and performance, conducting evaluations from multiple dimen-
sions. It more authentically reﬂects the operational eﬃcacy of models in real-
world applications, thereby providing more rational and reliable basis for model
optimization and practical deployment.
    In summary, the main contributions of this work are threefold:
. A novel open world framework in CPSS for person retrieval is proposed, over-
  coming the limitations of conventional approaches that address the problem
  solely from a single technical perspective.
. A new evaluation index that comprehensively considers computational com-
  plexity and performance is designed, which improves the evaluation system
  for person retrieval models in the open world.
. By focusing on the open world, a scenario of great practical signiﬁcance and
  challenge, the research on person retrieval is extended from the closed and
  ideal laboratory environment to the real and dynamic real world, signiﬁcantly
  expanding the application boundaries of person retrieval technology.


2     Open World Framework in CPSS for Person Retrieval
In this section, we introduce the proposed open world framework in CPSS for
person retrieval in detail. The CPSS is composed of three parts: the physical sys-
tem, the social system, and the cyber system. The physical system includes var-
ious entities in the real world and their interactive physical processes. Through
sensor networks and intelligent technologies, data from the physical system are
              Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training                          315

collected and transmitted to the cyber system. The social system consists primar-
ily of individuals, organizations, and complex social relationships within human
society. It interacts with the physical system and communicates with the cyber
system mainly through the Internet, serving as both a source and recipient of
data. The cyber system serves as the central hub for data storage and processing,
integrating data from both the physical and social systems. It performs analysis
and decision-making, and acts upon the physical system via control networks
and human interventions. Accounting for the complexity and speciﬁcity of per-
son retrieval in the open world, the proposed framework consists of three core
parts, namely the physical (P), social (S), and cyber (C) parts, as shown in Fig.
3.

2.1     P Part
Person retrieval aims to identify and locate a target individual within a
panoramic image gallery composed of visible spectrum images, using a query
image of any modality or type. Accordingly, the physical part of the proposed
framework comprises image data collected by a variety of sensors, as shown in
Fig. 4. In the open world, numerous sensing devices such as visible-light cam-
eras and infrared sensors, like the “eye” spread throughout the city, continuously
collect image data containing human information. These data are sourced from
diverse and dynamic real-world scenes, including streets, shopping malls, and
transportation hubs, and are inﬂuenced by various physical environmental fac-
tors such as weather conditions, illumination, and camera angles. This part serves
not only as the data foundation of the entire framework but also as the criti-
cal bridge between the physical world and social as well as cyber information
processing. The quality and diversity of the collected data directly impact the
accuracy and reliability of subsequent person retrieval models.
316    L. Yan et al.



                                        Camera


                                      Depth Sensor
                       Image Data


                                     Thermal Camera




                                          ......
                        Fig. 4. The P part of our framework.


    As the most fundamental data acquisition devices, visible-light cameras are
capable of capturing visual characteristics of individuals, including appearance,
clothing, and hairstyle. These devices are extensively deployed in public areas
such as schools, parks, supermarkets, stations and streets, forming a pervasive
visual perception network that covers the entire urban space. However, the qual-
ity of data collected by visible-light cameras deteriorates signiﬁcantly in chal-
lenging conditions such as low illumination, nighttime, or heavy smog. In such
scenarios, infrared sensors demonstrate unique advantages by detecting thermal
radiation emitted from object surfaces to produce infrared imagery. This modal-
ity enables clear representation of human silhouettes and positional information
even in complete darkness or adverse weather conditions, thereby compensating
for the limitations of visible-light data.
    Person retrieval data are typically characterized by substantial diversity and
dynamism. The diversity manifests in both the breadth of data sources and the
richness of modalities. Human behavioral patterns, clothing styles, and environ-
mental backgrounds vary signiﬁcantly across diﬀerent scenarios, all of which are
reﬂected in the collected data. The dynamism originates from the temporal vari-
ability of the open world. On the one hand, the behaviors and postures of people
are continuously changing, resulting in appearance variations for the same per-
son at diﬀerent moments. On the other hand, environmental factors such as light
intensity, weather conditions, and crowd density also ﬂuctuate over time. These
dynamic changes make the collected data always in an updated state, forming a
dynamically evolving dataset.
    The diversity of data facilitates the learning of more generalized feature rep-
resentations„ enabling robust performance when handling person retrieval tasks
across diverse scenarios and conditions. For instance, during model training, the
multi-modal and diverse data provided by the physical parts allow the model to
eﬀectively capture feature patterns of individuals under diﬀerent environmen-
tal conditions, thereby improving its adaptability and retrieval accuracy in open
environments. Consequently, the physical part serves not merely as a data collec-
tor, but more critically as the fundamental prerequisite and essential guarantee
for achieving eﬃcient and accurate person retrieval within the entire framework.
          Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training           317

2.2   S Part

In our framework, the social part serves as the core processing unit, integrating
a series of open world person retrieval models, as shown in Fig. 3. By lever-
aging advanced artiﬁcial intelligence techniques, this part extracts meaningful
information from the heterogeneous image data provided by the physical part,
enabling stable and accurate person retrieval in complex and dynamic scenes.
As shown in Fig. 5, its performance directly inﬂuences the overall applicability
and retrieval accuracy of our framework in the open world.

     Unlike the conventional person search task that use only visible-light pho-
tographs as query probes, person retrieval allows the use of other modalities
images of the target individual, such as sketch portraits, near-infrared images,
or far-infrared images. These other modalities images, although containing key
information about individuals, exhibit signiﬁcant diﬀerences from visible spec-
trum images in terms of imaging principles, visual characteristics, and data rep-
resentations. As a result, they cannot be directly utilized by conventional person
search algorithms designed for visible spectrum inputs. Therefore, the social part
introduces image translation techniques to convert sketches, infrared images, and
other non-visible modalities into visible spectrum images, thereby decompos-
ing complex multi-modal retrieval problems into image translation and visible-
image-based person search tasks. For conciseness, we abbreviate this translation
process as person image-to-image translation.
     Due to the complex scenarios and insuﬃcient sample labels in the open world,
it is diﬃcult to obtain a large number of paired images for supervised training of
person image-to-image translation models. Moreover, most existing unsupervised
image-to-image translation methods aim to generate realistic results without pre-
serving the identity information. Direct application of these methods to person
image-to-image translation often leads to identity information loss, which signiﬁ-
cantly compromises subsequent person identiﬁcation and matching performance.
318    L. Yan et al.

To address this issue, our framework incorporates an identity-preserving unsu-
pervised image-to-image translation method, which minimizes identity informa-
tion loss during the translation process to facilitate subsequent person identity
recognition and matching.
    Once multi-modal query probes are uniformly translated into visible spec-
trum images using an identity-preserving unsupervised image-to-image trans-
lation method, person search becomes the critical step in achieving the ﬁnal
retrieval objective. The core task of person search is to match and localize the
target individual in a large-scale panoramic image gallery using a visible spec-
trum image as the query probe. However, in the open world, the scenes of data
collection are complex and variable. Moreover, the prohibitive cost of manual
annotation makes it impractical to acquire suﬃcient labeled training data. These
constraints signiﬁcantly limit the eﬀectiveness of conventional person search
methods designed for closed, single-scenario applications. When confronted with
challenging conditions such as extreme illumination variations, severe occlusions,
and cross-camera viewpoint discrepancies, these methods exhibit substantial lim-
itations in model generalization capability, failing to meet the practical require-
ments of open world person retrieval. Consequently, the proposed framework
emphasizes the adoption of person search models capable of learning robust
pedestrian representation features under complex scenarios, thereby ensuring
stable retrieval performance in the open world.

2.3   C Part
As the core module for addressing data dilemma and enabling eﬃcient train-
ing, the cyber part is facing the serious challenge of scattered and large-scale
data in the open world. In such settings, massive volumes of data are contin-
uously generated and dispersed across surveillance devices, mobile terminals,
and various intelligent systems throughout the city, growing by terabytes or
more each day. Under these circumstances, conventional single-machine training
paradigms reveal multiple inherent limitations: not only do they demonstrate
prohibitively low training eﬃciency, failing to complete model iterations within
an acceptable time frame, but their exorbitant maintenance costs also render
large-scale data processing unsustainable. More critically, such centralized train-
ing architectures cannot eﬀectively integrate distributed data sources, thereby
severely limiting the extraction of deep feature representations and ultimately
compromising model generalization capability. Therefore, developing distributed
parallel training strategies speciﬁcally adapted for open world person retrieval
algorithms emerges as an inevitable choice to unleash model potential and facil-
itate technological deployment.
    To facilitate the deployment of open world person retrieval models into var-
ious intelligent surveillance systems to meet practical application needs, the
model should not have an excessively large number of parameters, and the
model training speed should be as fast as possible without compromising per-
formance. Thus, a data parallel strategy centered on large-batch training can be
             Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training                          319

adopted, which directly improves data processing eﬃciency by splitting large-
scale datasets into smaller sub-batches and distributing them to multiple com-
puting nodes for parallel processing. However, diﬀerent from classic visual tasks
such as image classiﬁcation and object detection, person retrieval models have
unique structural characteristics and task requirements, needing to complete
complex identity matching and positioning tasks. Their architecture typically
integrates multiple components including feature extraction and retrieval match-
ing. Direct application of existing large-batch training algorithms may not only
fail to optimize model performance but could also induce training instability and
degraded generalization capability. Notably, the proposed cyber part employs
distributed parallel training strategies speciﬁcally designed for open world per-
son retrieval models.

    As displayed in Fig. 6, the distributed parallel training strategies can be sys-
tematically optimized by integrating the network architecture and task-speciﬁc
characteristics of person retrieval models. For data parallelism, a dynamic adap-
tive learning rate adjustment mechanism can be employed. It intelligently adjusts
the training learning rate by monitoring the gradient distribution, model con-
vergence speed and other key indicators in the training process in real time to
maximize the training eﬃciency under the premise of ensuring model stability.
In terms of the model parallelism, for the complex architecture of model multi-
module collaboration, a hierarchical module partitioning strategy is adopted.
Model components are distributed across nodes based on their functional roles
and computational demands. In addition, a compression-aware communication
320     L. Yan et al.

algorithm can be introduced to reduce inter-node transmission overhead eﬀec-
tively. These strategies not only make full use of distributed computing resources
but also break through the limitations of traditional training methods in data
scale and computational eﬃciency, providing strong support for the rapid itera-
tion and optimization of models in open environments.


3     A Case Study for New Scenarios

In this section, we present a case study for new scenarios. First, we propose
a novel evaluation index that balances computational cost and retrieval per-
formance for assessing person retrieval models and their distributed training
strategies in the open world. Subsequently, we conduct experiments using an
end-to-end person search model, followed by detailed quantitative analysis of
the experimental results.


3.1   A New Evaluation Index: Balancing Computation
      and Performance

Considering the numerous challenges present in open environments, the evalu-
ation of person retrieval models and their distributed parallelization strategies
should not be limited to a single dimension such as computational cost or model
performance alone. Inspired by the Sun-Ni law [36], which considers parallel
acceleration under memory constraints, we propose a new evaluation index for
assessing open world person retrieval models and their distributed parallelization
methods.
     Let W denotes the problem size (or workload), n represents the number of
processors in the parallel system, and Ws indicates the workload of the serial
component. For the open world person retrieval task, we regard the model size,
i.e., the number of model parameters, as the workload. The proportion of the
serial component is then given by f = Ws /W . The proposed evaluation index S
is formally deﬁned by the following equation:

                                  Ws + (1 − f )W G
                            S=                                                (1)
                                 Ws + (1 − f )W G/n

where G = P F/W comprehensively reﬂects the model performance achievable
per unit of model parameters and the computational cost involved. Here, P
means the model performance, F stands for the total ﬂoating point operations
required by the model.


3.2   Experimental Analysis

In this subsection, we conduct some experiments to obtain evaluation results
based on the proposed index and perform a quantitative analysis of the results.
In open world person retrieval, image-to-image translation models are used to
                        Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training   321

convert the target person’s probe image into a uniﬁed visible-spectrum modal-
ity, after which the person search models perform localization and identiﬁca-
tion within the scene image gallery. Since the number of probe images used for
querying is far smaller than the number of panoramic images in the gallery,
the distributed parallel acceleration for person retrieval should mainly focus on
the person search component. Therefore, we select the end-to-end person search
model SeqNet [26] as a representative example and conduct experiments on the
publicly available CUHK-SYSU [46] dataset.
    SeqNet is a end-to-end network based on Faster R-CNN, which performs
detection and re-identiﬁcation sequentially. After generating a large number of
proposals through detection, it is necessary to further evaluate the features of
each proposal and calculate the bounding box scores. This step is highly suit-
able for parallelization, and thus we improve it using distributed computing
techniques.
    After completing model training, we evaluate SeqNet on the CUHK-SYSU
dataset using mean Average Precision (mAP) as the performance metric. Exper-
imental results show that SeqNet achieves 93.80% of mAP. The calculated total
number of model parameters is 48.42M, and the ﬂoating point operations amount
to 496.58 G. The parameter count for the serial component is 33.43M. Therefore,
the proportion of the serial component f is calculated as 0.69, and the balanced
parameter G is 9.62. When the number of processors n in the parallel system
is set to 2, the evaluation index S can be computed using Equation (1) and is
found to be 1.68. Similarly, we calculate the values of S for other values of n,
and the results are shown in Fig. 7.

and 5.14, respectively. Notably, when n increases from 64 to 128, S only improves
from 4.98 to 5.14, with an incremental gain of merely 0.16. This indicates that
as the number of processors n increases exponentially, the growth of S slows
down, which aligns well with our intuition that the marginal utility of adding
processors diminishes in practical parallel computing scenarios. The proposed
index eﬀectively captures this phenomenon and appropriately balances model
performance and computational cost.

4     Related Work
4.1   Person Retrieval
Since person retrieval can be decomposed into two subtasks: image-to-image
translation and person search, we introduce the related work of these two aspects
separately as follows.

Image-to-Image Translation. Existing methods can be broadly categorized
into supervised and unsupervised approaches. Supervised image-to-image trans-
lation methods, such as Pix2Pix [22] and Pix2PixHD [41] based on genera-
tive adversarial networks (GANs) [16], require paired source and target domain
images for supervised training. In addition to the aforementioned general super-
vised image-to-image translation approaches, researchers have also developed
specialized ones for tasks such as face super-resolution [61], image denoising [52]
and face photo-sketch synthesis [48], which have demonstrated promising per-
formance. In contrast, unsupervised image-to-image translation methods elimi-
nate this pairwise dependency. Among them, CycleGAN [63]is a representative
model that introduces a cycle consistency constraint to learn mappings between
unpaired domains. UNIT [28] implicitly enforces cycle consistency by incorpo-
rating the Kullback-Leibler divergence constraint in a shared latent space, while
MUNIT [21] extends UNIT to support one-to-many mappings. StarGAN [9]
enables multi-domain image translation with a single generator by leveraging
domain labels. Inspired by human vision systems, JND-GAN [60] introduces
a Just-Noticeable-Diﬀerence loss and generates more realistic target domain
images. IPGAN [49] introduces the heterogeneous image knowledge [50], focusing
on identity information preservation during translation, and achieves excellent
unsupervised photo-to-caricature translation performance.
    While methods based on cycle consistency constraint generally perform well
at transferring local texture features but often struggle with geometric trans-
formations. To address this issue, GANimorph [15] introduces deformable con-
volutions in the discriminator to enlarge its receptive ﬁeld and reformulates
the discrimination task as a semantic segmentation problem to encourage more
context-aware generation. CUT [32] maximizes mutual information between cor-
responding patches before and after translation by treating patches at the same
spatial location as positive pairs and those at diﬀerent locations as negatives. It
also incorporates multi-scale information to compute the contrastive loss. Build-
ing on CUT, NEGCUT [43] introduces a hard negative mining mechanism to
          Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training   323

enhance the quality of negative samples, while SRC [24] further regularizes the
consistency of similarity relationships before and after translation to preserve
spatial semantic structure and improve performance.
    Beyond GAN-based methods, recent research has also explored image-to-
image translation approaches based on diﬀusion models [19], which oﬀer alter-
native generative paradigms for high-quality and ﬂexible image synthesis. For
instance, Xiao et al. [44] present a denoising Brownian bridge model with dual
approximators for image-to-image translation.


Person Search. Existing person search methods can be categorized into one-
stage and two-stage methods. One-stage methods are typically modiﬁed from
pedestrian detection models to achieve person search using a single model in an
end-to-end manner. Early single-stage methods [45,46] often adopt the Faster
R-CNN [33] detection framework, which attaches a fully connected layer at the
tail end to output person re-identiﬁcation features. However, these approaches
generate excessive candidate bounding boxes at intermediate layers, resulting in
high storage and computational overhead. Thus, Liu et al. [27] propose a recur-
sive search strategy that progressively reﬁnes target locations without proposal
generation. Similarly, Chang et al. [5] develop a method based on deep rein-
forcement learning that performs person search without relying on candidate
proposals. Yan et al. [55] introduce an anchor-free person search framework to
further reduce dependency on predeﬁned anchor boxes.
    In addition to reducing the number of proposals, improving the discriminabil-
ity of pedestrian representation is also an important research direction. Chen et
al. [7] project person representation vectors into polar coordinates, using the
vector magnitude to distinguish between background and persons, and the angle
component for re-identiﬁcation. Yu et al.[57] adopt a cascading approach based
on the Cascade R-CNN [3] to learn more discriminative person representations
from coarse to ﬁne. Cao et al. [4] treat person search as a sequence prediction
problem and proposed an end-to-end solution based on Transformer [12]. Zhang
et al. [59] propose a hierarchical architecture to jointly optimize instance-aware
and part-aware embeddings. Yan et al. [47] introduce an additional unknown-
aware branch to fully leverage unlabeled or unknown instances and facilitate the
learning of discriminative features.
    In contrast, two-stage approaches decouple pedestrian detection and per-
son re-identiﬁcation into two distinct models. Cheng et al. [6] design a mask-
guided two-branch convolutional neural network, where one branch models fore-
ground pedestrians while the other processes the original image. Han et al. [18]
develop a diﬀerentiable region of interest transformation module to drive the
re-identiﬁcator to ﬁne-tune the detector results, enabling pedestrian bounding
boxes to exclude interference from the background and non-target pedestrians.
Wang et al. [39] employed hybrid training datasets combining ground-truth and
detected boxes to reduce train-test discrepancy.
    Meanwhile, some research eﬀorts focus on weakly supervised person search
paradigms. One type of weak supervision setting is that only the identities
324     L. Yan et al.

present in the gallery are known, without information about the speciﬁc images
or positions where these individuals are located [51]. That is, each image con-
tains neither identity annotations nor bounding box annotations. Built upon
this setting, a weakly supervised sketch-based person search method [53] is pro-
posed. Another type of weak supervision setting [17,38,54] provides bounding
box annotations while omitting pedestrian identity labels. In addition, Li et al.
[25] introduce an unsupervised domain adaptation setting into person search and
propose a DAPS framework. Almansoori et al. [1] further improve this framework
by introducing a domain adaptive bridging mechanism.

4.2   Distributed Parallel Training of Deep Neural Networks
The distributed parallel training of deep neural networks is mainly divided into
three categories: data parallelism, model parallelism, and hybrid parallelism. In
data parallelism, the training dataset is partitioned and distributed across mul-
tiple worker nodes, each maintaining a complete replica of the model. After each
iteration, the gradients computed by each node are synchronized and aggregated
to update the global model parameters before proceeding to the next iteration.
Model parallelism decomposes large models into sub-models distributed across
worker nodes, or allocates inter-layer parameters to diﬀerent hardware devices
for concurrent training. Hybrid parallelism integrates both data and model par-
allelization mechanisms to optimize training eﬃciency.
     In data parallelism, training with large batches eﬀectively increases through-
put and reduces the time required for each iteration cycle. As a result, large-
batch training to maximize data parallelism has become an important research
direction. However, training with large batches can lead to rapid convergence to
sharp local minima, which negatively impacts generalization performance [10].
Some researchers [34] eliminate the generalization performance gap by manually
adjusting the learning rate. Recently, adaptive learning rate adjustment tech-
niques have gained signiﬁcant attention. For example, LARS [56] adjusts the
learning rate of each layer based on the magnitude of its weights and gradients,
enabling ResNet-50 to be trained on ImageNet with a batch size of 32k while
substantially reducing training time. Liu et al.[29] further expand the batch size
to 96k using the idea of adversarial learning. SAM [14] introduces a strategy
that jointly minimizes the loss value and its sharpness to close the generaliza-
tion gap, but its requirement for two gradient computations per iteration makes
it less computationally eﬃcient. To address this problem, Du et al. [13] propose a
stochastic weight perturbation mechanism combined with a sharpness-sensitive
data selection strategy.
     Regarding model parallelism, earlier strategies are designed and implemented
based on expert experience. For example, Sutskever et al. [37] allocate diﬀer-
ent layers of deep learning models to heterogeneous devices according to their
distinctive characteristics, thereby achieving distributed parallel training strate-
gies for complex models. Sun et al. [35] propose a random partitioning method
based on the backbone network, which reduces model complexity by retaining
key operators in the network structure without compromising performance. In
          Open World Person Retrieval and Its Distributed Parallel Training      325

recent years, automatic model parallelism has become a research hotspot. Jia
et al. [23] construct a high-dimensional search space under a given cluster envi-
ronment and build a performance evaluation model to guide the dynamic pro-
gramming search for optimal parallelization strategies. On this basis, Wang et
al. [40] employ recursive partitioning and graph coarsening techniques to reduce
the search time for distributed parallel strategies and enhance model scalability.
Chen et al. [8] propose an automatic parallel framework, which uses the actual
execution time of distributed parallel strategies as a penalty factor for the long
short-term memory model to update the model parallelism plan.


5   Conclusion
In this paper, we propose a novel open world person retrieval and its distributed
parallel training framework. Inspired by CPSS, our framework consists of three
parts, including a physical part that collects image data from various sensors, a
social part that incorporates open world person retrieval models, and a cybler
part that implements distributed parallel training strategies for open world per-
son retrieval algorithms. Furthermore, to enable a more comprehensive and prac-
tical evaluation, we introduce a novel index that jointly considers computational
cost and retrieval performance, speciﬁcally designed for assessing both the per-
son retrieval model and its training strategy under the open world. The proposed
framework and evaluation index oﬀer foundational insights for future research
in open world person retrieval.
