         WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model
             for Satellite Image Recognition
          and Segmentation of Forest Wildfires

Juan Luo(B) , Tianyang Liu , Kexuan Feng , Guogen Zeng , and Fan Li

    The College of Computer Science and Electronic Engineering, Hunan University,
                                  Changsha, China
                                juanluo@hnu.edu.cn



        Abstract. Thermal infrared remote sensing is widely used for wild-
        ﬁre monitoring, but its low spatial resolution makes it diﬃcult to accu-
        rately delineate ﬁre boundaries, especially in small-scale or edge cases. To
        address this, we constructed a wildﬁre image dataset for the Australian
        region, named WildﬁreForest-S2, which better aligns the model with the
        satellite monitoring environment. In addition, we propose WSRNet, an
        image segmentation approach based on U-Net, speciﬁcally designed for
        satellite-based wildﬁre detection. WSRNet integrates classiﬁcation infor-
        mation to reﬁne and guide segmentation features, enhancing the accu-
        racy and eﬃciency of wildﬁre detection in satellite images. The model
        is capable of not only identifying the presence of wildﬁre events in a
        given image but also segmenting ﬁre regions with high precision. Exper-
        imental validation on the WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset demonstrates that
        WSRNet achieves notable improvements in ﬁre region segmentation. At
        the same time, it also demonstrates strong performance in ﬁre classiﬁca-
        tion, greatly enhancing the accuracy of wildﬁre monitoring.


        Keywords: Multi-task learning · ﬁre monitoring · satellite imagery


1     Introduction
Wildﬁres are a natural disaster that cause signiﬁcant losses worldwide [1]. They
threaten human lives and have multiple impacts on the environment, economy,
and society. In 2019, Australia experienced one of the worst wildﬁres in its
history. This disaster led to at least 33 deaths, thousands of injuries, and the
destruction of over 3,000 buildings, with losses estimated in the billions of dollars.
This disaster highlights the importance of timely and eﬀective ﬁre monitoring.
Good monitoring can quickly identify ﬁre sources, reduce losses, and provide
critical support for emergency response.
    Among the current ﬁre monitoring methods, drone detection, manual patrols,
and sensor monitoring can oﬀer some ﬁre warnings, but each has clear limita-
tions. Drone detection employs high-deﬁnition cameras and thermal imaging
for real-time aerial monitoring capable of covering extensive areas. However, its
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 330–348, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_18
     WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition       331

operational duration is limited by battery life, and operating in harsh weather
conditions can be challenging, potentially leading to inaccuracies in data acqui-
sition.
     Manual patrols are the oldest monitoring method, that rely on trained pro-
fessionals to regularly check speciﬁc areas. Its main limitations are ineﬃciency,
limited coverage, and susceptibility to subjective human judgment which can
result in missed detections.
     Sensor monitoring tracks environmental changes in real time through the
ground sensor networks. Although it can quickly detect ﬁres, its eﬀective range
is limited, and the layout and maintenance costs are high.
     In contrast, satellite remote sensing can gather information over large areas.
It helps identify ﬁres by analyzing satellite images. The main advantages of
satellite monitoring are its wide coverage and eﬃcient data collection. This makes
satellite remote sensing have a unique value in ﬁre monitoring and can make up
for the shortcomings of traditional ﬁre monitoring methods.
     Sentinel-2 is part of the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Copernicus program
and features high spatial resolution (ranging from 10 to 60 m) and multispectral
imaging capabilities, which provide signiﬁcant support for ﬁre monitoring [2].
However, how to achieve high-precision ﬁre monitoring through satellite data
remains a challenge that needs to be addressed.
     To address these issues, we have adopted three strategies:
Strategy 1: Sentinel-2 data consists of 13 spectral bands, with ground res-
olutions of 10 m, 20 m, and 60 m. We conducted a selection process for each
spectral band and their combinations, ultimately choosing bands B12, B11, and
B8a for our analysis. This combination eﬀectively highlights the characteristics
of ﬁre-aﬀected areas, ensuring the feasibility of ﬁre monitoring and wildﬁre seg-
mentation.
     Taking the 2019 Australian wildﬁre as an example, we processed all collected
satellite data to create the WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset. The satellite images were
sourced from various regions during critical time points of the Australian ﬁre
events, ensuring the dataset’s usability for analysis.
Strategy 2: We propose WSRNet, a U-Net-based architecture designed to
improve the segmentation of ﬁre-aﬀected areas. To enhance feature quality and
enable the model to better focus on critical regions, we introduce the HAFE
module. In addition, we adopt a multi-task learning strategy and propose the
CGFR module, which uses classiﬁcation information to guide the segmentation
task during joint ﬁre detection and segmentation.
     Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

• We constructed a satellite image dataset called WildﬁreForest-S2 focusing on
  the Australian wildﬁre. WildﬁreForest-S2 is more closely aligned with satellite
  monitoring scenarios compared to existing datasets.
• We innovatively propose the WSRNet method, which combines the U-Net
  architecture with modules such as HAFE and CGFR. Through a multi-task
  learning approach, the model simultaneously performs classiﬁcation and seg-
332    J. Luo et al.

  mentation tasks, providing technical support for satellite wildﬁre monitoring
  tasks.
• By applying the WSRNet method, we signiﬁcantly improved the performance
  of satellite wildﬁre monitoring tasks and achieved a maximum accuracy of
  99.53% in the classiﬁcation task.



2     Related Work
2.1   Wildfire Datasets
Northern Arizona University and other institutions jointly released the FLAME
and FLAME 2 datasets, including visible light imagery and infrared thermo-
graphs collected by drones during planned burns of accumulated debris in pine
forests in Arizona [3,4]. These datasets comprehensively and multi-angularly
capture critical information from the ﬁre scenes. The FLAME 3 dataset was
created by Clemson University and several partner institutions [5]. It includes
synchronously collected visible spectrum and thermal imaging images, provid-
ing high-resolution RGB and thermal TIFF ﬁles, which is suitable for computer
vision and wildﬁre modeling tasks.
    The wildﬁre dataset includes 2,700 aerial and ground images, which are
planned from various online platforms such as government databases, Flickr,
and Unsplash [6]. Mesogeos is a large-scale, multi-purpose dataset speciﬁcally
designed to wildﬁre modeling in the Mediterranean region. It integrates variables
representing wildﬁre drivers—such as weather, vegetation, and human activity—
along with 17 years (2006–2022) of historical wildﬁre ignition and burn area
records [7].
    The Fire Dunnings dataset oﬀers more granularity, and is divided into two
categories: ﬁre and non-ﬁre classes, including ﬂame images segmented into super-
pixels, enabling precise localization and recognition [8].
    The FireNet dataset focuses on the application of lightweight networks, fea-
turing videos and images of ﬁre and non-ﬁre scenarios, making it particularly
suitable for real-time ﬁre detection in IoT environments [9].
    The existing datasets primarily consist of ground and drone images.
WildﬁreForest-S2 is speciﬁcally designed for satellite scenarios, aiming to facili-
tate on-board forest ﬁre monitoring.

2.2   Wildfire Monitoring
Currently, ﬁre monitoring still relies on traditional methods such as manual
surveillance and drone detection [10–12]. Rodrigo De la Fuente et al. proposed
a forest ﬁre monitoring system that integrates monitoring towers, surveillance
balloons, and drone technology. They developed a compact mixed-integer linear
programming model that includes location decisions for various monitoring tech-
nologies and route planning for drones between monitoring facilities to achieve
the most extensive terrain coverage. [13].
      WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition      333

    Liu et al. created a dataset using UAV aerial photography for image fusion
and proposed a method of forest ﬁre identiﬁcation that combines visual and
infrared images,which sloved the problem of the high rates of false positives and
missed detections in forest ﬁre monitoring [14].
    While ground monitoring and UAV monitoring methods have their advan-
tages, they also exhibit signiﬁcant limitations, being susceptible to issues such
as monitoring costs, coverage areas, weather factors, and natural conditions. In
contrast, satellite remote sensing technology provides extensive and real-time
ﬁre monitoring capabilities, overcoming the spatial and temporal deﬁciencies of
ground and UAV methods.
    Moreover, satellite monitoring is not constrained by ground conditions
or weather, allowing for continuous operation in complex environments and
enabling comprehensive surveillance of ﬁre events [15–19].
    Current satellite ﬁre monitoring data often relies on radar and various sen-
sors, lacking image-based ﬁre satellite data. To address this gap in satellite mon-
itoring scenarios, we collected image data during Australian ﬁre events using
Sentinel-2 to create the WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset and proposed the WSRNet
method. This method leverages the rich visual information captured by satel-
lites to improve the accuracy and eﬃciency of ﬁre monitoring eﬀorts.




            Fig. 1. Geographic distribution of data in WildﬁreForest-S2.




3     Dataset
The WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset contains image data from diﬀerent locations and
times during wildﬁre events in Australia. This dataset is speciﬁcally designed for
satellite-based wildﬁre recognition and segmentation tasks.

3.1   Image Collection
The image data for this dataset comes from the Copernicus Data Center of the
European Space Agency, covering ﬁre-related images collected from November
7, 2019, to January 28, 2020. The study area includes the southern and eastern
regions of New South Wales, the eastern and northeast parts of Victoria, South
East Queensland, and Kangaroo Island, among others, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
334     J. Luo et al.




Fig. 2. (a) MSI Natural Colors (B4, B3 and B2). (b) MSI False-color Infrared (B8, B4
and B3). (c) MSI Atmospheric Penetration (B12, B11 and B8a).


    Sentinel-2 L1C is an atmospheric top-of-atmosphere reﬂectance product that
has undergone orthorectiﬁcation and geometric correction, but has not been
atmospherically corrected. However, the L2A data mainly contains atmospheri-
cally corrected bottom-of-atmosphere reﬂectance data, which users need to pro-
duce according to their requirements. To address this, we used the Sen2cor
plugin, released by the European Space Agency, to perform atmospheric cor-
rection of the acquired data [20,21]. This dataset comprises 13 spectral bands,
and we employed band combinations to better interpret the feature character-
istics within the images. We explored all available combinations and ultimately
selected the three infrared bands with a 20 m resolution that are most suitable
for ﬁre monitoring: B12, B11, and B8a, as illustrated in Fig. 2. In the dataset,
we segmented the images into small pieces of 256 × 256, and ﬁlter out portions
containing and without ﬁre events.

3.2   Image Annotation
We used the Labelme tool to annotate the images and exported the labels in
PNG format [22]. After completing the image annotations, we invited experts
to review and validate the labels to ensure annotation quality, resulting in the
ﬁnal annotated dataset.

3.3   Dataset Statistics
The WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset has a total of 1,714 images,of which 857 contain
ﬁre scenes. We split these ﬁre images into test sets and training sets in a ratio of
2:8. We also picked 857 images in the area that did not include ﬁre scenes and
seperated them in the same proportion.
         WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition                                                                                                 335

    In the end, the training set has 1,376 images, and the test set has 338 images
of which the number of the ﬁre and no-ﬁre pictures is the same.


4      WSRNet Architecture

WSRNet introduces the concept of multi-task learning to enhance the U-Net
method and incorporates a wildﬁre recognition task [23]. First, we propose a
speciﬁc feature enhancement module to improve the features during the down-
sampling process [24]. Next, we propose a guidance module that directs the
segmentation task using the classiﬁcation results, further enhancing the segmen-
tation performance. Additionally, we incorporate an extra cross-entropy loss for
the wildﬁre recognition task. This approach allows the two tasks to mutually
beneﬁt from each other, thereby improving the model’s performance.

4.1       Technical Overview

As illustrated in Fig. 3, WSRNet adopts a dual-decoder architecture. The back-
bone employs a shared encoder and incorporates our proposed Hierarchical
Attention for Feature Enhancement (HAFE) module at multiple levels to empha-
size critical information, thereby improving the quality of feature representation.
Under a multi-task learning framework, the model jointly performs segmentation
and classiﬁcation using shared features, which enhances both representational
power and generalization capability.
    Moreover, we propose a guidance module named Class-Guided Feature
Reweighting (CGFR) to fuse classiﬁcation outputs with segmentation features.
This module applies a class-guided feature reweighting mechanism to semanti-
cally modulate the segmentation features, resulting in more accurate and dis-
criminative segmentation outcomes.
336     J. Luo et al.

Fig. 4. HAFE module integrates highlight features, dilated convolutions (ASPP), chan-
nel attention, and edge-guided spatial attention, and employs learnable gating and
scaling to achieve multi-dimensional feature enhancement for ﬁre imagery. It receives
the feature map (x ∈ RB×C×H×W ) from the previous encoder as input and outputs an
enhanced feature map (y ∈ RB×C×H×W ) to the next encoder, with consistent input
and output dimensions for seamless feature consistency and eﬃcient information ﬂow.


To enhance the representation of critical regions in satellite ﬁre imagery, we pro-
pose the Hierarchical Attention for Feature Enhancement (HAFE) module, as
illustrated in Fig. 4. HAFE integrates multi-scale context extraction, channel-
wise reweighting, spatial saliency reﬁnement, and edge-aware modulation in a
uniﬁed attention framework, eﬀectively enriching semantic features while pre-
serving structural cues.
    Given an input feature map X ∈ RB×C×H×W , HAFE performs the following
steps:
Step 1: High-Response Highlighting: First, a 1×1 convolution is applied
to the input feature map for channel-wise linear transformation, which reduces
redundancy and enhances the response of important channels. Then, a 3×3 con-
volution is used to capture local spatial context and further highlight ﬁre-related
features. Both convolution layers are followed by ReLU activation functions to
strengthen the non-linear representation capability.

                                                                                                               (2)
Step 2: Multi-scale Context Extraction (Lightweight ASPP): After
obtaining the initially enhanced highlight features, we introduce a lightweight
     WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition      337

Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module to further strengthen the
model’s perception of multi-scale ﬁre regions. Speciﬁcally, the highlight features
are fed into multiple parallel 3×3 dilated convolution branches with diﬀerent
dilation rates to extract contextual information at various receptive ﬁelds. Each
branch is followed by Batch Normalization and ReLU activation to ensure stable
training and richer non-linear representation. The outputs from all branches are
then concatenated along the channel dimension and fused via a 1×1 convolution
to generate the ﬁnal multi-scale representation.

             Fdi = ReLU BN Conv d3×3
                                  i
                                     (Xcat )           ,   di ∈ {1, 3, 5}     (3)


             Fms = ReLU (BN (Conv 1×1 (Concat(Fd1 , Fd3 , Fd5 ))))            (4)

where di ∈ 1, 3, 5 denotes the dilation rate.
Step 3: Channel Attention with Learnable Gating: Global average pool-
ing and max pooling are applied to the input feature map to obtain two dis-
tinct channel descriptors. These descriptors are then passed through a shared
multilayer perceptron (MLP) for nonlinear transformation. Finally, channel-wise
attention weights are generated to emphasize informative channels, improving
the model’s sensitivity to salient ﬁre regions.

            Mca = σ (MLP(AvgPool(Fms )) + MLP(MaxPool(Fms )))                 (5)

    A learnable scalar gate β adaptively fuses attention-enhanced and original
features:


                      Fca = β · (Fms     Mca ) + (1 − β) · X                  (6)

Step 4: Edge-Aware Spatial Attention: To enhance the model’s attention
to ﬂame edges and salient regions, a Sobel-based edge extraction module is intro-
duced and integrated with a spatial attention mechanism. First, ﬁxed Sobel ﬁl-
ters extract horizontal and vertical gradients to model edge structures. Then, the
average-pooled map, max-pooled map, and edge map are concatenated along the
channel dimension and passed through a 7×7 convolution to generate a spatial
attention map. Let E denote the edge map computed via Sobel ﬁlters:

                   E=     (Sobelx (F̄ca ))2 + (Sobely (F̄ca ))2 +             (7)

where F̄ ca is the mean across channels of F ca, and is a small constant. Spatial
attention map:

             Msa = σ (Conv7×7 (Concat(Avg(Fca ), Max(Fca ), E)))              (8)

Step 5: Final Output with Learnable Scaling: Finally, the spatial attention
map Fca is element-wise multiplied with the channel-reﬁned feature map Msa ,
338         J. Luo et al.

enabling joint modeling of spatial and channel-wise saliency. A learnable scaling
factor α is applied to adaptively modulate the ﬁnal attention-enhanced output.

                                             Fout = α · (Fca            Msa )                                                          (9)

   By hierarchically integrating semantic, contextual, and structural cues,
HAFE signiﬁcantly enhances the discriminability of ﬁre-related features while
maintaining spatial precision.

4.3       CGFR Module


        Input        Segmentation Features      Class-Guided Reweighting Map       Class Activation Map        Classification Logits
      256x256x3        256x256x32                        256x256x32                     256x256x2




                                                                            1x1 Conv                      Expand
                                                                                                                       [0.9,0.1]
                             32                            32




                                                                    1x1 Conv + Sigmoid


                                                   32


                                                                                                     Output
                                                                                                    256x256x3



Fig. 5. CGFR module enhances segmentation features using classiﬁcation predictions.
The logits are expanded into spatial masks, projected via a 1×1 convolution, and
fused with segmentation features through element-wise multiplication for class-aware
modulation.


The Class-Guided Feature Reweighting (CGFR) module is designed to lever-
age the classiﬁcation branch to semantically guide the segmentation process, as
illustrated in Fig. 5. This process is formally deﬁned as:
Step 1: Generation of Class Probabilities: The raw logits from the clas-
siﬁcation branch are passed through a sigmoid activation to produce class-wise
conﬁdence scores in the range [0, 1]:


                                             Mcls = σ(Pcls ) ∈ RB×C                                                                (10)

where σ(·) is the sigmoid function, where B is the batch size and C is the number
of semantic categories. The resulting vector indicates the likelihood of each class
being present in the input image, providing high-level semantic cues
Step 2: Construction of the Class-Guided Mask: To adapt the classiﬁ-
cation cues for spatially distributed segmentation, the conﬁdence vector Mcls is
expanded along spatial dimensions to match the size of the segmentation feature
      WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition    339

map Fseg ∈ RB×Cseg ×H×W . A 1×1 convolution is then applied to project the
expanded class mask into the segmentation feature channel space:
               exp
              Mcls = Conv1x1(Expand(Mcls )) ∈ RB×Cseg ×H×W                  (11)

    where Expand(·) denotes spatial broadcasting and Cseg is the number of
channels in the segmentation feature. This expansion acts as a coarse spatial
attention mechanism, aligning global category-level activations with the local
receptive ﬁelds of segmentation.
                                                                           exp
Step 3:Semantic Feature Reweighting: Finally, the class-aware mask Mcls
is element-wise multiplied with the original segmentation feature map:
                                             exp
                              Fout = Fseg ⊗ Mcls                            (12)

where ⊗ denotes element-wise multiplication, and Fout is the reweighted seg-
mentation feature. This reweighting process suppresses features unrelated to
predicted classes and enhances the activation of semantically relevant regions,
improving the model’s focus and robustness, especially in ambiguous or noisy
scenes.
    This mechanism eﬀectively injects high-level semantic cues into the segmen-
tation branch, enabling the model to better focus on category-relevant regions.


4.4   Classification Decoder

The design of this image classiﬁer consists of two main modules: the ASPP
module (Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling) and the Recognition Decoder. These
two modules together form an eﬃcient framework for multi-scale context feature
extraction and classiﬁcation. An overview of the network architecture is pre-
sented in Fig. 6, which illustrates the ﬂow of data through the key components
of the model.
    Traditional convolutional layers acquire image information through local
receptive ﬁelds. However, when processing large objects or distant contextual
information, the receptive ﬁeld may be insuﬃcient. The ASPP module addresses
this limitation by utilizing dilated convolutions with varying dilation rates
to extract contextual features from diﬀerent scales. This approach eﬀectively
expands the receptive ﬁeld, enabling the model to capture richer global infor-
mation without signiﬁcantly increasing computational cost. By extracting both
local features and broader contextual information, the ASPP module enhances
the model’s discriminative power.
    The primary function of the Recognition Decoder is to process the multi-scale
contextual features extracted by the ASPP module and ultimately produce the
classiﬁcation output.
340        J. Luo et al.

                                    1x1 Conv
                                    Dilation=1

                                    3x3 Conv
                                    Dilation=6
                    1x1 Conv                     1x1 Conv   MaxPooling   Linear   [0.9,0.1]
                                    3x3 Conv
  512
                                   Dilation=12

                                    3x3 Conv
                                   Dilation=18




Fig. 6. Overview of the Image Classiﬁcation Architecture. The input features ﬁrst
pass through a 1x1 convolution to reduce the number of channels to 256. Then, four
parallel dilated convolution layers with diﬀerent dilation rates (1, 6, 12, and 18) are
applied to capture multi-scale contextual information. The outputs of these layers are
concatenated and passed through another 1x1 convolution for feature fusion. Afterward,
global average pooling is applied to reduce the spatial dimensions, and the features are
ﬂattened into a 1D vector. Finally, a linear layer outputs a classiﬁcation probability in
the range of [0, 1].


   To provide a clearer understanding of the internal mechanisms of this classi-
ﬁcation decoder, the main implementation steps are detailed as follows:
Step 1:Channel Reduction Preprocessing: A 1×1 convolution is applied
to reduce the number of channels (256), followed by batch normalization and
ReLU activation:

                           Freduced = ReLU(BN(Conv1 × 1(Fseg )))                       (13)

    where Fseg ∈ RB×Csig ×H×W is the input feature map with 512 channels,and
Freduced ∈ RB×Cout ×H×W is the output feature map after channel reduction, typ-
ically with Cout = 256.
Step 2: Multi-scale Context Extraction: The reduced feature map Freduced
is fed into the Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module, where four
parallel convolutions extract context at diﬀerent scales:

                           F1 = ReLU(BN(Conv1×1 (Freduced )))                          (14)
                           F2 = ReLU(BN(Conv3×3,r=6 (Freduced )))                      (15)
                           F3 = ReLU(BN(Conv3×3,r=12 (Freduced )))                     (16)
                           F4 = ReLU(BN(Conv3×3,r=18 (Freduced )))                     (17)

        These outputs are concatenated and projected back to 256 channels:

                 FASPP = ReLU(BN(Conv1×1 (Concat[F1 , F2 , F3 , F4 ])))                (18)

   where FASPP ∈ RB×CASPP ×H×W and CASPP = 256.
Step 3:Global Feature Aggregation: The fused multiscale feature FASPP
undergoes global average pooling, reducing its spatial dimensions to 1×1, result-
ing in a single feature vector for each sample. This operation aggregates global
spatial context and produces a compact representation used for classiﬁcation.

                               Fgap = GAP (FASPP ) ∈ RB×256×1×1                        (19)
       WSRNet: A Multi-task Learning Model for Satellite Image Recognition               341

Step 4: Classification Head and Prediction: Finally, the global feature
Fgap is ﬂattened and passed through a fully connected (FC) layer to produce the
prediction score for each class.
                          Pcls = F C(F latten(Fgap )) ∈ RB×Ncls                          (20)
    where Pcls is the classiﬁcation score for each class.
    The proposed recognition decoder leverages channel reduction and an ASPP
module to eﬀectively integrate multi-scale contextual features, thereby enhancing
the model’s ability to detect ﬁre occurrences of varying sizes in satellite imagery.
The use of global average pooling and a classiﬁcation head further enables eﬃ-
cient aggregation of discriminative features, leading to robust and accurate ﬁre
detection in complex remote sensing scenarios.

4.5    Training and Inference
Training Stage. We want to optimize the loss functions for both tasks at the
same time so that the model can learn features of both classiﬁcation and seg-
mentation together. Since the model handles two tasks, we have created separate
loss functions for each one.
    For the classiﬁcation task, we use the Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss to
measure the diﬀerence between the model’s predicted probability and the ground
truth labels. The BCE loss function is deﬁned as follows:
                     N
                 1
      Lclass =         −yiclass · log(ŷiclass ) − (1 − yiclass ) · log(1 − ŷiclass )   (21)
                 N i=1

   where yiclass represents the true classiﬁcation label of the i-th sample, ŷiclass
denotes the classiﬁcation prediction result of the model, and N is the total num-
ber of training samples.
   For the segmentation task, we use the Cross-Entropy Loss to measure the
diﬀerence between the model’s predicted segmentation results and the ground
truth segmentation masks. The Cross-Entropy Loss function is deﬁned as follows:
                                             N    C
                                         1
                             Lseg = −                         seg
                                                  y seg log(ŷi,c )                      (22)
                                         N i=1 c=1 i,c
           seg
where yi,c     represents the ground truth label of the i-th sample for the c-th
        seg
class,ŷi,c denotes the predicted probability of the c-th class by the model, and
C is the total number of classes.
    To jointly optimize the classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks, we weight the
loss function of the classiﬁcation task and then sum it with the segmentation
task’s loss to obtain the ﬁnal multi-task loss function:
                                  Ltotal = Lseg + λ · Lclass                             (23)
where λ represents the weight of the classiﬁcation task.
Inference Stage. We input the organized test set data into the model, and the
corresponding classiﬁcation and segmentation results to obtain.

5     Experiments
Dataset. We use the WildﬁreForest-S2 dataset to evaluate our model. All of
which contain 1,714 images in total. These are split into 1,376 training images
and 338 test images. In both the training and test sets, half of the images show
ﬁre events, and the other half do not. This keeps the dataset balanced for fair
evaluation.
Evaluation Metrics. In order to evaluate the performance of our model, we
have selected the following core indicators.
    For the segmentation task, we used mean Intersection over Union (mIoU)
that gives a clear idea of how accurate the segmentation is [25]. To check how
good the model is at ﬁnding target areas, we added Recall (Rec) and the F1-
score [26]. These help measure the model’s ability to detect what matters. We
also included the Kappa coeﬃcient to make sure the evaluation is fair, especially
when some classes are much rarer than others. These metrics together give a full
picture of the performance of the model.
    For the classiﬁcation task, we added the Area Under the Curve (AUC) to see
how well the model can tell diﬀerent categories apart [27]. We also used other
common metrics like accuracy, sensitivity, speciﬁcity, F1-score, and Matthews
Correlation Coeﬃcient (MCC) [28]. These help us understand how precise, bal-
anced, and reliable the model’s predictions are.
Experimental Setup. To ensure the fairness and reproducibility of our exper-
iments, we describe the detailed experimental setup and parameter choices.
Table 1 shows the hardware conﬁguration and key parameters used in the exper-
iment.

performance, not only surpassing other methods in segmentation accuracy but
also excelling in other metrics. This enables WSRNet to have high stability and
reliability when handling wildﬁre segmentation tasks.

eﬀectiveness of the HAFE module for wildﬁre detection in satellite remote sens-
ing scenarios. These analyses not only demonstrate the accuracy of our approach
in wildﬁre area identiﬁcation but also elucidate the mechanisms by which the
model enhances key features and suppresses redundant information.

remote sensing scenarios.

5.3    Ablation Study

To validate the eﬀectiveness of each module in WSRNet, we conducted ablation
experiments by removing key modules and evaluated the performance on both
classiﬁcation and segmentation tasks.

• WSRNet w/o HAFE: We removed the HAFE module, directly passing
  the output of the previous layer to the next layer in the encoder.
• WSRNet w/o Classifier: We removed the Classiﬁer Encoder and eliminated
  the classiﬁcation loss from the loss function.
• WSRNet w/o CGFR: We removed the CGFR module and directly decode
  the raw segmentation features.

cation tasks, playing a crucial role in improving overall model accuracy. More-
over, the guidance provided by the CGFR module also eﬀectively improves
the segmentation accuracy. It is evident that the multi-task learning approach
improves the accuracy of both tasks simultaneously through joint loss optimiza-
tion and feature-guided mechanisms. When all components are included, WSR-
Net achieves its optimal performance.


6     Conclusion
We constructed a wildﬁre dataset covering Australia called WildﬁreForest-S2 and
we proposes a new method called WSRNet, which based on multi-task learning
for wildﬁre identiﬁcation and segmentation tasks in satellite images. WSRNet
achieves high-precision wildﬁre detection and accurate ﬁre area segmentation by
sharing feature extraction networks and task-speciﬁc decoders, while optimiz-
ing identitication tasks and segmentation tasks. Experimental results show that
WSRNet is supper to existing methods in indicators such as mIoU and F1-score
for the segmentation task and achieves exceptionally high accuracy in the classi-
ﬁcation task. In the future, we plan to expand the geographical coverage of the
dataset and optimize the computing eﬃciency of the model support real-time
use.

        SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought
                  Guardrail Model

    Yuxuan Lin1,2 , Shi Liu1,2 , Dongqin Liu2 , Wei Mi2 , and Xuehai Tang2(B)
    1
      School of Cyberspace Security, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences,
                                   Beijing, China
2
  Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
          {linyuxuan,liushi,liudongqin,miwei,tangxuehai}@iie.ac.cn

        Abstract. The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) in intel-
        ligent applications has introduced critical safety challenges concerning
        input and output content moderation. Current guardrail solutions suﬀer
        from inadequate performance in small-parameter models while exces-
        sive resource overhead in large-parameter models, limited capacity for
        ﬁne-grained rule customization, and improvable out-of-distribution gen-
        eralization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SCoT Guard,
        a novel reasoning-based guardrail framework that dynamically acquires
        ﬁne-grained judgment criteria through contextual learning from exam-
        ples. Our approach leverages a meticulously curated training dataset of
        40,000 high-quality instances generated using DeepSeek-R1, incorporat-
        ing comprehensive safety detection reasoning chains and rule-learning
        mechanisms. We implement LoRA ﬁne-tuning on the Qwen2.5-1.5B-
        Instruct model to achieve optimal performance. At inference time, SCoT
        Guard utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to identify simi-
        lar examples, extracts their underlying judgment principles, and applies
        these learned rules to evaluate the new sample, thereby accommodat-
        ing evolving safety requirements. Comprehensive experimental evalu-
        ation demonstrates that SCoT Guard substantially surpasses 9 base-
        line methods across 6 benchmarks (e.g., OpenAI Moderation, Toxic-
        Chat, BeaverTails). These results conﬁrm the eﬀectiveness of integrat-
        ing chain-of-thought reasoning with RAG in enhancing the performance,
        interpretability, and adaptability of guardrail models. With its compact
        1.5B parameter architecture, SCoT Guard enables direct deployment on
        resource-limited IoT edge devices, facilitating real-time local inference
        while eliminating cloud dependency and ensuring data privacy. Both the
        training dataset and model weights will be open-sourced.


        Keywords: Large Language Models · Safety Guardrails ·
        Chain-of-Thought · Retrieval-Augmented Generation · Edge AI ·
        Fine-tuning


1    Introduction
With the rapid iteration of artiﬁcial intelligence technology, large language mod-
els (LLMs) [1–10] have achieved revolutionary breakthroughs in diverse scenarios
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 349–363, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_19
350     Y. Lin et al.

such as chatbots, search engines, recommendation systems, and agent interac-
tions, owing to their exceptional natural language processing capabilities. As
the core driving engine of next-generation intelligent systems, while unleashing
productivity, LLMs also expose signiﬁcant safety risks [11–16]: privacy leakage
from training data, harmful content generation triggered by malicious instruc-
tions, and automation support for illegal activities have become key bottlenecks
constraining their large-scale application. Therefore, reliable safety guardrails
are needed to automatically detect safety risks in the inputs and outputs of
large language models, thereby enhancing the safety and reliability of various
intelligent systems.
    Existing LLM-based safety guardrails primarily adopt two approaches. The
ﬁrst relies on powerful general-purpose LLMs [1–10], utilizing prompt engineer-
ing to leverage the models’ excellent generalization capabilities and instruction-
following abilities for text safety detection. The second involves collecting content
moderation data across various categories, constructing supervised ﬁne-tuning
datasets to post-train LLMs into specialized guardrail models, such as LLaMA
Guard [3,17], ShieldGemma [18], Aegis Guard [19,20] and ShieldLM [21]. How-
ever, existing LLM-based safety guardrails still face the following limitations:
(1) Existing guardrail models have large parameter sizes (typically .≥ 7B) and
incur substantial resource overhead, making them diﬃcult to deploy on resource-
constrained edge devices (e.g., IoT terminals), whereas small-parameter models
often suﬀer from inadequate detection performance. Dependence on cloud ser-
vices not only introduces network latency and privacy risks but also increases
system operational costs. IoT scenarios urgently require lightweight, low-power
and high-performance localized safety detection solutions; (2) They typically
rely on zero-shot descriptions of detection rules to support safety standards
for speciﬁc scenarios. In practical applications, however, safety standards often
change dynamically depending on speciﬁc contexts, making it diﬃcult to debug
the model to formulate eﬀective and universally applicable detection rules. (3)
Their detection performance (F1 score) on out-of-distribution datasets is still
improvable.
    To address these challenges, we propose SCoT Guard, a small reasoning
guardrail model that supports analyzing and learning safety judgment rules from
contextual examples, enabling more ﬁne-grained and customized safety detec-
tion. In real-world detection scenarios, the criteria and thresholds for harmfulness
often vary signiﬁcantly across diﬀerent content instances. Simply adding batch
zero-shot descriptions in prompts struggles to achieve ﬁne-grained, instance-
speciﬁc customized detection. Our model addresses this by analyzing and learn-
ing safety judgment rules from few-shot examples during the reasoning process.
    We utilize the current SOTA reasoning LLM, DeepSeek-R1 [6], to synthesize
chain-of-thought (CoT) data for text safety detection scenarios. This includes
synthesizing CoT data speciﬁcally designed for learning safety judgment rules
from contextual examples. This constructs a training dataset with explicit rea-
soning processes, enabling the model to train the capability to reference similar
examples during analysis. During inference detection, the Retrieval-Augmented
                  SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model        351




           Fig. 1. Limitations of Existing LLM-based Safety Guardrails.


Generation (RAG) component retrieves the top-.n most similar examples from
an exemplar knowledge base. When analyzing a new sample, SCoT Guard aligns
its judgment criteria with these similar examples, achieving customized detec-
tion tailored to each speciﬁc input and supporting more ﬂexible dynamic safety
standards. Trained with only 40k high-quality examples via LoRA ﬁne-tuning
based on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, SCoT Guard achieves excellent performance
on multiple safety benchmark datasets at minimal training and inference costs.
Its F1 score surpasses current mainstream LLM guardrail models (e.g., LLaMA
Guard, ShieldGemma, ShieldLM). We will open-source our high-quality training
dataset and model weights to support future research and the advancement of
LLM safety.


2   Related Work
LLM Safety. Large language models have demonstrated exceptional perfor-
mance across various domains, yet their potential safety risks are increasing sig-
niﬁcantly and cannot be overlooked. To achieve safety alignment for LLMs [22],
researchers employ strategies such as ﬁltering toxic training data [23] and imple-
menting post-training techniques including SFT [24], RLHF [25], and DPO [26].
These methods aim to make model outputs more compliant with ethical and
legal standards. However, such alignment training inevitably leads to model
performance degradation. To address this trade-oﬀ, external guardrail models
play a crucial role in balancing model performance and safety. Moreover, exter-
nal guardrail models better support ﬂexible and continuously evolving safety
standards.
Guardrail Model. LLM-based guardrail models primarily adopt two technical
approaches. The ﬁrst leverages powerful general-purpose LLMs (e.g., GPT [1],
DeepSeek [5,6], Qwen [7,8,10]) with strong generalization and instruction-
following capabilities, utilizing carefully designed prompt engineering to function
as text safety detectors. The second involves constructing ﬁne-tuning datasets
352     Y. Lin et al.

to train specialized guardrail models for text safety detection. Notable open-
source implementations include the following: LLaMA Guard [3,17] and Aegis
Guard [19,20] analyze samples based on predeﬁned safety guidelines, outputting
the unsafe category to which each unsafe sample belongs; ShieldGemma [18],
which enhances robustness through extensive adversarial dataset synthesis; and
ShieldLM [21], which supports customizable zero-shot judgment rules while pro-
viding explanations for decisions.
Reasoning LLM. Recent research has revealed that reasoning-enhanced LLMs
exhibit superior performance in domains such as mathematics and coding,
where extended chains-of-thought (CoT) signiﬁcantly improve out-of-domain
generalization. Initially, researchers guided LLMs to think step-by-step via
prompt engineering [27,28]. Subsequently, researchers explored diﬀerent modes
of thinking such as self-criticism, reﬂection, and planning [29–34], which further
improved the model’s performance. Contemporary reasoning LLMs–represented
by models like OpenAI-o1 [35], DeepSeek-R1 [6], QwQ [9], and Kimi k1.5 [36]–
internalize reasoning capabilities, enabling spontaneous deliberation, reﬂection,
and problem-solving attempts before generating answers. These models achieve
remarkable results across diverse ﬁelds, motivating our exploration of incorpo-
rating reasoning mechanisms into small-parameter LLMs to enhance their per-
formance in text safety detection.


3     Methodology
This section outlines the methodology of SCoT Guard, a reasoning model that
dynamically learns safety judgment rules from contextual examples during infer-
ence and applies them to the current sample. Leveraging DeepSeek-R1, we
synthesize high-quality Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data for text safety detection,
achieving exceptional safety detection performance on small models with mini-
mal training and inference costs.


3.1   Problem Deﬁnition

SCoT Guard formalizes text safety detection as a dynamically constrained deci-
sion problem. Safety standards for harmful content categories (e.g., hate speech,
illegal activities) vary across samples and dynamically evolve with temporal
shifts, regional diﬀerences, and cultural changes. Moreover, identical content may
receive diﬀerent safety labels under varying standards–observed both in open-
source datasets (contradictory annotations across datasets) and real-world appli-
cations (diﬀerences in safety criteria across countries and cultures). For instance,
satirical religious cartoons may be protected expression in secular countries like
France but deemed blasphemous in certain Islamic communities. This inherent
variability motivates our dynamic constraint approach. When processing a sam-
                     SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model               353

3.2    Training Pro cess
Figure 2 illustrates SCoT Guard’s end-to-end training and inference pipeline.
The training process comprises three stages:
Stage One: We use BeaverTailsTrain [37] as the original dataset and employ
DeepSeek-R1 to analyze each sample for generating chain-of-thought (CoT)
data. The temperature is set to 1.2, and each sample is analyzed ﬁve times
to produce multiple CoT candidates. CoTs with incorrect predicted labels are
ﬁltered out, and the remaining ones are evaluated automatically by DeepSeek-
R1 on four dimensions: accuracy, logical rigor, clarity, and completeness. The
top-performing CoTs are then selected, resulting in a high-quality dataset for
text safety analysis.
Stage Two: For each original sample, we use the TF-IDF algorithm (concatenat-
ing .Pj and .Rj ) to retrieve its three most similar examples. Using DeepSeek-R1
354     Y. Lin et al.




                     Fig. 2. Overall Architecture of SCoT Guard.


with a temperature of 1.2, we again analyze each sample ﬁve times, following the
same ﬁltering and evaluation procedure as in Stage One. At this stage, however,
the CoTs ﬁrst verify whether the retrieved examples truly correspond to similar
scenarios as the current sample. For those conﬁrmed to be similar, the CoTs ana-
lyze and learn their safety judgment criteria, then apply these learned rules to
evaluate the current sample. These processes produce two subsets: CoTs without
similar examples (.N1 = 21458) and CoTs with similar examples (.N2 = 22946).
From each subset, we sample 20k examples while maintaining a 1:1 ratio of
safe to unsafe labels, resulting in a 40k high-quality training set. This dataset
enables the model to learn to ﬂexibly switch between independent analysis and
example-guided reasoning, while enhancing its ability to analyze and learn from
contextual examples.
 Stage Three: We perform supervised ﬁne-tuning (SFT) on Qwen2.5-1.5B-
 Instruct using the constructed dataset. SFT adapts pretrained models to down-
 stream tasks using labeled data [25]. Given .S, .P , .R, and similar examples
.E = {e1 , e2 , e3 }, guardrail .G generates CoT (.T ) and label (.L). The loss function
 is:
                       .Lscot = −     E     log PG (T, L | S, P, R, E)               (2)
                               (P,R,E)∼D

By optimizing the model parameters .G to minimize the objective loss function,
the ﬁnal SCoT Guard model is obtained. During training, LoRA (Low-Rank
Adaptation) [38] was adopted to further reduce training overhead. LoRA achieves
this by freezing the original model weights .W and training only their incremental
updates .ΔW . Through low-rank matrix decomposition .ΔW = BA, it exclusively
                  SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model         355

trains the low-rank parameters .A and .B, signiﬁcantly reducing GPU memory
consumption and computational load.

3.3   Inference Detection
The ﬁne-tuned SCoT Guard model takes the sample to be detected and its sim-
ilar examples as input, engaging in reasoning before outputting the ﬁnal classiﬁ-
cation label. During this reasoning process, the model ﬁrst veriﬁes the similarity
between the given examples and the current sample. It then learns safety judg-
ment rules and standards from the conﬁrmed similar examples, prioritizing the
application of these learned rules and standards to evaluate the target sample.
To detect the safety of user input instead of LLM responses, the prompt tem-
plate shown in Fig. 3 can be modiﬁed by replacing the user input with “Just say
something.” while positioning the target user input in the LLM response slot,
enabling text safety detection for user inputs (Fig. 3).

    The above workﬂow applies to scenarios where few-shot examples are pro-
vided for the model to learn safety detection rules and standards. When zero-
shot descriptions are needed to guide rule learning, prompt engineering can be
employed to make the LLM generate one or more concrete examples, thereby
maintaining compatibility with zero-shot scenarios. Compared to using zero-shot
descriptions alone, this approach supports more ﬁne-grained safety detection
rules and standards. Furthermore, the reasoning process .T of SCoT Guard pro-
vides interpretability for text safety detection tasks, ensuring traceable decision-
making. This reasoning mechanism also signiﬁcantly enhances the detection per-
formance of the 1.5B-parameter model deployable on edge devices.


4     Experiments

To comprehensively evaluate SCoT Guard, we conducted comparative experi-
ments against 9 baseline models across 6 benchmarks. Our key ﬁndings show
that SCoT Guard, despite having only 1.5B parameters, surpasses models that
are 5 times larger or more in safety detection performance, demonstrating excep-
tional capability. Furthermore, incorporating similar examples via retrieval for
analysis and learning consistently enhances all detection metrics.


4.1   Experimental Setup

Training Environment: All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA
V100 GPU with 32 GB VRAM and can be reproduced on consumer-grade GPUs
(e.g., 3090/4090 or lower). During inference, SCoT Guard requires only 3 GB
VRAM in ﬂoat16 mode, enabling deployment on common edge devices (e.g.,
Raspberry Pi with external NPU modules), meeting the stringent power and
computational constraints of IoT scenarios. We performed supervised ﬁne-tuning
on the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct using the LLaMA Factory framework with LoRA
to reduce resource consumption. The training dataset contains 40k samples with
a 1:1 ratio of safe/unsafe labels and a 1:1 ratio of data without/with similar
examples. Training hyperparameters: batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation=8
(eﬀective batch_size=16), learning_rate=1e-4, epochs=5, max_gradient_norm
=1.0,                        compute_type=bf16,                          trun-
cation_length=32768; LoRA conﬁguration: rank =16, alpha=64, dropout=0.1,
target_layers=all; checkpoint saved every 2500 steps, optimizer=adamw, learn-
ing_rate_scheduler=cosine, warmup_steps=0.All experimental parameter set-
tings are based on the empirical settings commonly used in most research.
Inference Setting: For prompt harmfulness detection tasks, we set the user
input A to “Just say something.” in the prompt template, as illustrated in
Fig. 2, and position the target prompt in the LLM response slot. SCoT Guard
                                                               ∗
leverages RAG to retrieve the top .n most similar examples .Ej,n   with similarity
scores exceeding threshold .τ (set to 0.17 in experiments, empirically determined
through manual inspection of 100 samples where scores above this threshold
                  SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model          357

consistently indicated referentially similar scenarios) for dynamic safety detec-
tion. The retrieval process uses TF-IDF algorithms, concatenating user input and
LLM response for retrieval. We intentionally choose this basic retrieval method to
validate the fundamental feasibility of our approach. In practice, more advanced
retrieval models (e.g., BERT-based) can be employed during training data con-
struction and inference to further enhance performance. This setup validates
the performance improvement from learning safety judgment rules from similar
examples.
Benchmarks: We evaluated safety detection performance on six guardrail
benchmarks:
– Prompt Harmfulness Detection: OpenAI Moderation [39], ToxicChat [40]
– Response Harmfulness Detection: BeaverTails [37], SafeRLHF [41], Wild-
  Guard [42], HarmBench [43]
Baselines: We compared SCoT Guard against 9 baselines:
– Guardrail Models: OpenAI Moderation [39], Aegis Guard Defensive 7B, Aegis
  Guard Permissive 7B [19,20], LLaMA Guard 3 8B [3], ShieldGemma 2B,
  ShieldGemma 9B [18], ShieldLM 14B [21]
– General LLMs: QwQ-32B [9], DeepSeek-R1 [6], GPT-4 [1]

Evaluation Metrics: We report three core metrics: Accuracy, F1-unsafe (con-
sidering unsafe as positive class), and F1-safe (considering safe as positive class).

4.2   Experimental Results
We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of SCoT Guard against 9 baseline
models across 6 guardrail benchmark datasets. The experimental results are
presented in Table 1. The analysis reveals two key conclusions: (1) Superior
Detection Performance: For both prompt harmfulness detection and response
harmfulness detection, SCoT Guard demonstrates signiﬁcantly superior perfor-
mance compared to baseline models. Despite its compact 1.5B parameter size, it
achieves results where a small model outperforms larger ones, matching or even
surpassing models with 5.× or more parameters. (2) Unique Value of Long
Chain-of-Thought: By explicitly generating safety detection reasoning chains,
SCoT Guard provides interpretability for model outputs, which enhances user
conﬁdence in safety decisions and enables developers to identify model weak-
nesses for targeted optimization.
Prompt Harmfulness Detection: Without RAG, SCoT Guard (1.5B) already
shows competitive performance (achieving 72.51% F1 on the OpenAI Modera-
tion dataset). When combined with RAG, it reaches 73.11% F1 on OpenAI
Moderation and 75.89% on ToxicChat, signiﬁcantly outperforming specialized
guardrail models. For example, on ToxicChat, it exceeds LLaMA Guard 3 (8B)
by 22.77% and surpasses general models like GPT-4 by 7.77%. Notably, with
only 1.5B parameters (1/5 to 1/21 the size of comparison models), SCoT Guard

Response Harmfulness Detection: SCoT Guard combined with the RAG
mechanism demonstrates remarkable performance advantages. Experimental
data shows the model achieves 86.15% F1 on BeaverTails and an exceptional
92.30% on SafeRLHF. Compared to guardrail model ShieldGemma (9B), SCoT
Guard achieves substantial performance improvements across multiple datasets:
F1 scores increase by 22.54%, 28.51%, 28.56%, and 26.69% on BeaverTails,
SafeRLHF, WildGuard, and HarmBench respectively. Remarkably, on Beaver-
Tails, SCoT Guard’s F1 surpasses large general models QwQ (32B), DeepSeek-
R1 (671B), and GPT-4 by 4.52%, 6.56%, and 5.28% respectively. These results
fully validate the eﬀectiveness of small-parameter models (1.5B) achieving per-
formance breakthroughs through high-quality safety detection reasoning chains,
highlighting the advantage of combining RAG for customized safety detection
capability.
Interpretability and Engineering Value: The advantages of SCoT Guard
extend beyond numerical performance improvements. Its unique long chain-of-
thought reasoning mechanism provides crucial interpretability for safety detec-
tion processes. By explicitly outputting reasoning steps including example com-
parative analysis and safety rule learning, it not only increases user conﬁdence
in detection results but also facilitates developers’ observation of the model’s
decision logic in speciﬁc cases, aiding in summarizing root causes of false pos-
itives or false negatives. This traceability provides clear direction for subse-
quent iterative optimization–by analyzing logical ﬂaws or knowledge gaps in
                               SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model                                                                             359

the reasoning chains, targeted improvements can be made, forming a closed-
loop “detection-analysis-correction” optimization process. This fundamentally
enhances the robustness and reliability of safety detection systems, address-
ing the debugging challenges inherent in traditional black-box models in safety
detection scenarios.


4.3          Ablation Study

To clarify the speciﬁc contributions of the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reason-
ing mechanism and the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) component to
SCoT Guard’s performance, we conducted an ablation study. The results are
presented in Table 2 and Table 3. We evaluated four conﬁgurations across six
guardrail benchmark datasets. The study used a controlled variable approach to
assess the individual contribution of each core module, validating the eﬀective-
ness of key components in the model design.
    The conﬁgurations were as follows: (1) “Only Label” serves as the baseline,
where the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning mechanism was removed during
training, and the model was trained to output only the predicted safety labels.
(2) “CoT + Label” introduced the CoT reasoning mechanism in both train-
ing and inference stages, but did not use the Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG) component to retrieve similar examples. (3) “CoT + Label + RAG”
extended conﬁguration (2) by incorporating the RAG mechanism during infer-
ence to retrieve similar examples as references for reasoning; however, the model
was not explicitly optimized during training to learn from these retrieved exam-
ples. (4) “Full SCoT Guard” built upon conﬁguration (3) by further optimizing
the model during training to eﬀectively leverage retrieved examples for detect-
ing. All conﬁgurations were based on the same 1.5B-parameter model (Qwen2.5-
1.5B-Instruct) and used an identical training setup.

360       Y. Lin et al.

      Three core conclusions emerge from the results in Table 2 and Table 3:
(I) Eﬀectiveness of CoT Reasoning: The “Only Label” baseline exhibited sig-
    niﬁcant performance degradation across all datasets compared to models with
    CoT reasoning. For instance, comparing “Only Label" to “CoT + Label”, the
    average accuracy improved from 79.43% to 84.42% for prompt harmfulness
    detection, and from 82.99% to 86.38% for response harmfulness detection.
    This indicates that removing the reasoning process strips the model of its
    ability to perform ﬁne-grained analysis of safety detection tasks, validating
    the critical role of CoT in enhancing detection eﬀectiveness and interpretabil-
    ity.
(II) Impact of RAG Optimization: The results reveal that simply adding
    RAG without proper training optimization is insuﬃcient. The “CoT + Label
    + RAG” conﬁguration showed inconsistent performance compared to “CoT
    + Label” alone, with prompt harmfulness detection average accuracy declin-
    ing from 84.42% to 83.88%, and some metrics even performing worse than
    the CoT-only approach. This occurs because during training, the model was
    not optimized to eﬀectively learn from retrieved similar examples. In con-
    trast, “Full SCoT Guard” incorporates training optimization that enables the
    model to leverage retrieved examples eﬀectively, resulting in superior perfor-
    mance across all metrics. This demonstrates that RAG’s eﬀectiveness depends
    critically on training the model to properly utilize retrieved contextual infor-
    mation.
(III) Robust Cross-Task Performance: The Full SCoT Guard consistently
    achieved the best performance across both prompt and response harmfulness
    detection tasks, demonstrating remarkable robustness. The method showed
    particularly notable improvements in F1-unsafe scores, with the average met-
    ric improving from 61.76% (Only Label) to 74.50% (Full SCoT Guard) for
    prompt harmfulness detection. Compared to “CoT + Label + RAG", the full
    model improved average accuracy by 4.59% for prompt harmfulness detection
    and 2.45% for response harmfulness detection, indicating superior capability
    in identifying harmful content across diverse safety detection scenarios.
    Further analysis reveals that the CoT mechanism makes the model’s deci-
sion process observable, while RAG contextualizes safety rules through concrete
examples, reducing dependency on the training data distribution. Their combi-
nation not only enables the model to achieve “small defeating large” but also
establishes an interpretable and debuggable safety detection framework. This
provides foundational support for rule iteration and risk assessment in practical
deployments, enabling LLM safety protection on IoT endpoints at computational
costs aﬀordable for edge devices.


5      Conclusion
We present SCoT Guard, a reasoning guardrail model that learns safety judg-
ment rules from in-context examples and enables ﬁne-grained, customizable
                  SCoT Guard: A Safety Chain of Thought Guardrail Model            361

safety detection. Our core contributions are: (1) The construction of a 40k
high-quality chain-of-thought dataset for text safety detection; (2) Designing
a retrieval-based similar example learning mechanism; (3) The achievement
of high-performance safety detection on a 1.5B-parameter model, delivering a
deployable guardrail for IoT edge devices, reducing reliance on cloud computing,
and improving response speed and privacy. Experimental results demonstrate
that SCoT Guard comprehensively outperforms mainstream baseline models
(including LLaMA Guard 3-8B, ShieldGemma-9B, ShieldLM-14B and so on)
across six safety benchmarks such as OpenAI Moderation, ToxicChat and so
on. With RAG, it reaches an F1 of 75.89% on ToxicChat, signiﬁcantly outper-
forming LLaMA Guard 3’s 53.12%. Moreover, the explicit safety-detection rea-
soning chains oﬀer interpretable rationales, while the RAG mechanism supports
dynamic safety-standard modeling and real-time policy updates; the model can
improve simply by reﬁning the example library, without requiring costly retrain-
ing. To advance AI safety research, we will open-source the model weights and
training datasets described in this paper at https://github.com/JosueLin/SCoT-
Guard.


6   Ethical Considerations

This research aims to enhance the safety of large language models (LLMs) by
training a practical guardrail. Our goal is to ensure model outputs are better
aligned with human values. The datasets used contain potentially harmful con-
tent, which may be disturbing. These materials are used strictly for academic
research purposes.
