       Abstract. To handle the high volume of requests, large-scale services
       are comprised of thousands of instances deployed in clouds. These ser-
       vices utilize diverse programming languages and are distributed across
       various nodes as encapsulated containers. Given their vast scale, even
       minor performance enhancements can lead to signiﬁcant cost reductions.
       In this paper, we introduce Atys (Atys, known as the god of tracking and
       discovery, is often portrayed as a skilled hunter and scout in mythology),
       an eﬃcient proﬁling framework speciﬁcally designed to identify hotspot
       functions within large-scale distributed services. Atys presents two key
       features. First, we propose a function selective pruning (FSP) strategy to
       enhance the eﬃciency of aggregating proﬁling results. Then, we develop
       a frequency dynamic adjustment (FDA) scheme that dynamically mod-
       iﬁes sampling frequency based on service status, eﬀectively minimizing
       proﬁling cost while keeping accuracy. Cluster-scale experiments on two
       benchmarks show that the FSP strategy achieves a 6.8% reduction in
       time with a mere 0.58% mean average percentage error (MAPE) in stack
       traces aggregation. Additionally, the FDA scheme ensures that the mean
       squared error (MSE) remains on par with that at high sampling rates,
       while achieving an 87.6% reduction in cost.


       Keywords: Data center · performance proﬁling · distributed system ·
       cloud computing


1    Introduction
Large-scale online services like Google search [16] and Amazon [2] play a vital role
in our daily life. To manage massive requests, these applications rely on numer-
ous instances(or replicas). For example, a one-day trace in Meta’s production
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 367–386, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_20
368     J. Sun et al.

environment shows its microservice topology contained 18,500 active services and
over 12 million service instances. The most replicated service www has as many as
557,000 instances, as it handles the most incoming requests [20].
    Identifying and optimizing hotspot functions in large-scale cloud services can
signiﬁcantly improve resource eﬃciency. These hotspot functions account for a
signiﬁcant portion of service resource consumption. Due to their vast scale, even
minor performance enhancements can lead to substantial cost savings.
    Large-scale services markedly diﬀer from traditional monolithic applications
in hardware and software architectures, as well as deployment strategies. In the
view of hardware, these services spread across numerous distributed worker nodes
in clouds [5]. On the software side, they employ various programming languages,
encompassing both compiled and interpreted types. The rise of container technol-
ogy has also transitioned deployment methods in clouds from virtual machines
to containers [25].
    Administrators usually employ performance proﬁling tools to identify hotspot
functions. Current proﬁling tools can be divided into single-machine and
multi-machine proﬁlers, both of which face challenges in proﬁling large-scale
distributed services. Single-machine proﬁlers are often language-speciﬁc. For
instance, system-level tools like Perf [24] can only collect native symbols, prevent-
ing them from recognizing user-deﬁned functions and ﬁle names in interpreted
languages like Python. Additionally, proﬁlers such as Intel VTune [21] and gprof
[18] are not suitable for large-scale distributed environments. On the other hand,
multi-machine proﬁlers, while leveraging single-machine proﬁlers for individual
node call stack tracing, struggle with access restrictions and usability issues.
Google Wide Proﬁling (GWP) [35] is restricted to internal users, while HPC-
Toolkit [1] necessitates speciﬁc commands for application initialization, limiting
direct process attachment. Additionally, constructing multi-machine proﬁlers on
monitoring platforms, as shown by Pyroscope [33], is achievable. However, indis-
criminate use of single-machine proﬁlers in multi-instance services can lead to
considerable performance overhead.
    In this paper, we present a distributed proﬁling framework named Atys,
which leverages existing proﬁling tools to identify hotspot functions in a cost-
eﬀective and non-invasive way. Our design principle focuses on the unique char-
acteristics of large-scale microservices, typically emphasizing cost eﬃciency.
    Firstly, Atys enables hotspot function proﬁling for both compiled and inter-
preted languages within containers by utilizing specialized proﬁling tools. Sec-
ondly, acknowledging the multi-threaded nature of highly concurrent microser-
vices, Atys implements a function selective pruning (FSP) strategy that con-
solidates proﬁling results at the thread level, facilitating cost-eﬀective proﬁling.
Lastly, Atys introduces a frequency dynamic adjustment (FDA) scheme that
adaptively adjusts sampling frequency based on previous proﬁling results, sig-
niﬁcantly lowering proﬁling costs while keeping accuracy.
    To evaluate the eﬀectiveness of Atys, we conducted experiments on a cluster
consisting of 13 nodes, using typical Java and Python workloads Specjbb2015
[39] and VGG16 [38] as benchmarks. The experiment results show that:
                                     Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework       369

– The FSP strategy reduces aggregation time by 6.8% while retaining the 99th
  percentile (P99) hotspot threads, resulting in a mean absolute percentage
  error (MAPE) of just 0.58% for the top 50 hotspot functions.
– The FDA scheme, averaging a sampling rate of 3,578 Hz, yields results with a
  mean squared error (MSE) comparable to a 10,000 Hz sampling rate, at only
  12.4% of the cost.
– We demonstrate the scalability of Atys; when sampling 1,000 service
  instances concurrently, the central server’s average memory usage is merely
  175 MB, with overall CPU usage remaining below 6%.
Overall, Atys demonstrates signiﬁcant versatility, accuracy, and cost-
eﬀectiveness in a non-invasive manner within containerized and distributed envi-
ronments, meeting the requirements of modern large-scale cloud services.
   The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
– We present an eﬃcient proﬁling framework called Atys, speciﬁcally designed
  for large-scale microservices in production data centers.
– We propose an eﬃcient function selective pruning strategy along with an
  adaptive scheme for adjusting sampling frequency, signiﬁcantly reducing pro-
  ﬁling costs.
– We implement a prototype1 of Atys and evaluate its performance through a
  series of experiments.


2     Related Work
2.1    Proﬁling Paradigms
Performance proﬁling involves analyzing a program’s runtime behavior by cap-
turing its hardware or software metrics. Proﬁlers generally rely on sampling for
higher eﬃciency or code instrumentation for higher precision.

Sampling. Sampling-based proﬁling, or stack tracing, captures periodic snap-
shots of a program’s function call stacks. The last function in these traces repre-
sents the active function during sampling. As samples accumulate, the frequency
of each function’s appearance reveals its resource consumption over the observed
time window.
    Recent studies indicate that this paradigm exhibit inaccuracies [42,44]. Xu
et al. identify that the function represented in the sample may not always corre-
spond to the executed one, a phenomenon known as the skid eﬀect [42]. Similarly,
Intel’s Precise Event Based Sampling (PEBS) also suﬀers from a similar shadow
eﬀect [44].
    However, sampling incurs low CPU overhead, as it interrupts the program
only upon receiving speciﬁc signals. Furthermore, it is deemed non-invasive since
it does not necessitate modiﬁcations to the proﬁled program. Consequently, its
eﬃciency contributes to its popularity in major proﬁling tools such as Perf [24],
HPCtoolkit [36], and Intel VTune [21].
1
    The code of Atys can be accessed at: https://github.com/ottoSJTU/Atys.
370    J. Sun et al.

Code Instrumentation. Code instrumentation entails integrating supplemen-
tary code into the target program. The modiﬁed program generates performance
data during execution, which is subsequently utilized for report generation.
    This paradigm ensures accuracy by collecting metrics only when target func-
tions are active, thereby mitigating issues like the shadow eﬀect [44] and skid
eﬀect [42] identiﬁed in recent studies. However, this technique often requires ser-
vice restarts or recompilation, leading to signiﬁcant overhead. Furthermore, the
additional instructions from proﬁling code can degrade service response times
and increase resource consumption [4,9].
    Modifying source code, recompiling, and restarting services are impractical
in large-scale microservice environments. Therefore, non-invasive sampling-based
proﬁling is favored in this scenario for its minor interference on target services.


2.2   Proﬁling Tools

Current proﬁlers are categorized into two categories: single-machine proﬁlers and
multi-machine proﬁlers, with the latter typically built on the former’s founda-
tion. Single-machine proﬁlers operate on individual worker nodes to trace the
call stack of an application. However, they are insuﬃcient for proﬁling multiple
instances across distributed worker nodes. Consequently, multi-machine proﬁlers
are built by integrate single-machine proﬁlers with data links, databases, dash-
boards, and other components, to eﬀectively capture large-scale applications and
manage proﬁling metrics cohesively.


Single-Machine Proﬁlers. When analyzing application performance on a sin-
gle worder node, the Linux-based tool Perf [24] is widely utilized. However, Perf
does not support all interpreted languages. Fortunately, most of these languages
have built-in proﬁlers, such as pprof for Golang [17], cProﬁle for Python [34],
and V8 proﬁler for Node.js [27]. These proﬁlers are tailored for their speciﬁc lan-
guages, enabling precise metric collection at the line level and directly linking
metrics to their source. Although built-in proﬁlers oﬀer high compatibility, they
necessitate modiﬁcations to the source code.
    To address this issue, external proﬁlers have been created for speciﬁc pro-
gramming languages. Notably, Async-proﬁler [3] and JProﬁler [14] are widely
utilized for Java. These proﬁlers operate as Java agents, leveraging the Java
Instrumentation API [29]. They can be easily launched or attached to the Java
Virtual Machine (JVM), enabling stack trace sampling on demand. These tools
are not only user-friendly but also provide language-speciﬁc enhancements. For
instance, Async-proﬁler employs the AsyncGetCallTrace API from OpenJDK
[30] to mitigate the prevalent safepoint bias issue in Java proﬁling. In the realm
of large-scale distributed services, these agents are particularly advantageous as
they can be seamlessly integrated into individual nodes with minimal disruption
to the host system.
                                     Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework        371

Multi-machine Proﬁlers. Notably, Google’s continuous proﬁling infrastruc-
ture for data centers, known as Google-Wide Proﬁling (GWP) [35], oﬀers high
scalability and the ability to attribute metrics to source code using symbols.
However, GWP is exclusive to Google, with limited public information accessi-
ble. Other proprietary multi-machine proﬁlers include Prodﬁler [28] and Google
Cloud Proﬁler [15], both of which oﬀer limited functionality in their free versions.
    Developers can create custom monitoring systems as multi-machine proﬁlers.
For example, Performance Co-Pilot (PCP) [37] and Zabbix [45] use agents to
gather various performance metrics from individual targets. In Prometheus [32],
this is termed as exporter. Regardless of terminology,they primarily function as
single-machine proﬁlers. Pyroscope [33] employs a similar approach, utilizing the
same proﬁling backend as Atys (async-proﬁler for Java and py-spy for Python).
However, directly deploying these kernels without optimizations leads to signif-
icant performance degradation, as discussed in Sect. 5. In Atys, we implement
a similar architecture while reducing proﬁling overhead compared to traditional
multi-machine proﬁlers.


2.3   Proﬁling Optimization Techniques

In addition to engineering methods, current research focuses on enhancing pro-
ﬁling accuracy while minimizing costs, which aligns with our objectives. From
a bottom-up perspective on proﬁling tools, the levels include microarchitecture,
event, sampling strategy, and system. Existing work primarily optimizes around
these levels.
    At the microarchitecture level, current researches are dedicated to accurately
obtaining the cost consumed by each CPU instruction. Gottschall et al. demon-
strate that each static CPU microinstruction impacts overall execution time dif-
ferently, leading to the development of time-proportional Per-Instruction Cycle
Stacks (PICS) [40]. Recognizing that long-latency memory accesses in data-
intensive applications (epochs) can be overlapped with useful computations or
with one another, Carlson et al. propose an epoch-based microarchitectural anal-
ysis to model the performance eﬀects of microarchitecture interactions with these
applications [10].
    At the event level, a signiﬁcant challenge is the disparity between the limited
number of metric registers and the vast array of target events. Modern micro-
processors can capture only a few hardware metrics simultaneously, which is
inadequate given the number of target events. To address this issue, researchers
have proposed time interpolation techniques that allow for the collection of dif-
ferent metrics at various time points, subsequently interpolating the results to
facilitate reasoning across all metrics at the same time points [26].
    At the sampling strategy level, researchers focus on dynamically optimizing
the sampling process based on current results during system operation, rather
than following ﬁxed parameters beforehand. Ehlers et al. utilize time series anal-
ysis of operational response times alongside the architectural information of the
372      J. Sun et al.

target system to facilitate rule-based monitoring adaptations for sampling cov-
erage [12]. Cho et al. introduce a sampling-based code instrumentation tech-
nique known as instant proﬁling [11]. Rather than directly sampling stack traces
or instrumenting the entire execution, they periodically interleave native and
instrumented executions, eﬀectively determining which code segments to instru-
ment through this sampling strategy.
    On the other side, academic research on multi-machine proﬁlers primarily
addresses system-level challenges. In distributed proﬁling systems, comparing
timestamps across diﬀerent machines is essential, as the relative behavior of sys-
tem components is captured by timestamping signiﬁcant events on each machine
[6]. Benavides et al. introduce FreeZer, a timestamp synchronization algorithm
that eﬀectively bounds timestamp inaccuracies within a speciﬁed time interval
by analyzing the relative frequency and zero bounds between clock pairs [8]. To
tackle the timestamp synchronization issue in big data processing environments,
Cloudproﬁler has been developed to measure event durations within a streaming
framework. It leverages time-stamp counters (TSCs) during network quiescent
periods to achieve accuracy within tens of microseconds [43].
    In large-scale microservice environments, eﬃciency is paramount. Thus, Atys
distinguishes itself by optimizing the sampling strategy to attain high eﬃciency
while maintaining an acceptable level of accuracy.


3     Design of Atys
3.1     System Overview
Overall Architecture. The architecture of Atys is depicted in Fig. 1, consist-
ing of three key components. 1) Local Proﬁler: Sampling and processing stack
traces from the target microservice, subsequently exposing metrics that indicate
hotspot functions to the Prometheus server. 2) Controller: Receiving user com-
mands and manages local proﬁlers. 3) Prometheus Server2 : Pulling metrics
exposed by local proﬁlers and provides services for data storage, analysis, and
visualization.
    The design principle of Atys is to adapt to the distributed architecture
and varied workloads of large-scale microservices. This entails deploying local
proﬁlers equipped with multiple proﬁling kernels on each worker node while
establishing central nodes for uniﬁed control and data processing. This design
presents two key advantages. First, the workload of Atys is mainly concentrated
on the Prometheus server side. By ensuring that local proﬁlers utilize minimal
CPU time, this design reduces interference with the target microservices. Second,
the functionalities of various components are loosely coupled, which improves the
system’s maintainability and scalability.


2
    Prometheus [32] is an open-source monitoring system that has gained signiﬁcant
    traction in monitoring large-scale distributed systems. In Atys, the persistent data
    storage and data transmission link are built on Prometheus.
                                    Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework      373




                        Fig. 1. The architecture of Atys.


3.2   Local Proﬁler

A local proﬁler primarily identiﬁes hotspot functions on individual worker nodes.
It consists of two components: proﬁling kernels and the agent.


Proﬁling Kernels. Atys provides eﬃcient and non-invasive proﬁling across
various programming languages in containerized environments. It employs spe-
cialized profiling kernels on worker nodes to execute stack tracing without
altering or disrupting the target service. These kernels leverage the hardware
Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU) to gather runtime stack traces triggered
by speciﬁc events.
    Each stack trace records the sequence of function calls leading up to the
sampling point. For example, in a trace such as F unc1 → F unc2 → F unc3,
Func3 represents the currently executing function, called by Func2, which was
in turn called by Func1. Identical stack traces are counted to indicate their
frequency of occurrence.
    The selected proﬁling kernels for Atys must adhere to speciﬁc criteria. They
should not necessitate program modiﬁcations or restarts, should be sampling-
based, and must oﬀer comprehensive support for the target language. In line with
these requirements, async-proﬁler [3] is chosen for Java, py-spy [7] for Python,
and Perf [24] for compiled languages.


Agent. The agent acts as a mediator connecting three core components of the
system. It initially responds to the controller’s instructions by automatically
activating the appropriate kernels with dynamic frequencies. Subsequently, it
processes the raw stack traces from these kernels, utilizing a function pruning
strategy to minimize data aggregation costs. Finally, it converts the aggregated
stack traces into Prometheus-compatible metrics, ensuring accessibility to the
Prometheus server (Fig. 2).
374     J. Sun et al.




                  Fig. 2. Internal interactions in the Local Proﬁler.


3.3   Controller

The controller in Atys serves as the central hub for routing user commands to
the system’s components. Upon the user triggering proﬁling tasks, the controller
interprets the conﬁguration, establishes communication with local proﬁlers, and
assigns proﬁling tasks based on the user’s speciﬁcations. Furthermore, the con-
troller allows users to manage existing proﬁling tasks.


3.4   Prometheus Server

The Prometheus server in Atys collects metrics from the monitored ports of
worker nodes. These metrics, reﬂecting the performance of hotspot functions,
are generated by local proﬁlers from raw stack traces and formatted according
to Prometheus standards [31].
    In managing hotspot functions, the server employs a straightforward yet eﬀec-
tive strategy: it adds a function to the trace if it has not been previously recorded
or updates the existing trace with new resource consumption data from the lat-
est proﬁling. Consequently, the Prometheus server oﬀers a comprehensive data
management suite for the tracked hotspots, encompassing persistent storage,
querying, analysis, and visualization capabilities. This allows users to monitor
resource consumption trends or export data for in-depth evaluation.
                                     Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework        375




Fig. 3. Number of samples and the ratio of sample sum to total for each subthread in
Specjbb2015.


4     Eﬃciency Optimization

As noted in Sect. 1, in large-scale distributed microservices, even minor cost
reductions in collecting and aggregating stack traces can lead to substantial
savings throughout the system. To achieve this, we focus on optimizing the
eﬃciency of Atys based on two key observations.
Existence of Massive Daemon Threads: Stack traces from numerous dae-
mon threads often lack informative data for pinpointing hotspot functions, as
these threads typically handle background tasks unrelated to performance bot-
tlenecks. By eliminating stack traces from these daemon threads, we can improve
the eﬃciency of the aggregation process.
Periodic Variation of Hotspot Functions: Previous studies have shown that
microservice workloads display periodic variation in user requests [19]. This is
further illustrated by the Java server benchmark Specjbb2015 [39]. By recog-
nizing and leveraging this periodicity, we can dynamically adjust stack trace
sampling frequency, resulting in reduced sampling costs while enhancing accu-
racy.


4.1   Function Selective Pruning (FSP) Strategy

In this subsection, we demonstrate that it is unnecessary to consider every stack
trace when identifying hotspot functions. We then introduce an eﬃcient method
for selectively pruning less relevant function calls.
    In complex production environments with high concurrency, the target ser-
vice initiates a signiﬁcant number of threads [13]. A pertinent example is the
Java benchmark Specjbb2015 [39]. Figure 3 illustrates the distribution of sample
counts across various threads during a speciﬁc run. The threads are ordered by
descending sample counts, with their ranking based on sample volume displayed
on the horizontal axis. The left vertical axis represents the number of samples
per thread, while the right vertical axis indicates the cumulative percentage of
samples contributed by the top n threads relative to the total sample count.
The data indicate a notable concentration of activity among a small subset of
376     J. Sun et al.

threads. Speciﬁcally, approximately 25% of the threads–namely, the top 444 out
of 1,840–account for 90% of the samples, deﬁning the 90th percentile or P90
threads. The majority of threads outside this core group remain inactive, often
functioning as daemon threads. Furthermore, the P99 threads, comprising the
top 838 threads, demonstrate that the remaining 1,002 threads contribute only
1% to the total sample count.
    In multithreaded services, analyzing the performance of individual threads is
crucial for understanding the service’s operational dynamics. However, examin-
ing stack traces from a single thread does not provide a complete picture of the
overall performance landscape. Thus, it is essential to combine stack trace data
from all threads to gain a comprehensive view of performance hotspots. Although
it may seem thorough to include every stack trace in the aggregation to avoid
overlooking relevant data, this indiscriminate approach can increase computa-
tional overhead. More importantly, it risks cluttering the analysis with irrelevant
information, obscuring the actual performance bottlenecks. Consequently, prior
to aggregation, it is vital to carefully assess the signiﬁcance of each stack trace.
To enhance the eﬃciency and eﬀectiveness of the aggregation process, it is rec-
ommended to ﬁlter out stack traces that contribute minimally to identifying
hotspot functions. This pruning is executed by the local proﬁler in Atys, which
aggregates only the signiﬁcant raw call stacks.
    In Atys, the agent captures stack traces from threads and organizes them
by the number of samples per thread. Given that the number of threads is
signiﬁcantly lower than the number of stack traces, the sorting cost is negligible.
The agent retains threads with the highest sample counts, such as P99 threads,
while discarding samples mainly from inactive daemon threads. This method
enables focused analysis of the most active threads, improving proﬁling eﬃciency
without being burdened by less relevant data. Experiments demonstrate that this
approach yields negligible error and high cost savings.


4.2   Frequency Dynamic Adjustment (FDA) Scheme

Through experiments and data analysis, we have made two key observations
regarding the relationship between sampling frequency and accuracy, as well as
the periodic variation of hotspot functions.
    Firstly, proﬁling at a higher sampling frequency is widely recognized as a
way to improve accuracy due to the increased number of samples. However,
this approach incurs higher costs, which makes this an inviable solution in the
context of multiple instances. Consequently, a trade-oﬀ should be made between
cost and accuracy.
    Secondly, our research reveals that certain workloads exhibit periodic ﬂuc-
tuations in their hotspot functions. To investigate this pattern, we conducted
experiments using two benchmarks: the widely recognized Java benchmark
Specjbb2015 [39] and a representative deep learning inference task employing
the VGG16 architecture [38], which iteratively processes the CIFAR dataset
[22]. We meticulously monitored the variations in the top 10 hotspot functions
                                      Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework         377




      Fig. 4. The periodic variation of hotspot functions in typical workloads.


during the execution of these benchmarks. We speciﬁcally analyze the propor-
tion of time spent on the top 10 hotspot functions as a probability distribution.
By employing the Jenson − Shannon(JS) divergence [23], we quantify the dif-
ferences between the current and previous distributions at 10-s intervals. The
ﬁndings, illustrated in Fig. 4, highlight two signiﬁcant trends: 1) High levels of
JS divergence are consistently observed at the beginning and end of the applica-
tion’s lifecycle, indicating rapid changes in hotspot functions during these phases.
2) During stable application operation, a cyclical variation pattern in hotspot
functions emerges, characterized by recurring spikes in JS divergence at regular
intervals, reﬂecting shifts in hotspots that subsequently return to lower levels
before the next cycle commences.
    Motivated by these observations, we propose a dynamic frequency adjustment
scheme that adaptively modiﬁes the sampling rate based on proﬁling results. The
goal is to minimize proﬁling costs while maintaining accuracy. The fundamental
idea is to increase the sampling frequency when signiﬁcant changes in hotspots
are detected, and to either maintain or decrease it when they stabilize, thereby
improving the accuracy of low-frequency sampling results with high-frequency
samples.
    The principle behind this approach can be outlined as follows: leveraging
high-frequency sampling results as reference points to enhance the accuracy of
low-frequency sampling outcomes. Initially, we gather precise results through
high sampling rates, followed by obtaining data at lower sampling rates. If the
discrepancy between low and high-frequency sampling results is minimal, it indi-
cates that the hotspot functions have remained relatively stable. Consequently,
the high-frequency results can substitute the low-frequency sampling outcomes.
Conversely, signiﬁcant diﬀerences suggest that the hotspot functions are chang-
ing rapidly, rendering previously obtained high-frequency results no longer appli-
cable. In such instances, the sampling rate should be increased to acquire new,
accurate reference points.
    The frequency in Atys is adjusted exponentially, where the new frequency
is determined by multiplying the current frequency by a user-speciﬁed decaying
coeﬃcient λ. To assess the similarity of the sampling results, we employ the JS
378      J. Sun et al.

Ensure: f : sampling frequency for next time window
 P0 ← Distribution of functions in R0
 P ← Distribution of functions in R
 D ← JS divergence(P, P )
 if D > θ then
    f = f /λ
 else if D ≤ θ in more than the speciﬁed number of consecutive newline time win-
 dows3 then
    f ←f ∗λ
 else
    f ←f
 end if
 return f



divergence of the distributions of hotspot functions. Speciﬁcally, we treat the
percentage of time each function occupies in the results of two consecutive sam-
ples as two probability distributions. Thus, Pi = {fi,1 , fi,2 , . . . , fi,n }, where Pi
denotes the distribution obtained from the ith sampling, and fi,k indicates the
proportion of time that the kth function occupies across all samples collected
at the ith instance. We can then compute the divergence between two distribu-
tions. Two distributions are considered signiﬁcantly diﬀerent when the condition
DJS > θ is satisﬁed, where θ is a user-deﬁned threshold determining the strict-
ness of frequency adjustment. The pseudo-code of this approach is presented in
Algorithm 1.
    To adjust the strictness of similarity evaluation, users can set the thresh-
old θ. The optimal value of θ may vary across diﬀerent programs. To establish
an initial suitable value, users can perform a initialization stage by a low-cost,
coarse, and oﬄine proﬁling before large-scale proﬁling. This determined value
can subsequently be applied directly, incurring no additional costs during ongo-
ing monitoring activities.
    To reduce computational costs, not all functions in the sampling results are
considered when calculating DJS , due to the typically large number of functions.
In most workloads, the top 10 hotspot functions account for a signiﬁcant por-
tion of the total cost, highlighting the primary performance bottlenecks of the
target service. In our speciﬁc implementation, we demonstrate the use of the
top 10 hotspot functions for calculating DJS , though this selection is ﬂexible.
Users can adjust this parameter; increasing its value incorporates more func-
tions, enhancing accuracy in identifying changes in hotspot functions, albeit at
a higher computational cost.

3
    This threshold is adaptable based on user preferences. For our experiment, we set it
    to 5.

4.3   Initialization Stage

The essential purpose of both Function Selective Pruning and Frequency
Dynamic Adjustment is to balance cost and accuracy, which requires knowing
how they vary according to diﬀerent parameters. Moreover, diﬀerent services
have diﬀerent performance characteristics and access patterns, and the proﬁl-
ing cost and accuracy of proﬁling kernels themselves are also diﬀerent. It is
impossible to know in advance the eﬀects of diﬀerent parameters before proﬁl-
ing in practice. Therefore, to determine the optimal parameters for them, we
need an initialization stage by performing a pre-proﬁling before large-scale pro-
ﬁling. Since our target is long-running large-scale distributed services, the cost
of this one-time initialization process is usually acceptable compared to the cost
of subsequent long-term monitoring.
    For the pruning standards of Function Selective Pruning, there is a nearly
functional relationship between the percentage of pruned threads, the time
reduced, and the mean average percentage error(MAPE) caused for the tar-
get service, as shown in Fig. 5. We can ﬁt this relationship through the results
of pre-proﬁling and appropriate models. Therefore, given the acceptable maxi-
mum MAPE, we can calculate the maximum pruning percentage to achieve the
maximum time reduction within the error range. This can be formalized as the
following optimization problem:

                               min      T (p)
                                p                                             (1)
                               s.t. M AP E(p) ≤

where p is the pruning percentage, while denotes the maximum acceptable
MAPE. The functions T (p) and M AP E(p) illustrate the ﬁtted relationships
between p and the corresponding time reduction, as well as the MAPE induced
by p, respectively. Since T (p) and M AP E(p) are both monotonically increasing,
this problem can be easily solved.
    For the example Specjbb service, we choose linear model for T (p), and log-
arithmic model for M AP E(p) (MAPE of the top50 hotspot functions). The
results are T (p) = −1.0614p + 114.44, ﬁtting MAPE=4.75; and M AP E(p) =
984.368∗log(−0.001p + 1.099), ﬁtting MAPE=15.73. It should be noted that the
MAPE of the logarithmic model before P99 is only 1.66, and at P99, the overall
relative error increases due to the small absolute value of the error. This means
that the predicted values are highly accurate in most feasible regions of this
optimization problem. Given a threshold in the example, we can thus calculate

    As for the determination of the threshold of Frequency Dynamic Adjustment
Scheme, user can derive an image of JS divergence over time like Fig. 4 through
pre-proﬁling. Through this image, user can easily see the migration of hot func-
tions of the service, and thus set an appropriate JS divergence threshold for
frequency adjustment. The general target is to make the small changes in the
hotspot function of the service do not reach the threshold most of the time, while
those drastic changes reach it.

5     Evaluation
5.1   Experiment Setup
We conduct experiments on a 13-node cluster to evaluate the eﬀectiveness of
function selective pruning and frequency dynamic adjustment strategies, along
with the scalability of Atys. Speciﬁcally, we utilize SPECjbb2015 [39] as the
Java benchmark and async-proﬁler [3] as the Java proﬁling kernel. Additionally,
we employ the VGG16 network inference [38] for Python benchmarking, using
py-spy [7] as the proﬁling kernel.
   The Specjbb2015 runs in HBIR (High Bound Injection Rate) mode, indicat-
ing it seeks HBIR before exiting. The VGG workload is set up to employ the
VGG16 network for repeated classiﬁcation on the CIFAR-10 dataset [22]. All
benchmark programs are deployed via Kubernetes [41], with Atys installed as
a daemon on the target node. All tests are performed on identical worker nodes,
as detailed in Table 1.

5.2   Baselines
Our advancements in proﬁling kernel eﬃciency enhance the kernels’ optimiza-
tions. This indicates that the optimization techniques outlined in Atys can be
applied to both single-machine and multi-machine proﬁlers. Furthermore, due
to the inherent performance disparities among diﬀerent kernels, it would be
inappropriate to evaluate distinct kernels using our optimization techniques.
Consequently, our experiments concentrate on assessing the optimizations on
the same kernel, rather than merely deploying the kernel from previous studies.
We select the open-source multi-machine proﬁler pyroscope [33] as the baseline,
which employs the same Java and Python proﬁling kernels as Atys.


             Table 1. Conﬁguration of worker nodes in the experiments

        OS              Alibaba Cloud Linux release 2.1903 LTS
        CPU             Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8269CY CPU @ 2.50GHz
        Core Number 104
        Memory Size 187GB




5.3   Eﬀect of FSP Strategy
We employ the function selective pruning (FSP) strategy, as detailed in Sect. 4.1,
on the stack traces gathered from a speciﬁc execution of Specjbb2015. We then
analyze the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of the execution time for
the top n most sampled functions, alongside the aggregation time under varying
pruning thresholds, with n set to 5, 10, 20, and 50. Notably, the time to sort
                                    Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework       381

Fig. 6. CPU cost and MAE with diﬀerent sampling frequencies by Atys, single-

1,840 threads by sample count is minimal compared to the aggregation cost of
hundreds of MBs of raw stack traces. Therefore, our primary focus is on the
aggregation process’s time cost for comparison.
    The results are depicted in Fig. 5, showing that for the top 5, 10, 20, and
50 hotspot functions, the FSP strategy in Atys yields signiﬁcant time savings,
surpassing the marginal error incurred. Speciﬁcally, with the P99 pruning thresh-
old, a mere 0.58% MAPE is introduced for the top 50 hotspot functions, while
aggregation time decreases by 6.8%. Therefore, the P99 standard is established
as the default pruning threshold in Atys.


5.4   Eﬀect of FDA Scheme

To evaluate the eﬀectiveness of the frequency dynamic adjustment (FDA)
scheme, we initially select six time-consuming (> 5%) business logic functions
from Specjbb2015, as detailed below:
382       J. Sun et al.


      –   AssociativityOfCategoryTransaction.execute
      –   SupermarketAudit.analyze
      –   SupermarketAudit.summarizeReceipt
      –   InStorePurchaseTransaction.doCheckout
      –   InStorePurchaseTransaction.doPurchase
      –   OnlinePurchaseTransaction.doCheckout


In addition, we select four functions essential for neural network inference from
the VGG16 benchmark:

      –   forward (torch/nn/modules/linear.py)
      –   _conv_forward (torch/nn/modules/conv.py)
      –   _max_pool2d (torch/nn/functional.py)
      –   relu (torch/nn/functional.py)


    We have instrumented the benchmark code to accurately measure the CPU
time consumed by each function. For the Java benchmark, we achieve this by
invoking threadMXBean.getCurrent ThreadCpuTime() before and after the func-
tion’s execution. In the case of the Python benchmark, we employ the CProﬁle
[34] library. Furthermore, we extrapolate the CPU time based on proﬁling results.
The percentage of time consumed by these hotspot functions is then converted
into a distribution. Finally, we compute the diﬀerence between the distribution
derived from proﬁling and the actual time consumption, expressed in terms of
mean average error (MAE).
    We calculate the MAE and CPU consumption of proﬁling across various sam-
pling frequencies using diﬀerent proﬁlers. The parameters for the FDA scheme
are set as follows: the JS divergence threshold θspecjbb = 0.5, θvgg = 0.05, and
the decay rate λ = 0.8.
    Several observations can be made from the results depicted in Fig. 6. Firstly,
as the sampling frequency increases, sampling costs generally rise while sampling
error decreases, conﬁrming the trend discussed in Sect. 4. Secondly, in the Python
benchmark, Atys consistently achieves lower error and costs than both py-spy
and pyroscope across all tested frequencies using our FDA strategy. Its MAE
approaches that of pyroscope at 800 Hz, with CPU utilization at only 53% of
pyroscope’s. Thirdly, in the Java benchmark, Atys has an average sampling
frequency of 357.8 Hz, with CPU usage comparable to async-proﬁler at 5,00 Hz.
However, it demonstrates a signiﬁcantly lower MAE than async-proﬁler at this
frequency, nearing the performance at 1,000 Hz while incurring only 12.4% of
the sampling cost. Additionally, Atys’ MAE remains notably lower than that
of pyroscope across all frequencies. These results demonstrate the eﬀectiveness
of Atys’s FDA strategy, achieving high accuracy while signiﬁcantly minimizing
performance overhead.
                                     Atys: An Eﬃcient Proﬁling Framework        383

5.5   System Scalability

When deploying Atys in production environments, the Prometheus server must
track and store extensive metrics, potentially resulting in signiﬁcant strain. Thus,
evaluating the server’s capacity to manage increased workloads during simulta-
neous monitoring of multiple instances is crucial. We conduct experiments in
which Atys concurrently monitors 0, 100, 500, and 1,000 instances of web ser-
vices over a period of 1,200 s. For each instance, Atys is conﬁgured to collect the
top 10 hotspot functions. The memory consumption of the Prometheus service
is recorded and presented in Fig. 7a.




Fig. 7. Memory and CPU usage of the Prometheus server with varying numbers of
monitoring instances.


    Initially, with no active monitoring, the Prometheus server’s memory usage
is approximately 50MB. As the number of monitored services increases, memory
consumption rises accordingly. However, even when monitoring up to 1,000 ser-
vice instances, the memory footprint remains below 250MB, which is negligible
compared to the worker node’s total memory of 184GB. The CPU usage of the
Prometheus service is also monitored, as illustrated in Fig. 7b. At its peak work-
384     J. Sun et al.

load, while monitoring 1,000 service instances simultaneously, the server utilizes
only about 6% of the host node’s total CPU.
    These results conﬁrm that the Prometheus server has ample capacity to man-
age numerous sampling tasks without strain. Furthermore, this demonstration
of the server’s resource eﬃciency underscores the suitability of Atys for meeting
the demands of extensive proﬁling tasks in production large-scale microservice
environments.

6     Conclusion
This work presents Atys, a highly eﬃcient proﬁling framework tailored for the
complexities of large-scale services in production environments. To enhance eﬃ-
ciency, Atys implements a function selective pruning strategy and a frequency
dynamic adjustment scheme to minimize proﬁling overhead. The performance
and eﬀectiveness of Atys have been validated through a prototype, which under-
went extensive experiments, showcasing its potential for practical deployment in
production environments.

        Path Optimization of USV Based on Stochastic
          Schemata Exploiter with New Exploitation
                          Strategy

                              Jianshan Liang1 and Yi Zuo1,2(B)
     1 Collaborative Innovation Center for Transport Studies, Dalian Maritime University,
                                   Dalian 116000, China
                                   zuo@dlmu.edu.cn
           2 Navigation College, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian 116000, China




        Abstract. In recent years, the rapid development of unmanned surface vessel
        (USV) navigation technology has driven a surge of interest in path planning algo-
        rithms. As a core technique in this field, traditional evolutionary algorithms have
        been widely applied to solve USV path planning problems under multiple con-
        straints. However, these algorithms commonly encounter limitations such as low
        search efficiency and slow convergence. Based on the latest advances in path opti-
        mization, this paper proposes a novel stochastic schemata exploiter (SSE) algo-
        rithm. SSE adopts the framework of genetic algorithms and uses integer encoding
        to map feasible paths to chromosomes. It breaks through the traditional selection–
        crossover model of subpopulation generation by extracting common schemata
        through semi-ordered permutation and combination strategies to guide offspring
        evolution. Specifically, SSE integrates schema theory into the iterative process,
        prioritizing the retention of high-fitness individuals and extracting advantageous
        schemata. A bounded mutation operation is further employed to enhance search
        capability, enabling both strong global exploration and rapid convergence. Simu-
        lation experiments under multiple constraints—including path length, navigation
        safety, and path smoothness—demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of
        the SSE algorithm. Comparative experiments with genetic algorithm (GA), ant
        colony optimization (ACO), and the Q-learning algorithm show that SSE achieves
        significantly better overall performance in path planning tasks.

        Keywords: evolutionary algorithm · path optimization · unmanned surface
        vessel · schema theory · integer encoding



1 Introduction
With the advancement of intelligent maritime technologies, unmanned surface vessels
(USV) have been increasingly deployed in a wide range of mission-critical scenarios,
including deep-sea exploration, disaster response, and maritime patrol [1]. These appli-
cations impose stringent requirements on autonomous navigation, particularly in terms
of real-time decision-making and robust path planning [2]. For instance, in ocean moni-
toring tasks, the accuracy of the USV’s trajectory directly determines the spatial coverage

© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 387–399, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_21
388       J. Liang and Y. Zuo

of environmental data [3]. In emergency response scenarios, timely and safe arrival under
harsh sea conditions is crucial to mission success [4]. In military operations, path con-
cealment and anti-interference capability are essential for avoiding detection and achiev-
ing strategic objectives [5]. Therefore, maritime path planning has become not only a
foundational element of autonomous navigation systems but also a pivotal technology
linking intelligent equipment performance to mission effectiveness [6]. The develop-
ment of planning algorithms that integrate global exploration with rapid convergence is
imperative for the future deployment of USVs in complex maritime environments [7].
    To address the challenges of USV path planning, a variety of classical algorithms have
been proposed [8]. The rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) algorithm is well-regarded
for its high efficiency in exploring complex spaces and is widely used in dynamic envi-
ronments. However, its outputs typically suffer from discontinuity and lack smoothness,
necessitating post-processing [9]. genetic algorithms (GAs), inspired by the process of
natural selection, are naturally suited for global search and multi-objective optimization.
Nevertheless, GAs often exhibit premature convergence, resulting in limited solution
precision [10]. ant colony optimization (ACO) mimics the foraging behavior of ants
and is effective in obstacle-rich environments through its positive feedback mechanism
[11]. Yet, ACO may suffer from slow convergence and limited diversity in solution sets
[12]. Other conventional approaches, such as artificial potential fields, grid-based A*
search, and cell decomposition techniques, demonstrate stable performance in structured
environments but generally encounter issues such as local optima, high computational
overhead, or compromised path quality [13]. A common shortcoming across these meth-
ods is their limited ability to simultaneously optimize multiple conflicting objectives,
such as minimizing path length, reducing energy consumption, and improving trajec-
tory smoothness—particularly under the dynamic and uncertain conditions typical of
maritime domains [14].
    To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel evolutionary algorithm
based on schema theory, termed the stochastic schemata exploiter (SSE) algorithm.
By integrating schemata extraction, stochastic replacement, and an adaptive balance
between exploration and exploitation, the SSE algorithm exhibits strong structural recog-
nition and optimization capabilities. The algorithm employs a semi-ordered mechanism
to form structured subpopulations and extracts common schemata from high-fitness
individuals to guide new solution generation. To preserve population diversity, muta-
tion is applied conditionally to prevent premature convergence. Unlike conventional
GA implementations, SSE performs mutation at the schema level rather than directly
on individuals. Simulation results of 100 times demonstrate that, compared to GA,
ACO, and Q-learning, the proposed SSE achieves superior performance. Specifically,
in path length, SSE (14.60 km) is shortest than GA (16.09 km), ACO (16.05 km) and
Q-learning(15.19 km). In algorithm execution time, it only takes 5.31 s, which is much
less than ACO (13.77 s) and Q-learning (86.65 s), and slightly lower than GA (2.09 s).
These experimental results indicate significant advantages of SSE in path planning of
USV.
    The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the USV
path planning environment modeling and the principles of the SSE in detail. Section 3
presents the simulation results and a comparative analysis of the performance of four
                Path Optimization of USV Based on Stochastic Schemata Exploiter         389

algorithms applied to USV path planning. Section 4 summarizes conclusions of this
paper.


2 Preparation of USV Path Planning and SSE Algorithm
This section introduces the environment of electronic chart, and presents environment
modeling, the path encoding method and detail of SSE algorithm.

2.1 Environment Modeling
Raster Map Modeling of Electronic Chart
In USV path planning, the navigation environment is typically derived from electronic
nautical charts, which provide reliable information about the target sea area. To facilitate
computational modeling, the maritime environment is discretized into a raster map that
transforms continuous space into a grid-based representation. This study adopts a raster-
based environmental model, which is widely used in evolutionary algorithm-based path
planning due to its simplicity and efficiency in representing navigable space and obsta-
cles. In the raster map, the target area is discretized into uniform, non-overlapping grid
cells, each assigned a specific color based on its environmental characteristics. Specifi-
cally, black grid cells denote non-navigable sea regions—such as islands, reefs, or buffer
zones—while white grid cells indicate navigable, obstacle-free regions. As illustrated in
Fig. 1, this representation allows the USV to recognize feasible routes and avoid collision
zones by evaluating the state of each cell along the path.




                Fig. 1. Environmental modeling example based on raster map


    Within this raster-based modeling framework, two common methods are used for
grid cell marking: the Cartesian coordinate method and the serial number method, which
maintain a bijective mapping for flexible conversion. The serial number method assigns
unique indices to grid cells following a strict left-to-right, bottom-to-top, ordering, as
visualized in Fig. 2. This sequential labeling ensures systematic path encoding by con-
verting coordinate-based waypoints into linear indices, which simplifies chromosome
representation in evolutionary algorithms.

Path Encoding
As shown in Fig. 3, path encoding is performed based on the environmental modeling
390         J. Liang and Y. Zuo




                               Fig. 2. Mapping raster to coordinates


and encoding described in the previous section. The start and end points of each path
are fixed, with each path node represented by an integer Pi and coordinates (x i , yi ). A
path consists of two or more nodes, and the number of nodes is variable.




                          Fig. 3. Graphical illustration of path encoding.


      Through integer encoding of the map, all path points can be effectively converted
from raw coordinate representation to integer representation. For example, the coordinate
representation of the path shown in Fig. 3 is Path = [(x s , ys ), (x 1 , y1 ), (x 2 , y2 ), …, (x i ,
yi ), (x i + 1 , yi + 1 ), …, (x e , ye )], it can be transformed into integer representation as Path =
(PS , P1 , …, Pi , Pi + 1 , …, Pn , PE ). Eq. 1 shows the method for converting the Cartesian
coordinates of a path point into the corresponding raster number,

                                       Pi = xi + C(yi − 1)                                         (1)

where Pi represents the unique integer number of the raster cell in the grid map, x i and
yi are the column and row indices of the point in the Cartesian coordinate system, C is
the number of raster map’s column.

Fitness Function
As a genetic algorithm-based method, the SSE algorithm employs a fitness function to
evaluate the quality of individual paths. In this study, the fitness function is designed to
comprehensively consider both path length and path smoothness, according to the path
length objective and path smooth objective, its function specified as follows:
                                                                               −1
                    fitness(P) = a ∗ length(P) + b ∗ smoothness(P)                                 (2)
                Path Optimization of USV Based on Stochastic Schemata Exploiter         391

where P means the Path from the starting point S to the endpoint E, length denotes
the total distance of the Path, and smoothness represents the degree of Path bending
and quantify the feasibility of a path, a and b are weight coefficients tuning the priority
between length and smoothness. This formulation ensures that shorter paths and smoother
trajectories contribute higher fitness values, aligning with the objectives of minimizing
energy consumption and navigation risks.

2.2 Stochastic Schemata Exploiter
This section introduces the Stochastic Schemata Exploiter (SSE) algorithm designed
for addressing USV path planning problems. It begins with an outline of the algo-
rithm’s framework, followed by a detailed explanation of the subpopulation generated
based on fitness rank, and schema generate. Finally, a detailed explanation of stochastic
replacement and schema mutation are presented.

The Framework of SSE
The SSE algorithm is a metaheuristic optimization method that represents potential solu-
tions using gene-based encodings inspired by natural evolution. In the context of genetic
algorithms, a schema refers to a common pattern shared across multiple individuals in
a population, representing a partial solution or building block that contributes to overall
performance. By preserving and combining such schemata, evolutionary algorithms can
effectively exploit promising search directions.
    In the SSE framework, schema theory is explicitly incorporated to guide the evo-
lutionary process. The algorithm extracts common schemata from subpopulations, pre-
serves them through elite-oriented selection, and introduces stochastic replacement or
mutation when all individuals converge to the same schema. This mechanism enables
SSE to maintain a balance between exploiting high-quality patterns and exploring new
search regions, thereby mitigating premature convergence while improving solution
diversity. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the main progress of SSE for USV path planning
include the following steps:
    Step1: Setting parameters for the SSE.
    Step2: The initial population POP1 is constructed by generating diverse individuals,
either randomly or based on heuristic rules.
    Step3: The newly generated individuals in POP1 are decoded into complete paths and
evaluated based on multiple performance metrics, such as path length and smoothness.
    Step4: Check the termination condition: if the stopping condition is satisfied (such
as the number of iteration), outputting the best solution of the latest generation, and stop
circulating; else, turn to step 5.
    Step5: High-fitness individuals are ranked using semi-ordered permutation based
on their fitness values. These elites are then recombined using a binary tree structure
to form subpopulations; after semi-order permutation and combination, subpopulations
were generated.
    Step6: For each subpopulation, a common schema is derived by preserving consistent
gene positions according to all individuals, while marking inconsistent positions with’*’;
    Step7: The positions with’*’ in the schema are filled with valid gene values selected
via a stochastic sampling process to enhance exploration, then turn to step 3.
392        J. Liang and Y. Zuo




                                 Fig. 4. Flowchart of SSE.


Initialization Strategies
In the SSE algorithm, each feasible grid cell on the raster map is assigned a unique integer,
and paths are encoded as chromosomes. The start and end points are fixed as the first and
last genes, while the remaining genes are randomly selected from non-obstacle cells. The
chromosome length is set according to the map size and task complexity. To ensure path
feasibility, each chromosome undergoes a continuity check. Disconnected segments
are repaired by interpolation or node replacement; if repair fails, the chromosome is
regenerated. This initialization strategy ensures that all individuals are collision-free
and diverse, providing a solid foundation for the SSE algorithm’s evolutionary process,
the Fig. 5 illustrated initialized population POP1 .




                           Fig. 5. Initialization of chromosomes.



Subpopulation Generates Procedure
In this section, a fitness-ranked combination strategy is employed to select individu-
als from the previous generation population POPi − 1 and construct the corresponding
subpopulations for generation Gi .
                Path Optimization of USV Based on Stochastic Schemata Exploiter        393

     The elite-oriented selection operation is a key component of the SSE algorithm.
Its objective is to select high-fitness individuals from the current population as elite
candidates for subpopulation generation. First, all chromosomes in the POPi − 1 are
sorted in descending order according to their fitness values. Then, the top n individuals
are selected and sequentially assigned to a new population set Pn , denoted as Pn = {a1 ,
a2 , …, an }.
     Based on the selected individuals in population Pn , a combination operation is per-
formed. A binary tree structure is used to arrange individuals according to their labels,
as illustrated in the Fig. 6.




                    Fig. 6. Semi-ordered permutation and combination.


    In this progress, each parent node can generate two child nodes: The left child is
generated by adding the next individual from the sorted list into the parent subpopulation.
The right child is generated by replacing the individual with the lowest fitness in the
parent subpopulation with the next individual.
    Through this iterative combination process, subpopulation nodes can be generated,
each representing a new subpopulation. This procedure lays the foundation for the
subsequent step of common schema generation.

Schema Generation
Schema is an important concept from biological evolution adopted in the proposed SSE
algorithm, used to represent the similarity or structural segmentation among chromo-
somes. SSE uses an encoding scheme of {‘integer’, ‘*’}, where ‘*’ denotes a gene that
can be replaced by any valid grid code along a feasible path. The schema generation
process is illustrated in the Fig. 7,




                               Fig. 7. Schemata generation.
394        J. Liang and Y. Zuo

    in this progress, a common schema for each subpopulation can be derived by compar-
ing identical gene positions across chromosomes within the same subpopulation. If the
subpopulation contains only one chromosome, that chromosome is directly retained as
the schema for the next generation. If the subpopulation contains multiple chromosomes,
the same gene positions among all chromosomes are extracted as the common schema,
different gene positions use ‘*’ to represent. The resulting schema is then supplemented
with valid gird number to ensure path continuity. The filled-in schema is incorporated
into the population POPi , serving as a source of elite individuals for the next generation.

Schemata Mutation Procedure
Through the above steps, after multiple iterations, a situation may arise in which all
individuals within the subpopulations at each node of the binary tree become identical.
If the same iterative logic continues to be applied under this condition, the algorithm will
lose its exploration capability in subsequent iterations, leading to premature convergence
and stagnation in a local optimum. Therefore, for this general case but special situation,
mutation operation is required to recall a stochastic replacement process to randomly
modify one position in common schema. To reduce the potential premature convergence,
this operation employs a more conservative mutation strategy, noted as follows:
• Random Schema Perturbation: Select an intermediate path node Pi (excluding start
  point S and end point E) from the rigid common schema and replace it with a wildcard
  ‘*’.
• Boundary Definition: Derive the coordinates of the preceding and succeeding nodes
  Pi − 1 = (X i − 1 , Y i − 1 ) and Pi + 1 = ( X i + 1 , Y i + 1 ) using coordinate transformation.
• Constrained Replacement: The replacement node Pn = (X n , Y n ) must satisfy:
                          ⎧
                          ⎨        Xn ∈ Xi−1 , Xi+1
                                   Yn ∈ Yi−1 , Yi+1                                            (3)
                          ⎩
                            Pn ∩ Obstacle, Pi−1 , Pi , Pi+1 = ∅

when newly generated schema does not represent a feasible path, repeat above operation.


3 Experiment and Simulation
This section presents the map configuration, algorithm parameter settings, and simulation
results.

3.1 Setting of Map and Parameters
In this section, we evaluate the performance of the proposed SSE algorithm by imple-
menting SSE and several baseline algorithms in MATLAB R2018a. The experiments
were conducted on a system equipped with an Intel Core i5 2.3 GHz processor and
16 GB of RAM. Based on the raster map modeling and encoding method described
in Sect. 2.2, simulation experiments for USV path planning were carried out using a
localized rasterized map of the target sea area, as shown in Fig. 8. The size of the map
was standardized to 50 × 50, 75 × 75, and 100 × 100 grid.
                   Path Optimization of USV Based on Stochastic Schemata Exploiter            395




              Fig. 8. Raster map modeling and coding for experimental sea area.


    In the experiments, we compared the proposed SSE algorithm with GA, ACO, and
the Q-learning in terms of planned path length. Table 1 lists the parameter settings
for each algorithm, including the common parameter of maximum iterations (MI). For
ACO, the parameters include the number of ants, pheromone factor, heuristic factor,
and pheromone evaporation coefficient for population size, crossover rate, and mutation
rate. Q-learning contains learning rate, discount factor, and exploration rate. For SSE,
only population size and mutation rate need to be specified.

a 30/200 denotes the population size of GA and ant number of ACO.



     Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the robustness of the
proposed SSE algorithm. Results indicate that the SSE algorithm exhibits exceptional
stability; owing to the unique characteristics of its structural design, variations in the
initial population size exert a negligible influence on its iterative process. Experimental
investigations demonstrate that as long as the number of initialized valid paths exceeds
396        J. Liang and Y. Zuo

2, the algorithm can rapidly converge to yield a suboptimal path in subsequent iterations.
Additionally, the number of offspring generated by the SSE algorithm is primarily gov-
erned by the binary tree branching algebra n. Further parametric experiments reveal that
when n is set to 5, a favorable trade-off between computational time and convergence
rate can be achieved.


3.2 Experimental Analysis

Experimental Comparison of Multiple Algorithms
As can be seen from the comparative experimental results of four algorithms (SSE, ACO,
Q-learning, and GA) on the three groups of algorithm trajectory maps (50 × 50, 75 ×
75, and 100 × 100) presented in Fig. 9, in each group of map experiments, all algorithms
successfully found collision-free paths after 100 iterations. It can be observed from the
three groups of trajectory maps that the red route representing the SSE algorithm is,
on the whole, the closest to the line connecting the red start point and the green end
point. Furthermore, combined with the convergence curves of path length, SSE shows
significant advantages in the shortest path experiments on these three maps: it converges
faster than other algorithms, and the shortest path length is also significantly better than
that of other algorithms.
    Table 2 data indicate that in the 100 × 100 experimental map, take the four algorithms
into account together, the SSE algorithm can plan shortest paths within a reasonable time
frame. This demonstrates the algorithm’s effectiveness.
    Analysis of Fig. 10 indicates that, after conducting one hundred experiments in
the 100 × 100 experimental map, the SSE algorithm demonstrated outstanding overall
performance. In terms of path length, SSE achieved a mean value of 14.60 km, sig-
nificantly outperforming ACO (16.09 km) and GA (16.05 km), and slightly surpassing
Q-learning (15.19 km). The short error bars further indicate a low standard deviation
in path length, highlighting the algorithm’s strong result stability. Regarding execution
time, SSE recorded an average of only 5.31 s, which is substantially lower than that of
Q-learning (86.65 s) and ACO (13.77 s), and only slightly higher than GA (2.09 s). More-
over, the short error bars suggest minimal fluctuation in runtime. Overall, SSE achieves a
favorable balance between path optimality and computational efficiency, offering supe-
rior practical advantages over GA, ACO, and Q-learning in USV path optimization
tasks.

4 Conclusion
This paper proposes a novel EA of SSE based on schema theory, which incorporates the
discovery of biological evolution, and utilizes swarm behavior in generation iterations.
One of the core concepts in SSE is to include common schemata for dividing individuals
from population into subpopulations, which contain individuals with similar genes, and
preserves these excellent genes via common schema. Another core concept is to involve
stochastic replacement, which can generate new individuals in wide and diverse search
space. During exploitation operation, SSE remains individuals with high fitness, which
can accelerate the population’s convergence to the optimal solution. During exploration
operation, SSE replaces individuals via stochastic process, which can increase population
diversity. Besides exploiter strategy, SSE also resets mutation operation on common
schema instead of individual, which can efficiently prevent premature convergence.
    In quantitative comparisons, SSE and other EAs are applied to solving the path plan-
ning problem of USV as experiment and simulation. Among all methods, SSE reveals
faster convergence, best solutions, and shorter run time. Additionally, SSE requires
fewer parameters than ACO and Q-learning (see details in Table 1), to enhance the
environmental adaptability and generalization of the algorithm.
