           On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy
       for Throughput Enhancement in V2V/V2I
                   Communications

            Weidong Yang1 , Xinzhuo Zhang1 , Yan Liu1(B) , Ranran Sun1 ,
                                and Yulong Shen2
      1
         Hangzhou Institute of Technology, Xidian University, Hangzhou, China
                {yangweidong01,liuyan,sunranran}@xidian.edu.cn,
                         24241215271@stu.xidian.edu.cn
    2
      School of Computer Science and Technology, Xidian University, Xi’an, China
                            ylshen@mail.xidian.edu.cn



          Abstract. This paper investigates the challenge of optimizing commu-
          nication performance in highway scenarios with discontinuous infras-
          tructure coverage. First, we propose an Adaptive Cooperative Strategy
          (ACS) that dynamically integrates Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) and
          Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communications in both same-direction and
          opposite-direction traﬃc ﬂows, adaptively selecting the optimal trans-
          mission path based on real-time vehicle positions and network condi-
          tions. Then, we develop a comprehensive analytical model, modeling
          the vehicular network as a stochastic process to capture the dynamic
          topology of the network and deriving a closed-form expression for the
          average achievable throughput. Finally, extensive simulations validate
          the accuracy of our analysis and evaluate the impact of key parameters
          on performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed ACS signif-
          icantly outperforms traditional single-mode strategies in scenarios with
          discontinuous infrastructure coverage. Our approach aims to maximize
          achievable throughput in infrastructure-sparse vehicular networks and
          promote the development of intelligent transportation systems.


          Keywords: Vehicular networks · Cooperative communication · V2I ·
          V2V · Throughput


1    Introduction

With the rapid development of intelligent transportation systems and the con-
tinuous maturation of vehicular network technology, Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V)
and Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) communications have become key techno-
logical foundations for realizing intelligent driving, traﬃc safety management,
and eﬃcient traﬃc coordination. In highway scenarios, the combination of high-
speed vehicle movement, dynamic network topologies, and uneven infrastructure
coverage creates a complex communication environment where traditional single
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 400–418, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_22
                                         On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy       401

communication modes struggle to adapt, resulting in unstable connections, low
data transmission eﬃciency, and signiﬁcantly limited performance of vehicular
communication systems. Therefore, how to eﬀectively utilize V2V and V2I com-
munications in dynamic vehicular network environments to optimize network
throughput presents a signiﬁcant technical challenge.
    Early research on vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs) primarily focused on
single communication modes, such as standalone V2I or V2V communication.
[1] analyzed the existence probability of connectivity paths between vehicles and
roadside units (RSUs) using a stochastic model and proposed an upper bound
for end-to-end packet delivery delay. However, standalone V2I communication
faces the challenge of limited coverage. As noted in [2], the high deployment
cost of base stations makes it diﬃcult to fully cover highways, resulting in large
“dark zones” and transmission interruptions. In terms of standalone V2V com-
munication, [3] investigated spectrum reuse optimization for V2V communica-
tion, employing stochastic geometry theory and homogeneous Poisson point pro-
cesses to characterize the random distribution of V2V transmitters. It derived
closed-form expressions for the success probability of V2V pair transmissions and
V2V broadcasts, and analyzed the problem of maximizing average throughput
under V2I communication interruption constraints. [4] proposed a cooperative
multi-hop transmission scheme for a two-way amplify-and-forward relay network.
Nevertheless, these single communication modes exhibit signiﬁcant limitations
in complex VANET environments, making it challenging to meet the demand for
eﬃcient and stable data transmission. This has prompted researchers to explore
hybrid communication modes.
    To overcome the limitations of single communication modes, hybrid commu-
nication strategies have become a research hotspot. In terms of unidirectional
V2V and V2I collaboration, [5] proposed the ChainCluster scheme, which selects
appropriate vehicles to form linear clusters on highways, with each member
retrieving a portion of a ﬁle from roadside infrastructure, signiﬁcantly improv-
ing the probability of successful ﬁle downloads. [6] introduced a dynamic col-
laboration scheme that generates adaptive multi-hop V2V paths for vehicles
located outside RSU coverage. In terms of bidirectional V2V and V2I collabo-
ration, [7] proposed a collaborative content dissemination scheme (CCDS) that
coordinates multiple infrastructures and bidirectionally moving vehicles to assist
target vehicles in downloading data. [8,9] proposed a collaborative store-carry-
forward (CSCF) scheme and an elastic segment-based collaborative strategy
(ESCS), respectively, utilizing bidirectional vehicle ﬂows as relays, signiﬁcantly
improving throughput. In single-hop collaboration, [10] proposed a cluster-based
resource management scheme that groups vehicles into clusters and selects opti-
mal vehicles as cluster heads to manage V2V and V2I connections, signiﬁ-
cantly enhancing the average throughput of cellular users. [11,12] investigated
cooperative medium access control (MAC) optimization techniques in RSU-
equipped VANETs, proposing distributed cooperative MAC schemes based on
the CSMA/CA protocol. [13] explored the use of vehicles traveling in the oppo-
site direction as single-hop relays. [14] further extended this approach, addressing
402    W. Yang et al.

the issue of enhancing network capacity in multi-user scenarios through cooper-
ative communication strategies. In terms of multi-hop V2V links, [15] employed
stochastic geometry to study the success probability in multi-relay cooperative
C-V2X networks, deriving analytical expressions for joint success probability
considering interference correlation. Regarding multi-hop V2V and V2I collabo-
ration, [16] investigated data dissemination in hybrid vehicular networks, using
bidirectionally moving vehicles as relays and proposing a distributed multi-source
scheduling algorithm that signiﬁcantly improved data dissemination eﬃciency.
[17] proposed a joint frequency scheduling and power control scheme, mapping
I2V and V2V links to tuple links, and signiﬁcantly enhancing network connec-
tivity and average throughput through the joint design of frequency schedulers
and power controllers. Additionally, [18] explored complex collaborative scenar-
ios and introduced a deep reinforcement learning-based task oﬄoading scheme
for vehicular edge computing. This scheme enables ﬂexible RSU-RSU collabora-
tion to transmit task results to the RSU currently serving the vehicle and oﬄoad
tasks from high-load RSUs to low-load RSUs, signiﬁcantly reducing overall task
processing costs. Despite signiﬁcant progress in various aspects, most existing
studies primarily focus on single multi-hop or single-hop, unidirectional or bidi-
rectional relaying V2V/V2I cooperative strategies, lacking comprehensive con-
sideration of multiple communication modes.
    Based on the above analysis, this paper proposes an Adaptive Cooperative
Strategy (ACS) suitable for highway scenarios with sparse infrastructure, com-
prehensively considering the characteristics of V2I and V2V communications,
dynamically adjusting same-direction multi-hop and opposite-direction single-
hop communication modes to optimize achievable throughput for long-distance
communications. Notably, although our analysis focuses on a straight highway
segment, the results extend directly to independent roads in 2D and 3D sce-
narios [14] (e.g., 2D grid networks and 3D multi-layer networks). In such cases,
the overall network capacity can be regarded as the sum of the capacities of
the individual roads. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows:

1. We propose an ACS that comprehensively utilizes V2I communication and
   bidirectional V2V communication, adaptively selecting communication modes
   based on the positions of same-direction and opposite-direction vehicles to
   improve the achievable throughput on bidirectional roads with discontinuous
   infrastructure coverage.
2. Based on the above results, we develop an analytical model to study the data
   transmission process in diﬀerent communication scenarios under dynamic net-
   work topologies. We formulate the data volume obtained in same-direction
   multi-hop communication as an optimization problem to maximize the data
   volume. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for the average
   achievable throughput.
3. Finally, extensive simulation experiments are conducted to illustrate the
   impact of RSU spacing, opposite-direction vehicle density, and same-direction
   vehicle density on the average achievable throughput. The results demonstrate
                                          On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy       403

    that the proposed ACS signiﬁcantly improves the throughput of vehicular
    networks compared to single-mode communication strategies.

   The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 describes the system
model and the ACS. Section 3 provides a theoretical analysis of the average
achievable throughput through V2I and V2V in one period. Section 4 validates
the theoretical analysis through simulations and discusses the impact of key
parameters on performance. Section 5 concludes the paper.


2     System Model and Adaptive Cooperative Strategy
2.1   System Model

As shown in Fig. 1, a bidirectional lane highway network includes a single request-
ing vehicle (i.e., requester) aiming to download a large data ﬁle from a central
server.




Fig. 1. A highway communication network scenario with a two-lane road within a
period. Vehicles traveling in the same direction communicate through multi-hop, while
those traveling in the opposite direction communicate through single-hop.



    This strategy achieves the download of large ﬁles by integrating V2I, opposite
V2V, and forward V2V communications. The ﬁxed deployment of RSUs, coupled
with their capability to connect to the central server via wired or wireless links,
establishes RSUs as reliable data relays for the requester in a dynamic environ-
ment. The requester is assumed to receive the exact data fragments required
404     W. Yang et al.

from RSUs, opposite-direction vehicles (i.e., carriers), and same-direction vehi-
cles (i.e., relays).
    We adopt the unit disk model for communication modeling, where the data
transmission rate remains constant within the range, and no transmission occurs
beyond this range. Furthermore, in time-varying channels, V2I and V2V data
transmission rates may be approximated by their time-averaged values [13]. V2I
and V2V communications operate in half-duplex and unicast modes, utilizing
distinct channels to prevent mutual interference. Assuming an inﬁnitely long
road, the lane width is negligible. RSUs equipped with wired or wireless com-
munication capabilities for receiving information from the central server are uni-
formly distributed along the road at intervals d. The communication radius of
each RSU is rI , and the transmission rate to vehicles is RI . Vehicles traveling in
same-direction and opposing lanes exhibit densities ρ1 and ρ2 , correspondingly.
The vehicle count adheres to a Poisson distribution, while the spacing between
vehicles conforms to an exponential distribution. In the same and opposite direc-
tions, vehicles maintain uniform velocities of v1 and v2 , respectively. The commu-
nication radius of each vehicle is rV , and the inter-vehicle data transmission rate
is RV . Moreover, each vehicle is equipped with a GPS module for localization.
In the common scenario considered, rI > rV and RI > RV are satisﬁed.

2.2   Adaptive Cooperative Strategy
Based on the aforementioned communication scenario, we propose an ACS to
optimize the achievable throughput for the requester. The speciﬁc implementa-
tion process of this strategy is detailed below.




                  Fig. 2. The requester communicates with RSUs.


    Our analysis focuses on a period during which the requester travels a distance
d. As shown in Fig. 2, this period spans from the requester entering the trans-
mission range of Ii to just before entering the transmission range of Ii+1 . During
this period, due to the larger transmission range rI and higher data transmission
rate RI of the RSU, the requester prioritizes communication with Ii to maximize
                                           On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy        405

the amount of data acquired. Upon leaving the communication range of Ii , the
requester engages in V2V communication over the remaining distance d − 2rI ,
prioritizing interaction with carriers and secondarily with relays.




                  Fig. 3. The requester communicates with carriers.


   If carriers are within the requester’s communication range, as shown in Fig. 3,
the requester utilizes the carriers to perform single-hop V2V communication
using the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) strategy. Figure 3a and Fig. 3b illustrate the
scenarios where the requester is at the boundary of Ii ’s transmission range and
beyond this boundary, respectively. In both cases, the carriers provide a brief
yet eﬃcient single-hop communication opportunity, enabling the requester to
rapidly acquire data to meet the needs after disconnection from Ii . Speciﬁcally,
the requester selects the carrier that entered its communication range earliest and
continues communication until that carrier leaves the communication range or
the data is fully transmitted. Subsequently, the requester selects the next carrier
that entered its communication range earliest to continue transmission. In the
period considered, there are N carriers, denoted as V1 , V2 , . . . , VN . The distance
406     W. Yang et al.

between consecutive carriers Vi−1 and Vi is indicated by li , for i = 2, 3, . . . , N ,
while l1 represents the distance from the left boundary of the requester’s com-
munication range to the ﬁrst carrier V1 . According to [19], the distance li follows
an exponential distribution with an expected value of E[li ] = ρ12 .




                  Fig. 4. The requester communicates with relays.


    If there are no carriers within the communication range of the requester,
multi-hop communication via relays is considered. This process is shown in Fig. 4,
we adopt a farthest multi-hop selection strategy. As illustrated in Fig. 4a, when
the requester is at the boundary of the transmission range of Ii , it checks whether
there are relays within its communication range. If there are, it selects the relay
that is within both the communication ranges of the requester and Ii and is
farthest from the requester as the ﬁrst relay vehicle M1 . As depicted in Fig. 4b,
when M1 reaches the boundary of the transmission range of Ii , it selects the
relay that is within both the communication ranges of M1 and Ii and is far-
thest from M1 as the next relay vehicle M2 . This process continues until no
more relays are available. Let Q denote the number of relays in the multi-hop
                                         On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy       407

communication link formed when the requester moves beyond the transmission
range of the RSU Ii . This forms a connected multi-hop link between Ii and the
requester, with Q + 1 hops including Q hops from the Q relay vehicles to the
requester and one hop from Ii to the last relay vehicle MQ . We deﬁne Pdi , for
i = 1, 2, . . . , Q, as the distances associated with the relays. Pd1 represents the
distance between the requester and the ﬁrst relay M1 , while Pdi for i ≥ 2 denotes
the distance between consecutive relays Mi−1 and Mi . A store-and-forward app-
roach is adopted, where each relay vehicle Mi can receive a data amount Ei
from the Ii while within its transmission range. The data amount received by
the requester from relays within a period is denoted by Zi . By selecting the far-
thest relay vehicle, the coverage range per hop is maximized, thereby reducing
the number of hops required. This multi-hop link is activated only when there
are no carriers within the communication range of the requester. This combi-
nation of strategies aims to maximize the requester’s data acquisition eﬃciency.
By establishing a priority hierarchy (RSUs > carriers > relays), the system can
ﬂexibly switch communication modes across diﬀerent scenarios, adapting to the
high dynamics of highway traﬃc and the complexity of the communication envi-
ronment. It is worth noting that the ACS presented here is not the only possible
approach.


3     Theoretical Analysis of Average Achievable Throughput
3.1   Average Achievable Throughput

We model the communication within a period as a renewal reward process, where
the update process captures the switching of data transmitters interacting with
the requester within a time interval dt, and the reward process quantiﬁes the
volume of data received by the requester following a transmitter switch. To
evaluate the performance of this process, the average achievable throughput is
used as the metric.
   While the requester travels within a period, the average achievable through-
put is expressed as follows [13]:

RSUs, carriers, and relays. The total expected data volume is given by:

                       E[D] = E [DI ] + E [DR ] + E [DS ] .                     (2)

Furthermore, according to [13], the expressions for the expected data E [DI ]
received directly from the RSUs via V2I communication and the expected data

follows:

    In Fig. 9, the variation of achievable throughput for the three strategies with
RSU spacing is illustrated under the conditions of ﬁxed densities of opposite-

DCS because requester encounters more carriers than relays on an inﬁnitely long
road, enabling the requester to receive a greater amount of data from carriers
within the same time frame. Compared to CCS and DCS, our proposed ACS
performs the best, as it receives data from both carriers and relays.
    In Fig. 10, the achievable throughput of the three strategies with respect to

the achievable throughput of DCS increases with the rise in ρ1 , because the
increase in the density of same-direction vehicles facilitates the establishment
of multi-hop links, thereby enabling the requester to obtain more data from
relays. Since CCS only considers carrier nodes, its achievable throughput remains
constant as ρ1 increases. Compared with DCS and CCS, ACS has the optimal
achievable throughput, which is the advantage of utilizing bidirectional lanes.
    In Fig. 11, the achievable throughput of the three strategies with respect to
the density of opposite-direction vehicles is illustrated under the conditions of
ﬁxed density of same-direction vehicles and RSU spacing. It can be noted that the
achievable throughput of CCS rises with an increase in ρ2 , as the greater density
of opposite vehicles enable the requester to acquire more data from carriers. In
contrast, since the DCS solely relies on relays, its achievable throughput remains
constant as ρ2 increases. It can be found that the achievable throughput of ACS
consistently exceeds that of CCS, with the gap between them narrowing as ρ2
increases. This occurs because, as the density of opposite-direction vehicles ρ2

increases, requester encounters more carriers. Due to prioritization, requester
communicate more frequently with carriers, consequently reducing opportunities
for communication with relays.

4.4   Discussion
The use of the unit-disk model and the assumption of a constant transmission
rate within the communication range are admittedly idealized, as they do not
account for interference or channel fading. However, since the main contribution
of this work lies in the ACS rather than in detailed physical-layer modeling, such
abstractions are adopted to facilitate isolating and verifying the beneﬁts of the
proposed ACS. In future work, we plan to incorporate more sophisticated chan-
nel models to examine how interference and fading inﬂuence the performance of
ACS. In practical vehicular networks, the speed of individual vehicles may devi-
ate from the average. As shown in results [13], although such deviations can lead
to vehicle overtaking, their eﬀect on throughput performance remains negligible.


5     Conclusions
In this paper, we propose an ACS for V2I and V2V communications as well
as vehicular mobility. In the V2V communication area, the strategy leverages
vehicles on bidirectional lanes to perform opposite single-hop communication
and forward multi-hop communication, thereby enhancing the average achiev-
able throughput in highway vehicle networks. Theoretical analysis and exten-
sive simulation results demonstrate the eﬀectiveness of the strategy and reveal
                                            On Adaptive Cooperative Strategy         417

the impact of key parameters on the average achievable throughput. Further-
more, compared to strategies that use only forward multi-hop communication
or opposite single-hop communication, the proposed strategy exhibits signiﬁcant
advantages in improving the average achievable throughput. In addition, deep
learning, as a broadly applicable methodology, presents a promising avenue for
future work in optimizing our scenario.

       Abstract. With the widespread adoption of deep learning across indus-
       tries and academia, the energy consumption of AI computing clus-
       ters has surged, creating signiﬁcant economic and environmental chal-
       lenges. Improving AI server energy eﬃciency has therefore become a
       critical research focus. Traditional dynamic voltage and frequency scal-
       ing (DVFS) research has primarily focused on regulating either CPU or
       GPU/NPU frequency in isolation, which cannot fully unlock the energy-
       saving potential of AI servers. Naively applying joint DVFS requires
       exhaustively evaluating all frequency combinations to ﬁnd the most
       energy-eﬃcient one, which becomes prohibitively expensive with many
       frequency states.
          To address this limitation, this study proposes CoDVFS, a Coordi-
       nated Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling framework that employs
       Bayesian optimization to rapidly converge to optimal frequency conﬁgura-
       tions for both CPUs and GPU/NPUs. Experimental results on AI servers
       running HPL-MxP workloads demonstrate that CoDVFS enhances server
       energy eﬃciency by 17%, achieving signiﬁcant energy savings. We also
       analyze the relationship between whole-server and accelerator-only energy
       eﬃciency, proposing an optimum alignment criterion. On our device, the
       optima of both metrics coincide. However, the criterion reveals that if
       server and accelerator power scale diﬀerently on other devices, optimiz-
       ing accelerator eﬃciency alone may not reﬂect true server eﬃciency.

       Keywords: energy eﬃciency · DVFS · server


1    Introduction
Advancements in artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) spanning natural language process-
ing and computer vision have driven substantial demand for computational
resources. Research institutions and enterprises worldwide heavily invest in AI
clusters, relying on GPUs/NPUs (Neural Processing Units) for eﬃcient training
and inference. However, computational growth brings soaring energy costs. For
example, GPT-3 training consumed 1,287 MWh (502t CO2 , equal to 8 cars’
lifetime emissions). Computing facilities like Aurora peak at 38.7 MW [20],
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 419–439, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_23
420    Y. Zhang et al.

potentially costing $30M/year and emitting 140,000t CO2 annually. As a result,
improving the energy eﬃciency of AI servers is now critical.
    Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) is an important technique
to control energy consumption and improve energy eﬃciency [1–5,8,10,12,14–
17,19,22,24,25,27–31]. By applying DVFS, we dynamically adjust a processor’s
operating frequency and supply voltage: increasing frequency and voltage under
heavy load to ensure performance, and lowering frequency and voltage under
light load to reduce power usage. This technique allows processors to minimize
energy consumption whenever possible.
    However, existing studies focus solely on applying DVFS to individual compo-
nents [1–5,8,10,12,14–17,19,22,24,25,27–31]—either the CPU or GPU—while
overlooking the fact that, in real tasks, the CPU and GPU work in coordina-
tion to complete computations. If DVFS is applied only to the CPU, the GPU
may still remain in a high-power state; likewise, optimizing only the GPU fre-
quency may result in CPU power consumption or execution performance failing
to match the GPU’s processing pace. Such isolated control strategies often fall
short in unlocking the full energy eﬃciency potential of an AI server.
    As a result, joint frequency and voltage scaling for both CPU and GPU
becomes important. Guided by this motivation, we propose CoDVFS, a Coordi-
nated Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling framework tailored for AI servers.
This framework can be applied across diﬀerent workloads and minimize power
consumption or maximize overall system energy eﬃciency by simultaneously
tuning the operating frequency and voltage of both the CPU and GPU.
    To facilitate optimization, we adopt a Bayesian optimization approach to
eﬃciently search for the optimal processor frequency combination, making the
control strategy more adaptive and precise.
    To validate the eﬀectiveness of CoDVFS, we conducted experiments on a
DGX server equipped with 8×GPU V100. We used external power monitor-
ing equipment to measure the energy consumption of the server while running
benchmarks. The experimental results show that, compared to the default DVFS
setting, CoDVFS improves server energy eﬃciency by 17% (HPL-MxP) and 12%
(HPCG), signiﬁcantly lowering overall electricity usage. Compared with DVFS
strategies applied only to CPU or GPU individually, the coordinated control
approach further exploits the system’s overall energy-saving potential.
    Since measuring full server power consumption is more challenging than
monitoring GPU power alone, prior GPU DVFS studies have typically focused
solely on GPU power measurements [1,3–5,8,12,14,16,22,24,25,28,30,31]. To
overcome this limitation, we present a detailed description of our methodology
for server-wide power measurement. More importantly, by comparing the GPU
power reported by the nvidia-smi tool with the total power measured by exter-
nal power meters, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the diﬀerences between
whole-server energy eﬃciency and GPU-only energy eﬃciency.
    Our analysis reveals that the point of optimal GPU energy eﬃciency does
not necessarily coincide with the point of optimal whole-server energy eﬃciency,
especially when the power consumption of other components, such as fans, mem-
ory, and the motherboard, varies diﬀerently with GPU frequency. We propose an
           CoDVFS: Improving the Energy Eﬃciency of AI Servers Through        421

optimal alignment criterion demonstrating that when GPU power and non-GPU
power grow at equal rates, their optimal operating points coincide. On the other
hand, when these growth rates diﬀer, optimizing GPU energy eﬃciency alone
may not accurately represent the overall server energy eﬃciency. This highlights
the importance of evaluating power consumption from a holistic perspective in
order to accurately assess energy eﬃciency. These ﬁndings may oﬀer new per-
spectives for future system-level energy eﬃciency optimization.


2   Background

Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) is a key technique used to
control the power consumption and performance of processors by adjusting
their operating voltage and frequency [1–5,8,10,12,14–17,19,22,24,25,27–31].
The dynamic power of a processor can typically be approximated by the for-
mula P ∝ CV 2 f [9], where C is the capacitance, V is the voltage, and f is the
frequency. This equation indicates that reducing the voltage and frequency leads
to a decrease in dynamic power consumption. Compared with other power man-
agement methods that require changes to application codes or hardware archi-
tecture, DVFS oﬀers several advantages: it is non-intrusive to user applications,
easily applicable, and provides fast response times as DVFS adjustment usually
ﬁnishes within 30 milliseconds [21]. As a result, DVFS is widely integrated into
modern CPUs and GPUs.
    Current CPUs and GPUs typically do not expose voltage control interfaces
to users. Instead, on-chip logic automatically adjusts the voltage based on the
conﬁgured frequency, and voltage scales approximately linearly with frequency.
In practice, this means that adjusting the processor’s operating frequency is
suﬃcient, with the corresponding voltage being managed internally by the pro-
cessor. The frequency-voltage curves can be found in [13,18]. In this study, we
regulate the frequencies of CPUs and GPUs, thereby indirectly managing their
supply voltages.
    Research on applying DVFS to CPUs has a long history. Numerous stud-
ies have explored how to achieve optimal power and performance trade-oﬀs
under various workloads and scenarios by adjusting CPU frequency and volt-
age [2,7,10,17,19,27,29]. This includes precise modeling of CPU power consump-
tion and the design of optimal frequency-setting strategies. With the widespread
adoption of multi-core CPU architectures, researchers have begun to investigate
the feasibility of applying diﬀerentiated frequency control to individual cores on
the same chip [19], as well as independent DVFS control of the uncore compo-
nents [10,27] (which include on-chip caches and memory controllers) to further
tap into energy-saving potential.
    Over the past decade, the widespread application of deep learning has driven
GPUs to the forefront of high-performance computing. Consequently, research
on GPU DVFS has also seen rapid growth [1,3–5,8,12,14–16,22,24,25,28,30,
31]. Many studies focus on modeling GPU performance and power consumption
under diﬀerent frequency settings, seeking to identify frequencies that strike a
422    Y. Zhang et al.

balance between energy eﬃciency and computational performance. For GPUs
that support memory frequency scaling, some research has also explored the
additional optimization opportunities that GPU memory DVFS can provide for
task execution [23].
    Most existing studies, however, focus on applying DVFS to either the CPU
or GPU in isolation and rarely explore the optimization potential of coordinated
CPU-GPU control. In addition, most prior experiments measured only the power
of the CPU or GPU chip itself, lacking a comprehensive analysis of whole-server
power usage. In fact, when server-level energy eﬃciency is assessed by using the
actual power of the entire server as the denominator, the resulting conclusions
may diﬀer from those drawn from GPU-only measurements.
    To address this limitation, our study measures and analyzes the power con-
sumption of the entire server to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the
energy eﬃciency beneﬁts of coordinated DVFS in data center servers. Table 1
compares the diﬀerence between our work and previous research, showing that
most prior studies lack investigation into coordinated frequency scaling and
whole-server power measurement.

3     CoDVFS: A Coordinated Dynamic Voltage
      and Frequency Scaling Framework

Existing frequency and voltage scaling techniques primarily target individual
computing components—either the CPU or GPU—for optimization. To address
this issue, it is essential to adopt a holistic perspective and perform coordinated
energy eﬃciency optimization across both the CPU and GPU.
    A straightforward way to implement joint CPU-GPU DVFS is to evalu-
ate all possible combinations of CPU and GPU frequencies exhaustively, and
then select the conﬁguration that yields the highest energy eﬃciency. However,
while exhaustive search is conceptually simple, it becomes prohibitively expen-
sive when the number of frequency states is large. Suppose the CPU has M
frequency states and the GPU has N states. If each combination is tested R
times to ensure measurement stability, then M × N ×R experiments are required
in total. For example, if M = N = 11 and R = 5, a total of 605 experiments
would be needed, which could take several hours or more. This time and resource
expenditure is impractical in AI computing environments.
    To overcome this limitation, we propose CoDVFS, a coordinated dynamic
voltage and frequency scaling framework for CPU-GPU systems. The core idea
of CoDVFS is to leverage Bayesian Optimization to eﬃciently approximate the
optimal solution in high-cost experimental environments. This allows the system
to discover the optimal CPU/GPU frequencies with few experiments.
    When using this framework, it can be applied to any target program requiring
optimization. CoDVFS will then automatically perform experimental evaluations
and iteratively identify the best frequency conﬁguration. The source codes of
CoDVFS are available at https://github.com/zyjopensource/CoDVFS.


3.1    Optimization Objective

The objective of the optimization process is to maximize the energy eﬃciency,
which is deﬁned as the ratio of performance to power usage:


                          Performance   Workload/Duration   Workload
      Energy Eﬃciency =               =                   =          .
                             Power       Energy/Duration     Energy

    According to this formula, when running the same workload (with a ﬁxed
computational demand), maximizing energy eﬃciency is equivalent to minimiz-
ing total energy consumption. During optimization on a server, performance,
power, and runtime duration are all measured directly while the program is
executing. Each experiment typically lasts tens of seconds to several minutes.
    The input variables for the optimization process are the combinations of
CPU and GPU frequencies (fCPU , fGPU ). Since most processor hardware auto-
matically adjusts voltage according to the selected frequency, it is suﬃcient to
directly set the frequencies externally.
424    Y. Zhang et al.

3.2   Reason of Using Bayesian Optimization
Bayesian Optimization is a global optimization method based on probabilistic
models. It is particularly well-suited for optimizing functions that are expen-
sive or time-consuming to evaluate. In our case, because AI computing servers
are complex systems, the relationship between energy eﬃciency and CPU-GPU
frequency combinations cannot be described with an explicit analytical formula
unless complex modeling is done in advance. As a result, traditional methods
such as derivation-based or gradient-descent approaches are not applicable for
optimizing energy eﬃciency.
    Furthermore, since each experiment is relatively time-consuming, naive
brute-force search incurs a prohibitive computational cost. Bayesian Optimiza-
tion avoids the need for an analytical formula by constructing a probabilistic
model of the objective function. This model is then used to intelligently select
the next sampling point in the search space, allowing the optimization process
to eﬃciently approach the function’s optimum with relatively few experiments.

3.3   CoDVFS Framework Architecture
The proposed CoDVFS framework is implemented in Python and comprises key
modules: a Bayesian optimizer, workload runner, performance/power monitor-
ing, and CPU/GPU frequency control (Fig. 1).
    The Bayesian optimizer selects the next CPU-GPU frequency combination
using historical data and probabilistic modeling to maximize energy eﬃciency.
The workload runner executes the target program across frequency settings
for performance measurements. The performance monitoring module evaluates
workload execution based on program-reported metrics, and the power monitor-
ing module collects real-time power data from meters. Frequency control lever-
ages hardware-speciﬁc interfaces to adjust CPU/GPU frequencies.
    CoDVFS features adaptable interfaces for diﬀerent server setups, allowing
quick integration with new platforms by modifying frequency control calls. This
design ensures core optimization logic while enabling ﬂexible task execution,
monitoring, and coordinated CPU-GPU DVFS across servers, oﬀering a uniﬁed
solution for system-wide energy eﬃciency in real-world deployments.




                         Fig. 1. The CoDVFS Framework.
           CoDVFS: Improving the Energy Eﬃciency of AI Servers Through           425

3.4   Detailed Steps of Bayesian Optimization
Initialization of Sample Points. First, within the search space of CPU
and GPU frequencies, one or more initial frequency combinations are randomly
selected. For each combination, run the workload to collect performance/power
results and compute its energy eﬃciency.


Surrogate Model Construction. Using the data from the initial sample
points, a surrogate model is constructed to approximate the true objective func-
tion. A Gaussian Process (GP) is a commonly used surrogate model in Bayesian
Optimization. It characterizes the distribution of the objective function using a
mean function and a covariance function: f (x) ∼ GP(m(x), k(x, x )), where
x is the input variable (a CPU-GPU frequency combination (fCPU , fGPU )),
f (x) ∼ GP(·, ·) is the Gaussian process, m(x) is the mean function, k(x, x )
is the covariance function (also called the kernel), which describes the correla-
tion between inputs x and x .
    In Bayesian optimization, commonly used kernels include the RBF (Radial
Basis Function) kernel and the Matern kernel. Our implementation uses the
Matern kernel, which contains a few hyperparameters denoted as θ here.

Sampling Next Point. The core of Bayesian optimization lies in the sampling
of the next point. Based on the surrogate model, the next point is selected by
optimizing an acquisition function. The acquisition function evaluates the value
of each candidate point, which balances both exploration (gathering information
about unknown areas) and exploitation (reﬁning known good areas).
    Common acquisition functions include Expected Improvement (EI) and
Upper Conﬁdence Bound (UCB). Our implementation uses EI, which is:

                   EI(x) = max(μ(x) − f ∗ , 0)Φ(z) + σ(x)φ(z),                   (1)
where f ∗ is the current best energy eﬃciency value, μ(x) and σ(x) are the pre-
dicted mean and standard deviation of the Gaussian process at input point x, and
           ∗                 z             t2
z = μ(x)−f
      σ(x) . Also, Φ(z) = −∞ 2π exp − 2 dt is the cumulative distribution

function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution, and φ(z) = √12π exp − z2
is the probability density function (PDF) of the standard normal distribution.
max(·, ·) is used to ensure the improvement is non-negative.
    Based on function EI(x), the next frequency combination is selected by max-
imizing the EI function: x∗ = arg maxx EI(x). According to (1), when μ(x) is
much larger than f ∗ , EI is large, indicating a high expected improvement. Even
if μ(x) is not much larger than f ∗ , a large σ(x) can still yield a high EI, thereby
encouraging exploration in regions with high uncertainty.

Model Update. After the new sampling point x∗ is selected, an experiment
is run to measure its energy eﬃciency value, and the result y∗ is added to the

existing dataset. With this updated dataset, the Gaussian process (GP) model
will be recomputed to improve its accuracy.

Iterative Optimization and Convergence. Repeat the above sampling and
model updating steps, progressively searching for the optimal frequency combi-
nation. In each iteration, the updated model and acquisition function are used
to choose a new sampling point, gradually converging toward the optimum of
the objective function. After several iterations, when the value of the acquisition
function becomes suﬃciently small and the new sampling points oﬀer diminish-
ing improvements to the objective function, the optimization is considered to
have converged. At this point, the frequency combination returned by Bayesian
optimization is regarded as the optimal setting.


3.5   Computational Complexity

Assume the CPU oﬀers M distinct frequency states and the GPU oﬀers N ,
                                             (i)   (j)
leading to a discrete design space X = {(fCPU , fGPU ) | 1 ≤ i ≤ M, 1 ≤ j ≤ N } of
size K = M N .
    For the baseline exhaustive search, if each conﬁguration is evaluated R times
to suppress measurement noise, the baseline requires Cexh = R K = R M N
individual workload runs. With a single experiment taking wall time τ (tens of
seconds to a few minutes in our servers), the cost is Cexh τ .
    For the Bayesian-optimization-based CoDVFS, let T = T0 + TBO be the total
number of experiments: T0 random initial samples followed by TBO Bayesian-
guided iterations. Then, the experimental cost is T τ , which is typically 10-40
runs in our deployments, two orders of magnitude smaller than Cexh when both
M and N are greater than 10. The algorithmic overhead for each Bayesian
optimization iteration, Talg , is decomposed in the following:
           CoDVFS: Improving the Energy Eﬃciency of AI Servers Through        427

– GP posterior update. Naively O(t3 ) with t samples due to the matrix inver-
  sion operation of the kernel matrix. If implemented with rank-one Cholesky
  updates, the amortised cost can be reduced to O(t2 ).
– Hyper-parameter re-estimation. Performed every H iterations (typically H ≥
  5). Each call costs O(t3 ) but is infrequent.
– Acquisition maximization. For a discrete search we can enumerate only the
  unexplored points, costing O(K − T ) per iteration, or use a continuous opti-
  mizer whose complexity is O(Ld) where L is the number of L-BFGS steps
  and d=2 is the dimensionality.




                          Fig. 2. Experimental devices.


    Because t ≤ T K and d is small, the algorithmic overhead Talg is negligible
compared with the cost of running experiments itself.
    In summary, given T K and τ Talg , the practical runtime of CoDVFS is
dominated by T τ , yielding a speed-up factor ≈ Cexh /T = RM N/T ∼ 101 −102 .
As a result, CoDVFS reduces the number of costly workload executions by one
or two magnitude in practice, making coordinated DVFS feasible for AI servers.


4     Experimental Metho dology
This section describes the details of the hardware, workloads, power measure-
ment, frequency control, and baseline DVFS policies used in our experiments.

4.1   Server and Workload
The server used in this study is a DGX V100, as shown in Fig. 2(a). It is equipped
with two Intel Xeon E5-2698 v4 CPUs, providing a total of 40 physical cores and
80 threads, along with eight V100 GPUs. The GPUs run on CUDA 10.2. Each
GPU consumes an idle power of ∼42 W, and the total idle power of all GPUs is
∼336 W. The entire server consumes ∼750 W in idle state.
428     Y. Zhang et al.

    To evaluate the eﬀectiveness of our proposed CoDVFS framework, we used
HPL-MxP [6] as the primary workload and ran it inside the oﬃcial NVIDIA
container. HPL-MxP is a representative hybrid-precision workload based on the
traditional HPL benchmark, designed to leverage both CPU and GPU comput-
ing capabilities. It evaluates both double-precision computation in HPC scenarios
and low-precision operations commonly found in AI workloads. In addition to
HPL-MxP, we also tested the HPCG benchmark [11], which solves large sparse
linear systems using iterative methods. We used the GPU version of these bench-
marks released on the NVIDIA GPU Cloud platform.
    After setting both the CPU and GPU set to their maximum frequencies, we
conducted a grid search over the tunable parameters N (matrix size) and N B
(block size) of HPL-MxP. This search is a standard procedure, which runs tests
to identify the conﬁguration that delivers the server’s peak performance. After
completing the grid search, we used matrix size N = 204800 and block size
N B = 896 that yielded the highest performance. These two parameters were
ﬁxed in all subsequent energy eﬃciency optimization experiments, ensuring a
fair comparison of energy performance across diﬀerent control strategies under
consistent workload conditions.

4.2    Server/GPU Power Measurement Method and Frequency
       Control Method
In this study, we measured the server’s total power consumption using external
power meters (model GWGJ), as shown in Fig. 2(b). This power meter supports
TCP/IP-based communication via the SNMP protocol and can be controlled
through Python scripts with the pysnmp library, enabling remote real-time mon-
itoring and automated data logging. With a minimum valid sampling interval
of approximately 0.5 s, it is capable of capturing ﬂuctuations in dynamic server
power consumption.
    The DGX V100 server used in our experiments has four power supply units,
and its nominal maximum power consumption is 3500 W. To cover the full range
of server power draw, we deployed two power meters, each connected to two
power supply units, eﬀectively splitting the load. To obtain the total power,
we summed the readings from both meters. To set up the devices, each power
meter’s input side was connected to the rack’s power outlet, while the output
side was connected to two of the server’s power supply units.
    A simpliﬁed version of our codes for power meter reading is provided below:

    For monitoring GPU power consumption, we used the nvidia-smi tool,
which allows periodic readings of each GPU’s power usage with good preci-
sion [26]. This data helped us analyze the individual power trends of the CPU
and GPU and was also useful in later comparisons between GPU-only control
strategies and coordinated control strategies. It is worth noting that, because
measuring GPU power using nvidia-smi does not require deploying external
power meters, it is much easier than measuring whole-server power. This is one
of the main reasons why most prior GPU energy eﬃciency studies (as shown in
Table 1) have focused only on GPU power measurements. Section 6 will compare
whole-system energy eﬃciency with GPU-only energy eﬃciency in detail.
    For frequency control, we used the cpupower tool to set CPU frequencies.
The CPU frequency range was restricted between 1.2 GHz and 2.2 GHz, with
0.1 GHz intervals. For GPUs, we again used the nvidia-smi tool to set the
operating frequency. The GPU V100 we use oﬀers a tunable frequency range
from 135 MHz to 1440 MHz, with two adjustable frequency points every 15 MHz,
yielding a total of 175 frequency points. This provides a high degree of ﬂexibility
in tuning GPU frequency.


4.3   Comparison Strategies

In our experiments, we compare the proposed CoDVFS framework with several
common DVFS strategies to validate its eﬀectiveness:

– Only-CPU-DVFS: This strategy applies DVFS only to the CPU, while the
  GPU remains ﬁxed at its maximum frequency.
– Only-GPU-DVFS: This strategy applies DVFS solely to the GPU, keeping
  the CPU ﬁxed at its maximum frequency.
430    Y. Zhang et al.

– MaxFreq: In this strategy, both the CPU and GPU operate at their maxi-
  mum frequencies. This is the default conﬁguration applied in many clusters
  with the aim of maximizing performance.
– MinFreq: This strategy sets both the CPU and GPU to their minimum
  frequencies. It helps measure the power control range of the server and is
  applicable in scenarios with strict power caps, such as when participating in
  electricity curtailment plans.

   Our experiments mainly compare metrics including energy eﬃciency, perfor-
mance, and average power. For performance, we directly read the ﬂoating-point
computation performance reported by HPL-MxP and HPCG.

5     Experimental Results
In this section, we ﬁrst present the results from a coarse-grained DVFS brute-
force search. Then, we show the results of experiments using CoDVFS.

5.1   Coarse-Grained CPU-GPU DVFS Brute-Force Search
To analyze the value of coordinated CPU-GPU DVFS, we ﬁrst performed a
coarse-grained brute-force search over CPU and GPU frequency combinations.
In the experiment, we selected 11 frequency points for the CPU, ranging from
1.2 GHz to 2.2 GHz, and 11 frequency points for the GPU, ranging from 135 MHz
to 1440 MHz. For each frequency pair, we ran the HPL-MxP workload ﬁve times,
and the average of the ﬁve runs was taken as the ﬁnal measurement value.
    Figure 3 shows the results of this exhaustive search: Fig. 3(a) presents the
measured performance of HPL-MxP in TFlops; Fig. 3(b) shows the average
server power in watts, measured using the external power meters; Fig. 3(c) shows
the energy eﬃciency in GFlops/W.
    From Figs. 3(a) and (b), we observe that as the CPU and GPU frequency
increases, both overall performance and power show a gradual increase. The high-
est performance and power are achieved when both CPU and GPU frequencies
are set near their maximum values. At this point, server power reaches 1702 W,
signiﬁcantly higher than the 911 W observed at the lowest frequency combina-
tion. Although in practical scenarios it is uncommon to set both CPU and GPU
to their minimum frequencies due to performance demands, this extreme case
demonstrates that coordinated DVFS can regulate server power consumption
across nearly a 50% range. This has practical signiﬁcance for computing clusters
whose total power is constrained, such as in power-capped environments.
    Compared with the monotonic increases observed in power and performance,
the energy eﬃciency results in Fig. 3(c) reveal more interesting patterns. Energy
eﬃciency does not continuously increase with rising frequency. Instead, it reaches
a peak value of 122.6 GFlops/W when the CPU frequency is set to 2.1 GHz and
the GPU frequency to 915 MHz. This peak highlights the potential advantage of
coordinated CPU-GPU DVFS.
    These results show that if DVFS is applied to only the CPU or only the
GPU, it may not discover this optimal frequency combination, and such single-
component strategies are unlikely to achieve a comparable level of energy eﬃ-
ciency. These ﬁndings also emphasize that to fully exploit the potential of coor-
dinated CPU-GPU control, it is essential for both the CPU and GPU to sup-
port a suﬃcient number of adjustable frequency levels. If only a small set of
DVFS options is available, optimization accuracy will be greatly reduced, and
the resulting energy eﬃciency may fall short of the theoretical optimum.

5.2   CoDVFS Optimization Exp eriment
In this experiment, we ran the CoDVFS framework to perform Bayesian opti-
mization for coordinated CPU-GPU frequency control. Unlike the previous
432    Y. Zhang et al.




                   Fig. 4. Trajectory of Bayesian optimization.


section where GPU frequency selection was limited to 11 points, here we
expanded the GPU frequency search space to all 175 available frequency points,
aiming to ﬁnd the optimal solution in the complete frequency space.
    Experimental results show that CoDVFS was able to determine the opti-
mal frequency setting in just 20 iterations. For HPL-MxP, the obtained optimal
setting is CPU at 2.1 GHz and GPU at 1035 MHz, resulting in a server energy
eﬃciency of 123.2 GFlops/W. The optimization trajectory is illustrated in Fig. 4.
It can be observed that the algorithm balances exploration and exploitation and
eventually identiﬁes the frequency combination with the best energy eﬃciency.
    This result clearly demonstrates the eﬃciency of CoDVFS in coordinated
DVFS control. In contrast, using an exhaustive search approach would require
evaluating 11 CPU frequency points × 175 GPU frequency points = 1925 combi-
nations, which is impractical to execute on real-world systems. While experienced
engineers may be able to manually reduce the number of tests by heuristically
pruning the search space, manual tuning lacks scalability and automation, mak-
ing it diﬃcult to apply broadly in complex and dynamic cluster environments
across various programs.
    CoDVFS, by leveraging the eﬃcient search mechanism of Bayesian optimiza-
tion, can rapidly locate high-eﬃciency conﬁgurations even in large search spaces.
This oﬀers a practical and scalable solution for extending the framework to other
deep learning or high-performance computing workloads.
    In Fig. 5(a), we compare this optimal point with the baseline strategies, with
all values normalized against the MaxFreq strategy (i.e., both CPU and GPU set
to their highest frequencies). The ﬁgure shows that while MaxFreq can shorten
execution time to some extent, it signiﬁcantly reduces energy eﬃciency. In con-
trast, under the CoDVFS strategy, energy eﬃciency improves by 17.5% compared
to the MaxFreq baseline, while performance is only 4.3% lower, and average
power consumption drops by more than 18%. Considering that many computing

Fig. 5. Comparison of diﬀerent DVFS strategies, and comparison of whole-
server/GPU-only energy eﬃciency.


clusters default to running processors at their maximum frequencies, this result
demonstrates the importance of coordinated CPU-GPU DVFS.
    Furthermore, comparing with a scenario that applies CPU-only frequency
optimization (CPU at 2.1 GHz, GPU at 1440 MHz), CoDVFS still achieves a 17%
higher energy eﬃciency. When compared to GPU-only frequency optimization
(CPU at 2.2 GHz, GPU at 915 MHz), CoDVFS improves energy eﬃciency by
1.2%. These comparisons indicate that while optimizing a single component can
bring some energy eﬃciency gains, it is insuﬃcient to fully exploit the joint
potential of the CPU and GPU. Only by integrating DVFS strategies for both
components can we achieve the maximum possible energy eﬃciency.
    Similar results are observed for the HPCG benchmark. CoDVFS achieves an
energy eﬃciency of 15.63 GFlops/W at the optimal point found within 20 itera-
tions, representing a 12% improvement compared to MaxFreq’s 13.93 GFlops/W,
while the performance degrades by only 1%.

6     Discussion: Comparing Whole-Server Energy Eﬃciency
      and GPU Energy Eﬃciency

In previous work, it was often assumed by default that optimizing GPU energy
eﬃciency is equivalent to optimizing server energy eﬃciency. In this section, we
carefully analyze the diﬀerences between the two and provide a criterion for
establishing their equivalence.


6.1   The Distinction Between Two Metrics

In an AI computing server, components such as the CPU, GPU, motherboard,
fans, memory, storage, and network adapters collectively determine the total
server power consumption. Therefore, server-level energy eﬃciency is deﬁned
as the ratio of application performance to the total power consumption of all
components. In contrast, if we consider only the GPU, we are calculating the
ratio of performance to GPU power, resulting in the GPU energy eﬃciency.
    The distinction between the two can be clearly understood through the fol-
lowing formulas:
    GPU energy eﬃciency = (Performance)/(GPU power),
    Server energy eﬃciency = (Performance)/(GPU power + non-GPU power).
From the deﬁnition above, we also have:
    Server energy eﬃciency = GPU energy eﬃciency × GPU power ratio,
    GPU power ratio = (GPU power)/(GPU power + non-GPU power).
Clearly, when the GPU power ratio is constant, optimizing server energy eﬃ-
ciency is equivalent to optimizing GPU energy eﬃciency. However, in real-world
environments, the GPU power ratio varies dynamically, so we cannot directly
treat these two quantities as equivalent.
    In fact, during coordinated DVFS, the frequencies and voltages of both the
CPU and GPU are continuously adjusted, which not only aﬀects their individual
power consumption but also indirectly alters the power draw of other components
such as fans, memory, and the motherboard. This variability makes the GPU
power ratio no longer ﬁxed.
    In most prior research (see Table 1), due to experimental constraints, the
focus has been solely on GPU energy eﬃciency, using tools like nvidia-smi to
obtain GPU power data for analysis and optimization. However, comprehen-
sively evaluating whole-server energy eﬃciency requires external power meters
and power wiring reconﬁguration to measure total consumption, which is often
infeasible in real data centers. Consequently, research on whole-server energy
eﬃciency has been relatively limited.
    The problem of focusing on GPU energy eﬃciency is that the optimal point
for GPU energy eﬃciency does not always coincide with the optimal point for
server energy eﬃciency. Although the discrepancy was small in our experiments,
there is no guarantee that the alignment of the two optimal points will hold true
under diﬀerent hardware conﬁgurations and workloads.
            CoDVFS: Improving the Energy Eﬃciency of AI Servers Through                435

search, their actual optimal frequency points would not exactly coincide. How-
436    Y. Zhang et al.

ever, since energy eﬃciency curves tend to be relatively ﬂat near their extrema,
this discrepancy would not result in signiﬁcant performance or power loss.
    In other words, in this setting, if we choose to use GPU energy eﬃciency as
a reference, the resulting optimal frequency is likely to be close to the system-
wide optimal frequency. From a practical application perspective, this represents
a feasible approximation method.

server energy eﬃciency coincide, we present an analytical criterion.
    Let performance be denoted as f (x), GPU power as g(x), and non-GPU
power as h(x), all of which are smooth functions of frequency x. Then, the
GPU energy eﬃciency is deﬁned as U (x) = fg(x) (x)

    The solution to this equation is the shared optimum point. In other words, we
have the following Optimum Alignment Criterion: if at the GPU’s energy
eﬃciency optimal point, the relative growth rate of GPU power is equal to the
relative growth rate of non-GPU power, then this point is also the server’s energy
eﬃciency optimal point.
    In the last three rows of Table 2, we present the discrete diﬀerences between
adjacent columns to approximate the growth rates of each quantity across fre-
quency intervals. We observe that around 915 MHz, the growth rates of both
performance and non-GPU power begin to decline, while the growth rate of
GPU power increases rapidly, which is consistent with our criterion.
    We suspect that the operational behavior of the server’s cooling fans explains
why non-GPU power initially increases signiﬁcantly and later stabilizes as GPU
frequency increases. In our experiment, the CPU frequency was ﬁxed at 2.1 GHz,
meaning CPU-side power remained relatively stable. However, as the GPU fre-
quency rose, system heat output increased sharply, triggering an increase in fan
speed, which in turn boosted non-GPU component power.
    Once the fans approached their maximum speed, further increases in GPU
frequency no longer caused fan power increases, leading to a plateau in non-GPU
power, as shown by the green line in Fig. 5(c). This power trend is relatively
common in servers using air-cooling technologies. If alternative cooling methods
such as liquid cooling are adopted, the impact of the fans may be signiﬁcantly
reduced, which could also change the overall trend of non-GPU power. In such
cases, the deviation between GPU energy eﬃciency and server energy eﬃciency
may increase, necessitating further in-depth comparative study.
           CoDVFS: Improving the Energy Eﬃciency of AI Servers Through              437

    In summary, when comparing GPU and server energy eﬃciency, their two
optimal points do not necessarily align under DVFS control, due to the non-
constant GPU power ratio. However, in the workload and hardware conﬁguration
used in our experiment, the two optima were closely aligned, which validates
the feasibility of using GPU energy eﬃciency (which is easier to measure) to
approximate whole-server energy eﬃciency.
    At the same time, it’s important to recognize that in other setups, such as
liquid-cooled servers, cooling power characteristics may diﬀer signiﬁcantly. This
could widen the gap between GPU and server energy eﬃciency, underscoring
the need for further study. Deeper understanding of this issue will contribute to
more accurate system-level energy eﬃciency evaluation and optimization, and
provide new insights for future research in green computing and thermal design.

7   Conclusion and Future Work
This study proposes CoDVFS, a CPU-GPU joint frequency control framework
for AI server energy eﬃciency. Experiments on a DGX V100 show Bayesian opti-
mization eﬀectively ﬁnds optimal frequency combinations, achieving 17% higher
energy eﬃciency than default settings under HPL-MxP workloads. While GPU-
only and whole-server optima show minor diﬀerences, GPU eﬃciency serves as
a reliable proxy. Future work includes ﬁner-grained DVFS for multi-stage work-
loads, multi-task CPU-GPU coordination, and revisiting GPU-system eﬃciency
alignment under liquid cooling.

          Machine Learning and Data Statistics
          Based Scalability Bottleneck Detection

        Yuhan Cao, Haoming Zhan, Juan Chen(B) , and Mingyuan Zhang

    College of Computer Science and Technology, National University of Defense
                          Technology, Changsha, China
          {caoyuhan23,zhm441x,juanchen,zhangmingyuan}@nudt.edu.cn


       Abstract. The continuously expanding problem scale of scientiﬁc com-
       puting applications has demanded massive parallel computing resources.
       However, the scalability bottlenecks of parallel programs severely con-
       strain computational eﬃciency and performance gain. Current MPI par-
       allel program scalability bottleneck detection faces three main issues:
       inaccurate prediction of the parallel performance inﬂection at the pro-
       gram level; diﬃculty in locating the speciﬁc bottleneck segments at the
       segment level; and low eﬃciency in identifying key performance events
       from massive data at the performance event level. To address the above
       issues, we propose the machine learning and data statistics-based scalabil-
       ity bottleneck detection framework (POPP-SOPP-KER). POPP builds a
       decision tree model with aggregation of segment features to improve pre-
       diction accuracy of performance inﬂection. SOPP uses type-aware feature
       selection to reduce deviations in segment-level optimal parallelism pre-
       diction, precisely locating bottleneck segments. KER recognizes the key
       events through KL divergence and mutual information correlation-based
       statistical method, improving the recognizing eﬃciency. Experimental
       veriﬁcations are conducted on two compute clusters (x86 and ARM, each
       with 2048 cores). POPP achieves an average accuracy of 70% (x86) and
       60% (ARM) in performance inﬂection prediction, exceeding that of non-
       segmented methods. SOPP decreases prediction deviation of theoretical
       segment optimal parallelism by 13.2% (x86) and 11.88% (ARM) com-
       pared to using all features. KER eﬀectively recognizes key features within
       65 PMCs. By comparing key features based on performance inﬂection
       grouping, KER is proven beneﬁcial. The proposed framework employs
       data-driven approaches for scalability bottleneck detection, providing
       insights for optimizing the scalability of large-scale applications.


       Keywords: Scalability bottleneck · Optimal parallelism degree · MPI
       parallel program · performance optimization


1    Introduction
The potential of large-scale computing systems is often unrealized due to the
poor scalability of parallel programs [31]. Poor scalability prevents parallel pro-
grams from achieving higher performance, slowing problem-solving and wasting
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 440–461, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_24
                                      Machine Learning and Data Statistics      441

computing resources. Scalability bottlenecks stem from various aspects, such as
communication overhead, load imbalance, and contention for shared resources
[22]. Complex parallel programs exhibit behavioral changes during execution,
leading to potential shifts in scalability bottlenecks. Detecting scalability bot-
tlenecks in parallel programs has become a key issue in enhancing parallel com-
puting eﬃciency.
    Current research on the scalability bottlenecks of parallel programs mainly
focuses on three aspects. In terms of performance inﬂection prediction, exist-
ing research mainly relies on performance models [5,30,36]. However, prediction
accuracy tends to decrease when the parallel scale gets large [35]. In identify-
ing program bottleneck segments, existing performance analysis tools like HPC-
Toolkit [3] and TAU [29] oﬀer capabilities for detecting scalability loss. However,
Xuan et al. [33] note that current performance analysis tools still fail to pinpoint
the root causes of scalability issues. The mechanistic analysis typically relies on
manual expertise for optimization [20] or focuses on speciﬁc performance issues
[4,21]. In scenarios with massive performance data, manual feature analysis is
laborious, making automated methods essential.
    This paper focuses on the scalability bottleneck appearance and bottleneck
cause analysis of MPI (Message Passing Interface) parallel programs from pro-
gram, segment, and performance event levels, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Assume
the MPI parallel program runs at a certain parallelism. Three key issues are
encountered as below:
    (Issue 1) When Predicting the Performance Inﬂection at the Pro-
gram Level, the Neglect of Segment Behavior Leads to Inaccurate Per-
formance Inﬂection Predictions. Existing methods typically rely on global
performance metrics [15] (e.g., total instruction count) to reﬂect program behav-
ior. However, the scalability of a program is not determined by its “average”
behavior, but by the behavior of its individual segments. The neglect of segment-
speciﬁc implications may lead to inaccurate performance inﬂection predictions
p∗app , making it diﬃcult to balance the program runtime and resource costs.
    To analyze the causes of performance inﬂection, it is necessary to identify
which program segments and performance events are responsible for the scala-
bility bottlenecks.
    (Issue 2) At the Segment Level, Accurately Locating the Speciﬁc
Bottleneck Segments is Challenging Due to Signiﬁcant Diﬀerences
Among the Segments. The core of inﬂection cause analysis is to identify
which segments of the program cannot eﬃciently utilize the current level of par-
allelism, thereby limiting the overall application scalability. However, due to the
vast diﬀerences in communication or computation behaviors between program
segments, accurately assessing their optimal parallelism p∗seg is challenging, lead-
ing to poor bottleneck locating.
    (Issue 3) At the Performance Event Level, Manually Analyzing the
Vast Amount of Performance Event Data is Ineﬃcient and Impracti-
cal. The ﬁnal step in inﬂection cause analysis is to recognize key performance
events to ﬁnd the cause of the bottleneck. This requires analyzing the massive,
442     Y. Cao et al.




Fig. 1. Scalability bottleneck appearance and cause inference from program, segment,
and performance event levels.


high-dimensional performance event data generated during program execution.
Relying on manual analysis to search for causes, like memory bandwidth sat-
uration, from terabytes of data is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and almost
impossible to complete.
    To address the above issues, we develop a scalability bottleneck detection
framework based on machine learning and data statistics. The foundation lies in
dividing parallel programs into comm and non-comm segments to leverage the
segments’ performance features. Speciﬁcally, these performance features serve
to predict p∗app . Due to disparities between comm and non-comm segments, the
model input features are carefully diﬀerentiated to reduce prediction deviation
for p∗seg to accurately locate the bottleneck segments. By quantifying statistical
metrics of performance data, key performance events are recognized eﬃciently
in high-dimensional big-data scenarios.
    To sum up, our main contributions are summarized as follows:
– For issue 1, POPP is proposed to improve the program performance inﬂection
  p∗app prediction accuracy. POPP utilizes segment features to build decision
  tree prediction model.
– For issue 2, SOPP is proposed to predict optimal segment parallelism degree
  p∗seg , which aids in accurately locating bottleneck segments. SOPP distin-
  guishes input features for comm and non-comm segments based on resource
  needs in order to reduce prediction deviation
– For issue 3, KER is proposed to eﬃciently recognize the key events. Through
  quantifying data distribution diﬀerences by KL divergence and event cor-
  relations by mutual information, the key performance events of bottleneck
  segments and performance inﬂection are recognized.
– Experimental veriﬁcations are conducted on two compute clusters (x86 and
  ARM, each with 2048 cores). POPP exceeds non-segmented methods in per-
  formance inﬂection prediction with an average accuracy of 70% (x86) and 60%
  (ARM). SOPP decreases prediction deviation of theoretical segment optimal
  parallelism by 13.2% (x86) and 11.88% (ARM) compared to methods without
  feature selection. KER eﬀectively recognizes key performance events within
  65 PMCs. Group comparisons of key features based on performance inﬂection
  validate the eﬀectiveness of KER.
