2     Motivation
2.1   Segment Features Aﬀect MPI Program Optimal Parallelism
Choosing an inappropriate number of processor cores may negatively impact the
performance of large-scale parallel programs. The prolonged execution times of
large-scale computing tasks not only hinder progress in scientiﬁc and engineering
research but also result in substantial energy waste and economic costs. However,
the naive approach of repeatedly executing the application with diﬀerent core
numbers to ﬁnd the optimal parallelism degree is prohibitively expensive in terms
of both time and computational resources. Therefore, methods for accurately
and rapidly predicting optimal parallelism need to be investigated to avoid this
exhaustive testing process.
    The program optimal parallelism is probably inﬂuenced by its segments’
properties. Parallel programs exhibit distinct computation or communication
characteristics at diﬀerent phases during execution. As shown in Fig. 2, one
comm segment and one non-comm segment of LU (D) (p∗app =512) consistently
decrease with increasing core number. In contrast, the two segments of CG (C)
(p∗app =64) exhibit signiﬁcant time growth over 64 cores. However, most existing
prediction methods rely on global performance metrics (total execution time and
instruction count) [15]. Such metrics average all segment behaviors, making it
hard to identify behavioral variances between segments with diﬀerent attributes,
resulting in low prediction accuracy.


2.2   Bottleneck Segments Aﬀect the Performance Inﬂection
      Formation

Bottleneck segments are speciﬁc parts of a parallel program that experience
severe performance degradation when the program-level optimal parallelism
(p∗app ) exceeds their individual optimal parallelism (p∗seg ). p∗seg is deﬁned as the
parallelism degree where a segment achieves its minimal execution time during
444     Y. Cao et al.

program runs across parallelism conﬁgurations. Crucially, when p∗seg is substan-
tially lower than p∗app , that segment may suﬀer severe degradation at higher
program-level parallelism. This localized performance collapse not only hinders
overall program computing eﬃciency but forms scalability bottlenecks. Such seg-
ments constitute the fundamental cause of performance inﬂection points. How-
ever, obtaining p∗seg through exhaustive testing is computationally expensive,
making it necessary to predict it instead.
    Existing prediction methods often suﬀer from large prediction deviations,
resulting in unreliable location results. These methods typically utilize Per-
formance Monitor Counters (PMCs) as features, selected through correlation
analysis or empirical heuristics [27,32]. Their major limitation is adopting ﬁxed
feature sets universally, overlooking fundamental diﬀerences between compute-
intensive and communication-intensive segments. Accurate prediction of p∗seg
requires input features that eﬀectively reﬂect distinctions between computational
and communication behaviors.

2.3   Cause Analysis of Scalability Bottleneck Depends on Key
      Performance Events

Key performance events refer to program behaviour events that aﬀect the scal-
ability of parallel programs, which are captured in performance proﬁle data
[8]. Recognizing key events often requires expertise in both software and hard-
ware, typically accumulated through repeated execution and observation of pro-
grams on a speciﬁc platform. For instance, determining whether a program is
memory-bound on a given architecture requires experience gained from analysis
of extensive program execution. Furthermore, performance proﬁle data has high
dimensionality and large volume, which makes manual analysis ineﬃcient. It is
impractical for experts to examine hundreds of metrics individually to recognize
key events reliably.
    Eﬀectively leveraging the performance event data to analyze bottlenecks
remains a critical issue. The performance events arise from interactions across
hardware, system, and application layers, each contributing collectively to
performance and further complicating the identiﬁcation process. Hardware
features reﬂect physical operation eﬃciency, system features represent data
access/management eﬃciency, and application features capture problem-solving
eﬃciency.


3     Scalability Bottleneck Detection Framework
Figure 3 illustrates the machine learning and data statistics-based scalability
bottleneck detection framework. The framework is based on the communication
and non-communication segment features of MPI programs, with the following
implementation steps. First, the SOPP method is proposed to predict the opti-
mal parallelism of each program segment (pseg ) by type-aware feature selection,
aiming to accurately identify the speciﬁc bottleneck segment (solving Issue 2).
                                      Machine Learning and Data Statistics     445




Fig. 3. Machine learning and data statistics based scalability bottleneck detection
framework


Next, the POPP model is built to predict the performance inﬂection (papp ) of
the program through aggregating segment features, thus enabling rapid determi-
nation of the optimal core count (solving Issue 1). Finally, the KER method is
applied to automatically analyze the causes of the bottleneck, replacing manual
analysis (solving Issue 3).

3.1   Segmentation Algorithm Based on MPI Communication
Since communication characteristics signiﬁcantly aﬀect the performance of par-
allel programs, the program’s execution is divided into comm segments and non-
comm segments for subsequent performance bottleneck analysis. Communication
time is often discontinuous on the program execution time axis and is determined
by the parallel program algorithm. The communication time exhibits multiple
short-duration characteristics on the program runtime timeline, with the commu-
nication start time determined by the algorithm; the non-communication periods
are relatively long, during which the program performs computation and memory
access.
    The segmentation algorithm is based on MPI communication events, aggre-
gating consecutive communication timestamps into segments, thereby obtaining
comm segments and non-comm segments, as shown in Algorithm 1. First, if a
timestamp has comm counts or comm volume, it is determined to be a comm
timestamp. Then, consecutive comm timestamps are merged into comm seg-
ments, resulting in a comm segment list COM M s. Finally, the non-comm seg-
ment list nonCOM M s is obtained by computing the complement of the comm
segments on the program execution time axis.

3.2   SOPP: Type-Aware Feature Selection Based Theoretical
      Segment Optimal Parallelism Prediction
Selecting features for the optimal parallelism prediction model requires taking
into account diﬀerent communication patterns [25,32]. The core bottleneck of the
comm segment may lie in global communication, where its eigenvectors should
446    Y. Cao et al.

Algorithm 1. Segmentation algorithm based on MPI communication
Require: parallel program performance dataset D, di ∈ D is composed of com-
    munication indicators with timestamp t ∈ [1, n]: countcomm and volumecomm
Ensure: comm segments COM Ms and non-comm segments nonCOM Ms
 1: iscomm[t] ← False                                 Initialize comm timestamp
 2: for t = 1 to n do
 3:    if countcomm ∨ volumecomm then
 4:       iscomm[t] ← True
 5:    end if
 6: end for
 7: COM Ms ← ∅, start ← None                           Initialize comm segments
 8: for t = 1 to n do
 9:    if iscomm[t] ∧ start = None then
10:       start ← t
11:    else if ¬iscomm[t] ∧ start = None then
12:       end ← t − 1
13:       COM Ms ← COM Ms ∪ {(start, end)}
14:       start ← None
15:    end if
16: end for
17: if start = None then
18:    COM Ms ← COM Ms ∪ {(start, n)}
19: end if                                                Obtain the comm segs
20: nonCOM Ms ← Complement(COM Ms )                  Obtain the non-comm segs
21: return COM Ms , nonCOM Ms



prioritize metrics like comm time and data volume (x_comm). While the non-
comm segment prioritizes computation and memory access features (x_comp).
The feature vector of one program x consists of n1 comm-related features and
n2 computing-related features, with the vector length n = n1 + n2 . The diﬀer-
entiation selection is as follows: n1 ≥ n2 for comm segments, that is, choosing
more comm-related features, while n1 = 0, n2 > 0 for non-comm segments.
    The theoretical optimal parallelism prediction of segments is based on the
idea of using small-scale data to predict large-scale conﬁgurations [7]. The the-
oretical optimal parallelism of segments represents the performance mutation of
speciﬁc segments. The Artiﬁcial Neural Network (ANN) structures have the nat-
ural advantages in solving nonlinear mapping problems based on feature data,
which can be used to solve the problem of capturing performance mutations.
First, organize the segment’s q-dimensional feature data (the speciﬁc q features
depend on the segment type) under p small parallelisms into a p · q feature
vector as training input data; then, use an artiﬁcial neural network model to
learn the correlation between the feature vector and the optimal parallelism.
The algorithm ﬂow is shown in Algorithm 2.

Ensure: Target segment optimal parallelism predicted value p̂seg
 1: type = classif ier(x_settarget ), type ∈ {0, 1}               t=0 represents
    non-comm-seg, t=1 represents comm-seg
 2: if t = 0 then
 3:    return non-comm feature set x_setnon
 4: else
 5:    return comm feature set x_setcomm
                                  Feature selection based on target segment type
 6: end if
 7: p∗ _set = AN N (x_setnon , train) or p∗ _set = AN N (x_setcomm , train)
 8: p̂seg = AN N (x_settarget , predict)
 9: return p̂seg



     The SOPP prediction values are used to locate bottleneck segments. Locat-
ing bottlenecks in parallel programs requires comparing the theoretical optimal
parallelism of a segment (p∗seg ) to the program optimal parallelism (p∗app ). Here,
p∗seg represents the maximum number of processor cores that the segment can
eﬀectively utilize to reach its top performance, while p∗app indicates the paral-
lelism for best program performance. A larger diﬀerence between p∗seg and p∗app
indicates that the segment is less suited for high parallelism. The bottleneck
segment locating rule is shown as Eq. 1: the logarithmic diﬀerence between the
p∗seg and p∗app is greater than zero.

                            log2 (p∗app ) − log2 (p∗seg ) > 0                   (1)


3.3   POPP: Program Optimal Parallelism Prediction Based
      on Aggregation of Segment Performance Features

Segment performance features reﬂect local program properties. Selecting the
theoretical optimal parallelism of segments as input features quantiﬁes the local
scalability of parallel programs, providing a more accurate basis for predicting
parallelism conﬁgurations.
    Since diﬀerent programs often contain diﬀerent numbers of program seg-
ments, using raw features may directly result in inconsistent input dimensions,
making them unsuitable for model training. To address the issue of inconsis-
tent segment counts, the POPP algorithm applies zero-padding to construct
ﬁxed-length feature vectors by standardizing all feature vectors to the same
length. Then, the input feature set and labels are organized by aggregating each
ﬁxed-length feature vector to form the complete input feature set for the par-
allel program set. The true optimal parallelism degree of each parallel program
is used as the training label, corresponding to its ﬁxed-length feature vector.
448     Y. Cao et al.

Algorithm 3. POPP: program optimal parallelism prediction
Require: the number of parallel programs m, the set of the theoretical opti-
    mal parallelism of n segments of each program X = {x1 , . . . , xn }, optimal
    parallelism pi of ith program, max segment count N of one program
Ensure: program optimal parallelism predicted value p̂app
 1: if n < N then
 2:     {xn+1 , . . . , xN } = 0, X = {x1 , . . . , xN }         uniform input length
 3: end if
 4: training_set = {(X1 , p1 ), . . . , (Xm , pm )}                  build training set
 5: pˆi = T reeRegression(training_set, train)           Train decision tree regression
    model
 6: p̂app = T reeRegression(target_set, predict)
 7: return p̂app



Based on this collection of feature vectors and the corresponding optimal par-
allelism labels at the program level, a decision tree regression model is trained,
as illustrated in Algorithm 3. The decision tree regression model automatically
determines which features are most critical for prediction, capturing the non-
linear relationship between segment-level parallelism and overall performance.
The goal of model training is to minimize the deviation between predicted and
actual parallelism, thereby improving prediction accuracy.


3.4   KER: Key Event Recognition Based on Data Statistical
      Methods
Data statistical methods are ideal for recognizing key performance events due to
their quantiﬁability and ability to handle complex, high-dimensional data. Key
event recognition focuses on two aspects: during program execution, anomalous
events within bottleneck segments are detected by comparing their distributions
against the program’s overall distribution; across diﬀerent degrees of parallelism,
the events most strongly correlated with changes in execution time are identiﬁed.
    It is worth noting that the key performance events identiﬁed by KER are typ-
ically abnormal performance events that cause performance bottlenecks, while
the feature selection method of SOPP focuses on selecting features for improving
the accuracy of the prediction model. The performance features selected by the
two methods are independent and not directly related.


Key Event Recognition for Bottleneck Segments Based on KL Diver-
gence. The core idea is to detect discrepancy in performance event distributions
between bottleneck segments and the overall program proﬁle. Speciﬁc root causes
of bottlenecks (like resource contention) typically manifest as abnormal patterns
in key metrics (e.g., cache hit rate). By comparing these distributions, anomalous
events indicative of bottlenecks can be directly identiﬁed.
                                      Machine Learning and Data Statistics    449

    The Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence is selected as the discrepancy metric.
KL Divergence requires no prior assumption about the underlying data distribu-
tion, making it broadly applicable to diverse performance metrics. Its principle
involves quantifying the information diﬀerence when approximating the bottle-
neck segment distribution (P) with the global distribution (Q). A larger KL value
indicates a greater discrepancy. The calculation formula is shown in Eq. 2. Ulti-
mately, by independently computing the KL Divergence values for each event
and ranking the results, the key events with the most pronounced distribution
anomalies can be automatically recognized.

                                                            P (x)
                       DKL (P      Q) =          P (x)log                     (2)
                                                            Q(x)
                                           x∈X

x represents the event value in the sampled data. P (x) or Q(x) denote the
probability of the event taking value x in the bottleneck segment or during the
program execution. X indicates the set of all possible event values.


Key Event Recognition for Performance Inﬂection Based on Mutual
Information. The core idea is analyzing the correlation between various per-
formance events and the execution time of parallel programs under diﬀerent
parallelism degrees. By quantifying the correlation between events and execu-
tion time, the core factors causing performance degradation can be pinpointed.
    Mutual Information (MI) is chosen as the correlation metric. MI captures
any statistical dependency, making it ideal for analyzing parallel program perfor-
mance variations. Crucially, unlike Pearson correlation, MI quantiﬁes non-linear
and non-monotonic relationships (e.g., periodic ﬂuctuations) between events and
execution time. The MI value I(X; Y ) measures how much knowing event X
reduces uncertainty about execution time Y . A higher MI value indicates a
stronger association, meaning event X more signiﬁcantly explains variations in
performance (Y ), as shown in Eq. 3.

                                                           p(x, y)
                    I(X; Y ) =             p(x, y) log(            )          (3)
                                                          p(x)p(y)
                                 x∈X y∈Y

X and Y represent the discrete sets of values for event X and execution time Y.
p(x) and p(y) represent the marginal probability distributions of X and Y, while
p(x, y) represents the joint probability distribution of X and Y.


4     Experiments
4.1   Experimental Design
Validation of Scalability Bottleneck Appearance Prediction. The opti-
mal parallelism prediction employs a stepwise validation approach. First, a base-
line Artiﬁcial Neural Network (ANN) model is established, using all available
performance metrics collected from program runs at small-scale parallelism (4,
450    Y. Cao et al.

                        Table 1. Platform Speciﬁcations

                           x86 Platform                   ARM Platform
        CPU Name           Intel Xeon Platinum 8358P ARMv8-based
        Frequency          2.6 GHz                        2.2 GHz
        #Sockets           2                              8
        #Cores             64                             64
        RAM                512 GB                         128 GB
        Thread(s)/core 1                                  1
        #Nodes             32                             32
        #total cores       2048                           2048


8, 16 cores) to predict segment optimal parallelism or the program optimal par-
allelism. Next, the eﬀectiveness of the Segment Optimal Parallelism Prediction
(SOPP) is veriﬁed by comparing its predictions against this baseline. Finally,
the Program Optimal Parallelism Prediction (POPP)’s eﬀectiveness is validated
using the segment optimal parallelism values (p∗seg ) as input features.

Validation of Scalability Bottleneck Cause Inference. First, verify the
accuracy of bottleneck segment identiﬁcation: compare the baseline model and
the SOPP, analyzing their eﬀects in identifying bottleneck program segments.
Second, verify the eﬀectiveness of key event recognition: group segments and
parallel programs according to their optimal parallelisms. If similar events are
recognized for programs within the same group, the key event recognition method
is validated as eﬀective.

Experimental Environment. The above methods are validated on x86 and
ARM computing clusters (64 cores per node), with hardware conﬁgurations spec-
iﬁed in Table 1. Each cluster includes 32 nodes, with 2048 cores supported.
    Three benchmark suites are used: NPB [26], HPCG [18], and Graph500 [14].
Each process occupies one core by default. PMC, system load, and memory
usage metrics are collected by Linux perf, top, and free on both platforms.
Communication events are captured via the mpiP tool [1].
    In the training process of SOPP and POPP models, the feature sets from pro-
grams other than the target program are used as training data. SOPP employs
a three-layer ANN structure. The input layer has a feature dimension ranging
from 90 to 120, while the two hidden layers contain 128 and 100 neurons, both
utilizing the ReLU activation function. The dataset for SOPP is randomly split
into training and test sets in a 9:1 ratio for model training and evaluation. For
the POPP model’s decision tree regression algorithm, a grid search is conducted
on the tree depth hyperparameter, and the model with the optimal predictive
performance is selected for ﬁnal prediction.
                                      Machine Learning and Data Statistics     451

   Prediction accuracy and prediction deviation are metrics for evaluating the
optimal parallelism prediction. Prediction accuracy measures the proportion of
programs for which the optimal parallelism is correctly predicted, out of the total
number of test programs. Prediction deviation measures the prediction eﬀect of
each sample, which is calculated as the absolute logarithmic diﬀerence between
predicted and actual values, as shown in Eq. 4 (e.g., the deviation between 256
and 512 is 1).

            deviation =| log2 (actual_value) − log2 (predicted_value) |        (4)


4.2   The Bottleneck Segment can be More Accurately Identiﬁed
      Based on the SOPP Prediction
SOPP Accuracy and Deviation. Based on the SOPP feature selection
method based on segment types, speciﬁc input features of comm and non-comm
segments are chosen through multiple runs of the prediction model. Only those
features that contribute to improving predictive accuracy are retained. SOPP
selects 20 input features for comm segments, including 12 communication fea-
tures and 8 others, such as branch instructions and CPU migration. Non-comm
segments have 30 input features, including features related to branch instruc-
tions, CPU state, cache/memory access, and page tables. The speciﬁc input
features are selected by experience. The baseline method uses all 65 features
without feature selection.
    As shown in Fig. 4, SOPP outperforms the baseline in prediction deviation
and accuracy. The average deviation of SOPP on the x86 platform is 1.88, a
13.2% decrease compared to the baseline. On the ARM platform, SOPP reduces
the average deviation by 11.88% compared to the baseline, with the average
deviation being 1.93. SOPP improves the prediction accuracy by 11.07% and
8.09% on the x86 and ARM platforms compared to the baseline. From the anal-
ysis of program segment types, SOPP demonstrates more accurate predictions
for non-comm segments on the x86 platform, with a lower prediction deviation
(1.65) compared to comm segments (2.21). On the ARM platform, the opposite
is observed: SOPP shows a lower prediction deviation for comm segments (1.66)
than for non-comm segments (2.14). These results indicate that both the hard-
ware platform and program segment type inﬂuence the predictive performance of
the SOPP model, highlighting considerable room for improvement in prediction
capability across diﬀerent architectures and segment types.

The Accuracy of Bottleneck Segment Identiﬁcation. Table 2 shows that
SOPP improves the accuracy of localizing program bottleneck segments. If the
optimal parallelism predicted by the baseline method (e.g., 1024 for seg1) is used
for judgment, this value is signiﬁcantly higher than the program’s optimal par-
allelism (512), leading to the erroneous classiﬁcation of seg1 as a non-bottleneck
segment, even though it is actually a bottleneck. In contrast, the SOPP method
predicts an optimal parallelism (e.g., 128 for seg1) closer to the actual optimal

parallelism of the segment (256), correctly identifying seg1 as a bottleneck seg-

values than the baseline’s, resulting in more accurate identiﬁcation of bottleneck
segments.

(performance denotes parallel program execution time) under POPP prediction
reaches an average of 84.75% and 75.00% of the actual optimal performance
on x86 and ARM platforms. Figure 6 illustrates relative performance for typical
programs under predicted optimal parallelism (p̂app , POPP) and using maximum
platform core (pmax , baseline) , normalized against performance under actual
optimal parallelism (p∗app , best). The smaller the relative performance of POPP
than that at max cores and the closer the relative performance is to one, the
better the performance improvement eﬀect. If the relative performance is equal
to 1, it indicates accurate prediction (p̂app = p∗app ).
    The relative performance of POPP is close to the actual optimal parallel
performance, with signiﬁcant gains over using max cores. The average perfor-
mance improvements over baseline under POPP value are 45.43% and 36.3%
on ×86 and ARM platforms; the average diﬀerences from optimal performance
are 24.1% and 87.9%. This shows that on the x86 platform, the performance
improvement under POPP is greater, and the gap to the optimal performance
is smaller. On the ARM platform, the average performance under POPP shows
much worse than the average optimal performance, mainly due to the large
performance ﬂuctuations of the IS (D) program with varying numbers of pro-
cesses. For the IS (D) program, the execution time under POPP is 185 s, while
the fastest execution time is 53 s, a diﬀerence of more than double.


4.4   KER Can Eﬀectively Recognize Key Events
To validate the eﬀectiveness of the key event recognition method, the experi-
ment employs a grouped comparison strategy. For bottleneck segments, the dif-
ferences of key events between the severe and the general bottleneck groups are
compared; for performance inﬂections, the diﬀerences of key events between the
high-p∗app and the low-p∗app program groups are analyzed. If both experimental
comparisons show signiﬁcant diﬀerences in event distribution between groups
(e.g., speciﬁc events are more prevalent in the more severe bottleneck group), it
will demonstrate that this method can eﬀectively identify key events.
                                       Machine Learning and Data Statistics      455




Fig. 6. Relative performance is the performance normalized against the best perfor-
mance. The closer the relative performance is to one, the better the performance
improvement.




Fig. 7. The performance events of severe bottlenecks are diﬀerent from the general
bottlenecks, validating the eﬀectiveness of the key event recognition for bottleneck
segments.


Key Event Recognition for Bottleneck Segments. Bottleneck segments
are classiﬁed as severe or general based on the deviation between segment-level
(p∗seg ) and program-level (p∗app ) optimal parallelism. Using the NPB (x86) as exam-
ples to analyze, CG (D) and LU (D) show severe bottlenecks (deviations: 7, 6),
while IS (D) and EP (C) exhibit general bottlenecks (deviations: 1, 2).
     There are signiﬁcant diﬀerences between the performance events of the two
groups, validating the eﬀectiveness of the key event recognition for bottleneck
segments. Figure 7 compares the count of key events about diﬀerent aspects rec-
ognized in the two groups separately. Severe bottlenecks primarily stem from
systemic issues (the front events), like frequent TLB misses (dTLB/iTLB) and
memory access events (MEM), linked to address mapping and memory eﬃciency.
General bottlenecks mainly reﬂect software issues (the behind events), like cache
ineﬃciencies and branch mispredictions (branch_inst), often caused by algorith-
mic limitations or poor data locality.
456     Y. Cao et al.




Fig. 8. The correlation value between events and performance with mutual information.


Key Event Recognition for Performance Inﬂection. Figure 8 shows the
mutual information correlation values between multiple events and performance
for four programs in NPB (x86). A higher mutual information value indicates a
stronger correlation between the event and performance. CG (D) and LU (D)
exhibit high p∗app (1024, 512), respectively; CG (C) and EP (C) show low p∗app
(64, 64).
    ram_used (memory usage) and energy (energy consumption) show a strong
positive correlation with performance across all four programs, particularly CG
(C) and EP (C). This suggests that programs with low p∗app may be resource-
constrained, either by memory or other factors. Switches refers to the number
of CPU context switches. A higher correlation (0.51 and 0.60) is observed in the
two more scalable programs, indicating that CG (D) and LU (D) may suﬀer from
signiﬁcant context switching overhead.
    The last four events are more relevant in low p∗app programs. These four
events, which are iTLB misses, NUMA local memory access misses, icache misses,
and LLC misses, reﬂect key events of CG (C) and EP (C). (1) Instruction and
data locality issues: high iTLB misses and icache misses (0.44 and 0.400 for
EP(C)) indicate low instruction fetch eﬃciency. (2) NUMA eﬀects: high node
misses (0.369 for CG(C)) reﬂect high overhead from cross-node memory access,
potentially becoming a bottleneck.
    The mutual information correlation values reﬂect diﬀerent key events of two
program types, validating the eﬀectiveness of key event recognition for perfor-
mance inﬂections. Programs with low p∗app (CG (C) and EP (C)) are more likely
to be constrained by resource limitations (memory/energy) and architectural
bottlenecks (instruction/data locality, NUMA eﬀects).


4.5   Discussion

The scalable bottleneck detection framework excels at accurately and eﬃciently
predicting performance inﬂection and analyzing the causes of bottlenecks. The
model assists users in tuning parallel execution strategies to optimize program
performance.
                                    Machine Learning and Data Statistics    457

    The framework still oﬀers opportunities for enhancement in speciﬁc areas.
First, the framework is currently applied to a limited number of benchmark
programs. In the future, it is considered to apply this framework to large-scale
scientiﬁc computing applications for validation and iteration. Second, the pre-
dictive ability of POPP and SOPP still needs improvement. E.g., the accuracy
of POPP for rare samples, like programs with exceptionally low or high perfor-
mance inﬂections, is lower than others. For the bottleneck identiﬁcation mech-
anism, the SOPP deviation may still introduce imprecision. Third, the KER
methodology may exhibit sensitivity to performance event ﬂuctuations under
certain conditions. Future work will focus on these aspects to improve predic-
tion consistency and reliability.


5   Related Work

Performance modeling is essential for optimizing parallel programs. PMCs are
widely used for performance models. Ding et al. [12] propose the APMT frame-
work, which utilizes hardware counters to identify key computational kernels
and construct performance models. Barry et al. [8] propose a PMC analysis
methodology that maps hardware events to programming concepts. Andrade
et al. [6] propose a hardware event-based program execution time modeling
method by analyzing the correlation between hardware events. Others utilize
the parameter of application and systems to build performance models. Hut-
ter et al. [19] leverage tensor decomposition techniques to overcome the lim-
its of high-dimensional parameter space modeling. Ritter et al. [28] develop an
enhanced Extra-P analysis framework to analyze nonlinear relationships between
parameters and performance.
    Program phase modeling distinguishes phases with similar behavior dur-
ing program execution, aiding resource optimization and performance predic-
tion [10]. Oﬄine phase detection approaches rely on post-execution trace analy-
sis, whereas online methods [11] identify phase changes in real time, enabling
transparent optimization without code modiﬁcations. For oﬄine approaches,
Siesta [25] extracts MPI program communication-computation traces to gen-
erate parameterized code snippets that simulate behaviors across diﬀerent exe-
cution phases. The DwarfCode [34] performs phase representation by merging
MPI event traces and compressing repetitive patterns. Lozano et al. [24] com-
bined GMM clustering with LSTMs for CPU workload phase prediction. Phase-
aware methods are also applied in runtime conﬁguration optimization. Aurora
[23] dynamically adjusts thread counts by monitoring OpenMP parallel loop
behaviors at runtime.
    Communication characteristics impact the program performance, particu-
larly in large-scale parallel computing [16]. Chen et al. [9] demonstrated that
communication event intervals follow a power-law distribution. Abubaker et
al. [2] optimized point-to-point scheduling to minimize per-processor messages.
The EventGraD algorithm [13] optimizes parallel stochastic gradient descent via
event-triggered communication, reducing the communication overhead. Hoeﬂer
458     Y. Cao et al.

et al. [17] map the application’s communication graph to the physical network
topology to minimize overhead.


6     Conclusion

The scalability bottleneck of MPI parallel programs severely limits their compu-
tational eﬃciency. This paper proposes a machine learning and data statistics-
based scalability bottleneck detection framework to address the issues of detect-
ing scalability bottlenecks. Experimental veriﬁcation is conducted on two 2048-
core ×86 and ARM clusters. The POPP method utilizes MPI comm and non-
comm segment features for p∗app prediction, achieving an average prediction accu-
racy of 70% (×86) and 60% (ARM), exceeding the non-segmented prediction
methods. SOPP, based on diﬀerentiated feature selection, reduces the p∗seg pre-
diction deviation by 13.2% and 11.88% compared to methods without feature
selection. Key event recognition, combining KL divergence and mutual informa-
tion, improves the eﬃciency of identifying bottleneck performance events. This
framework is capable of eﬀective performance inﬂection prediction, bottleneck
localization, and key performance event analysis, oﬀering insight for parallel
application performance optimization.

        Abstract. Traditional e-commerce review methods face diﬃculties in
        identifying implicit evaluation targets and extracting features from both
        local details and overall semantic levels. To address this, this paper pro-
        poses an aspect term extraction model integrating auxiliary sentence
        construction and a hybrid neural network (EBERT-CBAC). This model
        ﬁrst constructs auxiliary sentences to mine potential aspect term infor-
        mation and incorporates part-of-speech (POS) tags, enabling the tra-
        ditional BERT model to capture multi-dimensional POS word struc-
        tures. After obtaining contextual embeddings, it uses a CNN layer to
        extract local contextual features, followed by a BiGRU layer to capture
        global contextual features within the sentence. Considering that a single
        attention mechanism cannot capture important sentence features from
        diﬀerent perspectives, a multi-head attention mechanism is introduced
        to process sentence-level information. Finally, sequence labeling is com-
        pleted in the CRF layer to accurately identify both explicitly expressed
        and semantically implicit aspect terms in reviews. Experimental results
        show that, compared to the baseline model BERT-BiLSTM-CRF, the
        proposed model achieves an average F1-score improvement of 2.48% on
        three benchmark datasets, eﬀectively enhancing the accuracy of aspect
        term extraction.


        Keywords: Aspect Extraction · Attention mechanism · Deep learning


1     Introduction
With the rapid development of the internet, the quantity and inﬂuence of online
reviews on e-commerce platforms have grown exponentially. The valuable user
feedback they contain has become a crucial basis for optimizing products and ser-
vices. However, e-commerce reviews are characterized by ﬂexible sentence struc-
tures and colloquial expressions, posing signiﬁcant challenges for aspect term
extraction. For example, users may use implicit expressions like “slow delivery” to
reﬂect dissatisfaction with “logistics speed”. Such expressions often lack explicit
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 462–477, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_25
                  Aspect Term Extraction Method Based on EBERT-CBAC           463

aspect term indicators, making it diﬃcult for traditional methods based on asso-
ciation rules or shallow semantic models to eﬀectively capture implicit sentiment
information. Therefore, accurately identifying both explicit and implicit aspect
terms in reviews has become an important and challenging issue in the current
ﬁeld of sentiment analysis.
    Aspect term extraction (AE) can be treated as a sequence labeling task [1].
Research methods have roughly evolved through the following stages:
    Rule-based and Lexicon-based Algorithms: Early rule-based and lexicon-
based algorithms relied on manually constructed linguistic rules and sentiment
lexicons to identify text, such as using keyword matching and predeﬁned syntac-
tic templates to extract aspect terms. These methods are easy to implement and
show certain eﬀectiveness in speciﬁc scenarios, but they have poor adaptability to
corpus variations, weak scalability, and require signiﬁcant manual intervention,
making them diﬃcult to apply to large-scale real reviews. Subsequent research
introduced traditional machine learning methods like Hidden Markov Models
(HMM) [2] and Conditional Random Fields (CRF) [3].
    Traditional Machine Learning Methods: Compared to rule-based approaches,
traditional machine learning methods show improvements in accuracy and gen-
eralization capabilities, but they demand substantial annotated data.
    Topic Model-based Methods: Subsequently, topic modeling methods like LDA
(Latent Dirichlet Allocation) [4] were introduced for aspect term extraction
tasks. Mukherjee and Liu [5] proposed an approach combining predeﬁned seed
words with the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model to guide the extrac-
tion of latent aspect topics from product reviews. However, relying on word
co-occurrence frequencies struggles to eﬀectively capture syntactic structures
and contextual semantic dependencies in text, resulting in limitations in the
granularity of aspect terms.
    Deep Learning Methods: With the development of deep learning techniques,
neural networks have shown signiﬁcant advantages in natural language process-
ing tasks. Hammerton [6] was among the ﬁrst to apply Long Short-Term Mem-
ory networks (LSTM) to sequence labeling tasks, addressing vanishing gradient
issues. Subsequently, by combining BiLSTM and CRF, Lample et al. [7] pro-
posed the BiLSTM-CRF model. BiLSTM extracts features from both directions
and gradually improved the accuracy of various sequence labeling tasks. Beyond
recurrent structures, based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Xu et al.
[8] proposed the DE-CNN model, introducing general and domain-speciﬁc dual
embedding mechanisms and performing feature extraction through hierarchically
stacked CNNs, demonstrating the potential of deep convolutional structures in
aspect extraction tasks. Wang et al. [9] proposed the RNCRF model, combin-
ing a recurrent neural network with a CRF model to simultaneously identify
aspect terms and associated opinion expressions in text, enhancing the model’s
overall performance. While current methods exhibit improved precision, their
heavy reliance on explicit aspect-opinion associations renders them ineﬀective
against implicit aspects. Additionally, their global sentence-level analysis fre-
464     Y. Wu et al.

quently fails to capture nuanced local contexts, particularly when processing
negations or adversative constructions in reviews.
    In summary, this paper proposes an aspect term extraction model integrating
auxiliary sentence construction and a hybrid neural network (EBERT-CBAC).
The innovative ideas are as follows:
    (1) Propose an auxiliary sentence generation method jointly driven by L-LDA
and semantic distance. First, an aspect category-seed word association library
is constructed from annotated corpora. Then, BERT computes the semantic
similarity between input words and seed words to dynamically generate explicit
interrogative auxiliary sentences, thereby verbalizing implicit aspect terms.
    (2) Optimize the semantic-syntactic integration for domain adaptation. On
the semantic side, BERT dynamic encoding is leveraged to adapt to domain-
speciﬁc expressions. On the syntactic side, optimization is achieved through POS
tagging.
    (3) Design a multi-level hybrid neural network architecture (CNN-BiGRU-
MHA) integrating local-global features, extracting complementary informa-
tion from local contexts, long-distance dependencies, and multi-head attention,
respectively. Sequence labeling is ultimately completed in the CRF layer.


2     Related Principles and Methods
2.1   L-LDA

Labeled Latent Dirichlet Allocation (L-LDA) [10] is an extension of the LDA
model. Its core idea is to introduce document label information as a prior dis-
tribution to extract semantic features highly relevant to predeﬁned categories.
Through label constraints, L-LDA restricts the topic distribution of a document
to its labeled speciﬁc categories, ensuring the generated topics are closely related
to domain knowledge. The generative process of L-LDA is shown in Table 1:


                       Table 1. Generative Process of L-LDA

               Generative Process of L-LDA
               For each topic k ∈ {1, . . . , K}:
                 → Generate: βk = (βk,1 , . . . , βk,V )T ∼ Dir(· | η)
               For each document d:
                 For each topic k ∈ {1, . . . , K }:
                                    (d)
                   → Generate: Λk ∈ {0, 1} ∼ Bernoulli(· | Φk )
                 → Generate: α(d) = L(d) × α
                 → Generate: θ(d) = (θl1 , . . . , θlMd )T ∼ Dir(· | α(d) )
                 For each i ∈ {1, . . . , Nd }:
                                            (d)       (d)
                   → Generate: zi ∈ {λ1 , . . . , λMd } ∼ Mult(· | θ(d) )
                   → Generate: wi ∈ {1, . . . , V } ∼ Mult(· | βzi )
                     Aspect Term Extraction Method Based on EBERT-CBAC                            465

Table 1 lists the complete generative process of the L-LDA model. This process is
based on a Dirichlet-Multinomial two-level generative mechanism and introduces
a label projection matrix on top of standard LDA to constrain the global topic
space to the label set of each document. For clarity, the main mathematical
symbols involved in the table are explained in Table 2 below:


       Table 2. Explanation of Symbols in the Generative Process of L-LDA

Symbol Meaning
K      Total number of topics, equal to the number of unique label types in the corpus
V      Vocabulary size
βk     Word distribution for the k − th topic, a vector of dimension V
η      Hyperparameter of the Dirichlet distribution, controlling the sparsity of the word distribution
Λ(d)   Label of document d
Φk     Prior probability of label presence for the k − th topic
L(d)   Document label projection matrix of size Md × K
α      Dirichlet parameter vector for the global topic prior
α(d)   Document-speciﬁc Dirichlet hyperparameter vector, restricted to label-related topics
θ(d)   Topic distribution for document d
zi     Topic number assigned to the i − th word
wi     Index of the i − th generated word
Nd     Total number of words in document d
Md     Number of labels for document d (i.e., size of λ(d) )




2.2    BERT Pre-training
In the ﬁeld of Natural Language Processing, the Transformer architecture pro-
posed by Vaswani A et al. [11] broke through the sequence modeling limitations
of RNNs through the self-attention mechanism. Its parallel computation proper-
ties signiﬁcantly improved model eﬃciency and led to the emergence of genera-
tive pre-trained models like GPT and the landmark bidirectional encoder model
BERT [12].
    BERT uses Transformer encoder layers to achieve fully bidirectional semantic
representation. Its input integrates three types of embedding information: token
embeddings, position embeddings, and segment embeddings [13]. By scaling the
hidden layer dimension to 768 and utilizing a 12-head self-attention mechanism,
BERT optimizes feature extraction capability. The BERT model learns linguistic
patterns through a dual-task pre-training strategy: Masked Language Modeling
(MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). The MLM task randomly masks
15% of tokens (80% replaced with [MASK], 10% replaced with random words,
10% left unchanged), forcing the model to predict masked content using bidirec-
tional context. The NSP task models logical relationships between sentences by
contrasting positive and negative samples. The pre-trained BERT can be quickly
adapted to downstream tasks through ﬁne-tuning, requiring only a small amount
466    Y. Wu et al.

of labeled data to adjust parameters in the top-layer network, eﬀectively allevi-
ating the sensitivity of deep learning models to small-sample scenarios.


2.3   BiLSTM-CRF Model

In the ﬁeld of sequence data processing, improved models based on LSTM have
continuously driven technological advancements. The Bidirectional Long Short-
Term Memory Network-Conditional Random Field (BiLSTM-CRF) architecture
proposed by Huang et al. [14] has become a benchmark model in this domain.
    The model adopts a three-stage processing pipeline: First, it transforms dis-
crete symbols into a continuous vector space through distributed representations.
Next, it employs bidirectional networks to capture contextual features. Finally,
it utilizes a probabilistic graphical model to optimize sequence labeling. Speciﬁ-
cally, given an input sequence x ={x1 ,x2 ,...,xn }, the word embedding layer maps
each lexical unit xi to a d-dimensional dense vector wi ∈ Rd . For the tempo-
ral characteristics of sequential data, RNN and its enhanced variant, the LSTM
network, demonstrate unique advantages. LSTMs establish a selective memory
mechanism through gated units, controlling information ﬂow and mitigating the
gradient explosion problem common in traditional RNNs. However, unidirec-
tional LSTMs can only capture forward contextual features, limiting their per-
formance in tasks requiring bidirectional context reasoning. To address this, the
BiLSTM employs a parallel dual-channel architecture, where the forward LSTM
layer and backward LSTM layer process the sequence separately. The bidirec-
tional features are then fused to form a comprehensive semantic representation,
as calculated in Eqs. (1), (2) and (3):
                             →                  →
                             ht = LST M (wt , ht−1 )                          (1)
                             ←                 ←
                             ht = LST M (wt , ht+1 )                          (2)
                                   →    ←
                             ht = [ht ⊕ ht ]                                  (3)
       →      ←
where ht and ht represent the forward and backward hidden states at time step
t, respectively, which are concatenated via the ⊕ operation.


3     Model Design

The main contribution of this paper is the EBERT-CBAC model. This model
constructs auxiliary sentences and extends the BERT architecture to integrate
syntactic standards. It employs CNN to extract local features, BiGRU to capture
global context, combines MHA to attend to key information, and ﬁnally identiﬁes
explicit and implicit aspects through a CRF layer. An illustration of the model
is shown in Fig. 1.
                 Aspect Term Extraction Method Based on EBERT-CBAC           467




                Fig. 1. EBERT-CBAC Model Framework Diagram


3.1   Auxiliary Sentence Construction and POS Tagging Method

Since words of the same type exhibit similar positional distances in semantic
vector space (as shown in Fig. 2), for implicit aspect terms not directly present
in sentences, L-LDA is utilized to extract a set of seed words for each poten-
tial implicit aspect from an annotated e-commerce domain corpus (see Table 3).
Aspect category items are generated from corresponding seed words. The seman-
tic distance between each word in the input sentence and the target seed words
is calculated. Words meeting a speciﬁc threshold are considered semantic can-
didates. An auxiliary sentence is constructed based on the semantic distance
between aspect-dependent seed words and the target sentence. This auxiliary
sentence serves as an expanded feature of the original sentence and is input into
the model.
    In the example sentence from Fig. 3, the explicit aspects are “sports shoe”
and “price”, both directly present in the sentence. However, the phrase “quickly
received” implies information about the implicit aspect term “delivery speed”,
which is not explicitly stated in the original sentence. Accordingly, an auxil-
iary question will be generated: “What do you think of the delivery speed?” to
explicitly extract this implied aspect.
468    Y. Wu et al.




Fig. 2. Example Illustration of Similarity Coherence Distribution in Word Embedding
Space

               Table 3. Top 4 Seed Word Examples from Laptop Dataset

       Aspect Word Seed Word
       delivery-speed received, fast, slow, postage, deliver, ...
       service         eﬃcient, friendly, inconvenient, troublesome, ...
       price           expensive, cheap, aﬀordable, cost, buy ...
       sports shoe     comfortable, durable, lightweight, breathable, ﬂexible ...



Then, Stanford POS Tagger is employed to generate part-of-speech tags for each
word. Considering adjectives and adverbs are central to sentiment expression
while nouns and their relationship with subjects help identify key aspect tar-
gets, three syntactic rules (adjective modiﬁcation, nominal subject relation, and
adverbial modiﬁcation) are applied to preserve POS tags. These processed tags
are ﬁnally fed into the EBERT-CBAC model for extraction tasks. Taking the
sentence “The customer service is very friendly and the product quality is good.“
as a sample input, its processing ﬂow is illustrated in Fig. 4.

3.2   EBERT Layer

Currently, the generic BERT model generates vector representations for text W
by summing and concatenating three embeddings: word embeddings ew , sentence
embeddings es , and position embeddings ep . Here, word embeddings capture the
semantic meaning of characters, sentence embeddings indicate sentence mem-
bership to provide basic text classiﬁcation capabilities, and position embeddings
record word order information to preserve input sequence temporality [12].
    Since generic BERT cannot fully represent all information, this work intro-
duces an additional embedding layer for POS tagging recognition. This layer is
integrated with character embeddings to capture POS tag features. The EBERT
model takes both text characters and their corresponding POS tags as input.
While retaining the original three-layer embeddings (ew , es , ep ) for character
vectors, we employ One-Hot encoding to uniformly represent POS-tagged enti-
ties and non-POS entities, aligning them with BERT’s vector space. The entity
vectors are then summed and concatenated with character vectors to form the
ﬁnal representation ea , as formalized in Eqs. (4), (5) and (6):

                              epos = OneHot ( T ag )                               (4)
                              ea = epos + ew + es + ep                             (5)
                              ea = EBERT ( ea )                                    (6)

EBERT integrates character vector representations with corresponding POS tag
information during word vector construction. Since aspect terms predominantly
appear as nouns and often form evaluation phrases with adjectivesâĂŤfor exam-
ple, in “I found the best deals at the new store downtown,” store functions as a
noun denoting a physical location, while in “You can store all your photos in the
cloud easily,” it serves as a verb meaning to save. In the original BERT model:
“store” is represented by the vector v = (v0 , v1 , ..., vn ) in sentence 1, “store” is
represented by the vector v = (v0 , v1 , ..., vn ) in sentence 2. Though contextual-
ized, the absence of POS tagging causes v and v to remain numerically close,
hindering model discrimination. EBERT addresses this by converting POS cat-
470    Y. Wu et al.

egory labels into vectors and superimposing them onto original character vec-
tors, thereby widening the numerical distance between v and v and signiﬁcantly
enhancing aspect term identiﬁcation capability.

3.3   CNN Local Feature Extraction Layer
In many cases, aspect terms are positioned close to the words determining their
sentiment polarity [13]. Therefore, prior to convolution operations, input matri-
ces require padding: m columns of 0 vectors are added to both left and right
sides to align CNN layer input/output dimensions. Subsequently, a convolutional
layer extracts local contextual features, with the kernel dimensions conﬁgured
as l × de , where: l = 2m + 1 denotes the kernel length, de represents the ker-
nel width, indicating that the convolutional kernel will extract local semantic
relationships between the current character and its surrounding m characters.
    During feature extraction, dh convolutional kernels perform multi-kernel con-
currency for parallel computation, as formalized in Eqs. (7) and (8):

obtained as h = [h1 , h2 , ..., hn ] ∈ Rn×dh .

tures long-range dependencies and is ideal for aspect extraction (e.g., processing
both “battery life is excellent” and “screen quality is mediocre” in one sentence).
More eﬃcient than RNNs for e-commerce data, BiGRU encodes EBERT embed-

3.5   Multi-head Attention (MHA) Layer
For the e-commerce domain, massive volumes of reviews often contain redundant
information. BiGRU may also face challenges when extracting critical informa-
tion from sentence sequences. The attention mechanism can more eﬀectively
allocate weights to key information, helping the model better understand the
                   Aspect Term Extraction Method Based on EBERT-CBAC                471

semantics of sentence sequences. The multi-head attention mechanism projects
inputs into multiple vector spaces and computes contextual representations of
characters within their respective vector spaces. Finally, these distinct results are
concatenated to obtain a comprehensive contextual representation. The compu-
tation of MHA (Multi-Head Attention) is shown in Formula (12), Formula (13),
and Formula (14) [11].

                                                  (QK )
               Attention(Q, K, V ) = Sof tmax( √             )V                    (12)
                                                        dk
               M (Q, K, V ) = concat(score1 (ytg ), ..., scoreh (ytg ))W           (13)
               scorei (ytg ) = Attention(QWiQ , KWiK , V WiV )                     (14)

Among them, Q, K, and V are respectively the query, key, and value matrices, all
represented by multi-dimensional vectors; ytg represents the output of the BiGRU
layer; h is the number of heads of the self-attention mechanism; W , Wiq , Wik
and Wiv are all the weight matrices to be learned; the self-attention mechanism√
calculates the scaling dot product through the Attention function, where dk is
the scaling factor. It is used to prevent the QK dot product result from causing
Softmax saturation (the gradient approaches zero) when the dimension is large,
thereby aﬀecting the training stability of the model (this setting is derived from
the standard scaling attention mechanism in the Transformer structure).
    After processing through the multi-head attention mechanism, the model can
integrate the global feature information of the input sequence and pass it as input
to the CRF layer. The method involves selecting the label with the highest score
as the corresponding sequence labeling result for independent decoding. It is
worth noting that the aspect term extraction task exhibits certain particularities
at the labeling level [13]. The dataset in this paper mostly adopts the BIO format
for label annotation, where the I-label must immediately follow the B-label. If
this condition is not met, the label combination loses semantic consistency. The
advantage of CRF lies in its ability to learn constraint relationships based on
the correlations between adjacent labels. Let the input be I = {I1 , I2 , I3 , ..., In }
and the labels s = {s1 , s2 , s3 , ..., sn }, where P (s|I) represents the conditional
probability, as shown in Eq. (15).

                                        s       t=1

Here, S(I) denotes the set of all possible labels, and the score function
f (st−1 , st , I) is used to simultaneously evaluate the transition state between
labels (from st−1 to st ) and the feature score corresponding to the current posi-
tion st . The optimal label path is obtained by maximizing the output probabil-
ity P (s|I) under the conditional probability distribution for the entire sequence.

further improvement.

5     Conclusion
This paper addresses the challenge of aspect term extraction in e-commerce
reviews by proposing an extraction model that integrates auxiliary sentence con-
struction with a hybrid neural network. Aiming at the diﬃculties in identifying
implicit aspect terms within e-commerce reviews and the limitations of tradi-
tional methods that rely on explicit co-occurrence relationships, this work intro-
duces semantics-driven auxiliary sentence construction and incorporates POS
embedding features to surface implicit aspect terms. Building upon the BERT
model, we designed the EBERT-CBAC architecture, which employs CNN and
BiGRU to capture local and global contextual features within sentences, respec-
tively. Subsequently, a multi-head attention mechanism is utilized to learn weight
information for words in the entire sentence from diﬀerent perspectives, enabling
the accurate identiﬁcation of both explicit and implicit aspect terms. The results
demonstrate that EBERT-CBAC achieves F1-scores of 83.47%, 88.86%, and
76.44% on the Laptop, Restaurant, and Twitter datasets, respectively. This rep-
resents an average improvement of 2.48% over the best baseline model, BERT-
BiLSTM-CRF. Ablation studies further conﬁrmed the contributions of auxiliary
sentence generation, POS tags, and the multi-head attention mechanism to the
overall performance, providing reliable aspect terms for aspect-level sentiment
classiﬁcation tasks. Future research could explore the introduction of large lan-
guage models (LLMs) to generate more diverse and richer auxiliary sentences
through semantic rewriting and multi-turn questioning mechanisms. This app-
roach holds the potential to overcome the limitations of current methods based
on seed words and similarity thresholds, thereby further enhancing the perfor-
mance of aspect term extraction.
