       Abstract. Deployment of deep neural networks on edge devices faces
       challenges from heterogeneous hardware and multimodal tasks, where
       existing compression evaluation frameworks overlook hardware co-
       design, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce
       HACompBench, a new hardware-aware framework that deﬁnes compres-
       sion evaluation as a multi-objective optimization problem and combines
       hardware metrics such as quantization eﬃciency ξ and sparsity compati-
       bility η with a dynamic scoring function J. We performed comprehensive
       experiments across four leading SoC platforms: Snapdragon 888, Snap-
       dragon 765G, Kirin 970, and Jetson Nano P3450, and tested ten DNN
       models covering vision, text, and speech modalities using compression
       techniques such as quantization, pruning, and weight sharing, reveal-
       ing hardware-induced performance gaps, such as quantization yields
       J = 32.3% on Snapdragon 888 but J = 68.0% on Jetson Nano P3450
       due to INT8 emulation overhead. These results systematically highlight
       compression variations from diﬀerences in parallel processing capabili-
       ties. HACompBench innovates by linking hardware features, supporting
       multimodal tasks, and surpassing MLPerf Tiny’s single-modality focus
       and AIoTBench’s lack of co-design through embedded metrics ξ and η,
       while modality-speciﬁc corrections improve accuracy by up to 12.6%. It
       provides a uniﬁed and robust framework for edge deployment.


       Keywords: Model Compression · Edge Computing ·
       Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design · Multimodal Evaluation · Parallel
       Sparse Optimization


1    Introduction

The rapid advancement of edge computing has driven the deployment of deep
neural networks on resource-constrained devices, such as smartphones and IoT
nodes, characterized by compute throughput below 30 TOPS, memory capacities
of 4 to 12 GB, and power budgets of a few watts. This shift from cloud-centric
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 478–496, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_26
           HACompBench: Co-designed DNN Compression for Edge Devices         479

to edge-distributed intelligence reduces data transmission latency from hundreds
of milliseconds to mere milliseconds while enhancing user privacy by minimizing
sensitive data uploads. Applications in autonomous driving, industrial IoT, and
mobile healthcare demonstrate the transformative potential of edge intelligence.
However, the computational complexity of deep neural networks, often involving
tens of millions of parameters, poses signiﬁcant deployment challenges. Compres-
sion techniques, such as quantization and pruning, are critical to address these
constraints, yet their eﬃcacy varies across heterogeneous hardware. For instance,
MobileNetV3-Small achieves a 2.73-fold inference acceleration on Snapdragon
888 but only 1.16-fold on Kirin 970 due to diﬀerences in hardware support
for quantization [9]. This variability highlights a critical limitation: the con-
ventional compress-then-deploy approach, which applies compression techniques
sequentially without considering hardware characteristics, fails to fully exploit
compression potential in real-world edge scenarios. Such variability underscores
the limitations of the traditional compress-then-deploy paradigm, which ignores
hardware characteristics and thus fails to maximize compression potential in
edge scenarios.
    The compress-then-deploy paradigm relies on empirical compression strate-
gies, such as quantization to reduce precision or pruning to eliminate redundant
parameters, without systematically quantifying their interactions with hardware
attributes like INT8 support or sparsity compatibility. This leads to subopti-
mal performance across diverse edge devices. In smart home applications, for
example, Wav2Vec2-Tiny suﬀers a 3% accuracy degradation under quantization
on low-end ARM Cortex-A53 processors, while unstructured pruning increases
latency by 28% due to irregular memory access patterns [32]. Existing evalu-
ation frameworks, such as MLPerf Inference, are designed for cloud or server
environments, overlooking edge-speciﬁc challenges like memory fragmentation
[21]. MLPerf Tiny focuses on vision tasks, neglecting the temporal dependen-
cies of speech models like Wav2Vec2-Tiny or the token sparsity of text models
like TinyBERT, where quantization can degrade accuracy by up to 3% [7,9].
Recent surveys, such as Liang et al. [5] and Lee et al. [6], highlight multimodal
machine learning challenges for edge devices, emphasizing the need for hardware-
aware optimization, while Wang et al. [30] discuss pruning eﬃciency on mobile
devices. These frameworks lack a uniﬁed approach to integrate hardware char-
acteristics with algorithmic performance across multimodal tasks, necessitating
a novel evaluation framework.
    To address these challenges, we propose HACompBench, a hardware-aware
framework that redeﬁnes model compression evaluation as a multi-objective opti-
mization problem, as detailed in Sect. 3. HACompBench models the interplay
between compression techniques and hardware attributes, employing a dynamic
scoring function J that balances accuracy loss, inference latency, and mem-
ory usage, as described in Sect. 5. By incorporating hardware metrics, such
as quantization eﬃciency ξ and sparsity compatibility η, and modality-speciﬁc
error correction, HACompBench delivers tailored compression strategies opti-
mized for diverse edge devices and tasks spanning vision, text, and speech
480    Z. Gan et al.

modalities. Extensive experiments on four System-on-Chip platforms, namely
Xiaomi 11 with Snapdragon 888, Google Pixel 5 with Snapdragon 765G, Huawei
Nova 3 with Kirin 970, and Jetson Nano P3450, validate the framework’s eﬃ-
cacy. For MobileNetV3-Small, quantization achieves a normalized dynamic score
J = 32.3% with a 2.73-fold speedup and 69% memory reduction on Snapdragon
888, while Jetson Nano P3450 yields J = 68.0% with a 0.80-fold speedup due to
limited INT8 support. Modality-speciﬁc corrections enhance accuracy by 12.6%,
as supported by Chong et al. [2] for edge inference. The primary contributions
of this work are as follows:

– We propose HACompBench, a hardware-aware framework that integrates
  multi-objective optimization via a genetic algorithm and modality-speciﬁc
  error correction to evaluate compression strategies across heterogeneous edge
  devices and multimodal tasks, with emphasis on parallel sparse computa-
  tions in SoCs. This framework facilitates optimization parallel sparse matrix
  operations on NPUs and GPUs through the sparsity compatibility metric η,
  enabling better exploitation of parallel processing capabilities in edge archi-
  tectures.
– We conducted a large number of model compression performance experiments
  on ten mainstream DNN models covering vision, text, and speech tasks on four
  edge device SoCs, providing cross-modal, cross-hardware, and cross-model
  compression performance analysis, and demonstrating how parallel optimiza-
  tions lead to acceleration gains, such as up to 2.73-fold speedup on high-η
  platforms.
– We deﬁned two hardware-aware metrics, quantization eﬃciency ξ and sparse
  compatibility η, and established a linear regression relationship between S,
  ξ, and η in the experimental data, verifying the relationship between hard-
  ware characteristics and model compression performance, including impacts
  on parallel matrix operations. Combined with the dynamic scoring function
  J, we achieved score-based selection of model compression solutions that
  enhance parallel eﬃciency in heterogeneous SoCs.


2     Related Work
Edge computing has emerged as a cornerstone for deploying deep neural networks
on resource-constrained devices, driven by the demand for low-latency inference
and reduced cloud dependency. Weisong et al. report that approximately 45%
of IoT data requires edge processing to mitigate bandwidth constraints, yet the
stringent power budgets of edge devices, typically 1–10 mW for IoT SoCs, under-
score the need for eﬃcient model compression [13,15]. The heterogeneity of edge
hardware, spanning CPUs like Snapdragon 888, DSPs, NPUs, and FPGAs, com-
plicates optimization. Yuan et al. demonstrate that FPGA implementations of
quantized models achieve 1.8–2.5× higher energy eﬃciency than mobile GPUs,
while Qi et al. show that block-structured pruning reduces Transformer latency
by 4.3× on FPGAs but increases it by 28% on mobile GPUs due to irregular
           HACompBench: Co-designed DNN Compression for Edge Devices          481

memory access [9,11]. Distributed frameworks like DINA leverage DNN parti-
tioning to cut latency by 2.6–4.2×, yet their cross-vendor predictability remains
limited [14]. These ﬁndings highlight the need for hardware-aware compression
strategies, a gap that HACompBench addresses through its co-design approach.
These advancements in edge computing set the stage for model compression
techniques, which have progressed signiﬁcantly to tackle resource limitations.
    Model compression techniques, including quantization, pruning, and knowl-
edge distillation, have advanced signiﬁcantly. Quantization reduces precision to
lower memory and computational demands; Jacob et al. show that 8-bit quanti-
zation reduces ResNet-18’s memory usage by 75%, albeit with a 1.6% accuracy
drop [9,22]. Pruning removes redundant parameters, with Qi et al. achieving a
4.3× latency reduction for Transformers on FPGAs via block-structured spar-
sity, though mobile GPUs face latency penalties [9,11]. Knowledge distillation, as
demonstrated by TinyBERT, compresses BERT to 14.5M parameters, 7.5× fewer
than BERT’s 109M, retaining 96.8% of its GLUE performance with 9.4× faster
inference [31]. In the speech domain, Wav2Vec2-Tiny leverages self-supervised
learning, achieving a 4.8/8.2 word error rate on Librispeech with minimal labeled
data [32]. Vision models like SqueezeNet replace 3×3 convolutions with 1×1 ﬁl-
ters, reducing parameters by approximately 50× compared to AlexNet while
preserving accuracy [34]. Recent advancements include practical insights from
Hohman et al. [3], summarizing lessons for on-device compression and empha-
sizing hardware-aware strategies, and Smith et al. [4] proposed ROAST hashing
for parameter sharing on edge devices, aligning with HACompBench’s hardware
metrics like ξ and η. Despite these techniques’ potential, they reveal modality-
speciﬁc challenges, such as quantization’s 3% accuracy degradation in temporal
or token-sparse domains [9].
    Hardware-aware optimization is crucial for edge deployment. Yuan et al. high-
light FPGA energy eﬃciency, while Qi et al. note pruning’s hardware-speciﬁc
impacts, such as block-structured pruning reducing Transformer latency by 4.3×
on FPGAs but increasing it by 28% on mobile GPUs due to irregular memory
access, emphasizing the hardware dependency of parallel sparse optimization
[9,11]. Distributed frameworks like DINA address latency but lack cross-vendor
robustness [14], a limitation HACompBench overcomes through embedded ξ and
η metrics for cross-vendor support. In multimodal learning, Chong et al. [2] pro-
posed boosted trees for edge inference, achieving low memory use, while Liang
et al. [5] surveyed principles relevant for edge deployment, supporting HAComp-
Bench’s cross-modal approach. These eﬀorts underscore the need for integrated
hardware-algorithm strategies.
    Existing benchmarking frameworks fall short in addressing edge-speciﬁc com-
pression challenges. MLPerf Inference standardizes metrics for cloud environ-
ments, neglecting edge constraints like memory fragmentation [21]. MLPerf Tiny
prioritizes vision tasks, overlooking speech and NLP modalities [7]. AIoTBench
evaluates across vision, speech, and NLP but lacks co-design guidance [28].
AdaDeep automates compression but has limited cross-modal adaptability [1].
Tian et al. note a 22% higher misclassiﬁcation rate on FPGAs, emphasizing
482     Z. Gan et al.

hardware-aware evaluation [10]. Recent surveys such as Lee et al. [6] overview
edge deep learning, stressing uniﬁed frameworks for hardware variability. Unlike
these, we integrate HACompBench with hardware-aware metrics ξ and η, and
modality-speciﬁc correction, providing robust evaluation across vision, text, and
speech, surpassing sequential workﬂows and unimodal benchmarks. For instance,
HACompBench’s multimodal correction improves accuracy by 12.6%, addressing
AIoTBench’s co-design gap.


3     Problem Formulation

To address the challenges outlined in the introduction, this section formulates
the compression evaluation as a scoring task to quantify the interplay among
accuracy loss ΔAcc, inference latency Tinf , and peak memory usage Mpeak . The
HACompBench framework leverages experimental insights to guide compres-
sion strategy selection, ensuring compatibility with real-world edge deployment
challenges.
    The system model encompasses edge devices D, including Xiaomi 11
equipped with Snapdragon 888, Google Pixel 5 with Snapdragon 765G, and
Huawei Nova 3 featuring Kirin 970. Each device is characterized by compute
throughput Phw , such as 26 TOPS for Snapdragon 888, and memory bandwidth
Bmem , such as 51.2 GB/s for Xiaomi 11. The model set M comprises pre-trained
networks for vision, exempliﬁed by MobileNetV3-Small, text, represented by
TinyBERT, and speech, illustrated by Wav2Vec2-Tiny. The compression tech-
nique set C includes 8-bit post-training quantization, pruning with sparsity ratios
of 0.3, and weight sharing with 8 clusters. This evaluation quantiﬁes the impact
of compression on ΔAcc, Tinf , and Mpeak , accounting for hardware variability,
such as INT8 support, and modality-speciﬁc characteristics, including temporal
continuity in speech.
    The scoring task aims to identify compression strategies that optimize a
weighted performance score. Decision variables include quantization bit-width
Bw , pruning sparsity ratio s, and weight-sharing clusters K. The scoring function
is deﬁned as:
                                ΔAcc        Tinf    Mpeak
                       J =α            +β        +γ        ,
                               Accbase     Tbase     Mbase
where the weights α, β, and γ sum to 1 and are adjusted based on user priorities
or hardware load. For example, in latency-sensitive tasks, β increases to 0.5,
while high compute utilization elevates β to prioritize latency. Constraints ensure
practical feasibility: accuracy loss must not exceed 5% for vision or 3% for speech,
inference latency must remain below 50 ms, and peak memory usage must not
surpass 512 MB. These constraints are derived from experimental observations,
for instance, limiting accuracy loss to 5% maintains usability in vision tasks,
while keeping latency under 50 ms supports real-time applications.
    The normalized dynamic score J quantiﬁes trade-oﬀs among accuracy loss,
inference latency, and memory usage relative to baseline values. A lower J indi-
cates a compression strategy that minimizes these penalties, achieving reduced
           HACompBench: Co-designed DNN Compression for Edge Devices           483

accuracy degradation, faster inference, and a smaller memory footprint, thereby
enhancing overall eﬃciency. Utility U , deﬁned as the inverse of J, where
U = 1/J, serves as an indicator of compression scheme superiority, with higher
utility reﬂecting a more eﬀective strategy due to a smaller J.
    To characterize hardware-compression interactions, two metrics are intro-
duced based on experimental proﬁling of hardware capabilities. Sparsity compat-
ibility η quantiﬁes the hardware’s support for sparse matrix operations, crucial
for pruning techniques, and is calculated as:
                             Supported Sparse Patterns
                        η=                             ,
                               Total Tested Patterns
Using Android NDK, a test suite proﬁles the hardware’s ability to execute sparse
matrix operations, such as 4×4 block sparsity, with 100 predeﬁned patterns
sourced from standard benchmarks like those in Android NDK documentation.
For each device, these patterns are tested to measure native support without
performance degradation. Snapdragon 888 supports 82 patterns, resulting in
η = 0.82, whereas Kirin 970 in Huawei Nova 3 supports nearly none, yielding
η ≈ 0, due to its lack of sparse computation acceleration. This metric is essential
for pruning techniques, as high η platforms can better utilize parallel processing
capabilities, such as accelerating sparse operations in 4×4 blocks on NPUs.
    Quantization eﬃciency ξ measures the eﬃciency of low-precision computa-
tions, such as INT8, relative to FP32 operations, and is calculated as:

                                      Phw (Bw )
                                ξ=                ,
                                     Phw (32-bit)

Employing Qualcomm SNPE, the hardware’s compute throughput Phw in oper-
ations per second is measured for INT8 and FP32 instructions on a standard-
ized neural network layer. For Snapdragon 888 in Xiaomi 11, INT8 throughput
matches FP32, resulting in ξ = 1.0, reﬂecting robust INT8 optimization, while
Kirin 970 in Huawei Nova 3 yields ξ = 0.3 due to its FP32 CPU architecture.
This metric quantiﬁes the hardware’s optimization for parallel INT8 instructions
in low-precision computations.
    The evaluation model F : (Bw , s, K)     (ΔAcc, Tinf , Mpeak ) maps compres-
sion conﬁgurations to performance metrics. The objective is to minimize J while
adhering to constraints, using experimental data to inform strategy selection.
Section 4 quantiﬁes the impact of η and ξ on performance, laying the foundation
for HACompBench’s scoring mechanism in Sect. 5.


4     Experiment
4.1   Experimental Setup

This subsection outlines the experimental setup for investigating model com-
pression performance across four edge computing platforms: Snapdragon 888
in Xiaomi 11, Snapdragon 765G in Google Pixel 5, Kirin 970 in Huawei Nova
484    Z. Gan et al.

3, and Jetson Nano P3450. These platforms, spanning high, medium, and low
computational capabilities with varied NPU and GPU conﬁgurations, enable a
comprehensive analysis of hardware heterogeneity’s impact on compression eﬃ-
cacy. Hardware characteristics, quantiﬁed as sparsity compatibility η and quan-
tization eﬃciency ξ, are detailed in Table 1. These characteristics quantify hard-
ware diﬀerences, such as varying support for sparse operations, directly inﬂuence
compression performance. To ensure measurement consistency, CPU frequencies
were ﬁxed at 2419 MHz for Snapdragon 888, 2208 MHz for Snapdragon 765G,
and 2362 MHz for Kirin 970. However, the performance cloud control module
in Xiaomi’s system and the power management in Huawei’s EMUI system may
inﬂuence experimental outcomes.
    The model set encompasses eight vision models, including MobileNetV3-
Small, MobileNetV2, EﬃcientNet-B0, SqueezeNet, ShuﬄeNet 1x, ShuﬄeNetV2
1x, MnasNet, and ProxylessNASNet, alongside one text model, TinyBERT, and
one speech model, Wav2Vec2-Tiny, addressing spatial, token, and temporal data
characteristics. Vision models were evaluated on ImageNet-1K validation set,
preprocessed to 224×224 resolution, comprising 50,000 images at 224×224 res-
olution, using Top-1 accuracy. TinyBERT was tested on the SST-2 task from
GLUE, with 67,349 reviews, employing accuracy and F1 score. Wav2Vec2-Tiny
was assessed on LibriSpeech test-clean, containing 2,620 audio clips, using word
error rate. Compression techniques comprised 8-bit post-training quantization,
pruning with sparsity ratios of 0.3 and 0.5, and weight sharing via K-means clus-
tering with 8 and 16 clusters. Performance metrics included accuracy loss ΔAcc,
or ΔF 1 for TinyBERT and ΔW ER for Wav2Vec2-Tiny, inference latency Tinf ,
peak memory usage Mpeak , and compression ratio CR, measured via TensorFlow
Lite for inference and Android NDK for proﬁling. Peak memory was calculated
as:
                              L
                   Mpeak =         (|Wl |Bw + |Xl |Ba ) + Mcache ,             (1)
                             l=1

where Wl and Xl denote layer weights and activations, Bw and Ba represent their
bit-widths, and Mcache is the runtime cache, monitored through the Android
Debug Bridge.
    These settings establish a robust foundation for evaluating hardware-
compression interactions, directly informing the design of HACompBench’s pro-
ﬁling, evaluation, and optimization components in Sect. 5. With this setup, we
now analyze hardware heterogeneity’s eﬀects on compression performance.

compatibility η, as deﬁned in Sect. 3, aﬀect the inference acceleration ratio S and
memory change ratio Mcomp /Mbase for MobileNetV3-Small under quantization,

4.4   Compression Technique Eﬃcacy
This subsection evaluates the eﬃcacy of quantization, pruning, and weight
sharing across ten models, including eight vision models: MobileNetV3-Small,
MobileNetV2, EﬃcientNet-B0, SqueezeNet, ShuﬄeNet 1x, ShuﬄeNetV2 1x,
MnasNet, and ProxylessNASNet, one text model, TinyBERT, and one speech
model, Wav2Vec2-Tiny, on four System-on-Chip platforms: Snapdragon 888 in
Xiaomi 11, Snapdragon 765G in Pixel 5, Kirin 970 in Huawei Nova 3, and Jet-
son Nano P3450. The analysis explores the relationship between platform char-
acteristics, quantiﬁed by ξ and η, and the normalized dynamic score J, which
balances accuracy loss ΔAcc, ΔF 1, or ΔW ER, inference latency Tinf , and peak
memory usage Mpeak . The scoring function, deﬁned in Equation (3), employs
initial weights α = 0.4, β = 0.4, and γ = 0.2, determined by task priorities for
latency, memory, or accuracy loss, enabling uniﬁed comparisons across platforms,
models, and techniques.

combination strategies.
    These ﬁndings inform HACompBench’s design in Sect. 5, particularly the
Scoring and Optimization module in Sect. 5.4. The lower J scores of quantiza-
tion, such as 32.3% for MobileNetV3-Small on Snapdragon 888, validate the opti-
mization of J. Dynamic weight adjustment, increasing β to 0.5 for high compute
utilization CUavg = 0.85, aligns with Sect. 4.2, while ξ and η guide compression
selection, prioritizing quantization for high-ξ SoCs and weight sharing for low-η
SoCs, ensuring hardware-aware recommendations.

4.5   Experimental Conclusions
The experiments yield four key ﬁndings that shape HACompBench’s design
in Sect. 5. 1. Hardware heterogeneity signiﬁcantly inﬂuences compression out-
comes. Platforms with high quantization eﬃciency, such as Snapdragon 888 with
ξ = 1.0, achieve up to a 2.73-fold quantization speedup, whereas those with low
sparsity compatibility, such as Kirin 970 and Jetson Nano P3450 with η = 0.0,
incur a 0.96-fold and 1.05-fold pruning performance, respectively. Regression
analysis, as shown in Equation (2), quantiﬁes ξ’s dominance in quantization,
contributing a 2.37-fold per unit ξ, and η’s role in pruning, contributing a 1.05-
fold per unit η (with Pearson correlations of 0.95 and 0.92, respectively), guid-
ing HACompBench’s hardware proﬁling in Sect. 5.2. 2. Multimodal tasks exhibit
distinct sensitivities. Text models, such as TinyBERT with a 0.5% ΔF 1, demon-
strate greater robustness than vision models, with a 2.85% ΔAcc, and speech
models, with a 2.75% ΔW ER, on Snapdragon 888, as visualized in Fig. 2. A
12.6% accuracy improvement through modal validates HACompBench’s modal-
ity correction in Sect. 5.6. 3. Quantization outperforms other single techniques,
490    Z. Gan et al.

achieving a 2.73-fold speedup and J = 32.3% for MobileNetV3-Small on Snap-
dragon 888, with consistent trends across platforms, as shown in Fig. 3. 4. The
scoring function J eﬀectively balances accuracy, latency, and memory, with lower
J scores, such as 32.3% for quantization versus 73.0% for pruning on Snapdragon
888, correlating with higher utility, 3.1 versus 1.37, providing a robust metric
for HACompBench’s scoring mechanism that surpasses unimodal benchmarks
like MLPerf Tiny by incorporating multimodal support and hardware metrics.
These ﬁndings establish a data-driven foundation for HACompBench, ensuring
hardware-aware, task-adaptive, and optimized compression recommendations.
Future experiments could extend to FPGA platforms to further validate parallel
optimizations.

5     HACompBench Framework Design
This section presents the design of HACompBench, a hardware-aware frame-
work for evaluating and optimizing model compression strategies on resource-
constrained edge devices. Guided by experimental insights from Sect. 4,
HACompBench integrates hardware characteristics, modality-speciﬁc correc-
tions, and multi-objective optimization to recommend compression conﬁgura-
tions that balance accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The framework is val-
idated on four System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms: Snapdragon 888 (Xiaomi 11),
           HACompBench: Co-designed DNN Compression for Edge Devices         491

Snapdragon 765G (Google Pixel 5), Kirin 970 (Huawei Nova 3), and Jetson Nano
P3450. Below, we detail the framework’s workﬂow, components, and validation,
emphasizing its operational principles and alignment with experimental ﬁndings.


5.1   Workﬂow Overview

HACompBench operates through four core modules, as illustrated in Fig. 4:
Hardware Proﬁling, Compression Evaluation, Scoring and Optimization, and
Eﬀect Validation. The Hardware Proﬁling module quantiﬁes SoC-speciﬁc met-
rics, such as sparsity compatibility η and quantization eﬃciency ξ, using Qual-
comm SNPE and Android NDK, aligning with ﬁndings in Sect. 4.2 that high
ξ enhances quantization performance, achieving a 2.73-fold speedup on Snap-
dragon 888. The Compression Evaluation module applies compression tech-
niques, including quantization, pruning, and weight sharing, and measures per-
formance metrics, such as accuracy loss ΔAcc, inference latency Tinf , peak mem-
ory usage Mpeak , and compression ratio CR, via TensorFlow Lite benchmarking.
The Scoring and Optimization module computes a dynamic score J to select con-
ﬁgurations that minimize J while adhering to constraints, ensuring peak mem-
ory usage does not exceed 512 MB. Finally, the Eﬀect Validation module veriﬁes
the recommended conﬁgurations across SoCs, ensuring robust performance. This
workﬂow is based on experimental insights from Sect. 4, such as high ξ improving
quantization performance.


5.2   Hardware Proﬁling

The Hardware Proﬁling module quantiﬁes SoC characteristics to guide compres-
sion strategy selection by measuring sparsity compatibility η and quantization
eﬃciency ξ, as deﬁned in Sect. 3. Using Qualcomm SNPE and Android NDK, the
module executes a test suite to proﬁle sparse matrix operations and low-precision
computation throughput. For example, Snapdragon 888 exhibits high quantiza-
tion eﬃciency with ξ = 1.0 and sparsity compatibility with η = 0.82, enabling
eﬃcient quantization and pruning, with η = 0.82 supporting eﬃcient parallel
sparse operations. While Kirin 970’s low quantization eﬃciency of ξ = 0.3 and
sparsity compatibility of η = 0.0 favor weight sharing. These metrics are stored
in a hardware characteristics table, such as Table 1, for use in subsequent mod-
ules, prioritizing quantization for SoCs with high ξ and weight sharing for SoCs
with low η.


5.3   Compression Evaluation

The Compression Evaluation module applies compression techniques and mea-
sures their impact on performance metrics. It operates as follows:

– Technique Application: Compression methods, including 8-bit post-
  training quantization (PTQ), pruning (sparsity s = 0.3, 0.5), weight sharing
492    Z. Gan et al.

  (K = 8, 16 clusters), and combinations (e.g., quantization + weight shar-
  ing), are applied to models such as MobileNetV3-Small, TinyBERT, and
  Wav2Vec2-Tiny using TensorFlow Lite.
– Performance Measurement: Metrics are measured using TensorFlow Lite
  for inference and Android NDK for proﬁling, including ΔAcc (or ΔF 1,
  ΔW ER), Tinf , Mpeak , and CR.

   This module provides the performance data necessary for computing J and
optimizing conﬁgurations, aligning with Sect. 4.4 ﬁndings on combination strat-
egy eﬃcacy.


5.4   Scoring and Optimization

The Scoring and Optimization module orchestrates the evaluation and reﬁne-
ment of compression conﬁgurations by computing a performance score J, adapt-
ing weights to real-time hardware conditions, and optimizing conﬁgurations
through a multi-objective genetic algorithm that searches for optimal sparsity
patterns, emphasizing parallel sparse matrix operations on NPUs and GPUs.
Executed over approximately 5 s, this module ensures hardware-aware compres-
sion strategies that balance accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The process
begins with an initial scoring phase, where the scoring function J is applied to
100 initial compression conﬁgurations using user-speciﬁed default weights, such
as α = 0.4, β = 0.4, and γ = 0.2, which are validated for balance in Sect. 4.4.
For instance, applying single quantization to MobileNetV3-Small on the Snap-
dragon 888 yields a baseline J = 31.5%, establishing a reference for subsequent
optimization. This step, completed in 0.3 s using Python with TensorFlow Lite
APIs, provides a foundation for assessing the suitability of default weights and
initializing the optimization process.
    Following initial scoring, the module monitors real-time hardware load to cap-
ture dynamic computational and memory demands. Compute utilization (CU )
and memory stress index (M SI) are collected every 100 ms via Android NDK
and ADB, with a sliding window of 10 samples (1 s) computing averages, such as
CUavg = 0.85 and M SIavg = 1.2 for Snapdragon 888. This 0.3-second process,
aligned with load correlations from Sect. 4.2, informs the need for weight adjust-
ments by quantifying resource bottlenecks. The load data directly drives the
dynamic weight adjustment phase, which reﬁnes the scoring function to reﬂect
real-time conditions. If CUavg exceeds 0.8, indicating a computational bottle-
neck, β increases by 0.1 to 0.5 to prioritize latency, while α decreases to 0.3,
and γ remains 0.2; similarly, M SIavg above 1.5 would increase γ. For the Snap-
dragon 888 scenario, the adjustment to β = 0.5 reduces latency by 32%, and J
is recomputed, yielding J = 29.8% for the combination strategy. This 0.4-second
step ensures the scoring function adapts to hardware demands, enhancing opti-
mization relevance. The process is shown in Fig. 5.
    After obtaining the J value, ﬁlter out conﬁgurations that violate constraint
conditions, such as conﬁgurations with peak memory usage exceeding 512 MB.
           HACompBench: Co-designed DNN Compression for Edge Devices          493




      Fig. 5. Dynamic Weight Adjustment for Scoring Function Optimization.


Subsequently, select the conﬁguration with the lowest J value from these conﬁg-
urations. Achieving J = 29.8% for Bw = 8 and K = 8 on Snapdragon 888 with
a 3.21-fold speedup. The module concludes by recommending this conﬁguration,
validated in Sect. 5.5, ensuring alignment with Sect. 4.4 ﬁndings on combina-
tion strategy eﬃcacy. The genetic algorithm uses a population size of 50 and 20
iterations, selected based on convergence tests in experiments to minimize com-
putational overhead (approx. 5 s), to search for optimal sparse patterns, focusing
on parallel matrix operations on NPUs/GPUs.


5.5   Eﬀect Validation

The Eﬀect Validation module assesses the performance of recommended conﬁg-
urations across four SoCs. For Snapdragon 888, quantization for MobileNetV3-
Small achieves a normalized dynamic score J of 32.3%, a 2.73-fold speedup, and
a 69% memory reduction, consistent with ﬁndings in Sect. 4.4 on compression
eﬃcacy. On Snapdragon 765G, with quantization eﬃciency ξ = 0.7, quantization
yields a J of 40.3%, a 1.62-fold speedup, and a 2.85% accuracy loss. For Kirin
970, with ξ = 0.3 and η = 0.0, quantization results in a J of 52.6%, a 1.16-fold
speedup, and a 2.85% accuracy loss. For Jetson Nano P3450, with ξ = 0.3 and
η = 0.0, quantization yields a J of 68.0%, a 0.80-fold speedup, and a 2.85%
accuracy loss. These results align with correlations of 0.95 for quantization and
0.92 for pruning reported in Sect. 4.2 on hardware eﬀects. Compared to prun-
ing, quantization improves utility signiﬁcantly, for example, from 1.37 to 3.1 on
Snapdragon 888. Compared to benchmarks like MLPerf Tiny, HACompBench
reduces J by 20% on average while supporting multimodal tasks, conﬁrming its
eﬃcacy in hardware-aware optimization.
494     Z. Gan et al.

5.6   Modality-Speciﬁc Correction

To enhance cross-modal robustness, HACompBench applies a modality-speciﬁc
correction factor modal , calibrated at 2.1% for vision, 1.5% for text, and 3.8% for
speech, based on Sect. 4.3 ﬁndings. This factor adjusts ΔAcc to mitigate accuracy
losses, with computational overhead less than 1 s using 10% of the dataset for
calibration, improving evaluation accuracy by 12.6% for TinyBERT, 12.2% for
Wav2Vec2-Tiny, and 7.9% for MobileNetV3-Small across SoCs, ensuring consis-
tent performance across diverse tasks. This correction ensures consistency across
tasks, surpassing single-modality benchmarks.


6     Summary

In summary, this study presents HACompBench, a hardware-aware framework
for optimizing deep neural network compression on resource-constrained edge
devices across vision, text, and speech tasks. HACompBench addresses limita-
tions of traditional compress-then-deploy approaches by formulating compres-
sion evaluation as a multi-objective optimization problem, integrating quanti-
zation eﬃciency ξ, sparsity compatibility η, and a dynamic scoring function J
to balance accuracy, latency, and memory, with a focus on enhancing paral-
lel sparse computations in edge architectures. Experiments on four SoC plat-
forms, namely Snapdragon 888, Snapdragon 765G, Kirin 970, and Jetson Nano
P3450, tested ten models using quantization, pruning, weight sharing, and com-
binations, revealing key performance trade-oﬀs. For example, quantization on
MobileNetV3-Small achieves J = 32.3%, a 2.73-fold speedup, and 69% memory
reduction on Snapdragon 888, versus J = 68.0% and 0.80-fold speedup on Jetson
Nano. Combining quantization and weight sharing yields J = 29.8%, a 3.21-fold
speedup, and an 8.1% utility gain on Snapdragon 888. Modality-speciﬁc correc-
tions enhance accuracy by 12.6%. HACompBench improves on MLPerf Tiny’s
vision-only scope and AIoTBench’s lack of co-design via ξ and η, supported by
regression analysis. This framework provides a uniﬁed approach that quantiﬁ-
ably advances edge deployment through hardware-algorithm co-design. Future
work will explore FPGA acceleration to further leverage hardware parallelism in
sparse optimizations, integrate neural architecture search with parallel process-
ing for automated model design, develop adaptive compression for dynamic edge
environments to handle varying loads, and extend to federated learning scenarios
with distributed parallel computations for collaborative edge intelligence.

content of this article.

          Are We There Yet? Unraveling the
      State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed
                    Optimizations

                 Mingliang Liu, Shanlin Deng, and Baojian Hua(B)

       School of Software Engineering, Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research,
        University of Science and Technology of China, Suzhou 215123, China
       {liumingliang,dengshanlin}@mail.ustc.edu.cn, bjhua@ustc.edu.cn



       Abstract. Binary feedback-directed optimization (BFDO) is a novel
       technique for optimizing program binaries by leveraging dynamic pro-
       ﬁles, showing promising potential in various domains including data cen-
       ters, clouds, and embedded systems. However, state-of-the-art BFDO
       approaches primarily focus on speciﬁc instruction set architectures and
       programming languages, while overlooking the architectural discrep-
       ancies, language diversity, and compiler optimization options. Conse-
       quently, a comprehensive study of BFDO is still lacking, hindering its
       broader applications.
          In this paper, to address this gap, we present the ﬁrst systematic study
       of BFDO, providing insights into its current capabilities, key grand chal-
       lenges, and future research opportunities. Speciﬁcally, we ﬁrst conduct
       an empirical study using a novel end-to-end evaluation tool to assess
       the eﬀectiveness of BFDO. Our analysis identiﬁes three root causes of
       BFDO failures and highlights three factors inﬂuencing its optimization
       eﬀectiveness. Based on these ﬁndings, we propose four best practices
       and outline three promising research opportunities, oﬀering guidance
       for future advancements. Applying our best practices to RISC-V bench-
       marks improves performance by an average of 4.57%, eﬀectively mitigat-
       ing existing relocation failures.


       Keywords: Compiler optimizations · binary feedback-directed
       optimizations · Proﬁle-guided optimizations


1    Introduction
Binary feedback-directed optimization (BFDO) [32,36,37,40,48] is a promising
post-link compiler optimization that directly enhances a target program’s binary
by leveraging the dynamically collected runtime proﬁles. Since BFDOs can more
accurately map runtime proﬁles to binaries [10] than to high-level program source
code or compiler intermediate representations, they oﬀer performance improve-
ments beyond those typically achieved by static compilers or traditional proﬁle-
guided optimizations (PGOs) [9,22,31,35]. For instance, BOLT [36], a recently
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 497–517, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_27
498    M. Liu et al.

proposed BFDO, achieved speedups of up to 7.0% for data-center applications on
x86-64. Over the next decade, the growing demand for greater program eﬃciency
in data centers, cloud computing, and embedded systems, along with the need
for lower energy consumption, will make BFDO an increasingly valuable opti-
mization technique.
    While existing BFDOs have demonstrated promising potential for achiev-
ing signiﬁcant performance improvements in practical workloads, they remain
limited in terms of architectural independence, language diversity, and compiler
optimization neutrality. First, existing BFDO studies [36,37,40,48] primarily
focus on a single architecture, x86-64, while neglecting others. We speculate
that this focus on x86-64 stems not only from its widespread adoption in data
centers and cloud environments but also from its hardware functionalities, such
as Last Branch Record (LBR), which are essential for generating precise run-
time proﬁles. However, as RISC architectures like AArch64 and RISC-V are
increasingly deployed, we argue that the advantages of BFDO on x86-64 do not
necessarily extend to RISC architectures for several technical reasons. First, the
static disassembly required for BFDOs remains an unsolved challenge [3], which
is particularly diﬃcult for RISC architectures due to the frequent intermixing of
data and instructions [25]. Second, proﬁling hardware on RISCs exhibits signif-
icantly diﬀerent capabilities [46], meaning that proﬁles generated by this hard-
ware may lack the precision required for eﬀective BFDO optimization. Therefore,
a comprehensive understanding of BFDOs on RISC architectures is urgently
needed.
    Second, existing BFDOs primarily focus on speciﬁc languages such as
C/C++, neglecting support for other emerging languages. Although C/C++ are
widely used in cloud computing, data centers, and embedded systems [19,44,50],
languages like Go and Rust are also gaining traction [43]. For instance, Go
has been extensively adopted by vendors like Google and has facilitated the
development of major open-source projects such as Docker and Kubernetes [38].
Similarly, Rust is being deployed in Firefox [34] and the Linux kernel [28]. Fur-
thermore, binaries compiled from these languages exhibit distinct characteristics
compared to those compiled from C/C++, due to diﬀerences in compilation tech-
niques and runtime organizations. For example, Go’s binaries contain extensive
runtime information, including garbage collection mechanisms, while binaries
from functional languages such as ML consist of numerous smaller basic blocks
due to the use of continuations [4,26]—both of which are absent in C/C++
binaries. Consequently, evaluating the eﬀectiveness of BFDO across diverse pro-
gramming languages and binary structures is crucial.
    Third, existing BFDO studies [32,36,37,40,48] have largely overlooked the
impact of compiler optimizations on target binaries, making it challenging for
developers to tune optimization options for optimal BFDO performance. Since
compiler optimizations are applied in the early compilation stage without explic-
itly considering the post-link binaries, they may inadvertently reduce the eﬀec-
tiveness of state-of-the-art BFDOs. For example, the default optimization level
(O0) may hinder sample-based proﬁle generation by producing a large number
    Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations     499

of smaller basic blocks, while linker relaxation optimizations [11] may interfere
with function reordering by replacing call instructions with those of narrower
ranges (e.g., jalr to jal). Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of how
compiler optimizations aﬀect BFDO eﬀectiveness is essential.
    In light of these limitations, in this paper, we present the ﬁrst comprehen-
sive study of state-of-the-art BFDOs to investigate their current capabilities, key
grand challenges, and future research opportunities, providing insights into their
continued development. To achieve this, we design BinInsight, a novel auto-
mated and scalable tool, to aid in our investigation, and employ both quantitative
and qualitative methodologies on micro-benchmarks and real-world workloads.
We then conduct a qualitative study to investigate BFDO failures and their root
causes, current limitations and mitigation strategies, best practices, and future
research directions.
    Speciﬁcally, our investigation addresses the three aforementioned limitations
of existing BFDOs. First, we study BFDOs on three representative architectures:
x86-64, AArch64, and RISC-V. These architectures are chosen not only because
they represent distinct application scenarios—including cloud, embedded, and
mobile systems—but also due to their diﬀering dynamic proﬁling capabilities,
which are crucial for BFDO eﬀectiveness. Second, we study binaries compiled
from four programming languages: C/C++, Go, ML, and Rust. These languages
are selected because they are not only widely adopted but also represent diverse
programming paradigms, including imperative, object-oriented, and functional
programming. Third, we experiment with various compile-time optimization
options as well as link-time optimizations, such as linker relaxation. Moreover,
thanks to the scalable design of BinInsight, our system is not restricted to those
speciﬁc combinations and can be extended to explore potential combinations of
architectures, languages, and optimization strategies.
    Our study yields signiﬁcant ﬁndings and insights. First, we identify three pri-
mary root causes of BFDO failures, originating from issues in disassembly and
symbol relocation. Second, we reveal three key factors—compiler support code,
biased proﬁles, and branch prediction failures—that substantially aﬀect BFDO
eﬀectiveness. Based on our ﬁndings, we propose four best practices for using
BFDOs, and point out three potential directions for future studies. By applying
our best practices to RISC-V benchmarks, we achieve an average performance
improvement of 4.57% over state-of-the-art while simultaneously preventing relo-
cation failures.
    To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first step towards
gaining a comprehensive understanding of state-of-the-art BFDOs. In summary,
our work makes the following contributions:

– Comprehensive study. We systematically analyze state-of-the-art BFDOs
  using both quantitative and qualitative methodologies.
– Findings and insights. We identify three root causes for BFDO failures,
  and three factors aﬀecting their eﬀectiveness.
– Best practices and suggestions. We propose four best practices for
  improving BFDOs and outline three promising research directions.
500    M. Liu et al.

– Open source. We open source our software prototype, benchmarks,
  test scripts, and evaluation results to promote open research at:
  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15058804.


2     Background
To be self-contained, in this section, we present the background knowledge for
this work on Feedback-directed optimization (FDO) (§ 2.1), and proﬁle genera-
tion (§ 2.2).

2.1   Feedback-Driven Optimization (FDO)

History. Feedback-driven optimization (FDO), also known as Proﬁle-guided
optimization (PGO), has been extensively studied with a long history [27] due
to its potential to leverage runtime proﬁles for guiding compiler optimization.
Recently, with advancements in hardware support and more accurate proﬁle
utilization techniques, FDO has garnered renewed research interest with notable
variants and applications (e.g., AutoFDO [9], SamplingPGO [35], and CSSPGO
[22]).
Workflow. FDOs employ a two-stage
build process as shown in Fig. 1. In the
ﬁrst stage, the source code is compiled
(①) to binary, which is then executed to
obtain proﬁles (②). Speciﬁcally, two pri-
mary approaches are utilized for proﬁle
acquisition: instrumentation-based and
                                             Fig. 1. Workﬂow of FDO and BFDO.
sample-based. The instrumentation-
based approach instruments the target program to collect important runtime
information such as execution frequency of basic blocks, functions, and loops,
whereas the sample-based approach leverages specialized hardware features such
as x86-64 LBR to periodically sample instructions to approximate execution fre-
quencies. Guided by proﬁles collected in stage one (③), the second stage compiles
the source to binary again (④), to further improve program performance (e.g.,
more precise inline decisions for frequently called functions).
    Traditional FDOs face two technical challenges. First, binary-only programs
lack source code, making it diﬃcult if not impossible to instrument sources. Sec-
ond, compiler optimizations in phase (①) may dramatically change code layout,
defeating the feasibility of binary proﬁles to source programs. Binary Feedback-
directed Optimizations (BFDOs) [12,32,36] are introduced to address these chal-
lenges. As Fig. 1 presents, BFDOs directly instrument the executable binary to
generate proﬁles which are then utilized to optimize the binary (⑤), without
requiring program source code. Compared to FDOs, BFDOs (e.g., HALO [39],
Lighting BOLT [37], and Propeller [40]) often have a global view of the bina-
ries as they process post-link programs, enabling more aggressive optimizations
      Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations   501

including code layout, data compaction, hot/cold code splitting, alignment, and
peephole optimizations.
Application. As a promising compiler optimization, FDO has been widely
deployed in many applications. FDO is now supported by mainstream com-
pilers [29], and has demonstrated eﬀectiveness in optimizing diverse real-world
programs (e.g., Chrome [9] and Linux kernel [51]). Furthermore, FDO is also
rapidly adopted by industry to optimize production applications in production
environments. For example, FDO is used by Google [40] to optimize warehouse-
scale applications, and by Meta to optimize compute-bound services [22].

2.2    Profile Generation

Proﬁle generation is essential to perform eﬀective FDO, as proﬁles directly guide
optimization. Existing proﬁle generation approaches can be classiﬁed into four
categories: instrumentation-based, sample-based, hardware-based, and deep-
learning-based.
Instrumentation-Based. Instrumentation-based proﬁle generation inserts
instructions into the code to track accurate execution counts for various pro-
gram paths, and has been deployed in many tools (e.g., Atom [41], Clang [30],
and BOLT [36]). While the instrumentation-based approach generates precise
data, it introduces substantial runtime overhead as well as considerable code
size increases to instrumented binaries, hindering its use in production scenar-
ios.
Sample-Based. Sample-based proﬁle generation employs operating system
mechanisms like clock interrupts to periodically capture program state snap-
shots as proﬁles. Traditional sample-based proﬁling is a statistical approxima-
tion which may produce inaccurate proﬁles. To mitigate this problem, precise
sampling such as continuous proﬁling [2,20] is proposed to signiﬁcantly enhance
the precision.
Hardware-Based. Hardware-based proﬁling [1,10,14] collects proﬁles leverag-
ing hardware performance counters, which critically rely on the underlying archi-
tectures. Fortunately, most modern architectures support performance counters
(e.g., Intel x86-64’s Last Branch Records (LBR) [15], AArch64’s Embedded Trace
Macrocell (ETM) [5], and RISC-V’s Hardware Performance Monitor (HPM),
among others), which enable the generation of proﬁles with negligible runtime
costs [17,42].
Deep-Learning-Based. Deep-learning-based approaches generate proﬁles by
estimating program branches statically. Once deemed impractical in the 1990s
[7], deep-learning-based approaches have shown promising potential in optimiz-
ing binaries [33].
502    M. Liu et al.

3     Approach
This section presents our approach to conducting the evaluation. Performing
such an evaluation of various datasets on multiple platforms is challenging, due
to two key reasons: automation and scalability. First, the evaluation must be
fully automated to eﬃciently evaluate a large number of projects; human inter-
vention is only required for tasks that cannot be automated by machines, such
as root cause analysis. Second, the evaluation must be scalable to study diﬀerent
combinations of architectures and programming languages, even potential ones
not covered in this study.
    To this end, we design and implement an automated software prototype,
BinInsight, to aid in our evaluation. We ﬁrst present an overview of BinIn-
sight (§ 3.1), and then each component, including compilation (§ 3.2), opti-
mization (§ 3.3), metric measurement (§ 3.4), and root cause analysis (§ 3.5).

3.1   Overview
BinInsight is designed with the key
principle of modularity and extensi-
bility, making it straightforward to
accommodate diﬀerent needs, such as
adding new test projects, new pro-
gramming languages, and architec-
tures.
    Figure 2 provides an overview of
BinInsight, which comprises four
key components: compilation, opti- Fig. 2. An overview of BinInsight’s work-
mization, measurement, and root ﬂow.
cause analysis. First, the compilation component (①) takes the test cases as
input, compiles and links them with relocation information according to the
user-speciﬁed conﬁguration, generating an unoptimized binary. Second, the opti-
mization component (②) receives the unoptimized binary and samples the binary
during execution to produce proﬁles, which guide the optimizer to optimize the
target binary and generate an optimized version. Third, the measurement com-
ponent (③) measures and records metrics for both the unoptimized and opti-
mized binaries. Finally, the root cause analysis module (④) enables root cause
studies for failures, upon which best practices and suggestions are composed.

3.2   Compilation
The compilation module compiles and links source code into binaries with relo-
cation information according to a user-speciﬁed conﬁguration. A critical aspect
of this process is selecting toolchains that support the link options required by
BFDOs [36]. Speciﬁcally, the compiler toolchain must support emit relocations
option (i.e., --emit-relocs or -q in most linkers). However, we have observed
that while mainstream linkers (e.g., BFD, Gold, and lld) generally support the
      Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations   503

relocations option, some do not. For instance, gc, the oﬃcial Go compiler, lacks
support for this option whereas other Go compilers, such as gccgo [18] and gol-
lvm [21], provide the necessary functionality. For this reason, we use gccgo to
evaluate Go programs (§ 4). The key takeaway is that developers must carefuly
select a compiler toolchain that supports relocation, otherwise BFDOs may fail
to take eﬀect without any explicit warning.


3.3    Optimization

The optimization component optimizes the target binaries and produces opti-
mized ones by leveraging proﬁles in two steps: 1) Proﬁling: collect proﬁles during
execution using performance tools like perf [16] to sample the CPU-cycles event
and taken branch stack. To minimize potential noise and ensure more accurate
proﬁles, essential measures should be taken, including terminating irrelevant pro-
cesses, increasing process priority, and setting CPU aﬃnity. 2) Optimization: the
binary is optimized using the proﬁles and options speciﬁed by the user.
    During our experiments, we observed that the taken branch stack is arguably
the most critical information for BFDOs, as it records a series of consecutive
taken branches, thus providing accurate counts for critical edges to improve the
resilience against imprecise sampling [36] (see § 4). Therefore, it is essential to
enable this hardware feature if it is supported by the underlying hardware.


3.4    Quantitative Measurement

The measurement component calculates metrics for both the original and opti-
mized binaries. Key metrics essential for measuring BFDOs include, but are not
limited to, the following:
CPU Cycles. This metric represents the number of clock cycles spent executing
the program and is the primary target for reduction through binary optimization.
Branches and Branch Misses. This metric reﬂects the eﬀect of branch pre-
diction after basic block reordering, which can be reduced by eﬀective block
reordering.
Cache and Cache Misses. This metric encompasses both instruction cache (I-
cache) and data cache (D-cache). BFDOs aim to improve instruction locality by
reducing I-cache occupation, grouping hotspot code, and folding identical code.
However, a trade-oﬀ between I-cache and D-cache optimization is often necessary,
as optimizing both simultaneously can be challenging.
TLB and TLB Misses. This metric indicates instruction and data locality at
the page level, which is larger than cache size, and thus is useful for analyzing
large programs.
    These metrics can be measured by utilizing performance tools like perf.
Meanwhile, the measurement should be repeated multiple times to minimize
noise, before calculating the average speedups according to Eq. (1).
504     M. Liu et al.

                                                unopt−opt
                                       repeat     unopt
                         speedup =                                           (1)
                                          repeat

3.5   Root Cause Analysis

The root cause analysis component identiﬁes the underlying causes of optimiza-
tion failures, proposes suggestions, and provides ﬁxes. We conduct manual anal-
ysis when automated analysis is impossible, following prior studies on optimiza-
tion failures and performance degradation [3,13,24,25,45,49]. Furthermore, we
identify impactful factors for performance improvements, and provide best prac-
tices and suggestions to enhance the whole ecosystem.


4     Evaluation

In conducting the evaluation, we aim to answer the following research questions:
RQ1: Programming Language Diversity. Is BFDO eﬀective on binaries
compiled from diﬀerent programming languages? What are the performance dis-
crepancies for these binaries from diﬀerent languages, if any?
RQ2: Architecture Independence. Is BFDO dependent on diﬀerent archi-
tectures, as these architectures have diﬀerent hardware performance facilities?
RQ3: Optimization Neutrality. How do compiler and linker optimizations
aﬀect BFDO? What are the optimization traps and pitfalls?

4.1   Experimental Setup

We conduct experiments on three current representative architectures: x86-64,
AArch64, and RISC-V, as shown in Table 1. For Intel CPUs, all experiments
are performed on Performance-cores (P-cores). Additionally, for RISC-V CPUs,
we use Debian instead of Ubuntu because our RISC-V machine only provides
the Debian images, which does not introduce any bias because our experiments
do not depend on speciﬁc OS features. We use BOLT to optimize their I-cache
locality with the following options:
- reorder - blocks = ext - tsp - dyno - stats - split - functions
- split - all - cold - split - eh - reorder - functions = hfsort

   We collect proﬁles using perf record with options -e cycles:u -j any,u.
We then use perf2bolt tool to convert the proﬁles to BOLT format, with a -nl
option if the corresponding architecture does not support branch stack sampling.
      Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations                                     505

4.2     Datasets

We construct two datasets to conduct the evaluation: 1) micro-benchmarks; and
2) real-world workloads, which are distributed in our open source.
Micro-benchmarks. We create a set of micro-benchmarks as a uniﬁed standard
for four languages: C++, Go, Rust, and Standard ML (SML), which are compiled
by clang, rustc, gccgo, and MLton, respectively.
Real-World Workloads. We select diverse real-world open-source projects
from GitHub based on the following selection criteria: 1) compiler support, and
2) performance priority. First, we select projects that satisfy the compiler require-
ments outlined in § 3.2, otherwise BFDO cannot be applied. Second, we select
projects prioritizing performance, for which BFDOs are of more practical impli-
cations.

4.3    RQ1: Programming Language Diversity
To answer RQ1 by demonstrating the eﬀectiveness and eﬃciency of BFDO
across multiple languages, we ﬁrst conduct experiments on micro-benchmarks,
as shown in Table 2. For all three architectures, C/C++ demonstrates speedups
of 1.82%, 1.76%, and -5.69% on average, respectively, Go shows speedups of
3.38%, 2.63%, and -6.60% on average, respectively, whereas SML shows speedups
of 3.4%, 1.23%, and 1.25% on average, respectively. While Rust exhibits the
best optimization eﬀects of 15.26% on x86-64, it performs poorly on RISC-V.
In contrast, SML exhibits the worst optimization results on x86-64 and RISC-V
but also the lowest variance.
    Next, we evaluate real-world workloads, as presented in Table 3. Across all
three architectures, the performance improvement for C/C++ achieves 4.17%,
and 4.07% on average, while Go achieves 4.74% and 3.35%, followed by Rust’s
4.36%. These results demonstrate that BFDO is eﬀective in uniformly improving
the performance of real-world workloads for all three languages.

      Table 3. Performance for real-world workloads (% speedup, per test case).

Root Cause Analysis. We then investigate the root cause leading to perfor-
mance discrepancies and identify the following factors. First, Rust and Go con-
tain more cold code because they integrate more complex runtimes than C/C++,
      Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations     507

including stack overﬂow check, array bounds check, Drop trait code, and sup-
port libraries. Such mechanisms aﬀect instruction locality hence beneﬁt BFDOs.
We identify that in our micro-benchmark, the cold code of C/C++ programs
accounts for 57% of the code, while Go and Rust account for 84% and 96%,
respectively, which results in section sizes 23x and 122x larger than C/C++.
These metrics indicate that Go and Rust have greater optimization potential.
    The second root cause for performance discrepancies is the machine code
style generated from diﬀerent languages. We reveal that BFDO disassembles
binaries at the function granularity determined by the granularity of relocation
information, which does not ﬁt well with functional languages that often leverage
continuation-passing style (CPS) transformation leading to many small functions
(i.e., chunks). Furthermore, we observe that the MLton compiler invokes the
generated functions via indirect function pointer dispatches rather than direct
calls, which complicates both the function disassembly and the ﬁnal control-ﬂow
graphs. To this end, existing BFDOs still face grand challenges for functional
languages.

failures.


4.4    RQ2: Architecture Independence
To answer RQ2, we investigate BFDO’s dependency on diverse architectures,
as presented in Table 2. We observe that x86-64 improves the performance of
all four languages, while AArch64 improves three among them except for Rust.
RISC-V is the worst to manifest performance degradation for all languages, as
508    M. Liu et al.

depicted in Fig. 3. We then conduct experiments on real-world workloads, as
detailed in Table 3. The results align closely with those from micro-benchmarks,
conﬁrming that x86-64 delivers the best performance, while RISC-V performs
the worst. Furthermore, as Table 3 shows, AArch64 and RISC-V encounter more
compilation, disassembly, and relocation errors, leading to optimization failures.
Root Cause Analysis. We then investigate the root causes of optimization fail-
ures and performance degradation, and identify four key root causes: 1) custom
instructions, 2) relocation exception, 3) biased proﬁling, and 4) failed predic-
tion. First, custom instructions in RISC-V lead to optimization failures. Specif-
ically, as an open-source architecture, RISC-V allows chip vendors to incorpo-
rate custom instructions. While such customizations bring ﬂexibility, they pose
challenges to disassembly, an essential step for BFDO. Figure 4 shows a failure
example we observed when disassembling from grpc-go. The values 0x01a0000b
and 0x0246000b in the .insn directive encode the custom instructions SYNC.I
and DCACHE.CVAL1 respectively on Xuantie C910 processor [8], which defeat the
disassembler, leading to optimization failures.




            Fig. 5. PC-relative relocations lead to optimization failures.


    The second root cause leading to optimization failures is relocation excep-
tions. Speciﬁcally, we identify that optimization failures for Rust on RISC-V
are due to the exceptions that the optimizer failed to ﬁnd the corresponding
%pcrel_hi modiﬁer. This exception stems from the relocation type PC-relative
TLS GD GOT reference used in RISC-V multithreaded programs, which is used
to load the address of a symbol into a register (via the pseudo directive la or
la.tls.gd for thread-local storage (TLS)). On most architectures, such load
operations typically use PC-relative addressing, which requires two instructions
on RISC-V, as shown in Fig. 5. The %pcrel_hi modiﬁer represents the high 20
bits of the relative address between the program counter (PC) and the target
symbol, and the %pcrel_lo modiﬁer represents the low 12 bits. In this example,
to load the address of symbol into register a0, auipc instruction uses the high
20 bits of the relative address between PC and symbol as source operand HI,
storing P C + (HI << 12) into register a0. Then addi instruction takes regis-
ter a0 and the low 12 bits of the relative address between corresponding auipc
instruction and symbol as source operands, adding them and storing the result in
register a0. The instructions in foo and bar, though written diﬀerently, perform
    Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations    509

similar functions. They load normal symbols and TLS symbols, respectively, and
produce two distinct relocation types: R_PCREL_HI20 and R_TLS_GD_HI20. We
identify that BFDO fails to resolve the R_TLS_GD_HI20 relocation type, lead-
ing to optimization failures. Furthermore, we reveal that such relocation types
are common in Rust binaries even for non-multithreaded programs but are rare
in C/C++ and Go binaries. Thus we believe existing BFDOs have spaces to
improve the relocation type resolution in Rust binaries.
    The third root cause leading to performance degradation is biased profiles.
Speciﬁcally, while sample-based proﬁling is eﬀective for generating proﬁles with-
out any special aid from instrumentation, it may not reﬂect the real execution
frequency of the program’s basic blocks. This inaccuracy stems from factors such
as sampling frequency, basic block size, and sampling environment. We observe
that among all these factors, the basic block size is the most critical yet chal-
lenging factor to tune by adjusting sampling options. Furthermore, sample-based
proﬁling may introduce bias because it is usually performed at OS interrupt
granularity, in which larger basic blocks with more instructions have a larger
sampling probability while smaller basic blocks are rarely sampled. Although
increasing the sampling frequency can improve the sampling probability of small
basic blocks, it simultaneously increases the sampling probability of large basic
blocks, making it diﬃcult to achieve balanced proﬁling.
    We present in Fig. 6 an exam-
ple leading to optimization failures
due to biased proﬁles. Basic block
B1, B3, and B4 have the same exe-
cution count. However, basic block
B3 is rarely sampled due to its small
size (one instruction). Consequently,
BFDOs may classify B1 and B4 as hot
basic blocks while B3 are classiﬁed
as cold block based on the sampling
results. Thus the optimization lever-
ages the hot/cold split algorithm to
split them into distinct sections that Fig. 6. Biased proﬁles lead to optimization
are far apart in address space, causing failures.
each loop to jump twice between the
hot and cold sections. Such extra jumps introduced by the optimization lead to
severe performance degradation of I-cache locality, and in the worst case lead to
a 1.5x increase in execution time.
Failed Branch Prediction is the fourth and last root cause we have identiﬁed. Dur-
ing BFDO, the optimizer reorders basic blocks by adjusting the target of branch
instructions, placing hot basic blocks in fallthrough areas and cold basic blocks
in cold sections. However, the reordered basic blocks may be too far away and
beyond the addressing range (typically ±4KB) of the conditional jump instruc-
tion that reaches them, as shown in Table 4. To address this issue, the optimizer
can insert an unconditional jump instruction following the conditional jump, but
510    M. Liu et al.




           Fig. 7. Failed branch predictions lead to optimization failures.


this approach may incur signiﬁcant branch prediction failures. We present two
failed branch predictions leading to optimization failures in Fig. 7. In the ﬁrst
case, the branch prediction will take cold block B1 as the predicted branch, which
is not an eﬃcient layout. After optimization, the cold block B1 is placed into the
cold section, and an unconditional jump instruction to B1 is inserted in the orig-
inal position of B1. However, while such a code layout improves code locality, it
does not improve branch prediction accuracy. In the second case, the situation is
even worse. To jump to cold basic block B2, the optimizer reverses the condition
of the conditional jump instruction and inserts an unconditional jump before
basic block B1, incurring a branch prediction failure for each jump to B1. We
observe that when the improvement from code locality cannot compensate for
the overhead of branch prediction failures, the overall performance will degrade.
Speciﬁcally, we identify that branch prediction failures in if statements incur a
performance degradation of about 6%.
