                  Type                  x86-64 AArch64 RISC-V
                  unconditional jump ±2GB ±128MB ±1MB
                  conditional jump      ±2GB ±1MB          ±4KB



4.5   Optimization Neutrality

To answer RQ3 by investigating optimization neutrality of BFDO, we conduct
experiments by applying compiler and linker optimizations when generating the
binaries.
   We ﬁrst experiment with diﬀerent compiler optimization options, and reveal
that lower optimization levels (e.g., O0) will degrade performance because they
tend to generate more complex control-ﬂow graphs with numerous tiny basic
blocks. For instance, we observe a 4.0% performance improvement when run-
ning C/C++ micro-benchmarks on RISC-V by simply switching the compiler
optimization option from O0 to O2. Therefore, we argue that full compiler opti-
mizations should be utilized to maximize the beneﬁts of BFDO.
    Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations    511

    We then conduct experiments to test the eﬀects of link-time optimizations
on BFDOs. We reveal that BFDO often assumes symbol locations remain
unchanged after linking, but binary optimization breaks that assumption and
thus may lead to optimization failures. Speciﬁcally, we observe that the Cppcheck
workload encounters the relocation exception on RISC-V where R_RISCV_JAL
relocation exceeds its address range. Upon investigating the source code, we
identify that this exception is triggered by the linker relaxation optimization.
The linker relaxation optimization is a link-time optimization aimed at reducing
code size. Unfortunately, the binary optimizations in BFDO, including function
reordering, basic block reordering, and the hot/cold code split, will change the
symbol locations, triggering exceptions. To investigate mitigations, we recompile
the Cppcheck workload with the --no-relax option to disable linker relaxation
optimization, and observe a performance improvement of 21.02%.


5   Best Practices and Future Directions

In this section, we present best practices for using BFDOs and outline directions
for future studies.
Better Support of Relocation Information. We argue that a key step to uti-
lize BFDOs is selecting compilers that support the export of relocation informa-
tion. Speciﬁcally, since BFDOs require precise disassembly and relocation infor-
mation, compilers should export symbol table and precise relocation information
to binary ﬁles. While many compilers support symbol table well, some do not
support relocation information (e.g., the gc compiler for Go). Besides, optimizer
support for certain relocation types, such as R_RISCV_TLS_GD_HI20, remains
limited. Therefore, using unsupported relocation types should be avoided. This
is a trade-oﬀ between performance and program implementation.
Do Not Use BFDOs on Unoptimized Binaries. We argue that BFDOs
supplement existing compilation optimizations but do not replace them. We
observe from our evaluation that unoptimized binaries (e.g., generated from the
compiler via O0) often contain numerous tiny basic blocks and complex jump
structures, which are more susceptible to biased proﬁles, especially on RISC
architectures like RISC-V. Applying BFDOs on such binaries often leads to
performance degradation rather than improvements.
Avoid Using Linker Relaxation. We argue that although linker relaxation
can reduce binary size and improve performance, it has negative impacts on
BFDOs, especially for large binaries. To this end, we suggest that linker relax-
ation should be avoided during BFDOs. In the long term, we believe that the
conﬂict between linker relaxation and BFDOs should be addressed by introduc-
ing more sophisticated optimization heuristics that take into account the eﬀects
of BFDOs on code layouts. We identify that this idea is integrated into the recent
version of BOLT, but regrettably, it does not work correctly, at least as of this
study.
512     M. Liu et al.

Improve Sampling Accuracy. We argue that sampling accuracy is essential
for BFDOs and thus should be carefully tuned. We reveal from our experi-
ments that it is often eﬀective to adjust the sampling frequency to improve
accuracy (e.g., the -F option in perf), when the performance improvement is
suboptimal. Furthermore, due to the imprecision of sample-based proﬁling for
tiny basic blocks, we argue that sample-based proﬁling can be complemented by
instrumentation-based proﬁling to determine more precise proﬁles. We believe
this best practice is especially valuable for hardware that lacks powerful perfor-
mance measurement units.
Better Disassembly and Hardware Support. We argue that eﬀective
BFDOs comprise two key sub-tasks: binary disassembly and optimization. Unfor-
tunately, both sub-tasks are well-known NP-complete problems and thus eﬀec-
tive heuristics must be leveraged. To this end, we believe better disassembly
support will beneﬁt BFDOs, especially for RISC binaries in which the mixture
of code and data often defeats disassembly. Furthermore, we observe that cur-
rent architectures, especially AArch64 and RISC-V, still have limited hardware
proﬁling support, which undermines BFDOs. Addressing this limitation requires
attention and eﬀort from hardware vendors.

6     Discussion and Threats to Validity
Like any empirical study, there are threats to the validity of our results. We
discuss the most signiﬁcant ones, along with possible mitigations.
External Validity. Threats to external validity concern the generalizability
of ﬁndings across experimental settings, primarily stemming from three factors:
the selected programming languages, architectures, and benchmarks. To mitigate
these threats, we selected four programming languages spanning distinct appli-
cation domains and encompassing varied programming paradigms. Additionally,
we evaluated three representative architectures. Finally, for benchmarks, we used
both micro-benchmarks and real-world workloads applied across various ﬁelds.
Internal Validity. As for threats to internal validity, a critical threat stems
from random variance in execution times of benchmarks, caused by subtle ﬂuc-
tuations in the host OS’s state that may manifest as signiﬁcant deviations. To
mitigate this threat, we conducted multiple trials for each benchmark, using
the mean execution duration as the evaluation metric while calculating tempo-
ral variance to quantify runtime volatility. For micro-benchmarks whose execu-
tion speed exceeds measurement resolution thresholds, we incorporated repeated
invocations to amplify temporal observables, thereby compensating for sampling
inaccuracies.
Construct Validity. We evaluated the eﬀectiveness of BFDOs through compar-
ative analysis of runtime data collected from benchmarks before and after opti-
mization. Although many benchmarks on RISC-V platforms were non-executable
due to compilation errors or optimization failures, these instances serve as critical
validation indicators for assessing the cross-platform validity of BFDOs.
    Unraveling the State-of-the-Art Binary Feedback-Directed Optimizations      513

7   Related Work

Binary Optimizations. There are numerous studies on binary optimizations.
Panchenko et al. [36] presented a static binary optimizer BOLT for data-center
applications, demonstrating that proﬁle data can be used more precisely at the
binary level. Williams-King and Yang et al. [48] implemented CodeMason, which
performs static binary rewriting based on the binary rewriting platform called
Egalito [47]. Panchenko et al. [37] demonstrated Lightning BOLT based on the
work of BOLT. They addressed the CPU and memory overhead of BOLT by
introducing parallel processing and selective optimizations. Zhou and Jones et
al. [52] presented a framework called Janus to address the challenge of automatic
binary parallelization. Savage and Jones et al. [39] proposed a post-link proﬁle-
guided optimization tool called HALO to improve the layout of heap data to
reduce cache misses automatically.
     However, existing work mainly focuses on the x86 CPU architecture and
binaries compiled from C/C++. Our work studies the eﬀectiveness and perfor-
mance improvement of other platforms and programming languages, aiming to
ﬁll this gap.
Profiling Techniques. Proﬁling techniques are a key component of binary opti-
mization. Instrumentation-based proﬁling is a common method for collecting
precise proﬁle data, but it often incurs non-negligible runtime overhead. To mit-
igate this issue, Ball et al. [6] optimized probe placement using minimal spanning
tree. Additionally, Cho et al. [23] proposed a novel instrumentation framework
that reported an average runtime slowdown of 3% to 6%. Since the overhead
of instrumentation-based proﬁling remains undesirable for production deploy-
ment, sample-based proﬁling is widely adopted by many tools. He et al. [22]
proposed a pseudo-instrumentation technique as a supplement to sample-based
proﬁling to improve proﬁle quality without incurring the overhead of traditional
instrumentation. Moreira et al. [33] enhanced static proﬁling technique called
Evidence-Based Static Prediction (ESP), originally proposed by Calder et al.
[7], which enables the generated proﬁles to be used for binary optimization.
    However, although leveraging proﬁling techniques as foundational infrastruc-
ture, our contribution lies in systematically evaluating BFDOs’ eﬀectiveness and
eﬃciency. This focus dictates our selection of the most compatible and relatively
accurate sample-based proﬁling in our study.


8   Conclusion

In this work, we present the ﬁrst study on binary feedback-directed optimiza-
tion, aiming to evaluate its current capabilities, remaining limitations, and future
research directions. By designing and implementing a software prototype, we
investigate the eﬀectiveness and eﬃciency of binary optimization across three
representative architectures and four programming languages. We reveal three
root causes of optimization failures and performance degradation, along with
514     M. Liu et al.

three best practices for improved optimization outcomes. Additionally, we out-
line three promising directions for future research. We believe that our study
provides valuable insights that can guide future research eﬀorts in leveraging
modern hardware performance measurement capabilities through advanced com-
piler technologies.

           Yang Liu1,2 , Zexin Wang1,2 , Xinyin Zhang1,2 , Zenghui Ren1,2 ,

       Abstract. Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamen-
       tal computational kernel widely used in scientiﬁc computing. Due to
       its irregular memory access patterns and the diverse sparsity structures
       present in real-world matrices, optimizing SpMV is challenging. This
       paper proposes an adaptive SpMV optimization framework and SpMV
       implementation method, which integrates deep insights into matrix char-
       acteristics, algorithmic strategies, and hardware architectures. By com-
       bining these three complementary aspects with a hierarchical decision
       tree model, the framework dynamically selects the most suitable opti-
       mization strategy for a given matrix and target hardware platform.
          The framework consists of three key components: (1) A matrix feature
       extraction pipeline that analyzes non-zero element distribution, sparsity
       patterns, and algorithmic properties to generate feature descriptors; (2)
       An interpretable adaptive model based on hierarchical decision tree that
       examines key parameters to eﬀectively guide the selection of comput-
       ing kernels and their conﬁguration; and (3) A collection of specialized,
       lightweight candidate SpMV kernels designed to cover diverse scenarios
       and validate the framework’s adaptability.
          Extensive experimental evaluation on modern GPU architectures
       demonstrates that the framework delivers consistent performance
       improvements over a wide range of sparse matrices with diﬀering spar-
       sity characteristics. The model-enhanced SpMV kernels achieve an over-
       all speedup ranging from 1× to 6× compared to the baseline, with an
       average speedup of 1.31×, compared to hipSPARSE, the average solution
       speed is improved by a factor of 1.22×. Furthermore, it maintains robust
       and stable performance while automatically adapting to matrix proper-
       ties, highlighting its potential for practical deployment in heterogeneous
       computing environments.

       Keywords: Heterogeneous computing · Parallel optimization ·
       Adaptive optimization

1   Introduction
Sparse matrix vector multiplication (SpMV) represents a critical computational
kernel in high performance computing (HPC), serving as a fundamental building
block for numerous scientiﬁc applications, including neural networks, ﬁnite ele-
ment analysis, large language models, and linear system solvers [3,11,24]. Despite
its widespread use, achieving optimal SpMV performance remains challenging
due to three primary bottlenecks: limited memory bandwidth utilization, irregu-
lar memory access patterns leading to poor cache eﬃciency, and load imbalance
across parallel processing units.
    To address these bottleneck, various innovations in storage formats and algo-
rithmic techniques have been proposed to improve the computational eﬃciency
of SpMV. These include tiling-based partitioning schemes [14], compression
techniques that exploit cache hierarchy awareness [9], row-based decomposition
methods [16], and hardware-speciﬁc optimizations [15]. However, due to diﬀer-
ences in the distribution of non-zero elements leading to signiﬁcant heterogene-
ity among matrices, a single SpMV kernel cannot achieve optimal performance
across all sparse matrices.
    With the development of machine learning techniques, auto-tuning frame-
works have emerged as eﬀective solutions for SpMV optimization. yaSpMV [22]
introduces an automated framework for optimizing sparse matrix storage struc-
tures and thread conﬁgurations; Huang et al. [7] present a sophisticated per-
formance modeling methodology for heterogeneous memory systems to predict
optimal data placement; Gao et al. [6] develop a machine learning approach for
predicting optimal thread conﬁgurations in CSR-format operations; and Li et
al. [12] propose a runtime selection framework utilizing three neural networks
to dynamically select from eight specialized kernels. Alphasparse proposes an
approach to machine-designed sparse matrix storage and related SpMV kernel
implementations [5].
    Most frameworks focus on single optimization objectives (such as kernel selec-
tion, storage format selection, or parameter conﬁguration), and neural network-
based models employ completely black-box designs by unifying all parameters
for training, making it diﬃcult to explain the rationale behind optimization deci-
sions, which limits the model’s credibility and adaptability in practical applica-
tions.
    The eﬃcient implementation of SpMV algorithms hinges on the ability to
analyze the distribution of non-zero elements and eﬀectively utilize available
computational resources. This insight motivates the development of our hybrid
adaptive optimization framework.
    Through analysis of real-world applications and representative sparse matri-
ces, we have identiﬁed several structural patterns that signiﬁcantly impact SpMV
computational performance: (1) Diagonal-dominant patterns; (2) Block struc-
tures; (3) Band structures; (4) Irregular scatter patterns. These structural pat-
terns frequently appear either individually or in combination within large-scale
sparse matrices, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
520    Y. Liu et al.




          Fig. 1. Matrices sourced from SuiteSparse Matrix Collection [4].


    By leveraging matrix characteristics, kernel design strategies, and hardware
conﬁgurations, we aim to maximize both algorithmic and hardware perfor-
mance. For computational kernels such as SpMV, performance is tightly coupled
with data properties and resource utilization. Our framework models and ana-
lyzes structural features that impact performance, substantial speedups can be
achieved through informed optimization.
    We propose an adaptive SpMV optimization framework that extracts a range
of row-oriented sparse matrix structural features, uses classiﬁcation models to
identify key parameters, and builds an interpretable optimization model. This
model enables the framework to automatically select the suitable kernel and
its optimal parameter conﬁguration. The key contributions of our work are as
follows:

– We design a GPU-oriented feature extraction pipeline that systematically
  integrates sparse matrix structural characteristics, SpMV kernel computa-
  tional properties, and GPU architectural features, providing comprehensive
  feature support for the adaptive optimization framework.
– We highlight that parameter conﬁguration is critical in achieving eﬃcient
  SpMV performance. We propose an interpretable hierarchical classiﬁcation
  framework that jointly addresses both kernel selection and parameter tuning.
  The model is trained in two stages: the ﬁrst level determines the optimal
  kernel choice, while the second level optimizes the parameters for the selected
  kernel. This hierarchical formulation provides ﬁne-grained, multi-level feature
  analysis respectively.
– We conducted experimental validation on two platform. The results demon-
  strate that the framework exhibits adaptive performance across various sparse
  matrix characteristics.


2     Background and Motivation
2.1   SPMV Optimization Method
The SpMV operation is deﬁned as y = Ax, where each element is computed as
y i = k A(i,k) xk . Despite its mathematical simplicity, SpMV typically achieves
only a small fraction of the peak ﬂoating-point performance, and achieving
                                    Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework         521

 optimal computational performance remains challenging. Extensive research
 has been dedicated for SpMV optimization to develop various optimization
 approaches.
     The research on SpMV kernel mainly focuses on two optimization direc-
 tions:(1) improving data locality and memory access eﬃciency, and (2) enhanc-
 ing parallel execution and load balancing. For example, BCSR [2,20] exploits
 block-level to enable dense BLAS operations. CSR-k introduces a multilevel
 compressed sparse row format that organizes rows into hierarchical super-rows,
 improving memory locality and parallelism across diﬀerent cache levels [8]. CSR-
 5 introduces tile-based partitioning for better SIMD utilization and automatic
 load balancing [14]. These format-level optimizations demonstrate the impor-
 tance of data organization in achieving high performance, particularly in terms of
 eﬃcient thread and warp-level workload distribution, improved memory coalesc-
 ing, and enhanced vectorization opportunities. In addition, optimization meth-
 ods for speciﬁc matrix patterns, such as compression techniques and Mixed preci-
 sion method [13,16,17], further improve computational performance by reducing
 memory footprint and computation cost.
     Furthermore, machine learning-based auto-tuning and prediction models for
 SpMV have been extensively studied. These include thread conﬁguration opti-
 mization [8], prediction models for sparse matrix storage format selection [10,18],
 as well as performance prediction and load balancing strategies [1,19,21,23].
 Auto-tuning and prediction models can also provide feedback to existing eﬃ-
 cient SpMV implementation algorithms, which can further optimize the design
 of existing high-performance algorithms and break through the performance of
 existing calculations.

 2.2   SPMV with Modern GPU Architectures
 There are several key challenges in optimizing SpMV in modern GPU architec-
 ture, stemming from the fundamental mismatch between irregular sparse matrix
 access patterns and GPU’s Single Instruction, Multiple Threads (SIMT) exe-
 cution model. Modern GPUs adopt a hierarchical execution paradigm centered
 around Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), Work-Group Processors (WGPs), or
 other execution units, as illustrated in Fig. 2 Each execution unit can support
 thousands of resident threads, organized into thread blocks or warps.
    For SpMV operations, The GPU architecture presents three primary perfor-
 mance bottlenecks:

(1) Memory Access Latency: One of the primary bottlenecks in SpMV is the
    high memory access latency caused by irregular and indirect memory access
    patterns, particularly when fetching elements from the input vector x. These
    patterns signiﬁcantly hinder spatial and temporal locality, leading to ineﬃ-
    cient cache usage and poor memory coalescing on GPU architectures. As a
    result, SpMV implementations often fail to saturate the available memory
    bandwidth. Furthermore, the high latency of global memory access ampliﬁes
    this ineﬃciency, making eﬀective cache reuse and memory hierarchy-aware
 522    Y. Liu et al.




 Fig. 2. Architectural overview of modern GPU memory hierarchy and execution units.


    optimizations—such as shared memory blocking and register tiling—crucial
    for performance.
(2) Thread Divergence: The irregular distribution of non-zero elements across
    matrix rows leads to thread-level workload variability within a warp. In the
    GPU’s SIMT execution model, this variability causes warp divergence—where
    threads in the same warp follow diﬀerent control ﬂow paths—resulting in
    serialized execution. Such divergence signiﬁcantly degrades parallel eﬃciency,
    particularly in matrices with highly imbalanced non-zero counts per row. This
    mismatch reduces the eﬀective utilization of GPU cores and limits through-
    put.
(3) Load Imbalance: The non-uniform sparsity structure of real-world matri-
    ces induces multi-level workload imbalance during parallel execution. At the
    intra-warp level, threads may process rows with varying numbers of non-zero
    elements; at the block and device level, thread blocks mapped to regions
    with denser rows incur longer execution times, leading to load imbalance
    across streaming multiprocessors (SMs). This imbalance is exacerbated by
    the GPU’s bulk-synchronous execution semantics, where slower threads delay
    warp or block-level progress, resulting in low occupancy, idle cores, and sub-
    optimal hardware utilization.


 3     The Adaptive Optimization Framework
 To enhance the computational performance of SpMV across diverse sparse matri-
 ces on GPU, we propose an adaptive optimization framework. The framework
 is as illustrated in Fig. 3, This framework including several designed SpMV ker-
 nels, adopting a systematic optimization strategy by employing a hierarchical
 decision tree model to analyze key matrix features, enabling an intelligent kernel
 selection mechanism that adaptively chooses the optimal SpMV computation
 strategy based on matrix characteristics.
                                                  Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework                          523




                Fig. 3. The Adaptive SpMV Kernel Optimization Framwork.


3.1       Sparse Matrix Features

The distribution of non-zero elements in sparse matrices is often highly diverse.
Some matrices exhibit regular banded patterns that align well with the GPU’s
SIMT execution model, thereby achieving eﬃcient computation. In contrast,
other matrices display irregular distributions of non-zero elements, characterized
by signiﬁcant row length variations and scattered sparsity patterns.
    For matrices with substantial row length variation, adopting a ﬁxed thread
allocation strategy often results in underutilization of GPU resources and severe
computational imbalance. Additionally, matrices with highly dispersed non-zero
elements impose substantial memory access overhead, especially under high spar-
sity conditions. In such cases, eﬃcient exploitation of the GPU’s multi-level cache
hierarchy becomes crucial for performance optimization.
    Motivated by these observations, we design a row-oriented feature extraction
mechanism that captures both intra-row and inter-row structural patterns. These
extracted features guide the adaptive framework in selecting appropriate SpMV
kernel strategies, enabling targeted optimizations based on matrix structure.


                    Table 1. Matrix Features for the Adaptive Framework

nnz_variance        Variance of non-zero counts per row
col_variance        Variance of column index gaps between consecutive non-zeros
bandwidth           Average bandwidth, deﬁned as the average distance between the ﬁrst and last non-zero in each row
sparsity_imbalance Ratio between the number of non-zeros in sparse regions and dense regions

   The speciﬁc feature extraction results are presented in Table 1. These fea-
tures are designed to capture the distribution of non-zero elements in row-wise
dimensions, providing a foundation for adaptive performance tuning in SpMV
algorithms. The basic matrix dimensions are represented as m, n, and nnz,
denoting the number of rows, columns, and non-zero elements, respectively. To
describe row-wise sparsity distribution, we include the maximum, minimum, and
average number of non-zeros per row, along with the variance of row-wise non-
zero counts:

    col_variance measures the variance of column index diﬀerences between

3.2   Candidate Kernel Set

We adopt the Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format as the data storage for-
mat and develop lightweight sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) kernels
speciﬁcally optimized for this format. It is well established that eﬀective storage
format conversions and matrix reordering techniques can often enhance compu-
tational intensity eﬀectively [2,9], as demonstrated by numerous studies, many
adaptive models incorporate the selection of storage formats as a tunable variable
to optimize performance [1,10,12]. However, in scenarios where SpMV operations
are invoked infrequently, the overhead associated with format conversions can
become signiﬁcant relatively. Moreover, in many practical applications—such
as sparse linear system solvers, graph-based learning models, and multi-stage
numerical pipelines—matrix reordering often alters the structural characteristics
of the original sparse matrix, which typically requires additional recovery steps
to restore the original indexing or data layout. Both factors introduce further
complexity and computational overhead to the overall workﬂow. Therefore, this
paper does not delve into format conversion or matrix reordering strategies. Our
kernel design focuses on eﬃcient thread mapping and load balancing strategies,
combined with optimizations leveraging GPU shared memory and cache hierar-
chies, as well as vectorization and warp shuﬄe techniques to improve execution
eﬃciency.
                                  Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework       525

   SpMV kernel ❶ employs thread-level parallelism, where each thread is
mapped to a single matrix row, and thread blocks cover consecutive rows. The
kernel exploits the structural regularity of by preloading a ﬁxed-size window of
the input vector into registers. Combined with loop unrolling and vectorized
memory access, this kernel is suitable for banded matrices.


Algorithm 1. SpMV Kernel❶
 1: Input: A, x, y, bandwidth
 2: Output: y = α · A · x + β · y
 3: row ← blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x
 4: if row < num_rows then
 5:     for i = 0 to cache_size − 1 do
 6:        col ← row      bandwidth/2 + i
 7:        if 0 ≤ col < num_rows then
 8:            x_cache[i] ← x[col]
 9:        end if
10:     end for
11:     sum ← 0
12:     for j = row_ptr[row] to row_ptr[row + 1] − 1 step vector_size do
13:         vec_size ← min(vector_size, row_ptr[row + 1] − j)
14:         for k = 0 to vec_size − 1 do
15:            col ← col_ind[j + k]
16:            cache_idx ← col − (row     bandwidth/2 )
17:            if 0 ≤ cache_idx < cache_size then
18:                sum ← sum + values[j + k] × x_cache[cache_idx]
19:            else
20:                sum ← sum + values[j + k] × x[col]
21:            end if
22:         end for
23:     end for
24:     y[row] ← α × sum + β × y[row]
25: end if



    SpMV kernel ❷ applies a sub-warp-level parallelism strategy by dividing
each warp into multiple sub-warps, each responsible for computing a single row.
Threads within a sub-warp cooperate to process the row’s nonzero elements in
parallel. Warp-level reduction using __shﬂ_down_sync is employed to aggre-
gate partial results, __ldg is used to optimize read-only memory accesses. This
approach is suited for matrices with relatively balanced and long rows.
    SpMV kernel ❸ targets matrices with highly irregular row lengths by adopt-
ing a dynamic row-block partitioning strategy. Threads process rows within
assigned blocks in a cyclic manner to balance workload across threads. Loop
unrolling is applied to improve memory throughput. This method helps mitigate
load imbalance and enhances kernel eﬃciency for unstructured sparsity patterns.
    SpMV kernel ❹ serves as a baseline warp-level parallelism kernel, where each
warp is responsible for one row and threads within the warp process nonzero
526    Y. Liu et al.

Algorithm 2. SpMV Kernel❷
 1: Input: A, x, y, sub_warp_size
 2: Output: y = α · A · x + β · y
 3: threads_per_row ← sub_warp_size
 4: rows_per_block ← blockDim.x/threads_per_row
 5: row ← blockIdx.x · rows_per_block + threadIdx.x/threads_per_row)
 6: lane ← threadIdx.x mod sub_warp_size
 7: if row < m then
 8:     sum ← 0
 9:     for j ← row_ptr[row] + lane to row_ptr[row + 1] step sub_warp_size do
10:         sum ← sum + values[j] · x[col_ind[j]]
11:     end for
12:     for of f set ← sub_warp_size/2 to 1 step of f set/2 do
13:         sum ← sum + shuﬄe_down(sum, of f set)
14:     end for
15:     if lane = 0 then
16:         y[row] ← α · sum + β · y[row]
17:     end if
18: end if

Algorithm 3. SpMV Kernel❸
 1: Input: A, x, y, row_blocks
 2: Output: y = α · A · x + β · y
 3: block_start ← row_blocks[blockIdx.x]
 4: block_end ← row_blocks[blockIdx.x + 1]
 5: for row ← block_start + threadIdx.x to block_end step blockDim.x do
 6:     row_start ← row_ptr[row]
 7:     row_end ← row_ptr[row + 1]
 8:     sum ← 0
 9:     for j ← row_start to row_end do
10:         sum ← sum + values[j] · x[col_ind[j]]
11:     end for
12:     y[row] ← α · sum + β · y[row]
13: end for



elements cooperatively in a strided fashion. Warp-level reduction is used to accu-
mulate results, and loop unrolling is applied to improve memory access eﬃciency.
The design provides a reference for evaluating alternative kernel strategies.
   These kernels integrate parallelization optimizations tailored to common
sparse matrix patterns, and combining GPU hardware feature optimization tech-
niques include cache-aware data reuse, warp-shuﬄe based reductions, adaptive
workload partitioning, and register-level optimizations to enhance performance.
   The conﬁguration parameters for the four SpMV kernels are shown in Table 2.
These parameter values are selected based on the architectural characteristics
and resource constraints of modern GPUs. For each parameter, we choose a
representative range of values commonly used in GPU kernel design.
                                    Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework        527

   To serve as a performance baseline, one value from each parameter set is
randomly selected as a default conﬁguration, allowing us to compare the adaptive
tuning performance against a ﬁxed, non-optimized setting.

                Table 2. Conﬁguration Parameters of SpMV Kernels.

       Kernel            Parameters      Values               Default Values
       SpMV Kernel❶–❹ Dim(Block)         32, 64, 128, 256, 512 256
       SpMV Kernel❶      Bandwidth       32, 64, 128, 256     64
       SpMV Kernel❷      sub_warp_size 4, 8, 16, 32           16
       SpMV Kernel❸      row_size        16, 32, 64, 128      128
       SpMV Kernel❹      N/A             N/A                  N/A




3.3   Hierarchical Decision Tree Model
As mentioned above, the characteristics of diﬀerent matrices, such as the dis-
tribution of non-zero elements, vary signiﬁcantly. Diﬀerent SpMV kernels are
often optimized for speciﬁc types of matrices and cannot adapt to all matri-
ces. Therefore, a reasonable approach is to employ a classiﬁer to dynamically
select the optimal SpMV kernel for diﬀerent matrices. Commonly used machine
learning models for such classiﬁcation tasks include decision trees, support vec-
tor machines (SVM), random forests, and neural networks. Although neural
networks excel at capturing complex nonlinear relationships, decision tree clas-
siﬁers provide better interpretability because they can assess the importance of
diﬀerent features and observe their splitting boundaries.
    Unfortunately, a naive decision tree can only classify the SpMV kernels, while
diﬀerent SpMV kernels have distinct conﬁguration parameters and their per-
formance is quite sensitive to these parameters. Without additional handling,
even if the optimal SpMV kernel is selected, the performance is likely to be
suboptimal due to inaccurate parameter conﬁguration. Therefore, as illustrated
in Fig. 3, we constructed a hierarchical decision tree structure to address both
kernel prediction and parameter prediction. The ﬁrst layer of the decision tree
performs coarse-grained classiﬁcation of kernel types, while the second layer con-
sists of multiple independently trained parameter conﬁguration decision trees,
each modeling ﬁne-grained parameter selection for a speciﬁc kernel type. This
structure eﬀectively captures the heterogeneity in parameter distribution across
diﬀerent kernels, signiﬁcantly enhancing the overall prediction accuracy.

Training Stage. During the training phase, we ﬁrst generate a large number
of training samples, with each matrix corresponding to an optimal kernel and
optimal parameter conﬁguration. We use an exhaustive approach, traversing all
candidate kernels and their candidate parameter spaces (as detailed in Table 2)
528     Y. Liu et al.

for each matrix and recording the actual execution time for every conﬁguration.
After obtaining the execution times for all conﬁgurations, we can easily iden-
tify the best kernel and parameter conﬁguration for each matrix. And as we
mentioned that we also consider hardware information when selecting candidate
parameter spaces to enhance the algorithm’s robustness and portability.
    After generating the data, we use these labeled samples to train the hier-
archical decision tree. Speciﬁcally, for each training sample, we ﬁrst perform
feature extraction to identify representative features of the sparse matrices and
best execution time as labels. The sample then undergoes iterative optimization
within the decision tree. The loss in the hierarchical decision tree consists of two
components: one is the loss from kernel selection in the kernel base, and the
other is the loss from parameter selection in the parameter tower. Each sample
enters only one of the parameter towers. Both components of the loss utilize the
cross-entropy loss function. For training stability, the maximum depth of each
decision tree is limited to 3, and each internal node requires at least 15 samples
to split.


Testing Stage. During the testing phase, for each new incoming sparse matrix,
we similarly perform feature extraction. The extracted features are then fed into
the trained hierarchical decision tree, resulting in the prediction of the optimal
kernel and its best parameter conﬁguration.


Discussion. This hierarchical decision tree framework allows each subproblem
to be modeled using the most relevant features and splitting strategies, improv-
ing overall prediction capability. The layered structure enables each kernel type
to maintain a dedicated parameter tree and encoding scheme, with each deci-
sion tree minimizing its own entropy-based loss. This design prevents interference
from unrelated categories and reduces the impact of irrelevant features or imbal-
anced classes, thereby enhancing both prediction accuracy and generalization.
Furthermore, it balances diﬀerences in parameter space and optimal conﬁgura-
tion across kernel types.
    At deployment, the runtime overhead introduced by our framework mainly
stems from extracting matrix structural features and performing decision tree
inference. As the structural properties of sparse matrices are typically static
in most applications, the inference process only needs to be executed once. In
addition, the proposed framework is highly modular and extensible, allowing for
integration of new SpMV kernels to support and optimize a broader range of
sparse workloads.


4     Experimental Evaluation

To evaluate the eﬀectiveness of the proposed adaptive optimization framework,
we conduct a series of experiments across two computing platforms and various
                                   Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework          529

sparse matrices. The evaluation emphasizes both the improvement in computa-
tional eﬃciency over the original kernels and the eﬀectiveness of performance
prediction enabled by the adaptive model.


4.1   Experimental Setup
Hardware and Software Environment. Experiments are conducted on two
heterogeneous computing platforms. The hardware and software information of
the two platforms. The NVIDIA platform is equipped with Tesla V100 GPU,
uses with 64 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and 32 GB of HBM2 memory
per GPU, manages warps consisting of 32 threads. The software environment
includes CUDA 12.4, the NVIDIA driver version 550.76, and GCC 11.3.0 as the
host compiler. The AMD platform features Instinct MI60 GPUs with 64 CUs per
GPU and 16 GB of HBM2 memory, where a wavefront consists of 64 threads.
The system runs on ROCm 5.4.0 with the HIP runtime, and also uses GCC
11.3.0 for compilation.
    Our experiments were conducted on two platforms, where most of the results
exhibited similar trends. Except for cases speciﬁcally highlighted, we selected
the results obtained on the NVIDIA GPU platform as representative examples
for illustration.


Matrix Dataset. We choose 600 large matrices (with the row number n >
50,000, the nonzero number nnz> 100,000) from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collec-
tion [4] for the experiments. During the tests, we use double precision for matrix
values and repeat each kernel function 50 times to measure the average perfor-
mance. We adopt stratiﬁed random sampling to divide the dataset into training
(80%) and testing (20%) subsets.

4.2   Overall Performance of the Hierarchical Decision Tree

To demonstrate the eﬀectiveness of the hierarchical classiﬁer, we evaluated its
classiﬁcation performance, as shown in Table 3. Our method achieved an F1-score
of around 0.8, even when trained on less than 500 matrices. This suggests that
many sparse matrices share similar features. With more diverse and abundant
training data, the model’s accuracy could be further improved.
    Moreover, the parameter tower also achieved high prediction accuracy for
diﬀerent SpMV kernels, with many parameters exceeding an accuracy of 0.8.
Notably, the accuracy for the bandwidth parameter reached over 90%. This
demonstrates the eﬀectiveness of our matrices feature extraction and the eﬀec-
tiveness of hierarchical structure in predicting kernel and parameters separately.
However, the variation in accuracy across diﬀerent parameters indicates that
precise prediction for all parameters is relatively challenging. This is an area for
further optimization in our future work.

4.3   Execution Time of Dynamic SpMV Kernel
We discuss the importance of kernel selection. To this end, we selected 300 sparse
matrices and evaluated their performance across multiple SpMV kernels with
varying parameter conﬁgurations. The experimental results (see Fig. 4) reveal
diﬀerences in execution time among the kernels, particularly as the matrix size
increases. For example, SpMV kernel ❹ exhibits a more pronounced increase in
execution time as matrix rows grow.
    Furthermore, we compared the performance under ﬁxed and optimized
parameter settings in Fig. 4. The results demonstrate that parameter tuning
has a notable impact on the performance of kernel ❶,❷,❸, especially for large-
scale matrices. In contrast, the performance of kernel ❹ is relatively insensitive
to parameter changes, as its conﬁguration mainly aﬀects the thread block dimen-
sions during kernel launch.




Fig. 4. Execution time for SpMV kernels of default parameters and optimal parameters.


    In order to gain a more intuitive understanding of how kernel selection and
parameter conﬁguration aﬀect SpMV performance, we listed several SpMV exe-
cution times for kernel ❷ and kernel ❸ as examples, as illustrated in Fig. 5.
The results show that, for some matrix, diﬀerent kernels yield varying execu-
tion times with ﬁxed parameters, indicating that certain sparse matrices are
inherently better suited to speciﬁc kernel algorithms due to distribution char-
acteristics of non-zero elements. Furthermore, for matrices such as Freescale1,
circuit5M_dc, and Delaunay_n23, where the execution times of ﬁxed param-
eter kernels are relatively close, further tuning of kernel parameters can still
lead to noticeable performance improvements. These observations underscore
                                  Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework         531

the importance of not only selecting an appropriate kernel but also performing
ﬁne-grained parameter optimization to achieve optimal SpMV eﬃciency.




Fig. 5. Execution time of SpMV Kernel ❷ and Kernel ❸ with ﬁxed and optimized
parameters on matrices.


    These ﬁndings highlight the necessity of kernel selection and parameter tun-
ing in achieving eﬃcient SpMV computation and validate the motivation and
signiﬁcance of our work in this direction.
    Next we evaluate the eﬀectiveness of our prediction model. The dataset of
600 matrices was partitioned into a training set of 480 matrices and a test set
of 120 matrices. The trained model was used to predict the optimal kernel and
parameter conﬁgurations, which were then applied to actual SpMV executions.
We compared the model’s performance with a static baseline—SpMV kernel ❹—
conﬁgured with a ﬁxed block dimension of 256. As shown in the Fig. 6, our
method achieves faster execution times than the baseline on the majority of the
test matrices, with an average speedup of 1.31×. This conﬁrms the eﬀectiveness
of our model and demonstrates its ability to support both kernel selection and
parameter tuning.

4.4   Ablation Study

To demonstrate the eﬀectiveness of our proposed hierarchical decision tree model,
we compared the execution times of a naive single-layer decision tree model and
our hierarchical decision tree model across diﬀerent matrices. The naive single-
layer decision tree model refers to using only one decision tree to predict the
optimal kernel, while the kernel’s parameters are set to default values. The box
plots of execution times for diﬀerent decision tree models are shown in Fig. 7. We
can observe that for all kernels, the execution time of the hierarchical decision
tree model is consistently shorter than that of the naive single-layer decision
tree model, especially for the SpMV kernel ❷. This highlights the importance of
parameter selection in the SpMV execution process and demonstrates that the
hierarchical decision tree model is a reliable solution to this challenge.

4.5   Decision Tree Analysis

The hierarchical decision tree generated by the model clearly demonstrates the
decision-making logic, facilitating the understanding of how the model utilizes
features for classiﬁcation. Based on multiple runs of the hierarchical decision tree
model and its visualization analysis, we conducted an in-depth investigation of
feature importance.
    In the ﬁrst-level classiﬁcation (kernel classiﬁer), max_nnz serves as the pri-
mary feature to distinguish diﬀerent categories, followed by the nnz_variance,
sparsity_imbalance and the col_variance as key features for further reﬁnement.
Speciﬁcally, SpMV kernel ❶ mainly clusters in regions with relatively small
max_nnz and nnz_variance; SpMV kernel ❷ is primarily distributed where
max_nnz and avg_nnz are small; whereas SpMV kernel ❸ concentrates in areas
                                   Eﬃcient SpMV Optimization Framework         533

with relatively large max_nnz, nnz_variance, and avg_nnz. This observation
aligns with our structured analysis of the matrices and the design of the ker-
nels, as the implementation of our kernel algorithms takes these distinct sparsity
structure features into account.
    At the second-level model, the emphasis on parameter conﬁguration varies
across diﬀerent kernels. For SpMV kernel ❶, a coarse classiﬁcation is ﬁrst per-
formed based on the total number of nnz, followed by a ﬁner parameter tun-
ing using features such as col_variance, avg_nnz, and bandwidth. For SpMV
kernel ❷, avg_nnz is the most critical feature; meanwhile, features including
sparsity_imbalance, m, and col_variance play key roles in selecting the dimen-
sion block parameters. The adjustment of sub_warp_size parameters relies
more heavily on avg_nnz, sparsity_imbalance, max_nnz, min_nnz, as well as
col_variance.
    By visualizing the model, it is possible to further optimize the matrix feature
extraction parameters, remove non critical features, and preserve and reﬁne key
features. This is also the reason why we chose the decision tree model, and the
hierarchical decision tree model we used makes the analysis of parameters more
reﬁned and accurate.

4.6   Compared With hipSPARSE
To further evaluate the performance advantages of the adaptive framework, we
compared its computational eﬃciency with hipSPARSE on AMD GPU. Figure 8
shows the comparison between the optimized SpMV kernel implementation of
the adaptive framework and the computation time of hipsparseDcsrmv. The
experimental results shows that our execution time is generally shorter than that
of hipSPARSE SpMV kernel, and without relying on complex implementation
algorithms and data storage structures, our average solving speed is 1.22x faster
than the hipSPARSE implementation.




        Fig. 8. The comparison of our SpMV execution time vs hipSPARSE.
534     Y. Liu et al.

5     Conclusion
In this paper, we have presented an adaptive optimization framework for SpMV
computation that eﬀectively addresses the challenges posed by irregular mem-
ory access patterns and diverse sparsity structures. The key contributions of
our work include a triple-aware optimization framework that integrates matrix
feature awareness, algorithmic characteristic awareness, and hardware archi-
tecture awareness, providing a comprehensive approach to SpMV performance
optimization; A layered decision tree performance optimization model, which
enables accurate prediction of optimal kernel selection and parameter conﬁg-
uration based on matrix characteristics; An eﬃcient implementation of SpMV
framework that achieves consistent performance improvements across diﬀerent
hardware platforms.
    This comprehensive optimization approach, which considers matrix charac-
teristics, hardware architecture features, and algorithmic properties, reduces the
need for manual tuning while providing a foundation for incorporating and opti-
mizing existing complex algorithms to break through the performance limita-
tions of original computations, achieving signiﬁcant performance improvements
without relying on complex kernel implementations.

Program of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (No.XDB0500101).

         GMS-YOLO: A Lightweight Algorithm
         for SAR Ship Target Detection Based
                    on YOLOv8n

            Xiaozhang Liu, Xinting Zhou, Xiulai Li(B) , and Jiajing Xu

           School of Computer Science and Technology, Hainan University,
                              Haikou, China 570228
                              lxzh@hainanu.edu.cn


       Abstract. To address the problems of noise interference, small target
       size, and complicated backgrounds in ship detection using synthetic aper-
       ture radar (SAR), this study proposes the GMS-YOLO, a lightweight
       model. This study uses the lightweight GhostConv to reduce compu-
       tation and model parameters. To enhance feature representation while
       maintaining the model’s lightweight design, this study designs a C2f-M
       module based on the mixed local channel attention (MLCA) mecha-
       nism. Furthermore, SPPFAS is intended to improve detection perfor-
       mance for targets at various scales. Lastly, this study introduces the
       Wise-IoU to resolve the issue of unfavorable gradients caused by occur-
       rences of low quality in the training dataset for target detection. The
       ﬁndings of the experiment show that, compared to YOLOv8n, the pro-
       posed GMS-YOLO algorithm achieved higher R, mAP50, and mAP50-
       95 on the SSDD dataset by 2.4%, 0.7%, and 1.3%, and on the HRSID
       dataset by 1.4%, 1%, and 1.1%. Additionally, the parameters and FLOPs
       were reduced to 2.8M and 7.8G, respectively, for both datasets. In
       the comparative experiments with other deep learning approaches, the
       GMS-YOLO algorithm still performed better, achieving a good balance
       between lightweight and accuracy.


       Keywords: synthetic aperture radar (SAR) ship detection ·
       GMS-YOLO · C2f-M · SPPFAS · Wise-IoU


1    Introduction
Synthetic aperture radar (SAR), due to its high resolution, all-weather capability,
and insensitivity to weather conditions [1], holds signiﬁcant value in ﬁelds such
as Earth observation [2], environmental monitoring [3], military reconnaissance
[4], agricultural yield estimation [5], disaster early warning [6], and ship rescue
[7], and it plays a particularly crucial role in ship detection. As deep learning
technology continues to advance, it has become a common technique for the
automatic detection of ships in SAR imagery. However, this ﬁeld continues to
face numerous challenges. Currently, SAR ship detection algorithms are mainly
categorized into traditional and deep learning-based algorithms [8].
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 537–554, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_29
538     X. Liu et al.

    The primary focus of traditional methods is on manual feature extraction and
image segmentation techniques, which rely heavily on the experience of profes-
sionals and have low detection eﬃciency. Examples include wavelet transform-
based detection methods [9], constant false alarm rate (CFAR) methods [10],
template matching methods [11], and so on. Although these methods show some
eﬀectiveness in detection, inherent limitations, such as dependence on experience
and high computational complexity, lead to low eﬃciency in practical applica-
tions.
    In recent years, as artiﬁcial intelligence technology has advanced quickly, deep
learning-based methods have achieved notable advancements in SAR ship target
detection [12]. Two types of deep learning-based methods for target detection
are categorized as follows: two-stage and one-stage target detection methods.
    The two-stage detection methods ﬁrst generate candidate frames and then
classify them in a regression. These methods mainly include R-CNN, Faster
R-CNN, and Mask R-CNN. Girshick et al. [13] proposed Region-based CNN
(R-CNN), a simple and scalable detection method. This algorithm generates
candidate regions through selective search and performs feature extraction and
classiﬁcation regression on each region to achieve target detection, signiﬁcantly
improving target detection performance on the PASCAL VOC dataset. Ren et al.
[14] designed a region proposal network (RPN) that reduces the computational
cost of candidate region generation through an end-to-end training approach,
thus improving the eﬀectiveness and precision of object detection. He et al. [15]
designed Mask R-CNN, which achieves eﬃcient instance segmentation and target
detection by incorporating a parallel branch into Faster R-CNN for predicting
the segmentation mask of targets. This approach increases the precision of seg-
mentation. One-stage methods, in contrast to two-stage methods, eliminate the
need for candidate region extraction, achieving faster detection speeds, lower
computational costs, and maintaining high accuracy.
    One-stage detection methods mainly include you only look once (YOLO)
series [16–21] and single-shot multibox detector (SSD) [22]. Jeong et al. [23]
designed a method for object detection to raise the accuracy of traditional SSD.
By optimizing the structure near the classiﬁer network, the method enhanced
the eﬀective utilization of feature maps, achieving high performance with 78.5%
mAP on the Pascal VOC 2007 test set while maintaining fast detection speed.
Wang et al. [24] introduced a SAR object detection approach based on SSD,
which achieves multi-scale feature learning through data enhancement and trans-
fer learning strategies, and the experimental ﬁndings demonstrate that this app-
roach outperforms other detection techniques in terms of detection performance.
Sun et al. [25] developed a BiFA-YOLO for detecting arbitrarily oriented SAR
ships based on the YOLO framework. This method eﬀectively aggregates multi-
scale features and accurately obtains ship angle information through an angle
classiﬁcation structure and a bidirectional feature fusion module, improving the
detection accuracy and speed of ships in arbitrary directions and dense arrange-
ments in high-resolution SAR images. Bai et al. [26] proposed FEPS-Net, a novel
SAR ship detecting network, which raises the eﬀectiveness of small ship detection
             GMS-YOLO: A Lightweight Algorithm for SAR Ship Detection         539

in SAR imagery by designing feature enhancement pyramids and shallow fea-
ture reconstruction modules. Yasir et al. [27] proposed an upgraded YOLOv5s
technology, which improves the model’s backbone and neck by combining C3
and FPN+PAN structures with attention mechanisms. This eﬃciently addresses
problems such as complicated background interference and the blurring of small
ship features while achieving high detection rates for multi-scale SAR ships. Tang
et al. [28] improved a SAR ship detection approach called N-YOLO, built upon
YOLOv5. By incorporating a SAR target potential area extraction (STPAE)
module, a noise level classiﬁer (NLC), and the YOLOv5 detection module, this
method enhances The eﬀectiveness and precision of SAR ship detection. Guo et
al. [29] introduced a reﬁned detection approach based on YOLOv5. This method
enhances the learning of feature information in both spatial and channel dimen-
sions, along with the integration of multi-scale target information by integrating
the bidirectional feature pyramid network (BiFPN) and the convolutional block
attention module (CBAM). This eﬀectively reduces the issue of detection leakage
in multi-scale targets.
     The above studies have achieved signiﬁcant results in enhancing ship detec-
tion accuracy in SAR imagery. Nevertheless, in practical applications, they
face the challenge of high algorithm complexity. Xu et al. [30] improved Lite-
YOLOv5, a lightweight star-borne SAR ship detection model, built upon the
YOLOv5 algorithm. By designing the lightweight cross stage partial (L-CSP)
module, applying network pruning, and integrating several optimization mod-
ules, it achieves both a lightweight architecture and high detection accuracy. Ren
et al. [31] developed YOLO-Lite, a lightweight network designed for SAR ship
detection. By designing lightweight feature enhancement backbone (LFEBNet),
channel and position enhancement attention (CPEA) modules, and enhanced
spatial pyramid pooling (EnSPP) modules, and combining these with a multi-
scale feature fusion network (MFFNet) and a novel conﬁdence loss function,
they achieved both reduced computational cost and high-precision ship detec-
tion. Tang et al. [32] designed YOLO-SARSI, based on YOLOv7 with an atten-
tion mechanism multi-scale receptive ﬁeld convolution block (AMMRF), For
detecting ship targets in SAR ocean images with high resolution. This method
enhances the capacity to diﬀerentiate between ships and the background by fully
utilizing the positional information of feature maps and channel relationships.
Thus, the enhancement of ship detection performance, coupled with the opti-
mization of the lightweight model, continues to be a focus of investigation, with
the aim of striking a balance between computational complexity and detection
eﬀectiveness.
     To address the above challenges, this study proposes GMS-YOLO, a light-
weight model that increases SAR ship detection accuracy while keeping a light-
weight architecture. The following are the main contributions of this study:

– To address the feature redundancy problem, this study introduced Ghost-
  Conv, replacing the Conv of the YOLOv8n backbone with GhostConv, which
  extracts a large number of features through a small amount of computa-
540    X. Liu et al.

  tion, eﬀectively solving the redundancy problem in the procedure for feature
  extraction.
– To address the issue of insuﬃcient feature extraction due to background com-
  plexity while maintaining lightweight, this study proposed the C2f-M mod-
  ule, which combines C2f with the mixed local channel attention mechanism
  (MLCA) to enhance the network’s ability to capture useful features by com-
  bining local and global features as well as channel and spatial feature infor-
  mation.
– To address the problem that SPPF in YOLOv8 ignores the global feature
  information of the input image, this study proposed the SPPFAS module. By
  fusing the global max pooling and global average pooling operations into the
  SPPF module and introducing SEBlock, this module acquires more image
  information and enhances target detection at various scales.
– To address the problem of low-quality images in SAR ship datasets, this
  study adopted WIoU-v3, which uses a gradient gain assignment strategy and a
  dynamic non-monotonic focusing mechanism to increase the model’s detection
  accuracy and robustness.




                       Fig. 1. The structure of GMS-YOLO.




2     Methods

The overall network structure of GMS-YOLO based on YOLOv8n proposed in
this study is shown in Fig. 1. The following four main improvements are made
             GMS-YOLO: A Lightweight Algorithm for SAR Ship Detection        541

in GMS-YOLO. In the backbone section, GhostConv replaces Conv, which con-
tributes to the improvement of lightweight algorithms. In the neck section, SPP-
FAS is designed instead of SPPF, capturing more diverse feature information
and enhancing the capacity to detect targets at various scales. Additionally, the
C2f-M module integrates the lightweight MLCA module into C2f, combining
the beneﬁts of the C2f and MLCA mechanism. This integration maintains the
model’s lightweight nature while better capturing key features. Consequently,
target detection performance is improved. In addition, WIoU is used in place of
the algorithm’s loss function to enhance the recall of objects and increase the
detection boxes’ precision.




                Fig. 2. The process of Conv(a) and GhostConv(b).




2.1   GhostConv

Given that the feature maps generated by contemporary mainstream convolu-
tional neural networks (CNNs) frequently include a signiﬁcant number of redun-
dant features, some of which are similar to one another, this increases computa-
tional cost in addition to adding more parameters. To address this issue, Ghost-
Net [33] proposed an innovative method that extracts many features with few
computations, eﬀectively solving the redundancy problem in the feature extrac-
tion process. Inspired by this advantage, this study introduces GhostConv, a
novel convolutional layer that is diﬀerent from conventional convolutional oper-
ations.
    As illustrated in Fig. 2, GhostConv divides the convolution operation into
two steps: ﬁrstly, it performs a standard convolution, which involves obtaining
feature maps using a standard convolution and extracting intrinsic feature maps
542    X. Liu et al.

with a convolution layer of kernel size; secondly, it performs a lightweight linear
transformation operation, which involves applying a convolution with a kernel
size of 5 to the intrinsic feature maps from the previous step, generating addi-
tional feature maps. The feature maps obtained from these two steps are spliced
in the channel dimension to generate the ﬁnal feature map. This method can
generate feature maps comparable to normal convolution with fewer parameters
and computational resources, thus achieving a lightweight model.


2.2   C2f-M Mo dule

The C2f module is one of the basic modules in the YOLOv8 network archi-
tecture, capable of providing rich gradient ﬂow information while keeping the
lightweight network. However, the original C2f module primarily employs stan-
dard convolutions and bottleneck structures. While these can extract features
eﬀectively, they fail to focus adequately on the target regions. This study designs
the C2f-M module, integrating an attention mechanism to improve the model’s
capability for feature extraction, based on the C2f module’s excellent character-
istics. The attention mechanism enables the model to focus on the key features
of targets, thus increasing the precision of detection. In this study, the MLCA
mechanism [34] is introduced to improve detection by combining local and global
feature information with channel and spatial feature information while maintain-
ing computational eﬃciency.




                          Fig. 3. The structure of C2f-M.


   MLCA is a lightweight attention mechanism that improves detection accu-
racy with a negligible increase in parameter count. The MLCA mechanism is
             GMS-YOLO: A Lightweight Algorithm for SAR Ship Detection          543

shown in Fig. 3. The input feature maps are ﬁrst processed by local average pool-
ing (LAP) and global average pooling (GAP) [35] to capture the local spatial
information and the statistical information of the entire feature maps, respec-
tively, to enhance the representational capability of the model. The features
obtained from global pooling and local pooling are subject to transformation
through 1D convolution (Conv1d) to maintain the spatial dimension while com-
pressing the feature channels. The features after 1D convolution are rearranged
(Reshape) to ﬁt subsequent operations. For the local pooling features, after 1D
convolution and rearrangement before being integrated with the original input
features using a “multiplication” operation (×), which is equivalent to a fea-
ture selection to highlight valuable features. For the features obtained from
global pooling, they undergo 1D convolution and rearrangement before being
integrated with the local pooling features using an ‘addition’ operation, achiev-
ing the fusion of global contextual information. Lastly, the operation of unpool-
ing (UNAP) returns the feature maps that have been enhanced by both global
and local attention to their original spatial dimensions. By integrating MLCA,
the model preserves computational eﬃciency while improving the capacity for
feature extraction.
    The C2f-M module is illustrated in Fig. 3. The integration of the MLCA
mechanism with the C2f module of the YOLOv8 architecture brings great advan-
tages for SAR ship detection. Due to the complexity of the background, ship
feature learning is signiﬁcantly aﬀected, which leads to insuﬃcient ship fea-
ture extraction. The module maintains computational eﬃciency while optimiz-
ing feature representation by integrating global and local information to high-
light important features. This makes the model more capable of capturing useful
features, eﬀectively mitigating interference from non-target backgrounds, thus
enhancing the model’s performance.

2.3   SPPFAS Mo dule
Although the traditional SPPF has adopted three strategies of max-pooling to
improve the capacity to extract features, there are still some shortcomings: Max-
pooling can only extract the maximum value of the input features and can
only represent the local information of the input features while ignoring the
input image’s global feature information. For SAR images that contain noise
and complex backgrounds, this processing method results in insuﬃcient infor-
mation about targets and backgrounds at diﬀerent scales and interference from
background noise. Therefore, this study proposes the SPPFAS module, which
integrates global average pooling and global max pooling operations into SPPF
to obtain the global background and global edge information of the images. SPPF
extracts features through diﬀerent pooling layers, combining global background
and edge information, which allows the model to better capture information from
multi-scale features, thereby boosting its capability to detect targets of diﬀerent
sizes. This information is then spliced together with the local feature maps to
form a feature map containing the global view. And ﬁnally, the SEBlock is intro-
duced to optimize the feature expression by adaptively recalibrating the weights
544    X. Liu et al.

of each channel to improve the diﬀerentiation between targets and backgrounds,
so as to enhance detection performance and lessen the inﬂuence of complicated
backgrounds. The structure of the SPPFAS is illustrated in Fig. 4.




                       Fig. 4. Structure of the SPPFAS module.




SEBlock. The SE attention mechanism [36] involves two stages: squeeze and
excitation. As shown in Fig. 4, where Ftr is the convolutional structure, and X
and U are the input and output, respectively. The SEBlock learns the correla-
tions between diﬀerent channels and adjusts the weight of each channel, using
the attention mechanism to enhance the information between feature map chan-
nels, thereby improving the network’s representation. This module will slightly
increase the computational load, but better prediction results can be achieved.
The following is the derivation process for the SEBlock:

1. The feature map U is subjected to global average pooling to obtain the vector
   z.

   where uc (i, j) represents the value of the c-th channel in the feature map at
   position (i, j), and zc is the global descriptor of channel c.
2. Obtain the vector s by learning with two fully connected layers(FC).

                            s = Fex (z, ω) = σ (ω2 δ (ω1 z))                  (2)

SPPFAS. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the SPPFAS module comprises a max-pooling
layer, a global max pooling layer, and a global average pooling layer, as well as
a SEBlock. This feature map is fed into three consecutive max-pooling layers,
producing three distinct feature maps. Additionally, it undergoes global average
pooling and global max pooling, producing two global feature maps that lessen
noise impact and enhance the model’s robustness in complex contexts. Then,
concatenate these six generated feature maps to produce richer feature maps.
Finally, the fused feature map is generated by applying the Conv module. Then,
the SEBlock is used for channel attention weighting to emphasize important
features while suppressing less relevant ones, and ultimately, the feature map is
output. The whole calculation process can be expressed by equations (4)-(6).

                                X0 = Conv(Xin )                               (4)



      ymax = Concat(M ax(X0 ), M ax(M ax(X0 )), M ax(M ax(M ax(X0 ))))        (5)


          Fout = SEBlock(Conv(Concat(X0 , ymax , Am(X0 ), Aa(X0 ))))          (6)
    In Eq. Xin denotes the input features, Conv is the convolution operation,
Max denotes the max-pooling operation, Am represents the global max pooling
operation, Aa represents the global average pooling operation, Concat is the
feature splicing operation, ymax represents the maximally pooled branch’ output
features and Fout represents the ﬁnal output.


2.4    Loss Function

In the SAR ship detecting ﬁeld, the accuracy of target localization is particu-
larly important. YOLOv8 adopts the component Intersection over union (CIoU)
[37] loss function. CIoU incorporates considerations of shape features in the
process of bounding box regression. By incorporating the aspect ratio of both
the predicted and ground truth bounding boxes, it can eﬀectively optimize the
prediction of the bounding box. Nevertheless, the computational complexity of
CIoU is larger, which leads to a higher computational burden while training
the model. Furthermore, SAR images include many low-quality images, and
geometric metrics like aspect ratio and distance exacerbate the penalties for
546     X. Liu et al.

these images, causing a reduction in the performance of the model’s general-
ization. When the target frames and the anchor overlap well, the optimal loss
function should reduce the geometric penalty, avoid excessive interference with
results of training, and increase the model’s generalization capacity. Therefore,
The dynamic non-monotonic focusing mechanism employed in this study is the
WIoUv3 loss function [38], which is based on attention-driven bounding box loss
(Wise-IoU v1). It employs a non-monotonic focusing coeﬃcient to adjust the
gradient gain dynamically based on the anchor boxes’ outlier degree, optimizing
model training. This enables the model to provide diﬀerent levels of attention
to various types of anchor boxes at diﬀerent stages of training, thus retaining
more high-quality anchor box information in the early stages, and the negative
consequences of low-quality anchor boxes are lessened in the later stages.
    The calculation of Wise-IoU v1 is given by Eqs. (7)–(8).

                             LW IoU v1 = RW IoU · LIoU                         (7)

                                        (x − xgt )2 + (y − ygt )2
                        RW IoU = exp(            2          ∗       )          (8)
                                            (W g + Hg 2 )
where RW IoU is the distance attention factor, denoting the normalized distance
between the centroids of the ground truth and the predicted bounding boxes.
LIoU denotes the loss of IoU. (x, y) and (xgt , ygt ) represents the coordinates of
the predicted and ground truth boxes’ center points, respectively. Wg and Hg
denote the minimum bounding box’s width and height, respectively. * separation
from the computation graph.
   WIoUv3 is calculated based on WIoUv1 and represented by equations (9)-
(10).
                                     L∗IoU

where β denotes the outlier degree, which is utilized to explain the quality of
the anchor boxes, L∗IoU denotes the gradient gain of the IoU loss, and k is the
non-monotonic focusing coeﬃcient, denoted by the hyperparameters α,δ (in this
study, α,δ were set to 1.9 and 3, respectively).

To assess the performance of the GMS-YOLO detection model, the recall,
mAP0.5, mAP0.5:0.95, the parameters, and FLOPs were used as evaluation

ranging from 0.5 to 0.95. (with a value interval of 0.5).

3.4   Ablation Experiments

To validate the eﬃcacy of the model enhancements proposed in this study, abla-
tion experiments were performed on the SSDD and HRSID datasets to evaluate
how changes to various modules inﬂuence detection performance. The results
are illustrated in Table 3.

                          Table 3. Ablation experiments

GhostConv C2f-M SPPFAS WIoU SSDD                HRSID               Params/M FLOPs /G
                            R/% mAP50/% mAP95/% R/% mAP50/% mAP95/%
                          94.8 97.5    66.7    81.9 91.5    66.5    3.0      8.1
                          94.2 97.5    65.6    83.2 91.3    65.4    2.8      7.7
                          94.4 97.8    67.0    80.6 91.4    67.2    2.8      7.7

                          97.2 98.2    68.0    83.3 92.5    67.6    2.8      7.8




    The table shows that applying the GhostConv module to the YOLOv8n
model reduces the parameters and computation for both datasets, albeit with
slightly degraded performance. This is because GhostConv achieves these reduc-
tions by generating multiple smaller feature maps, which, however, weakens the
model’s capability to detect objects. Overall, the introduction of the Ghost-
Conv module allows the model to maintain a high level of performance while
simultaneously reducing parameters and computation. With the introduction of
C2f-M on top of this, while maintaining lightweight, the recall rate on the SSDD
dataset improved by 0.2%, mAP50 increased by 0.3%, and mAP50-95 improved
by 1.4%. On the HRSID dataset, although the recall rate decreased slightly,
mAP50 increased by 0.1%, and mAP50-95 improved by 1.8%, which indicates
that the C2f-M module, by improving the ability to capture local and global
feature information and improving feature representation, can focus more eﬀec-
tively on critical features and improve the performance of detection. The addi-
tion of the SPPFAS module enhanced the overall performance on both datasets.
Finally, the algorithm’s performance was signiﬁcantly enhanced by incorporat-
ing the WIoU optimization loss function. Compared to the YOLOv8n model,
GMS-YOLO showed a reduction of 0.2G in parameters and 0.4G in FLOPs. On
the SSDD dataset, recall increased by 2.4%, mAP50 by 0.7%, and mAP50-95
by 1.3%. On the HRSID dataset, recall increased by 1.4%, mAP50 by 1%, and
mAP50-95 by 1.1%. These experimental results fully demonstrate the eﬀective-
ness of the lightweight optimization of the GMS-YOLO, as well as the model’s
good generalization ability across diﬀerent datasets.
    Figure 5 shows the visualization of detection results on SSDD and HRSID.
It can be observed that in the complex nearshore scene, YOLOv8n incorrectly
identiﬁed some targets as ship targets and failed to detect one of the small ships,
while GMS-YOLO accurately detected these ship targets without any missed
detections. For detecting small targets in low-quality, high-noise scenarios, and
550    X. Liu et al.

simple scenarios, both YOLOv8 and GMS-YOLO performed well, but GMS-
YOLO had higher conﬁdence. This indicates that GMS-YOLO has excellent
performance in ship target detection, outperforming YOLOv8 on both datasets,
proving its eﬀectiveness and generalization in SAR ship detection.


3.5   The Impact of IoU on Algorithm Performance
Using the YOLOv8 algorithm as the baseline model, replaced the backbone
network Conv with GhostConv, the neck network SPPF with SPPFAS, and C2f
with the C2f-M module to assess the eﬀects of various IoUs on the model’s
performance. Table 4 shows the performance of diﬀerent IoU metrics (CIoU,
DIoU [37], EIoU [41], GIoU [42], SIoU [43], and WIoU) on the SSDD and HRSID
datasets. The experimental results indicate that WIoU performs better than all
other IoUs. On the SSDD dataset, R increased by 1.7%, mAP50 by 0.5%, and
mAP50-95 by 0.8%. On the HRSID dataset, R rose by 0.2%, mAP50 by 0.5%,
and mAP50-95 by 0.3%.

and YOLOv8n. The comparison experiment results of the various approaches on
the SSDD and HRSID datasets are provided in Table 5 and Table 6, respectively.

demonstrates optimal detection performance on both datasets, with parame-
ters and FLOPs being nearly the lowest. On the SSDD dataset, compared to
YOLOv5n with the lowest parameters and FLOPs, the parameters and FLOPs
of this model only increase by 0.3M and 0.7G, respectively. However, on the

4   Conclusions

This study proposes GMS-YOLO, a lightweight model for SAR ship detection.
Firstly, GhostConv introduced in this study successfully reduced the model
parameters and computation. Secondly, the designed C2f-M eﬀectively improves
the feature representation. In addition, the SPPFAS module improved the detec-
tion capability for targets of diﬀerent scales. Finally, the WIoU eﬀectively mit-
igated the adverse eﬀects of low-quality instances on training. This study con-
ducted extensive experiments on two SAR datasets, SSDD and HRSID. The pro-
posed model demonstrated outstanding performance and lower computational
costs under various scales of ship targets, strong noise, and complex background
interference, validating the eﬀectiveness and generalization of the GMS-YOLO
method in SAR ship target detection tasks. It not only enables more accurate
detection in SAR images but also achieves lightweight implementation, providing
an eﬃcient and precise solution for SAR ship target detection.
