          ERL-CDR: Evolutionary Reinforcement
            Learning with Causal Decoupling
                    Representation

    Zuohao Wu1 , Guang Li2(B) , Zihao li3 , Jiaqi Wei4 , and Mingsheng Shang2
    1
      Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Chongqing, China
    2
     Chongqing Institute of Green and Intelligent Technology, Chinese Academy of
                        Sciences Chongqing, Chongqing, China
                                 liguang@cigit.ac.cn
  3
    School of Computer Science and Technology, University of Chinese Academy of
                               Sciences, Beijing, China
                              2022441629@cqust.edu.cn
4
   School of Electrical Engineering, Chongqing University of Science and Technology,
                                  Chongqing, China


         Abstract. Evolutionary Reinforcement learning (ERL) algorithms
         eﬀectively address the sample eﬃciency problem in continuous state-
         action spaces by integrating gradient-based reinforcement learning (RL)
         with gradient-free evolutionary algorithms (EAs). However, traditional
         ERL methods still face limitations, including insuﬃcient processing of
         the state space in collected samples, diversity-limited ﬁtness evaluation
         based solely on rewards leading to reduced sample diversity, and dif-
         ferences in EA-RL sample distributions that hinder the value function
         learning. This paper proposes Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning -
         Causal Decoupling Representation (ERL-CDR). which addresses the
         issue of insuﬃcient state space processing by introducing a causal repre-
         sentation learning mechanism that disentangles task-irrelevant features
         from decision-critical features. A behavioral diversity mechanism is used
         to evaluate the population, promoting more comprehensive exploration
         of the sample space and increasing sample diversity. Finally, a novel value
         function is introduced to better represent the sample space of policy pop-
         ulations, which, together with the RL value function, eﬀectively guides
         policy learning. Experimental results show that this method signiﬁcantly
         improves convergence speed, stability, and ﬁnal performance in complex
         continuous control tasks. These methods are of research signiﬁcance for
         complex continuous reinforcement learning tasks.

         Keywords: Causal Representation · Diversity Evaluation · Value
         Function


1       Introduction
Reinforcement Learning (RL) [1] has achieved signiﬁcant success in ﬁelds like
robotics [2], game AI [3], and autonomous driving [4], mainly due to its eﬃcient
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 555–570, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_30
556    Z. Wu et al.

policy learning with deep neural networks. However, RL still suﬀers from insta-
bility, limited exploration, and diﬃculties in environments with sparse or noisy
gradient signals.
     Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) [5] are black-box optimization methods that
maintain a population of solutions and optimize them through selection, inheri-
tance, and mutation, without relying on gradient information. EAs oﬀer better
exploration, robustness, and stable convergence [6], but suﬀer from low sample
eﬃciency due to the need for extensive population evaluations, especially as the
policy space grows [7].
     EAs with RL leverage the complementary strengths of both approaches for
more eﬃcient policy optimization. Recent research has mainly focused on the
integration of EAs with RL, such as Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL)
[8], which combines Genetic Algorithms (GA) [9] with a Deep Deterministic Pol-
icy Gradient (DDPG) [10]. In ERL, a population of agents interacts with an
RL agent, allowing both components to beneﬁt from each other. Improvements
include using the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [11], gradient-based genetic
operators, and multiple RL agents [12]. However, most methods focus on col-
lecting diverse policy samples, often overlooking the ability of the value function
to learn complex state representations, which limits the performance of evolu-
tionary reinforcement learning.
     Inspired by causal reinforcement learning [13], this paper introduces causal
representation learning to unravel environment dynamics, task-irrelevant fea-
tures, and decision-critical features. The proposed ERL-CDR algorithm improves
on the original ERL framework by designing a decoupled representation net-
work that extracts key task features from complex environmental information.
In addition, a world model is incorporated to guide the training of the decou-
pled representation network. This enables the ERL algorithm to better isolate
critical information relevant to the task, thereby enhancing the generalization
and sample eﬃciency of the learned representations, and eﬀectively addressing
the problem of feature redundancy in high-dimensional and complex tasks.
     The main contributions of our work are as follows.
     (1) A novel ERL algorithm is proposed, in which a causally disentangled
representation network is introduced to enable agents to better perceive the
state space and decouple task-critical features.
     (2) A new population ﬁtness metric for the policy population is designed,
incorporating a diversity mechanism to guide the optimization of the diversity
of the policy population.
     (3) By employing diﬀerent value functions, the method is able to eﬀectively
learn distributional diﬀerences within the sample space.
     Finally, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of ERL-CDR against strong
baseline ERL methods and representative RL algorithms on MuJoCo continuous
control tasks and the DeepMind Control Suite, including systematic studies such
as ablation experiments and hyperparameter analysis.
                                                                     ERL-CDR         557

2    Background
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is formulated as a Markov Decision Process
(MDP), represented by the tuple S, A, P, R, γ, T . At each time step (t), the
agent selects an action at ∼ π(st ) according to its policy π based on the current
state st ∈ S. The environment then transitions to the next state st+1 according
to the transition function P (st , at ), and the agent receives a reward r(st , at ).
The return, deﬁned as the cumulative reward, is the discounted sum of future
                                 T
rewards, expressed as Rt = i=t γ i−t ri , where γ ∈ [0, 1) is the discount factor
and T is the maximum episode length. The objective of RL is to learn an optimal
policy π ∗ that maximizes the expected return. DDPG [10] is a well-known oﬀ-
policy actor-critic algorithm. It consists of a deterministic policy (the actor) and
an approximate state-action value function (the critic), parameterized by ω and
ψ, respectively. The critic is optimized using temporal diﬀerence (TD) learning
[14], while the actor is updated by maximizing the estimated value (Q). The loss
                                                                              2
functions are formulated as: L(ψ) = ED r + γQψ (s , πω (s )) − Qψ (s, a)         and
L(ω) = −ED [Qψ (s, πω (s))] are sampled from the replay buﬀer D, and ψ and ω
denote the parameters of the target networks. TD3 [15] further improves DDPG
by employing clipped double Q-learning to mitigate overestimation bias.
Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) [16] are a class of black-box optimization
methods that iteratively evolve a population of policies. The population is indi-
cated as P = π1 , π2 , . . . , πn , and policies evolve in each iteration. During each
iteration, all agents interact with the environment to obtain Monte Carlo M C
estimates of policy ﬁtness, f (π1 ), f (π2 ), . . . , f (πn ), where ﬁtness is deﬁned as:
              e      T
[f (π) = 1e i=1      t=0 rt | π ] Here, rt is the reward at time step t and T is the
duration of the episode. Policies with higher ﬁtness scores are more likely to be
selected as parents for the next generation. Various selection mechanisms exist,
such as Genetic Algorithms (GA) [9] and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)
[17]. The oﬀspring are generated using genetic operators: two parents πi and πj
are randomly selected, and the oﬀspring πi and πj are produced by crossover
or mutation in GA. Speciﬁcally, the crossover operator combines parts of the
parent networks to generate new oﬀspring: πi , πj = Crossover(πi , πj ) Alterna-
tively, the mutation operator generates a child policy by applying small random
perturbations to the parent policy: [πi = Mutation(πi )] In most existing meth-
ods, crossover and mutation are performed at the parameter level. Due to the
diversity introduced by a large number of candidate solutions and the contin-
uous variation from genetic operations, evolutionary algorithms exhibit strong
exploration capabilities.


3    Related Work
EAs, with their gradient-free nature and diversity, provide valuable samples for
RL in complex environments but suﬀer from low sample eﬃciency. RL, optimized
558    Z. Wu et al.

via neural networks and gradient descent, often gets stuck in local optima, mak-
ing high-reward policy discovery diﬃcult in continuous control tasks. Integrating
EAs and RL has emerged as a promising direction, enabling eﬃcient policy opti-
mization [8,18], improving action selection, assisting in hyperparameter tuning
[19,20], and enhancing EA performance in multimodal problems.
    The core contribution of this study lies in the integration of EAs and RL
to achieve more eﬃcient policy optimization. ERL [8] was the ﬁrst to pro-
pose a hybrid framework in which an RL agent and an evolutionary popula-
tion are trained simultaneously. The RL agent can explore a wider variety of
samples through the EAs population, and copies of the RL agent are periodi-
cally injected into the EAs population. Furthermore, CEM-RL [11] combines the
Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) with TD3 for optimization. CERL [7] extends a
single RL agent to multiple RL agents with diﬀerent hyperparameters to address
the issue of hyperparameter sensitivity in RL. PDERL [21] introduces Q-ﬁltering,
distillation crossover, and proximal mutation to mitigate policy collapse caused
by traditional parameter-level genetic operations.
    The motivation for adopting the causal decoupling representation network
stems from the need to explicitly separate diﬀerent causal factors in complex rein-
forcement learning environments. In such environments, the agent must distin-
guish between features that drive environment dynamics, those that are decision-
critical, and those that are irrelevant to the task. By designing a multi-branch
structure, our approach enables each branch to focus on a speciﬁc causal fac-
tor, which aligns with the principles of causal inference–such as intervention and
counterfactual reasoning–proposed by Pearl (2009) [22]. This explicit separation
allows the agent to better generalize and adapt when the environment or task
changes, as each causal factor can be independently manipulated or analyzed.
    Unlike unsupervised disentanglement methods such as β-VAE [23] and Fac-
torVAE [24], which encourage independence among latent variables without con-
sidering their causal roles, our approach is tailored for reinforcement learning.
It ensures that the learned representations correspond to distinct causal mecha-
nisms relevant to decision making and environment dynamics. The independence
loss further enforces this separation, making the branches as independent as pos-
sible and thus more interpretable from a causal perspective.
    In summary, our design is guided by the intuition that eﬀective reinforcement
learning requires not only disentangled representations, but also representations
that reﬂect the underlying causal structure of the environment. This facilitates
robust policy learning and transfer across tasks with varying causal factors.


4     The Algorithm Framework Of ERL-CDR
In this section, we present the overall framework of ERL-CDR, explain how the
ERL-CDR model is derived from the general framework, and detail the speciﬁc
implementation of the three key components.
                                                                                  ERL-CDR   559

4.1   Representation Learning of Causal Decoupling




Fig. 1. The ERL-CDR framework is shown in this ﬁgure. The environment state st
is input to a shared representation network with three branches S1 , S2 , S3 , extracting
causally disentangled features for environment dynamics, task-irrelevant information,
and decision-critical factors. These features are concatenated as the shared representa-
tion, which serves as input for both the policy and value networks in RL, and provides
a uniﬁed feature basis for multiple EA policy individuals (w1 , w2 , w3 ), enabling syn-
ergy between EA and RL. The world model acts as an auxiliary task, optimizing the
shared representation network via environment state transition prediction to improve
modeling and generalization of dynamics.



Representation Learning of Causal Decoupling. Let the raw state of the
environment at time t be st . We design a multi-branch shared representation
network Zφ that maps st to causally disentangled multimodal features (Fig. 1):

                                 zt = Zφ (st ) = concat(ztdyn , ztirr , ztdec )             (1)
where  ztdyn ,   ztirr ,
                   and             ztdec
                             denote the environment dynamics features, task-
irrelevant features, and decision-critical features, respectively. The ﬁnal shared
representation zt is obtained by concatenating these features.

Orthogonality-Independence Loss. To achieve disentanglement among the
branch features, we employ an orthogonality loss to constrain the correlation
between outputs of diﬀerent branches:
                                                              (i)   (j)
                                      Lindep =         Cov(zt , zt )                        (2)
                                                 i=j

                 (i)       (j)
where Cov(zt , zt ) denotes the covariance between the i-th and j-th branch
features. The objective is to minimize the correlation among branches, making
them as independent as possible.
560     Z. Wu et al.

World Model Auxiliary Loss. A world model fψ is introduced, which takes
the shared representation zt as input to predict the next state ŝt+1 . The mean
squared error (MSE) is used as the auxiliary loss:
                                                        2
                           Lwm = E |fψ (zt ) − st+1 |                            (3)

This loss enforces the shared representation network to learn features that can
accurately model the environment dynamics.

Total Loss Function. Finally, the training objective of the representation
network is a weighted sum of multiple loss terms:

                       Lcausal = αLpolicy + βLindep + γLwm                       (4)

where Lpolicy is the policy loss, and α, β, and γ are the weighting coeﬃcients for
each loss term.

pute similarity, which is combined with reward-based ﬁtness to promote more diverse
population evolution.

within an episode be {s1 , a1 , s2 , . . . , sn }. We use the state embedding network

                                    zt = Zφ (st )                                (5)

   The trajectory embedding hi for individual i is obtained by applying average

4.3    Population Experience-Driven Auxiliary Critic for Actor
       Guidance


Population Experience-Driven Auxiliary Critic. Let each individual i
in the current population collect a trajectory in the environment, denoted as
τi = (sit , ait , rti , sit+1 , . . . , sin , ain , rni ). We introduce an auxiliary critic network Qψ,
whose parameters are independent from the main critic. This network is trained
using the sampled experiences from all individuals in the population, aiming to
comprehensively model the value distribution of population behaviors (Fig. 3):
                                Qψ (s, a) ≈ E[R | (spop , apop )]                                (11)
562     Z. Wu et al.




Fig. 3. This ﬁgure shows the auxiliary critic, which learns from the population’s sam-
pling distribution and, together with the main critic, guides the actor toward high-
reward regions.


Multi-Source Sampling and Generalization Enhancement. The training
samples for the auxiliary critic are drawn from collected episodes of the entire
population, thus covering a diverse range of policy distributions. Compared
to single-policy sampling, this multi-source approach signiﬁcantly enhances the
critic’s generalization over the state-action space and reduces the risk of overﬁt-
ting.Formally, the population experience buﬀer Bpop is constructed as:

              Bpop = {(s, a, r, s ) | (s, a, r, s ) ∈ Bi , i = 1, 2, . . . , N }   (12)

where N is the population size, and Bi denotes the experience buﬀer of individual
i. The auxiliary critic is trained on samples (s, a, r, s ) ∼ Bpop, ensuring coverage
of diverse state-action pairs.

Collaborative Policy Optimization. During actor training, the loss func-
tion is designed to jointly maximize the outputs of both the environment reward
critic and the auxiliary critic Qψ . Speciﬁcally, the actor’s objective is not only
to improve the output of the environment reward critic, but also to increase the
value estimated by the auxiliary critic Qψ for its actions. This collaborative guid-
ance enables the actor’s parameter updates to be informed by both environment
rewards and the auxiliary critic, leading to higher-quality policy optimization.
    The actor loss can be formulated as:

                 Lactor = −Es ∼ D [Qφ (s, μθ (s)) + Qψ (s, μθ (s))]                (13)

   where Qφ is the main critic, Qψ is the auxiliary critic, μθ is the actor policy,
D is the experience buﬀer.
                                                                   ERL-CDR      563

Training and Update Mechanism The auxiliary critic is trained using the
same temporal-diﬀerence (TD) loss as the main critic:
                                                                            2
          Lcritic = E(s,a,r,s )∈PopBuﬀer (Qψ (s, a) − (r + γQψ (s , a )))       (14)

where (s, a, r, s ) are sampled from the population experience buﬀer, and a
denotes the next action. The auxiliary critic can be periodically reset and
retrained with the latest population experiences to maintain adaptability to the
current population distribution.
    In practice, the auxiliary critic network is periodically trained in batches
using population-sampled data. After training, it is used to evaluate actor poli-
cies. The actor’s loss function combines the outputs of both the environment
reward critic and the auxiliary critic, and parameters are updated to jointly
maximize both.

5   Experiments
To comprehensively evaluate the eﬀectiveness and generalizability of our pro-
posed causal decoupling representation network, we selected the MuJoCo and
DeepMind Control (DMC) environments as benchmark tasks. The choice of these
environments is motivated by several key considerations:
    First, both MuJoCo and DMC are widely recognized in the reinforcement
learning community for their diversity and complexity. MuJoCo provides a suite
of continuous control tasks, such as locomotion and manipulation, which feature
high-dimensional state spaces and complex physical dynamics. These character-
istics present signiﬁcant challenges for representation learning, as the agent must
extract meaningful and disentangled features from rich sensory inputs to achieve
robust control.
    Second, the DMC suite oﬀers a variety of tasks with diﬀerent levels of reward
sparsity and dynamic complexity. Some tasks, such as “walker-walk” or “eetah-
run,”nvolve sparse or delayed rewards, which require the agent to perform eﬃ-
cient exploration and causal reasoning to identify the key factors that inﬂuence
long-term success. Other tasks present dense rewards but involve intricate inter-
actions between multiple state variables, further testing the model’s ability to
disentangle and utilize relevant causal features.
    Third, by including both MuJoCo and DMC environments, we ensure that
our method is validated across a broad spectrum of reinforcement learning sce-
narios. This allows us to demonstrate that the proposed approach is not limited
to a speciﬁc type of task or reward structure, but is generally applicable to envi-
ronments with high-dimensional observations, complex dynamics, and varying
reward signals.
    In summary, the selection of MuJoCo and DMC environments is intended to
highlight the strengths of our method in handling high-dimensional state spaces,
sparse and dense rewards, and complex causal relationships. This comprehensive
evaluation underscores the versatility and practical relevance of our approach for
real-world reinforcement learning applications.
564    Z. Wu et al.

5.1   Experimental Setups
We evaluated two categories of baseline methods: (1) standard reinforcement
learning algorithms (PPO [25], SAC [26], DDPG [10]); and (2) ERL methods
(ERL [8], CERL [7], PDERL [21]), all using DDPG as the RL backbone. Perfor-
mance comparisons were conducted on Mujoco tasks with identical initialization
and tuned population sizes. Key module weights and diversity ﬁtness weights
were set for diﬀerent environments (for example, in the Ant environment, the
loss function weights were α = 0.5, β = 0.25, γ = 0.25 and the diversity ﬁtness
weights were α = 0.5, β = 0.5). Hyperparameters for all algorithms were sim-
ilarly optimized. We also evaluated performance in the DMC environment by
integrating RAD-based data augmentation with ERL variants.

5.2   Hyperparameter Selection
This section provides a detailed description of the hyperparameter settings for
diﬀerent tasks. Some hyperparameters remain consistent across all tasks. The
population size is set to 5, and the mutation operator’s α is set to 1.0. The
number of environment interaction episodes for surrogate ﬁtness is 1. The value
of γ is 0.99. Since ERL-CDR is built upon ERL, other settings remain unchanged.
Table 2 and Table 3 lists other speciﬁc hyperparameters of ERL-CDR that vary
across diﬀerent tasks.

5.3   Performance Evaluation

During the MUJOCO experiments, we compared the DDPG implementation
of ERL-CDR with baseline methods. As shown in Fig. 4, ERL-CDR outper-
forms other ERL methods and traditional reinforcement learning algorithms on
most MuJoCo continuous control tasks. For example, in the Swimmer environ-
ment, ERL-CDR converges to the optimal value within 600,000 steps, while other
methods typically require 800,000 steps. In the Humanoid environment, the ﬁnal
reward increases from around 1,200 to about 3,200. However, in simpler environ-
ments with relatively limited state spaces, the performance improvement is less
pronounced. This may be because, in simple action spaces, each state dimension
is closely related to decision-making, making the beneﬁts of the causal disen-
tanglement representation network less signiﬁcant. In these cases, improvements
mainly result from the design of the diversity ﬁtness function and the auxiliary
critic. In environments like DMC, where state inputs are pixel-level, as shown
in Table 1, the causal disentanglement network can eﬀectively extract important
causal representations to facilitate better policy learning for RL. Overall, these
ﬁndings indicate that ERL-CDR achieves progress on most benchmark tasks,
maintains strong performance, and reduces sample exploration requirements.

increasing from around 3,500 to about 4,800, demonstrating its advantage. Next,
in Fig. 6, we examined whether the auxiliary critic helps achieve faster conver-

0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. As shown in Fig. 8, gradually increasing the independent dis-

state network can better separate state features. For example, in the Swimmer
environment, the score increased from around 330 to 350. The second category
involves the weights of the diversity ﬁtness function, α and β, which correspond

6     Conclusion
We propose an innovative method called ERL-CDR, which builds upon tra-
ditional ERL algorithms by introducing a causally disentangled representation
extraction approach. This enables agents to distinguish key environmental fac-
tors in complex states. Sample diversity is further enhanced through diversity-
based ﬁtness estimation, and an auxiliary critic is used to independently learn
from the population distribution, improving convergence speed. Experimental
results show that through the interaction of the three modules, ERL-CDR
improves the ﬁnal reward by about 5–20% over various baselines in most envi-
ronments. Although the reward improvement is smaller in some cases, the num-
ber of samples required for convergence can be reduced by 10–20%, ultimately
achieving strong performance.

7     Limitations and Future Work
7.1   Limitations
Despite the promising results achieved by our proposed causal decoupling rep-
resentation network, there are several limitations that should be acknowledged.
    First, the method introduces additional computational overhead compared
to baseline approaches. The multi-branch architecture and the associated loss
terms increase the complexity of both the forward and backward passes during
training, resulting in longer training times. This increased time cost may limit
the scalability of our approach, especially when applied to large-scale or real-
time reinforcement learning tasks. Tabel 4 presents the time consumption of
diﬀerent algorithms on MUJOCO every 10,000 steps. The additional time cost
mainly comes from the training of the auxiliary critic and the causal decoupling
network. All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Ti GPU and
an Intel(R) Core i5-12600F CPU.
    Second, while our experimental results consistently demonstrate performance
improvements over existing methods, our approach currently lacks formal the-
oretical guarantees. The eﬀectiveness of the causal decoupling representation
network is supported by empirical evidence, but a rigorous theoretical analysis
of its properties and limitations has not yet been established. This may aﬀect
the generalizability and interpretability of the method in broader contexts.
    In summary, although our method shows clear empirical advantages, further
research is needed to address its computational eﬃciency and to establish the-
oretical guarantees, thereby enhancing its practical applicability and scientiﬁc
rigor (Table 4).

7.2    The Future Work
In future work, we plan to further optimize the computational eﬃciency of our
causal decoupling representation network, for example by exploring lightweight
architectures and distributed training strategies. Additionally, we aim to estab-
lish formal theoretical guarantees for our method to better understand its prop-
erties and limitations. We also intend to extend our approach to more complex
and diverse reinforcement learning environments, including those with partial
observability and multi-agent interactions. Finally, investigating the integration
of causal representation learning with other advanced techniques, such as meta-
learning and hierarchical reinforcement learning, will be an important direction
to enhance the adaptability and generalization of our framework.

          Based Diﬀerential Evolution Algorithm
             for Mixed-Variable Optimization

               Qing Chen, Xiaogang Dong(B) , and Changshou Deng

    School of Computer and Big Data Science, Jiujiang University, Jiujiang 332005,
                                      China
                                dongxg@jju.edu.cn



        Abstract. Optimization problems play a pivotal role in the develop-
        ment of various ﬁelds. Among them, mixed-variable optimization prob-
        lems (MVOPs) involving both continuous and discrete variables war-
        rant particular attention, as they are prevalent in engineering design
        and pose substantial computational challenges for solution methods. To
        this end, this paper proposes a novel variant of diﬀerential evolution
        (DE), termed the model archive and ensemble learning-based diﬀeren-
        tial evolution algorithm (MEDE). Speciﬁcally, a data enhancing strategy
        based on dynamic opposition-based learning is ﬁrst devised to improve
        the diversity of the dominant population. Furthermore, a model archive
        is designed to store the probabilistic distribution models learned during
        the early-stage evolutionary process, which enables the algorithm to eﬃ-
        ciently exploit learned probabilistic distribution models while preventing
        premature convergence. Finally, by utilizing stacking ensemble learning,
        the model’s predictive accuracy and generalization capability have been
        enhanced, thereby improving the overall optimization performance of
        the MEDE algorithm. To validate the eﬀectiveness and eﬃciency of the
        proposed algorithm, 28 artiﬁcial benchmark functions are selected to
        conduct performance evaluation experiments. The experimental results
        clearly show that compared with other similar algorithms, i.e., AEDA,
        S-PSO, .ACOmv , and .DEmv , the proposed algorithm shows signiﬁcant
        advantages in terms of quality and eﬃciency.


        Keywords: Mixed-variable optimization · Diﬀerential evolution
        algorithm · Dynamic opposition-based learning · Model archive ·
        Stacking ensemble learning


1     Introduction

Optimization problems denote the search for solutions that can make the objec-
tive function achieve the optimal state under the premise of satisfying a series of
established constraints. Within the context of optimization problems, the deci-
sion variables serve as the core elements, and the process essentially involves
 c The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026
H. Liu et al. (Eds.): ICA3PP 2025, LNCS 16383, pp. 571–589, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-95-8405-5_31
572     Q. Chen et al.

determining their speciﬁc values to ﬁnd the optimal solution. Based on the
form of variables, decision variables are classiﬁed as continuous variables and
discrete variables [1]. Consequently, optimization problems can be divided into
continuous optimization problems and discrete optimization problems. However,
optimization problems in the real world are far more complex than simple contin-
uous and discrete optimization problems. For example, there are pressure vessel
design problems [2], aircraft wing design problems [3], and welded beam design
problems [4] in mechanical structures. The decision variables in these problems
include both continuous variables and discrete variables. Such problems are clas-
siﬁed as mixed-variable optimization problems (MVOPs).
    As a simple yet eﬃcient optimization algorithm, the evolutionary algorithm,
such as diﬀerential evolution (DE) [5] which has demonstrated outstanding opti-
mization performance in recent years, has been successfully applied in various
industries. JADE [6], LSHADE-RSP [7], and iDE-EDA [8] are all improved ver-
sions of DE. However, the improvement of these algorithms revolves around
simple continuous optimization problems. So when faced with mixed-variable
optimization problems, these algorithms still have certain performance deﬁcien-
cies, which make it diﬃcult for them to solve these problems eﬃciently and
accurately.
    Based on the above description, a new solution scheme is proposed for solv-
ing mixed-variable optimization problems, namely model archive and ensemble
learning-based diﬀerential evolution algorithm (MEDE). In this paper, the algo-
rithm incorporates dynamic opposition-based learning to increase data diversity.
In addition, the model archive is innovatively proposed to store the probabil-
ity distribution models generated throughout the evolutionary process. Further-
more, combining the stacking ensemble learning method improves the precision
and reliability of models. The main contributions of this study can be concluded
as follows:
• A data enhancing strategy based on dynamic opposition-based learning and
  model archive strategy are proposed. The model archive strategy that stores
  probability distribution models in the algorithm evolution process eﬀectively
  solves the problem of insuﬃcient data diversity at the later stage of the algo-
  rithm.
• The stacking ensemble learning method is added to MEDE. Speciﬁcally, three
  models are randomly selected from the model archive to serve as weak learners
  for stacking ensemble learning, which eﬀectively enhances the accuracy and
  generalization of the generated samples.
• Through eﬀectiveness analysis experiments and performance comparison
  experiments, the study veriﬁed the feasibility of the proposed algorithm.
    The structure of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the clas-
sical diﬀerential evolution algorithm and its relevant variants. Section 3 elabo-
rates on the proposed MEDE algorithm and its algorithmic framework. Section 4
oﬀers a comparative analysis of the experimental results, focusing on the eﬀec-
tiveness assessment and performance comparison between MEDE and other algo-
rithms. Section 5 draws the conclusion.
                                              MEDE for Mixed-Variable Optimization   573

2      Related Works
2.1     The Original DE
Diﬀerential Evolution (DE) is a population-based stochastic optimization algo-
rithm. It utilizes a population with a size of .N P to solve various types of opti-
mization problems through an iterative evolutionary process. The core oper-
ations of this algorithm encompass three key steps: mutation, crossover, and
selection. During the algorithm’s initialization phase, it is necessary to initialize
this population in a D-dimensional space according to Eq. (1).

                                  Xi = LB + rand · (U B − LB)

 where .i ∈ {1, 2, 3, · · · , N P } represents the index of an individual within the
 population. .LB and .U B denote the lower and upper search boundaries of the
 problem.
    In the mutation stage, the mutation vector .Vi is generated from individual
.Xi in the population according to the preset mutation strategy to enhance the
 diversity of the population. Here are six classic mutation strategies:
    (1) DE/rand/1:

2.2   Some Advanced DE Version
(1) JADE
    The JADE algorithm is an adaptive diﬀerential evolution algorithm with
optional external archive. In the process of algorithm optimization, the success-
ful individual information of the current population is used to adjust the param-
eters, namely the scaling factor .F and the crossover probability .CR. In addition,
an external archive mechanism is introduced to save the individuals that have
been replaced during the iteration process to provide the direction of evolution.
Through these two strategies, the exploration and exploitation capabilities of
algorithms in the search process are eﬀectively balanced.
(2) LSHADE-RSP
    LSHADE-RSP, one of the winners of the IEEE CEC 2018, is an improved
algorithm based on the LSHADE algorithm. The algorithm improves the muta-
tion operation with rank-based selective pressure strategy, which performs better
performance when solving complex multi-model optimization problems.
    The initialization strategy of the LSHADE-RSP algorithm is the same as that
of the classic DE, as shown in Eq.(1). The mutant vectors .Vi is generated based
on the mutant strategy with rank-based selective pressure named "DE/.current−
to − pbest − w/.r", as shown in the following:

3     Proposed Approach
3.1       Data Enhancing Based on the Opposition-Based Learning
When dealing with complex optimization problems, traditional algorithms tend
to fall into local optimums. Opposition-Based Learning can enhance the ability
to jump out of the local optimal by generating the reverse solution of the current
solution. As a consequence, a number of opposite-based learning strategies have
been devised and their eﬀectiveness has been demonstrated in many evolutionary
algorithms.
    As mentioned previously, iDE-EDA uses .N Pd dominant individuals to estab-
lish a probability model. However, as the population undergoes sustained evolu-
tionary progression, the crowding degree of dominant individuals progressively
                                       MEDE for Mixed-Variable Optimization      577

intensiﬁes, thereby substantially diminishing the diversity of model training data.
As a result, the trained model may exhibit a signiﬁcant degradation in sampling
performance due to the above phenomena. To address this limitation, we pro-
pose the data enhancing scheme based on the opposition-based learning, which
is termed as DOL. The details of DOL are as (25).

                .OPdi =Pdi + r1 ∗ (r2 ∗ (LB + U B − Pdi ) − Pdi )               (25)
                     s.t. :
                         i ∈ [1, |Pd | ∗ 0.3]
                        i ∈ [1, |Pd |]
                        i = f (i)

where, .LB and .U B represent the lower and upper bounds of the individual
population, respectively. .| · | denotes the modulo operation. .f (·) is an injective
mapping between .i and .i .
   DOL is constructed based on opposition-based learning, with the main
objective of performing data enhancing on dominant individual populations to
improve the model’s generalization capability. In the implementation of DOL,
there are two critical aspects that need to be noted.

• The dynamic opposition-based learning strategy is used to further improve
  the performance of data enhancing.
• To conserve evaluation resources, only the 30% of dominant individuals are
  randomly selected to perform the dynamic opposition-based learning.


3.2   Model Archive

Recent years, the archive strategies have been increasingly widespread and eﬀec-
tive in the ﬁeld of evolutionary algorithms. The core advantage of these strate-
gies lies in their ability to dynamically and eﬃciently balance exploration and
exploitation during the search process of evolutionary algorithms, thereby sig-
niﬁcantly enhancing their overall performance and convergence speed. However,
it should be noted that most current archive strategies primarily focus on the
storage and management of individual solutions, which, to a certain extent,
limits their capacity to further explore the search space and adapt to complex
optimization problems.
    Therefore, we propose an innovative archive strategy for storage models,
which is based on the key problems of the model-assisted diﬀerential evolution
algorithm for solving complex optimization problems, such as insuﬃcient data
diversity and overﬁtting of data diversity of probability distribution models, to
enhance the robustness and search eﬃciency of the algorithm.
    In terms of algorithm implementation, we design a set of ﬁne archival struc-
ture and archival update mechanism. During each iteration of the iDE-EDA
algorithm, the currently generated model is saved to the model archive .Amodel .
578    Q. Chen et al.

The speciﬁc structure of .Amodel as in Eq. (26). In the archive management mech-
anism, the archive only stores the model generated during the ﬁrst 50 iterations
corresponding to the current number of iterations.

                                      μ1 , μ2 , . . . , μm
                           Amodel =
                           .                                                  (26)
                                      C1 , C2 , . . . , Cm

where .μm and .Cm are the mean and covariance of the .m model in .Amodel , the
value of .m is 50. .[·] is the matrix. Here are the considerations.
• The .m value is too large, which increases the computational cost and limits
   the exploitation capacity. If it is too small, the data diversity will be poor,
   and it is easy to fall into the local optimization. Experiments have shown that
  .m is more eﬀective with 50.
• The model update strategy adopts the proposal of Li et al. [9] ﬁrst-in-ﬁrst-out
   (FIFO) archive updates policies to maintain model diversity.


3.3   Ensemble Learning
As a cutting-edge and inﬂuential machine learning method, ensemble learning is
based on the principle of improving model performance by integrating the predic-
tion results of multiple learners. Speciﬁcally, ensemble learning usually combines
multiple weak learners to build a strong learner with excellent performance,
resulting in more stable and accurate prediction results. Common combination
strategies include Bagging, Boosting, and Stacking. In the MEDE algorithm, in
order to further improve the model performance and generalization ability, the
stacking ensemble learning method is added in an innovative way. This method
trains multiple weak models and uses the prediction results of these weak models
as new features to train a strong model to make the ﬁnal prediction. Improve
overall performance by combining the strengths of diﬀerent models. Provides
more robust model support for solving complex problems.
    In the speciﬁc method, in the ﬁrst 50% iterations, the same model prediction
strategy is used as the iDE-EDA algorithm. In the last 50% iterations, three
models are randomly selected as weak learners in the model archive. Use the
three weak learners ( .M1 , .M2 and .M3 ) to generate .q individuals separately and
merge these individuals to form a new data set .inds, as shown in Eq. (27). The
mean of the set .inds .muE and the covariance .CE are obtained as parameters
for the strong learner.

          inds = samplingq (M1 ) ∪ samplingq (M2 ) ∪ samplingq (M3 )
          .                                                                   (27)

   The current model .M C is used to generate .(1 − λ) · N PE individuals and
the strong learner .M E is used to generate .λ · N PE individuals, where .λ is the
sampling weight of the strong learner. Then combine the individuals to form a
population .XE as Eq. (28).

              XE = sampling(1−λ)·N PE (M C ) ∪ samplingλ·N PE (M E )
              .                                                               (28)
                                   MEDE for Mixed-Variable Optimization       579

3.4   MEDE Framework
In this subsection, an in-depth exploration is conducted on the integrated appli-
cation of three innovative strategies, namely dynamic opposition-based learning,
model archive mechanisms, and stacking ensemble learning techniques. The syn-
ergy of these strategies is aimed at enhancing the performance of evolutionary
algorithms. Based on this, an improved variant of DE, named MEDE, is pro-
posed. The complete operational framework of the MEDE algorithm is presented
in pseudocode within Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1. The procedure of MEDE
Input: f ,[xmin , xmax ] ,F ESmax .
Output: xbest .
 1: N Pinit = 30, D = 50, D1 = 25, N Pinit = 4, F Es = 0, A = ∅, Amodel = ∅,
    count = 1.
 2: Initialize population X by using Eq. (1).
 3: Apply round(·) to dimensions D1 through D.
 4: Evaluate X to determine their ﬁtness.
 5: F ES = F ES + N P .
 6: while F ES < F ESmax do
 7:    Determine P r as Eq. (12) and Ranki as Eq. (13)
 8:    MCR,H = 0.9 , MF,H = 0.9 ,SCR = ∅ , SF = ∅.
 9:    for i = 1, 2, · · · , N P do
10:       Calculate F wi by Eq. (11) and generate mutant vector Vi using Eq. (10).
11:       Generate trial individual Ui .
12:       if f (Ui ) < f (Xi ) then
13:          Update external archive A.
14:          Xi = Ui , f (Xi ) = f (Ui ), SCR = Cri ∪ SCR , SF = F ri ∪ SF .
15:       end if
16:    end for
17:    Update MF and MCR as Eq. (14) and Eq. (15).
18:    Sort X and select the ﬁrst N Pd individuals to form Xd .
19:    Select 0.3 ∗ N Pd individuals from Xd for DOL as Eq. (25).
20:    Learn Gaussian probability model by Xd and obtain the mean and covariance.
21:    Update Amodel by FIFO strategy.
22:    if F Es >= 0.5 ∗ F Esmax then
23:       Select three models M1 ,M2 ,M3 randomly.
24:       Sample inds using Eq. (27), and Check bound-constraints.
25:       Obtain strong learner parameters, and generate XE as Eq. (28).
26:    else
27:       Sample XE by current model.
28:    end if
29:    F Es = F Es + N P + N PE .
30:    X = X ∪ XE , f (X) = f (X) ∪ f (XE )
31:    Calculate N P according to Eq.(18).
32:    Shrink X and A by discarding the worst individuals.
33: end while
580     Q. Chen et al.

3.5   Complexity Analysis

Obviously, the MEDE algorithm introduces three additional components in
comparison with the iDE-EDA algorithm, namely the computation of dynamic
opposite-based learning, the save of model archive, and the operation of stacking
ensemble learning.
    The complexity associated with computing dynamic opposite-based learning
is closely related to the population size .N P per iteration and the total number
of iterations .iter. To be more speciﬁc in MEDE, select 30% of the dominant
individuals for dynamic opposite-based learning, where the number of dominant
individuals is 50% of .N P . Speciﬁcally, the complexity of this part is .O(0.15 ∗
N P ∗ iter). The model archive’s save operation mainly stores the model’s mean
and covariance. The time complexity of this process is negligible.
    In the context of the stacking ensemble learning procedure, during roughly
the latter half (approximately 50%) of the total iterations, a random selection
process is carried out to pick three individuals from the model archive. Following
this selection, the mean and covariance values for these three chosen individuals
are computed. These computed mean and covariance metrics are then leveraged
to generate new individuals, which are introduced into the learning process. Upon
a thorough evaluation, the complexity of this particular segment of the stacking
ensemble learning operation can be succinctly expressed as .O(0.5 ∗ iter ∗ 6).
    Based on the above analysis, the additional complexity introduced by the
MEDE algorithm is .O(0.15 ∗ N P ∗ iter + 0.5 ∗ iter ∗ 6).


4     Experimental Results and Study

In the subsequent experimental section, we employ 28 artiﬁcial benchmark func-
tions sourced from the IEEE CEC 2013 test suite [10]. All experiments are con-
ducted in a 50-dimensional .D = 50 search space. For each benchmark function,
every algorithm is executed independently 25 times.
    Regarding the algorithm parameters, the population size .N P for each algo-
rithm is set to 30, and the maximum number of function evaluations .F Esmax is
100,000. Additionally, the decision variables are partitioned into two distinct seg-
ments. Speciﬁcally, the ﬁrst 25 dimensions of the decision variables are treated as
continuous variables, while the remaining dimensions are designated as discrete
variables.
    In the analysis of experimental results, use symbols for clarity. “+” means
our algorithm outperforms others under metrics. “-” shows it’s inferior. And “.≈”
indicates similar performance within an acceptable error range. The symbols
“Mean” and “Std” represent the average function error and standard deviation.
    To comprehensively assess the capabilities of various algorithms in address-
ing the aforementioned problems, we have devised two experimental studies:
an eﬀectiveness analysis and a performance comparison for mixed-variable opti-
mization.

4.1   Eﬀectiveness Analysis

With the aim of conducting a scientiﬁc and comprehensive evaluation of the
eﬀectiveness of the MEDE algorithm, we have deliberately and meticulously
selected its original version as well as other relevant algorithms JADE, LSHADE-
582     Q. Chen et al.

RSP, and iDE-EDA as comparison counterparts. During the experiment, the
four algorithms are compared in the same experimental setup, and the results
are shown in Table 1.
     According to the results, compared to the JADE algorithm, MEDE is better
in 27 functions and similar in 1 function, and no function is inferior to the JADE
algorithm. Compared to the LSHADE-RSP algorithm, MEDE achieves superior
performance in 8 functions, is similar in 17 functions, and is slightly inferior to the
LSHADE-RSP algorithm in 3 functions. Compared with the original algorithm
iDE-EDA, MEDE is better in 8 functions, similar in 19 functions, and slightly
inferior to iDE-EDA in only 1 function.
     Under the same experimental setup (each test function is run independently
25 times and the mean value is taken to generate the convergence curve and
Y-axis in .log10 scale), the detailed convergence process is compared as shown
in Figs. 1, 2, 3 and 4. In the test function presented in Fig. 1, the convergence
performance of the MEDE algorithm is signiﬁcantly better than that of the other
three comparison algorithms. For the test function in Fig. 2, the convergence
results of the MEDE algorithm are similar to the other three algorithms and
are signiﬁcantly better than the JADE algorithm in the Fun 4, 5, 19, and 21
functions. Among the functions involved in Fig. 3, for Fun 1, Fun17 and Fun18,
the convergence performance of the MEDE algorithm is slightly inferior to that
of the LSHADE-RSP algorithm, but better than other algorithms. For Fun13
and Fun14 functions, the convergence performance of the MEDE algorithm is
slightly weaker than that of LSHADE-RSP and iDE-EDA algorithms, but it is
still stronger than the JADE algorithm.In Fig. 4, the convergence results of the
MEDE algorithm reach the same level as those of the other three algorithms.
     A detailed summary of the MEDE algorithm and other algorithms is shown
in Table 2, the MEDE algorithm has signiﬁcant advantages in 43 functions and
is similar in 37 functions and slightly worse in 4 functions than the other three
algorithms.
     Through the analysis of the above experiments, it can be seen that the
MEDE algorithm has signiﬁcant advantages in solving the mixed-variable opti-
mization problems. This result fully veriﬁes that a series of improved strategies
implemented for MEDE are highly eﬀective and adaptable to mixed-variable
optimization problems. These improvements not only increase the algorithm’s
search ability in complex mixed variable spaces but also signiﬁcantly improve
global optimization performance.

   Through the above performance analysis, it can be seen that the MEDE
algorithm far exceeds other representative algorithms in performance. In the
experiment, our algorithm MEDE is signiﬁcantly better than the comparison
algorithms in terms of convergence speed and optimal solution quality, and its
performance advantages are highly signiﬁcant after Friedman testing.

5     Conclusion
This paper introduces a novel variant of DE, termed MEDE, speciﬁcally designed
to deal with MVOPs. MEDE uses dynamic opposition-based learning strategy to
enhance population diversity. Furthermore, model archive strategy is introduced
to eﬀectively mitigate the issue of diminishing data diversity in the later stages of
algorithm evolution by storing probability distribution models generated during
the evolutionary process. Additionally, stacking ensemble learning method is
incorporated into the algorithm to eﬀectively address the overﬁtting problem
associated with probability distribution models.
    In future work, there are two possible directions that can be addressed.
Firstly, the eﬃciency of model archive utilization is further investigated. Sec-
ondly, the MEDE framework incorporates stacking ensemble learning, while fur-
ther investigation into alternative ensemble methods remains promising.
